text: This grammar provides a comprehensive English-language reference description of Hokkaido Ainu, the primary indigenous language of Hokkaido, Japan.

The object of description is the language's phonological, morphological, morphosyntactic, and discourse structure as documented across the Hokkaido dialect cluster — principally Saru, Chitose, Shizunai, Tokachi, Horobetsu, Mukawa, and Ishikari — drawing on the full range of prior scholarship from Kindaichi and Chiri through the modern reference grammars of Tamura ; , Refsing , Shibatani , Satō , Bugaeva , and Nakagawa .
The intended readership is broad but assumes linguistic training.

The grammar is addressed to professional linguists working on polysynthesis, evidentiality, applicatives, alignment, or the typology of head-marking languages; graduate students and advanced undergraduates in descriptive and typological linguistics; Ainu studies researchers whose primary language of scholarship is English or Japanese; documentation workers engaged with Ainu language materials; and community members who approach the language through formal description.
Readers without prior knowledge of Ainu will find a structural overview in and the historical and cultural setting in .
Those already familiar with the Japanese-language descriptive tradition may proceed directly to whichever domain interests them.

A reference grammar is comprehensive in both depth and breadth: it covers every major grammatical domain, provides attested examples for every claim it makes, states where the literature disagrees and how seriously, and offers a quantitative profile of the phenomena it describes wherever the data permit.
The benchmark for breadth here is Nakagawa (2024) , which organizes its description across 28 top-level chapters — the most extensive single-authored description of Hokkaido Ainu yet published.
The present grammar targets roughly double that topic coverage, distributing 176 leaf chapters across 23 structural parts.

The organizing sequence is the standard structural-descriptive one: phonetics and phonology → morphophonology → word classes and nominal morphology → possession → pronouns and demonstratives → personal affixes → verbal morphology → valency and voice → TAM → evidentiality and modality → negation → basic clause structure → complex sentences and clause linkage → discourse and information structure, bracketed by front matter, sources and conventions, and back matter (diachrony, dialectology, contact, and texts).
Comprehensiveness means integrating all prior descriptions rather than supplanting them.
Every chapter cites the relevant treatments from the existing scholarship and states where they agree, where they diverge, and what the grammar takes from each.
The grammar claims comprehensiveness of coverage and integration; it does not claim priority over any individual analysis.
Hokkaido Ainu is the primary object of description.

It commands the great majority of the accumulated corpus and the bulk of the modern descriptive literature, and its several dialects differ enough to make dialect-internal comparison informative without requiring a separate comparative grammar for each.
The principal dialects drawn on are Saru (the most copiously documented), Chitose, Shizunai, Tokachi, Horobetsu, Mukawa, and Ishikari.
Finer locality distinctions — Nibutani within Saru, Biratori, Honbetsu within Tokachi — are recorded in the place field of each example rather than as separate dialect labels.

Sakhalin Ainu (also referred to as Enciw) and Kuril Ainu appear as external contrast material throughout the grammar, presented in dedicated contrast boxes with their dialect tags (SA, KU) whenever they illuminate a specifically Hokkaido structural choice.

Several features of Hokkaido Ainu — the pitch-accent system, the four-term evidential paradigm, the system of applicative preverbs, noun incorporation as a productive syntactic operation, and the elaborate oral-literature register — have no direct counterpart or show divergent organization in the Sakhalin variety; these receive expanded first-class treatment, with Sakhalin drawn into comparison where the contrast is instructive.
The sociolinguistic situation, including the present state of the revitalization movement, is treated in .

The modern revitalization register — the standardized orthography and coined vocabulary current among new-speaker communities — is described as a synchronic variety alongside the documented oral tradition, with coinages and standardized forms explicitly flagged when they differ from documented historical usage.
The grammar's corpus frequency counts draw on historical texts and conversation recordings rather than revival-norm materials, and the distinction is maintained throughout.
This is a grammar.
Lexical material appears only as grammatical evidence: in examples, in paradigm cells, and in class diagnostics.

The grammar does not define senses of individual lexemes beyond what is needed to gloss an example, and it links out to the available dictionary resources rather than reproducing or paraphrasing their content.
The dictionaries and lexicographic records that underpin the grammar are surveyed in ; the ethnographic and cultural context is treated in .
Four commitments run through every chapter.
They are not segregated layers but part of how each phenomenon is described from the outset.

Every frequency claim in the grammar is backed by counts from a large aligned corpus of Hokkaido Ainu oral-literature and conversation data that includes material from the NINJAL Corpus of Ainu oral literature and the Glossed Audio Corpus of Ainu Folklore .

The corpus is treated as a register archive: genre labels (uwepeker 'prose tale', yukar 'human epic', kamuy yukar 'divine epic', ritual prayer, conversational recordings) permit per-genre frequency breakdowns.
This genre-level detail bears directly on several claims about TAM, evidentiality, and information-structural phenomena whose distribution is register-conditioned.
No predecessor grammar reports systematic corpus frequencies for Hokkaido Ainu.
The sampling methodology, dialect weighting, and the conventions for citing figures are set out in full in .
Each grammatical domain is placed against a named cross-linguistic framework.

At the level of the language as a whole, the grammar produces a feature profile comparable to what WALS or Grambank would supply for a set of typological parameters: overall structural type (polysynthetic, head-marking, head-final, postpositional, modifier-before-head), morphological alignment, valency-changing morphology, evidential paradigm type, number marking, and numeral base.

Within individual domains, standard typological reference works supply the comparative scaffolding — the frameworks cited range from general morphosyntactic typology to the specific literatures on alignment, evidentiality, applicatives, nominalization, and noun incorporation.
The purpose is to supply the comparative context that makes descriptive choices legible to readers approaching from general linguistics.
provides a condensed structural thumbnail of the whole language that serves as an orientation map into the granular chapters.
Proto-Ainu reconstruction and grammaticalization pathways are embedded in the chapters treating the relevant synchronic phenomena rather than quarantined in a separate historical chapter.

Where a diachronic source is established — the derivation of the evidential formal nouns from possessed sensory nouns, the grammaticalization of postpositions from relational nouns, the Sakhalin vowel-length correspondence to Hokkaido pitch accent — it is stated in the synchronic chapter, with forward reference to the diachrony and contact parts of the grammar (Parts XX–XXI).
The genetic position of Ainu as a language isolate and the history of its internal classification are treated in ; the periodized history of its scholarly description is in .

Five domains of Hokkaido Ainu grammar have attracted sustained formal theoretical attention: alignment and the personal-affix system (see and ), the applicative preverb system (), noun incorporation (), the nominalization-plus-copula evidential paradigm (), and clause linkage and switch-reference-like phenomena ().

For these five domains the grammar provides an optional formal-analysis layer — explicit theoretical framing beyond the descriptive synthesis — clearly sectioned so that readers interested only in the description can skip it without losing continuity.
Original re-analysis is confined to these five domains; in every other chapter the grammar reports, synthesizes, and triangulates the existing literature.
Every nontrivial or novel claim in the grammar carries an explicit evidence-grade label.
Six grades are in use.
Consensus marks claims on which all major sources agree and which are not in dispute.
Contested marks genuine disagreements among sources: the competing positions are stated, and none is declared settled.
Corpus-confirmed marks claims checked against the corpus and borne out by the data.
Corpus-suggested marks claims the corpus data point toward but do not conclusively establish.
Speculative marks plausible but unverified hypotheses, typically diachronic ones.
Original-needs-review marks new analyses proposed by the present grammar; this grade is restricted to the five formal domains listed in the previous section and is flagged for editorial review.
Claims left ungraded are treated as consensus.
A grade is placed at the end of the clause or sentence it scopes, written as a small-caps label in guillemets: ‹contested›, ‹corpus-confirmed›, and so on.
This is a working apparatus, not a rhetorical device: a contested grade commits the grammar to stating the actual positions, and a corpus-confirmed grade commits it to showing the relevant counts.

A full survey of the descriptive tradition — from the Edo-period wordlists and Batchelor through Kindaichi, Chiri, and the modern era — appears in , and a source-criticism audit of the major grammars, dictionaries, and text corpora is in .
The table below summarizes the book-length treatments that define the field this grammar enters.
Each work contributes something indispensable.
Kindaichi and Chiri establish the basic morphological architecture that all subsequent grammars build on .
Refsing provides the most systematic morphosyntactic account in English of any single Hokkaido dialect .
Shibatani places Ainu within a typological account of the languages of Japan .
Tamura's Saru dictionary and grammar monograph remain the central data source for that dialect ; .
Satō's grammar gives the most thorough treatment of the Chitose verb system and Hokkaido morphosyntax in the modern Japanese-language literature .
The Bugaeva Handbook supplies extensive English coverage across topics from phonetics to oral literature and from Hokkaido to Sakhalin .
Nakagawa's grammar brings the description of Hokkaido Ainu to its greatest single-volume comprehensiveness .
The grammar works from all of these, citing each directly.

What the present description adds is a corpus-quantified layer — systematic frequency counts for morphological cells, evidential paradigm members, alignment environments, and sandhi rates — alongside cross-dialect integration extending beyond the Saru–Chitose pair that dominates the modern literature, and an explicit typological scoring at both the language level and within each domain.

Where prior analyses disagree — on the number of formal persons, on the morphological alignment of the paradigm, on the word-class status of property concepts, on the syntax of the evidential constructions — the disagreements are stated explicitly and graded.
Two bodies of material outside the formal research literature bear on specific domains.

The aynu-corpora Discord community has accumulated analytical discussion of Ainu grammar across several thousand archived messages, including morpheme identifications, pattern observations, and occasional structural hypotheses .
These contributions are treated as leads: points of departure for corpus investigation and source-checking.
Where a community observation has been verified against the scholarly literature or the corpus it is integrated under the appropriate evidence grade and cited with the contributor's handle.
Where it has not been verified it is not included.
Ijäs (2023) provides an accessible English-language learner grammar of Ainu, available as an online guide.
Its structural analyses are cited where they present a reading of a construction not covered in the research literature, and graded accordingly.
It is also cited for its treatment of revival-register conventions.
Being addressed primarily to learners rather than to the documentary record, its analyses of the teaching norm and of the historical oral corpus are distinguished when citing it.

The grammar can be read linearly — beginning with for a structural orientation, then moving through the sources and conventions chapters of Part II before entering the substantive description — or consulted chapter by chapter for specific phenomena.
Chapter numbering is sequential and book-wide, but cross-references are always given by chapter title and slug, so individual chapters can be read independently without knowing their sequence number.
The interlinear glossing conventions — the four-line format, morpheme-boundary symbols, and the Ainu-specific gloss inventory — are documented in ; the full abbreviation list is in .
The Latin phonemic transcription used throughout the grammar is explained in .
The oral-literature and spoken-language data sources that supply most of the attested examples are surveyed in .
The optional formal-analysis sections in the five theory-magnet domains are clearly delimited within each chapter.

Readers who want the descriptive account without the formal apparatus can skip those sections; cross-references from the formal sections into the descriptive content are one-directional, so the descriptive text stands without them.
The bibliography at the close of each chapter is generated automatically from the citations that appear in it and lists only works actually cited in that chapter.
Hokkaido Ainu has no demonstrated genetic relationship with any other language family ; .

Proposals connecting Ainu to Japanese, Korean, Altaic branches (Tungusic, Mongolic, Turkic), Austronesian, Nivkh, or Chukotko-Kamchatkan have each failed to produce the systematic sound correspondences and shared morphology that genetic relationship requires.
The fuller treatment of the isolate status and the history of macro-comparison controversies belongs to .
The isolate argument has a structural dimension that goes beyond the absence of lexical correspondences.

Bugaeva's analysis frames Ainu as "a head-marking language of the Pacific Rim" — after the framework of — and treats the structural mismatch between Ainu's head-marking profile and the dependent-marking profile of all its geographical neighbours as a positive argument against relatedness .

Head-marking is "well attested in the Americas and Melanesia but vanishingly rare elsewhere" and characterizes the Greater Pacific Rim (GPR) macroarea — a population of languages whose distribution Nichols traces back more than ten millennia .

Northeast Asia is predominantly dependent-marking: Japanese, Korean, Tungusic, Mongolic, and Turkic all mark syntactic relations on the dependent NP (nominal case, adnominal genitive, uninflected postpositions governing case).

The head/dependent-marking parameter is among the most diachronically stable typological features known ; its consistent divergence between Ainu and every language proposed as its relative accordingly constitutes evidence independent of the lexical record .
In a single typological characterization: Hokkaido Ainu is SOV, agglutinating, polysynthetic, incorporating, and head-marking at both clause and phrase level ; .
The sections that follow treat each dimension of that profile in turn, closing with a WALS-style feature summary.
Nichols' parameter classifies languages by the locus of the morphological signal of a syntactic relation: on the head of the phrase, on the dependent, or on both.

Head-marking correlates — verbal cross-reference of arguments, noun incorporation, instrumental/directional affixes on verbs, inflected adpositions, pronominal affixes on nouns — differ systematically from dependent-marking correlates — case on nouns, adnominal genitive marking, agreement suffixes on attributives, uninflected adpositions governing case .
Hokkaido Ainu shows the head-marking correlates and lacks all the dependent-marking ones across both clause and noun phrase ; .
The grammatical role of a noun phrase in the clause is signalled by person indexes on the finite verb, not by case suffixes on the NP itself.
A transitive verb carries an A-index for the agent/transitive-subject and may carry an O-index for the patient; an intransitive verb carries an S-index.
The NP argument is caseless.
Third-person arguments are zero-indexed; first and second persons carry overt prefixal indexes for A/S and O roles ; ; .
The absence of morphological case in an SOV agglutinating language is cross-linguistically unusual.

Japanese and Korean, Ainu's closest geographical neighbours, pair SOV order with elaborate nominal case systems; Ainu makes the same constituent order work without case, relying entirely on verbal person-indexing and semantics for argument tracking ; .
WALS-type surveys classify Hokkaido Ainu as "borderline" or "zero" in case inventory .

The full architecture of the S/A/O paradigm — four formal persons, the side-encoding of intransitive S versus transitive A, portmanteau exponents, and the mixed alignment that results — is set out in .
In the noun phrase the same head-marking logic operates.

A possessed nominal does not require a case-marked genitive possessor; instead the head noun itself carries two signals of the possessive relation — a personal prefix agreeing with the possessor, and an affiliative suffix marking the noun as standing in a possessed relation ; .

Within the nominal domain Ainu distinguishes obligatorily-possessed (inalienable) nouns — body parts, kin terms, and spatial-relational nouns that must carry a possessor — from nouns that are non-possessible .
These possessive classes are absent from the surrounding Northeast Asian languages and align Ainu with GPR-type possessive-class systems.
The full classification, the morphophonology of the affiliative suffix, and the appositive possessive construction are treated in , , and .
Hokkaido Ainu is genuinely polysynthetic in Nichols' sense of open head-marking: there is no fixed closed paradigm of what categories may accumulate on the verb .
A single verb word can stack person indexes, applicative prefixes, reflexive or reciprocal prefixes, incorporated nominals, and a number suffix while remaining one phonological word.
The density of such accumulation is most visible in Classical Ainu, particularly in the heroic epic genre yukar ; :

In ordinary Hokkaido speech, a comparable degree of stacking is less frequent; a transitive verb routinely carries two person indexes and one or two derivational prefixes, and a single incorporated nominal already constitutes a polymorphemic complex.
The register difference between Classical Ainu and everyday speech — and what it implies for the grammar/lexicon boundary — is a live research question ‹contested›.
Satō (2016; 2022) provides the fullest typology of Ainu noun incorporation, identifying four types that differ in their effect on verbal valency ; :
The valency effects of each type — and in particular the A-incorporation type, unusual cross-linguistically — are treated in , , and .
How productive and how polysynthetic Ainu incorporation is in formal terms is contested.

Shibatani (1988) analysed Ainu incorporation as a productive type-I lexical compounding process without semantic bleaching of the incorporated nominal, placing Ainu at the strong end of the polysynthesis scale .

Bugaeva's (2022) characterization as "open head-marking" identifies why: the inventory of what may be incorporated or stacked is unconstrained by a fixed paradigm, unlike the closed agreement paradigms of dependent-marking languages ‹contested›.

The applicative system (e-, ko-, o-) further intersects with incorporation: an applicative argument can be simultaneously incorporated in ways that bear on the syntactic status of both operations ; these interactions are treated in .
The basic constituent order of Hokkaido Ainu clauses is SOV: subject precedes object, the finite verb closes the clause, and the clause is strictly head-final throughout.

Modifiers precede their nominal heads; subordinate clauses precede the matrix verb; postpositional phrases — built on relational nouns and postpositions — follow the head noun with the adpositional element in final position ; ; .
The relational-noun system and the postpositional inventory are treated in and .
The SOV/head-final pattern sits in a typological tension with the head-marking type.

GPR head-marking languages tend toward verb-initial order; Ainu's SOV gives it a surface resemblance to its dependent-marking neighbours (Japanese, Korean, Turkic) that does not extend to structural organization .

Bugaeva accounts for this via pragmatic right-dislocation of subject and object NPs: when arguments are shifted rightward for discourse reasons, the resulting surface order approaches verb-initial, aligning Ainu with the pragmatically common patterns of the GPR grouping .
The full syntax of constituent order and argument realization is in .

Community member @aomidori_cs_ (aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-01-29) has proposed that the SOV order is not original to Ainu but the result of contact with Northeast Asian SOV-dominant neighbours, citing the preverbal position of the negator as a cross-linguistic diagnostic found in SVO languages ‹speculative›.
No comparative reconstruction of proto-Ainu word order is currently available to evaluate the proposal.
The person-affix paradigm of Hokkaido Ainu shows a typologically mixed alignment.
The first-singular row is nominative–accusative: the same prefix ku= marks both S (intransitive subject) and A (transitive subject), opposed to en= for O.
The second-person rows are neutral: e= (2SG) and eci= (2PL) cover S, A, and O alike.
The third person is zero in all three roles.
The first-plural exclusive and the fourth person are tripartite: S is marked by a suffix (=as, =an) while A is marked by a prefix (ci=, a=) and O by a distinct prefix (un=, i=) ; .

This side-encoding — prefix for transitive A, suffix for intransitive S — is the morphological basis on which Bugaeva characterizes the overall system as "mixed, with elements of tripartite alignment" .
The detailed person paradigm, portmanteau exponents, and the full alignment debate — tripartite, hierarchical, inverse — are treated in and .
The split-intransitive question, which in Ainu surfaces in verb classes and valency morphology rather than in the agreement paradigm, is treated in .
The fourth person (also termed the indefinite person) is a feature of the Ainu person system unusual enough to warrant mention here.

A single form-set covers first-person-plural inclusive ('we including you'), indefinite/impersonal agent, second-person honorific address, and logophoric (protagonist) reference in oral-narrative direct speech ; ; .

Terminology for the set is unsettled across sources: Nakagawa uses "fourth person", Tamura lists the same forms as separate sub-persons, and Bugaeva analyses the quotation use as logophoric ; ‹contested›.
The full referential range is catalogued in and .
Ainu nouns divide into two classes in the syntax of spatial phrases ; .

Ordinary nouns require a locative noun as an intermediary head (, , , ) to form a spatial phrase; locative nouns can head a spatial phrase directly, as in pet or ta 'at the river' (river + place + LOC).
The locative/ordinary distinction helps track grammatical relations when the third person is zero-marked: a locative noun heads a spatial phrase and is not parsed as a bare object NP.
The full system is treated in .
Property concepts that would be expressed by adjectives in related languages function as stative verbs in Ainu, with no separate adjective class ; this is treated in .
The numeral system operates on a base-20 (vigesimal) frame, typologically unusual in the region.
Ochiai (2021) documents a historical shift in the reckoning strategy within that frame — from a subtractive to an additive counting method — on the basis of dialect comparison .

Verbal number is separately marked by suppletive singular/plural stem pairs (ek / arki 'come', arpa / paye 'go') and by the pluractional suffix -pa ; ; the full treatment of numeral morphology is in and ; verbal number in .
Hokkaido Ainu encodes the speaker's source of information periphrastically through a nominalization-plus-copula construction.

Four formal (defective) nouns — , , , and — combine with the copula to yield a four-term paradigm encoding a visual-trace / inferential evidential, a direct-visual / situational evidential, a reportative, and a non-visual sensory evidential respectively ; ; .
The system is built on the grammaticalization of sensory nouns into a nominalization slot, a structural type unusual in Northeast Asia.
All four terms and the schema they instantiate are treated in .
The table below assembles the major typological parameters of Hokkaido Ainu.
Sources for each feature are given in the preceding sections; primary reference is and .

The head-marking profile aligns Ainu with the GPR typological cluster; the SOV order gives it a surface resemblance to Northeast Asian dependent-marking languages that does not carry into morphological organization.

The combination of polysynthesis, a four-term analytical evidential system, and the incorporation-plus-applicative interaction makes the structural profile of Hokkaido Ainu distinctive even within the GPR grouping.
The word aynu is a common noun meaning 'person, human being'; it is also the ethnic self-designation of the people whose language this grammar describes ; .
In its ethnic use the term identifies a person as a member of the Ainu community, as distinct from the gods (kamuy), and marks the boundary against neighbouring peoples.
Its territorial correlate is Ainu Moshir (aynu mo-sir) 'Ainu land', the indigenous name for the homeland .

A second self-referential term, utar 'people', appears in affiliative form as utari 'relatives, our people'; it was used as the basis for the name of the Hokkaidō Utari Kyōkai (北海道ウタリ協会), the main Ainu civic organization for much of the twentieth century .
The Sakhalin Ainu have a distinct self-designation, enciw, which their modern descendants in Japan have adopted as a distinguishing label .
The exonym "Ainu" (in older literature also "Aino") is now standard in both Japanese and international usage.

Through much of the twentieth century the Japanese government applied the term 旧土人 (kyū-dojin, 'former aborigines') in official documents, most notably as part of the 1899 legislation that governed the Ainu's legal status .
This usage was formally abandoned with the abolition of that legislation in 1997.

Within the Hokkaido Ainu community, the relative weight of "Ainu" versus "Utari" as preferred public designations was contested during the 1980s and 1990s, and the discussion reflects continuing negotiations over political identity ‹contested›.
Hokkaido, the northernmost of Japan's main islands, was the core of the historical Ainu territory ; .

The same ethnic population extended across the full chain of the Kuril Islands and across the southern half of Sakhalin (Japanese: Karafuto; Ainu: Karapto); a marginal Ainu presence on the southernmost tip of Kamchatka is also attested in ethnonymic and archaeological sources .
Evidence for an earlier, more southerly range on Honshu comes principally from toponymy.

The endings and , both characteristic of Hokkaido river names, appear in dense clusters across the Tōhoku and Kantō regions, pointing to Ainu (or an immediately ancestral variety) having been spoken well south of Hokkaido at some period ; .

Linguistic borrowing evidence — potential Ainu-derived words in early Japonic texts — has been advanced as additional support for a Honshu range , though the direction and scale of those loans remain a matter of specialist debate ‹contested›.
The southern limit of former Ainu territory on Honshu cannot be fixed with precision on present evidence ‹contested›.
The genetic position of the language within this spatial history is treated in .

Within Hokkaido the Ainu dialect cluster is internally diverse: the dialects of the Saru, Chitose, Ishikari, Tokachi, Horobetsu, Shizunai, Asahikawa, and Yakumo areas differ phonologically and morphologically in ways that the corpus chapters track in detail.
Sakhalin Ainu (abbreviated SA in this grammar) and the now-extinct Kuril variety (KU) are cited comparatively; the dialect sample and method are set out in .
Ainu subsistence in the historical period centred on fishing, hunting, and gathering, with strong seasonal and ecological patterning ; .

Settlement followed rivers and coastlines, and the vocabulary reflects this orientation: the various stages of the salmon's life cycle are distinguished by roughly twenty distinct lexical items, and some fifty words for harbour seals and more than twenty for types of whale point to the centrality of sea-mammal hunting in the coastal zones .

Among land animals, bears held a special ceremonial role: the word serves both as the generic term for the divine and as a specific designation for the bear, which was understood as a mountain god that brought its meat to the village .
Dogs figure prominently in subsistence and ceremony alike.

The precolonial Ainu maintained a diversified economy that also included small-scale horticulture and, via the Santan trade, the exchange of furs, dried fish, and lacquerware for metal goods and silk manufactured further inland on the Asian continent .
Population size is uncertain for the precolonial period; a figure close to 25,000, possibly more, has been suggested for Hokkaido alone .

A rich tradition of oral literature — the heroic epics called , the divine epics called , and the prose folktales called — was the principal medium for transmitting cultural knowledge and was performed in a register distinct from everyday speech.
The oral tradition and its register differences are directly relevant to grammar because the kamuy yukar corpus contains the densest concentration of older morphological forms and archaic vocabulary.

The oral-literature genres and their linguistic properties are treated in the corpus chapters; the grammatical differences between the oral-literary and colloquial registers appear throughout the descriptive chapters.

The ancestors of the historical Ainu arrived on Hokkaido in connection with the Satsumon culture (c. 700–1200 CE), an archaeological complex that spread northward from Honshu and replaced the earlier local Epi-Jōmon traditions in southern Hokkaido .

The linguistic lineage that became Ainu has roots in the Jōmon period on Honshu; Ainu can therefore be described as a "Jōmonic" language in the sense that it likely preserves features that were broadly characteristic of pre-Yayoi Japan .

As a consequence, Hokkaido itself is a secondary territory for the Ainu; their earlier homeland was on Honshu, from which the Satsumon complex — and the ancestral Ainu language — was displaced northward by the Yayoi and subsequent Yamato expansion .
The Satsumon expansion on Hokkaido encountered the Okhotsk culture (c. 600–1600 CE), a littoral and maritime complex that had spread to northern Hokkaido from Sakhalin .

The interaction and gradual absorption of Okhotsk populations by the Satsumon bearers contributed both genetic and cultural material — and potentially some linguistic features — to the complex that became the historically attested Ainu ethnicity.

The chronology of the Ainu territorial expansion can be traced approximately from this archaeological evidence: northern Hokkaido was under Ainu ethnic domination by roughly 1000 CE; southern Sakhalin was reached by roughly 1300 CE; and the Kurile Islands, including the Northern Kuriles, were occupied by Ainu speakers as late as c. 1500–1600 CE .

All these dates are approximations, and the specific identification of the Satsumon bearers as Ainu-speakers rests on an inference from archaeological continuity rather than direct linguistic evidence ‹contested›.
Japanese contact with the Ainu of southern Hokkaido predates formal political control by centuries.
The earliest surviving written records of the language, including the Matsumae no koto — Ezo kotoba no koto of c. 1600 with 117 words compiled for use by merchants, come from this trade context .

The Matsumae domain (松前藩), established at the southern tip of Hokkaido under Tokugawa authority, held a monopoly on trade with the Ainu through the Edo period; Ainu communities in the interior of the island and in the Kurile Islands remained outside this domain's political control .
Commerce in furs, dried fish, and eagle feathers constituted the principal economic link between the Ainu and the Japanese domains.

Episodic tensions over trade terms escalated into armed conflicts, most notably the Shakushain War of 1669–1672 and the Menashi-Kunashir uprising of 1789, both of which ended with Ainu defeat and tightened Matsumae control ‹contested›
(the interpretation of Ainu agency and objectives is debated).

The broader trade network extending from Sakhalin into the Amur basin and ultimately connecting with Qing China — the Santan trade (山丹交易) — supplied the Ainu with metal goods and silk in exchange for northern products .
This trade also fostered sustained contact between the Sakhalin Ainu and their Nivkh and Uilta neighbours, the linguistic traces of which are reviewed in the Handbook's chapter on language contact .

Russian exploration and colonization of Kamchatka from the early eighteenth century brought a second colonial power into contact with the Kurile Ainu; Sakhalin was transferred from Manchu to Russian control by the Treaty of Peking (1860), and the island's status was subsequently settled between Japan and Russia by the Treaty of St.
Petersburg (1875), which assigned Sakhalin to Russia and the Kurile Islands to Japan .
The formal annexation of Hokkaido by the Meiji state and its opening to Japanese colonization in 1869–1870 ended the Ainu's position as the dominant population of the island within a few decades .
Japanese settler immigration proceeded rapidly: from a figure close to the precolonial Ainu population of roughly 25,000, settlers came to outnumber the Ainu by an ever-growing margin .

The Hokkaido Former Aborigines Protection Act of 1899 (北海道旧土人保護法) placed the Ainu in a defined legal category as wards of the state, assigned them small agricultural land plots, and legislated their assimilation into Japanese society .

No formal legal prohibition of the Ainu language was enacted, but the use of the language was restricted or effectively banned in schools, and children were pressured to learn Japanese in place of Ainu; administrative discrimination reinforced the suppression of public language use .
The human cost of this period appears in the census figures available, though the figures must be read with awareness that assimilation policy itself distorted their collection.

The 1940 census recorded 16,170 Ainu in Hokkaido; the 1935 census put the Sakhalin Ainu population at 1,512; the Kurile Ainu were relocated to Shikotan in 1884, and by 1933 only forty-one descendants survived — that variety of Ainu is now extinct .
After 1945, Sakhalin Ainu communities were evacuated to Hokkaido; the last speaker of Sakhalin Ainu died in 1994 .

Intercommunal marriage and the discontinuation of Ainu census categories make reliable demographic estimates for the late twentieth century difficult; figures reported in earlier surveys suggest a population of roughly 16,000 to 24,000 persons with Ainu ancestry in Hokkaido, with wide uncertainty depending on self-identification criteria ‹contested›.
By the second half of the twentieth century the language had ceased to be transmitted to children in most Hokkaido communities .
The present sociolinguistic situation and the documentation record are taken up in .
The 1899 act was abolished in 1997, when the Japanese Diet enacted the Ainu Culture Promotion Act (アイヌ文化の振興並びにアイヌの伝統等に関する知識の普及 及び啓発に関する法律).
This legislation provided institutional funding for cultural activities and language classes for the first time, but did not recognize the Ainu as an indigenous people with specific rights .
A unanimous resolution by the Japanese parliament in 2008 recognized the Ainu as the indigenous people of Japan, though without statutory force .

The Act on Promoting Measures to Realize a Society in Which the Pride of the Ainu People Is Respected, enacted in April 2019, superseded the 1997 act: it provides the statutory definition of the Ainu as an indigenous people, establishes support mechanisms for cultural and language activities, and authorized the establishment of the National Ainu Museum (Upopoy), which opened in Shiraoi in 2020 .

The linguistic implications of revitalization policy — including the standardization pressures that accompany institutionalized language classes and the rise of new-speaker varieties — are discussed in .

The documentary record that this grammar draws on is a product of this entire history: the bulk of the attested Hokkaido Ainu material was collected in the early-to-mid twentieth century from elderly speakers in communities where the language was already in decline.

The unevenness of that record — richer for some dialects (Saru, Chitose) and thinner for others — directly shapes what can and cannot be described with confidence, and the corpus chapters note coverage gaps as they arise.
The history of Ainu language description and the main grammars and dictionaries consulted in this work are surveyed in ; the corpus method and dialect sample are set out in .
The language-shift history of Ainu is inseparable from the political transformation of Hokkaido after 1868.

Under the Matsumae domain system a bilingual interpreter class — (< Jp 通事／通詞) — had mediated trade contact, but the Meiji government's annexation of Hokkaido and its enactment of the Hokkaido Former Natives Protection Act (北海道旧土人保護法) of 1899 reconfigured the position of Ainu speakers decisively .

The Act registered Ainu as Japanese subjects, abolished traditional fishing and deer-hunting rights, and assigned Ainu children to segregated schools (旧土人学校) where Japanese was the sole medium of instruction.

No statute explicitly prohibited the Ainu language, but its use in institutional settings was discouraged and children were penalised for speaking it, producing a generation-by-generation shift to Japanese .
The pressure of that period is recorded from within the community in composed Ainu prose.

Recalling the era of assimilation policy in the Ainu Times, a Saru–Chitose speaker describes both ritual and everyday speech as placed under prohibition — using the prohibitive construction X kuni hattoho an 'there was a prohibition against doing X':
The last generation with full first-language command was born approximately between 1900 and 1910; their children acquired Japanese as the primary language and did not transmit Ainu in the home ; .

A subsequent cohort born in the 1940s and 1950s, whose parents had already shifted to Japanese, in some cases acquired partial Ainu from grandparents while parents worked away from the village; these individuals suspended active use on entering the Japanese school system but retained partial receptive and productive competence.
Members of this cohort — sometimes called "rememberers" — have since been recruited as language resources and participants in the revival movement .
The same transmission loss is thematised from within the reviving community in composed Ainu prose.
Writing in the Ainu Times newsletter, a Saru–Chitose speaker states the breakdown directly, casting the whole proposition in the reportative hawe ne frame:
Reliable statistics on Ainu speakers do not exist.

The Hokkaido-resident Ainu population has been estimated at approximately 24,000 on the basis of a 2005 survey by the Hokkaido Department of Environment and Life (北海道環境生活部), but this census identifies community members by self-declaration, not language ability .

Before the 2019 Ainu Policy Promotion Act the government did not legally recognise Ainu as indigenous people, which meant that self-identifying as an Ainu-language speaker amounted to disclosing sensitive personal information subject to discrimination risk; speaker counts were therefore practically impossible to collect in any systematic form .
The closest available measure in the literature is Ōno's assessment that fluent first-language speakers are today "almost nil" .
The active revival community consists of L2 learners, heritage speakers of varying competence, and a small number of elder rememberers.
All instruction is now conducted by instructors who are themselves L2 speakers working from recordings and transcriptions of deceased native speakers.
The dialect situation and the corpus on which this grammar rests are described in and .
An era of documentation preceded the organised revival.

The foundational document is , a collection of thirteen kamuy yukar (divine epics) compiled by Yukie Chiri (知里幸恵, 1903–1922) of Horobetsu and published the year of her death — the first book of Ainu texts compiled and published by an Ainu, written in Roman script.
Her brother Mashiho Chiri produced the major mid-century dictionaries and lexicological studies but framed his programme as recording rather than revival .
The newsletter アイヌ・モシリ (Aynu-mosir), founded by Tasuke Yamamoto (山本多助) and colleagues, ran eighteen issues between 1957 and 1965 in text written almost entirely in Ainu .
The shift toward active revival is associated principally with two first-language speakers.

Shigeru Kayano (萱野茂, 1926–2006) of Nibutani (Biratori) collected cultural objects, tools, and audio recordings; his 1974 collection of was printed in katakana so that community members without access to academic Roman-script editions could read their own oral tradition.
Kayano held that the language had to remain a medium of living exchange.
He founded the first private Ainu language school at Nibutani in 1983 — after official permit applications had been rejected — and delivered the first Diet speech in Ainu in 1994 .

Tatsujirō Kuzuno (葛野辰次郎, 1910–2002) of Shizunai coined the phrase katsu-hozon (活保存, 'living preservation') as the alternative to shi-hozon (死保存, 'posthumous preservation'), a formulation that became a slogan of the revival movement .

The Ainu Association of Hokkaido (北海道アイヌ協会; formerly Hokkaido Utari Association) launched structured Ainu Language Classes (アイヌ語教室) in 1987, beginning at Nibutani and Asahikawa and growing to fourteen classes across Hokkaido, subsidised by the Hokkaido Board of Education .
The classes functioned as community gathering spaces as much as formal instruction.
They were restructured in 2010 and abolished in 2012 .
Parallel programmes operated in the Kantō region: classes run by the Kantō Utari-kai from 1989 (with Hiroshi Nakagawa as instructor) and Tokyo Ainu Association courses.

The 1997 Ainu Cultural Promotion Act (アイヌ文化振興法) established the Foundation for Research and Promotion of Ainu Culture (FRPAC; 財団法人アイヌ文化 振興・研究推進機構), which funded Ainu-language courses, instructor training and dispatch, and cultural programming .
The annual Itak-an ro ('Let's speak!') Ainu-language speech contest was inaugurated under FRPAC in 1998.

In the same year, the Sapporo District Court's Nibutani Dam ruling — with Kayano Shigeru and Kaizawa Kōichi as plaintiffs — for the first time judicially recognised the Ainu as an indigenous minority under Japanese law .
A 2008 Diet resolution called on the government to recognise the Ainu as indigenous people, following Japan's endorsement of the 2007 UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

The 2019 Ainu Policy Promotion Act repealed and superseded the 1997 law and extended for the first time formal statutory recognition of the Ainu as indigenous, with provisions for cultural preservation, ethnic business support, and education .

Leader-training programmes for Ainu-language instructors had been running from Shiraoi since 2008, graduating 23 trainees through 2020, with subsequent cohorts at Biratori; the Sapporo University Urespa Club, founded 2010, trains university students in Ainu language and cultural skills .

The institutional centrepiece of the 2019 framework is the National Ainu Museum and Park — Upopoy (ウポポイ, lit. 'many people singing together') — at Shiraoi on the Pacific coast, opened in July 2020 after delay from the COVID-19 pandemic .
The Upopoy project required the coining of approximately 180 new Ainu words for museum facilities and signage (see the neologisms section below).
Ainu has no indigenous writing system ; text has been rendered in katakana or Roman script since the nineteenth century, and both systems remain in use.

Katakana is preferred for community publications and public signage but requires a set of more than ten specially devised small subscript consonant characters — most prominently small ㇰ for syllable-coda k, small ㇷ゚ for coda p, and small ㇳ for coda t.
The sequence tu requires either the archaic ト゚ or the modern トゥ; font and encoding problems have been a recurring obstacle in digital contexts .
Roman script needs no special characters and handles digital text more readily, but unfamiliarity among community members who learned to read in Japanese has limited its uptake .
Several conventions are now standardised.
The digraphs ch and sh, used in Batchelor and many early transcriptions, have been replaced throughout the contemporary literature by c and s (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-08).

The convention of marking personal-index clitic boundaries with = and derivational boundaries with - originated in Nakagawa's 1986 annotated collection and has since become the norm in academic publications, including this grammar ; (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-09).
Active debates remain unsettled ‹contested›.

The spelling of the pre-labial nasal in Japanese loanwords divides an etymological approach — writing kampi (< Jp 紙 kami) with m, preserving the underlying form — from a surface-phonological approach that writes kanpi with n because the nasal is neutralised before p; academic sources and Ainu Association textbooks diverge on this point (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-16).

Word-division is similarly variable: the phrase sisam itak ('Japanese-person speech') and the compound sisamitak ('the Japanese language, as a named entity') carry different denotational scopes, yet editorial practice on whether to write them as one or two tokens remains inconsistent (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-05).

A century of disuse created a vocabulary gap that native word-formation had no opportunity to close. Ōno documents the diagnostic asymmetry: during the Meiji period, while Ainu was still in daily use, speakers coined tunas-kampi ('fast paper', i.e. telegram, Asahikawa) for a new technology and assembled the transparent compound a=e-i-nu-p ('the thing with which one hears', i.e. telephone) from native morphological material; by contrast, words for television, computers, and modern administrative institutions were simply borrowed from Japanese untranslated, because Ainu was no longer anyone's daily language when those things spread .
Systematic neologism-coining since the 1980s attempts to reverse this.

The most productive neologism stem is — a Japanese loanword (< Jp 紙; see ) that already carried an older sense 'written order, official document' in the oral-literature corpus — now extended to school and information-technology vocabulary: kampi-pu 'library' (paper + storehouse), uepeker-kampi 'explanatory leaflet' (storytelling + paper), and the school-level set pon kampinukatcise (elementary school), haykannu kampinukatcise (middle school), poro kampinukatcise (high school) .
The morphological apparatus underlying these coinages — object noun incorporation and compounding — is described in and .

The Upopoy project assembled approximately 180 new words for museum facilities and signage, ranging from tumamka-us-pe 'poster' (lit. 'thing that hangs prominently') to multi-word institutional names such as aynu teetawano ankur kampinuye cise sekor an pe ('Center for Ainu and Indigenous Studies') .
