A hortative drinking toast was needed for contexts calling for Japanese kanpai:

Formulaic expressions for marriage congratulations, condolences, and other life-event occasions remain without established Ainu forms; Ōno documents the tendency to revert to Japanese at such moments .
The general constraint on coinage is that new words must conform to Ainu grammar and morphological patterns .
The spread of individual coinages remains unmeasured: no corpus of new-speaker production exists, and Ijäs explicitly notes that it is unknown how widely specific coinages have been adopted .
The transition to all-L2 instruction has structural consequences for the variety being acquired.
All teaching is now delivered by instructors whose first language is Japanese, a situation Ōno identifies as likely to affect phonology, morphology, and discourse organisation in learner output .

The direct-method approach developed for Māori (Te Ataarangi) has been imported in experimental form to reduce dependence on the grammar-and-translation model that had discouraged community members uninterested in formal linguistic analysis .
The structural features of new-speaker Ainu have not been systematically described in the accessible literature ‹speculative›.
Dialect choice is a further pressure.
No standard variety exists across Hokkaido, and few revival participants see the need for one; Ōno anticipates that more than one regional standard may emerge independently .
The practical resolution is for learners to revive the dialect of their ancestral village where documentation is available.

For several communities — Hakodate, Erimo, Rumoi, Otaru — Japanese settlement displaced Ainu speech before any systematic linguistic recording took place, making reconstruction there "almost impossible" .

Where ancestral-dialect records are absent, the best-documented variety, Saru, serves as a fallback; dialect mixing arises when instructors have drawn on materials from more than one regional tradition .
The overall dialect classification and the structure of the available record are set out in .
The contact history with Japanese that produced the modern loanword stratum is documented in and .
The influx of untranslated Japanese vocabulary into Ainu marks precisely the period of disuse: it records when Ainu ceased to be productively applied to new domains of experience.

The recovery of that productivity — through the systematic neologism efforts described in the preceding section and through the reviving speaker community — proceeds without a standard variety as its target.
Ainu has no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other language or language family.

Every attempt to connect it — whether to Japonic, Altaic, Austroasiatic, Austronesian, or Nivkh — has failed to produce the regular sound correspondences across a systematic body of cognates that the comparative method requires ‹consensus›.
The assessment is stated plainly by : Ainu "does not show unambiguous indications of being associated with any other language family".
adopts the same position and explicitly sets aside all prior affiliation proposals to concentrate on what can be recovered by internal analysis alone.
Within its own lineage, Ainu is a small family.
refers to it as "Ainuic" (or "Kurilic", from the Russian exonym for the Kuril-speaking population), with three member varieties: Hokkaido, Sakhalin, and the Northern Kuriles.

The internal comparison among these three is the only comparative operation available to Ainu linguistics; it is treated in depth in , , and , and the classification of Hokkaido dialects within the Ainuic family is the subject of .
The Sakhalin variety branched off first, approximately 800 years ago; the Kuril variety diverged less than 600 years ago, following what calls the "Great Migration" of the 13th century ‹consensus›.
The deep genealogical history of the family, and the ethnogenesis of the Ainu people, are treated in .
Typologically, Ainu is distinct from all its geographic neighbours, including Japanese.
notes it may be placed under the broad rubric of North Pacific Rim typology, but stands apart even within that areal grouping.

For a language with no established relatives, three analytical tools are available, in decreasing order of probatory force : (i) internal reconstruction — working backwards from dialectal and morphophonological alternations to recover earlier forms — which calls "by far the most powerful" for Ainu; (ii) contact-induced change analysis, chiefly Ainu interactions with Japanese and, on Sakhalin, with Nivkh; and (iii) typological reasoning, to be "used with utmost caution" since structural parallels between languages provide heuristics for the reconstruction scenarios but carry no genealogical weight.
The time depth reachable by internal reconstruction is shallow.
Without a comparative method drawing on related sister languages, reconstruction "with wild speculation excluded" takes Ainu back roughly 1,000 years .
The one firm external date is the 13th-century separation of Common Ainu into its descendant varieties (§).
The Pre-Proto-Ainu and Proto-Ainu stages reconstructed by and revised by rest entirely on internal reconstruction, without an external comparative check.

The standard for assessing claims of genetic relationship is the presence of regular sound correspondences across a sizeable set of basic-vocabulary items — correspondences that cannot be explained by borrowing, universal sound-change tendencies, or chance resemblance.

Typological similarity (shared SOV order, similar phoneme inventories) and individual look-alike pairs fall short of this standard, as does the observation that two languages share structural features that typologists group together aareally.
The macro-comparison proposals surveyed below are evaluated against this criterion.
The following table summarises the major genetic or deep-contact proposals for Ainu, their principal evidence, and their present standing.
Detailed assessment follows.
Proposals linking Ainu to Altaic languages (Turkic, Mongolic, Tungusic) and to the "Ural-Altaic" macro-family circulated in comparative philology from the 19th century onward.
explicitly sets aside all such proposals — "ignoring all previous attempts at seeking relatives" — to work on internal reconstruction alone.
The Altaic hypothesis itself lacks consensus status, and no systematic cognate set with regular Ainu correspondences has been advanced in the peer-reviewed literature ‹speculative›.

Community members have proposed individual Mongolic or Korean connections for specific Ainu words (antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord 2024–2025 ), but isolated look-alike pairs — the kind of comparison that motivated the earliest hypotheses — are precisely what the comparative method excludes as evidence.
Without a systematic correspondence set covering basic vocabulary, such proposals cannot be evaluated as genetic claims ‹speculative›.

The most consequential internal methodological problem in Proto-Ainu reconstruction arose from 's choice to use Austroasiatic as the typological template for his consonant inventory, positing a bloated 12-consonant stop system to explain the distribution of the affiliative suffix.
All three published reviewers of independently concluded that this background assumption vitiates the consonant reconstruction: Sidwell (1996), Abondolo (1997), and Witczak (1999), as summarised by .
's revised reconstruction abandons the Austroasiatic template and proposes a leaner inventory that better matches the Ainu phonological profile (see ) ‹speculative›.
Ainu and Nivkh (Ghilyak) share an extensive zone of contact, centred on Sakhalin, and lexical material has moved in both directions.

document items including kaya (from Nivkh, 'fish-skin garment, sail'), san (from Nivkh cʰaŋ, 'offering shelf'), and the shared term tunakay 'reindeer' (→ Japanese トナカイ tonakai), reconstructed from Pre-Proto-Ghilyak *tola-ŋa.y.
These are contact items, not inherited cognates; Ainu and Nivkh are both independent isolates, and their structural differences exclude the hypothesis of common descent ‹consensus›.
The contact layer is the subject of .
The label "Paleo-Asiatic" (or "Paleosiberian") groups Ainu, Nivkh, Yukaghir, Chukotkan languages, and Itelmen on geographic grounds.

It is a useful shorthand for geographically unaffiliated languages of Siberia and the North Pacific, but carries no implication of common ancestry; each member is an independent isolate or small family ‹consensus›.

The relationship between Ainu and Japonic (the family including Japanese and Ryukyuan) is the most actively debated contact question, even though the genetic claim — that the two descend from a common ancestor — is rejected by the specialist consensus ‹consensus›.
Three distinct positions exist in the literature, and they need to be held apart.

Japonic as a recent intrusion. places the Japonic languages' arrival in the Japanese archipelago in the Yayoi/Kofun period (roughly 900 BCE–500 CE), as a migration from the Korean Peninsula that replaced or marginalized the Jōmon languages.

On this account, Ainu is not related to Japonic but to the substrate population that Japonic replaced or absorbed; structural features shared between Ainu and Japanese reflect Jōmon-language influence on the incoming Japonic varieties — what calls "Jōmonization of Japanese" — rather than common descent.
This position, sometimes termed the substrate hypothesis, explains the typological resemblances without positing genetic relatedness ‹consensus›.
Early Japanese loanwords in Ainu. A secure stratum of Old Japanese loans in Hokkaido Ainu is attested by phonological fossils.

sippo 'salt' and pasuy 'chopstick' preserve Old Japanese features — word-initial *p and the diphthongoid *uy — that had already been lost by the time Old Japanese sources were compiled, placing the borrowing "around the middle of the first millennium CE" .
The culturally significant term kamuy 'deity' also belongs to this early contact stratum.

Later loans, such as Saru cikenki (Standard Japanese つけぎ tsukegi 'matches') and antuki (Standard Japanese 小豆 azuki, with prenasalization from the Tōhoku substratum), document the continuing contact through the medieval period .
These loanwords are treated fully in ‹consensus›.

Ainu loans in Old Japanese — Vovin's reverse-direction thesis. argues the traffic also ran in the other direction: that Ainu was once spoken throughout the Japanese archipelago (from the Kantō and Tōhoku regions to Kyūshū) and left identifiable loanwords in the earliest Japonic records, notably in eastern and western Old Japanese poetry of the 万葉集 Man'yōshū.

Proposed loans include iruka 'dolphin' (< Ainu rika 'whale-fat'), kuta 'house' (< kotan 'village, settlement', with a household↔village semantic shift parallel to Latin vicus), porö 'large' (< poro), and a set of place names in the Kantō and Tōhoku regions.
The loan phonology proposed by includes: Ainu *-kk- → OJ *-k-; Ainu medial *-k- (half-voiced) → OJ *-ŋg-; and Ainu final consonants lost before OJ vowels.
This is a live claim that has attracted attention but has not achieved consensus ‹contested›; it is evaluated in full in .
Ainu's roots lie in the Jōmon period (12,000+ BP), and Ainu is the sole surviving representative of the Jōmon language complex, its continuity into the present "an accident" of demographic history .
The Jōmon population spoke a range of languages, of which only the Ainu lineage is traceable; the others were absorbed or replaced.
The geographic picture is counterintuitive: Janhunen argues that Ainu's homeland is Honshu, not Hokkaido.

The ancestors of the modern Ainu people moved northward, associated with the Satsumon material culture (c.700–1200 CE), colonizing Hokkaido (northern areas c.1000 CE), southern Sakhalin (c.1300 CE), and the Kuril Islands (c.1500–1600 CE) .
The Emishi (蝦夷) of northern Honshu — a recurrent presence in early Japanese historical sources — are viewed as a "generic proto-historical complex" ancestral in part to the Ainu .
The Sakhalin ethnonym enciw (cognate with emi₁si, Ebisu, Ezo, *emisV~*emiciV; Kindaichi 1960, via ) preserves the Honshu connection at the vocabulary level ‹corpus-suggested›.

A community member has proposed that the Sarunkur group of the Saru valley represents an Aomori-origin migrant population with connections to the Jōmon cylindrical-pottery culture (aomidori_cs_, aynu-corpora Discord 2023 ).
The proposal is consonant with Janhunen's Honshu-origin thesis, but the specific pottery connection is not supported by the archaeological record as presented in the accessible sources ‹speculative›.
In the north, the Ainu population on Sakhalin absorbed the Okhotsk culture (c.600–1600 CE), whose language may have been an early form of Ghilyak/Amuric .
This contact episode introduced the items documented by and helped shape the morphological distinctiveness of the Sakhalin variety.
The linguistic legacy of the Okhotsk-culture contact remains incompletely disentangled from the Ainu substrate ‹speculative›.
The linguistic lineage is, in Janhunen's terms, "the one ethnic marker traceable unambiguously back in time" for the Ainu people .

The ethnonyms aynu 'human being' (the endonym, of shallow diachronic formation) and utari 'people' are internally analysable; the exonym kur 'man', whose plural form (via Northern Tungusic -l) is the origin of the Russian Kuríly 'Kurils', and the term for the Japanese, sisam (reconstructed to Pre-Proto-Ainu *sii+sam/o), both point to a period of established ethnic differentiation predating the Hokkaido colonization.

What the available methods do support, for Hokkaido Ainu, is a two-stratum contact vocabulary — early Old Japanese loans dated to the first millennium CE (§ above) and a thinner Nivkh-mediated layer from the northern contact zone (§) — and a body of internal reconstructions reaching back at most ~1,000 years.
Within that depth, internal reconstruction has produced robust results.
The most celebrated is the etymology of in Saru.
Two Eurasian Wanderwörter appear in the Hokkaido lexicon and locate Ainu in a network of long-distance cultural contact.
is an Eurasian Wanderwort of continental origin ; it is among the most frequent Hokkaido nouns (rank 56 in the Hokkaido oral-literature corpus).
The term is reconstructed to a Tungusic source (Ikegami 1980, via ), pointing to archaic northern contact predating the Sakhalin-era Ainu–Nivkh–Uilta interaction.
These items signal cultural exchange, not genealogical relationship ‹consensus›.

The grammaticalization pathways recoverable through internal reconstruction — the possessive suffix -hV from the noun hi 'thing', the evidential nominalizers ruwe, siri, hawe, and humi from possessed sensory nouns, and the applicative prefixes e-, ko-, and o- from locative/relational nouns — are among the best-documented results of Ainu historical linguistics and are treated in .

As Alonso notes, "when it comes to functional words and TAM formatives, the etymology is still transparent" ; it is in the basic vocabulary where external comparison would be decisive — and where it has consistently failed to produce the requisite correspondence sets.
The macro-comparative and deep-contact debates are returned to in full detail in , which assembles the correspondence-set evidence — or its absence — for each proposal in one place.

The earliest systematic documentation of the Ainu language dates from the Edo period (17th–19th centuries), when Japanese interpreters and officials stationed at trading posts on Hokkaido compiled word-lists, phrase-books, and glossaries for practical administrative use.

The most comprehensive of these, described by , is the 蝦夷方言藻汐草 (Ezo hōgen moshiogusa, 'An Ezo dialect miscellany'), compiled by the interpreter Uehara Kumajirō and the official Abe Chōzaburō and first issued in 1792.
It contains roughly three thousand lexical entries organized by semantic field, a list of common phrases, and short texts, and it served as a primary reference for subsequent Japanese scholarship.
The late Meiji period added further lexical resources, among them the Saru-dialect topical conversation dictionary of .
The Edo-period manuscript tradition has received philological attention in recent scholarship.
examines the Kaga-ke (加賀家) documents — a set of administrative and linguistic records from the Matsumae domain — in a dissertation that subjects these materials to systematic critical scrutiny.

The Sino-Ainu glosses embedded in the 蝦夷島奇觀 (Ezoshima kikan) have been studied by , contributing to a digitally oriented philological programme that bridges the manuscript tradition and modern corpus resources.
These sources function primarily as practical aids for Japanese-Ainu communication rather than as linguistic analyses.

They provide invaluable lexical witnesses, particularly for varieties spoken in regions where communities ceased to transmit the language before systematic recording was possible, but they contain no morphological analysis and their phonological transcriptions require careful critical interpretation.
Their evidentiary status is assessed in .

Basil Hall Chamberlain's 1887 monograph marshalled detailed linguistic arguments against relating Ainu to Japanese or any Altaic family, concluding that it must be treated as genealogically unclassifiable.
His points were subsequently reviewed and extended by Kindaichi Kyōsuke, and the isolate status has remained the scholarly consensus; the question is examined in .
The most influential early description available in a European language came from John Batchelor, a British Anglican missionary who spent several decades working among the Hokkaido Ainu.

His dictionary — held in this project's sources in the edition and in its final revised form of — combined Ainu-English-Japanese glosses with a grammatical sketch, and it remained outside Japan the most accessible major source material on the language for several decades .
Among Batchelor's contributions was a Roman-alphabet transcription system for Ainu, the most direct antecedent of the Latin-script orthographic tradition examined in .

The limitations of the dictionary, however, were noted by his Japanese successors: Refsing documents Chiri Mashiho's extended criticism cataloguing mistranslations, phantom entries, and unreliable forms, and concludes that the work requires a critical and cautious approach.
The grammatical sketch shares the presupposition of European missionary-grammar categories and requires verification against the later native-speaker-based record.
Bronisław Piłsudski's collection , compiled from fieldwork on Sakhalin, supplies an early and substantial documentary record of the Sakhalin Ainu variety.
The significance of that collection for Sakhalin phonetics, phonology, and morphosyntax has been reassessed in , and the texts have been re-edited with translation and grammatical notes by .

The Sakhalin materials feature in this grammar as systematic external contrast, marked with the dialect tag sa; the historical and geographic setting shared between Hokkaido and Sakhalin Ainu is outlined in .

Kindaichi Kyōsuke (1882–1971) established Ainu studies as a recognized academic discipline in Japan, bringing sustained scholarly productivity and the institutional standing of the Tokyo Imperial University to a field that had previously lacked both.
His primary interest lay in the oral-literature tradition — particularly the heroic epics known as yukar — and his grammatical work was conceived as an instrument for that philological programme .

Among the textual materials he drew on were yukar notebooks compiled by the Ainu narrator Kannari Matsu, who wrote down her repertoire in romanized Ainu over several years in Kindaichi's home, eventually filling seventy notebooks .
The oral-literature tradition itself is surveyed in .
Kindaichi's analytical contributions to Hokkaido Ainu grammar were substantial.

Refsing identifies two advances in particular: he demonstrated that the language's person-indexing elements are personal affixes on the verb rather than the free pronouns that Batchelor's description had posited, and he distinguished the abstract nominal form from the personal-reference-bearing concrete (possessed) form — an opposition later refined by Tamura and central to the nominal morphology of this grammar .

Chiri Mashiho (1909–1961), an Ainu scholar, studied under Kindaichi at Tokyo Imperial University — the first Ainu student admitted to that institution — and his graduation thesis became the joint grammar , アイヌ語法概説 ('An outline of Ainu grammar'), co-authored with Kindaichi.
Published in 1936, it remained the standard Japanese reference work for decades.
Chiri subsequently undertook fieldwork on Sakhalin and produced a grammar centred on the Sakhalin dialects .

His later scholarly career turned toward lexicography and etymological research; he began a projected ten-volume classified dictionary of Ainu, completing three volumes on plants, animals, and human beings respectively before his death in 1961 .

Chiri Yukie (1903–1922) compiled the first published collection of Ainu kamuy yukar (divine epics) with Japanese translations , a text-publication project that established the model of romanized Ainu with facing-page translation and drew the oral-literary tradition into print for the first time.

The descriptive framework of Kindaichi and Chiri organized grammar around traditional Japanese parts-of-speech categories — noun, pronoun, adjective, adverb, verb, particle — with grammatical relations treated semantically: the analyst begins from a meaning-type (nominative, locative, dative) and asks how the language expresses it.

Refsing notes that this approach presupposes categories from the analyst's prior framework rather than deriving them from the distributional behavior of Ainu morphemes, and produces a coherent overview whose ordering reflects the analyst's starting-point as much as the structure of the language .
The contrast between this tradition and the formal-distributional analysis of Tamura is a recurring reference point in the history of Ainu grammaticography.
Post-war descriptive work began with two large comparative projects by Hattori Shirō.

The lexicostatistic study he undertook with Chiri Mashiho surveyed 19 Ainu localities — 13 on Hokkaido, 6 on Sakhalin — using a 200-item Swadesh list and established the first quantitative basis for internal dialect classification .

The Ainu dialect dictionary he subsequently edited covers the same 19 localities and remained the foundational pan-dialectal lexical resource for decades; the current state of the dialect classification that builds on that data is described in .
The Sakhalin variety was described in the grammar of , later re-edited and annotated by .
Asai Tōru produced a grammar of the Ishikari dialect , extending the descriptive record to a variety north of the Saru basin.
Tamura Suzuko — publishing through the 1950s and 1960s under her maiden name Fukuda — built the Saru dialect into the best-described variety of Hokkaido Ainu.

Her early articles on Saru verbal morphology , auxiliary verbs , and particle systems applied distributional criteria to morpheme classification, departing from the semantic ordering of the Kindaichi-Chiri tradition.

Refsing's comparison shows that Tamura was among the first to delimit morpheme classes by formal and positional behavior — for instance, restricting the possessed (belonging) form to a defined semantic class of nouns, where Kindaichi had treated the opposition as applicable to all nouns .
Her Saru-dialect dictionary remains the most comprehensive single-dialect Ainu dictionary and is used throughout this grammar as a primary lexical resource.
The English-language grammar made the Saru description accessible to non-Japanese readership, though it was not available to this project for direct consultation.

Refsing's 1986 monograph on the Shizunai dialect applied the distributional programme more explicitly, organizing morpheme classes by positional evidence alone and providing substantial coverage of a Hokkaido variety otherwise under-described in the literature.

Its introduction — a critical survey of the history of research through the early post-war period — is the most thorough historiography of Ainu linguistics available in English prior to the Handbook, and large parts of the historical account in the present chapter draw on that survey.

Shibatani's 1990 chapter on Ainu , in his typological survey of the languages of Japan, situated the language within the cross-linguistic typological literature at a scale that earlier descriptions had not attempted.

He characterized Hokkaido Ainu as head-marking, polysynthetic, SOV, and organized for evidential distinctions through a nominalization-plus-copula construction — a characterization confirmed and refined by subsequent scholarship; see .
His 1988 article had placed Ainu noun incorporation within the cross-linguistic typology of polysynthesis, establishing a framework for the incorporation analysis taken up in later work.

Satō Tomomi's grammar is the most comprehensive Japanese-language description since Tamura's, covering Hokkaido Ainu morphology, syntax, argument structure, valency operations, and information structure, with particular depth on the Chitose variety.
Together with Tamura's Saru dictionary and grammar, it forms one of the two principal Japanese-language reference works against which this grammar triangulates its analyses.

The scholarship of the early 21st century has advanced on two fronts simultaneously: deeper domain-specific analysis of grammatical subsystems, and the development of digitally accessible annotated corpora.

Article-length studies have addressed domains that the reference grammars treated only summarily, and the resulting findings have in several cases revised or substantially refined the standard analyses.
Bugaeva Anna's research has reshaped understanding of several grammatical subsystems.

Her work on Ainu applicatives provided a cross-linguistically situated analysis of the three applicative prefixes e-, ko-, and o-; her analysis of the antipassive placed Ainu within the comparative typology of antipassive constructions; and her work on possession and causatives has refined the standard valency analysis.
Her treatment of the diachrony of anticausatives extends the historical dimension of the valency description.

The Handbook of the Ainu language , which she edited, assembles specialist treatments of every major domain: phonology , verbal valency , dialectology , oral literature , historical and comparative linguistics , and the revitalization movement .
The Handbook constitutes the most comprehensive reference work on Ainu available in English.
Nakagawa Hiroshi's — アイヌ語広文典 ('An extensive grammar of the Ainu language') — is the most recent single-author reference grammar of Hokkaido Ainu.

It surveys the full grammatical range from phonology through complex clause-linkage, drawing primarily on Saru and Chitose data, and provides detailed paradigm tables with Japanese translation throughout.
It is the primary reference grammar for this work, cited throughout by section.
A critical review of its analyses and relation to earlier grammars is available in .
Domain-specific monographs and dissertations have contributed substantially alongside the reference grammars.
Dal Corso's dissertation on Ainu evidentiality provided a semantico-pragmatic account of the formal-noun evidential system and a morphosyntactic analysis of its construction and clause-final frames.
Historical phonology has been examined by , who established the diachronic correspondence between Sakhalin Ainu vowel length and Hokkaido Ainu pitch accent.
The Handbook chapter by critically reviewed earlier Proto-Ainu reconstruction proposals, including those of , and advanced a revised segmental and suprasegmental inventory.
Dialectological classification has been reconsidered by and in subsequent quantitative analyses.
The documentary and corpus infrastructure of Ainu linguistics has grown substantially since the 1970s.

The annotated oral-literature text editions published by Nakagawa and others, the NINJAL Corpus of Ainu oral literature , and the Glossed Audio Corpus have made the oral-narrative tradition available in digitally accessible, aligned, and partially glossed form.
Natural-language-processing-oriented work, including the philological study of Sino-Ainu materials by , marks a further extension of the field's methodological range.
The sources underpinning this grammar's corpus layer are described in and .
The revitalization movement and the emergence of new-speaker varieties constitute a distinct strand of contemporary research.
Its history is surveyed in and treated in depth in .
The typological profile of the language is mapped in , and the genetic-relationship question is treated in .
The chronological account of how the descriptive tradition developed — from the Edo-period glossaries through Batchelor and Kindaichi to the modern typological turn — is given in .
The present chapter identifies the specific works this grammar draws on: reference grammars, dictionaries and lexical resources, and the philological record.
Spoken corpus sources are treated in .
The foundational work in the modern Japanese descriptive tradition is , a collaborative outline grammar by Kindaichi Kyōsuke and Chiri Mashiho.

It introduced the numbered person-form system and identified the auxiliary verb paradigm and the evidential nominalizers, establishing the analytical categories that all subsequent Japanese-language description built on.

Its Hokkaido dialect coverage is uneven by contemporary standards, and many of its morphological analyses have been revised since, but it remains the indispensable point of entry into the classical tradition.
Chiri's separate grammar of the Sakhalin dialect falls outside this grammar's primary scope; it is cited when the Hokkaido–Sakhalin structural comparison in requires a Sakhalin-side primary source.
is the only pre-2020 monograph grammar dedicated to a single Hokkaido variety: the Shizunai dialect of the Hidaka region (SHI).

It covers morphology and syntax in full paradigm tables and remains an important comparator for the Saru baseline used in this grammar, given that Shizunai belongs to the southwest Hokkaido group and the correspondences to Saru are close.
For features where Shizunai and Saru diverge, dialect tags signal which variety a cited form comes from; the systematics of the southwest group are discussed in .
includes an Ainu chapter in his typological survey of the languages of Japan.
The coverage is sketch-level, but its framing in terms of polysynthesis, noun incorporation, and alignment introduced Hokkaido Ainu to a wide comparative-linguistics audience.
It is cited here when a brief typologically-oriented reference is needed for a structural property treated in detail in .
is the most comprehensive Japanese-language descriptive grammar available for the Saru–Chitose core.
The treatment spans phonology, the full verbal template, the person-affix system, aspect, evidentiality, nominalization, and clause linkage, with extensive paradigm tables and elicited examples.

It is held locally and constitutes one of the two primary structural references throughout this grammar; its analyses of the auxiliary verb system and person forms are the starting point for the corresponding chapters.
provides a compact English sketch of southern Hokkaido Ainu, covering the Saru–Chitose varieties.
As the most accessible single English-language overview of the core dialect group, it is cited when a concise English-language reference is needed alongside the more detailed Japanese treatments.
is a multi-author handbook in the De Gruyter Mouton series on the Japanese language and linguistics (HJLL 12).
Its chapters, each by a specialist on a specific grammatical domain, offer the broadest cross-dialect coverage of any single reference work currently available.

This grammar cites Handbook chapters under their respective author keys throughout the content chapters; where a Handbook treatment and the analyses of Satō or Nakagawa diverge, the disagreement is stated explicitly.
is the most recent and most comprehensive single-author grammar of the Ainu language.

It covers the full range of Hokkaido dialects with attention to micro-variation, incorporates data from large annotated corpora, and provides substantial sections on syntax and discourse that earlier grammars left largely undescribed.

It is held locally and serves as the principal structural reference for this grammar, particularly for the phonology, the person-marking system, the auxiliary and evidential constructions, and the formal-noun nominalization paradigm.
Where the present grammar departs from Nakagawa's analysis, the departure is stated and the reasoning given.
is an English-language grammar sketch of Saru Ainu, adapted from Tamura's 1988 Japanese encyclopedia article.
It is not held locally and carries the reported status explained in the section below.
Structural claims that rely on it alone are cross-checked against Satō and Nakagawa; the Saru dictionary (see below) provides the primary-data complement.
is the comprehensive Ainu–Japanese dictionary of the Saru dialect.
Beyond word-forms and definitions, it records grammatical category membership, possessed forms, and aspect alternations for individual lexical items.

In this grammar it functions as a primary data source for Saru morphological evidence — affiliative forms, valency-class membership, paradigm alternants — that goes beyond what the grammar texts directly supply.
Although not held locally in the project corpus, individual entries are cited throughout the content chapters when lexical-paradigmatic evidence is needed.
and cover the Chitose and Saru dialects respectively.
Both carry the reported status in this grammar; they are accessible through the db.aynu.org catalogue, and their evidence is cross-checked against and the spoken corpus where possible.
Together, the three dictionaries supply the lexical–paradigmatic backbone for the Saru–Chitose core that the structural chapters draw on when individual morpheme forms are at issue.
is the comparative dialect dictionary, covering nineteen localities across Hokkaido and Sakhalin with a 200-item basic-vocabulary list per site.
Its word-form data underpin all subsequent Hokkaido dialect classification, and it is cited in the dialectological chapters as a reported source.
The dialect-classification literature built on it is treated in .

Chiri Mashiho's multi-volume classified dictionary , arranged by semantic field (plants, animals, humans), is the standard reference for cultural-semantic vocabulary and has been cited extensively in toponymic and ethnobotanical research.
It is not held locally and is cited here as a reported source; structural claims resting on it alone are flagged accordingly in the relevant content chapters.

Batchelor's Ainu–English–Japanese dictionary, first published in 1905 and revised through four editions to a fourth in 1938 ; , includes a grammar sketch of the Ainu of the northwestern Hokkaido region as it was spoken in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Both editions are cited in this grammar with the philological witness role and the reported status: Batchelor's transcription conventions and analytical categories diverge substantially from those of the mid-century Japanese tradition, and his structural claims require verification against the Saru–Chitose baseline before they can bear analytic weight.
The phonological transcription system he used is discussed in .

The Kaga-ke monjo (加賀家文書), a collection of Edo-period manuscript records preserved at the National Ainu Museum and other repositories, contains Ainu-language material — glossaries, word lists, and transcribed phrases — predating systematic grammatical description.
provides a philological study of this collection, and this grammar accesses Edo-period lexical and phonological evidence through that work.
The Sino-Ainu glosses of the illustrated document known as the 蝦夷島奇觀 (Ezoshima kikan) are studied by , whose linguistic analysis is the entry point for that early attestation.

Neither document furnishes sufficient structural data to affect grammatical analyses directly; both are relevant to the historical phonology of , to which the interested reader is directed for their philological use.

Several works that descriptive practice requires citing are not directly consulted in this grammar: the full text is either unavailable locally or was not read in preparation for the chapter in question.
These sources carry the reported marker in the auto-generated references list and are flagged with a badge wherever they appear.

The convention is defined in : claims that rest solely on a reported source are not treated as independently verified, and where a structural analysis depends on such a claim, an independent supporting source is required or the uncertainty is stated explicitly.

Among the grammars, is the most significant reported source: its analytic coverage of Saru is cited throughout the secondary literature, but the full text is not held in the project corpus, and its grammatical claims are consistently cross-checked against and .

Among the Sakhalin-side sources, — a reedition of Murasaki's West Sakhalin materials with grammatical notes — is cited as reported; its evidence enters this grammar only where the Sakhalin contrast in requires a philologically worked Sakhalin source.
The transcription systems, citation formats, and abbreviation conventions used throughout this grammar are set out in .

The relationship between the transliteration schemes of individual sources — Batchelor's romanization, the NINJAL practical orthography, Nakagawa's extended Latin transcription — and the phonemic transcription adopted here is explained in and .
The grammar of Hokkaido Ainu is documented overwhelmingly through its oral-literary and recorded spoken tradition.

Written records from before the twentieth century are sparse and linguistically unreliable; the descriptive grammars and dictionaries treated in rest in turn on recordings made between the 1920s and the 1990s from a contracting community of native speakers.

The corpus underlying this grammar — approximately 209,878 aligned sentences across 45,225 distinct token types — consists almost entirely of transcribed and annotated performances of traditional oral genres: heroic epics (/), divine epics (/), prose folktales (/), ritual prayer (/), and a smaller body of composed prose (the Ainu Times newsletter and comparable texts).
For the genre system and its grammatical correlates see ; for poetic register, ; for corpus method and dialect sampling, .

The earliest published Ainu-language oral-literature collection is — seventeen Iburi (Horobetsu) divine epics with Ainu text and Japanese translation, compiled by Chiri Yukie 知里幸惠 (1903–1922) in the final years of her life.
Linguistically, the collection is anchored in the Horobetsu idiolect of its compiler, who drew on repertoires transmitted within her family.

Its hero-narrators are indexed throughout by the exclusive first-person plural prefix ci= and suffix =as deployed as a singular narrator-voice — a convention characteristic of Iburi divine epics and distinct from the Saru and Chitose practice of using the fourth-person a=/=an in the same role ; .
This person-marking contrast and its grammatical motivation are taken up in and .

Kindaichi Kyōsuke's parallel scholarly activity in the 1930s–1940s — editing transcriptions made by Kubodera Itsuhiko from speakers across Hokkaido — produced the main pre-war inventory of heroic-epic texts ; .

Kindaichi's yukar grammar established the five-syllable line as the canonical metrical unit , a description subsequently refined by Okuda's two-metre analysis distinguishing syllable-count from accent-oriented verse ; the metrical system is treated in .
The pre-war editions are read here through Endō and Okuda and are cited as reported.
The bulk of the aligned corpus derives from recordings made in the three decades after World War II.
The most extensively analysed set is the Biratori Town oral-literature archive , held by the National Ainu Museum (国立アイヌ民族博物館) and available online.
Principal narrators include 鍋澤ねぷき (Nabesawa Nepuki), 貝澤とぅるしの (Kaizawa Torusino), and 川上まつ子 (Kawakami Matsuko), all from Biratori in the Saru basin.
The archive covers kamuy yukar, menoko yukar (female heroic epic), and uwepeker; it supplies many of the attested examples cited throughout this grammar.

The ILCAA Ainu materials — recordings made at the Tokyo University of Foreign Studies Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa, 1976–1984 — cover Saru and Shizunai narrators performing uwepeker, kamuy yukar, and prayer texts.
The primary narrators are 川上まつ子 (Saru) and 織田ステノ (Shizunai); their performances are available with transcription, Japanese translation, and audio at ainugo.aa-ken.jp.

Tamura Suzuko's contemporaneous field recordings in Biratori (principally 平賀サダモ and others) underlie her Saru dictionary and the folktale and lyric texts from which Dal Corso and Hirosawa draw evidential examples ; .
An independent line of post-war documentation covers Iburi and neighbouring dialects.

Satō's study of an Abuta (虻田) yukar narrated by 遠島タンケ extends coverage east of Horobetsu and establishes that yukar grammar — aspect marking, the prospective anki, comparative , and fourth-person indexing — is continuous with the prose grammar of the same dialects .
Nakagawa's Chitose dictionary provides a parallel primary reference for the genre terms, the sakehe system, and ritual vocabulary in the Chitose dialect.

Nakagawa Hiroshi's 24-volume annotated text series (2000–2025) presents Chitose-dialect kamuy yukar and uwepeker narrated principally by 白沢ナベ (Shirasawa Nabe), with interlinear glossing and Japanese commentary.
This is the most extensively annotated single-narrator Hokkaido corpus available in print.
Its Chitose data complement the Saru-centred Biratori and ILCAA collections and support dialect comparisons for person marking, aspect, and evidential distribution across the corpus.
The online NINJAL Ainu oral-literature corpus aggregates recordings with audio across dialects (primarily Saru and Chitose, with additional localities).
The Chiba University materials add Horobetsu and related dialect texts.
The Glossed Audio Corpus provides interlinearly glossed Chitose and Saru folktale texts online.
The Ainu Times (アイヌタイムズ) newsletter , published from 1991, supplies the main body of composed Ainu prose from after the period of intensive oral recording.
Contributors include speakers from Saru, Chitose, and Samani; genres include first-person prose narration, prayer texts, and songs.

These texts differ from the transcribed oral record in being written compositions; their register draws on the traditional prayer-language inventory (see ) and on the poetic-elegant conventions of , but their grammatical profile is shaped partly by literacy practices rather than performance conventions.

The collections differ not only in dialect but in the grammatical constructions they make available.

Verse genres (yukar, kamuy yukar) deploy the elegant poetic register (atomte-itak), featuring applicative prefixes in place of case particles, expanded polysynthetic verb forms, and a distinct lexicon; they also show the fourth-person prefix a=/=an as the hero-narrator's voice in Saru and Chitose texts (and ci=/=as in Iburi, per Chiri 1923), a number-agreement override under which ek-an 'I come.SG' is grammatical where everyday speech requires k-ek, and formulaic couplet phrasing throughout .

Prose folktales use a more conversational register with dense quotative marking and a characteristically one-directional, low-variation intonation that Tamura distinguishes from the rising pattern of conversational interaction (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024; ).
These differences are the empirical basis for , , and .

The contrast between verse and prose registers can be heard in native metalinguistic commentary within the corpus. 川上まつ子 describes the menoko yukar genre explicitly in terms of the sakehe (refrain): performing with the refrain marks the piece as menoko yukar, while omitting it and delivering the same content in prose style makes it an uwepeker — a speaker's formulation that identifies the sakehe as the primary formal diagnostic.
The sakehe system and its verse structure are analysed in ; rhetorical couplets and formulaic phrases in .

The evidential framing that pervades the corpus differs by genre: ruwe ne marks the narrator's asserted knowledge of story-world events in prose tales, while the formulaic ceremonial close ruwe tapan na appears in prayer and ritual contexts .
For the evidential system see and .

The aligned corpus is heavily weighted toward the Saru and Shizunai dialects, which together account for roughly 121,000 of the 209,878 sentences; Chitose adds approximately 4,400 (plus 5,753 classified as Saru–Chitose combined), Mukawa 13,424, and Horobetsu 3,098.
Tokachi contributes 1,550.
Northern and eastern Hokkaido — the localities of the sakorpe heroic epic and the distinct eastern song traditions — are represented thinly .
This geographic bias reflects the concentration of twentieth-century fieldwork in the Saru basin; comparable systematic recording of eastern and northern varieties did not occur at comparable depth.
Genre coverage is similarly uneven.

The kamuy yukar is well documented across multiple dialects (Saru, Chitose, Iburi); the uwepeker is well represented in Saru and Chitose; prayer texts are attested in Saru (川上まつ子, ILCAA), Shizunai (織田ステノ), and revival prose (Ainu Times).

The caranke (rhetorical negotiation-speech), which Kindaichi ranks immediately below yukar for elegant-register density , is identified in the scholarly literature but does not appear as a genre tag in the aligned corpus.
Songs (upopo, yaysama) are attested but their short lyric texts contribute comparatively little to the grammatical evidence base for the phenomena analysed in this grammar.
Several features of the record limit what the corpus can establish.

The transcription history is uneven: Chiri Yukie's 1923 edition and the pre-war Kindaichi-era texts were produced before modern phonemic conventions; their representations of coda consonants, the glottal stop, and pitch accent vary from the orthographic norms used in this grammar (see the orthography chapters).

The ILCAA and Biratori recordings, made with audio and transcribed against the audible record, are phonologically more reliable but reflect the idiolects of a small number of elderly Saru-basin speakers.
The aligned corpus is not genre-tagged as a queryable facet.
Genre must be inferred from document titles (e.g. "uwepeker 民話8", "kamuy yukar フム パㇰパㇰ") rather than a controlled metadata field.

Per-genre frequency counts — for instance, the density of quotative sekor in yukar versus uwepeker — are not directly retrievable from the database; only whole-corpus token counts are available, and these include metalinguistic uses of genre terms alongside performance tokens.
Certain corpus documents present genre-boundary ambiguities that resist the standard taxonomy.

One ILCAA text narrated by 織田ステノ — a kamuy yukar titled "怠け者の子供" — combines a long sakehe with a short narrative body and closes as a first-person human self-narration (yayeisoytak), making it not straightforwardly assignable to the kamuy yukar or yukar categories ‹contested›
(gengojiro, aynu-corpora Discord 2025-12-12; ).
Genre fuzziness of this kind is consistent with Endō's observation that regional repertoires vary and that speaker practice does not always track scholarly category boundaries .
A further philological note concerns Chiri Yukie's Ainu Shin'yōshū.
The kamuy yukar section headings appear in full capitals in the original edition (e.g.
AEKIRUSHI KAMUY).
The title element AEKIRUSHI has been proposed, after Katayama Ryūmine 2003, to parse as a=e-kir-usi 'the place one has memory of' rather than as a form of ekiru 'turn back' ‹contested›
(0penke, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-03-19; ).
The analysis is morphologically plausible but remains community-proposed and has not been confirmed in independent philological commentary.
It is noted here without grammatical commitment.

The grammatical features conditioned by genre and register — fourth-person narration and its logophoric function, TAM and evidential framing in verse versus prose, elegant-register morphology — are analysed in , , , and .
Verse structure and the sakehe refrain belong to and ; the honorific and ritual registers of prayer texts to .
Hokkaido Ainu was spoken in regionally differentiated forms whose systematic divergences bear on morphology, phonology, and lexical semantics alike.
The grammar takes the Saru (SAR) and Chitose (CHI) varieties as its descriptive core.

Saru is the most extensively documented Hokkaido dialect: Tamura's 1996 dictionary supplies a dense lexical record; Nakagawa's annotated oral-literature text collections from Nibutani and Biratori narrators give a genre-diverse discourse corpus ; and Nakagawa's 2024 grammar takes Saru as the default Hokkaido reference throughout .

Chitose is the second depth-documented variety: Nakagawa's 1995 dictionary provides the foundational Chitose lexical record ; Satō's 2008 grammar integrates Chitose systematically alongside Saru comparisons ; and the NINJAL Glossed Audio Corpus of Folklore contributes additional Chitose material .

Six further dialect areas enter the description where sources allow: Shizunai (SHI), documented most fully by ; Horobetsu (HOR), the subject of Takahashi's morphosyntactic studies ; Tokachi (TOK), whose dialect is documented in Takahashi's Tokachi example collection and evidentiality and deixis studies ; Ishikari (ISH), described by ; and the more sparsely attested Asahikawa (ASA) and Yakumo (YAK) areas.
The tag HK marks data not assignable to a specific locality.
