Nakagawa characterizes it as 円唇後舌母音 ('rounded back vowel'), and notes that /o/ is also protruded, making the distinction between /o/ and /u/ difficult in casual speech.
To Japanese-speaking ears, /u/ sounds close to [o], which is why early Japanese records transcribed aynu 'person' as アイノ and inaw 'ritual stick' as イナオ .
/i/ and /u/ devoice when flanked by voiceless consonants; /e/ is occasionally affected in the same environment.
The phenomenon is well documented across Hokkaido dialects, with the earliest systematic account in Kindaichi (1931) and detailed treatment in Tamura (1998), both discussed in .
Representative forms: ci̥se 'house', su̥tu 'root', se̥ta 'dog'.
The degree of devoicing shows heavy inter-speaker and inter-dialectal variation.
Northern dialects devoice more frequently.

A longitudinal comparison reported by Tamura (1998) — two Saru speakers from different generations — showed the younger speaker (b. 1912) devoicing approximately 25 times more often than the older (b. 1890) and in a wider range of phonological environments, including closed syllables under accent and consecutive vowels (eci̥ci̥snupehe 'your tears'); this is discussed in .
The syllable types most prone to devoicing are si and ci; the types tu, pi, and pu are reported never to devoice — a contrast with Japanese, which devoices ピ and プ in the same environment .
A Chitose-dialect recording shows eci=kay realized as [et͡sɨ̥kaj], with devoiced [ɨ̥] in the ci sequence (nukopoli, 2024-12-20) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
L2 learners influenced by kana spelling tend to over-devoice, applying devoicing beyond its natural distribution (Tamura 1998: 55, cited in ).
The interaction of devoicing with consonant voicing and the /s/ palatalization pattern is discussed in and .
Hokkaido Ainu has no phonemic vowel length.
All length observed in performance is allophonic, arising from two distinct sources ; .
First, monosyllabic CV words lengthen the vowel in isolation or in pause-final position: kaː 'thread', toː 'lake', niː 'tree'.
Second, the vowel of the accented syllable lengthens in polysyllabic words: ˈnuːman 'yesterday', poˈroː 'big'.

Both processes are automatic and "not conducted consciously" by speakers (Kindaichi 1931: 4, cited in ); this accent-conditioned lengthening is why the yukar epic was formerly written ユーカラ (accent on yu) .

A grammaticalized emphatic lengthening, distinct from the allophonic process, breaks the extended vowel with a glottal onset: wen 'bad' → weʔen 'very bad'; to 'lake' → toʔo 'faraway' (Kindaichi 1931; ).
The glottal element here marks the emphatic lexical expansion, not a phonemic long vowel.
Sakhalin Ainu, by contrast, maintains genuine vowel-length oppositions (e.g.
‹SA›
niisah vs.
nisah) corresponding to the Hokkaido pitch-accent contrast (HA nísap 'suddenly' vs.
nisáp 'shin') ; .
The reconstructed diachronic relationship — vowel length as the older opposition, later replaced by pitch-accent in Hokkaido — is argued at length in and discussed in the prosody chapters .
Sequences such as ay, aw, uy, ew, and oy are phonetically falling diphthongs — [ai̯], [au̯], [ui̯], [eu̯], [oi̯] — but their phonological analysis is not as diphthongs in the classical sense.

The elements -y and -w behave as syllable-coda consonants in morphological tests (they trigger the consonant allomorph of the nominalizer -pe rather than the vowel allomorph -p: okay-pe, siw-pe) and cannot carry accent independently ; .
The full analysis — including the phonemic status of /y/ and /w/, glide insertion at hiatus, and the diphthong vs. coda-glide question — is given in .
Morphophonological consequences of vowel hiatus at morpheme boundaries are treated in .

/a/ is the most frequent vowel in the Hokkaido corpus, a point in common with Japanese. /e/ is markedly more frequent than in Japanese, a characteristic that persists when person-affix tokens (a=, =an, and related forms) are excluded from the count (nukopoli, 2024-09-25) ‹corpus-suggested›.

The corpus tools available for this grammar count word tokens rather than phoneme occurrences, so these frequency ranks cannot be reproduced from per-segment counts at this writing; the underlying pattern is, however, consistent with the high frequency of the participial suffix -e, the applicative prefixes, and the evidential formal nouns all containing /e/.

In two morphological contexts — the suffix that derives transitive verbs from intransitives, and the vowel suffix that forms the possessed (affiliative) form of nouns — the choice of suffix vowel is conditioned by the vowel of the root: kay → kay-e 'break (tr.)', mos → mos-o 'wake (tr.)', yak → yak-u 'crush'; possessed tek → tek-e 'hand', nan → nan-u 'face' ; .
Chiri (1952) named this pattern 母音調和 ('vowel harmony'), hypothesizing that the suffix was originally -i (the 3sg possessive), which underwent full assimilation to the root vowel .
The characterization as vowel harmony is contested.

The pattern is confined to two derivational contexts; it is absent from the plural suffix -pa (kom-pa, not *kom-po), from personal prefixes (ku-kor, not *ko-kor), and from underived forms; and no backness or tongue-root feature uniformly characterizes the alternating set ; ; .
The phenomenon is therefore better described as a morphologically restricted vowel co-occurrence pattern than as productive harmony ‹contested›.
The morphophonological analysis of the possessed-form suffix, including the competing accounts of the assimilation mechanism, is pursued in .
While the five-vowel inventory is constant across Hokkaido dialects, vowel quality shifts are attested in individual dialect records.

In recordings of the Mukawa dialect (Katayama corpus), /i/ is realized as a lowered, fronted vowel approximating [e], and /e/ as a more open [ɛ]; the shift is general in the recording, though /i/ retains a canonical [i] realization outside the affiliative form in some tokens (nukopoli, 2024-03-18) ‹corpus-suggested›.

The pattern is consistent with a lowering chain in which the entire front series shifts one step downward; whether it is a stable feature of Mukawa or reflects idiolectal or recording conditions is not settled by the available evidence.
The Shizunai (静内) and Samani dialect areas are accentless (), which affects the realization of vowels under accent but does not alter the underlying inventory.
Systematic acoustic comparisons of vowel space across Hokkaido dialect regions remain a gap in the literature .
Hokkaido Ainu has a single fricative phoneme, /s/ (see ).
Its phonetic realization depends on syllabic position.
In onset function /s/ appears as a laminal sibilant with a degree of palatalization that varies by speaker and vowel context.

In coda function the realization splits by the preceding vowel: after /i/ the coda /s/ surfaces as [ɕ], merging perceptually with the initial consonant of Japanese シ; after /a/, /e/, /o/, and /u/ it surfaces as a partially palatalized laminal [sʲ]~[ʃ], intermediate between Japanese ス and シ.
A third context overrides the coda rule: immediately before the glide /w/ at a following syllable or word boundary, the coda /s/ surfaces as a plain [s] ; .
Because /s/ is the only fricative in the Hokkaido Ainu phoneme inventory, the alternants [sʲ], [ʃ], [ɕ], and [s] are all allophones of one underlying segment, never contrastive with each other.

The distribution does, however, produce perceptual near-mergers that led early transcribers working within a Japanese kana frame to hear palatal colouring in unexpected environments, and it creates systematic difficulty for Japanese-background listeners distinguishing morphological structures that differ in syllabic affiliation rather than in the consonant itself.
In onset position /s/ is realized as a laminal alveolar fricative.

A community phonetics survey characterizes it as [s̻] — with the blade of the tongue making the primary constriction rather than the tip — and notes a perceptible difference from the palato-alveolar [ɕ] of Japanese シ even when both are heard as "sh-like" (nukopoli, 2023-12-11) ‹speculative›.
The palatalization tendency of onset /s/ in older recordings extends beyond the environment of a following /i/.

Community phonetic analysis of early twentieth-century audio reports that the onset /s/ was palatalized in a wider range of vowel environments than is typical of the better-documented mid-century speakers (nukopoli, 2023-12-05) ‹corpus-suggested›.
Shiraishi describes Ainu /s/ as "often palatalized" , citing Kindaichi (1931: 9) and Tamura (1988b: 13) for the forms sini [ʃini] and as [aʃ] as early printed attestations.
Early Japanese transcriptions of Ainu rendered the onset sa, su, se, so syllables with the digraphs シャ, シュ, シェ, ショ rather than サ, ス, セ, ソ, reflecting a palatal impression before non-high vowels.

Tamura (1996) states that in Saru "the fricative is /s/ alone, close to the consonant of シ, but with individual variation; sa, se, so, su vary between a サ-type and a シャ-type pronunciation, while si is invariably シ" (reported via , nukopoli, 2023-12-11; corroborates the general pattern) ‹speculative›.
The realization of coda /s/ is conditioned by the vowel of the syllable nucleus it closes.
When that vowel is /i/, the coda /s/ surfaces as [ɕ]; when it is /a/, /e/, /o/, or /u/, the coda surfaces as a partially palatalized [sʲ]~[ʃ].
The rule as stated in and corroborated by can be formulated:
The following table gives attested examples in word-citation (pause) form.
All coda forms are taken from ; the general rule applies equally to coda /s/ after /u/, though no dedicated example is cited there.
The near-merger between coda /s/ after /i/ and onset /s/ before /i/ generates a systematic perceptual difficulty.

The pair tures 'younger sister' — with coda /s/ in the syllable /res/ — and tures-i 'his/her younger sister' — in which the same /s/ resyllabifies as the onset of the following possessive suffix -i, giving the syllable /si/ [ɕi] — both approach [tureɕ] at their right edge as heard by Japanese listeners, even though they are structurally distinct .
For Ainu speakers the difference is in the syllabic affiliation of /s/ (coda vs. onset), recoverable from morphological structure.
Resyllabification at morpheme boundaries is treated in ; the morphophonology of the possessive suffix is taken up in .
The onset /s/ before /i/ participates in the same [ɕ] realization.
The reflexive prefix surfaces as [ɕi], the same phonetic output as coda /s/ after /i/.
The two environments converge on [ɕ] from different structural positions (coda conditioned by preceding /i/, onset conditioned by following /i/) without forming a phonemic /ɕ/ distinct from /s/.
At a juncture before the labio-velar glide /w/, the coda /s/ surfaces as plain [s] rather than the [sʲ]~[ʃ] expected from the non-/i/ conditioning rule.

Tamura (1996) describes as 'stand' in isolation as アㇱ ([aʃ]), but the same verb followed by the conjunctive particle becomes アㇲワ ([aswa]), with the fricative shifting to a plain sibilant before the /w/ onset (aomidori, 2023-12-11, reporting Tamura 1996); see also for the coda-/s/ allophony frame within which this constraint operates ‹corpus-suggested›.
The phonetic interpretation is straightforward: the labial co-articulation of /w/ suppresses the palatal colouring that the coda /s/ otherwise carries.

Whether this is best analysed as anticipatory labial assimilation blocking palatalization, or as a context-sensitive allophone rule that takes precedence over the general coda rule, is not resolved in the sources consulted.
The broader sandhi environment in which /s/ participates at word junctures — including the /r/+/s/ cluster that produces progressive effects (see ) — is treated there.
The [ɕ] that appears as the coda /s/ allophone after /i/ and as the onset /s/ allophone before /i/ is phonetically distinct from the Japanese palato-alveolar [ɕ] of シ.

Community phonetic analysis characterizes the Ainu surface [ɕ] as having less high-frequency friction than its Japanese counterpart, placed somewhat further back in the oral cavity — on the boundary between Japanese [ɕ] and an English postalveolar [ʃ] — while never reaching a full retroflexed or postalveolar [ʃ] (nukopoli, 2023-12-11) ‹speculative›.
The analysis characterizes it as a laminal sound, with the tongue blade rather than the tip engaged, which distinguishes it from the Japanese [ɕ] even within the palato-alveolar region.
This distinction has no phonemic status: there is no /ɕ/ phoneme in Hokkaido Ainu separate from /s/; the [ɕ] surface form is entirely predictable from the vowel context.

The use in earlier descriptions of /ʃ/ as a coda symbol (as in Shiraishi's notation as [aʃ], and Tamura's representation of coda -s after /i/ as シ) reflects the impressionistic transcription of the fully palatalized allophone, not a phonemic /ʃ/ distinct from /s/ .
The degree of coda palatalization shows inter-speaker variation within and across dialects.

Analysis of NINJAL recordings identifies Hiraga Sadamo (平賀さだも, Saru dialect) as producing "pure [ɕ]" at the coda and onset-before-/i/ position, while Mukawa dialect recordings from the same archive frequently show a reduced variant [ɕ̱̥] — a partially devoiced, laminal palato-alveolar — in the same environment (nukopoli, 2024-03-24) ‹speculative›.

The Mukawa variant suggests an interaction between coda /s/ palatalization and the vowel devoicing that affects /i/ between voiceless consonants (treated in ): when /i/ devoices in the environment of the coda /s/, the palatalization feature is retained on the fricative but the overall phonetic output moves toward a devoiced palatal fricative [ç] or a devoiced [ɕ̥].
These inter-speaker differences have not been quantified from published acoustic measurements in any directly-read source.
The phonetic detail is graded accordingly.
The vowel devoicing pattern that creates the relevant environment in Mukawa is independently attested in and .
A sporadic case of progressive palatalization has been observed in NINJAL corpus recordings of the compound word sirsak .
The underlying form /sir.sak/ has initial /si/ → [ɕi] by the regular onset rule, followed by the coda /r/ of sir and then the onset /s/ of sak.

In the speech of 木村きみ (Kimura Kimi, Saru), the coda /r/ after /i/ is palatalized ([ɾʲ]), and this palatalization carries forward progressively onto the following /s/, shifting it from the expected laminal [s̻] toward a laminal postalveolar [ᶘ], as in [ɕiɾʲᶘak˚]; an alternative surface realization is [ɕiɾʲɕak˚] (nukopoli, 2026-05-11) ‹speculative›.

The speaker 小田イト (Oda Ito, also documented in Saru at the same NINJAL site) does not show the same progressive shift: her realization is [ɕiɾʲis̻ak˚], with an echo vowel after the /r/ coda (a property of coda /r/ discussed in ) and a plain laminal [s̻] — not a palatalized [ᶘ] or [ɕ] — as the onset before /a/ (nukopoli, 2026-05-11) ‹speculative›.

The contrast between the two speakers illustrates two independent strategies for the /ɾʲ.s/ juncture: progressive coarticulation of palatality from [ɾʲ] onto the following /s/ (Kimura), versus insertion of an echo vowel that interposes a vocalic buffer between the palatalized rhotic and the onset /s/ (Oda).

The observation is idiolect-specific in the available NINJAL data, has not been confirmed in other compounds or other speakers in any read source, and the IPA transcription reflects community analysis rather than published spectral measurement ‹speculative›.
The broader /r/+/s/ sandhi environment — where a coda /r/ interacts with a following /s/ onset — is treated in .
Hokkaido Ainu has one rhotic phoneme, /r/, the sole coronal sonorant that is neither a nasal (/m/, /n/) nor a glide (/y/, /w/) in the eleven-consonant system described in ; ; .

The phoneme occurs in both onset and coda positions within the canonical (C)V(C) syllable, and its coda realization — carrying a distinctive vocalic release and triggering a dense assimilation system — makes it the most morphophonologically active segment in the language.

The full assimilation rules are given in ; the present chapter covers the phoneme's phonetic realization, the echo-vowel phenomenon, and the diagnostics that separate /r/-final syllables from genuine /rV/ syllables.
In syllable-onset position /r/ is realized as an alveolar flap [ɾ] ; .
Speaker variation and historical change produce a broader allophonic range; the table below collects documented realizations.
The allophonic range — flap, trill, dental-approximant — places Ainu /r/ in a different perceptual space from Japanese ラ行, whose typical word-initial and post-nasal realization leans lateral.

Tamura's Saru dictionary grammar is reported by community members to emphasize this perceptual distance explicitly (aomidori, 2023-12-11, citing Tamura 1996) ‹speculative›; the source most directly available, Shiraishi (2022: §3.1), records [l] and [d] as occasional allophones attributed to Tamura (1988b: 13) rather than as the default, which remains the flap [ɾ].
In Sakhalin Ainu the cognate of Hokkaido /r/ is described as retroflex [ʈ], acoustically close to [t] and distinct from the Hokkaido flap .

The coda realization of /r/ carries a vocalic release — known variously in the literature as the re-sounding, the echo-vowel, or the echoing vowel — that has attracted sustained analysis since the earliest systematic descriptions .
In careful speech the release is audible as a short vowel copying the nucleus of the syllable: kar [kaɾ(a)], kor [koɾ(o)], sir [siɾ(i)].
In recitation or emphatic delivery the release extends to a full vowel: [piriˑka], [mokoroˑ] .

Batchelor (1905) and the early Kindaichi transcriptions wrote post-/r/ vowels as full phonemic segments — hence spellings such as koro, pirika, Ainurakkuru — without distinguishing a genuine /rV/ syllable from the echo-vowel release of a /r/-final syllable ; .

Yukie Chiri (知里幸恵), in correspondence with Kindaichi around 1923, established that /r/-final words form a coherent phonological category and that the post-/r/ releases in Batchelor's transcriptions are phonologically spurious .
She identified three diagnostics that separate /r/-final from /rV/-final words ; :

The echo-vowel weakens before a vowel-initial suffix; a genuine final vowel does not. In mokor=an 'sleep.4S' the echo is reduced before the suffix, whereas the final /o/ of poro=an 'be.big.4S' remains unreduced.

Coda /r/ undergoes morphophonological sandhi; /rV/ does not. The /r/-final verb a=kor 'have' assimilates its coda before the onset of a following word (a=kor nispa → [akonˈnispa] 'a wealthy man'), whereas a word ending in /rV/ such as poro 'big' shows no corresponding change.
The sandhi system is treated in .
The nominalizer selects its consonant-allomorph after coda /r/. The nominalizer surfaces as -pe after a consonant and -p after a vowel.
A /r/-final stem takes -pe:

The minimal pair etor [etoro] 'snot' versus etoro [etoːro] 'to snore' is now well established in the literature: in the /rV/-final word the vowel preceding /r/ is measurably longer, whereas the echo-vowel in the /r/-final word is audibly shorter ; .
Asai (1976) confirmed the length difference acoustically .
An additional independent diagnostic, noted by Satō (2000), is that in pre-pausal position the final vowel is repeated only for /r/-final words .

The direction of vowel-copying is predominantly anticipatory: pirka surfaces as [pirĭka] and arki as [ariki], with the echo anticipating the following vowel rather than perseverating the preceding one .
A perseveratory case, citarpe [citarube] (Asai 1976), shows that the copying direction is not categorically fixed .
Northern dialect speakers vacillate between -r and -rV in certain lexical items (kikir ~ kikiri), suggesting ongoing redistribution between the two categories in those varieties .

One articulatory account of the echo-vowel, proposed within the community, treats it as a timing offset: the tongue-tip flap gesture begins before the mouth has finished the preceding vowel, so the flap releases into the vowel-gesture and produces an audible copy of the nucleus (nukopoli, 2023-12-11) ‹speculative›.
Published treatments describe the release as a phonological property of coda /r/ without committing to a specific articulatory model .

In casual connected speech, word-final /r/ is susceptible to deletion, producing reduced forms such as ku for kur 'person' and ko for kor 'have', while the verb koro tends to stabilize its full form in many contexts (nukopoli, 2024-12-11) ‹corpus-suggested›.
This casual reduction is distinct from the diachronic Sakhalin coda-/r/ → /h/ change treated in .
When the onset of a CVC syllable is a voiceless stop /k/, /p/, or /t/, the coda /r/ is devoiced to [ɾ̥].
The verb nukar 'look at' illustrates the pattern: the final syllable kar has onset /k/ and coda /r/, and the rhotic surfaces as [ɾ̥], giving [nukaɾ̥] (aomidori, 2023-12-11) ‹corpus-suggested›.

The pattern is phonetically parallel to the partial devoicing of sonorant codas reported for other languages after voiceless-onset syllables; Shiraishi's description of /r/ as a flap with voicing-conditioned variants is consistent with the conditioning, though no instrumental study targeting this specific alternation has been found in the sources read for this grammar.

The devoiced coda in turn affects the echo-vowel: when [ɾ̥] releases, the following vocalic copy is likewise voiceless, yielding a realization such as [nukaɾ̥ɨ̥h] in citation-form speech (aomidori, 2023-12-11).

Vowel devoicing in comparable environments — high vowels between voiceless consonants — is independently attested in Hokkaido Ainu and is described in ; the rhotic devoicing here extends the same voicelessness-spreading dynamic to the coda rhotic of CVC syllables with voiceless onsets.
Coda /r/ is the dominant trigger of the regressive assimilation rules described in .
When a /r/-final morpheme or word precedes a consonant-initial morpheme or word, the /r/ assimilates to, or is absorbed into a geminate with, the following consonant.

The principal alternations, drawn from Nakagawa (2024: 35–37) and Shiraishi (2022: §6.1), are: /r/ + /t/ → [tt] (a=kor tar → [aˈkottar]); /r/ + /n/ → [nn] (a=kor nispa → [akonˈnispa]); /r/ + /c/ → [tc] (retar cikap → [retatˈcikap] 'swan'); /r/ + /s/ → [ss] (ar suy → [asˈsuy] 'once'); and, uniquely, a dissimilatory /r/ + /r/ → [nn] (ku=kor rusuy → [kukonˈrusuy] 'I want it') ; .

Unlike nasal-place assimilation (which is bounded by the phrase in Shiraishi's 2001 analysis), /r/-sandhi operates across phrasal and sentence boundaries as a postlexical rule ; (antitwilight, 2024-11-23) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The rules are not written in standard orthography, which notates underlying forms; they are fully productive in speech .
Personal-affix junctures that feed the same /r/-sandhi rules are treated in , and the echo-vowel's interaction with possessive-form derivation is treated in .

Across Hokkaido varieties, coda /r/ shows at least one documented lexically specific neutralization: in some dialects mokor 'sleep' surfaces as mokon, with /r/ replaced by [n] (keycja, 2024-07-20) ‹speculative›.

Nakagawa and Fukazawa's dialect classification documents extensive morphophonological isoglosses across the Hokkaido area , though the specific /r/ → /n/ change in this lexical item has not been mapped to a named dialect zone in the sources read for this grammar.
The broader picture of dialectal consonant correspondences is taken up in .
In Sakhalin Ainu, coda /r/ has merged with /h/ in syllable-final and word-final position, so that Hokkaido kor 'have' corresponds to Sakhalin koh.

The change is attested in the Sakhalin corpus, and the distribution of Sakhalin -h vis-à-vis the retained /rV/ type has been the subject of dedicated distributional analysis (cited in nukopoli, 2024-12-19).
Because the Sakhalin /r/ → /h/ shift belongs primarily to the diachronic and comparative treatment, details are routed to .
The Sakhalin onset cognate of Hokkaido /r/ is the retroflex [ʈ] mentioned in §2 above, distinct both from the Hokkaido flap and from the Sakhalin /h/ that the coda reflex produces.
Hokkaido Ainu has one laryngeal phoneme, /h/, and a phonetically audible glottal closure [ʔ] whose phonological status divides analysts.

The two laryngeal elements have distinct distributional profiles: /h/ occupies the onset of its syllable with vowel-conditioned allophony; [ʔ] marks the onset of vowel-initial syllables as a phonetically automatic boundary cue in the majority analysis, though it functions as a lexically contrastive phoneme in the accentless Shizunai dialect ; ; .
A glottal onset [ʔ] is phonetically present before every vowel-initial syllable in Hokkaido Ainu — word-initially and at internal morpheme and word junctures.
traces the earliest systematic observation to Kindaichi (1928), a Tōhoku-Japanese speaker who characterized Ainu as inserting a glottal closure before each vowel-initial syllable.
The stop's auditory salience varies with phonetic context.

Tamura (1970: 586–587, cited via ) distinguishes a perceptible stop — arising when the following vowel carries lexical accent and/or occurs in a closed syllable — from a barely perceptible transition that amounts to no more than the syllable-division point.
Attested forms in which the stop is clearly audible include [aˈʔep] 'food', [aˈʔoypep] 'tableware', [oˈʔatteke], [eˈʔunpipka], and [teˈʔeta] 'long ago' (Tamura 1970: 586, cited via ).
The HA syllable canon (C)V(C) permits at most one onset consonant per syllable (see ).
When a preceding morpheme ends in a consonant, that consonant resyllabifies as the onset of the following vowel-initial syllable: cip-o → [ci.po] 'board a boat', mat-ak → [ma.tak] 'younger sister' .
No [ʔ] appears in those resyllabified forms, because the onset slot is already filled.
The glottal closure thus marks syllables whose onset position remains empty — a phonetically automatic default rather than a lexically specified segment.
Whether [ʔ] constitutes an underlying phoneme /ʔ/ in Hokkaido Ainu is contested .
Two positions have been held since the mid-twentieth century:
The accent argument applies only in pitch-accent varieties.
In the accentless Shizunai dialect it does not hold, and phonemic /ʔ/ has been demonstrated there (§ below).
The non-phonemic analysis stands for the accent-dialect majority and is adopted here for those varieties ‹contested›.
The phonetic realization of [ʔ] at morpheme and word boundaries varies with the prosodic integration of the flanking elements.
Three degrees of boundary tightness are audible in a single compound across careful and casual speech.

In itakorapiru=an 'be telling the story in full', the most separated pronunciation is [itak|orapiru…] with a full juncture stop; an intermediate version shows [itak⁀orapiru…] with partial resyllabification alongside an audible [ʔ]; and the most integrated realization is [ita.ko.rapiru…] with full resyllabification and no glottal.
Acoustic measurement confirms that the presence or absence of a voiceless interval between the coda /k/ and the following /o/ distinguishes the [−C.ʔV] and [+C.V] realizations ‹corpus-suggested›
The suffix =an (fourth-person intransitive subject) provides a clear test after a stop-final stem.
After the suffix =an does not trigger resyllabification of the coda /p/ onto the following vowel; a juncture [ʔ] appears instead, yielding [sapʔan] ‹corpus-suggested›
The prefixes ku=, e=, ci= are prosodically integrated with their stem, forming a single prosodic word and triggering vowel-deletion and accent-shift processes (see and ).
The prefix a=, which does not shift lexical accent, is accordingly less tightly bound .

Acoustic observation of a=kor itak 'there is speech' yields [a.ko.rəʔi.tak]: the echo vowel [ə] follows coda /r/ in kor, and [ʔ] appears at the compound boundary before itak, while the a=–kor boundary shows no juncture stop ‹corpus-suggested›

These observations together point to a gradient of boundary tightness within the person-marking system: the productive object/agent prefix class (ku=, e=, ci=) is the most integrated; the a= boundary is tighter than a compound word boundary but looser than the productive-prefix class; and the =an suffix boundary is the least integrated of the person-marking elements examined here.
Glide insertion at hiatus and the broader juncture phonology are treated in .
The accentless Shizunai dialect (静内; classified as 無アクセント by ; see ) presents an environment in which [ʔ] and [w] carry lexical contrast.
Okuda (2025), drawing on fieldwork by 志賀雪湖, reports a minimal pair for juncture types that in accent varieties are kept distinct by pitch placement rather than by the laryngeal itself :
Because Shizunai lacks distinctive pitch accent, the contrast [suwat] : [suʔat] cannot be attributed to accent-placement differences as it would be in an accent dialect.

Okuda (2025) concludes that in Shizunai both the glide /w/ and the [ʔ] at transparent compound boundaries are phonemic, and adds the explicit caution that this finding does not generalize: "one cannot say, without specifying dialect, that the transitional glide y/w is non-phonemic" .
Parallel contrasts are reported for /uʔa/ : /uwa/ and /iʔo/ : /iyo/ in Shizunai ‹contested›.
The glide phonemicity question across Hokkaido dialects is examined in .
A morphologically conditioned process inserts [ʔ] to break a repeated vowel in emphatic or intensified word forms, shifting or heightening the form's meaning.
The set of participating roots is lexically restricted.
Kindaichi (1931, cited via ) documents the pattern in Saru:
The [ʔ] in emphatic forms carries semantic weight and is invariant under conditions that suppress the boundary glottal elsewhere.
This distinguishes it from the phonetically automatic onset [ʔ] discussed above, which yields to resyllabification.
The phoneme /h/ occurs only in syllable-onset position in Hokkaido Ainu, categorically excluded from the coda ; .
Three allophones are conditioned by the following vowel ; :
The conditioning is audible but less categorical than in standard Japanese.
Tamura (1998: 41, cited via ) reports that speakers born around 1900 showed only weak vowel-coloring of /h/, with the [ɸ] before /u/ approaching a glottal quality in particular tokens.
All three realizations are predictable allophones of a single phoneme /h/; no minimal pair distinguishes them for the same following vowel (see ).
Coda /h/ is absent as a synchronic segment in Hokkaido Ainu: no native Hokkaido word carries a laryngeal in coda position ; .

In Sakhalin Ainu, by contrast, a coda breath-release /h/ (realized as a voiceless breath, not [x]; Hattori 1964: 34, cited via ) is productive and reflects historical HA coda /r/ among other sources (see ).
Within Hokkaido Ainu, the possessed form siki-h-i 'his/her eyes' (from ) contains an epenthetic /h/ inserted before the possessive suffix.
This /h/ is a morphological insertion restricted to the affiliative formation and does not represent an underlying coda in the root (Kindaichi & Chiri 1936: 14, cited via ).

Whether certain citation forms of stems carry an underlying final /h/, and what diachronic relationship that /h/ bears to the Sakhalin coda and to Sakhalin vowel length, is the 'final-h question' treated in .
The Hokkaido Ainu syllable has the shape (C)V(C): an optional onset consonant, a single vowel nucleus, and an optional coda consonant ; ; .
Four syllable types result:
Every syllable contains exactly one vowel.
Two or more consonants in sequence occur only at a syllable boundary, never within a single syllable: the shapes CCVC, CVCC, and CVVC are all excluded ; .
The word toop 'far away', which looks like CVVC in the Latin transcription, parses as two syllables to.op (CV.VC), the syllable boundary falling between the two successive vowels .
The phonemic vowel inventory is described in and the consonant inventory in .

Nakagawa (2024: 25) characterizes Hokkaido Ainu as having relatively few phonemes and a straightforward syllable structure, noting that the five-vowel inventory is constant across all Hokkaido dialects — dialect differences are comparatively small.

In contrast, Sakhalin Ainu (SA) allows a long-vowel nucleus alongside a coda consonant, producing CVVC syllables absent from Hokkaido: SA aa, ruu correspond to Hokkaido a, ru, and the SA length contrast niisah : nisah corresponds to the Hokkaido pitch-accent contrast nísap : nisáp .
The diachronic SA-length ↔ HA-pitch correspondence is treated in .
Whether every vowel-initial syllable has an underlying glottal stop /ʔ/ is disputed.
Under the /ʔ/-as-phoneme view (Hattori 1961; Tamura, earlier work) the template reduces to just CV and CVC, eliminating V and VC shapes.

Nakagawa rejects this on the grounds that no minimal pair exists in monomorphemic forms and that positing /ʔ/ requires many costly deletion rules , a judgement shared by Refsing and Chiri (1942) as reported by .
The debate is covered in ; the majority position — /ʔ/ as a phonetic boundary element rather than a phoneme — is followed here, retaining V and VC syllable shapes in the template ‹contested›.
Nakagawa (2024: 43) provides a three-step algorithm for assigning syllable boundaries in the Latin transcription:
Split between two adjacent vowels: VV → V.V.
Split between two adjacent consonants: CC → C.C.
In a VCV sequence, split before the consonant: VCV → V.CV.
The algorithm applied to several representative words:
(Nakagawa 2024: 43.) The algorithm treats /y/ and /w/ as consonants, so aynu = ay.nu (CVC.CV) and kamuy = ka.muy (CV.CVC).
The arguments for treating /-y/ and /-w/ as coda consonants rather than as the second element of a diphthong are presented in .

A minimal pair that turns on syllable count exists in Saru and Chitose: yayrayke 'commit suicide' = yay.ray.ke (CVC.CVC.CV, three syllables) versus yairayke 'give thanks' = ya.i.ray.ke (CV.V.CVC.CV, four syllables).
The sequence -ay- in the first word is a single closed syllable (CVC); the -ai- in the second is two syllables separated by a morpheme boundary.
These words carry different accent patterns that follow from the syllable count , a distribution governed by the iambic placement rule in .
Syllabification applies across morpheme boundaries through resyllabification: a coda consonant on one morpheme is re-parsed as the onset of a following vowel-initial morpheme.
The compound mat-ikor (woman + possessions) thus surfaces as macikor [ma.ʨi.kor], with the underlying coda /t/ shifting to the onset of the second syllable and palatalizing before /i/ ; :
The palatalization rule t+i → [ʨi] is categorically obligatory wherever the coda /t/ of one morpheme and the onset /i/ of the next come into contact; it is covered in detail in .
Resyllabification is blocked when the following vowel bears secondary accent or when the boundary separates a reduplicant from its base, where a glottal boundary element appears instead .
The interaction of resyllabification with the morphophonology of personal affixes is treated in .
Nine of the eleven consonant phonemes occur in coda position.

The two excluded from coda position in Hokkaido Ainu are the affricate /c/ [ʨ] and the laryngeal /h/; the remaining nine — stops /p t k/, fricative /s/, nasals /m n/, rhotic /r/, and glides /y w/ — all appear as codas ; ; .
The coda stops /p t k/ are realized as unreleased [p̚ t̚ k̚] — closure is maintained but no burst follows, a pattern similar to Korean final stops and unlike English ; .
In older recordings, a full release was sometimes heard; the degree of implosion also varies across speakers (aomidori\_cs\_, 2023-12-05) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The coda allophony of /s/ — [ɕ] after the vowel /i/ versus a more front [sʲ] after other vowels — is treated in .
Coda /n/ undergoes place assimilation: it surfaces as [ŋ] before /k/ and as [m] before /p/ or /m/ .
So honkor 'be pregnant' is pronounced [hoŋkor] and anpe 'true thing' is [ampe].
The orthographic convention records the underlying /n/ throughout.

Coda /r/ carries a vocalic release — usually a copy of the preceding vowel — that was long confused with a final full vowel in early transcriptions; its phonemic status and sandhi behavior are covered in .

The frequency figures in this section are drawn from a syllable count over the headwords of three dictionaries of southern Hokkaido dialects: Tamura's Saru dictionary , Nakagawa's Chitose dictionary , and Kayano's Saru (Nibutani) dictionary .

After removing bound affixes, clitics, multi-word headwords, and forms containing letters outside the Latin transcription of the Hokkaido phoneme inventory, the three sources yield 13,891 distinct single-word types; 13,872 of these parse exhaustively into (C)V(C) syllables, giving 51,003 syllables in all.
The 19 residues are transcription errors in the source files.
Headwords include derived and compound stems, so the figures describe the lexicon as dictionaries record it; cluster counts in particular reflect morpheme seams as well as root-internal sequences.
Open syllables outnumber closed ones by a little over two to one (68.9% against 31.1%), and syllables with an onset outnumber onsetless ones nearly six to one.
Words run from one to twelve syllables, with three- and four-syllable words together making up over half the types; the mean is 3.7 syllables per word.
About a third of word types (4,927 of 13,872) begin with a vowel.
Among nuclei, /a/ leads with 29.7% of all syllables, followed by /e/ (21.0%), /o/ (17.2%), /i/ (16.7%), and /u/ (15.5%).
The most frequent onset is /k/ (9,277 of 43,446 filled onsets, 21.4%), with /r s p t n/ each between 4,600 and 5,200; /w/ is the rarest onset at 1,058.
Coda frequency splits sharply by position in the word.

Word-finally /r/ dominates (1,119 of 4,664 final codas), ahead of /p/ and /k/; word-internally /n/ leads (2,322 of 11,178 internal codas), followed by /y/ — a reflection of the many -Vn- and -Vy- sequences in derived stems.

The sample contains no coda /h/ whatsoever, and the nine orthographic coda-/c/ tokens all trace to transcription errors in the source files, so the count confirms the categorical exclusion of /c h/ from coda position stated above.
Of the 99 heterosyllabic coda-onset combinations the nine codas and eleven onsets permit, 98 are attested at least once.
The single systematic gap is *t.y, consistent with the affrication of /t/ + /y/ to /c/ at morpheme boundaries (see ).

The distribution is heavily skewed: the ten commonest junctures (n.k 625, r.k 578, n.n 553, y.k 524, k.k 488, and so on) account for over 40% of all cluster tokens, while the rarest attested combinations (p.w, w.h) occur once each, at compound seams.
Vowel hiatus (V.V) is likewise common — 2,376 sequences — with e.a the most frequent pairing (237) and i.i the least (24).
Several syllable shapes that the (C)V(C) template formally permits are absent or near-absent from the native lexicon.
The best-established gaps, from Nakagawa's onset-×-vowel table (2024: 43–45), are the following:

Among the starred onset+vowel combinations, /-c/ and /-h/ are also categorically excluded from coda position (see the preceding section), and the /-c/ exclusion from coda means that *-ac, *-ec, etc., are all absent.
The full discussion of the affricate /c/ and its distribution belongs to .
The exclusion of CVVC syllables has a direct morphophonological consequence.

In southern Hokkaido dialects (Saru, Chitose, Mukawa), the vowel /u/ of the first-person agent prefix ku= deletes before a stem-initial /a e u o/, and the vowel /i/ of an /i/-initial stem weakens to the glide /y/ in the same environment.

The weakening applies when the stem's first syllable is open (CV onset + vowel): ku=ipe 'I eat a meal' surfaces as ku=ype [kúype], since the first syllable of ipe is open (V) and weakening to /y/ gives the licit shape CVC + CV (ku.ype).
When the stem's first syllable is closed (CVC), weakening is blocked.

The form is ku=ikra [ku.ík.ra], not *ku=ykra: if /i/ weakened to /y/, the resulting sequence /kuykra/ would be unsyllabifiable under (C)V(C) — the three-consonant cluster /ykr/ cannot be distributed between two (C)V(C) syllables without creating either a CC onset or a CC coda ; (nukopoli, 2024-11-28) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

Nakagawa's published example for this blocking is kuínkar (not *kuynkar) 'I look' (2024: 53): the first syllable of inkar is closed (/in/), so the hiatus is retained rather than resolved by weakening.
The contrast between the two environments:
The same principle holds for the second-person prefix e=: e=itak → eytak 'you speak' (open stem, weakening permitted), but e=ikra [e.ík.ra] 'you send' (closed stem, hiatus retained) .
The full allomorphy paradigm for ku=, e=, and ci= under vowel deletion and glide-weakening is set out in .
Loanwords that contain consonant clusters or CVVC structures are adapted to fit the (C)V(C) template by vowel epenthesis.
The epenthetic segment is typically /o/ or a copy of the nearest adjacent vowel (nukopoli, 2024-12-11) ‹corpus-suggested›.

In Hokkaido the donor language is Japanese; Russian borrowings belong to the Sakhalin varieties, so the clearest illustration of the repair comes from there ‹SA›: potoloko (← Rus. потолок 'ceiling') breaks up both a word-initial CC onset (/pt/) and a word-final CC cluster (/lk/) with epenthetic /o/.
Its single corpus attestation is Sakhalin, in Sentoku Tarōji's letters — keta potoloko kasiketa okay=ahci ‹corpus-confirmed›.
A hypothetical English loanword like Christmas would enter as something like kurisumas, with each cluster split by an inserted vowel .
The identity of the epenthetic vowel is not always /o/: a copy of the adjacent vowel also occurs, and the choice may reflect the phonological neighborhood rather than a single underlying default.

Loan adaptation across contact periods — Japanese into Hokkaido Ainu, Russian into the Sakhalin varieties — shows the (C)V(C) template operating as a consistent filter, with epenthesis as the principal repair strategy ‹corpus-suggested›.
Hokkaido Ainu words frequently end in sequences pairing a vowel with a following y [j] or w [w]: áynu 'human', kamúy 'spirit', ohaw 'soup', kéwtum 'heart', ináw 'prayer-wand'.
Two analyses have been proposed for these sequences.
The first treats the final element as a coda consonant — /y/ or /w/ — parallel to the coda stops, nasals, and /r/ of the inventory.

The second treats the sequences as falling diphthongs, with the final element a non-syllabic vowel ([i̯] or [u̯]), giving bimoraic nuclei [ai̯], [au̯], [ei̯], [eu̯], [oi̯], [ui̯] (nukopoli, 2023-12-11).
Phonetically the two analyses are indistinguishable: both produce the same output, and neither predicts any difference in production or perception (nukopoli, 2023-12-11).
The question is whether post-vocalic y/w behave morphologically and prosodically as consonants or as the second element of a vowel nucleus.
This chapter covers the phonemic status of coda y and w and the related question of the marginal onset sequences yi, wi, and wu.
The full phoneme inventory is in and ; the (C)V(C) syllable canon in .
The allophonic glide that appears at morpheme-boundary hiatus — the [j] in i-y-ekarkar — is a separate process treated in .
The standard modern analysis treats post-vocalic y and w as coda consonants, assigning syllables like ay, muy, haw, and kew to the CVC slot of the (C)V(C) canon alongside cep, sin, and ker ; .
Three diagnostics converge on this position.
The participant/event nominalizer has two allomorphs conditioned by the final segment of the base: -p attaches to vowel-final stems and -pe to consonant-final stems ; .
The selection is phonological and applies without exception across the lexicon.
Stems ending in y and w consistently take -pe, grouping with the consonant-final class.
For the full treatment of these nominalizers see .

On the diphthong analysis the final element of okay and siw is a non-syllabic vowel, which should trigger the vowel allomorph -p; the occurring forms okay-pe and siw-pe would then be exceptions requiring an auxiliary stipulation.
On the consonant analysis they are regular: /y/ and /w/ are consonants, and -pe is the expected allomorph .
The same consonant–vowel boundary governs the distributive plural suffix, which surfaces as -te after a consonant-final stem and -re after a vowel-final stem.

The plural of ante is okayte (< okay + -te), selecting the consonant allomorph on the evidence that stem-final /y/ is a consonant; vowel-final stems take -re (nukopoli, 2025-12-03) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The pattern mirrors the nominalizer allomorphy: /y/ at stem-end triggers the consonant-class allomorph in both environments independently.

In the pitch-accent dialects of Hokkaido Ainu (Saru, Chitose, Horobetsu, and related varieties), accent placement is determined by the weight of the first syllable: a closed (CVC) first syllable bears the rising pitch nucleus (↗), while an open (CV) first syllable passes the peak to the second syllable .
The system is described in full in .
Words whose first syllable ends in y or w pattern as CVC-closed (Rule 1), not as open syllables followed by an additional vowel:
áynu /áy.nu/ has two syllables; the first is CVC-closed and thus high under Rule 1.

Under the diphthong analysis, ay is a V+V nucleus rather than a CVC syllable, and Rule 1 — which keys on the presence of a coda consonant — has no basis to apply; an additional rule or stipulation would be required.
The consonant analysis lets the standard placement rules cover these forms without exception ; (nukopoli, 2023-12-11).
The same simplification holds in compounds: kamúy in kamúynomi 'pray to a spirit' retains its Rule 2 accent as the first element, the coda /y/ keeping the compound syllable count transparent; see .
Kindaichi & Chiri (cited via ) analysed post-vocalic y and w as the second elements of falling diphthongs.

Early romanization and katakana transcription followed this view: kamuy was written カムイ (four kana), treating the final element as a full vowel; aynu appeared as アイノ, reflecting the approximate quality of the rounded unstressed second element .

The orthographic reform that Chiri Yukie (知里幸恵, c. 1923) introduced — kamuy, ohaw, kewtum for カムイ, オハウ, ケウトゥム — was motivated by exactly the morphological and prosodic evidence set out in §2, not by any change in phonetic realization .
Phonetically the diphthong analysis is accurate.
The sequences are realized as falling diphthongs — [ai̯], [au̯], [ei̯], [eu̯], [oi̯], [ui̯] — in which the second element is non-syllabic (nukopoli, 2023-12-11).
Nothing in the acoustic signal distinguishes a coda consonant from a non-syllabic vowel in this position: the two analyses predict identical phonetic outputs.

The diphthong analysis is a coherent phonetic description; its weakness is at the morpho-phonological level, where it forces the statement that a "non-syllabic vowel" triggers the consonant-class allomorphs of both the nominalizer and the plural suffix.

The fullest structuralist defence of the diphthong view is Simeon's, who classes /w y/ as "nonsyllabic vowels" on four grounds: phonetic similarity to /u i/, a clustering pattern unlike that of the consonants, the narrow allophonic range they share with the vowels, and their undergoing the same elision as syllabic vowels .

The cost of the analysis shows in his inventory of units: alongside rising and falling diphthongs he must admit a triphthong yay and a "geminate diphthong" ayay 'baby' — sequences the coda analysis parses without any new unit types, as yay (CVC) and a.yay (V.CVC).
His own morphophonemics also lists the elision and clustering behavior that the consonant analysis takes as diagnostic, so the same data sorted by modern criteria land on the opposite conclusion.
The consonant analysis is adopted by Nakagawa , Shiraishi , and Satō , and is the working assumption of this grammar ‹consensus›.

The three diagnostics in §2 — nominalizer allomorphy, plural-suffix allomorphy, and pitch-accent placement — all turn on the same categorical distinction (consonant vs. vowel-final stem), and all place /y/ and /w/ in the consonant class without exception.

The diphthong analysis requires an auxiliary rule reclassifying the non-syllabic vowels as consonant-class triggers in three separate morpho-phonological environments; no evidence favours this stipulation over the simpler consonant phonemicization ‹contested›.

The community formulation captures the symmetry: reading /y/ and /w/ as consonants makes the consonant-like morphological behaviour fall out; reading them as vowels makes the phonetic falling-diphthong character explicit; neither reading misrepresents the phonetics (nukopoli, 2023-12-11).

Post-vocalic y and w are phonological coda consonants /y/ and /w/; their surface realization as the non-syllabic elements [i̯] and [u̯] of falling diphthongs is their expected phonetic output in that position.
Word-initial and post-consonantal y [j] and w [w] are onset consonants without analytical controversy: , , , .

Their onset and coda realizations are phonetically identical — onset [j] = coda [i̯], onset [w] = coda [u̯] — which is consistent with a single phoneme appearing in both positions, parallel to /m n r/ in Hokkaido Ainu ; .
Three onset–vowel sequences are absent from Hokkaido Ainu monomorphemic roots: yi, wi, and wu.

Nakagawa states that no root has any of these as its initial syllable, and that syllables of the shape yi-C, wi-C, wu-C do not exist in the language ; the same point is made in Shiraishi , with attribution to Kindaichi 1931:13 and Tamura 1988b:14.

A palatal glide before a high front vowel ([ji]) and a labio-velar glide before a high back rounded vowel ([wu], [wi]) are articulatorily near-redundant transitions, and similar restrictions are typologically common.
The phonotactic constraint is parallel to the absence of the onset ti from Ainu roots — its place in the table is empty, not filled by a rare allophone .
The sequences [ji] and [wu] arise at morpheme boundaries through resyllabification.

When a /y/-final coda immediately precedes an /i/-initial syllable across a morpheme or compound boundary, the coda resyllabifies as the onset of the following syllable, producing surface [ji]; the analogous process generates [wu] at a /w/–/u/ juncture.
Shiraishi cites yayirwakikor (< yay irwaki kor) as a compound containing surface [ji] at an internal boundary, and awun mimtar (< aw un mimtar) as containing [wu].
These are boundary-derived occurrences, not root-internal.
Whether yi, wi, and wu should be recognized as phonemic onset sequences — rare but not impossible — is genuinely disputed ‹contested›.
Nakagawa treats them as categorically restricted to morpheme boundaries and derives their surface occurrences entirely from resyllabification.

The position attributed to Tamura in community discussion holds that they are independent onsets comparable in phonemic status to word-initial [j] in English year or [w] in would, and that the rarity of roots with these onsets is a phonotactic gap rather than a categorical exclusion (nukopoli, 2024-11-28).
The dispute partly tracks the glottal-stop question.

On Nakagawa's no-glottal-stop analysis, vowel-initial syllables begin with a bare syllable boundary; a /y/-final coda abutting an /i/-initial syllable produces boundary-derived [ji] by resyllabification.

On the glottal-stop analysis (Hattori, Tamura), a contrast between /y/-onset and /ʔ/-onset is available at precisely those positions, which in principle licenses phonemic onset status for [ji], [wi], and [wu] (nukopoli, 2024-11-28); .
The glottal-stop debate is developed in .
The minimal pair yayráyke 'commit suicide' (three syllables, /yay.ray.ke/) vs.

yaírayke 'give thanks' (four syllables, /ya.i.ray.ke/) illustrates the practical stakes of syllabification at this juncture : the two words differ in syllable count and in whether the reflexive morpheme yay- is present, but neither read source provides acoustic data bearing on whether the i in yaírayke ever surfaces as [ji] in connected speech.

In the accent dialects — Saru, Chitose, and related varieties — the accentual contrast between fossilized and transparent compounds renders the question of /w/ phonemicity at hiatus redundant: pitch, not glide presence, carries the contrast.
In Shizunai (east Hidaka), an accentless dialect, this alternative is unavailable.
Okuda reports a minimal pair from a Shizunai speaker (Oda Steno) that is unique in the Hokkaido documentation:
suwat [suwat] and su'at [suʔat] are phonetically distinct.

In an accent dialect this contrast would be carried by pitch — the fossilized compound would have a fixed accent pattern differing from the transparent form; in Shizunai, where pitch is not distinctive, the glide vs. glottal-stop difference bears the entire lexical distinction.
Parallel contrasts for /y/ at front-vowel hiatus in Shizunai — /u'a/ ~ /uwa/, /i'o/ ~ /iyo/, /i'e/ ~ /iye/ — extend the argument beyond this single pair .
Okuda's conclusion: "one cannot say, without specifying the dialect, that the glides y/w are non-phonemic" ‹contested›.
The Shizunai data do not overturn the Nakagawa–Shiraishi analysis of Saru and Chitose, where accent carries the contrast the glide would otherwise mark.
They demonstrate that /y/ and /w/ phonemicity at hiatus is a dialect-dependent property: phonemic in accentless Shizunai, non-phonemic in the accent dialects ; .
For the classification of Shizunai as accentless and its implications, see .
The coda-consonant status of /y/ and /w/ has one further prosodic consequence.

When ku= or e= prefixes to a stem beginning with /i/ or /u/, vowel-weakening converts the vowel to a glide, producing a CVC-closed first syllable: ku= + ipe → ku=ype /kúype/ (σ1 = /kuy/, closed, Rule 1: accent on σ1) .
The derived coda /y/ is treated by the accent system in exactly the same way as root-internal coda /y/ in áynu.
The full treatment of vowel-weakening and person-prefix accent shifts is in and .
Hokkaido Ainu has a pitch-accent system in which the prominent syllable is marked by a pitch rise, not a pitch fall.

The theoretical distinction matters because Standard Japanese pitch accent is analysed as a falling nucleus (下り核) — the distinctive cue is where pitch drops — whereas Ainu has a rising nucleus (上り核アクセント) — the distinctive cue is where pitch rises from low to high ; .

A word's accent identity is therefore fixed by the syllable at which the L→H transition occurs; post-nuclear syllables may continue high, or fall at the utterance edge, without changing the word's accent class.
The contrast is illustrated by the near-minimal pair nísap 'suddenly' (accent on σ1) vs nisáp 'shin' (accent on σ2).

nísap can be produced with both syllables at high pitch (nísáp) without changing its identity, because the rising-nucleus cue is already satisfied at σ1; the same flat-high production of nisáp would be heard as 'suddenly', since the σ2-rise is missing .
The Ainu accent system thus records where pitch begins to be high; the Japanese system records where it ceases to be high.
Accent is marked in this grammar with an acute diacritic on the vowel of the prominent syllable: kamúy (accent on σ2), áynu (accent on σ1).
The same event is representable with a rise arrow: ka↗muy, ↗áynu.
In IPA, a high-tone mark (◌́) on the nucleus of the accented syllable expresses the same.

Community participants summarize the typological point concisely: ku↗a–ni and ku↗a↘ni are equivalent pronunciations of the first-person pronoun; ku↘ani is deviant (nukopoli, 2024-12-09; corroborated by ).
Accent marks appear in citation forms and interlinear examples throughout this grammar and are suppressed in running text.
The theoretical question of whether the system is better modelled as a culminative accent (one H per prosodic word) or as an autosegmental tonal melody (L…LH…) is examined in .
Intonation and sentence-level prosody are treated in .
The pitch-accent placement rules described in this chapter apply to the standard-accent dialects.
Hokkaido Ainu divides into three prosodic classes ; :
Nakagawa (2024: 49–50) includes Bihoro, Shizunai, and the eastern Hidaka localities (Samani, Urakawa) among the accentless varieties.

Refsing (1986: 73) had earlier classified Shizunai as an accent dialect with rules analogous to Saru; archival evidence — scattered accent marks from a single Shizunai speaker showing both nisáppone and nísappone for 'suddenly' — supports Nakagawa's accentless classification ‹contested›.
Unaccented varieties and the phonological consequences of accent loss are treated in .
In standard-accent dialects, the position of the accent depends entirely on the structure of σ1 — the first syllable of the prosodic word — regardless of total word length ; ; .
Two rules cover the system:
Rule 1: If σ1 is closed — i.e. has the shape (C)VC — σ1 bears the accent.
Rule 2: If σ1 is open — i.e. has the shape (C)V — σ2 bears the accent.
Shiraishi (2022: §5.1) recasts these as an iambic (LH) pattern: a light (open) first syllable predicts accent on σ2; a heavy (closed) first syllable predicts accent on σ1.
Kindaichi and Chiri reached the same characterization: "the iambic rule is dominant" (Kindaichi & Chiri 1936: 11, reported via ).
The rule is strictly local to σ1: no further syllable weight is consulted.
A word of any length whose first syllable is closed carries σ1-accent (yáykosiramsuypa, nine syllables but σ1 = yay [CVC] → σ1-accent); an open σ1 gives σ2-accent regardless of what follows .

In Yakumo, Rule 2 applies one syllable further rightward when both σ1 and σ2 are open: standard notákam corresponds to Yakumo notakám; standard sinúye to Yakumo sinuyé; standard hoyúpu to Yakumo hoyupú.
When σ2 is closed, Yakumo and standard dialects agree (parúnpe in both).
Some Yakumo forms are additionally exceptional (hopúni, osórusi) ; .
Accent placement in compounds and under person-marking prefixes, where the rules reapply over the enlarged prosodic word, is covered in .
The syllable shapes that feed these rules — closed vs open, and the consonant-status of coda -y and -w — are established in .

The phonetic realization of the accent in standard-accent dialects follows a consistent contour: syllables preceding the accent syllable are at low pitch; from the accent syllable onward pitch is high.
In connected speech a fall at the utterance boundary is typical, but this is a phrasal boundary effect and is not the cue that identifies the accent class.
What is contrastive is solely the location of the L→H transition ; .
For a two-syllable word with σ2-accent, such as kamúy [ka(L) ↗muy(H)], the first syllable is produced at a low pitch and the rise occurs at the onset of σ2.
For a word with σ1-accent, such as áynu [↗áy(H) nu(H or ↘)], the pitch is high from the start of the word.

The community characterization of the overall pattern — syllables before the nucleus are low; from the nucleus onward pitch stays high; a fall occurs toward the end of the prosodic phrase — contrasts with the Tokyo Japanese pattern in which the diagnostic event is a drop after the nucleus (nukopoli, 2024-12-09; corroborated by ) ‹corpus-suggested›.

In some northeastern dialects, the accented vowel is slightly lengthened, an observation that underlies earlier romanization conventions such as ユーカラ for yukar (accent on yu, hence formerly written with a long vowel: Nakagawa 2024: 26, reported via ).
Phonemic vowel length is not otherwise contrastive in Hokkaido Ainu; the vowel inventory is discussed in .
A set of words with open σ1 carry accent on σ1 despite the prediction of Rule 2 (open σ1 → σ2-accent).
These must be stored in the lexicon; they cannot be derived from the placement rule.
Nakagawa (2024: 51) lists the following as the principal exceptions in Saru/Chitose:

cápe 'cat', húci 'grandmother', húra 'smell', húre 'red', káni 'I (free pronoun)', kéra 'taste', míci 'father', mína 'laugh', nína 'gather firewood', nísap 'suddenly', núman 'yesterday', páse 'heavy', sápo 'elder sister', sések 'hot', síno 'really', sísam 'Japanese person', túki 'cup', túnas 'fast', úsey 'hot water', yúpo 'elder brother'.
Several exceptions pair minimally or near-minimally with regular-rule forms:

The exceptions are not random: each corresponds to a Sakhalin Ainu form with a long first vowel (see the following section), and as a group they reflect the older vowel-length contrast that has been restructured as lexical accent in Hokkaido.
A quantitative analysis of the exception set and its contrastive residue against the rule-conforming majority is given in .

Hokkaido Ainu pitch accent stands in a systematic correspondence with Sakhalin Ainu vowel length: a Hokkaido word with accent on σ1 (including exceptions to Rule 2) has a long vowel in σ1 in Sakhalin; a Hokkaido word with accent on σ2 (regular Rule 2 output) has a short vowel in σ1 in Sakhalin ; .
(SA forms from .)

Hattori (1967, reported via and ) interprets the Sakhalin vowel-length opposition as diachronically prior, with Hokkaido pitch accent having developed from it; the diachronic relationship is argued in detail by (not consulted directly).
Satō dissents on the direction of the change () ‹contested›.

The Hokkaido accentless varieties listed in the preceding section represent a third path: they have lost the length opposition without acquiring pitch contrast, and are not converging on the standard-accent system (Nakagawa & Fukazawa 2022 §3.1, reported via ).
Sakhalin vowel length and its relationship to the Hokkaido vowel inventory are discussed in .
Hokkaido Ainu has lexical pitch accent: the position of high pitch within a phonological word is specified in the lexicon and contrasts meaning.

Pitch is not assigned to every mora or syllable independently, as in a tone language; a single accent nucleus per word marks the site of the rising boundary, and syllables before it are uniformly low ; ; .
The system involves no lexical tone and no vowel reduction correlating with accent position .
All three primary sources for Hokkaido Ainu agree on this characterization ‹consensus›.

The surface output phonetically resembles Standard Japanese pitch accent — Tamura (1988b: 13) remarked on the similarity (reported via ) — but the two systems are organized in structurally opposite ways, as the next section sets out.

Within the pitch-accent type, the further question of whether the accent nucleus is best formalized as a feature of the syllable or of the mora is taken up in § Mora or syllable?; the question of whether the system could be described as a restricted tone or register system is addressed in § Accent versus tone.
Not every description has found the system.

Simeon, eliciting at dictation speed from rememberer-speakers in 1967, reported no minimal pairs for stress and tied primary prominence to the final syllable of his "contour" unit, leaving secondary stress unpredictable — this in Hiratori, the same dialect area where Tamura was concurrently documenting lexical accent contrasts of the nísap : nisáp type.

The discrepancy is best explained by method: list intonation in slow elicitation overwrites lexical pitch with phrase-level prominence, so the accent system is invisible unless connected speech or paradigmatic contrast is examined.
The episode is a standing caution for reading any pre-Tamura Western description of Ainu prosody ‹speculative›.
The decisive structural difference from Japanese is directional.
Standard Japanese is a falling-nucleus system (下り核): the nucleus marks the position after which pitch drops, and syllables up to and including the nucleus are high.

Hokkaido Ainu is a rising-nucleus system (上り核アクセント): the nucleus marks the onset of the accented syllable, the pitch rises at that point, and syllables following the nucleus remain high without further contrast .
The same asymmetry was recognized under the term 昇り核 'rising kernel' by Hattori (1961) and Tamura (1970), reported via .
The consequence is that sustaining or extending the post-accent high plateau does not change a word's identity, whereas shifting the pitch rise to a different syllable does.

The community illustration of this point is apt: the first-person pronoun kuáni may be produced with a flat high plateau after the rise (ku↗áni) or with a fall after the peak (ku↗á↘ni) without any change of meaning, but a fall before the accent (ku↘áni) is perceived as anomalous or contrastive (nukopoli, 2024-12-09; corroborated by ) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
In the minimal pair nísap 'suddenly' : nisáp 'shin', only the syllable at which the ↗ rise occurs differs; the high plateau that follows is common to both .

The accented vowel also tends to lengthen allophonically in polysyllables, particularly in north-eastern accent dialects — Kindaichi (1931: 4) noted forms such as ˈnuːman 'yesterday' and poˈroː 'big', describing the lengthening as "not conducted consciously" (reported via ).
This allophonic lengthening is distinct from the phonemic vowel length of Sakhalin Ainu (§ Diachrony below) and carries no accent-analytical implications.
Accent placement in the standard accent dialects (Saru, Chitose, and their neighbors) follows a two-rule system sensitive exclusively to the syllable structure of σ1 :
Only σ1's shape matters; word length beyond two syllables is irrelevant to placement.
Shiraishi reformulates the same pattern as an iambic (LH) foot: accent on σ2 when σ1 is light, on σ1 when σ1 is heavy — a weight-sensitive rhythmic pattern widespread across languages .
Kindaichi and Chiri (1936: 11) concluded from their materials that "the iambic rule is dominant" (reported via ).
A class of lexical exceptions breaks the default: when σ1 is open yet accent falls on σ1, the word must be memorized.

Nakagawa lists around twenty such items, including cápe 'cat', húci 'grandmother', húre 'red', kéra 'taste', míci 'father', mína 'laugh', nísap 'suddenly', páse 'heavy', sísam 'Japanese person', síno 'really', túki 'cup', túnas 'fast', and yúpo 'elder brother' .
These exceptions produce minimal accent pairs:
These pairs establish that accent position is phonemically contrastive and that the weight rule, though dominant, does not determine accent in the exception class.
The full inventory of such pairs is the subject of ; accent behavior under compounding and affixation is treated in .
In Japanese pitch accent the mora is the accent-bearing unit: a CVC syllable may, in principle, bear accent on either of its two moras.
For Hokkaido Ainu the evidence points to the syllable as the relevant domain.
Three observations converge on this conclusion.
First, the placement rule (§ above) is stated entirely in terms of whether σ1 is open or closed — syllable weight rather than mora count.
No sub-syllabic accent position within a CVC syllable is ever distinctive; all coda consonants (/p t k m n r s y w/) are equivalent in their weight-conferring effect.
Second, the phonetic realization — the pitch rise — is timed to the onset of the accented syllable, not to an internal mora boundary.

Third, the analysis of coda /-y/ and /-w/ as consonants rather than as the second element of a diphthong (argued independently in on morphological and phonotactic grounds) is consistent with syllable-based accent: ka.muy 'deity' (two syllables, σ2 = CVC) receives accent on σ2 as an undivided unit; there is no evidence that the internal /-y/ constitutes a separate accent-bearing mora ; .
Person-prefix accent shift provides additional evidence.
The prefixes ku=, e=, and ci= integrate with the stem as a single phonological word; the weight of σ1 in the new word is recalculated with the prefix included.
A stem whose open σ1 would otherwise take σ2 accent by 原則2 shifts its accent one syllable toward the word boundary ; :
The contrasting prefixes a= and eci= do not trigger the shift: omáre → a=omáre retains the stem's accent .
These two prefixes are prosodically less integrated with the stem, a gradient that parallels their position in the person-affix paradigm (see and ).

A moraic restatement of 原則1/2 is formally possible: a closed σ1 has two moras (CV + C), so accent could be described as associating with the second mora of the word — belonging to σ1 when σ1 is heavy, to σ2 when σ1 is light.
This restatement covers the same data but posits mora-counting that is not independently evidenced elsewhere in Ainu phonology.
The sources consulted do not argue for it: Shiraishi characterizes the pattern as iambic and syllable-based , and Nakagawa states the rule in syllable-structure terms ‹contested›.

The pitch-accent label is used in two overlapping senses in the Japanological tradition: as a cover term for any system in which pitch is phonemic, and in the narrower sense of a system with one positionally specified nucleus per word.
All three primary sources use it in the narrow sense as applied to Hokkaido Ainu.
Pre-nuclear syllables are uniformly low; post-nuclear syllables are uniformly high; no syllable-by-syllable tonal specification is posited.
Ainu is not a tone language in the cross-linguistic typological sense ‹consensus›.
Two analytical positions on the structure of the exception class merit explicit grading.
Position A — gradient weight-sensitive accent with a lexical exception class ‹consensus›.
The system is weight-sensitive iambic accent; the exception class is a bounded set of forms with lexically specified initial accent.
The default rule accounts for the vast majority of the lexicon; exceptions must be memorized individually.
This is the position of Nakagawa , Shiraishi , and Satō , as well as Kindaichi and Chiri (1936: 11) (reported via ).
Position B — two prosodic word-classes ‹speculative›.

The exception class (open σ1, initial accent) and the default class (weight-conditioned accent) could be reframed as two lexical register classes: Class I words carry a lexical feature placing accent on σ1 regardless of weight; Class II words are unspecified and realize weight-determined accent.
This account is structurally parallel to two-register systems described for some East Japanese and Ryukyuan pitch-accent varieties.

The Sakhalin vowel-length correspondence (§ Diachrony below) supplies a diachronic motive: the HA exception class corresponds systematically to SA long-vowel forms, suggesting the two HA classes may reflect a former segmental length distinction rather than a discrete tonal specification.
This reanalysis has not been proposed in the sources consulted; the synchronic data do not require it; it is noted here as a possible alternative formalization ‹speculative›.
Community discussion noted a phonetic resemblance between Hachijō-language intonation and Ainu pitch contours (nukopoli, 2024-12-08).

No systematic published comparison of the two systems has been consulted here; the significance of any resemblance — intonational, accentual, or areal — cannot be assessed from the sources consulted ‹speculative›.
Not all Hokkaido varieties have contrastive pitch.
Nakagawa and Fukazawa classify Hokkaido dialects into three prosodic types ; :

The irregular accent of Yakumo shifts the iambic peak one position right when both σ1 and σ2 are open: compare Yakumo notakám vs Saru notákam, Yakumo sinuyé vs Saru sinúye, Yakumo hoyupú vs Saru hoyúpu; but when σ2 is closed both varieties agree: parúnpe in both ; .
The accentless status of Shizunai is contested.
Refsing (1986: 73) treated it as an accent dialect with rules parallel to Saru .

Nakagawa argues from museum-archive recordings that the same word appears in both accent patterns across tokens from one speaker — nisáppone five times vs nísappone twice — and reads this as accent-neutralization, not a stable system ‹contested›.

One phonological consequence of Shizunai's accentless status: the contrast between glide [w] and glottal stop [ʔ] at a hiatus position must carry the functional load that pitch contrast carries elsewhere, as argued for the pair suwat 'pothook' vs suʔat 'pot bail' in ; see .
The accentless dialects differ in their accentless origin.
Bihoro, Kushiro, and Shiranuka lost the pitch contrast without a compensatory change.
Sakhalin Ainu is also accentless but preserves a vowel-length opposition where Hokkaido developed pitch; neither opposition has neutralized in Sakhalin .
Dialect-level consonant features that intersect with accent — including eastern h-elision when accent falls on σ2 — are treated in .

The correspondence between HA accent class and SA vowel length runs through the lexicon systematically: HA exception-class words (open σ1, initial accent despite the weight rule) correspond to SA long-vowel forms; HA regular-class words (weight-conditioned accent) correspond to SA short-vowel forms ; :

Hattori (1967) reconstructed vowel length as the earlier contrast: Proto-Ainu had a long-vowel/short-vowel distinction, Hokkaido replaced it with accent while Sakhalin retained length (reported via ; ).
On this account the HA exception class reflects historically long syllables; the weight-conditioned default (原則2) is a Hokkaido innovation.
Satō dissents on the directionality in his contribution to the Handbook (reported via ) ‹contested›.

Itabashi (2001) argues the length–pitch diachrony in detail ; that study was not consulted directly for this grammar and the claims attributed to it here rest on its treatment in Nakagawa (2024) and Nakagawa and Fukazawa (2022).

The correspondence also supplies diachronic motivation for Position B (§ above): if the HA exception class reflects historically long vowels rather than a distinct tonal category, then the two HA accent classes may be the synchronic residue of a former segmental opposition rather than evidence of a register system in Proto-Ainu.
Whether this warrants a formal two-class reconstruction is a question for the comparative work in and ‹speculative›.
The placement rules of the accent dialects — if σ1 is closed (CVC), σ1 bears high pitch; if σ1 is open (CV), σ2 bears high pitch — assign accent to the large majority of the Hokkaido Ainu lexicon .
Shiraishi terms this the iambic (LH) pattern: words with a heavy (closed) first syllable are trochaic in accent, and words with a light (open) first syllable are iambic .
The full statement of these rules and their interaction with syllable weight is the subject of .
The rules leave a residue of words with open σ1 that are accented on σ1 against the prediction.
These carry lexically stored accent and must be individually memorized.

lists roughly twenty such items: cápe 'cat', húci 'grandmother', húra 'smell', húre 'red', káni 'I (emphatic)', kéra 'taste', míci 'father', mína 'laugh', nína 'gather firewood', nísap 'suddenly', núman 'yesterday', páse 'heavy', sápo 'elder sister', sések 'hot', síno 'really', sísam 'Japanese person', túki 'cup', túnas 'fast', úsey 'hot water', yúpo 'elder brother', and further items beyond the list given there.
Every word in the accent dialects is either rule-assigned or lexically specified; there is no third status.
The person-marking prefixes ku=, e=, and ci= are incorporated into the prosodic word and can shift accent relative to its base; a= and eci= do not trigger a shift.
Compounds suppress the accent of all but the initial element.
These morphological and compositional effects on accent placement are treated in and, for the person-affix interaction, in .
The exception-list words create lexical contrasts wherever a segmentally identical (or near-identical) word follows the regular rule.
Three such pairs are established in the descriptive literature ; :
In each pair, form A carries lexical exception accent on σ1 and form B is rule-derived with σ2 accent.
The critical phonetic property is the rising nucleus (上り核アクセント): what is distinctive is where the pitch ↗ rises, not where it subsequently falls.
A word accented on σ1 begins with high pitch and may remain high throughout with no change of meaning, because the system encodes the onset of the high span.
A word accented on σ2 requires a ↗ rise at σ2; pronouncing it with an σ1-initial high instead misidentifies it as the σ1-accented form .
This stands in contrast with Standard Japanese, whose falling nucleus (下り核アクセント) marks the syllable after which pitch drops .

A community observation from the Saru dialect captures the asymmetry: the pronouns ku↗ani and ku↗a↘ni are both acceptable, but ku↘ani (Japanese-style falling nucleus) is perceived as deviant — the rise position, not the fall, is what matters ‹corpus-confirmed›
The nísap : nisáp pair also has a diachronic dimension.
Sakhalin Ainu preserves vowel-length distinctions in exactly the positions where Hokkaido Ainu carries an accent distinction:
The long Sakhalin vowel occupies the syllable that carries initial accent in the Hokkaido exception word; the short Sakhalin vowel corresponds to the Hokkaido rule-derived form.

This correspondence underpins the reconstruction of a proto-system in which these syllables were prosodically marked — by vowel quantity, retained in Sakhalin and restructured as pitch in Hokkaido ; .
The direction of that change and whether the ancestral contrast was quantity-based or pitch-based remain disputed ‹contested›
The SA–HA length–pitch correspondence independently confirms that the three minimal pairs above represent genuine lexical contrasts.
The contrastive yield of the accent system is limited.
The placement rules account for the large majority of the lexicon; the exception list is closed and memorizable rather than an open accidental class.

The three pairs documented above appear to constitute the best-established minimal/near-minimal set in the literature; acknowledges the list to be incomplete, which implies further near-minimal contrasts in principle — any exception word whose segmental shape matches a rule-derived word — but such additional pairs are not systematically tabulated in the available sources.
Lexical disambiguation relies primarily on morphosyntactic context, and the segmental form alone resolves ambiguity in most encounters.
The typological character that emerges is a pitch-accent system with a predominantly predictable accent assignment and a limited lexically stored residue.
The formal typology of rising versus falling nuclei and the mora-syllable question are treated in .
The contrastive relevance of accent varies across dialects.
In Shizunai, Urakawa, Samani, Bihoro, Kushiro, and Shiranuka, pitch placement is not phonemically distinctive ; , and the three contrasts above are neutralized.

Whether Shizunai should be classified alongside the accent dialects — the position of — or treated as accentless, as argues on the basis of variable archival transcriptions, has not been settled ‹contested›.
The practical consequence is that the minimal pairs in this chapter are attributes of the Saru-type accent system and cannot be assumed for the accentless eastern and southeastern varieties.
The dialect typology is addressed in .
The Yakumo and Oshamambe varieties retain pitch distinctiveness but apply a rightward-shifted rule: when both σ1 and σ2 are open, accent falls on σ3 rather than σ2 ; .

Forms that contrast in Saru by the exception-versus-rule distinction may therefore pattern differently in Yakumo, since their accent is calculated from a shifted baseline — Saru notákam corresponds to Yakumo notakám, and Saru sinúye to Yakumo sinuyé ().
Whether the Yakumo rule interacts with the exception list in the same way as the Saru rule — and so whether the same minimal pairs surface in Yakumo — is not addressed in the available sources.
The Yakumo system is described in .
Loanwords are adapted to the Hokkaido Ainu (C)V(C) syllable canon — consonant-cluster repair, epenthesis, and syllable-boundary insertion — before entering the phonological system, as described in .
