Once adapted, they are in principle subject to the same placement rules as native words.

The Japanese borrowing tampaku 'tobacco' has its initial syllable closed by coda -m and would receive σ1 accent by 原則1 (támpaku); the Russian-origin form potoloko 'ceiling' begins with open σ1 and would receive σ2 accent by 原則2 (potóloko).

Neither nor states a loan-specific accent rule, and the application of the placement rules to adapted loanforms is an inference from the general description of the system rather than a directly documented observation.
Whether any loanword has joined the exception list with lexically stored non-rule accent is unattested in the available sources.
A community discussion observed a potential tension with the compound kamuynomi 'prayer ceremony' (kamúy + nomí → kamúynomi by first-element priority, ).
The Ainu accent on the first element is expected; the observation concerned the different prosodic placement that this term acquires when it is borrowed into Japanese-language usage ‹speculative›
That is a property of the borrowing in its receiving language.
Within Ainu, kamuynomi follows the first-element-priority pattern of all compounds, detailed in .
For reduplicated forms, direct evidence from phonetically transcribed accent-dialect texts is sparse.

A community observation reports that somósomo — the reduplicated form of somó 'even, also' — functions as a single prosodic word accented on σ2, matching the base, and that the two-word string ka somó ki 'even … too' assigns accent on the base word independently ‹speculative›

The pattern is consistent with first-element priority — in full reduplication the first copy retains its accent and the echo copy is de-accented — but primary-source confirmation from the phonetically transcribed descriptive literature is lacking.
The prosodic-word domain and its role in accent assignment are treated in .
In all standard-accent dialects of Hokkaido Ainu, high pitch is assigned to σ1 when σ1 is closed (has a coda), and to σ2 otherwise — with a memorized set of lexical exceptions (see ).

These rules evaluate the prosodic word as their domain: a prefix or compounding element that fuses with a base creates a new prosodic word, and the placement rules are reapplied from the new left edge ; ; .
Prefixation may therefore shift accent inward, and compounding suppresses all accent peaks after the first.
Affixes divide accordingly: those that enter the prosodic word of their base shift its accent; those that remain outside it leave the base accent intact.
The accent data thereby provide one of the clearest phonological diagnostics for the prefix/clitic boundary in the person-affix paradigm.

The Yakumo irregular system, where 原則2 shifts one position further right, produces different surface outputs for the same derivations but applies the same prosodic-word logic; its characterization is given in .
When two or more free forms combine as a compound noun, the result carries a single accent peak.
states the general outcome as a first-element priority rule: only the front element's lexical accent survives; all syllables belonging to rear elements are low.
For a polysyllabic front element, the accent it bears in isolation — as assigned by the placement rules to that element's own σ1 — is retained unchanged.
The accent positions follow from the placement rules applied to the front element in isolation.
kamúy has open σ1 (ka) → 原則2 → accent on σ2 mú; that accent is the sole high syllable of kamúynomi.
hórka has closed σ1 (hor) → 原則1 → accent on hór; that accent survives in hórkareyep.
The monosyllabic ni carries the single available accent, giving nítek.
For cisékorkur and kotánkorkur, the community reports that both are single words with the front-element accent as their sole peak (nukopoli 2024-12-09) ‹corpus-suggested›.

The assignments follow from the principle: cise 'house' has open σ1 (ci) → 原則2 → accent on sé, which becomes the sole peak of cisékorkur 'householder'; kotan 'village' has open σ1 (ko) → 原則2 → accent on tán, retained in kotánkorkur 'village chief'.
The first-element priority is a strong default.

notes a set of lexicalized compound nouns that carry the iambic pattern even when the front element's isolated accent would predict otherwise: hasínaw, cepétu 'fish snout', nayétok 'stream source' all show accent on σ2 of the compound, as if the form were an underived disyllabic root.
These represent lexicalized items requiring per-form verification ‹contested›.
The prosodic-unit question (mora vs syllable) bearing on the weight analysis is addressed in ; attested minimal-pair contrasts in compound accent are listed in .
The negative adverb illustrates the prosodic-word boundary transparently.
As an independent word, somo has open σ1 (so) and thus accent on σ2 by 原則2: somó.
This is its accent in phrases such as ka somó ki 'does not do even', where somo is a separate prosodic word.

When doubled to form the intensified negation somosomo 'not at all, definitely not', the pair becomes a single prosodic word: only the front element's accent survives, giving somósomo with a single high syllable on mó (nukopoli 2024-12-09) ‹corpus-suggested›.
The contrast ka somó ki (two prosodic words) versus somósomo (one prosodic word) instantiates the same mechanism as the compound table above.
The negation system and are treated in .
The reflexive prefix always opens the prosodic word as σ1.
yay is a closed syllable (CVC), so 原則1 places the accent on σ1 — on yáy — regardless of the shape of the following stem .
The published example is yáykoytak 'talk to oneself' (< yay-ko-itak).

The community additionally reports yáyesiru 'concentrate (on oneself)' as a further illustration that yáy holds the accent whether the following syllable is consonant-initial or vowel-initial (nukopoli 2024-11-10, attributed to ).
Lexicalized yay- derivatives may deviate and require per-form verification.
The distribution of yay- and the co-reflexive si- in Chitose is examined in ; the morphosyntax of both reflexive prefixes is set out in .
The applicative prefixes , , and open the prosodic word as a light (CV) σ1 when they attach to a base ; .
Because σ1 is open, 原則2 shifts the accent to σ2 of the new prosodic word, which is the σ1 of the original base.
The result is that prefixation moves the high syllable one position earlier in the string compared with the free base.
In ekótanne, the prefix e- creates a new light σ1 → 原則2 → accent on σ2 (kó).
The free word kotán accents σ2 (tán) by the same rule; in the applicative form the high syllable has moved one position to the left.
The ekótanne example is a community extrapolation from the general one-word analysis of applicative-prefixed forms (nukopoli 2024-11-10), consistent with the published epúni ‹corpus-suggested›.
The morphology and syntax of the applicative prefixes are treated in .
Derivational suffixes generally do not displace accent in Hokkaido Ainu .
The causative suffixes -re, -te, -e attached to monosyllabic bases retain the base accent: e → ére; ku → kúre; kar → káre.
The verb koré 'give' is a well-attested departure.
A regular causative derivation from kor 'have' + -e would yield *kóre (σ1 kor = CVC → 原則1 → σ1 accented); the attested form is koré, with accent on σ2 ; .

Nakagawa's account is that the morpheme boundary between kor and -e has eroded sufficiently for the form to be treated as a monomorphemic disyllabic root, whereupon σ1 ko is open → 原則2 → accent on ré.
The community proposes alternatively that koré is a phonological contraction of korpare 'give to someone', which independently yields σ2 accent (nukopoli 2024-12-26) ‹contested›.
Both accounts predict the same surface accentuation; the accent koré is attested in the Saru corpus:
The person-marking prefixes ku= (1SG agent/subject), e= (2SG), and ci= (inclusive 1PL) form a single prosodic word with their base ; ; .
Each prefix contributes a light (CV) σ1; 原則2 applies and the accent falls on σ2 of the new word — one position earlier than the base accent when the base's own σ1 was open:

In each case the base has open σ1 and accents σ2; after the CV prefix is added, σ1 of the new prosodic word is the prefix itself (open) and σ2 — which is the original σ1 of the base — receives the high pitch.
In Saru and Chitose, ku= and ci= additionally lose their vowel before a base-initial vowel other than i.
The conditions for this vowel deletion are described in and .
The accent shift precedes deletion, so the shifted accent survives in the contracted surface form: ku= + omáre → accent shift → ku=ómáre → vowel deletion → k=ómare; ci= + etú → c=étu .
Before a base-initial i, vowel deletion is blocked and glide formation (i → y) substitutes; the accent shift still applies: ku=ipe → ku=ýpe / kúype.
When the base-initial i is in a closed syllable, glide formation is itself blocked by the phonotactic constraint against CCC clusters: ku= + inkar → ku=ínkar with no glide and accent on σ2 .
The 1SG object prefix en= behaves analogously: it opens the prosodic word as a closed σ1 (en, CVC), so 原則1 places the accent on σ1.
In Nakagawa's textbook the phrase wa én=kore shows the accent on én, consistent with this rule (nukopoli 2024-11-10, attributed to ) ‹corpus-suggested›.
The indefinite-person prefix a= and the 2PL prefix eci= leave the accent of the base unchanged ; ; .
They attach outside the prosodic word of the stem:
a= and eci= also do not trigger the vowel contraction that the shifting prefixes undergo in Saru and Chitose after the accent shift.
The combined phonological evidence — no shift, no contraction — aligns with the morphosyntactic assessment in that a= and eci= are prosodic clitics, while ku=, e=, ci=, and en= are prefixes proper.
The position-class arrangement of person affixes in the verb word is set out in .
When a personal-number suffix (=an, =as) attaches to a vowel-final verb stem, the suffix carries a secondary (lower-level) accent alongside the primary stem accent .
The verb iruska 'be angry' with the plural suffix gives irúska=àn (primary accent á on rú, secondary accent à on àn); ipe 'eat' with =an gives ipé=àn.

When the stem ends in a consonant, the secondary accent on the suffix is lost: cis=an 'we cry' and sap=an 'we go out' carry only the primary accent on σ1 (both stems have closed σ1 → 原則1) with no secondary peak on =an .
The number-suffix paradigm is described in and .

The plural suffix -pa and the affiliative (possessed) suffix -hV — realizing as -hi, -he, -ha etc. according to the vowel-copy rule — are both accent-neutral: the stem's placement-rule accent survives into the suffixed form without adjustment ; .
They attach outside the prosodic word of the stem and do not produce the reapplication that the prefixal and applicative morphology triggers.
The morphophonology of the affiliative suffix and the echo-vowel alternation are treated in .
The accent patterns reviewed in this chapter offer a phonological diagnostic for grammatical category that is independent of morphological segmentation.

A morpheme that enters the prosodic word of its host and shifts the accent is a prefix in the prosodic sense; a morpheme that leaves the host accent untouched is a clitic or a non-incorporating suffix.
Applied to the Hokkaido Ainu person-affix paradigm, the test produces: prefixes — ku=, e=, ci=, en=; clitics — a=, eci= ; .
The same prosodic-word criterion distinguishes compound-internal structure (a single prosodic word, one accent peak) from phrasal juxtaposition (two prosodic words with independent accent peaks).
The compound formation discussed here and the sandhi processes of Part V share the same domain boundary.

Coda assimilation (r+t→tt, n+s→ys, etc.) applies most consistently within the prosodic word; the accent test provides an independent means of determining which phonological domain a given morpheme occupies before examining the assimilation data.
These interactions are taken up in and .
The underlying prosodic unit and the weight analysis are addressed in .

Hokkaido Ainu has a pitch-accent system in which the phonologically distinctive unit is the syllable at which F0 rises — a rising-nucleus (上り核アクセント) system — in contrast with Standard Japanese, whose falling-nucleus system marks the syllable at which F0 subsequently drops ; .

The word-level placement rules for the accent nucleus are stated in ; the theoretical question of whether the system is best analysed as culminative accent or as an autosegmental tonal melody is addressed in .

The rising-nucleus property means that F0 may remain high or drop after the accented syllable without changing the lexical identity of a word — only the position of the rise is phonologically distinctive.

For the Saru minimal pair nísap 'suddenly' vs nisáp 'shin', nísap may be realized with sustained high pitch on both syllables (nísáp) without shifting to nisáp; only a realization in which the lowest F0 point falls at σ1 would misidentify the word .

Community discussion illustrates the same point with the pronoun ku=ani 'I', whose accent falls on á (σ2, by regular rule): ku↗ani and ku↗a↘ni are both acceptable; ku↘ani, with the F0 minimum at the accented syllable, is not (nukopoli, 2024-12-09).
(; .) Words in the exception class — which includes nísap, nína, húre 'red', sísam 'Japanese person', and a score of others — have σ1 open (CV) yet accent σ1 instead of the regular σ2.
Their Sakhalin cognates show a corresponding long vowel at σ1: ‹SA›
niisah vs nisah, huure, siisam (Nakagawa 2024: 27, 51).
The diachronic relationship between Hokkaido accent and Sakhalin vowel length is discussed in ; additional minimal pairs are catalogued in .
The accented syllable is slightly lengthened in polysyllabic words, more markedly in north-eastern dialects (Asai 1972/1976, reported via ).
This allophonic lengthening explains older Japanese-script representations such as ユーカラ for yukar, where the long vowel corresponds to the accent on σ1 .
Lexically contrastive pitch is found only in the accent dialects.

Nakagawa and Fukazawa distinguish three prosodic classes: the standard-accent dialects (Saru, Chitose, Horobetsu, Asahikawa, Nayoro, Obihiro, Sōya), the irregular-accent dialects (Yakumo, Oshamambe, where the accent shifts one syllable rightward when both σ1 and σ2 are open), and the unaccented (無アクセント) varieties (Shizunai, Urakawa, Samani, Bihoro, Kushiro, Shiranuka), in which pitch is not lexically distinctive .
The dialect classification is treated in .
The utterance-intonation descriptions below rest on data from Saru and, to a lesser extent, Chitose; their applicability to the unaccented varieties is undocumented.

In Saru declarative utterances, F0 follows a natural declining course from the beginning to the end of the utterance, without a sentence-final intonation gesture — neither a terminal rise nor a marked fall (Tamura 1996: 4, reported via ).
Acoustic measurements on Saru speech confirm this pattern (Tamura and Motohashi 2002b; Makarova 2002, both reported via ).
Within this declination, the successive rising-nucleus accents of individual words produce a series of local F0 elevations against a gradually lowering baseline.

Simeon (1968, reported via ) characterizes the prosodic status of non-final clause boundaries in Ainu: a level or falling contour signals that the utterance is not yet complete and more follows, while a rising terminal marks the utterance as prosodically finished.

Under this description the default Saru declarative — ending with gradual declination but no added terminal gesture — has the profile of a continuation contour, and a clause that ends with a terminal rise (as in a polar interrogative or an exclamatory utterance) is the marked, utterance-final form.
Polar interrogatives in Saru carry a rising final intonation, with the F0 and intensity peak localized on the sentence-final particle.
An acoustic study of 35 Saru interrogative utterances found that the peak falls on the last word, normally one of the interrogative particles hawe, ya, a, or he (Makarova 2002, reported via ).

Tamura's Saru description extends the rising pattern to any utterance in which the speaker expects a reaction — a question, a report from the listener, a request, or an invitation (Tamura 1996: 4, reported via ).
The sentence-final particles themselves are described in ; interrogative strategies and the question particles are treated in .
One exception: the particle ya appears to select a falling rather than a rising contour in some Saru data.
A form transcribed as amkir_a (from amkir ya 'have you been?') was realized with falling pitch at the utterance end (Tamura and Motohashi 2002b, reported via ).

A contact explanation is plausible: Hokkaido Japanese uses falling intonation even in yes/no questions, and this influence has been suggested for some falling interrogative realizations in Ainu ‹contested›.
Whether the falling realization of ya-questions is a property of the particle, a speaker variable, or a contact phenomenon is not settled on current evidence.
A further contour type is documented when the sentence ends in a nominalized or conjunctive form without a final predicate verb.
In such cases the final F0 is level or falling, and the utterance communicates incompleteness or a request for confirmation rather than a settled assertion (, drawing on Tokachi data).
This aligns with the Simeon generalization noted above: absence of a terminal rise leaves the utterance prosodically open.

Exclamatory and optative utterances in Saru are produced at a pitch level elevated above the normal declarative baseline throughout, with the final syllable or syllables carrying a lengthened rise-fall (Tamura 1996: 4, reported via ).
The elevation is applied to the whole utterance, not only to the final position, so it interacts with the lexical accents of each word without displacing them.
The following Chitose example, drawn from Nakagawa's grammar, illustrates the construction:
The same elevated-register pattern extends to optative and invitation utterances, which share the whole-utterance F0 raise without necessarily carrying the lengthened final gesture.

No published instrumental study addresses intermediate prosodic phrasing in Hokkaido Ainu — the question of whether there are prosodic phrase boundaries between the word and the full utterance at which F0 resets, phrase-final lengthening occurs, or pauses are inserted systematically.
The available descriptions treat the utterance as the domain of F0 declination and the prosodic word as the domain of accent.
Two word-level prosodic facts bear on this question.
First, the person-affix paradigm distinguishes clitics by their degree of prosodic integration with the following stem.

Affixes ku=, e=, and ci= form a single prosodic word with their host and shift the stem's accent; a= and eci= do not shift accent and are prosodically less integrated (Kindaichi 1931; Tamura 1970, both reported via ; ).
This clitic-class distinction is treated in and ; it constitutes a gradient of prosodic bonding that may correlate with phrase-boundary placement in connected speech.

Second, personal suffixes such as =as (exclusive 1pl) and =an (4th person S) carry a secondary accent alongside the primary stem accent in open-syllable stems: iˈruska=ˌas 'we (excl.) are angry', ipˈe=ˌan (Kindaichi 1931; Tamura 1970, reported via ).
The secondary accent is lost when the stem ends in a closed syllable: ˈcis=an 'we cry', ˈsap=an.
The prosodic word template and the suffix interactions are treated in .
Community discussion of Ainu prosody has noted that the intonation patterns of Hachijō-shima Japanese feel "very close to Ainu" ( nukopoli, 2024-12-08).

Hachijō Japanese is known from the Japanese dialectological literature to have a rising-nucleus pitch-accent system, making it structurally parallel to the Hokkaido Ainu standard-accent dialects and distinct from the falling-nucleus system of Standard Japanese.

The perceived intonational resemblance is therefore typologically plausible — both languages share the consequence that the declarative default involves gradual F0 decline without a marked terminal gesture, and that interrogative intonation involves a terminal rise — but no published comparative acoustic study of Hachijō and Ainu intonation has been consulted for this grammar.
The observation is reported here at community grade: asserted and typologically grounded, but awaiting instrumental verification ‹corpus-suggested›.
Hokkaido Ainu has two intersecting regressive assimilation systems operating across morpheme, compound, and word junctures: coda /r/-sandhi and coda /n/-sandhi.
In /r/-sandhi, the coda /r/ of one morpheme is deleted and the following consonant geminates; /r/ is thereby the most morphophonologically productive segment in the language ; ; .

Independently, the coda nasal /n/ undergoes two distinct processes: it assimilates in place of articulation to a following labial or velar (an allophonic rule), and before following continuants /s/, /y/, and /w/ it triggers a morphophonological change — /n/-sandhi proper — which is more restricted in domain than /r/-sandhi ; .
A third, dialect-specific set of cluster simplifications is attested in eastern varieties, most prominently Bihoro, but Nakagawa (2024: 36) treats these as historically fixed rather than productive .
All rules described here are regressive: the coda segment adapts to the following onset.
None are notated in the standard romanization orthography, which writes underlying forms (ran wa, not ram ma); both sandhi types are nonetheless fully productive in speech .
The phoneme /r/ and its coda release are described in ; glide insertion at vowel hiatus is treated in ; the interaction of these rules with personal-affix clitics is treated in .
When a /r/-final morpheme immediately precedes a consonant-initial morpheme, the coda /r/ is deleted and the following consonant is lengthened, yielding a surface geminate.

The rule applies word-internally, at compound boundaries, and across word boundaries; it is not blocked by pauses within an utterance, and it crosses sentence boundaries without restriction (§4.1 below) ; .

Shiraishi (2022: §6.1), drawing on Shiraishi (2001), characterizes the trigger consonants as the coronal class — /n/, /c/, /t/, /r/ — with /s/ and /y/ also attested as triggers in northern dialects (Chiri 1956: 343, cited in ).
The assimilation can thus be stated as:
/r/ → C / _C[+coronal, ≠r]: the coda rhotic is deleted before a following coronal onset, which then geminates.
The earliest firsthand field record of this rule set is Simeon's 1967 survey of Hiratori, Horobetsu, and Higashi-Shizunai .

Working from citation forms with echo vowels (oara, koro, kuru, asiri), he states the same alternations — oat tuye 'he cut completely', ot teeta 'very ancient times', kon nispa 'my master', an kun ne 'it is a man', asin-no 'newly', and dissimilated ku kot cise 'my house'.

Two of his observations add texture the modern sources lack: the rules were mandatory in Higashi-Shizunai but optional in Hiratori and Horobetsu, where the unassimilated base form was the preferred variant; and his Hiratori informant — Kayano Shigeru — judged the assimilated variants "indicative of an older form of speech".
Both points suggest that by the 1960s the sandhi was receding in the Saru valley as a live process while remaining categorical further east ‹speculative›.
The sequence /r/+/r/ does not geminate to [rr] but dissimilates: the coda /r/ surfaces as [n] before a following rhotic onset.
Nakagawa (2024: 35) identifies ku=kor rusuy 'I want it' → [kukonrusuy] as the only published Hokkaido example of this dissimilation.
The complementary statement alongside the assimilation rule is:
/r/ → n / _r (dissimilation — avoidance of adjacent rhotics at syllable margins).
This dissimilatory outcome is the single exception within the /r/-sandhi system; all other coronal triggers yield total assimilation.
The derivations below move from underlying (orthographic) representations to surface phonetic forms.
Boundaries: = marks clitic attachment, space marks word boundary.
The coda nasal /n/ assimilates in place of articulation to a following labial or velar consonant: it surfaces as [m] before /p/ and /m/, and as [ŋ] before /k/.
These are allophonic realizations fully predictable from the following context.
The coda /m/ does not undergo velar assimilation before /k/ and remains [m] in that environment ; .
The orthography consistently writes /n/ in all environments (an=pe, hon=kor, hanku), never the allophonic surface values [m] or [ŋ].
Nakagawa (2024: 30) and Shiraishi (2022: §3) both treat [m], [n], [ŋ] as allophonic realizations of the two phonemes /m/ and /n/, with /n/ conditioned by the following consonant and /m/ invariant.
Whether /n/ and /m/ are phonemically neutralized before labials is a point of orthographic debate.
Forms such as matanpus ~ matampus are written with /n/ or /m/ before /p/ depending on the source; no consensus across dictionaries and authors has been established ‹contested›
The loanword kampi 'paper' (from Japanese kami) raises the same issue: an etymological kanpi versus a phonetically assimilated kampi (nukopoli, 2024-11-16) ‹contested›.

Before the [+continuant] consonants /s/, /y/, and /w/, a coda /n/ does not assimilate in place but is replaced by a glide or deleted: before /s/ and /y/ it surfaces as [j] (romanized y), yielding an apparent geminate with the following continuant; before /w/ the nasal is deleted and only /w/ remains.

Shiraishi (2022: §6.1), following Shiraishi (2001), characterizes the trigger class as the continuants and describes n-sandhi as the spread of the feature [+continuant] from the following onset onto the preceding coda.
The formal statement is:
The coda /m/ does not undergo this rule.

The form homsu (from hom-su) surfaces as [homsu], not *[hoysu], confirming that n-sandhi targets /n/ specifically and not the broader nasal class; /m/ and /n/ feed different morphophonological processes before continuants ‹corpus-suggested›
The /n/+/s/ output [js] — written as y in poy seta — behaves phonologically as a coda /y/ in the resulting syllable.
/r/-sandhi and /n/-sandhi share a regressive direction and a similar output structure (gemination or deletion), but they differ fundamentally in the phonological domain over which they apply.

Shiraishi (2022: §6.2), reporting on Shiraishi (2001), places /n/-sandhi within the prosodic phrase: it applies phrase-internally but never crosses a sentence boundary. /r/-sandhi carries no such restriction — it is a pure phonological rule that applies across all junctures including sentence boundaries.
The community independently observed this asymmetry: "r-連声は文境界を跨げるが n-連声は跨げない" (r-liaison crosses sentence boundaries; n-liaison does not) ‹corpus-confirmed›
(antitwilight, 2024-11-23).

The same contributor notes an account of n-sandhi's locality: because n-sandhi is mediated by nasalization in the coda, the sentence boundary disrupts the conditioning context, making the restriction predictable from the mechanism.
The formulation in Shiraishi (2022: §6.2) frames this as a distinction between a P-structure (phrase-internal) rule and a pure phonological (domain-free) rule.

The practical consequence is that inter-phrase /n/ sequences may or may not undergo sandhi depending on whether a phrase boundary intervenes, while /r/ sequences at any juncture assimilate in fluent speech regardless.
Neither alternation appears in the standard romanization .
Several Hokkaido Ainu lexical items preserve a sandhi output as their current lexical form, the underlying source either obsolete or reconstructed.
The best-documented case is .

The proto-form is reconstructed as at-rus; the Saru dialect attests an intermediate form ahrus (reflecting lenition rather than full assimilation); the general Hokkaido form attus reflects the lexicalization of /r/+/s/ → [ss] sandhi at the compound boundary (nukopoli, 2024-12-26) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

The word attus is attested 24 times in the corpus across multiple narrators and collections (小松哲郎, 神崎雅好, 相原典明, アイヌタイムズ; 平賀さだも, 平取町アイヌ口承文芸), confirming that the geminated form is the current lexical norm throughout Hokkaido.

A second piece of evidence for the productivity of /r/+/t/ → [tt] comes from a VITS-based Ainu TTS system: the model independently surfaced the sequence mosir ta 'land' + locative as [mositta] in generated speech, apparently learning the assimilation from training data without explicit phonological rules ‹corpus-suggested›
This anecdotal ML observation does not add to the primary-source evidence for the rule — established in and — but illustrates how pervasive /r/-sandhi is in connected-speech corpora.
Among other compound-boundary cases, ar suy 'once more' surfaces as [assuy] via /r/+/s/ → [ss]; retar cikap 'swan' surfaces as [retat̚cikap] via /r/+/c/ → [t̚c].
The compound-internal t+i → ci rule — illustrated by mat-ikor → macikor — is the one sandhi rule that applies without exception in all Hokkaido dialects and is treated in .

Additional lexicalized forms noted by the community include ketketcep (reconstructed from *ket~ket-se-pe) and nisatcawot (from nisat-sawot), both showing /t/+/s/ → [tc] assimilation at compound junctures ‹speculative›
(antitwilight, 2025-11-03).

Nakagawa & Fukazawa (2022: §3.3) document cluster simplifications in the Bihoro dialect — and to varying degrees in Obihiro, Kushiro, Asahikawa, and Nayoro — that go beyond the productive sandhi rules described above.
In these varieties, specific heterorganic sequences of two obstruents, or an obstruent plus fricative, are simplified to a geminate in specific lexical items.
Nakagawa (2024: 36) treats these as historical word-form changes rather than synchronic productive rules.

The diagnostic is substitution-productivity: a Kushiro speaker who produces hokke for 'lie down' does not produce *pek kari for pet kari 'the river did' in spontaneous speech, showing that the /tk/ → [kk] simplification is lexically specific and not a live rule generating [kk] from all /tk/ sequences .
The community endorses this analysis: the changes are word-specific in Bihoro and may reflect a proto-phoneme issue rather than a productive synchronic rule ‹contested›
(antitwilight, 2024-11-17, citing Nakagawa & Fukazawa 2022: §3.3).
The /rs/ → [ss] Bihoro cases are phonologically parallel to productive /r/+/s/ → [ss] sandhi in §2, but speakers do not generalize the alternation to new /rs/ sequences.
The broader dialect typology is treated in .
The productive rules of this chapter are collected below.
Formal statements follow the notation X → Y / Z (X undergoes change to Y in environment Z).

The principal structural asymmetry in the system — /r/-sandhi is domain-free, /n/-sandhi is phrase-bounded — is formulated by Shiraishi (2022: §6.2) as the distinction between a pure phonological rule and a P-structure rule.
Neither is written in the standard romanization; both apply in connected speech .
These rules interact with the personal-affix system (ku= before vowel-initial stems; en= assimilation), treated in , and with the possessed-form morphophonology of nouns.
The syllable structure that sets coda position is described in , and the consonant inventory from which all triggering segments are drawn is described in .
Morpheme composition in Hokkaido Ainu frequently places two vowels in adjacent position across a prefix or morpheme boundary.

Four main strategies resolve such hiatus sequences, each conditioned by the type of boundary and the phonological shape of the adjacent morphemes: (1) glide epenthesis, insertion of a transitional [y] or [w] between the boundary vowels; (2) vowel weakening, in which a stem-initial high vowel /i/ or /u/ reduces to a glide after a preceding prefix; (3) glottal insertion, in which [ʔ] marks the syllable onset; and (4) vowel deletion, in which one of the adjacent vowels is elided.
The present chapter covers strategies (1) and (2), together with the phonotactic constraint that blocks both of them in certain environments.
The glottal-insertion strategy is treated in , and vowel deletion in the context of personal-prefix sandhi is covered in .

Glide epenthesis applies only after specific prefixes — the indefinite/antipassive prefix , the reciprocal , and variably the reflexive — and only at a prefix boundary, not at a compound morpheme boundary.
Vowel weakening is also prefix-conditioned.

Both are blocked when a glide before a closed syllable would create an illicit onset cluster, because the (C)V(C) syllable canon of Hokkaido Ainu forbids consonant clusters within a single syllable: see .
Nakagawa defines わたり 'glide, transition' as the sound produced while the vocal tract reconfigures between two successive phonemic targets in normal-tempo speech.
In his analysis of Saru and Chitose, this transition is not an independent phoneme.

The word iyomante 'the bear-spirit-sending ceremony' — phonemically /i-omante/ (< the indefinite-object prefix + ) — is pronounced [iyomante] in connected speech, but the [y] between prefix and stem is a nonphonemic transition that standard orthography does not treat as a separate segment .

Likewise uwepeker 'tell each other stories' is phonemically /u-epeker/ (< + epeker, a stem posited by the analysis and not attested as a free word ‹speculative›), and the [w] at the prefix–stem juncture is a transitional sound rather than a grammatically independent consonant.
Two diagnostics establish non-phonemic status for Saru and Chitose.
The nominalizer allomorphy test: morphemes ending in a genuine /y/ or /w/ take the consonant-allomorph -pe of the nominalizer (e.g.
okay-pe, siw-pe), while vowel-initial stems take -p even when preceded by an epenthetic glide: iyomante-p, not *iyomante-pe ; .
The double-glide test (described in §5 below) provides a second criterion for vowel-weakening contexts.
The general analysis of /y/ and /w/ as consonant phonemes in the inventory — and the diagnostics that establish root-phoneme /y/ /w/ — is developed in .
Whether the transition [y]/[w] at morpheme boundaries is phonemic in varieties other than Saru and Chitose is a genuinely contested question, treated in §8.
Glide epenthesis operates at the juncture of a vowel-final prefix and a vowel-initial stem.
The relevant prefixes are the indefinite-object/antipassive and the reciprocal prefix ; .
After /i/ a [y]-glide appears; after /u/ a [w]-glide.
The rules:
R1 ∅ → y / i- ___ V  (at a prefix boundary) R2 ∅ → w / u- ___ V  (at a prefix boundary)
The epenthetic glide is determined by the prefix vowel — /i/ triggers [y], /u/ triggers [w] — independently of the quality of the following stem vowel.
Table 1 shows y-insertion before /o/, /oi/, /e/, and /u/, and w-insertion before /e/ and /o/.

Satō (1996, 2003, cited in Shiraishi 2022 §4.3) establishes on Chitose data that R1 and R2 are morphosyntactically conditioned: they apply only at a productive prefix boundary — after , , and variably — and not after the second-person-plural prefix , after applicative , nor at the juncture between an incorporated noun and its verbal host .

The contrast between a prefix boundary and a compound morpheme boundary is illustrated by a community observation: the compound i-o-ci (roughly 'the place where things are many') surfaces as ioci, not *iyoci, because the morpheme boundary is a compound juncture rather than a productive prefix–stem juncture (nukopoli, 2023-12-11) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The pair iyocispare vs.
niocire further illustrates the conditioning: in iyocispare the productive i- prefix triggers the glide; at the boundary in niocire the conditions for R1 are not met and no glide appears.
The bear-ceremony word iyomante is informative here.
Nakagawa , Okuda , and Satō all assign a glide-bearing form to this word because the i- + omante boundary retains sufficient compositional productivity for R1 to apply (cf.
kamuy-omante 'god-sending').
Okuda (2025) notes that in Shizunai, morphologically transparent instances may surface without the glide, as iomante.
The debate over this word is therefore incidental to the blocking question; it is the morphosyntactic conditioning, not this specific form, that divides the analyses.
Whether consistently triggers R1 across dialects is uncertain.
Satō (1996/2003, via Shiraishi 2022 §4.3) includes it in the trigger class, while community discussion notes dialectal variation in its behavior (nukopoli, 2023-12-11) ‹corpus-suggested›.
For the reflexive prefix itself, see .
The (C)V(C) syllable canon prohibits consonant clusters in onset position and disallows more than one vowel per syllable ; .
When glide formation at a morpheme boundary would produce a string that violates this canon, the process is blocked.
The first-person-singular agent prefix before a stem whose first syllable is closed (CVC) shows the blocking most directly.

In /ku-ikra/ 'I send it', weakening the stem-initial /i/ to [y] would place [y] immediately before the coda /k/ of ikra's first syllable, producing *[yk] — an illicit CC onset at the following syllable boundary.
The vowel is therefore not weakened: ku-ikra is the surface form, with the vowel hiatus [ku.ik.ra] maintained ; (nukopoli, 2024-11-28) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The applicative prefix before the same stem provides a parallel: /e=ikra/ cannot surface as *[eykra] because [yk] is an illicit onset.
The actual form is eíkra [e.ík.ra], where the /i/ of ikra bears accent as a syllable nucleus — confirming it has not been reduced to a glide ; (nukopoli, 2024-11-28) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The open-σ1 stems itasa and iwanke contrast with ikra: e= + itasa → eytasa; e= + iwanke → eywanke.
The open first syllable (CV) of those stems permits the glide without creating a cluster.
The constraint has direct practical consequences for corpus normalization.

The io→iyo and ue→uwe patterns cannot be applied uniformly across all morpheme boundaries: community member thegodofneet (2025-04-24, ) notes that no form *eciyoka for eci-oka is attested in the corpus ‹corpus-confirmed›.
A rule-based normalization that applied io→iyo or ue→uwe at every juncture would produce unattested forms.
Glide-bearing spellings are appropriate only where the morphosyntactic conditions of §3 and the phonotactic licence of §4 are jointly satisfied and where corpus evidence confirms the variant.
Vowel weakening (母音弱化) converts a stem-initial /i/ or /u/ to a glide after a preceding prefix.
No new segment is inserted; the high vowel already present at the stem onset is converted to a consonantal element and loses the ability to bear accent .
The process has been verified for Saru and Chitose; its distribution in other Hokkaido varieties requires further documentation .
The rules:
R3 /i/ → [y] / V= ___ (stem-initial /i/, open first syllable) R4 /u/ → [w] / V= ___ (stem-initial /u/, open first syllable)
In koytak (< ko= + itak), the stem-initial /i/ of itak 'speak' weakens to [y]; in yaykowepeker, the stem-initial /u/ of uepeker weakens to [w].
The open-first-syllable restriction of §4 applies here: weakening is possible only when the stem's σ1 is open (CV), so no onset cluster results.
A double-glide test distinguishes R3/R4 from the presence of an underlying /y/ or /w/ in the stem.
If the stem-initial segment were an underlying /y/ or /w/, weakening it to [y] or [w] would yield a geminate.
The verb iunin 'ache' has a phonemic stem-initial /i/ (not */yi/); with the prefix it surfaces in Chitose as [kuyunin], with a single [y], not *[kuyyunin] .
The same test in Saru: somo eyunin ya? (not *eyyunin).
The single [y] confirms that R3 weakens a stem vowel rather than inserting a new glide alongside an underlying one.
The accent consequences of vowel weakening — the nucleus shift when a formerly accentable σ1 vowel becomes a non-accentable glide — are treated in .
For the related deletion of the prefix vowel in ku- and ci- before non-/i/ vowels (ku-omare → k=omare), see and .
When the morphosyntactic conditions of §3 do not permit glide epenthesis and the adjacent vowel is non-high so that R3/R4 weakening does not apply, [ʔ] fills the hiatus.

Tamura (1970: 586–587, 1996: xv, cited in Shiraishi 2022 §4.3) notes that the glottal onset is most clearly audible when the second vowel is accented or belongs to a closed syllable: aˈʔep 'food', aˈʔoypep 'tableware', eˈʔikka, teˈʔeta 'a long time ago'.
In non-prominent environments the transition is gradual rather than sharply glottalized .

A morphologically restricted h-insertion applies within the affiliative (possessed) form of nouns when two vowels would be adjacent: onaa → ona-h-a 'his/her father'; sikii → siki-h-i 'his/her eyes' (Kindaichi & Chiri 1936: 14, cited in Shiraishi 2022 §4.3 n.8).
This process is restricted to possessive derivation and is treated in .
Whether [ʔ] at these junctures constitutes an underlying phoneme /ʔ/ or is a predictable boundary marker is contested; the debate is taken up in .
Vowel deletion provides a fourth resolution route, particularly for non-high vowels at morpheme boundaries where glide formation is unavailable.
Shiraishi documents: keran (< kera=an 'is delicious'), sisotta (< siso or=ta 'on the fireplace'), and noya noya (< noye a noye a).
Deletion is conditioned by speech rate and prosodic context and is not in free variation with glide epenthesis at the same boundary.
The full account, including the accent interactions that block resyllabification, is in .
Three analyses of the morpheme-boundary [y] and [w] bear on whether they are underlying phonemes or surface transitions, and the three rest on genuine cross-dialectal differences.

Nakagawa's non-phonemic analysis (Saru/Chitose). The transition [y] and [w] at prefix boundaries are non-phonemic in Saru and Chitose: their appearance is entirely predictable from the shape of the adjacent morphemes, and neither the nominalizer allomorphy diagnostic nor the double-glide test provides evidence for underlying /y/ /w/ at these junctures .

Okuda's phonemic analysis (Shizunai). In the Shizunai variety, which lacks contrastive pitch accent, the glide vs. glottal distinction at a morpheme boundary carries lexical weight that accent handles elsewhere.
The minimal pair first observed by 志賀雪湖 (Okuda 2025 ): [suwat] 'pothook' — an opaque, fused compound — vs. [suʔat] 'pot bail' — a transparent su- + at with the boundary maintained.
In an accentless dialect this /w/ vs. /ʔ/ contrast is phonemically distinctive, giving /suwat/ vs. /suʔat/ (= /suat/).

Okuda further documents the pairs /u'a/ ~ /uwa/, /i'o/ ~ /iyo/, /i'e/ ~ /iye/ as additional Shizunai minimal pairs, and concludes that "one cannot say, without specifying dialect, that わたり /y/ /w/ are non-phonemic" ‹contested›.

Satō's two-process analysis (Chitose). Satō (2003, cited in Shiraishi 2022 §4.3) proposes that in Chitose, [y] and [w] in sequences /ie/, /ia/, /io/, /iu/, /ue/, /ua/, /uo/ at a morpheme boundary occur in the same phonetic environment as their glottal-stop-bearing counterparts and contrast with them; he therefore posits underlying /y/ /w/ phonemes in those contexts.
The glide after ku- and e= prefixes, by contrast, arises through surface glide formation (i → y, u → w) — a distinct process from lexical /y/ /w/.
The analysis thus involves two interacting processes: underlying phonemes in some contexts, and surface-phonological glide formation in others ‹contested›.

In Saru and Chitose the nominalizer-allomorphy and double-glide diagnostics do not reveal evidence for underlying /y/ /w/ at the prefix boundaries treated in §3; the non-phonemic analysis is adopted for those varieties.
In Shizunai the accentless system exposes a contrast masked elsewhere, and the glides there are phonemically distinct from [ʔ].

The question is structurally linked to the /ʔ/-phoneme debate — positing /ʔ/ at all vowel-initial syllables reanalyses the Shizunai contrasts differently — and both are considered together in ‹contested›.
In Hokkaido Ainu the shape a morpheme takes when listed in a dictionary — its citation form — and the shape it takes when combined with an adjacent morpheme — its combining form — frequently differ.
The alternations are phonologically conditioned: the coda of one morpheme interacts with the onset of the next to produce assimilation, deletion, or consonant mutation.

Four processes govern the principal alternations treated here: (1) the behavior of coda /r/ at morpheme junctions and its vocalic release in citation position; (2) the categorical palatalization of coda /t/ before a following onset /i/; (3) vowel elision in the person prefixes ku= and ci= before vowel-initial stems; and (4) the historical compound assimilation visible in the elm-bark robe name attus (underlying at-rus).

The sandhi rules that propagate across word boundaries are described in ; the echo-vowel diagnostics for distinguishing /r/-final from /rV/-final words are analyzed in ; glide epenthesis at vowel hiatus is covered in ; the accent consequences of combining prefixes are treated in .

The affiliative suffix and the support vowels it introduces — the /i/, /e/, /we/ alternants in possessed forms such as hum-i, tek-e, ru-we — constitute a distinct citation/combining opposition routed to and .
The rhotic /r/ is phonologically exceptional because its citation (pre-pausal) realization and its realization before a following morpheme diverge in two distinct ways.
In citation position, coda /r/ releases into a vocalic echo that copies the preceding nucleus: kor [koɾ(o)], kur [kuɾ(u)], kar [kaɾ(a)].
The echo-vowel carries no accent, does not feed the nominalizer allomorphy, and disappears when /r/ resyllabifies before a following vowel-initial morpheme ; .
In combining position before a consonant-initial morpheme, /r/ instead triggers regressive assimilation (r-sandhi):
Sources: ; ; .
The full assimilation paradigm and its domain conditions — including the asymmetry between n-sandhi (bounded by the phrase) and r-sandhi (crossing phrasal and sentence boundaries) — are treated in .
In casual connected speech, word-final /r/ is susceptible to deletion, a reduction distinct from the productive sandhi above.
Attested reductions include kur 'person' → [ku] and the combining stem kor → [ko] (nukopoli, 2024-12-11) ‹corpus-suggested›.
Standard orthography notates underlying forms and does not write these reductions .
The independent verb behaves differently from the combining stem kor-.

The /o/ of koro is a genuine underlying segment, not an echo-vowel release, as confirmed by nominalizer allomorphy: the /r/-final combining stem takes the C-allomorph -pe (kor-pe → 'what one has'), whereas a genuine /rV/-final base would take the V-allomorph -p.
The diagnostics for separating /r/-final from /rV/-final words are fully described in .
The palatalization rule /t/ → /c/ [ʨ] before a following onset /i/ is the one sandhi alternation that applies categorically in all Hokkaido dialects without exception ; ; .
Its formal statement:
t → c / _ i (at a morpheme junction, where /t/ is the coda of morpheme 1 and /i/ is the onset of morpheme 2)

Resyllabification is prerequisite: the morphemic sequence …V.ti… resyllabifies to give …V.C, placing the erstwhile coda /t/ in onset position before the /i/ syllable; the resulting /ti/ then palatalizes to /ci/ [ʨi] ; .
The rule applies at compound boundaries, derivational boundaries, and inflectional (possessive) boundaries alike.
Sources: ; ; .
The derivation of macikor from + illustrates the two-step process:
Underlying: /mat-ikor/ — coda /t/ of mat at the left edge of the /i/-initial morpheme ikor
Resyllabification: /maˈtikor/ — coda /t/ moves to onset of the /i/ syllable, giving the sequence /ti/
Palatalization: /ti/ → /ci/ [ʨi] → macikor
The compound is well attested in Saru narrative speech:

The rule is subject to one phonotactic constraint: if the /i/-initial morpheme begins a closed syllable whose onset would create an impermissible three-consonant sequence, the resyllabification is blocked and palatalization does not apply.
See for the (C)V(C) canon and for the parallel blocking of glide weakening before closed /i/-initial syllables.
The possessive-boundary instances of the same rule are documented in .
The first-person singular agent prefix ku= and the first-person plural agent prefix ci= each have a reduced combining form before vowel-initial stems.
In the Saru, Chitose, and Mukawa dialects, the rule is:
/u/ → ∅ / ku= _ {a, e, u, o} (the prefix vowel elides before a stem-initial /a/, /e/, /u/, or /o/; parallel rule for ci=)
Before a stem-initial /i/, elision does not apply.
Instead, the stem /i/ weakens to the glide [y], giving the combining form ku=ype (from underlying ku=ipe) rather than *k=ipe ; ; (nukopoli, 2024-11-28) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Sources: ; ; (nukopoli, 2024-11-28).
The block on elision before /i/ is phonotactic.
If the prefix /u/ were deleted before a closed syllable beginning in /i/ (e.g.
ikra), the result *k=ikra would require a three-consonant onset, violating the (C)V(C) syllable canon.
Nakagawa (2024: 52–53) confirms the ungrammatical forms *k=ipe and *ku=ykra and *k=ikra alike, with only ku=ikra grammatical before the closed /i/-initial stem.
The same elision process accounts historically for the pronoun .

Community analysis traces kani to an underlying ku=an-hi (first-person + existential root + nominal suffix), with the prefix vowel /u/ elided before the /a/-initial stem — parallel to the reduction ci=ep → cep 'fish' (gengojiro, 2024-02-05) ‹speculative›.
On this account the historical combining form and the present-day independent pronoun are related by the same morphophonological rule, now lexicalized in kani.
The elision rule is restricted to southern Hokkaido (Saru, Chitose, Mukawa); most other dialects retain ku= and ci= uncontracted before all vowels .
For the personal-affix accent interactions triggered by prefix integration into the prosodic word, see and .
The elm-bark robe name attus (アットゥシ) derives from a compound at-rus, with at designating the elm-bark cloth.
Two dialect reflexes are reported:
General Hokkaido: attus — the onset /r/ of rus assimilates progressively to the preceding coda /t/ of at, producing a geminate /tt/ and collapsing the /t.r/ cluster: /at + rus/ → /at.tus/ → attus.
The form attus is corpus-confirmed (24 tokens) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Saru dialect: ahrus — a different outcome where the coda /t/ of at weakens to /h/ rather than geminating, while the /r/ is preserved.
This Saru form is reported by the community and has not been independently verified in a read primary source ‹speculative›.
The progressive assimilation /t + r/ → /tt/ producing attus is consistent with the cluster- simplification isoglosses documented in eastern dialects by (e.g.
tupte → tutte in Bihoro; hotke → hokke 'lie down').
treats such changes as historical word-form changes rather than synchronic alternations — a classification that applies equally to the lexicalized attus.
Broader dialect consonant-assimilation correspondences are treated in .
The verb presents a case where the synchronic combining-form analysis and a competing historical account remain unsettled.
Nakagawa's morphological analysis : koré is the combining stem kor 'have' plus the causative suffix -e, parallel to kay-e 'break (tr.)', tuy-e 'sell'.

The surface accent koré (σ2 high) rather than *kóre (σ1 high) follows from the iambic placement rule reapplying to the whole as if monomorphemic once lexicalization has obscured the morpheme boundary: /CV + CVC/ → σ2 accent.
The same accent pattern holds for the parallel lexicalized causatives treated in .
The community contraction account: koré is a contraction of korpare, the ditransitive root 'give to sb' (corpus frequency 153) (nukopoli, 2024-12-26).
Both koré and korpare are productive in attested narrative speech; the accent koré (not *kóre) is agreed under both accounts.
The corpus attests koré (accent-marked) 30 times and kore (unaccented, orthographic variant) 3120 times; the disparity reflects editorial marking practice rather than speaker frequency ‹contested›.

The two analyses make different predictions about the combining system: Nakagawa's account treats kor-e as a still-productive, if now lexicalized, causative combination; the contraction account treats koré as an opaque form derived from korpare by phonological reduction, making the kor + suffix boundary morphologically inert in this lexical item.
Neither is settled by the accessible sources.

A further class of citation/combining opposition involves the suffix vowel that consonant-final nouns receive when they take the possessed (affiliative) form: hum → hum-i 'his/her sound', haw → haw-e 'his/her voice', ru → ru-we 'the trace of —', tek → tek-e 'his/her hand'.
The vowel that appears after the root consonant is conditioned by the root's final vowel, following co-occurrence restrictions that are not simple spreading ; .
This constitutes a systematic citation/combining opposition — the citation form is the bare noun, the combining (possessed) form adds the suffix vowel — and is treated in and .

An additional morphologically restricted /h/-insertion between a vowel-final root and a following possessive vowel — ona-a → ona-h-a 'his father', siki-i → siki-h-i 'his eyes' (Kindaichi & Chiri 1936: 14, reported via ) — is also treated in .

The person markers of Hokkaido Ainu undergo systematic phonological changes at their juncture with a following verb or noun stem.
The most salient is the deletion of the vowel of ku= and ci= before stem-initial vowels other than /i/, a feature of the southern varieties (Saru, Chitose, Mukawa).
This deletion interacts with the prosodic-word formation and accent rules treated in and with the vowel-weakening mechanism described in .

The general sandhi processes that operate across all morpheme junctures — coda-/r/ assimilation, nasal-place assimilation — are the subject of ; the person-marker inventory and its morphosyntactic analysis are laid out in .

In Saru, Chitose, and Mukawa, the /u/ of ku= (first-person singular agent/subject) deletes before a stem-initial /a/, /e/, /u/, or /o/; correspondingly, the /i/ of ci= (first-person plural exclusive agent/subject) deletes in the same environments ; .
The vowel /i/ is excluded from the deletion domain: before a stem beginning with /i/, a distinct vowel-weakening process applies (§3 below).
Outside the southern zone, most Hokkaido dialects preserve the full marker forms without deletion ; .
The two deletion rules can be stated as:

Learners of Saru and Chitose frequently overgeneralize the deletion to /i/-initial stems, producing ungrammatical *k=ipe; the restriction to {a, e, u, o} is the corrective (nukopoli, 2024-11-28) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

When the stem begins with /i/, deletion of ku='s /u/ is blocked; the stem-initial /i/ instead undergoes 母音弱化 (vowel weakening), becoming the glide [j]: ku=ipe → ku=ype /kuˈype/, while *k=ipe is ungrammatical ; .
The same process operates with e=: e=itak → eytak [ejˈtak] 'your words / you speak' .
The weakening process (/i/ → [j] after a vowel-final prefix) is described in broader scope in .
A second environment blocks weakening: when the stem's first syllable is closed (CVC), the result of weakening would produce an illicit consonant cluster.
The stem ikra has σ1 = ik (coda /k/); weakening would yield the onset sequence /k-jk-/, which violates the (C)V(C) syllable canon ().
Accordingly ku=ikra is the only licit form: neither *ku=ykra nor *k=ikra arises ; (nukopoli, 2024-11-28) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
By contrast, stems with an open /i/-initial syllable do undergo weakening: eytasa (< e= + itasa) and eywanke (< e= + iwanke) both show the [j] glide (nukopoli, 2024-11-28) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The markers ku=, e=, and ci= form a single prosodic word with the following stem, so that the pitch-accent placement rules (原則1 / 原則2; ) are reapplied to the whole unit.
The crucial ordering point is that the accent shift occurs before vowel deletion: the surface accent is computed from the prefixed word, not re-derived from the contracted form ; .
The derivation of k=ómare illustrates the two-step ordering:
The same ordering holds with ci=: etú → ci=étu (accent on σ2 of the new unit) → c=étu [ˈcetu] .
For consonant-initial stems, deletion does not apply; only the accent shift operates: hopúni → ku=hópuni 'I rise' .

The markers a= (fourth-person agent/subject) and eci= (second-person plural agent/subject) behave differently: they do not form a single prosodic word with the stem, so the stem retains its underlying accent without shift.
Thus omáre → a=omáre (accent unchanged) ; .
Within the person-marker class as a whole, the degree of phonological integration with the host stem varies beyond the binary inner/outer accent-class split.

Community phonetic observation — uncorroborated by instrumental study in the sources read for this grammar — reports that the marker group binds more tightly to its host than a compound constituent does: a=kor itak 'speech one has' surfaces as [akorəʔitak], with a glottal catch at the word boundary after kor, rather than resyllabifying the coda /r/ across the compound juncture to *[ako.ri.tak] (nukopoli, 2024-03-18) ‹speculative›.

Within the marker paradigm, the inner-class markers (ku=, e=) are reported to be phonetically tighter than the outer-class markers (a=, =an), the latter tending to be realized more independently in measured speech (nukopoli, 2024-03-18) ‹speculative›.

The suffix =an (fourth-person S) shows a juncture pattern distinct from that of derivational suffixes: after a consonant-final stem, the coda does not resyllabify onto the following /a/ by the regular resyllabification rule of .
Instead the boundary is marked by a glottal stop or tense onset: sap=an → [sapʔan], not *[sa.pan] (nukopoli, 2023-12-27) ‹speculative›.
This contrasts with the morpheme-internal resyllabification seen in true derivational junctures such as sik-o → [si.ko] ; .
The =an suffix also carries a secondary accent when the verb stem closes with a CV(+) syllable: iˈruska-ˌan 'one is angry' retains both accents.
This secondary accent disappears when the stem ends in a CVC syllable: ˈcis-an 'one cries', ˈsap-an .
In fast or casual speech, the vowel-deletion process extends to sequences that have become partially lexicalized.
The independent pronoun kuani 'I' (analysed in ) reduces to kani by the same /u/-deletion that yields ciep → cep 'food (eaten thing)' (gengojiro, 2024-02-05) ‹corpus-suggested›.
Both kani and cep are the standard Saru/Chitose dictionary entries, showing that these contractions have become conventionalized rather than remaining casual variants.

The romanized orthography writes underlying (etymological) forms throughout — ku=omare rather than k=omare; ran wa rather than ram ma — while katakana practice tends to follow the phonetic output more closely ; (nukopoli, 2024-07-09) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

The sandhi forms are produced in speech but not written in standard transcription, so corpus searches for assimilated person-marker forms typically return nothing; the spoken distribution of the rule is consequently under-documented in the written record .
The wider romanization policy and its divergence from katakana practice are discussed in .
The coda /r/ of a verb stem can interact with person-marker sandhi when a /r/-final stem precedes a vowel-initial marker or suffix.
The regressive assimilation rules of operate on the coda /r/ first and produce the form that then serves as input to person-marker juncture rules.
The fast-speech deletion of word-final /r/ itself (kur → ku, kor → ko) is treated in .
Nakagawa's standard romanization applies the equals sign to all person markers at the left or right edge of the verb: ku=, e=, a=, ci=, eci=, en=, un=, =an, and =as .

The = is an orthographic device — Nakagawa states expressly that it is unrelated to the linguistic convention of marking clitics with an equals sign — so the notation itself carries no claim about clitic as against affix status.
The orthographic policy is discussed in .
The phonological evidence surveyed in this chapter shows that the personal markers — written uniformly with = — occupy different positions along the clitic-to-affix cline.
Three independent diagnostics converge on the same two-way split:
Accent shift: the inner class (ku=, e=, ci=) triggers prosodic-word formation and reapplication of accent rules; the outer class (a=, eci=) does not (§4 above; ; ).
Vowel deletion: only ku= and ci= lose their vowels before non-/i/ stems in the southern dialects, marking them as the most tightly bonded members of the marker paradigm (§2 above; ).

Juncture opacity: the =an boundary blocks the resyllabification that is otherwise permitted at morpheme-internal junctures, placing it above the level of a derivational suffix in phonological independence (§5 above; nukopoli, 2023-12-27, ‹speculative›).
The three criteria jointly define a gradient: inner clitics > outer clitics > independent words, with ku= and ci= the most tightly integrated members and =an the loosest.
A parallel gradation in morphophonological tightness across person-marking sub-classes has been documented for Sakhalin Ainu , providing a comparative point for the Hokkaido two-way split.
The morphosyntactic diagnostics for the Hokkaido system are taken up in and the template position of each marker in .
Hokkaido Ainu reduplication places a phonological copy of a verbal base alongside that base.

The process is most visible in iterative and distributive-plural forms, but this chapter is restricted to its phonological dimension: the shape the reduplicant takes, what happens at the boundary between reduplicant and base, how the general resyllabification and hiatus-resolution rules interact with that boundary, and how the sandhi assimilations documented in bear on the juncture when a suffix follows the reduplicated complex.
Aspect and iterative semantics belong to ; verbal-number pluractionality to ; nominalizer allomorphy consulted in §5 to .

Live morphological decompositions of reduplicated forms — full-copy, VC-echo (cirir), and final-syllable (hepokiki) types with their argument-structure annotations — are browsable in the Ainu morpheme database (mdb.aynu.org/processes).
Hokkaido Ainu reduplication is characteristically full: the reduplicant copies the complete syllable or CVC template of the base .

The syllable canon is (C)V(C), so each copy is an independently well-formed syllable (; ); consonant clusters at the juncture arise only when an assimilation rule applies (§§3–4 below), not from the copying itself.
The copying preserves coda consonants: a CVC base yields a CVC reduplicant; a CV base yields a CV reduplicant.
The coda shape of the copy is identical to the coda shape of the source form (see §5 on how coda alternation in the source propagates into the reduplicant).
The table below shows canonical mappings; phonetic representations are supplied in §3 where the boundary is discussed.
Accent follows the general iambic rule (): if the first syllable of the reduplicated complex is closed, it carries the primary accent; if open, the accent falls on the second syllable .
In ketketcep the first syllable is the closed ket, giving [ˈketketcep].
Lexicalized compounds with reduplicated elements follow the first-element priority rule governing all compounds (; ).
A reduplicant and its base do not form a seamless concatenation.
Across ordinary morpheme boundaries a coda consonant resyllabifies onto a following vowel-initial syllable: sik-o → [ˈsi.ko], mat-ak → [ˈma.tak] (; ).
Two blocking conditions suspend this rule and trigger glottal insertion instead:

Secondary accent on the following syllable. When the vowel of σn+1 carries secondary accent — as in paˈraparak-ʔan 'cry' — the accent domain prevents resyllabification; [ʔ] is inserted at the juncture.
The reduplicant-base boundary itself. ˈay-ʔay 'baby' shows glottal insertion at the REDUP-BASE juncture independently of whether the base vowel happens to be accented.
Both conditions are documented by Tamura (1998: 41–42), reported in .
Rule statement: ∅ → ʔ / VRED-final __ VBASE-initial at the REDUP-BASE juncture (or when the following V carries secondary accent at any juncture); resyllabification is otherwise suspended.

Productive glide insertion at person-prefix boundaries — e.g., i= + omante → iyomante — is a distinct operation in a different prosodic domain; it is morpho-syntactically conditioned and does not extend to the reduplicant-base boundary (; ).
The glottal option takes over at REDUP-BASE.
The blocking in §3 applies specifically at the internal REDUP-BASE boundary.
The junction between the reduplicated complex and a following affix is an ordinary morpheme juncture: sandhi rules operate there as they do everywhere else.
Progressive assimilation at an underlying /t/ + /s/ juncture yields [c] ([ʨ~ʦ]).
Nakagawa documents the pattern at compound and historical suffix junctures: pet-sam → petcam 'riverbank', sinot-sa → sinotca 'improvised song' ().
The compound ketketcep (a fish name) has been proposed as deriving from an underlying structure *ket~ket-se-pe ( antitwilight, 2025-11-03).
Derivation:
A parallel non-reduplicated case is nisatcawot ~ nisat-sawot 'Venus / morning star', the same /t/ + /s/ → [c] at a compound boundary.

The community analysis proposes that the rule applies only at historically underlying /t#/, not to /t/ that arose secondarily; this restriction has not been confirmed in a primary phonological source ‹speculative›
( antitwilight, 2025-11-03).
The palatalization rule t → c / __ i applies without exception in Hokkaido Ainu: mat + ikor → macikor, rekut-i → rekuci (; ).
The rule operates through resyllabification — coda /t/ moves to the onset of the /i/ syllable — so it shares the feeding mechanism that is blocked at REDUP-BASE (§3).

No attested /t/-final + /i/-initial reduplication pair has been identified in the sources read for this grammar; the blocking prediction follows from the interaction of the independently documented resyllabification block (§3) and the palatalization rule (; ) ‹speculative›.
Coda /r/ is the dominant regressive-assimilation trigger across all morpheme boundaries (; ).

In a reduplicated form with a /r/-final base, the coda /r/ of the reduplicant remains in coda position (resyllabification is blocked at REDUP-BASE), and could in principle trigger r-sandhi against the onset of the following base copy.
Nakagawa documents r-sandhi word-internally and across words (), and Shiraishi establishes it as a purely phonological rule with no prosodic-domain restriction ().
Whether r-sandhi applies at the REDUP-BASE juncture is not documented in the sources read here; corpus investigation is needed ‹speculative›.
The lexicalized compound attus (elm-bark robe), deriving from an underlying at-rus via r-sandhi (Saru intermediate ahrus), is attested 24× in the corpus ( nukopoli, 2024-12-26) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
This involves compound-internal r-sandhi, not the REDUP-BASE boundary; it is treated in .
Because the reduplicant copies the phonological shape of the source form, any alternation visible in the base propagates into the reduplicant.
A community observation on the verb illustrates this point.
The verb 'go up / ascend' appears in two forms: rikin, with final nasal coda /n/ (attested in corpus; see example below), and rikip, with final stop coda /p/.
In reduplication, either form may serve as the base that is copied, yielding alternant shapes; the alternation is summarized as rikin~rikip ( nukopoli, 2026-04-27) ‹speculative›.
The causative suffix attaches to the nasal-coda form only: rikinka is attested; *rikipka is not found ( nukopoli, 2026-04-27) ‹speculative›.
This asymmetry indicates that the nasal-coda form is the morphological base for further derivation, while the stop-coda form is a secondary shape.
The stop-coda form rikip is consistent with the nominalizer allomorphy: the nominalizer surfaces as -p after a vowel-final stem (; ).
If the root is vowel-final riki-, then riki-p = root + nominalizer.
The reduplicant then mirrors whichever form of the verb is being used as the base — nominalized or plain — without neutralizing or canonicalizing it.
The coda alternation in the reduplicant is thus an instance of morphological conditioning of the base shape feeding into the copying operation.
For the nominalizer system itself, see and .
Personal prefixes ku=, e=, and ci= attach to the full reduplicated complex as if it were a single prosodic word.
The iambic accent-placement rule — first closed syllable gets the nucleus; if the first is open, the second does — applies to the [prefix + REDUP + BASE] string as a unit (; ; ).

The vowel-deletion rule of ku= and ci= — prefix vowel deletes before stem-initial /a e u o/, but not before /i/ (; nukopoli, 2024-11-28) ‹corpus-confirmed› — applies at the prefix-reduplicant junction exactly as it does before any vowel-initial stem.
If the first syllable of the reduplicant is vowel-initial, the prefix vowel deletes; if consonant-initial, it does not.
The full morphophonology is treated in and .
No sandhi applies at the internal REDUP-BASE boundary in this example: the last syllable of the reduplicant (ri) is open, so there is no coda consonant to trigger the rules in §4.
The following particle wa attaches at the right edge of the whole reduplicated form; the only potential sandhi there is the progressive nasal-place assimilation documented for this particle ().

The regressive cluster assimilations of eastern Hokkaido dialects — tk → kk, pt → tt, rs → ss in Bihoro and related varieties () — are treated by Nakagawa as word-specific historical consolidations rather than active synchronic rules (; antitwilight, 2024-11-17).
No specific reduplicated compound showing these eastern assimilations is attested in the sources consulted here ‹corpus-suggested›.
The broader inventory of dialect-specific morphophonological isoglosses is treated in .
Word class in Hokkaido Ainu is determined by two converging criteria: grammatical role in the clause and formal (morphological) behaviour.

Meaning is explicitly excluded from the classification — words designating properties are verbs, words denoting events can be nouns, and the same root may function in more than one class without derivation ; .
Classes are prototype-based and their boundaries are gradient; between canonical members and the periphery lies a continuum of items sharing some but not all defining properties .
Three schemes dominate the modern literature.
Nakagawa's recognises six classes, distributing auxiliary verbs under particles and treating nominalizers as a grammatical role rather than a separate class.
His English Handbook chapter adds a seventh by splitting auxiliary verbs out of particles.
Satō , following Tamura's scheme, also arrives at six but subdivides noun to accommodate nominalizers and numeral nouns as distinct subclasses.
Ijäs follows the six-class scheme in her pedagogical grammar.

Refsing's Shizunai grammar collapses the inventory into three macro-classes (Nominals, Verbals, Particles), treating adnouns as particles and grouping conjunctions, interjections, and adverbs together ‹contested›.
The consensus at the macro level is solid: six or seven classes, with the treatment of auxiliary verbs as the only top-level disagreement.
Two deeper disputes — whether property-meaning words form an adjective class, and where nominalizers belong — are taken up in the no-adjective section and the nominalizer section below.
A verb can function as the head of a predicate without a copula and indexes its arguments with person affixes.
An intransitive verb takes one affix (the sole argument S), a transitive verb takes up to two (the transitive subject A and the object O), placed on different sides of the stem .
Verbs subclassify by valency: 0-argument existential (), 1-argument intransitive (), 2-argument transitive (), and 3-argument ditransitive ().
The full taxonomy is in , the valency system in , and the person-affix paradigm in .
Property-meaning words form no separate adjective class: they take the same S affix as action verbs, occur as bare predicates with no copula, and accept verbal derivational morphology.
The two examples below illustrate bare property-verb predicates:
The same 1SG intransitive-subject prefix ku= that marks the action verb ku=mina 'I laugh' marks the property verb ku=pewre 'I am young' .
The full argument for dissolving the adjective class is in .

A noun heads a noun phrase serving as a verb argument, does not occupy the predicate slot on its own, and carries at most one person affix — the possessive (transitive-subject) affix, not the nominative affix of verbs ; .
Four subclasses differ in independence, in relativisation potential, and in the type of person affix they admit:

The person-affix asymmetry is the sharpest diagnostic: the affiliative form of a common noun takes the possessive (A-type) affix — ku=tekehe 'my hand' — whereas a locative noun takes the objective (O-type) affix — en=sam 'my side' .
An affix cannot appear on a bare concept-form noun: *ku=tek is ungrammatical as a possessive.

Common nouns split by possession type: alienable possession uses a -construction (a=kor cip 'my boat'); inalienable possession uses the affiliative form (ku=tekehe 'my hand'); an appositive N₁ N₂(concept) construction marks attribute or scope rather than ownership (menoko tek 'a woman's hand', not replaceable by a possessive prefix) .
These constructions are developed in and .
Locative nouns (位置名詞) are a small, closed set expressing relative position ('on, beside, inside, behind').
Their basic forms require a preceding antecedent NP; their long forms can head a clause independently.
Both take the objective affix and always function as place arguments, distinguishing them formally from common nouns .
