The full inventory of locative nouns, their long-form morphology, and the Type-1/Type-2 divide are in .
Hokkaido Ainu nouns carry no grammatical number: the same form serves for one or many, and number marking is never obligatory ; .
The formal noun can optionally mark a plural or associative group; in the Saru dialects its range extends to inanimates on animist grounds, since all things carry a spirit in the Ainu worldview :

Community members have elaborated that (formally the affiliative form of ) carries a distinct semantic range — 'family, kinship companions' — with the possessed form implying a specific relational anchor in a way the bare plural marker does not (thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord 2025; ; corroborated by ) ‹contested›.
Transnumerality, the animacy-scope dispute, and the interaction with verb number are in ; the four noun subclasses are in .
Formal nouns (形式名詞, also called 名助詞 noun-particles) cannot head an NP without a preceding modifier and supply the nominal head of a nominalised clause ; .
Canonical members include /, , , , , and .
The allomorphy p after a vowel / pe after a consonant is phonologically conditioned .

Four formal nouns grammaticalise further into the evidential system: , , , and are affiliative forms of the sensory nouns , , , and that become the inferential, situational, reportative, and sensory evidentials; the full architecture is in .

A productive instrument-nominalisation pattern makes the clause-head role of formal nouns visible: ani 'with' plus a transitivised verb plus yields 'the thing for X-ing with' — ani e=kanpinuye p 'pencil' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2026; ).
The full inventory is in and the nominalizing function in .
Adverbs modify verb phrases without entering the predicate slot or argument structure.
They take neither the nominative person affix nor the possessive affix.
Formation types include bare underived forms (, ); intransitive verbs plus the adverbialiser (, ); and directionals built from locative-noun stems (, ) .
The adverbialiser and the degree/comparison system are in and .

A subclass of postpositional adverbs (後置副詞) takes an antecedent NP and functions like a postposition while remaining adverb in syntax: it can stand clause-initially and does not require its argument to be a place NP, unlike a locative case particle .
When the antecedent is pronominal, a postpositional adverb takes the objective person affix.
Canonical members include , , , , and .
Their relationship to the case system is in .
Adnouns (連体詞, also called prenominals) modify noun phrases directly and share none of the verbal properties: they do not head predicates, do not appear as arguments, and take no person affix.

The sole distributional privilege of the adnoun is that a case particle can attach to it directly, without an intervening formal noun — toan ta 'over there' joins a demonstrative prenominal with the locative particle directly, while a common noun requires a formal noun first .
Subclasses include demonstratives (, ), numeric (, ), interrogative (), indefinite, and general prenominals (, , ) .
A prenominal followed by the formal noun yields a demonstrative pronoun (, ); the demonstrative system is in .
The property verb occupies the same pre-noun position as an adnoun but retains full verbal morphology in the predicate, illustrating the verb/noun continuum developed further below:
Particles attach to autonomous clause elements and express grammatical relations without entering the predicate slot or argument structure.
Nakagawa recognises five subtypes: case particles (格助詞 — , , , , ), auxiliary particles (助動詞), adverbial/focus particles (副助詞), final particles (終助詞), and conjunctive particles (接続助詞).
Ainu has no nominative or accusative case particles: subject and object are identified through word order, person affixes, and context ; .
The four locative case particles all require a place argument and are distinct from postpositional adverbs that can stand clause-initially .
The Handbook chapter splits auxiliary verbs into a seventh class on the grounds that they head predicates but cannot stand as independent words.
Items such as and typically fuse with the preceding verb (arpa-rusuy=an 'I want to go'), while the perfective particle never does; the boundary is gradient rather than sharp ‹contested›.
Interjections stand alone as complete sentences with no syntactic relation to a surrounding clause .
They form a large and dialect-specific inventory of greetings (), calls, acknowledgements, and emotional expressions.
The class is treated in .
The most consequential classification decision in modern Hokkaido Ainu description is the absence of an adjective class.
Words translating English adjectives — , , , , , — are all intransitive verbs ; ; ; ; .

Historically, Kindaichi & Chiri still posited a 形容詞 class with its own person-inflected paradigm; Chiri's later work rejected the verb/adjective distinction and coined the unified term 用詞 for the merged class; all subsequent description has inherited that move — historically contested, now the consensus of the modern literature ‹consensus›.
Three arguments converge .
Syntactically, property words occupy the predicate slot with no copula, in exactly the same frame as action verbs.

Morphologically, causative (-re/-e/-ka) and applicative (e-/o-/ko-) affixes attach to property words under the same semantic conditions as to action verbs — i-ruska 'be angry at something' uses the applicative on .
Semantically, the same form serves both the stative reading ('be X') and the inchoative reading ('become X'): = 'be big' and 'become big'.
This stative/inchoative identity is general to Ainu intransitive verbs — , — and does not distinguish property words from action verbs ; .
The inchoative reading surfaces in imperatives:

In attributive position, property words precede the noun with no morphological change, in the same slot occupied by relative-clause verbs: pon hekaci 'small child' has the same surface structure as arki utar 'people who came', where is unambiguously a verb .

The residual adjective-like behaviour — the split between the linkers wa and no in conjoined VPs — reduces to a semantic (static vs dynamic) distinction in the whole VP, not a difference in the part of speech of its head .
The full argument with all diagnostics is in .

Intransitive verbs convert to nouns without morphological change: the same form is a predicate in one clause and a noun-modifier or compound-noun constituent in another, so the verb/noun boundary is positional and relational rather than marked on the word itself .

Compound-noun formation makes this visible: Nakagawa's arity-based analysis after shows that many items classed as N+N compounds have a verbal non-head — onture-p 'strawberry' (literally 'that which swims upstream') has a 1-argument-verb head .

Community observation has noted that Ainu has very few coordinate or exocentric pure-noun compounds (haca-hapo 'parents', po-at 'womb'); most nominal compound formation is verb-centred, in keeping with the near-universal convertibility of intransitives to nouns (antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord 2026; ) ‹contested›.
Compound structure is in ; nominal and verbal derivation in .
No independent conjunction class (接続詞) is set up.
Items glossed as conjunctions in earlier work — , , , , — are distributed between conjunctive particles and adverbs on the basis of their primary function ; .
Even Tamura, who had set up a conjunction category, noted that it was handled as conjunctive particles for convenience .
Refsing keeps conjunctions, interjections, and adverbs together in one macro-class — the counterpart of the modern distributed analysis ‹contested›.

The same item (oraun, kusu) receives the label conjunction, conjunctive particle, or postpositional adverb depending on the analytical framework, a terminological split with no consequence for the forms themselves.
The discourse-connective system is in .
The status of nominalizers is the deepest terminological split in the literature.
Satō distinguishes 名詞化辞 (nominalizer) — producing an internally complete content clause — from 形式名詞 (formal noun) — the head of a relative clause with a gap; both are noun subclasses in his system.

Nakagawa retains 形式名詞 as the word-class label and uses 補文標識 (complementizer) for the grammatical role a formal noun plays in certain clausal contexts, so that nominalising a VP and heading a relative clause are two uses of one class, not two classes.
Refsing uses "nominalizer" more broadly to cover what Chiri treated as mood morphemes (, , ) as one of four sentence-conversion types.
The three analyses are incompatible at the word-class level, though they agree on the inventory of forms involved ‹contested›.
A diachronic proposal that the affiliative suffix -i derives from the formal noun is Nakagawa's own and flagged as a hypothesis ‹speculative›.

Community discussion has noted that the absence of a true infinitive in Hokkaido Ainu — where head-marking and nominalisation-dependent grammar leave no role for a bare verbal noun — means that , , and nominalisations with auxiliary-like predicates handle what many languages express with infinitives or purpose clauses (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024; ) ‹contested›.
The formal-noun inventory is in and the nominalizing function in .
A noun is defined as a word that can form an NP and serve as a verb's subject or object .

Within the class, four subclasses are distinguished by two crossing diagnostics: whether the form can stand alone as an NP argument, and whether it can serve as the head of a relative-clause structure ; .
Crossing these two properties against the type of person affix the form takes and its status as a locative expression (⟨place⟩) yields a six-row grid.
The rows fall into an autonomy hierarchy.
Common nouns in the concept form are the most independent; common nouns in the affiliative form presuppose a possessor relation but can still stand as NP arguments.
Locative nouns are always ⟨place⟩ and take objective rather than nominative person affixes; the Type-1 basic form is the least autonomous among the locative forms, requiring an antecedent NP.
Pronouns can stand alone but cannot be relativised.
Formal nouns are the least autonomous of all: they require a preceding modifier or clause and cannot appear as bare NP arguments .
Pronouns and formal nouns receive full treatments in separate chapters: and .
Locative nouns are introduced in this chapter and developed in detail in .
Every common noun has two forms.
The concept form (概念形) presents the referent without anchoring it relationally to anything else.
The affiliative form (所属形) presents it in relation to a possessor or reference point, and it is the form that carries a personal prefix indexing that possessor.

Kindaichi & Chiri used the terms 抽象形 (abstract form) and 具体形 (concrete form) for the same distinction ; the current terminology, following Nakagawa and the Bugaeva Handbook, replaces those labels without changing the underlying analysis ; .
Three possession constructions are built on this opposition :

The decisive diagnostic distinguishing (2) from (3) is the person-prefix substitution test: the first NP of an inalienable construction can be replaced by a person prefix (ku=sikihi 'my eye' — concept form sik, affiliative sikihi), whereas the first noun of an attributive construction cannot (*ku=rus for 'bear-pelt'; only kamuy rus or kamuy rusihi 'that specific bear's pelt' is possible) .
The morphophonology of affiliative-form formation — the vowel-copy and echo-vowel suffixes — is treated in .
The full semantics of the concept/affiliative opposition, including its non-possessive (anaphoric and definiteness) uses, are developed in .
The inalienable construction (construction 2) covers several semantic fields.

Nakagawa identifies five main classes that favour the affiliative form when possessed: (a) body parts and items typically worn or carried (ku=tekehe 'my hand', a=tesmaha 'my snowshoes'); (b) part-of-whole nouns (op nicihi 'spear-shaft', sayo rurihi 'gruel broth'); (c) a subset of kinship terms (see below); (d) material-to-product nouns (ikaray ohawe 'nettle stew', top cise 'bamboo house'); and (e) a miscellaneous set including ataye 'price', (affiliative huraha), and kotanu 'village' .
Within the broader inalienable class, a distinction can be drawn by degree of boundness.
Common nouns in the body-part and part-whole classes retain an independent concept form that can appear in generic or classifier-like contexts: tek 'hand' can appear as a bare NP argument.

By contrast, the Type-1 basic forms of locative nouns (§ ) cannot appear at all as NP arguments without an immediately preceding antecedent, and formal nouns cannot appear without a preceding clause or prenominal modifier.
These two groups represent the strictly bound end of a gradient from "tends to be possessed" to "cannot appear without an antecedent" .
A long-standing descriptive question concerns what triggers the affiliative form specifically.

Tamura (1988a: 27–28, as reported by Nakagawa 2024: 228) proposed a specificity condition: N₂ appears in the affiliative form only when N₁ is specific and individuated (kamuy rusihi 'that specific bear's pelt' vs kamuy rus 'bear-pelt in general', which is almost a compound) ‹contested›.
Satō objects that the affiliative does appear with non-specific possessors — aynu opitta honihi kor 'all humans have a belly' — which would be excluded by a strict specificity condition ‹contested›.

Nakagawa's 2024 account resolves the tension by placing the conditioning in morphosyntax rather than semantics: whenever a person prefix is present, the affiliative form is required; specificity then emerges as a tendency rather than a categorical trigger, because inalienable possession of an individuated entity is simply the most common context for person-prefix use .

Nakagawa further notes that the sharp "has/lacks affiliative form" dichotomy, sometimes presented as a fixed lexical property, is overstated: given an appropriate relational context, most common nouns can in principle take an affiliative form .
The noun illustrates the gradient: as a formal-noun plural marker utar is uninflected, but as a common noun 'relatives, companions' it has an affiliative form utari(hi).

Community discussion has noted that, because it is hard to conceive of 'companions not belonging to anyone', this common noun surfaces almost exclusively in its affiliative form as 'N's family/companions' (thegodofneet, 2025-09-17) ‹contested›, extending Nakagawa's account of the same ambiguity at .
Kinship terms split into two sets with different possession constructions, and the assignment is lexically specified.
Terms using the kor-construction (concept form): ku=kor hapo 'my mother', ku=kor mici 'my father'.
Terms using the affiliative construction: ku=turesi 'my younger sister (sister's viewpoint)', ku=yupihi 'my elder brother' .
Within Hokkaido there is considerable dialect variation in the assignment of individual kinship terms to one set or the other .
A further division concerns address vs reference.

Several kinship terms — among them ona 'father', unu 'mother', yup 'elder brother', and sa 'elder sister' — are restricted to third-person reference and cannot be used in direct address; each has an address counterpart.

The restriction correlates with the grammatical pattern: only the affiliative form combines with a person prefix, so a term that cannot be addressed directly tends not to appear with first- or second-person possessor marking .
Kinship possession in full, including suppletive address forms and the dialect-by-dialect distributions, is treated in .
Inalienable-class membership is partly dialect-specific and partly lexeme-specific.
takes both the kor-construction and the affiliative construction equally in Saru; uses only the kor-construction (a=kor mosir; *a=mosirihi is ungrammatical) .
These lexeme-specific idiosyncrasies are part of the lexical entry and are not predictable from semantics alone.
Refsing notes comparable fluctuation in Shizunai, where some body-part stems allow either construction .
The full alienable/inalienable distinction, adnominal possession constructions, and the interaction of possession with nominal number and person marking are developed in , , and .
Locative nouns form a small, closed subclass expressing spatial and temporal relations ('above', 'below', 'in front of', 'beside', 'inside').
Four properties set them apart from common nouns ; :
The basic form cannot stand alone as an NP. Type-1 locative nouns require an immediately preceding antecedent NP (the spatial reference point).
Without it, *ka wa ran 'came down from above' with bare ka is ungrammatical; only the long form can head a clause independently (§ below).

Long-form derivation differs from the common-noun affiliative. Common nouns use a vowel-copy suffix (the -hV mechanism) predictable from the stem's final vowel; locative long forms use a distinct suffix set — -ke, -V, -si — that is lexically specified per item and follows different morphophonological patterns.
The overlap between the two systems may be historical: Nakagawa hypothesises that common-noun type-③-2 morphology was borrowed from the locative system ‹speculative›.

Both forms take the objective person affix. Common nouns in the affiliative construction take the nominative (possessive) prefix; locative nouns take the objective prefix: en=sam un 'to beside me' (1SG.O prefix en= on ) vs ku=tekehe 'my hand' (1SG.A/possessive prefix ku= on ) .
Both forms always function as ⟨place⟩. Locative nouns can be directly followed by the locative particle ta: kasi ta 'on top of it'.
A common noun cannot do this: *nupuri ta is ungrammatical; 'at the mountain' requires an intervening locative noun, nupuri or ta ('at [the inside of] the mountain') .
Nakagawa further divides locative nouns into two types .
Type-1 nouns require an immediately preceding antecedent NP in the basic form; in the long form they can head a clause alone.

Type-2 nouns can stand in the basic form without naming a reference point, making them syntactically closer to common nouns, though they retain the locative-noun properties of ⟨place⟩ status and objective-affix agreement.

The distinction between etok (front of a moving entity or linear path; temporal 'before') and kotca (front of a stationary entity) carries real semantic weight: i=etok omare 'placed in front of me [as a moving being]' means the referent was set ahead on the path, not merely in the visual field .
Similarly, oka (back of a moving entity; temporal 'after') and osmak (back of a stationary entity) form a paired contrast.
The locative noun has developed an extended use in several Hokkaido dialects, functioning as a broad oblique marker; its grammaticalization in Chitose is documented in .

Some researchers classify Type-2 locative nouns — kim, soy, rik, and the like — as common nouns on the grounds that they appear independently in the basic form, a property otherwise confined to common nouns.

Nakagawa retains them as locative nouns on two grounds: their long-form morphology follows the locative-noun pattern rather than the common-noun affiliative system, and their obligatory ⟨place⟩ status distinguishes them from any common noun, which would require a locative noun to mediate its use with ta ‹contested›.

One community observation proposes that the long forms of locative nouns carry a definiteness or high-specificity marking, which might explain why first- and second-person pronominal reference is expressed on the long form rather than the basic form (antitwilight, 2024-11-17) ‹speculative›.
This hypothesis is not attested in the primary-source grammars; it awaits cross-dialectal elicitation.
The directional adverbs derived from Type-2 forms (ekimne 'toward the mountains', okimne 'from the mountains'; esoyne 'outward') and the full locative-noun possessive paradigm are treated in .

Proper nouns form no grammatically distinct class in Hokkaido Ainu: they are an open subset of common nouns, distinguished by reference type rather than by any morphological marker, case distinction, or definiteness operator ; .
Many place names are transparently compositional: Poropet 'big river' (poro + ), Siretoko 'tip of the land' ( + etoko) .
One property that distinguishes proper nouns from common nouns in practice: Hokkaido personal and place names do not appear in affiliative forms under normal conditions, unlike many common nouns .
Sakhalin Ainu permits affiliative forms of personal names — ku=Harumihi 'my Harumi' is attested — but this pattern is absent from the Hokkaido data.

Personal-name avoidance, the practice of late and deliberately unflattering naming to deflect malevolent attention, and the classification of kamuy names as proper vs common reflect cultural conventions rather than grammatical rules .

Personal pronouns — kani 'I', eani 'you (2SG)', coka 'we (exclusive)' — share the common-noun property of standing alone as NP arguments but differ from common nouns in that they cannot head relative clauses: there is no grammatical Ainu equivalent of English 'the I who is sleeping' .
Their paradigms, dialect variants, and the fourth-person forms are treated in .
Formal nouns — also glossed as noun particles (名助詞) — occupy the bottom of the autonomy hierarchy.
Unable to appear as bare NP arguments, they nominalise a preceding clause or prenominal element into an NP head .
The class includes ~ , , , , , and the evidential nominalizers , , , and , whose possessed forms build the evidential paradigm .

The class is defined and its membership criteria set out in ; the nominalization function of p/pe and hi in relative-clause and complement constructions is treated in ; the four evidential nominalizers are treated in , , , , and .

Among the four noun subclasses of Hokkaido Ainu, the formal noun (形式名詞 keishiki meishi) occupies the lowest position in the independence hierarchy: none of its members can stand alone as a predicate argument.
Each must be preceded by a verb phrase, a prenominal, or — in one exceptional case — a bare noun, from which it draws its referential content ; .
The diagnostic that separates formal nouns from the three other subclasses (common, locative, and pronominal nouns) is set out in .
Nakagawa also calls them noun particles (名助詞 meijoshi), reflecting their particle-like attachment to the preceding element .
The terminology used for this class is unsettled ‹contested›.

divides what Nakagawa treats as a single class into two: nominalizers (名詞化辞 meishikaji) head content clauses with full argument structure, while formal nouns proper head relative clauses from which one argument is missing.
Both are distinct noun subclasses in his account.

Nakagawa keeps the single class label and instead distinguishes the role a formal noun plays clause by clause: as relativizer it heads a clause with a missing argument; as complementizer (補文標識 hōbun hyōshiki) it heads a clause with full argument structure, the diagnostic being arity — a clause summing to arity zero takes a complementizer, one with a net argument gap heads a relative construction .
uses nominalizer more broadly still, grouping items that other analyses class as mood-morphemes, complementizers, and relative-clause heads within a four-type nominalization typology ‹contested›.
The full accounts of relativization and complementation are in and ; the evidential constructions are in .
lists two sets.
The general set covers a range of relational senses; the sensory-evidential set (his Table 66) consists of affiliative forms of sensory nouns grammaticalized as evidential heads.
The four sensory-evidential formal nouns form a paradigmatic sub-set.
Each is the affiliative form of a sensory noun and heads one evidential construction ( Table 66):
The possessed morphology follows the standard affiliative pattern for monosyllabic open-syllable nouns: ru → ruwe(he), haw → hawe(he), and so on .
Four properties distinguish formal nouns from the other noun subclasses as a group .
Obligatory modification. A formal noun cannot constitute an NP on its own.
*pe, *hi, and *kur are not grammatical arguments in isolation.
This places formal nouns at the foot of the independence hierarchy set out in Nakagawa's Table 48 — below the locative noun's basic form, which at least requires only an immediately preceding NP.

No self-relativization. A formal noun cannot serve as the head of a separate modifying clause in the ordinary sense: *pirka ruwe 'a good track (as NP)' and *pon kur 'a small person (as NP)' are ungrammatical as true relativizations, where an external clause predicates something of the formal noun itself .

No free attributive modifier. When a prenominal demonstrative precedes a formal noun, the result is not a compositional NP but a fused pronoun-like form: tan + pe → tanpe 'this thing', toan + pe → toanpe 'that thing' .

Phonological fusion. p ~ pe and hi fuse prosodically with the preceding element, behaving synchronically like suffixes, even though each nominalizes the entire preceding VP rather than only the adjacent word .

Distribution asymmetry within the class. The antecedent constraint is not uniform: hi requires a VP antecedent; p ~ pe takes a VP or a prenominal but not a bare NP; utar exceptionally accepts a bare NP as well (cikappo utar 'small birds') ; .
The nominalizer ~ is the most productive member of the set.
It attaches to any VP and yields either a relative-clause head (entity reading, with a missing argument) or a content complement (propositional reading, full argument structure) ; .
The allomorph is phonologically conditioned: p follows a vowel-final VP; pe follows a consonant-final VP .
As a relative-clause head, p ~ pe nominalizes a VP with a missing argument:

A productive instrumental pattern uses p ~ pe to nominalize an applicative VP: ani X p 'the thing with which one does X', as in ani e=kanpinuye p 'pencil' (literally 'the thing with which you write') and ani humi a=aste p 'musical instrument' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-05-29) .
The instrumental ani fills the applicative argument slot while p nominalizes the whole VP ‹corpus-confirmed›.
When a prenominal demonstrative precedes pe, the result is a demonstrative pronoun: tanpe 'this (thing)', neap 'that previously mentioned thing', and the rest of the series treated in .
The full syntax of p ~ pe — its arity-based relativization/complementation split and clause-linker interactions — is in .
The formal noun accepts only a VP antecedent and characteristically nominalizes the state of affairs described by the clause — the content-complement reading — without a missing argument .
hi also supplies the morphological base of several personal pronouns.

The first-person singular kani derives from ku=an-hi 'the thing/fact of my existing', reduced by regular vowel contraction; c(i)oka(y) 'we (exclusive)' from ci=oka(y) + reduction; and asinuma from a= + sinuma ; .
The full pronoun paradigm is in .
hike 'the one (that …)' is an anaphoric relative head derived from hi by the concretizing suffix -ke — the same element that yields arke 'half' and sake 'refrain-melody' from their bases .

The suffix -ike that appears in lexicalized items such as onneike 'parent/elder' (< onne 'old' + -ike 'person/entity', per Chiri's gloss; noted by antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-15) may represent the same element in a lexicalized compound; the synchronic productivity of bare -ike as a nominalizing suffix is a proposed analysis ‹contested›.
katu 'state, manner' nominalizes the manner or condition described by a clause; it appears in the frame … katu ene an hi 'such is the state of affairs' as a manner complementizer .
uske 'place' and usi(ke) 'time/place' head NPs denoting the location or occasion of an activity:
The Tokachi/Ishikari form ihi is a regionally restricted variant confined in attested data to the fixed frame ene an ihi 'such a thing' .
Nakagawa's diachronic hypothesis — that hi is the historical source of the affiliative suffix -i (as in sik-i(-hi) 'its eye') — is discussed under ‹speculative›
The formal noun heads NPs denoting a person or agent.
As a relativizer it takes a VP antecedent.
As a class-term head it combines with the adnominal un to form demonyms: Sar un kur 'a Saru person', Iyoci un kur 'a Yoichi person' .
In the Hokkaido corpus kur ranks at position 98 (2,461 tokens), consistent with its dual role as agent-denoting nominalizer in narrative and as a class-term head.
The formal noun is the purpose and intention complementizer.

It follows a finite clause and establishes its content as a goal or the object of a mental-state verb: with the transitive verb ramu 'think/believe', the correct embedding is kuni a=ramu 'think that …', contrasting with the quotative frame sekor a=ye 'say that …', which selects a directly reported assertion rather than a propositional attitude (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-09) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The related carries a negative-purpose or indirect-question reading.
includes both in the nominalizer list alongside hi and p ~ pe.
Their full syntax — interaction with purpose adverbials, desiderative and abilitative predicates, and control — is in .
ruwe, siri, hawe, and humi are the affiliative forms of four sensory nouns and constitute the formal-noun stratum of the evidential system ; .
Each requires a finite VP antecedent, none stands alone as a predicate argument, and each is followed by a predicate — typically the copula ne — that closes the evidential construction.

A morphological point distinguishes evidential use from the full lexical affiliative: the lexical form may carry an additional extension (ruwehe, humihi), whereas the evidential formal noun blocks it — *ruwehe ne is ungrammatical as the inferential evidential .

Dialect variation affects the morphological shape: southern Hokkaido (Saru, Chitose) uses the possessed forms ruwe / siri / hawe / humi, while Tokachi and Ishikari often use the bare concept forms ru / sir / haw / hum in the same evidential construction .
Both shapes head the same frame.

The semantic distinctions among the four — the source-type hierarchy, the indirect evidential frames (siri an, hawe as), and the scope of the evidential over the embedded TAM system — are treated in the dedicated chapters: , , , and .
The architecture common to all four is in .
The sensory-evidential set makes the grammaticalization cline transparent.

The lexical noun denotes a physical trace; its affiliative form ruwe 'the trace of —' extends to any trace including an epistemic one; clause-final [clause] ruwe ne then asserts the clause content as established fact ; .
The parallel paths for sir, haw, and hum are transparent from the inventory table.

The result is only partial grammaticalization: the lexical source remains recoverable and the choice of post-nominal predicate (ne vs an) still matters, placing these forms at an intermediate point on the cline .
The non-evidential formal nouns stand at a later stage.

hi has no independent lexical noun use in modern Hokkaido Ainu; its original sense survives only in the pronoun-formation structures described above and, by Nakagawa's hypothesis, in the affiliative suffix -i.
p ~ pe is likewise fully bound; its affiliative-form origin in the monosyllabic open-syllable class (cf.
ru → ruwe(he), ci → ciye(he)) is preserved in the paradigm of monosyllabic nouns but no longer lexically active .

The two-stage path — lexical noun → possessed formal noun → complementizer or evidential head — is the mechanism through which Hokkaido Ainu builds clause-embedding without infinitives or dedicated particle complementizers.

The point has been noted in the community discussion (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-25) : in a head-marking language where every embedded clause carries its own person marking, the formal noun provides the NP wrapper that the embedding construction requires, substituting for the infinitive strategies of other language types ‹contested›.
The full treatment of relativization, complementation, and the arity diagnostic is in , , and .
Verbs are the class of words that head clausal predicates and carry person-marking for their arguments ; .
The class inventory and its formal diagnostics are established in .

Within the verbal class, Nakagawa organizes the subclasses along two partially independent axes: argument count (how many core nominal arguments the verb governs) and affix set (which portion of the person paradigm the verb admits) ; .
works within the same bipartite framework with slightly different labelling; both follow the scheme of .

places Ainu verbs in a broader macro-class (Verbals) that covers what the present taxonomy separates into intransitive, transitive, and copular verbs, without further subdivision by valence internally.
The pedagogical account in uses the person-affix set as its primary classificatory criterion, organizing the verb inventory in the same way.

Two further structural types cross-cut the table: locative-object verbs (場所目的語動詞), which take a locative phrase in the O position, and serial predicates (連動詞), in which two stems share argument slots.
Both are introduced below and described in depth in .
The valency-changing morphology that moves verbs between classes — applicatives, causative affixes, the antipassive prefix i-, and the transitivizer -ka — is treated in .
Assigning a verb to a subclass amounts to determining which argument roles its affixes encode.
The Hokkaido Ainu personal-affix paradigm distinguishes three roles: S (sole argument of an intransitive), A (subject of a transitive), and O (object of a transitive).
The full paradigm and its mixed alignment are set out in ; what matters here is its use as a classificatory probe.
A verb whose subject takes S affixes and permits no O affix is intransitive.
A verb whose subject takes A affixes and whose object takes O affixes is transitive.
A verb that takes A affixes on its subject but licenses no O-affix slot is copular.
The first singular provides the sharpest probe because 1SG distinguishes S=A (ku=) from O (en=).

At fourth person the contrast is still more transparent: the intransitive subject bears the suffix =an, the transitive subject the prefix a=, and the transitive object the prefix i= — three distinct exponences for three distinct roles ; .
Subclass membership is grammatical, not semantic.
The verb is transitive — it licenses A and O affixes — even though its meaning is stative.
The verb is intransitive for the same semantic domain.
The diagnostic difference is purely morphological.

This contrast was highlighted in community discussion: *sekor a=ramu an is ungrammatical because ramu requires the transitive A prefix a=, not the intransitive S suffix =an (nukopoli, 2024-11-09) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
One-place predicates assign a single S role.

The class is large and semantically heterogeneous: it encompasses motion predicates (, , , ), postural predicates (), cognitive and emotional predicates (, ), and the large class of property predicates (, , , ) that in other languages would be adjectives.
All share the S affix set; no O slot is available.
Property predicates — stative predicates describing qualities or states — take the identical S affixes as action intransitives, and head bare predicates without a copula.
The third person is zero, so a property verb in a simple declarative clause carries no overt person affix:
The argument for treating property predicates as intransitive verbs rather than as a separate adjective class — and the morphological evidence for that analysis — is developed in .
The predication of property concepts without a copula is treated in .

Within the intransitive class the descriptive literature distinguishes two semantic groupings: agentive intransitives, whose S argument is volitional and agent-like (motion, action, and activity predicates), and patientive intransitives, whose S argument is an experiencer or the subject of a state (property predicates, involuntary experience verbs).
The basic person-affix paradigm does not encode this contrast morphologically: both groupings select the same S affix set across all persons .
The agreement system is therefore not split-intransitive in the morphological sense — S-set assignment depends only on valence, not on the agent-vs-patient character of the S argument.
Whether semantic or lexical criteria support a deeper Split-S or Fluid-S analysis ‹contested› is examined in and .
Two-place predicates assign an A role to their subject and an O role to their object.
When both arguments are non-third-person, each may be person-indexed on the verb.
The ceiling is two indexes per verb — one A index and one O index — and a third argument is never indexed ; .
Third-person arguments surface as bare noun phrases.
One morphological consequence of transitivity is that verbal number marks plurality of the object, not the subject.

The suppletive pair and signals how many entities are killed, regardless of how many kill: the intransitive S and the transitive O are treated alike for number marking, in an ergative-like pattern (nukopoli, 2023-12-12) ‹consensus›.
The full system of number-sensitive stems and the pluractional suffix -pa are treated in .

A lexically small set of predicates takes three argument slots: subject (A), a primary object (typically a recipient or addressee), and a secondary object (typically a theme or propositional content).
The principal members are , , and , along with morphologically complex forms derived from them ; ; .
Because the verb carries at most two person indexes, the second object is unindexed when it is third person.
The indexed O slot falls on the recipient or the more animate participant; the theme or propositional content remains a bare noun phrase.
When both non-subject arguments are third person, only A is indexed:
A related pattern arises with the serial construction : its A role indexes on the action verb while the recipient role indexes on the relational noun , giving en=aske e=uk 'you invite me'.

Satō calls this type 連他動詞 (serial transitive); it is the clearest case of a wider class of serial predicates in which argument slots are shared between adjacent stems ; (nukopoli, 2024-11-17) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Whether the language is best analysed as secondary-object or secundative for this argument pattern, and how three-place structure interacts with applicative morphology, is taken up in and .
Three predicates hold a special position in the taxonomy: the copula , the existentials and , and the negative existential .
They function as predication operators and each admits a distinctive affix set.
The copula heads equative and classificatory clauses of the structure [NPsubject — NPpredicate — ne].
Its affix behaviour places it with the transitive class: the subject takes A-type affixes, not S.
At first singular this means ku=ne 'I am X', with the same prefix ku= that marks the A of a transitive verb.
The predicate nominal, however, carries no O person index regardless of its person or number.
Nakagawa groups this under a separate copular affix set — alongside the intransitive and transitive sets — precisely because it is A-marked on the subject yet has no object-affix slot ; .
The copula also covers the translative reading 'become X': the same form serves both equative and inceptive predication in context .
The full treatment of copular predication and its TAM and evidential extensions is in .
The existential is strictly intransitive.
It takes S affixes, and the located entity is its S argument; the locative phrase specifying the location is an oblique adjunct, not an O.

The diagnostic contrast with the transitive existential-locative is crisp: an requires a locative-case frame (cise or ta an 'is in the house'), while un takes the location as a direct O and may carry an O person affix (nukopoli, 2024-11-09) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The existential paradigm — an, oka, and their progressive and resultative extensions — is treated in .
The negative existential predicates non-existence of its S argument.
In possession frames it serves as the negative counterpart of .
Its inflection and possessed-construction interaction are treated in and .
One community observation bears noting: in certain negative frames (ka somo ne 'it is not the case that…') and occasionally elsewhere, ne appears without a person affix.
The reason is not settled in the accessible sources (nukopoli, 2023-12-25) ‹speculative›.
The negation–copula interaction is discussed in .
Nakagawa's arity framework reserves a zero-place (完全 / 0項) category for predicates that take no referential core argument .
The category is defined formally: a zero-place predicate has no argument-affix slot, not merely an impersonal or unspecified subject.

On the arity account, a clause whose total argument count resolves to zero takes a complementizer rather than heading a relative-clause nominalization , which connects this class to the complementizer-vs-nominalizer distinction treated in .
The sources read for this chapter did not bank specific lexical members of the zero-place class .
A fuller inventory and the syntactic treatment of avalent predicates — including weather expressions and impersonal event frames — are provided in .
Two structural types cut across the valence-based taxonomy and have word-class consequences.
Locative-object verbs (場所目的語動詞) take a locative noun phrase in the structural position of the O argument, and the locative receives an O-type person affix in the paradigm.
The subject of these verbs takes A affixes, making them transitive in their affix behaviour even though their object is a location rather than an entity.
The valency of verbs taking place or space as an argument is examined in ; .
Ambitransitive patterns arise where the same stem alternates between an S-marked (intransitive) frame and an A-marked (transitive) frame depending on whether an O argument is present.

The alternation is closely related to the productivity of denominal and deverbal derivation: Ainu intransitive verbs freely convert to noun-modifying and compound-forming roots, and transitivisers can reinstate a transitive frame ; .
Both types, and the full inventory of valency-alternating morphology, are described in .
The applicative system that promotes locatives into O position is treated in , and the antipassive that converts transitives to intransitives in .
Words expressing property concepts — , , , , , , , — are intransitive verbs in Hokkaido Ainu.

They take the nominative person affixes of the intransitive-subject set, predicate without a copula, derive manner adverbs with the suffix -no, and enter the same causative and applicative morphology as action verbs.
No separate adjective class is warranted ; ; ; ; ‹consensus›.
The clause-level consequences — property verbs predicating without a copula, the person-index frame, the interaction with negation — are treated in .
The word-class system as a whole, including the diagnostic criteria that separate verbs from nouns, adverbs, and adnouns, is established in .
The -no adverbializer is documented in ; causative counterparts of property verbs (e.g.

Three independently sufficient lines of evidence converge on the verbal classification of property words ; .

Property verbs occupy the predicate slot and receive the intransitive-subject (S) person prefix — the same prefix set as action intransitives, and distinct from the transitive-subject (A) set that nouns cannot host in this position at all.

Third-person predication is zero-marked — the same zero as on all third-person intransitive predicates, with no copula:
The same pattern holds prenominally: a property verb precedes the noun without any morphological change, identical to an action verb in attributive position.
pon hekaci 'small child' (property verb + noun ) deploys the same verb-before-noun construction as apkas utar arki ruwe ne 'the walking people came' (action verb prenominally) .
In neither case does the verb carry an attributive morpheme or particle.

The causative suffix -re (and its allomorphs -e, -ka) attaches to property verb stems when the semantics licenses a causative reading, producing transitive counterparts exactly as it does from action intransitives .

*hure ne for 'become red' and *poro ne for 'become big' are ungrammatical: the inchoative reading is already carried by the bare property verb, and the copula ne in that position constructs a nominal predicate ('be/become a —'), a structurally distinct construction treated in ; .
The three arguments above translate into a battery of formal diagnostics that separate property verbs from the other word classes in Nakagawa's inventory ; :
The first four diagnostics align property verbs with verbs and against both nouns and adnouns.

Diagnostic five — prenominal modification without morphological change — is shared between property verbs and adnouns, which accounts for the apparent adjective-like quality of items like and in noun-modifying position.
Diagnostic seven shows that property verbs also enter the -p/-pe nominalization slot exactly as action verbs do.
presents property verbs as intransitive stative verbs throughout the pedagogical guide, with no separate adjective paradigm and with stative versus inchoative readings resolved by context.
groups property words in the intransitive verb class without an adjective subclass.
reaches the same conclusion for the Shizunai dialect.
Three items have been taken to suggest a residual adjective class: (a) the adnoun (連体詞) class proper, (b) the specific items and , and (c) Kindaichi's pre-1942 grammar.
Nakagawa establishes a genuine adnoun class (連体詞) defined by morphosyntactic criteria: members modify a noun, cannot serve as a predicate, and take no person affix ; .

Its inventory comprises demonstratives (tan 'this', toan 'that', ne 'the aforementioned'), numeric prenominals (sine 'one-', tu 'two-'), interrogatives (hemanta 'which kind'), indefinites, and a residual set of general adnouns — oar 'one-of-a-pair', kes 'every', pinne 'male', matne 'female', oya 'other' .
None of these carries a property meaning in the sense relevant to adjective typology; class membership rests entirely on the morphosyntactic diagnostics above.
The demonstrative prenominals and their discourse-anaphoric subsets are treated in .
and appear as predicates — a=kor cise poro=an 'my house is big' (constructed) — and as prenominal modifiers — poro nupuri 'a big mountain'.
In prenominal position they are surface-identical to adnouns, because neither position displays person-affix morphology.
The predicate data, however, show that they take S-affixes like other property verbs; Nakagawa classifies them as verbs ; .

Place names attest their prenominal frequency particularly clearly: Poro-pet 'big river' and Pon-bets 'small river' are compounds of the type intransitive-verb-root + noun → nominal , the same formation available to any intransitive verb root.

The broader verb-centredness of Ainu nominal derivation — in which nearly every noun has a simultaneous intransitive-verb reading and noun-formation operates principally through verbal roots — supports classifying poro and pon as verbs whose prenominal distribution happens to be prominent (antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-06-02) ‹contested›.
§189–190 posits a 形容詞 (adjective) class with predicative person-inflection (形容詞の人稱變化), attributive use (連体形), and a participial form (分詞形容詞).
The predicative paradigm uses the same intransitive-subject prefixes as verbs — the observation that ultimately enabled the merger.

argued that since adjective-meaning words and action verbs share their full inflectional frame, their person-marking morphology, and their clause-final behaviour, positing two classes serves no formal purpose.
Chiri coined 用詞 (yōshi) for the merged class, and the no-adjective analysis has been standard since then ‹consensus›.
The term 用詞 is no longer in use; the merged class is simply 動詞 (verb) in current work ; .
A residual nuance concerns the clause-linking particles wa and no.
wa links clauses whose predicate describes a state (pirka wa 'since it is good'), while no links clauses describing a dynamic event (somo ipe no 'without eating').
Because property verbs cluster at the static pole, the contrast was sometimes read as a syntactic trace of an adjective/verb boundary.
demonstrates that the split tracks the static/dynamic semantic axis of the whole VP — it does not mark a part-of-speech boundary within the verbal system ‹consensus›.
The linking contrast is examined in .
Degree and comparison are expressed through verbal and adverbial means, not through dedicated adjectival morphology.

The postpositional adverb takes an object-marked antecedent and frames the comparison with a bare property verb predicate unchanged in form: en=pirka akkari pirka=an 'you are more beautiful than I am' (constructed).
Degree adverbs such as and modify a property verb directly, and the equative uses .
In every pattern, the property verb itself remains morphologically unchanged — which follows from its verbal status, since Ainu verbs in general carry no degree inflections.
These strategies are documented with corpus examples in .

In the typological survey of intransitive predication, languages range from those encoding property concepts in a dedicated open-class adjective (English, Russian) to those using a verbal strategy, where property words are simply intransitive stative verbs, to those using a nominal strategy ; .

Hokkaido Ainu falls squarely in the verbal-encoding type by every formal diagnostic: property words pattern with verbs in their morphology and predication, and no morphological or syntactic slot is reserved for adjectives alone ‹consensus›.
This places Ainu with Japanese and Korean, whose 形容詞 class is itself a closed verbal category.

Nakagawa draws the parallel explicitly: Ainu "adjectives" are verb-type — modifying a noun directly without an attributive morpheme — in contrast to the noun-type strategy where a linking particle or agreement marker intervenes .
states the outcome concisely: "adjective-meaning words become predicates without any copula, in exactly the same way as verbs."

A community hypothesis in the aynu-corpora discussion archive proposes that the existential in forms like pirka an 'be good; become good' might represent a distinct aspect marker for onset of state — parallel to ne an 'become X' alongside copular ne 'be X' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-15) ‹speculative›.

The bare corpus data show pirka an collocating with inchoative-oriented translations in certain narrative frames, but no primary source in the descriptive literature distinguishes a grammaticalized onset-of-state use of an here from its ordinary existential value.
The hypothesis is noted as a lead for further corpus investigation.
The principal derivational suffix operating on Hokkaido Ainu nouns for size and affect is , which attaches to a noun stem to yield a derivative meaning 'small X' or 'dear X' ; ; .
No productive augmentative suffix — a suffix encoding 'large X' — is described for Hokkaido Ainu in any of the grammatical treatments consulted.
Upward size modification relies on the prenominal property verb , used attributively before a noun without morphological change (see ).
Morphological encoding of size is therefore asymmetric: the diminutive has a suffix, the augmentative does not ‹consensus›.

Three features of merit individual treatment: its etymological identity with the free noun , its lexicalization into a subset of animal names where the base is no longer a free morpheme, and a Horobetsu colloquial meaning extension to 'deceased (intimate)' not reported for other dialects .
attaches to the concept form of a noun stem.
The output is itself a common noun in the concept form and may take the affiliative suffix in the normal way .

Nakagawa explicitly excludes the suffix from compound-noun formation: a form such as cikappo is a modifier-derived nominal, not a compounding element, and the person-affix and affiliative-suffix diagnostics that distinguish compounds from modifier–noun sequences classify derivatives as single-word outputs that function as ordinary free nouns .
The form is invariant across the Hokkaido dialects documented in the sources read here, and the suffix integrates phonologically with no reported junctural changes.
The table illustrates the range of base nouns: inanimate (supuya), animate non-human (cikap, cep), and human (menoko, okkay).
For the special status of okkaypo — which is ambiguous across dialects between the DIM reading and a noun–noun reading — see the section on the homophony below.
Kindaichi and Chiri describe as a 指小辞 meaning 'small thing / dear thing' and trace it etymologically to the free noun .
Two semantic values are present in the attested data and are recognized by subsequent treatments ; .
The diminutive value encodes that the referent is smaller than the prototype of its class.

For ceppo 'small fish' this is size in the physical sense; for supuyapo 'faint smoke' it is reduced quantity or intensity rather than spatial extent — a scalar application of the suffix to a non-count noun.
The affective / hypocoristic value encodes endearment or intimacy without implying reduced size.
Kindaichi's example ku=sampepo 'my dear one' (lit. 'my little heart') illustrates pure affect: the referent is a person, not a physically small object .
The two values are not in complementary distribution — the same form carries both potential meanings — and context selects the dominant reading.
The following attested examples from Saru and Horobetsu narrative texts show in productive use.

In all three, the DIM derivative freely combines with the associative-plural formal noun (treated in ), and in the second and third examples the prenominal property verb stacks with the DIM derivative, confirming that the suffix and the prenominal are independent strategies.
The Saru examples confirm that cikappo and ceppo behave as ordinary common nouns that take utar as a plurality marker ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The Horobetsu example shows the same stacking in a second dialect, with the focus particle hene 'even' scoping over the entire pon cikappo utar phrase.
The high frequency of okkaypo alone — 1,462 tokens, rank 136 in the Hokkaido sub-corpus — confirms that DIM derivatives are a live and frequent nominal class ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Several Hokkaido Ainu animal names contain a synchronically opaque -po where the base noun is not independently attested as a free form.
The best-known case is .
Two analyses have been proposed in community scholarship, both identifying -po as the diminutive suffix .

One analysis holds that ise is an onomatopoeia for the rabbit's high-pitched call, so isepo originated as 'the small/dear thing that goes ise' — an expressive base plus the diminutive (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-11; palestine_2026, 2024-08-28) ‹speculative›.

A related line invokes the productive pattern by which an onomatopoeic base followed by -se yields a verb (compare pawse 'a fox calls', where paw is the cry, and rimse 'dance'), and treats ise in isepo as the base of such a nominalized verb with -po added (palestine_2026, 2024-08-28) ‹speculative›.
Neither analysis has been confirmed by a read primary grammatical source; the status of ise as an independent morpheme in contemporary Hokkaido Ainu is unclear ‹speculative›.
The broader pattern of class-term residues in animal and plant names — where a frozen element meaning 'bird', 'fish', or 'tree' is embedded in a lexicalized form — is treated in .

The -po pattern is structurally distinct: rather than a class-term head retained from a transparent compound, it is a derivational suffix that appears to have frozen at an earlier productive stage, once the base ise lost independent currency.
The suffix is homophonous with the free noun , and Nakagawa attributes the homophony to a shared etymology .
In okkaypo the ambiguity is productive and dialect-sensitive.
In Saru and Chitose, okkay does not occur as a free noun — it appears only inside derivatives — so okkaypo parses unambiguously as [bound root okkay + DIM] 'young man'.
In dialects where okkay is a free noun meaning 'man', the form is genuinely ambiguous: [okkay + DIM] 'young man' versus [okkayo 'male' + po 'child'] = 'son'.
The unambiguous form for the N+N reading in those dialects is okkayopo with the full base .
The free noun has an affiliative form poho and enters the kinship paradigm as an inalienably-possessed term: po:poho 'child — one's child' .
See and .

The grammaticalization from free noun to suffix plausibly runs through a modifier-like compounding stage ('small/dear child of' → 'small/dear instance of'), consistent with the shared affective semantics, though no read source provides a detailed trajectory ‹speculative›.

Kindaichi records a Horobetsu colloquial pattern in which attached to a term denoting an intimate acquires a 'deceased' reading: ku=akipo 'my late younger brother' and ku=kor operpo 'my late daughter' .

The semantic path from 'dear' to 'dearly departed' is pragmatically transparent — the affective value of the suffix bleeds into memorializing reference — but the extension is attested only in Horobetsu colloquial in the sources read here, and no modern grammar corroborates it for other Hokkaido dialects.
It is recorded as a single-source, dialect-specific datum ‹corpus-suggested›.
The grammatical resources for noun-level size reference extend beyond .
The prenominal property verbs and modify a following noun in the same position that all attributive stative verbs occupy, without morphological change (see and ).
Three distinctions between the suffixal and prenominal strategies matter grammatically.

First, derives a new lexical item — a common noun in the concept form — while the prenominal is a syntactic modifier that can be independently relativized, negated, and causativized: porore 'make big' (causative of the property verb) has no morphological parallel on a DIM derivative.
Second, the corpus examples above show pon stacking freely with DIM derivatives (pon cikappo, pon ceppo), confirming that the two strategies are grammatically independent.
Third, the suffix asymmetry — for small, no suffix for large — is not mirrored at the prenominal level, where covers large size just as freely as covers small.
The sources do not explain the origin of this one-sided suffix system ‹consensus›.
For the wider system of noun-deriving morphology, including deverbal noun formation and the productive nominalizer suffixes, see .
For verbal number suppletives whose selection interacts with nouns headed by DIM derivatives, see .
Hokkaido Ainu forms compound nouns by combining two or more roots into a single phonological and morphological word.
The process is productive across the lexicon and supplies much of the vocabulary for tools, animals, plants, social roles, and place names .
Its dedicated structural study is , whose framework Nakagawa (2024: 261–272) reworks in terms of the valency of the constituent roots.
The base structural type is the concatenation of two nominal concept forms: a modifier root followed by a head root, the head carrying the compound's semantic class.

Because intransitive verbs and nouns share the same form in Hokkaido Ainu — the same root functions as either class without morphological change (see ) — roots of any valency can serve as compound constituents.
Nakagawa identifies six surface input patterns; all reduce to the same underlying N+N type once intransitive roots are treated as nominal .

The resulting compound is right-headed: the head is the rightmost constituent, which determines the grammatical class of the whole and hosts the affiliative (possessed) suffix and personal possessive affixes.
The diminutive -po is explicitly excluded from compound formation — it is a derivational suffix on a finished noun, not a compound constituent (see ) .
A two-root sequence might be either a compound noun or a syntactic noun phrase (attributive verb or modifier noun + head noun).
Nakagawa (2024: 261–264) gives four diagnostics, all exploiting positional differences between one-word and two-word structures .
A possessive personal affix attaches at the left edge of the word it marks.
In a syntactic phrase it appears on the head noun alone; in a compound it appears outside the entire compound.
The pair below has the same referent but different morphological structure.
In the compound both poro and yupi appear in their concept (bare) forms; the affix is placed outside both.
The affiliative (possessed) suffix marks the noun it heads.
In a syntactic phrase it attaches to the head noun, leaving the modifier unsuffixed; in a compound it attaches to the outermost right edge of the whole compound.
When the meaning of the combination is not predictable from its parts, the sequence is necessarily a compound.

{' '} is a transparent syntactic phrase meaning 'a white bird'; (where retat is a sandhi reduction of retar and cir does not occur as a free form) is a lexicalized compound meaning specifically 'swan' .
The bound status of the second element and the non-compositional meaning together confirm the compound analysis.

The most practical criterion is the observation that two nominal concept forms placed in immediate sequence without intervening morphology always form a compound: the absence of any overt linker or predicative marking removes any phrase-level analysis .
The series built on the head illustrates the pattern.
The same head kap combines with to give ni-kap 'bark', and with to give cep-kap 'fish scales / fish skin' — a productive derivational series .

Because property verbs such as occur in concept form without any morphological marking, the only reliable way to distinguish a compound from an attributive phrase in ambiguous cases is the positional diagnostics above.
Hokkaido Ainu compound nouns are head-final (right-headed): the right constituent is both the semantic and morphological head.
This follows directly from the diagnostics: person affixes and affiliative suffixes mark the word-level node — the compound as a whole — not the internal head constituent alone .
At the constituent juncture the modifier typically appears in its concept (bare) form, with no linking morpheme; this is the default for the N+N, 1-arg-V+N, and N+1-arg-V types.
In type ⑤ below the modifier appears in the affiliative (possessed) form instead.
The morphophonological behavior of the affiliative suffix at such junctures is treated in .
Prosodically the compound constitutes a single phonological word with a single accent peak.

Community observation (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-09) records that cisekorkur 'head of household' and kotankorkur 'village chief' each carry their accent on the second syllable of the compound as a single word, with no secondary peak on either internal constituent ‹contested›.
The general account of compound prosody is in .
Nakagawa (2024: 267–272), building on , distinguishes six input patterns by the valency of the constituent roots.
The classification is arity-based: because intransitive verbs freely convert to nouns in Hokkaido Ainu, types ②–④ surface as the same N+N morphological structure as type ① .
Types ⑤ and ⑥ are morphologically distinct: ⑤ uses the affiliative form of the first element, and ⑥ places a transitive verb in the head position.
For types ②③ the intransitive root — including property verbs such as and — appears in what is synchronically a nominal concept form, since no verbal morphology is available inside the compound .
In type ⑤ the modifier appears in the affiliative (possessed) form, giving the compound a relative-clause reading: 'the one whose N V-s'.
The two examples below share the same head verb .
The affiliative morphology of the first constituent makes the compound inherently relational: the head noun functions as an implicit argument of the modifier verb.
This pattern overlaps with the external-possession construction treated in .
In type ⑥ the first element is a concept-form noun serving as the implicit object of a transitive verbal head.
The compound names the entity characterized by performing that action on that object type.
Type ⑥ is structurally close to noun incorporation (see ), the distinction being that the result here is a lexicalized nominal, not a predicate frame with an internal incorporated argument .
The modifier-head relationship in Hokkaido Ainu compounds is consistently endocentric: the head names the class of the referent and the modifier restricts or characterizes it.
Three sub-patterns recur.
The largest group has a modifier specifying material, origin, location, or a characteristic property of the head referent.
Place names illustrate the pattern transparently: derives from + ('large river'), and from + ('land's tip, cape') .
The same structure governs common-noun compounds: sisam-itak 'the Japanese language (as a named category)' is restrictive with as modifier ‹corpus-confirmed›.
A productive sub-pattern combines a noun, the possession verb , and the formal-class noun to name a person who possesses or is in charge of the first noun.
This N-kor-kur template is one of the few fully productive three-constituent patterns in the language.
The compound accent data (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024, ) confirms that cise-kor-kur and kotan-kor-kur are single words with second-syllable accent ‹contested›.
The same template extends to mosir-kor-kur 'ruler of the land' and similar formations.

This construction must be distinguished from the syntactic alienable possession phrase a=kor cise 'my house', where kor is a fully inflected transitive verb taking its own person prefix, not a bound medial element .
The possession constructions are treated in .
Two surface-similar structures differ in their grammatical and semantic status.

The syntactic NP kane cise 'a metal house' uses as a free-standing attributive noun; the first element cannot receive a personal affix for this relationship (*ku=kane cise as 'my metal's house' is not a grammatical possessive frame here), and the combination is compositional and productive with any house material .
A genuine compound, in contrast, passes the person-affix and affiliative-suffix tests and typically names a culturally fixed category.

The same applies to sequences with : a contextual phrase kamuy cise 'a spirit's house (in this context)' is attributive; a lexicalized compound naming a specific object type would be non-compositional and semantically restricted.
Pure coordinate compounds (copulative; both elements of equal rank) and exocentric compounds (whose semantic head is not expressed) are marginal in Hokkaido Ainu.

Community discussion (antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-06-02) proposes that this sparsity reflects the verb-centred character of Ainu nominal derivation: because most roots can serve as intransitive verbs, noun formation proceeds through verb+noun or noun+verb frames rather than noun+noun coordination ‹contested›.
The attested examples cited in the same discussion — as coordinate and as exocentric — function as lexical items rather than templates for new formation .

Deciding whether a given modifier+noun sequence is a compound or a syntactic phrase has direct orthographic and grammatical consequences: compounds are typically written solid (no space), phrases with a space between elements.
The diagnostics in the preceding section provide the formal criteria; their application requires attention to both morphological form and meaning.

A minimal orthographic contrast illustrates the semantic stake: sisam itak (two words) means 'speech/language of a Japanese person (in context)', while sisamitak (one compound word) means 'the Japanese language (as a named category)' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-05) ‹corpus-suggested›.
The compound reading adds a categorical, language-name interpretation absent from the phrase.
Accent reinforces the distinction: the compound bears a single peak, the phrase retains peaks on both members (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-20) .
Full treatment of the prosodic test is in .

presents the compound–phrase distinction as a key point for learners of Ainu, treating the presence or absence of internal syntactic modification (TAM morphology, person marking) on the first element as the diagnostic: a root bearing its own grammatical morphology is in a phrase; a root appearing directly before the head with no such morphology is a compound constituent.
This matches the morphological diagnostics above and makes the distinction accessible without reference to accent.
The boundary also marks the limit of noun incorporation.
The object incorporation construction shares the surface appearance of an N+V compound, but the incorporated noun remains an internal verbal argument rather than a constituent of a new nominal word.

Community discussion (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-25) notes that verbs taking an intransitive-type modifier present an ambiguity between incorporation and lexicalized compounding that cannot always be resolved by surface form alone ‹contested›.
Deverbal and denominal noun derivation via -p/-pe and related suffixes is treated in .
Hokkaido Ainu has no separate class of deverbal suffixes standing apart from the rest of the morphology.
The same formal elements that nominalise whole verbal phrases at the syntactic level also operate at the word-formation level to produce stable lexical nouns.

Three morphemes dominate the lexical deverbal layer: the nominalizer -p/-pe, the possessive/affiliative suffix -i/-hi (with its vowel-harmonic variants -e/-we), and the lexical class-noun heads 'person' and 'place/time'.
The diminutive -po and the full range of noun-to-noun compounding belong to and ; the reverse direction — noun-to-verb conversion — belongs to .
The boundary between a lexical deverbal nominal and a syntactic nominalized phrase turns on the arity of the base.
When all argument slots of a transitive verb are filled by bound person morphology, the resulting -p-final form has no open relativizable gap and is reanalysable as a dictionary-listed noun.
When a gap remains — when one slot is left open for the matrix argument — the construction is a syntactic relative clause or complement, treated in .
Nakagawa formalizes this with an arity calculus: a clause whose arity sums to zero supplies a complement; one summing to +1 heads a relative clause .
The formal-noun subclass that these heads belong to, and the full complementizer syntax, are developed there and in .
The nominalizer appears as p after a vowel-final form and as pe after a consonant-final one ; .
The conditioning is phonological and holds across Hokkaido dialects ‹consensus›.
The most common word-formation output of -p/-pe at the lexical level is a patient or agent nominal produced when both argument slots of a transitive verb are filled by bound person morphology.

'food' is the canonical illustration: synchronically a common noun listed as a dictionary headword , its morphological shape is a=e-p — the indefinite fourth-person agent a=, the transitive verb , and the nominalizer — 'that which one eats'.
When a gap is not lexically filled and one slot remains open, the form heads a syntactic relative clause rather than a stable noun.
Nakagawa's example makes the contrast:

The lexicalized forms are patient nominals when the subject slot is filled and the nominalizer closes the object position, and agent nominals when the object is lexically saturated and the subject supplied by a person prefix.

The instrument or manner reading — 'the thing associated with this action' — arises when neither argument is left open but the predication describes an activity rather than a state; it is determined by the semantics of the verb, not by morphological marking ‹consensus›.

A set of lexicalized nominals was formed when both argument slots of a transitive base were filled — the subject slot by the first-person exclusive prefix ci=, the patient slot by -p — before the form stabilized as a dictionary entry.

The word is the most-discussed example: nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-06; ) proposes the analysis ci=e-p 'the thing that we (exclusive) eat', with phonological reduction cie-p → cep on a par with the attested contraction kuani → kani ‹contested›.
No primary source states the etymology directly; Tamura's Saru dictionary lists cep without internal analysis .

The same community discussion (nukopoli, 2023-12-08; ) identifies cikarkarpe 'manufactured thing, handcraft' as ci=kar-kar-pe — exclusive subject, reduplicated stem kar-kar 'make', nominalizer pe after the consonant-final stem — consistent with the allomorphy and the compositional meaning ‹contested›.

A denominal analysis for 'teaching, lesson' rests on the same skeleton: nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-10; ) reads ca-nu-p, with ca 'mouth' as the base, an associative element -nu, and -p as nominalizer — 'the thing one gives with the mouth, moral precept'.
The compound verb ecanupkar 'to teach' supports the noun status of canup; the internal segmentation remains unconfirmed in the accessible grammars ‹contested›.
Alongside the ci=-initial type, the fourth-person agent prefix a= fills the subject slot to produce indefinite-subject nominals: a=e-p → aep 'food'.
The alternation between ci= (exclusive: we-not-you) and a= (indefinite: one in general) reflects the person system described in , not a difference in the nominalization itself.
A productive word-formation pattern builds instrument nouns via the postpositional adverb followed by a verbal stem and the nominalizer: ani [V] p/pe = 'the thing with which one V-s'.

Nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-05-29; ) documents this as a regular instrument-nominalization frame: ani e=kanpinuye p 'pencil' (lit. 'the thing to write characters with'), ani humi a=aste p 'musical instrument' (lit. 'the thing to make sound with') ‹corpus-confirmed›.
In each form the verb's argument slots are filled and p closes the zero-arity predication; the instrument reading is contributed by ani.
The construction shows that the word-level nominalizer can co-occur with adverbial adjuncts — not only with person prefixes — to saturate the argument frame before nominalization.
Two criteria distinguish a lexical nominal from a syntactic one.
Argument opacity: a lexicalized form has all slots filled and admits no modification by a relativizing matrix argument; a syntactic form projects an accessible gap.

Compositionality: the meaning of a syntactic nominalization follows from the predicate and the gap's role; a lexicalized item may carry conventionalized meaning that has drifted from any compositional reading — 'fish' is not synchronically recoverable as 'what we eat'.

The community observation (nukopoli, 2024-11-09; ) that -p(e) nominalizes without dropping an argument, unlike relativized clauses, aligns with Nakagawa's arity account : a=i=ye p 'the thing that one says' is well-formed because both the subject slot (a=) and the object slot (i=) are filled, whereas substituting a bare head noun is impossible (*a=i=ye kamuy) ‹consensus›.
The full syntax of the construction — the headless-relative and complement continuum, TAM marking inside the nominalized clause, insubordination in Tokachi — belongs to .

The suffix that forms the affiliative (possessed) form of common nouns — -i/-hi in general notation, with -e/-we as the shape after certain base types — also operates as a derivational morpheme when applied to sensory and perceptual noun bases, producing formal nouns capable of nominalizing a preceding clause.
The resulting form is morphologically a possessed nominal: ru-we is 'the trace of —', its implicit possessor being the event described by the nominalized clause.
The same possessed-noun morphology underlies all four members of the Hokkaido evidential set ; .
The possessed-form suffix follows the same five-type conditioning that governs the general affiliative paradigm ; .
The short form and the long form carry no semantic difference; the choice is prosodic .
For the four sense-noun bases that grammaticalize as evidential formal nouns, the suffix type follows directly from the base-final segment:

Each short form (ruwe, siri, humi, hawe) is the form that heads the evidential construction; the corresponding long forms (ruwehe, sirihi, humihi, hawehe) exist as ordinary lexical possessed nouns but are blocked from the evidential slot — Tamura marks this explicitly for each item .
The blocking of the long form from the evidential slot shows that the formal-noun use has been grammaticalized beyond the general affiliative paradigm ‹corpus-confirmed›.

Refsing, from Shizunai, reanalyses the same set as nominalizers rather than possessed nouns, treating them as one of four sentence-conversion types alongside conjunctionalization, quotationalization, and adnominalization .
Nakagawa retains the formal-noun word-class label and treats the evidential role as a grammatical function (complementizer) that certain formal nouns fill when arity is zero .
The two framings are compatible at the descriptive level, differing in whether the category label or the functional role is foregrounded ‹contested›.

Full treatment of the evidential semantics and syntax belongs to and the sibling evidential chapters; what matters here is that the deverbal process is the possessive-suffix morphology, and the evidential construction is the grammaticalization endpoint of a path that begins at lexical word-formation.
Two common nouns operate as productive denominative heads: 'person' and (also usike) / .
Neither is an agreement morpheme; Hokkaido Ainu has no numeral classifier system .
They are ordinary common nouns that follow a modifier (NP or VP) and supply a semantic class specification for the resulting compound.
kur forms person-denoting nominals from place names via the allative particle un: Sar un kur 'a Saru person', Iyoci un kur 'a Yoichi person' .
Corpus rank 98 (2,456 tokens in the Hokkaido texts) reflects how productively it combines.
The word-class diagnostics that distinguish kur from the formal-noun subclass — it heads an independent NP, takes attributive modifiers, and takes possession marking — are set out in .
usi(ke) and uske head locational nominals from a verbal phrase.
Nakagawa lists them under the formal-noun inventory (2024: 257–258; ); their full syntax as heads of VP nominalization constructions belongs to .
