Many Hokkaido Ainu nouns have corresponding intransitive verbs with no overt marking of the class difference.
Property words like 'be big' serve as noun modifiers — poro cep 'a big fish' — without any derivational suffix; word-class membership is assigned by the syntactic slot, not the form ; .

This zero-conversion is the default mechanism in compound nouns where an intransitive verb appears as the first element: Nakagawa's taxonomy of compound types (2024: 267–272) — 1-arg-verb+N, N+1-arg-verb, and 1-arg-verb+1-arg-verb — all reduce to N+N because the verbal element is freely reanalyzed as nominal in the modifier position .
'prayer discourse' (compound of + ) illustrates this path: the intransitive verb inonno 'pray' modifies itak 'speech' as the first element of a V+N compound with no nominalizing suffix.
What signals the nominal reanalysis is the compound's function as a common-noun argument and the person-affix position outside the whole compound, not between its elements.
The formal diagnostics for whether a sequence is a compound or two syntactic words belong to .

Antitwilight (aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-06-02; ) observes that Ainu has very few pure-noun coordinate compounds or exocentric N+N combinations, because noun-formation is verb-centred — nearly every noun can also serve as an intransitive verb, so N+N and V+N compounds are morphologically indistinguishable at the surface ‹contested›.
This sharpens Nakagawa's (2024: 116) principle that word-class membership is defined by syntactic role rather than form.
The verbal-number suppletion patterns that some deverbal nominals feed (e.g. singular ek vs. plural arki 'come') belong to .
The morphemes treated here as word-formation devices extend along a grammaticalization cline into clause-level nominalization and then into evidential and sentence-final positions.

Takahashi's study of the Horobetsu dialect shows that the formal-noun nominalizers — including p/pe and the possessive-suffix set — undergo a further stage in Horobetsu, functioning as adverbial clause markers and conjunction-like linkers in contexts that the better-documented southern dialects (Saru, Chitose) handle with other strategies .
The lexicalized deverbal nominals treated here are the initial pole of the cline; the Horobetsu data mark the far end within Hokkaido ‹corpus-suggested›.
Bugaeva's comparison of Hokkaido and Sakhalin nominalization identifies Sakhalin Ainu as having innovated in the nominalization system relative to the common ancestor.

One index of this difference is the treatment of the evidential formal nouns: in Sakhalin varieties the long possessed form (ruwehe, sirihi) is used in the evidential slot, whereas Hokkaido restricts that slot to the short forms and blocks the long form from evidential use (see the conditioning table above).
Whether this blocking is a Hokkaido retention or an innovation is an open question; the Sakhalin data frame it as a candidate for Hokkaido-internal change ‹speculative›.
Full comparative treatment is in and the sibling evidential chapters.
Hokkaido Ainu nouns carry no grammatical number.
A bare noun names a referent without specifying whether one or several are intended: is the form for 'a stone', '(the) stone', and 'stones' alike; the same holds for , , and ; .
In Corbett's typology this is the transnumeral pattern: the noun is underspecified for number rather than syncretically encoding a singular or plural value through a single form .
Obligatory singular/plural agreement of the kind found in English or French is absent.
Plurality may be made explicit by the formal noun , but this addition is strictly optional.
In the 209,878-sentence Hokkaido corpus utar records 8,051 tokens (rank 30 among distinct types) — high frequency reflecting pragmatic salience, not grammatical compulsion ‹corpus-confirmed›.
utar belongs to the closed class of formal nouns — weakly autonomous items that form an NP only when preceded by another element ; .
Its syntactic distribution is uniquely wide within that class.

Whereas hi ('thing/matter') takes only a VP host, and p/pe ('thing/one') takes a VP or prenominal, utar follows a VP, a bare common noun, or a prenominal — the only formal noun that can immediately follow a noun without an intervening predication ; .
Sources: ; .
When following a bare noun, utar adds a collective or associative plural reading without predicational content:
The broader distribution of formal nouns is treated in .
For the p/pe nominalizer in clausal contexts see .
The meaning of utar in pluralizing use is associative rather than strictly additive.

Kindaichi and Chiri's example acha utar arki translates as 'uncle and his group came', not 'several uncles came': the form implies a cluster of associates gathered around the named referent, potentially including members of different categories .
Ijäs's pedagogical grammar presents the same associative reading .
Whether utar is restricted to animate referents is a genuine disagreement ‹contested›.

Kindaichi and Chiri state that utar applies to persons and animals (kamuy utar, ainu utar, seta utar 'dogs', cikap utar 'birds'), and that suma utar 'stones' and ni utar 'trees' are disallowed unless the referent is personified .

Nakagawa, working from Saru material, takes the opposite position: utar freely pluralizes inanimates (suma utar, ni utar, rus utar 'furs', coypep utar 'lacquerware'), the extension to all entities motivated by the animist conception that every being carries a spirit .
The Saru corpus attests inanimate utar directly:

The discrepancy most likely reflects dialect variation rather than a uniform pan-Hokkaido norm: the animacy restriction appears stronger in eastern and classical-norm speech, while Saru extends utar to inanimates within the animist conceptual frame.

The two textbook illustrations do not fare alike in the corpus: suma utar 'stones' does not occur, but ni utar 'trees' does, in a Saru/Chitose prose report — nítay or ta ni utar ka poronno a=momka 'in the forest many trees too were swept away'.
forms: nítay or ta ni utar ka poronno a=momka

text: The inanimate extension therefore has attested support, thin though it is: two occurrences against none for the stone example ‹corpus-confirmed›.
One nominal has grammaticalized a dedicated plural form through phonological fusion with utar: + utar contracts to , which serves as the fixed plural of 'child' ; .
The corpus records 297 tokens of hekattar (rank 509), confirming lexicalization ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The fused form can itself be followed by another utar — hekattar utar — for additional collective emphasis .

A separate nominal strategy for inherent plurality is reduplication: chaichai 'twigs', kaukau 'hailstones', kankan 'intestines', and ramram 'scales' carry plural semantics through their reduplicated structure without requiring utar .
These are lexicalized; reduplication is not a productive synchronic plural strategy.
The productive resource for ad hoc pluralization remains utar or the verbal number morphology described in .
The string utar covers two related but functionally distinct items.
The first is the formal noun pluralizer described above.
The second is a full common noun meaning 'relatives, kin, companions', with its own affiliative form (long form utarihi), which surfaces under possession :
The referential scope of k=utari is strictly third-person: in k=utari ku=tura 'I took my family', the speaker does not belong to the group named.
Likewise, a=utari opitta totek wa oka 'is your family all well?' takes a third-person verb because the referent is the addressee's relatives, not an inclusive 'you all' .

The -utari that enters Tokachi anutari 'we (inclusive)' combined with a fourth-person verb edges toward pronominal function — Nakagawa characterises the form as 'halfway between pronoun and common noun' — but the full treatment of pronominal -utari belongs to .
The corpus records 1,501 tokens of utari (rank 130), mainly as a possessed group or kinship noun.

Community analysis has proposed that the affiliative form is nearly obligatory in this function because 'companions belonging to no one' is semantically anomalous — the noun almost always surfaces possessed (thegodofneet, 2025) ‹contested›.
This aligns with the general behaviour of the affiliative form across the Ainu noun paradigm: the possessed shape presupposes a contextually available referent to which the named entity belongs .
The semantics of utar as a common noun extends to kinship idioms.
utar ni nare 'become utar with someone' carries the meaning 'to marry (into a family)', since marriage incorporates one into a kin group (thegodofneet, 2025) ‹corpus-suggested›.

Kinship compounds on -utari can also name a pair rather than a plurality of the base: onautari and unuutari (literally 'father-group' and 'mother-group') denote 'parents' collectively (nukopoli, 2026) ‹corpus-suggested›.
For kinship-term morphology in detail see .

When plurality is information-structurally relevant, Hokkaido Ainu has two independent resources: nominal utar and the verb's own number morphology — suppletive stem alternations (ek / arki 'come', arpa / paye 'go') and the plural suffix -pa .
The two are independent: a noun phrase can carry utar without triggering a plural verb, and a plural verb can appear without nominal utar.

Certain mass-like nouns — supuya 'smoke', hura 'smell' — consistently govern plural verb forms (supuya at, hura at) even without utar, encoding the diffuse nature of the referent at the verb rather than the noun .
The plural verb stem is also sensitive to quantitative context.

Small, specified counts (two, three) regularly co-occur with the singular stem (tu hekaci ek 'two children came'), while large or unspecified quantities take the plural stem (inne hekattar arki 'many children came'); uncountable referents remain with the singular stem even alongside 'many' (nukopoli, 2024; attributed to Satō) ‹corpus-suggested›.
On transitive verbs the plural stem tracks plurality of the object, following the absolutive-aligned pattern: rayke (singular object) / ronnu (plural object) (nukopoli, 2023) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
These agreement thresholds and the S/O alignment of verbal number are developed in and .

In verse, speakers sometimes apply utar to a semantically singular referent for metrical reasons, or omit it from a clearly plural one — evidence that the form adds meaning rather than enforcing obligatory number agreement (nukopoli, 2024) ‹contested›.
The Sakhalin varieties develop the cognate of utar into a more morphologically explicit system.

West Sakhalin has a suffix -(a)hcin (East -(a)hsin) attaching to the affiliative form of the noun — eci=setaha-hcin 'your dogs', an=niyehe-hcin 'our firewood' — alongside -utara as a separate suffix ; .

Sakaguchi distinguishes the two Sakhalin suffixes: -(a)hcin marks a homogeneous plural (all members standing in the same possessive relation), while -utara may mark homogeneous or approximative plurality and extends to personal names ; .

Despite the richer morphology, Sakhalin number remains optional and non-obligatory: -(a)hcin can attach even to nominalized clauses, so Sakhalin too lacks a grammatical number category in the strict typological sense .
An etymology linking Sakhalin utah to Hokkaido utar through historical final *r has been proposed but is disputed on comparative-phonological grounds (antitwilight, 2024) ‹contested›.
All prenominal modifiers in Hokkaido Ainu precede the head noun, and postpositional material follows it.
No agreement morphology links a modifier to its head; modification is juxtapositional throughout ; ; .

Positions need not all be filled; most NPs contain one or two pre-head elements.
When multiple positions are present, their order is fixed — a demonstrative cannot follow a numeral, nor a numeral follow a property verb.
