The line between an NP-internal modifier and a compound noun is drawn by four diagnostics (person-affix position, affiliative-suffix position, lexicalization, and the concept+concept rule) treated in after (via ).
The subclass properties of the head noun — which nouns can serve as argument heads, which can be relativized, and which require a modifier — are in .

The demonstrative system distinguishes two axes that Japanese conflates in a single この／その／あの series: on-site deixis (locating the referent in the shared perceptual field) and discourse-anaphoric deixis (tracking a previously mentioned referent) ; .
The vowel quality of the initial syllable of the on-site series correlates with distance: the narrow front vowel of tan encodes proximity and the wider back vowel of toan encodes distance.
This has been proposed as sound symbolism in the deictic system, with longer forms (taan) encoding more information content than shorter ones (tan) (nukopoli, 2025-12-27) ‹contested›.
The proposal has not been evaluated against the full corpus.
Non-Saru/Chitose dialects use nean where Saru has ne; eastern Shizunai has ikia/ikirok .
A demonstrative prenominal combined with the formal noun or yields a demonstrative pronoun: , , .
A demonstrative may be followed directly by a locative case particle — taan ta 'over there' — because the formal noun hi is historically elided in such constructions .
The full paradigm — including the interrogative ney and anaphora functions — is in .
Numerals occupy position 2, between a demonstrative and any adnoun or property verb.
A numeral precedes its head noun directly with no intervening classifier — a typological contrast with Japanese, which requires a numeral counter between numeral and noun ‹consensus›.
Nominalized numeral forms — , , — are pronoun-like count expressions, not prenominal quantifiers.

They cannot modify a noun directly: re mosir 'three worlds' is well-formed, but *rep mosir is not, because rep is already the nominalized form re + nominalizing enclitic -pe (nukopoli, 2024-11-09) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The vigesimal numeral system, ordinals, and quantifiers are in and .
Property-meaning words — , , , , — are intransitive verbs in Ainu.

In attributive position they immediately precede the head noun with no morphological change relative to their predicative form: the same pirka that takes a subject person index as a predicate appears zero-marked (third person) before the noun as its modifier ; .
The word-class analysis and the adjective controversy are in .
Beyond property verbs, a closed set of adnouns (連体詞, prenominals) occupies the same position.
Adnouns differ from property verbs in having no predicative use without the copula and in taking no person affix at all.

The Saru inventory includes gender specifiers (pinne 'male', matne 'female'), the pair-selector oar 'one of a pair', the universal quantifier kes 'every', and epistemic adnouns (sonno/sino 'true/genuine', yayan 'ordinary', oya 'other') .
A property verb or adnoun at position 3 scopes over the entire nominal complex to its right, including a following formal noun such as utar:
A full VP, including its person marking and aspectual material, can immediately precede a head noun and function as its modifier.
No relative pronoun or dedicated relative-clause morphology marks the construction; the head noun simply appears to the right of the modifying VP ; :

Relativizability is restricted by noun subclass (表47, ): common nouns can be relativized; formal nouns head argument-saturated nominalizations; locative nouns cannot be relativized; pronouns cannot be relativized ‹consensus›.

The arity account in distinguishes the relative-clause construction — which leaves an argument gap in the modifying VP that the head noun fills — from nominalization with -p~-pe, which nominalizes a VP without reducing its argument count.

A community analysis converges on the same point: relativization reduces the modifying clause's arity by one, whereas -p(e) nominalizes the entire clause without creating a gap (nukopoli, 2024-11-09) ‹contested›.
The construction and its gap types are in ; headless and internally-headed varieties are in ; argument-saturated nominalization is in .
Postpositional material follows the head noun and forms the outer boundary of the NP.
The postpositional layer consists of a locative noun in its basic or long form, optionally followed by a locative case particle (ta locative, wa ablative, un allative, peka perlative) .
The four locative case particles require a ⟨place⟩ antecedent; for a common noun, a locative noun must mediate:

Type-2 locative nouns (kim 'mountain-ward place', soy 'outside', ra 'low place') are inherently ⟨place⟩ and take a case particle directly without a preceding common-noun antecedent: kim ta arpa=an 'I went to the mountains' .
The full inventory of locative and relational nouns, their basic and long forms, and the case-particle restrictions are in .
Two nouns in their concept forms placed in sequence yield either apposition or an attributive-scope construction — both realizations of the same N(concept)+N(concept) surface pattern ; .
In the attributive use, the first noun specifies the type, quality, or scope of the second: kamuy rus means 'a pelt of the bear type' — kamuy functions as an attribute, not a possessor.

The diagnostic is substitution: an N₁ that is a true possessor can be replaced by a transitive-subject person prefix (a=kor cip 'my boat'), but an N₁ that is a mere attribute cannot — kamuy rus admits no person-prefix substitute for the bear .
When a specific animal's pelt is meant, the affiliative form marks the inalienable relation: kamuy rusihi (where rus-i-hi is the affiliative form of rus 'pelt').
Apposition in the narrower sense — two NPs coreferential with the same individual — uses the same juxtaposed structure without a copular linker.

The boundary with compound nouns runs through the four formal diagnostics in : a phrase allows person-affix placement and affiliative-suffix placement internal to the second noun, whereas a compound moves both to the outermost boundary.
The contrast between attributive juxtaposition, the inalienable affiliative construction, and the kor-construction is central to .
Three constructions express possession within the NP, selected according to the alienability of the relationship ; :

Pronominal possessors are expressed through the transitive-subject (A) person prefix — on kor in the alienable construction, or on the head noun in its affiliative form in the inalienable construction.
The possessive morphology — the affiliative-form paradigm, semantic classes of inalienable nouns, kinship-term dialect variation, and the double-marking construction — belongs to Part VII: , , and .
Hokkaido Ainu has no agreement morphology within the NP.
Demonstratives, property verbs, adnouns, and numerals do not change form as a function of any grammatical property of the head noun: there is no gender, case, or number agreement ; ‹consensus›.

A modifier at positions 1–4 appears in its uninflected citation form regardless of whether the head denotes one or many entities, whether it is animate or inanimate, or whether the NP occupies subject, object, or oblique position.
The plural marker is a postposed formal noun, not an agreement enclitic on the head or its modifiers.
It follows the entire nominal complex and is itself uninflected: wen cikappo utar and wen cikappo differ only in whether utar is present; the property verb wen is unchanged either way.

Community analysis confirms that Ainu plural is semantic addition rather than obligatory morphological agreement, and that verse can add or omit utar freely for syllable count (nukopoli, 2024-11-23) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Number, where grammatically encoded, surfaces on the finite verb through suppletive stem alternation (ek/arki 'come.SG/come.PL', arpa/paye 'go.SG/go.PL') — see .
The semantics and animacy conditions of utar, and the transnumeral character of Hokkaido nouns, are in .
Pronominal NPs are in , and derivation within the NP is in and .
Hokkaido Ainu has no genitive case-particle, no possessive preposition or postposition, and no adjectival inflection for possession.
Possession is instead expressed either by head-marking on the possessed noun itself or by a verb-based attributive clause using .
The language is "predominantly head-marking, exhibiting … polysynthesis, and having a robust alienability opposition" .
Bugaeva, Nichols & Bickel identify two independent grammatical dimensions that should not be conflated .
The first is possessibility — whether a noun's argument structure includes a possessor slot at all (optionally, obligatorily, or not at all).
The second is the coding strategy — whether the relationship, when licensed, is expressed by head-marking on the possessed noun or by a verbal attributive clause with kor.

These dimensions correlate with the traditional alienability distinction but the correlation is fixed grammatically rather than speaker-chosen: "a speaker does not decide to convey whether an item can be owned … the choice of a noun determines the possessive construction" .
Three surface patterns cover "N₁'s N₂" in Hokkaido Ainu.
The first two are possession constructions; the third is a modifier–head relation (quality, material, or kind) and is not possession ; :

The diagnostic that pattern (3) is not possession is person-substitutability: in patterns (1) and (2) the possessor N₁ can be replaced by a person-marking affix (ku=kor cip, ku=tek-ehe); in (3) it cannot — *ku=ru 'my footprint' is impossible, even though seta ru 'a dog's footprint' is well-formed .
The two possession constructions are in complementary distribution per noun: the construction is determined by noun-class membership, not by the speaker's choice at utterance time ; .
Where that membership is gradient or construal-sensitive, the picture is more complex (§4 below).
The morphophonology of the affiliative suffix is detailed in , and the concept/affiliative distinction as a noun-class parameter in .

In the alienable construction the possessed noun (N₂) remains in the concept form and is preceded by the transitive verb ; the possessor (N₁ or a person-marking prefix) is the transitive subject of that verb: a=kor cip 'my canoe', a=kor makiri 'my knife', a=kor hayokpe 'my armour' .
The semantics are those of alienable (transferable) possession: the possessed entity's existence is independent of the possessor's, and transfer to another person makes it theirs .
The negative counterpart replaces kor with ; predicative HAVE and BE schemas are treated in , and the particle kor 'while' that is homophonous with the verb in .

Bugaeva et al. analyse the kor construction as an appositive possessive with a verbal modifier: the attributive is a finite relative clause with kor whose object is gapped and coreferential with the head noun .
The construction retains relative-clause properties: kor can carry perfective and plural morphology and supports relative-clause stacking .

With a third-person possessor, kor loses overt person-marking and cliticises to the head noun — Anna katkemat kor-ninkari — a step toward head-marking that Bugaeva et al. characterise as ongoing grammaticalisation ‹speculative›.
The kor construction also extends to belonging and social dominion, not only transferable ownership.

When lexicalised in the compound N-kor-kur 'the one who holds N', it yields titles of authority such as kotan kor kur 'village chief' (lit. 'village-holding person') and the divine epithet nupuri kor kamuy 'the god who owns the mountain' ; :
The set of nouns attested in the kor construction is lexically bounded.

Drawing on Tamura's dictionary, Bugaeva et al. identify six classes of alienable nouns: people and kin (the largest class, 24 items including aynu, hapo, nispa), place and environment (11: kotan, mosir, pet), food and drink (7), tools and ritual objects (7: emus 'sword', ikor 'treasures'), domestic animals (including seta 'dog' and pewrep 'bear cub'), and human attributes (7: isoytak 'story', itak 'language', rametok 'bravery').
Wild animals and uncultivated plants are absent — nothing in the world is their owner ; .
A further affective use of kor with people nouns adds a nuance of endearment: a-kor pon menoko 'my dear young girl' .

In the inalienable construction the possessed noun takes the affiliative (possessed) form, derived from the concept form by a suffix that copies or echoes a vowel of the stem, and simultaneously carries a person-marking prefix drawn from the transitive-subject (A) set: ku= (1SG), e= (2SG), a= or an= (4th/indefinite), zero (3rd) ; .
Relational and spatial nouns deviate from this pattern by taking the objective (O) prefix set instead; they are treated in .
The A-prefix paradigm as a whole is set out in .

The possessor is thus encoded as a grammatical subject: Satō notes that e=paro 'your mouth' is literally 'you-subject mouth-in-relation', which reads oddly when translated word-for-word but reflects exactly the head-marking logic of the language .
The semantic classes of nouns that take the affiliative construction span five groups :
Body parts and normally worn or carried items. → sik-ihi; → par-o (irregular); → tek-ehe; → kema-ha.
Clothing normally worn is treated analogously (a=tesma-ha 'my snowshoes') and carried tools in some contexts (a=tasiro-ho 'my mountain-knife') .
Part–whole relations. at sinta atu-hu 'cradle cord'; rur sayo ruri-hi 'gruel broth' .

Kinship. A subset of kin terms takes the affiliative construction and obligatory person-marking; the full paradigm, the address/reference contrast, and dialect variation in kin-term assignment are set out in ; .
Material-to-product. ohaw ihawe-he 'the taste/essence of the soup' .
Miscellaneous relational. atay-e-he 'price'; hura-ha 'smell'; tokuy-e-he 'best friend'; asuru-hu 'rumour' .
The sensory nouns , , , and participate in the affiliative construction as ordinary possessed nouns before their possessed forms grammaticalised as evidential formal nouns (treated in ).
The possessive use of hawe 'voice' is attested in ILCAA oral-literature texts .

Community analysis of the form e=hawe aste 'raise your voice' similarly parses e=hawe as the possessed noun '2SG.POSS=voice' under the verb aste, confirming that hawe remains a productive possessed form alongside its evidential use (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2025-12-03; ) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The collective noun provides a further illustrative case.

A community-proposed analysis holds that utari(hi) is the affiliative form of utar, narrowing the sense toward '(someone's) companions / kin' in the same way the affiliative form generally specifies a relational reading against the more general concept form (thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord, 2025-09-17; ).
This is consistent with Nakagawa's treatment of k=utari as a possessed kin-group NP ‹contested›.
A related set of affiliative-type prefixes — e- 'its tip/head of' and o- 'its end/base of' — prefix to verbs and behave analogously to affiliative nouns in requiring a possessive antecedent .

These are homophonous with the applicative prefixes e-/o- that increase valency by one; Kobayashi distinguishes them by valency neutrality and by restriction to unaccusative intransitive hosts ‹contested›.
The applicative prefixes and the overlap with relational nouns are taken up in .
The core of the noun-class split is unambiguous.

Body parts, genealogical kin terms, and inalienable relational concepts are obligatorily possessed and take the affiliative construction; artefacts, domestic animals, and transferable resources take kor and cannot take a person-marking prefix directly .
Satō's diagnostic is exact: 'money' (kane) takes only ku=kor kane; the form *ku=kane is impossible. 'Mouth' (par) takes only e=paro; *e=kor par is impossible .
The two-construction distinction is documented in all major descriptive and pedagogical accounts ; ; .
Obligatorily-possessed nouns are bound: they almost never appear without possessive morphology.
When cited in isolation, speakers give the 3rd-person (zero-prefix) affiliative form — sik-ihi 'eye(s), his/her eye', never bare sik.
In riddles, where no specific possessor is identified, the 4th-person (indefinite) A-prefix takes over: a=sik-ihi 'people's eyes' .
These bound-noun properties, and the difference between nominal subclasses with and without obligatory possession, are developed in .

When an obligatorily-possessed noun is incorporated with a non-coreferential possessor, the antipassive prefix i- encodes the unspecified possessor and allows the bare noun root to incorporate: i-sapa-kar 'cut someone's head', i-rekut-tuye 'cut someone's throat' .

Hokkaido Ainu thus has two distinct de-specifying strategies: the indefinite A-prefix a=, which retains possessive morphology and keeps the noun as a free NP, and the antipassive i-, which suppresses the possessor and licences incorporation.
These are treated in .
Several nouns fall outside the clean bipartition.
The noun takes both constructions approximately equally: a=kor kotan ~ a=kotanu.
The noun takes only the kor construction in prose (*a=mosirihi is unattested, though mosiri appears in verse).

The noun is dialect-split: Saru, Chitose, and Horobetsu prose uses only kor for 'so-and-so's house', but verse and other dialects allow the affiliative cisehe; the compound uncise 'home, dwelling-place' takes the affiliative exclusively across dialects .
The clearest evidence for construal-sensitivity in class assignment comes from Nakagawa's discussion of the trap-bow (ku).
In the Ainu worldview, the prey animal chooses whose trap-bow to fall to, so the bow always pre-belongs to a specific person: it is construed as inalienable and takes the affiliative form :
The same bow, framed as an ordinary transferable object, takes the kor construction :
The inalienable frame foregrounds that the bow has a pre-assigned owner in a cosmological sense; the alienable frame treats it as a tool in ordinary human hands.
This pair is the strongest available evidence that the noun-class split, while grammatical in its effects, is not wholly referent-determined ‹contested›.

A parallel diachronic observation runs in the same direction: Bugaeva et al. note that loanwords such as kosonde 'kimono' enter as non-possessible and take kor, suggesting that unfamiliarity is the default entry point for new nouns and that possessibility can be acquired over time ‹speculative›.
The affiliative trigger has been debated in terms of both what the formal condition is and what typological category it instantiates.
The oldest question in the descriptive literature is whether the affiliative form is licensed by the specificity of the possessor or by a strictly grammatical condition.

Tamura held that N₂ takes the affiliative only when N₁ is specific: the contrast between kamuy rus-ihi 'the specific bear's pelt' and kamuy rus 'bear-pelt in general' was the key datum, the latter approaching the status of a compound .

Satō objected that the affiliative appears with non-specific possessors: aynu opitta hon-ihi kor wa okay pe ne 'all humans have a belly' — where aynu opitta 'all people' is maximally non-specific — carries the affiliative form hon-ihi ; ‹contested›.
forms: aynu opitta hon-ihi kor wa okay pe ne

text: Nakagawa's analysis shifts the frame entirely: the affiliative form appears wherever the noun carries a person-marking A-prefix or occupies the modifier slot of a relative-clause structure, regardless of possessor specificity .

Three constructions support this: the indefinite-person affiliative (a=teke munin pe ne na 'one's hand will rot', a general warning); affiliatives inside relative clauses (the modifier 'with a long tail' requires sara-ha tanne, not *sar tanne, because the modifier slot is a relative-clause position); and affiliatives triggered by quantifiers usa 'various' and nep 'whatever' ‹contested›.
Satō's personal-form (人称形) analysis, developed in , addresses a different aspect.

Once a person-marking prefix combines with the affiliative form to create a personal form, the result is a highly autonomous NP: Ø=sik-ihi alone — without any overt possessor NP — is a complete noun phrase 'his/her eye'.
At the same time, the possessor NP and its personal form need not be adjacent: the noun phrase menoko … anakne … kaskamuye 'the woman's guardian spirit' has the topic particle anakne intervening.
The personal form signals the presence of a possessor somewhere in context rather than forming a tight N-N genitive .

Bugaeva et al. converge on the same point: the possessed suffix "marks a noun as requiring a possessor (which is then indexed with a possessive prefix)" and "the possessor N₁ can easily be omitted without ambiguity as the possessed suffix signals its presence" .

Bugaeva et al.'s typological framing, drawing on , places the Hokkaido system within the Circum-Pacific appositive possessive type but distinguishes it by the fact that the modifier is a finite verbal clause (kor) rather than a nominal appositive .

The two constructions together give the language a mixed locus-of-marking profile: inalienable possession is head-marked on the possessed noun (A-prefix + affiliative suffix), while alienable possession is encoded as a verbal modifier.

The adnominal double-marking and appositive constructions that arise at the interface of these two strategies are examined in ; the external-possession and possessor-raising phenomena are treated in .

Huber's subjectivity analysis applies Ikegami's HAVE/BE-language typology and finds that Ainu patterns with English (a HAVE-type language where the possessor is foregrounded as subject) rather than Japanese (a BE-type language where the possessed entity is topicalised) .
Even in the inalienable construction the possessor is overtly indexed by the A-prefix — ku=tek-ehe ku=kikkik 'I clapped my hands' — unlike the dropped possessor of Japanese 「手を叩いた」.

Huber proposes treating inalienability as a subjectivity index and the possession-schema inventory as a gradient scale rather than a binary; this proposal is explicitly framed as preliminary in her paper ‹speculative›.

Every common noun in Hokkaido Ainu potentially has two citation shapes: a concept form (概念形) expressing the noun as a free-standing concept, and an affiliative form (所属形) expressing it as belonging to something or someone .
The concept form is the stem; the affiliative is a derivative, produced by a suffix on that stem .
Earlier scholarship described the contrast under the labels 抽象形 (abstract form) and 具体形 (concrete form) ; Nakagawa's own earlier work used 人称形 (personal form) for the possessed shape .
The alternation underlies Hokkaido Ainu's bifurcated possession system.
Inalienable nouns — body parts, kinship terms, part–whole pairs, and related classes — take the affiliative form when possessed and combine directly with a possessive person-prefix.
Alienable nouns remain in the concept form as the implicit object of the transitive verb ; .

The alienable/inalienable split itself is set out in ; the morphophonology of the affiliative suffix — the echo-vowel mechanism and suffix classes — belongs to ; the full double-marking NP (person-prefix plus affiliative suffix) is treated in ; and kinship-term idiosyncrasies appear in .
The affiliative suffix attaches to the noun stem.
Its shape is conditioned by the final segment of the stem ; .
Three types are recognised, each with a short and a long variant.
Type ① — vowel-final stems. The short affiliative is identical to the concept form; the long affiliative adds -hV₁ where V₁ repeats the stem's final vowel: → sapa / sapa-ha.
Type ② — stems in -y or -w. The suffix is -e(-he): → haw-e(-he); → patoy-e(-he).
Type ③ — other consonant-final stems. The basic (Type ③-1) suffix is -i(-hi): → sik-i(-hi).
Lexically listed subsets take an echo vowel matching the stem's last vowel (Type ③-2): → tek-e(-he); → kisar-a(-ha).
A small group with final a takes -u(-hu) (Type ③-3): → nan-u(-hu).
Types ③-2 and ③-3 must be memorised individually; Satō notes that the exceptions are numerous and must be learned one by one .
Monosyllabic open stems ending in i or u behave as Type ② rather than ③, taking -e(-he): → ru-we(-he) .
The affiliative ruwe of ru is the same form that serves as the evidential formal noun, and the possessed-noun origin underlies all four evidential nominalizers treated in .

When a consonant-final noun appears as the second element of a compound, it reverts to the ③-1 pattern regardless of its isolated affiliative class: → at-u(-hu) (③-2) in isolation, but tar-at → tar-ac-i(-hi) 'carrying-rope cord' inside a compound .
The distinction between an affiliative-suffixed noun in an NP and a phonologically similar compound link is discussed in .
For all three types, the suffix has a short and a long variant.
For consonant-final stems, the short form ends in the echo vowel alone (teke) and the long form adds a further syllable (tekehe).

The two variants carry no semantic difference; Satō writes that "the difference in meaning seems absent — how they are distributed remains unclear" ; Nakagawa confirms that the split follows prosodic and rhythmic preference rather than grammar .
The long form is more frequent in oral-narrative verse .
When a common noun appears in the affiliative construction, it combines with a possessive person-prefix drawn from the transitive-subject (A) affix set ; ; .
The possessor is thus grammatically encoded as the agent-like argument of the noun.
Satō captures the counterintuitive direction with a literal gloss: e=paro 'your mouth' parses as 'you [A] mouth', the possessor marked with the same form that marks a transitive subject on a verb .
Before vowel-initial stems, ku= reduces to k= and ci= to c=; accent falls on the syllable following the prefix for ku= and e= (e.g., ku-sápa) but not for a= or eci= .
The complete person-prefix system across all argument roles — intransitive-subject, transitive-subject, and object — is documented in .
Relational (locative) nouns such as and take the objective (O) affix set rather than the A-set; their possessed forms are treated in .
Nakagawa identifies five groupings of nouns that enter the affiliative construction when possessed :
Body parts and habitually worn items. The canonical inalienable class: , , , tears, nasal mucus, and so on.
Clothing and footwear normally worn on the body, and even commonly carried tools, are treated grammatically like body parts: ku=tesma-ha 'my snowshoes', a=tasiro-ho 'my mountain-knife'.
Part–whole relations. The part belongs inherently to the whole: sayo rur-i(-hi) 'the broth of the gruel'; nit op nic-i(-hi) 'the shaft of a spear'.
Material-product relations. The output belongs to its source: ikaray ohaw-e(-he) 'nettle stew'; top cise(-he) 'bamboo house'.
Kinship terms — a large subset whose allocation between the affiliative and the construction varies by term and dialect; see .
Miscellaneous inalienables whose belonging is inherent or relational: , , , , (variable; see below).
The classification is grammatically fixed: the noun's class membership determines the construction, not a speaker's inference about the nature of the possession .
A sword or dog is experientially "owned" but grammatically non-possessible and must take .
The contrast is sharpest in minimal pairs.
Satō's diagnostic example — ku=kor kani 'my money' (alienable; *ku=kanihi is ungrammatical) versus ku=teke-he 'my hand' (inalienable) — shows that the split cannot be inferred from semantics alone .
Two nouns sit on the boundary.
takes both constructions roughly equivalently: a=kor kotan ~ a=kotanu(hu).
is restricted to the concept construction in prose (a=kor mosir; *a=mosirihi unattested in prose, though mosiri appears in verse) .

is dialect-split: in Saru, Chitose, and Horobetsu prose the affiliative cisehe is not used for 'X's house', but verse and some other dialects allow it, and the verse-compound uncise 'home' is always affiliative (a=uncise, never *kor uncise) .

Cultural construal can also shift the construction for the same referent: a trap-bow () is usually alienable (ku=kor ku), but when the bow belongs existentially to whoever the prey chooses, the same object takes the affiliative kuwehe .
The inalienable/alienable line is therefore construal-sensitive for certain nouns, not fixed by the referent alone ‹contested›.

Community member thegodofneet (aynu-corpora Discord, 2025-09-17) proposed that utari(-hi) is the affiliative of , with the suffixed form narrowing the sense to 'X's companions/kin', on the grounds that companions belonging to no one are conceptually difficult to realise and the form consistently presupposes a possessor ‹contested›.
The corpus count for utari is 1,502 tokens.

The analysis extends — rather than contradicts — Nakagawa's observation that k=utari 'my family' is attested alongside the concept form ; the semantic narrowing under affiliation is the community's addition.
Body parts and kinship terms are obligatorily possessed: they almost never occur without a possessive prefix and affiliative suffix in natural speech .

When elicited in isolation — and in riddles, where no specific possessor is named — speakers supply the fourth-person (indefinite) prefix a=: a=sik-i-hi 'eyes (one's/ people's eyes)', not the bare stem sik .
These nouns function as bound stems in the sense defined in .

When an obligatorily-possessed noun is incorporated into a verb and the possessor is non-coreferential with any core argument, the derivational prefix encodes the unspecified possessor: i-sapa-kar usi 'a barber shop' (lit. 'a place where one does someone's head') .
This is the non-possessed-noun (NPN) marker, distinct from the antipassive i- that demotes the transitive object; the two homophonous prefixes are treated together in .
The fourth-person prefix a= (which retains affiliative morphology on the free noun) and the NPN i- (which enables possessor-less incorporation) are two distinct de-specifiers .
The combination of person-prefix plus affiliative-marked noun constitutes what Satō calls the personal form (人称形): the form the noun takes when it is related to a particular possessor .
Because the possessor is indexed on the noun itself, the personal form functions as an autonomous NP.
The third-person form siki(-hi) alone means 'his/her/their eye(s)' without any overt possessor pronoun — unlike Japanese 目, which requires 彼の to express the same content .
A consequence of this indexical autonomy is that the possessor NP and the possessed noun form a looser constituent than a Japanese genitive phrase.
Satō demonstrates that they can be separated by particles and intervening words, with the personal form presupposing only that some possessor NP is accessible in the discourse context .

Bugaeva's formulation is parallel: the possessive suffix "registers a possessor but does not index its properties", and "the possessor NP can easily be omitted without ambiguity as the possessed suffix signals its presence" .

Stacking of personal forms — where the possessor of one is itself a personal form — is structurally transparent, as the third-person (zero) prefix on the inner noun is sufficient to license retrieval of the outer personal form as its possessor.

Tamura identified the trigger for the affiliative as the specificity of the possessor N₁: kamuy rusihi 'that specific bear's pelt' (affiliative) versus kamuy rus 'bear-pelt in general' (concept form, approaching a compound) .
Satō challenged this with the counter-example aynu opitta honihi kor wa okay pe ne 'all humans have a belly' (honi-hi affiliative; possessor 'all humans' = non-specific) ‹contested›.
forms: aynu opitta honihi kor wa okay pe ne

text: Nakagawa argues that the constraint is grammatical rather than semantic: the affiliative appears wherever a person-prefix or a relative-clause structure demands it, regardless of the possessor's specificity .
Three classes of evidence bear on this.

General-warning contexts. a=teke munin pe ne na 'your hand will rot' (a warning about touching rainbows) uses the affiliative teke with the fourth-person prefix even though no specific person is addressed; the prefix alone forces the affiliative .

Relative-clause structure. 'A dog with a long tail' requires sara-ha tanne seta (affiliative sara(ha)), not *sar tanne seta, even with an indefinite dog: the NP structure in which the dog possesses its tail forces the affiliative on sar .

Quantifier and pro-form triggers. The quantifier usa 'various' and the pro-form nep 'what, whatever' independently induce the affiliative: usa kamihi usa cepihi 'meat and fish of various kinds' (Chitose); nep aynuhu e=ne 'whatever human you are' (aynuhu = affiliative of aynu) .

Nakagawa concludes that the received claim — that only some nouns possess an affiliative form — is overstated: given the right relational structure, potentially any common noun can take one ‹contested›.
The phonological boundary between a suffixed affiliative and a bare compound second element is discussed in .
The possessed form also feeds noun incorporation as discussed in .

Community member nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2025-12-03) parsed iteki e=hawe aste 'don't raise your voice' as [iteki [[e=hawe] aste]], with e=hawe (2SG possessive prefix + Type ② affiliative of haw 'voice') serving as a plain possessed-noun argument of aste 'raise' ‹contested›.
The analysis is consistent with the attested non-evidential, lexical use of hawehe in the example below.
The affiliative (possessed) form of a common noun differs from its concept form by a suffix whose vowel echoes the final vowel of the stem.

The suffix appears in two lengths: a short form consisting of the copy vowel alone (for vowel-final stems this adds nothing visible to the concept form), and a long form consisting of copy vowel + /h/ + copy vowel again, notated -hV₁ where V₁ is the stem's last vowel ; .
The two lengths carry no semantic distinction; the choice between them is governed by prosody and speaker rhythm, and Satō describes the usage split as "unclear" ‹contested›.

The possessive person-prefix that co-occurs with the affiliative form belongs to the transitive-subject (A) prefix set — identical to the verbal A paradigm — as set out in ; the full double-marking construction is treated in .

This chapter addresses only the morphophonology of the suffix: its shape, the conditioning environments of its three consonant-final classes, the irregulars, and the diachronic source of the /h/ element.
The conditioning sorts into three groups by the stem's final segment.
Vowel-final stems (type ①) produce the most transparent echo: the long form adds -hV₁, the short form adds nothing.
Glide-final stems (type ②) take the uniform suffix -e(he).

Consonant-final stems other than glides (type ③) belong to one of three lexically listed sub-classes: the default -i(hi), a minority echo-vowel class -V(hV), and a further minority -u(hu) class restricted to stems whose last vowel is /a/ .

When the concept form ends in a vowel, the short affiliative is identical to the concept form; a bare third-person (zero-prefix) vowel-final noun is therefore ambiguous between concept and affiliative readings and requires context for interpretation ; .
The long form adds -hV₁, repeating the stem-final vowel:
In each row the suffix vowel is identical to the stem-final vowel: /a/, /u/, /e/, /o/ respectively.

Because the short affiliative coincides with the concept form, corpus string-searches cannot separate them; frequency figures for long forms — sapaha 206 tokens in the present corpus — are the only clean affiliative counts for this class.
The paradigm itself follows .
When the concept form ends in the glides /y/ or /w/, the affiliative suffix is uniformly -e(he), regardless of the preceding vowel quality ; :
The affiliative of is attested as both an ordinary possessed noun ('X's voice') and, fully grammaticalized, as one of the four formal-noun evidentials treated in .
The two uses are morphologically identical; only context separates them .
A formally parallel subtype arises with monosyllabic open-syllable (CV) nouns whose concept form ends in /i/ or /u/.
These surface as vowel-final but take the type ② suffix -e(he) rather than the type ① echo -hV₁, as if an underlying glide — absent from the concept form — conditions the suffix :

Sakhalin Ainu, which preserves phonemic vowel length, has the corresponding nouns as cii, kuu — long-vowel forms plausibly reflecting an earlier *Ciy/*Cuw sequence and supporting the underlying-glide analysis ; ‹speculative›.

The affiliative ruwe is by far the most frequent of the four, since its grammaticalization as the recognized-fact evidential places it in clause-final position across a large share of narrative sentences; a clean affiliative count is not available by string-search because ruwe is homophonous with the lexical noun and with a reduced final particle .
Nouns whose concept form ends in a consonant other than /y/ or /w/ belong to type ③.
Three suffix shapes compete, and class membership within type ③ is in large part lexically determined ; .
The most frequent sub-pattern inserts /i/ before the optional long-form -hi, giving -i (short) or -ihi (long) regardless of the stem's vowel quality.

Kindaichi and Chiri's early description used sik / shikihi as the paradigm case of the distinction they called 具体形 'concrete form' versus 抽象形 'abstract form' ; the present grammar follows Nakagawa's terminology (concept/affiliative).
The kinship term takes the same ③-1 suffix as body parts, confirming that sub-type membership cuts across semantic domains.
The corpus attests yupihi at 759 tokens and sikihi at 133 tokens; the sub-type assignment follows .
The affiliatives siri and humi are lexically frozen in their short forms in the evidential construction; the long forms sirihi and humihi appear in the plain possessed-noun use only .

A lexically defined set of consonant-final stems takes a suffix whose vowel echoes the stem's last vowel (③-2) rather than defaulting to /i/; a smaller set inserts /u/ regardless of stem vowel quality (③-3, restricted to V₁ = /a/ stems).
Both sub-types accept the same optional long-form extension.
The conditioning matrix after Nakagawa 2024: 228, 表51:
V₁ = the stem's last vowel.
The /i/ column of ③-2 is empty because all consonant-final stems with V₁ = /i/ belong to ③-1.
For V₁ = /a/ stems three outcomes are possible (③-1, ③-2, ③-3), with no phonological cue distinguishing them; this is the hardest sub-case for morpheme recognition ; .
Nakagawa notes that ③-3 — the insertion of /u/ for V₁ = /a/ stems — "cannot be explained historically" ‹speculative›.
Sub-type ③-1 is the unmarked pattern.
A ③-2 or ③-3 stem that appears as the second element of a compound reverts to the ③-1 suffix, regardless of its own lexical class .
The noun alone takes the ③-2 long affiliative atu-hu (V₁ = /u/); as the second element of tar-at 'carrying-rope cord' the compound takes tar-ac-i(hi), the ③-1 form .
This alternation is the clearest synchronic evidence that ③-1 is phonologically basic and ③-2/③-3 are lexically marked ‹corpus-suggested›.
The same diagnostic applies to the evidential formal nouns.
The noun alone gives the short ③-1 affiliative siri, which grammaticalizes as the situational evidential.

The formal noun siri blocks the long extension in its evidential function — it is always the bare short form, never *sirihi — suggesting that grammaticalization has lexically frozen the short form in this use ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Two nouns have affiliative forms that none of the productive rules derives.
yields paro(ho), not the expected ③-1 *parihi.

Nakagawa traces this to the word's etymology: par is a compound of pa 'upper part' and or 'inside, place', so the ending -o(ho) is the locative long-form of or rather than an affiliative suffix proper .
The second irregular, → moru(hu), is attributed to a morphological re-analysis of an earlier stem moru ‹speculative›.

Kinship terms add further formal idiosyncrasies: address-form vs reference-form pairs where the two stems take different affiliative classes (e.g., reference yup ③-1 vs the address form yupo ①), and frozen dialectal variants.
These are treated in .
Types ① and ② are phonologically predictable from the concept form's final segment: any vowel-final stem belongs to ①; any /y/- or /w/-final stem (surface or underlying) belongs to ②.
Within type ③ the situation is different.
Satō states that "there are many exceptions … each must be memorised individually" , and Nakagawa 2024 concurs that ③-2 and ③-3 are lexically listed.
For V₁ = /a/ stems the task is hardest: a given noun may belong to ③-1, ③-2, or ③-3 with no phonological predictor.
For V₁ = /i/ the situation is simpler — all /i/-stem consonant-final nouns take ③-1 .
The pedagogical grammar of presents the consonant-final class under the label 'belonging form' and treats -ihi as the default suffix, consistent with the ③-1 analysis.
Ijäs does not distinguish ③-2 from ③-3 as labeled sub-classes; body-part forms with non-default suffixes are presented as items to be memorised.
For the obligatorily-possessed nouns that constitute the core affiliative class, the lexical class assignment is part of each noun's dictionary entry.
Chiri 1952 described the vowel quality of the affiliative suffix as an instance of vowel harmony spreading a feature from the stem .
The present description reframes this as vowel copy: the suffix vowel is a morphologically triggered copy of the stem's last vowel, not an autosegmental spread.
The distinction is empirically relevant: in type ③-2 the copy operates across an intervening consonant (tek → -e), where a strictly local harmony rule would require extra stipulation ‹contested›.
The origin of the ③-2 echo-vowel class is addressed separately by Nakagawa 2024: 228, 247–248, who proposes that it derives from the locative long-form suffix productive on relational nouns.

The relational noun takes the locative long form sutu; the same pattern recurs in the compound tap-sut 'shoulder' → tap-sut-u(hu), suggesting that the ③-2 suffix in such nouns was originally a locative ending that later spread into the common-noun affiliative paradigm.
Nakagawa describes the connection as "intimately related" , and notes that the ③-3 pattern (V₁ = /a/ → /u/) "cannot be explained historically" ‹speculative›.
Neither proposal has been independently replicated.
See for the relational-noun long-form paradigm.
The /h/ in the long-form suffix (-hV₁) has a proposed diachronic correlate.

Sakhalin Ainu, which preserves phonemic vowel length, has long vowels in nouns corresponding to Hokkaido affiliatives with -hV; Itabashi 2001 argues that proto-Ainu coda consonants were lost in Hokkaido and partially compensated by pitch accent, while their trace survives in Sakhalin long vowels .
Under this account the /h/ in sapa-ha, siki-hi, etc. reflects a historical boundary consonant or coda that became /h/ rather than zero in the possessive environment ; ‹speculative›.

Sakhalin Ainu uses the same vowel-copy mechanism but with the extended long form as the more consistent default: where Hokkaido freely alternates short hawe and long hawehe, Sakhalin typically retains the extended shape.

A community analysis of Sakhalin data observes that the stem san yields sanihi via san + insertion /i/ + -hi, and that makan similarly yields makanihi; the analysis further notes a Sakhalin variant -hike in a subset of forms (sani ike alternating with sanihi), where -ke may represent an additional nominal element appended to the affiliative (nukopoli, 2024-12-16) ‹speculative›.
The distributional and historical relationship between Sakhalin -hike and Hokkaido -hi has not been formally investigated in the accessible sources ‹speculative›.
A distinct element -ike appears in a small set of Hokkaido compound nouns where Chiri glosses it as 'person (who is X)' .

The eastern-dialect form onneke(he) 'parent/mother (Tokachi, Nemuro)' has been analysed as onne 'old' + -ike, with the compound then additionally taking the affiliative suffix (onneke-he), showing that -ike here is a stem-forming element and the affiliative suffix is separate (antitwilight, 2024-11-15) ‹speculative›.
The affiliation of this -ike to the affiliative paradigm, if any, is etymological rather than synchronic and is not a productive pattern in Hokkaido Ainu.
Hokkaido Ainu encodes adnominal possession without a genitive case particle or possessive adposition.
Two constructions divide the nominal lexicon by alienability.

Inalienable nouns — body parts, kinship terms, and a defined range of relational objects — carry a personal possessive prefix and an affiliative suffix directly on the possessed noun: ku=tek-ehe 'my hand'.
Alienable nouns — tools, animals, places — are possessed via the transitive verb , which takes the possessor as its A-argument: ku=kor seta 'my dog'.
The choice of construction is fixed by the noun class, not by the speaker's construal of ownership in a given context ; ‹consensus›.

The morphophonology of the affiliative suffix is treated in ; the concept/affiliative functional distinction in ; the bound-noun status of obligatorily-possessed nouns in ; kinship terms and their irregular affiliative forms in ; predicative possession in .

The present chapter addresses the NP-internal structure: the personal-prefix paradigm, the configuration in which both an overt possessor NP and a head-marked possessum appear together, nested possession, and the appositive kor construction.
The possessive prefix on an inalienable noun is the same form set as the transitive-subject (A) prefix documented in .
On a noun, the prefix indexes the possessor as the "subject" of the possessive relation — the same morphological slot that marks the agent of a transitive verb ; .
Satō notes the "backwards" feel: e=paro 'your mouth' is literally 'you-SUBJ mouth', the possessor marked by what looks like a nominative subject affix .
Accent shift and allomorphy follow the same rules as on verbs.
The prefixes ku= and e= move the pitch accent to the syllable immediately after the prefix: ku=sápa, e=páro.
The prefixes eci= and a= do not shift the accent: a=sapá, eci=sapá.
Before a vowel-initial stem, ku= reduces to k= and ci= to c=, with the accent on the first stem vowel: k=ótop-i .
Each inalienable noun has two affiliative shapes: a short form (the base with the minimal vowel-copy suffix) and a long form (short + -hV₁).
The two carry no semantic difference; the choice is prosodically conditioned and for many nouns is simply lexically inherited ; .
In the paradigm above, parenthesised endings mark the optional long-form extension: teke(he), sapa(ha), otopi(hi).
The prefix-plus-affiliative complex is what Satō calls the personal form (人称形 in his account): a noun form that presupposes and indexes a possessor .

A third-person personal form such as sik-ihi is referentially complete on its own — 'his/her/their eye(s)' — because the affiliative suffix alone signals the existence of a possessor in discourse context; the possessor NP can be omitted without ambiguity .
The same paradigm is presented in the Ijäs (2023) learner grammar under the label "possessive prefixes", with the A-set identity made explicit for learners .
A minimal illustration of the 2SG prefix in the possessed-noun slot: the noun has the affiliative (haw-e, type ②).
In iteki [[e=haw-e] aste] — proposed as 'don't raise your voice' — e=haw-e is parsed as the 2SG-possessed noun 'your voice' serving as the object of ‹contested›
(nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2025-12-03, proposed parse; the affiliative haw-e is independently attested as a plain possessed noun at ).
When the possessor is expressed as an overt noun phrase it is juxtaposed immediately before the possessed noun.
Ainu has no genitive case suffix or possessive adposition to mark the possessor constituent .

The result is a configuration in which the possessum bears both the person prefix and the affiliative suffix — the morphological load is carried entirely by the head noun — while the possessor NP is present but structurally unmatched.
This is head-marking in the sense of : the head of the NP, not the dependent, bears the relational morphology.
The following table summarises the semantic classes of nouns whose grammatical class requires the affiliative construction, following :
Class membership is grammatical rather than purely semantic.

The same object can fall into either class depending on cultural construal: a regular bow (ku) is typically alienable and takes kor, but a trap-bow is affiliative (kuwehe) because Ainu cosmology treats the prey's choice of whose bow to fall to as inalienable — yet the same trap-bow can also be expressed with kor when framed as an ordinary transferable object ‹contested›.

Whether the triggering condition for affiliative marking is the specificity of the possessor or the grammatical demands of the construction (a person prefix or relative-clause structure) is itself a live debate: the older analysis requires a specific referential possessor , while Nakagawa 2024: 227–233 argues the constraint is structural — the affiliative appears wherever a person prefix or relative-clause configuration demands it, regardless of possessor specificity ‹contested›.
The possessor NP and the possessed personal form are not tightly bracketed as a constituent.

Satō documents cases in which the possessor NP and the possessed noun are separated by topic particles or other intervening material, with the personal form functioning as a signal that a possessor NP exists somewhere in the discourse context rather than as part of a closely-bound syntactic constituent .
Bugaeva's parallel formulation is that the possessed suffix "registers a possessor but does not index its properties", so the overt possessor NP can be omitted without loss of grammaticality .

Community discussion in the aynu-corpora Discord (thegodofneet, 2025-09-17; ) proposes that the companion/group noun has an affiliative form utari(hi) — 'someone's companions/kin' — on the grounds that a group of companions is hard to conceive without a relational anchor, making it pragmatically obligatorily possessed like body-part and kin terms.
This is consistent with Nakagawa 2024: 251–252 on the behaviour of utar in narrative ‹contested›.
When the possessor is itself a personal form — an inalienable noun bearing its own person prefix and affiliative suffix — the result is a chain of possessed nouns, each indexed for its own possessor.
The innermost noun carries an overt person prefix; the next noun takes the innermost noun's referent as its possessor, which is then marked by a zero third-person prefix.
Nakagawa 2024: 224 (ex. 259) illustrates this in a Saru narrative passage:
Each noun in the chain takes its own personal prefix, and the chain as a whole is not syntactically tight: topic particles can interrupt it, as with the simpler two-noun case above.
Possessor-raising through noun incorporation — where the possessor of an incorporated body-part noun is promoted to the clause subject position — is a related but distinct phenomenon treated in .
Alienable nouns cannot receive the person prefix and affiliative suffix directly.

The transitive verb intervenes between possessor and possessum: the possessor fills the A-slot of kor as a person prefix; the possessed noun follows as the implicit relativised object, remaining in the concept (uninflected) form ; .

Bugaeva's analysis, based on the Pacific-wide typology of appositive possession, treats the kor construction as a finite relative clause headed by the transitive verb kor, with the possessum as the gapped object: [__ ku=kor] seta = 'the dog that I have' .

Evidence that kor retains full verbal syntax includes the availability of perfective marking (a=kor a kotan 'my former village'), plural suffixes, mirativity, and free stacking of relative clauses over the same head .
The construction is therefore classified as an appositive-verbal classifier — a Circum-Pacific possessive type in which a finite verb serves as the possessive head rather than a case affix .
With a third-person possessor, kor loses its overt A-prefix and can lean phonologically onto the following head noun, yielding units such as kor-ninkari 'X's earrings'.

Bugaeva (2021) reads this as an in-progress shift from the dependent-marking pattern of the full verbal construction toward a head-marking configuration in which kor has become a dependent marker on the possessed noun ‹corpus-suggested›.
This trajectory — verbal appositive classifier to head-marking dependent — parallels the path already completed in the inalienable system, where the affiliative suffix now sits squarely on the head.
The set of nouns attested in the kor construction is limited.

Tamura's Saru lexicon lists approximately fifty-seven such nouns, distributed across people (24), places and environment (11), food and drink (7), tools and ritual objects (7), domestic animals (1), and human attributes (7); wild animals and plants, owned by no one in the Ainu world, are largely absent ; .
The affective extension of kor — as in a=kor pon menoko 'my (dear) young girl' — adds a further function in oral literature beyond straightforward ownership .

Typologically, the inalienable affiliative construction is head-marking in the sense of : the relational morphology (person prefix plus affiliative suffix) is borne entirely by the head noun, with no case or adposition marking the possessor dependent.

The kor construction differs in placing the possessor index on the intervening verb rather than on the possessed noun head, a configuration that Huber (2025) places in a separate appositive-verbal column within her four-way attributive typology (head-marking / dependent-marking / zero-marking / double-marking) .
The broader Circum-Pacific context and its diachronic implications are laid out in .
Noun incorporation of possessed body-part nouns and the interaction with the kor set (alienable nouns cannot be incorporated in their possessed forms) are treated in .

External possession (EP) refers to a construction in which the possessor of a noun appears as a core argument of the main predicate rather than as a modifier inside the possessed NP; the possessor is thereby assigned a grammatical function — typically subject or object — by the verb rather than by the nominal head .
Hokkaido Ainu lacks a dative-shift EP construction of the type common in European languages ('the wave hit him on the shoulder').

The constructions available instead belong to three morphosyntactic domains: (1) body-part noun incorporation (NI) that promotes the possessor to intransitive-subject position; (2) natural-force NI that promotes the former object to intransitive subject; and (3) the applicative prefixes, which raise a possessor or beneficiary into direct-object position.
No read source applies the term "external possession" to Hokkaido Ainu directly; the label "possessor raising" (所有者の主語への昇格) enters the literature with and is restated in ‹contested›.
The constructional background lies in the possession system.
Body-part and kinship nouns are obligatorily possessed and take the affiliative form with the A-set person prefix whenever they occur with a specified possessor (see ).
When such a noun is incorporated into a predicate, the possessor — normally indexed on the noun — may migrate to a subject or object slot of the derived complex verb.
The most documented EP-equivalent in Hokkaido Ainu arises through body-part NI.

When a body-part noun in its affiliative (possessed) form is incorporated into an intransitive verb, the resulting stem loses the person prefix on the noun; that person — the possessor — resurfaces as the intransitive subject of the derived verb .

The derivational contrast is between the base clause, where the body-part affiliative carries an overt person prefix, and the incorporated clause, where the possessor appears only as the verb's subject suffix.
After NI, the possessor prefix detaches from the body-part noun and surfaces instead as the subject suffix of the complex predicate.
Satō (2012: 8, cited in ) and give the following contrast:

characterises the promoting force as the higher discourse salience of the possessor relative to the body part, citing Satō's observation that "body-part nouns are prone to backgrounding because the possessor is felt to be more salient" (Satō 2012: 20–21, as quoted in ).
This promoting force is NI-internal rather than a separate syntactic operation.
The construction overlaps with the possessor-stranding cases treated in , where the possessor NP remains in the clause while the body-part noun is incorporated.
A second incorporation pathway produces an unaccusative from a transitive by incorporating the natural-force subject (wave, wind, current) of the base verb.
Once incorporated, the natural force no longer occupies the subject position; the base object is promoted to intransitive subject of the derived verb .

shows that the derived unaccusatives from natural-force NI feed the affiliative-type prefixes e- and o- (treated in the following section), because those prefixes select exclusively for unaccusative hosts.

The two NI sub-types are therefore connected: body-part NI makes the erstwhile possessor the subject of a new intransitive; natural-force NI makes the erstwhile patient the subject of a new unaccusative that can undergo further derivation ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Alongside the full applicative system, identifies a set of affiliative-type prefixes (所属形的接頭辞): and .
These prefixes attach to a verb and function like the affiliative form of a possessed noun: they presuppose a contextual possessor without altering the verb's valence (valence impact: [0]).
The following forms are documented in :
e- and o- in this function attach only to unaccusative intransitives — verbs whose sole argument is a theme or patient — not to unergatives (agent-subject intransitives) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
This selectional restriction links the affiliative-type prefix to natural-force NI: a transitive that undergoes natural-force NI becomes unaccusative and can then receive e-/o-.
The strings e- and o- are homophonous with the e- applicative and the o- applicative, which increase arity by one.

The two uses are synchronically distinct in valence behaviour — the applicative adds an argument; the affiliative-type prefix does not — but this distinction requires verb-by-verb analysis and is not always surface-transparent ‹contested›.
The diagnostics for disambiguation are set out in and .
The applicative prefixes , , and each increase a verb's arity by one, promoting a peripheral participant — possessor, beneficiary, goal, or source — into the direct-object position ; ; .

When the promoted participant is the possessor of an NP already present in the clause, the result is a construction in which the possessor occupies object position rather than sitting inside the possessed NP — the closest Ainu structural equivalent of dative EP.

analyses a subset of these configurations as the interaction of NI with applicative formation: a body-part noun is incorporated while the applicative slot is filled by the body-part's possessor, yielding a complex predicate in which the possessor is the new object.
Hokkaido Ainu tolerates such NI-plus-applicative stacks; their ordering and feeding relations are treated in .
In 's typological survey (within the framework of ), the ko- applicative is the primary beneficiary/possessor-promotion prefix; e- adds a locative or goal; o- adds a source or endpoint.
The per-applicative EP readings are documented in , , and , with the system-level typological placement in .
When the possessor of an obligatorily possessed body-part or kinship noun is absent or non-coreferential with any clause argument, Hokkaido Ainu offers two morphological strategies .
The first is the fourth-person (indefinite) A-prefix , which keeps the noun in its full affiliative form and indexes an unspecified possessor (a=tekehe 'someone's hand').

The second is the derivational antipassive prefix , which enables the body-part noun to be incorporated without possessive morphology — functioning as a non-possessed-noun (NPN) marker, comparable in function to a nominal absolutive ; .
The two strategies differ in what they encode about the possessor.

The a= strategy retains affiliative morphology and implies a vague but retrievable possessor; i- suppresses the possessor argument entirely, producing what terms a non-possessible reading of the incorporated noun.
In EP terms, i- is the inverse operation to possessor-raising: it removes the possessor from the noun's argument frame rather than promoting it to clause level, enabling fully possessor-free NI.
For the broader function of i- as antipassive and detransitiviser, see .
A related use of i= as the fourth-person object index — homophonous with the antipassive prefix but distinct in status — is documented in .

The three mechanisms surveyed above have been described in distinct analytical vocabularies, and the descriptive literature does not converge on a unified formal account of "external possession" in Ainu.

, following , treats body-part NI possessor-raising as an NI-internal process: the incorporated noun's possessor is promoted to clause subject by virtue of the body-part's relative discourse-salience deficit, and the result is an unaccusative predicate.
This account is accurate at the descriptive level but does not determine whether the promotion is syntactic movement or base-generation of the subject.

approaches the same facts through the lens of obligatory possession and argument structure: the inalienable body-part noun requires a possessor as its argument, and when that possessor is suppressed (by i-) or left unspecified (by a=), the possessor slot is de-activated rather than raised.
She does not frame the resulting construction as possessor-raising.
The applicative account in treats the EP reading as the product of the applicative operation alone, with NI as an independent feeding process ‹contested›.

Whether these three routes — body-part NI promotion, natural-force NI promotion, and applicative object-promotion — constitute instances of a unified Ainu EP construction, or three typologically distinct processes that happen to yield similar interpretations, has not been resolved in the accessible literature ‹contested›.

Placing the Ainu facts within 's typology of NI types, body-part incorporation with possessor promotion would fall at the boundary between Type II (lexical-level compounding) and Type III (manipulation of discourse referents), but assigning the Ainu data precisely requires corpus evidence on whether an independent possessor NP can co-occur with the incorporated body-part noun — a question the sources consulted leave open ‹speculative›.

The natural-force and applicative mechanisms sit closer to Type I (simple argument reduction) and to applicative constructions respectively; their co-existence in a polysynthetic head-marking language is typologically expected .
Kinship terms in Hokkaido Ainu are bound nouns: they do not occur without possessive morphology in ordinary prose.
Like body parts, they are obligatorily possessed.

Unlike body parts, they split between the two possession constructions that organise the inalienable–alienable divide: some kin terms take the affiliative form with a direct person-prefix (ku=onaha 'my father'), while others remain in the concept form governed by the transitive verb (ku=kor hapo 'my mother') ; .
The assignment is lexically fixed and does not vary freely within a single dialect.

Bugaeva places kinship terms alongside body parts as the core of the obligatorily-possessed, inalienably-marked class in Ainu, yet the construction split shows that "inalienable" covers two morphosyntactically distinct sub-patterns rather than a single uniform category .

The general morphosyntax of both constructions and the affiliative-suffix morphophonology are treated in and ; the present chapter covers what is specific to kinship and to the honorific use of the 4th-person possessive.

Nakagawa organises Hokkaido kinship vocabulary into two sets: a concept-construction set, whose members take N kor and resist a direct person-prefix, and an affiliative-construction set, whose concept stem and affiliative form are both in use .
The concept-construction set contains principally senior-generation terms: , , , , , .
The affiliative-construction set is given below, with short and long affiliative forms and, where attested, address forms.
The affiliative-suffix allomorphs follow the same phonological patterns as body-part nouns, documented in .
Vowel-final stems (type ①: ona, unu, sa, po) take the optional suffix -hV₁ for the long form — ona→onaha, unu→unuhu.
Consonant-final stems mostly follow type ③-1 (-i(hi)): yup→yupi(hi), sut→suci(hi), mat→maci(hi), tures→turesi(hi).
For vowel-final stems the short affiliative is formally identical to the concept form; in the 3rd person a person-prefix is the only overt marker of the possessed reading ‹consensus›.
The two address affiliatives yupo and sapo carry an -o ending not predictable from the standard suffix classes.
Nakagawa lists them as lexically specified address forms without deriving the -o morpheme synchronically .
Seven affiliative-construction terms — ona, unu, sut, ekas, aca, yup, sa — are restricted to third-person reference and narrative use; they cannot be used to address the relative directly .
For elder siblings the address forms are yupo and sapo with ku=; for parents and grandparents the concept-construction terms (mici, hapo, ekasi, huci) serve as vocatives .

Satō confirms ku=sapo and ku=yupo as the securely attested direct-address (対称詞) forms; Nakagawa additionally reports ku=mataki and ku=matkarku as vocatives to younger kin, but their distribution is less fully documented ; ‹contested›.
The split is grammatical, not a register choice: the construction assigned to a kin noun determines what address form is even possible .
Narrative formulae use the reference forms in story-openings, where the logophoric narrator lists family members:
Whether a kin term belongs to the concept-construction or the affiliative-construction set, it does not appear bare in prose; every token carries possessive morphology.
When no discourse-salient possessor is active — in riddles, generic statements, or elicitation — the 4th-person A-prefix a= supplies a default unspecified-possessor value.
Bugaeva reports that kin and body-part forms elicited in isolation are supplied by speakers with a 3rd- or 4th-person index and the possessive suffix, never as a bare stem .
The general kin-group noun takes the affiliative form utari(hi) — k=utari 'my household', a=utari 'one's family (narrator's)' — and is among the higher-frequency kinship-domain tokens in the corpus .

The community member thegodofneet (aynu-corpora Discord, 2025-09-17) observes that the affiliative naturally narrows to a possessed reading because a kin-group not belonging to anyone is conceptually difficult to express; this parallels the bound-noun tendency across kin vocabulary ‹contested›.

Community member nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-06-15) further notes that the compounds onautari and unuutari, literally 'the father-group' and 'the mother-group', can designate 'parents' collectively ‹contested›.

The 4th-person prefix a= carries three uses that converge on kin affiliatives: (i) the unspecified-possessor default described above; (ii) the logophoric narrator first person in oral narrative; and (iii) an honorific use, where the speaker marks an esteemed third-party possessor — a deity (kamuy), a divine ancestor, or a high-status figure — with a= rather than the zero 3rd-person form, treating the referent as too elevated for the ordinary 3rd-person default ; .
The three values are formally identical; context, genre, and the referent's status together determine the reading.
The honorific-possession use is most consistent in kamuy yukar and ritual-register texts, where divine possessors regularly appear in kinship constructions with a=.
This is one reason the frequency of a= with kin affiliatives in the oral-literature corpus is conspicuously higher than pure third-person reference would produce alone.
The full treatment of the 4th-person paradigm and its logophoric and honorific functions is in and ; the register dimension belongs to .

The construction is the standard schema for story-opening family inventories:

The BE-type is unavailable for alienable nouns; its restriction to the inalienable domain is argued in .
The full typology of predicative-possession clauses is in .

Several kin-related meanings are expressed not by the full possession construction but through lexicalised incorporated-noun + kor compounds functioning as intransitive predicates denoting change-of-state or relational events rather than stative possession :
These compounds belong to a productive incorporation pattern; the reciprocal derivatives ukokor 'share (children)' and kopokor 'have a child with X' extend the set .
The incorporation pattern is treated systematically in .
The kinship lexicon shows some of the widest dialect spread in Hokkaido Ainu, and the construction assignments in each dialect interact with local lexical choices .
'Father' is the most variable kin term.

The oldest reconstructed form is aca (affiliative-construction; current in Sōya and Samani); mici (concept-construction) is the baseline for Horobetsu, Shizunai, Tokachi, Kushiro, Bihoro, and main Saru; iyapo appears in lower Saru; hampe in Ishikari; and hapo in Chitose.
Where hapo means 'father', 'mother' shifts to totto to avoid homonymy with the widespread hapo 'mother' .

The community member thegodofneet (aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-06-08) cites Chiri's dialect survey for the same mapping and notes that hapo extends further to 'elder sibling' in Kuril varieties ‹corpus-confirmed›.

Eastern Hokkaido fusion forms. In Tokachi the compounds konnarpe 'aunt' (< kor unarpe), koracapo 'uncle', and koruci 'grandmother' have grammaticalised to the point where internal structure is opaque; 'so-and-so's aunt' then requires kor konnarpe, treating the formerly bimorphemic form as a simplex concept-form noun ‹speculative›.

The younger-sister asymmetry reflects the bilateral-descent kinship system. 'Younger brother' is ak across Hokkaido; 'younger sister of a sister' is matak (all-Hokkaido, from mat-ak 'female younger-sibling'). 'Younger sister of a brother' varies: Saru uses matapa (from mat-apa, denoting a more distant relation), Chitose uses macirpe, and oral-narrative tradition generally uses tures(i) .
The form onneke(he) 'mother / parent', found in the Tokachi (Honbetsu) and Nemuro varieties, and onneike 'parent' in Asahikawa, follows the standard type-① affiliative pattern: onneke→onnekehe.

The community member antitwilight (aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-15) proposes the etymology onne 'old' + -ike 'person', with semantic narrowing from 'the elder [side of the household]' to 'parent' and further to 'mother' in some varieties ‹speculative›.

Across these variants the construction assignment — concept-set or affiliative-set — is stable within each dialect: variation affects which lexical item is chosen, not the morphosyntactic class it belongs to ‹consensus›.
Hokkaido Ainu marks person obligatorily on the finite verb; the independent personal pronouns are additive elements, not the primary vehicle of argument tracking.
Nakagawa assigns them arity 0 — they behave like adverbial adjuncts, are never obligatory, and cannot be incorporated into a verb stem, unlike other noun phrases of arity −1 .

Kindaichi and Chiri captured the same point by calling the pronoun a 贅語 'pleonasm', comparing kuani ku=eraman 'I know' to Latin ego scio and French moi je sais: the verbal index alone suffices, and the pronoun doubles it for emphasis .
Tamura's Saru description confirms the pattern — pronouns function syntactically like adverbs, appearing only when a specific pragmatic condition is met .

The practical result is that pronouns appear far less freely than in Japanese, and third-person forms are particularly rare: where Japanese uses 彼/彼女, Hokkaido Ainu overwhelmingly prefers demonstrative phrases (toan kur 'that person', nea menoko 'that woman') .
The sole pronoun that is dialect-invariant across all of Hokkaido is 2SG eani.

All other forms show at least some regional variation; the central division separates Saru and Chitose (1SG kani) from the rest of Hokkaido (1SG kuani), and the plural and fourth-person rows diverge considerably across zones .
The verbal affixes these pronouns reduplicate are described in .
Reflexive marking in Hokkaido Ainu is realized verbally, not by dedicated reflexive pronouns.
The prefixes yay- and si-, which redirect an action onto the subject or its possessor, are covered in and .

The emphatic 'I myself / you yourself' function that some languages express with a distinct intensive-pronoun series is realized in HA by the independent pronoun plus a focus or topic particle — the same pronouns described here, in their focus-hosting function.
The personal pronouns are not primitive forms.

Tamura's foundational analysis derives each one by attaching a person index to one of two existential roots — singular an 'exist (SG)' or plural oka(y) 'exist (PL)' — and then nominalizing the result with the possessed (affiliative) form suffix, whose base is the formal noun ; .
The formula is: person-index + existential root + hi.
A diagnostic point secures this analysis.
The plural pronouns use the transitive-subject / possessive person prefixes (ci=, a(n)=, eci=) rather than the intransitive-S suffixes (=as, =an) that a finite plural-existential verb would carry.
This shows that the base is a noun oka(y)+hi 'the (plural) being', which is possessed, not a finite verb oka(y) that is person-inflected ; .
The formal noun hi surfaces in the singular pronouns but is lost in the plurals.
The singulars preserve it: ku=an-hi → kani (with contraction), e=an-hi → eani, an-hi → anihi.
In the plural series the sequence okay-hi would produce an illicit syllable contact; hi is suppressed, and the final -y of okay further drops in Saru, yielding oka .

The 1SG contraction kuani → kani in Saru and Chitose follows the same vowel-deletion process as ciep → cep 'fish', where the high vowel of the prefix is absorbed by the adjacent syllable (gengojiro, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-02-05; asserted, corroborated by ).
Elsewhere in Hokkaido the uncontracted form kuani is maintained.
The full Hokkaido pronoun inventory spans six major dialect zones.
The singular/plural distinction is maintained throughout, though the plural and fourth-person rows show the greatest variation .
Corpus search returns kani at 522 tokens, eani at 716, and asinuma at 668; by contrast, the first-person exclusive plural coka reaches only 41 tokens ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The disproportion between singular and plural frequencies matches Nakagawa's description of the plural forms as genuinely marginal .
Clusivity in the first-person plural — exclusive ci=/=as versus the fourth-person inclusive — is treated in .
Beyond the existential-base type, two additional strategies contribute to the plural and third/fourth-person rows .
Type II — person-prefix + utari: Several dialects form plural pronouns with the associative-plural noun (possessed form utari): Tokachi ciutari (1PL), eciutari (2PL), anutari (4PL).
These forms retain the lexical sense of utari 'kin, associates' and stand "halfway between a pronoun and a common noun" .

The Saru/Chitose sequences k=utari, a=utari similarly mean 'my / their family' with a third-person (non-inclusive) verb, and only Tokachi anutari — which triggers a fourth-person (inclusive) verb — functions as a full plural pronoun 'we (including you)' .
Type III — sinuma base: The 3SG form sinuma and 4SG asinuma are built on a distinct base whose internal structure is unanalysed synchronically.
Kindaichi posited a literary 2SG form esinuma by analogy, but Nakagawa found no attested example and treats it as a phantom form ‹speculative›
Nakagawa identifies three conditions that trigger an independent pronoun where the verbal index alone would otherwise suffice .
A neutral predication ('I am here', 'he came') carries no pronoun; a self-introduction such as *asinuma anak … a=ne 'I am —' would be almost never said without special emphasis .
When a participant is singled out from alternatives ('I and not someone else will do it'), the pronoun precedes the verb and co-indexes the verbal prefix.
