When two participants are explicitly opposed in consecutive clauses — 'you do X; I do Y' — each is marked by the independent pronoun plus the topic marker anak=ne.
The following Saru dialogue from the Akor Itak teaching material pairs eani anakne (addressee) against kani anakne (speaker):
Focus and scalar particles such as ka 'even/also', anakne (topic-focus), and hem must attach to a noun phrase; they cannot host on a verbal index.
*ku= anakne and *ku= ka are ungrammatical.
An independent pronoun is therefore obligatory whenever such a particle scopes over a participant .
In the following Saru example, asinuma hosts the scalar particle ka:
The same constraint governs topic fronting: kani anakne … is the canonical pattern, impossible as *ku= anakne.
The broader implications for argument structure and pro-drop in HA are taken up in , and the particle paradigm in .

The fourth-person row is where the dialect paradigm shows its sharpest internal contradictions, providing, in Nakagawa's words, "an important hint for the historical origin of the fourth-person singular" that remains unresolved ‹contested›
In Saru and Chitose both the pronoun and the verb distinguish singular from plural: pronoun asinuma (SG) vs aoka (PL), paralleled by distinct singular and plural verbal forms.

Shizunai makes the opposite move: the pronoun preserves a singular/plural distinction (anani SG vs anoka PL), but the verb is invariably plural regardless of which pronoun is used — the pronoun-level contrast survives without a verbal counterpart.
Horobetsu shows the mirror image: the verb retains a singular/plural opposition, but the only available fourth-person pronoun is the plural-base aokay, used even for a single narrator .
These "opposite twists" are left as an open diachronic question by Nakagawa.

One community-proposed reconstruction treats the 4th-person prefix as a-/=an < *an-, with Shizunai anokay preserving the older form: the nasal-drop that produced Saru/western a= vs Tokachi/Ishikari an= would be blocked at pronoun level because the result would create hiatus (.k1270, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-03-22; ‹speculative›, attributed to Nakagawa).
The connection between this prefix form and the broader morphological alignment of the fourth person is discussed in and .
In oral narrative, the fourth-person pronoun asinuma functions routinely as the first-person narrative self, alternating with or supplementing the verbal index ku=/k=.
Corpus evidence places asinuma at 669 tokens, predominantly in Saru narrative texts.
The fourth-person pronoun appears in this function with topic-focus particles — the same focus-hosting role described above:
The honorific and logophoric uses of the fourth person — including the use of a fourth-person verb for a single esteemed addressee — are treated in .
The full debate over terminology (fourth person, indefinite, inclusive) and the referential range of the a=/=an/i= affix set is carried in .
Hokkaido Ainu demonstratives divide into two formally distinct sets.
One set — the deictic (on-site) forms — points to referents in the physical scene; the other — the anaphoric forms — tracks referents established in discourse.
Japanese uses a single three-way この/その/あの series for both functions; Hokkaido Ainu keeps the two apart with different lexical roots .

Kindaichi and Chiri's classical grammar already identified the deictic prenominals as fusions of three locative roots (te 'here', ta 'there', to 'yonder') with the copula an, while the anaphoric ne-series points in the discourse stream, not in space .

Refsing's Shizunai description formalises the whole system as a two-dimensional root paradigm ; the typological framing of Diessel's demonstrative taxonomy maps the anaphoric forms onto a recognitional–anaphoric cluster distinct from both exophoric pointing and grammaticalized definite articles .
Minor deictic prenominals in Saru include verse-register tanan (pl.
tanoka(y)) and emphatic tapan (pl.
tapoka(y)), the latter most frequent in Chitose address contexts .
The independent personal pronouns are treated in ; the interrogative and indefinite pro-forms in .
The etymology of the deictic prenominals is transparent.

Kindaichi and Chiri derive tan from ta + copula an, and toan from to + an; the medial taan is the long (information-richer) variant of tan, and the plurals tanokay / tonokay are formed by fusing the root with the plural existential okay ; .

The functional difference between tan and taan parallels Japanese この vs. その: tan is used when the referent is immediately at hand, taan when it lies within the speaker's perceptual sphere but is not immediately present, and toan when it is away from both speaker and addressee .

Community discussion has proposed an iconic account of the vowel gradient: longer form encodes more spatial distance-information, front raised vowel signals proximity, back lowered vowel signals remoteness ‹speculative›
The functional distribution is uncontroversial ; the iconicity explanation is unverified.

The distal toan is also the principal vehicle for nominal third-person reference: Hokkaido Ainu uses toan kur 'that person' or nea kur 'that person (aforementioned)' where languages with grammaticalized third-person pronouns use them, since the third-person pronouns of the paradigm treated in are rare in actual discourse .
The anaphoric prenominals — ne, nea, newaan — are formally separate from the deictic set and cannot be used to point at a scene-present referent.
nea picks up a referent already established in the discourse; in a narrative, nea menoko means 'the woman (who was just spoken of)' and does not admit a deictic (scene-pointing) reading .
The weaker ne marks a referent as immediately prior in the discourse; newaan is more emphatic.

Corpus counts confirm the predominance of the anaphoric function in narrative text: the surface string nea occurs approximately 1,984 times in the ainu-corpora aligned set — substantially more than toan (c. 735 tokens) and tanpe (c. 391 tokens) combined — consistent with its role as the primary anaphora-tracking device of narrative ‹corpus-confirmed›
(Surface counts conflate any homophonous forms and are upper bounds.)
Third-person reference. Where Japanese uses 彼 / 彼女, Hokkaido Ainu characteristically uses a demonstrative NP — nea menoko 'that woman (referred to)', toan kur 'that person (over there)'.

The third-person and fourth-person pronouns of the independent paradigm occur, but they are rare; the demonstrative NP is the default anaphora-tracking strategy in oral literature and in narrative prose .
The interaction of this strategy with pronominal-argument interpretations of the person affixes is considered in .

Dialect variation. nea is pan-Hokkaido; most dialects outside Saru and Chitose use nean (pronoun neanpe) — attested in Horobetsu, Shizunai, and Ishikari, with both forms occurring in some Horobetsu and Ishikari speakers .
Shizunai and the dialects to the east additionally have ikia (pl.
ikirok; pronoun ikiap), a second anaphoric prenominal functionally close to nea but more restricted in scope; it is rare in Saru .
The Ijäs pedagogical grammar covers the core nea forms alongside the deictic series .

Each prenominal may fuse with the formal noun (~pe) to produce a demonstrative pronoun referring to a thing rather than modifying a noun head: tan-pe 'this (thing)', toan-pe 'that (thing)', newaan-pe / nea-p 'the aforementioned thing', and the eastern ikia-p (Shizunai-and-east) .
The suffix alternation -pe / -p follows the phonological environment of the nominalizer, treated in .
The indefinite pronoun nep 'something / what' — formed from the same root ne- plus the nominalizer — is an interrogative/indefinite, not a demonstrative.
For anaphoric reference to a thing, Hokkaido Ainu uses newaanpe or neap, not nep .
This gap in the anaphoric pronoun paradigm is an incidental consequence of nep's grammaticalization as an indefinite/interrogative; the full indefinite and interrogative series are treated in .
The three roots , , and function as locative nouns taking case particles directly, not as prenominal modifiers.
Only ta and to enter the prenominal by fusing with the copula (ta-an → tan, to-an → toan).
The proximal root te does not produce a prenominal and cannot precede a head noun — *te menoko is ungrammatical; te only takes case particles (te ta 'here', te un 'this way', te wano 'from now') .

Case-marked forms of the deictic prenominals arise by ellipsis of the formal noun hi before the case particle: taan ta 'here' < taan hi ta 'the-place-of-this at'; toan un 'over there (toward)' < toan hi un .
These locative uses intersect with the relational-noun system; see .
Refsing's Shizunai description assembles the demonstrative, interrogative, and indefinite forms into a two-dimensional paradigm of roots and semantic dimensions .
It is the most explicit systematic statement of the opposition's internal logic in any published Hokkaido description.
Two observations follow from the grid.
The anaphoric root ne- is formally identical to the interrogative root of nep 'what', nen 'who', and neyta 'where', and to the copula ne.
Refsing flags this convergence as possibly more than coincidence ‹speculative›.
The place-row entry for the anaphoric column is empty — a systematic gap: there is no form *neta or *neyta functioning as 'the aforementioned place'.
Intra-Hokkaido variation affects chiefly the anaphoric prenominal and the distal pair.
nea vs.
nean. Saru and Chitose use nea; most other Hokkaido dialects (Horobetsu, Shizunai, Ishikari) use nean (pronoun neanpe), with both forms occurring in some Horobetsu and Ishikari speakers .
ikia / ikiap. Shizunai and the dialects east of it have a second anaphoric prenominal ikia (pl.
ikirok; pronoun ikiap), functionally close to nea but appearing to be more restricted in discourse scope.
It is rare in Saru .
toan vs.
toon. Saru favours toan; both forms occur in Chitose; Obihiro and Tokachi avoid toan; Ishikari lacks toon .
Takahashi's Tokachi description documents the local demonstrative system and the range of deictic forms available there .
Hokkaido Ainu has no grammatical article.

Neither the deictic nor the anaphoric demonstratives are obligatory in contexts where a definite-article language would require an article; bare nouns occur freely in argument position without referential specification ‹consensus›.
The language encodes identifiability through a cluster of constructions, none of which individually constitutes an article system:
Anaphoric demonstrative nea / ne marks a referent as established and salient in discourse — the functional counterpart of the definite article in post-introduction contexts.
Its high corpus frequency relative to the deictic forms (§3 above) is consistent with this article-like role ‹corpus-suggested›.
Possessive morphology. The personal possessor prefix combined with the affiliative form of an inalienable noun singles out the referent as uniquely identifiable relative to its possessor.
The alienable/inalienable split and the semantics of obligatory possession are treated in .
Proper nouns and naming are inherently referentially unique and carry no additional definiteness morphology.

Discourse position. A sentence-initial topic NP is typically presupposed as identifiable; first-mention NPs in non-topic position are indefinite by discourse default, without any morphological signal.
Whether nea should be analysed as a grammaticalized definite article is contested ‹contested›.

Against the article analysis: nea is absent from many clearly definite contexts where English or Japanese would require the article; it alternates with a bare noun in narrative without apparent semantic contrast; and its distribution is better described as anaphoric-recognitional — marking a referent as recoverable from discourse — than as an absolute definiteness category .
Refsing glosses the Shizunai cognate as 'the said', which aligns with recognitional use rather than a grammaticalized article .
In Diessel's typology, recognitional demonstratives track referents that are identifiable through shared knowledge or discourse memory but are not fully grammaticalized articles .
The related claim — that the affiliative form of certain nouns carries definiteness-like semantics in post-possessive contexts — is evaluated in that chapter.
For the clause-level question of how topics and foci interact with the demonstrative system, see .
The interaction of the demonstrative system with clausal interrogation — in particular with sentence-final question particles and with the interrogative existential frame — is treated in .
Hokkaido Ainu has a set of interrogative pro-forms covering the semantic slots that in other languages are filled by wh-words: things, persons, places, manners, times, quantities, and identity.
They are not a uniform part of speech.

Nouns (hemanta 'what', hunna 'who', hunak 'where'), adverbs (makanak 'how', hempara 'when'), and prenominals (hempak 'how many', inan 'which') all figure in the paradigm, each with distinct syntactic distribution .
The same forms — or a set of n-initial cognates — serve as indefinite pro-forms ('something', 'anyone', 'somewhere') when embedded in non-interrogative clauses or combined with focus particles.
Across Hokkaido, two competing root families divide the dialects: an hem-/hun- series in Saru and Chitose, and an nep/nen/ney/nekon series in most other varieties .

The clausal mechanisms that convert these wh-words into questions — the existential question frame, question particles, intonation — are treated in ; the present chapter covers the forms themselves, their morphological structure, their dialect distribution, and their indefinite function.
The Saru dialect uses an h-initial series for most interrogative slots.
The inventory and the part-of-speech classification of each form are given below :

hunak belongs to the locative noun (〈place〉) subclass and takes case particles directly — hunak ta 'where (at)', hunak un 'where (to)', hunak wa 'where (from)' — without the intermediate locative noun or 'place-of' .
The locative-noun subclass is set out in .
hemanta and hunna take the existential question frame rather than a copular predicate: 'what is it?' is hemanta an? and 'who is it?' is hunna an? .
The sequence hemanta ne is occupied by the 'why' periphrasis, where ne is the copula; a bare hemanta ne? therefore means 'why?' not 'what is it?'.
'Why' has no monomorphemic form.
The three periphrases share the core hemanta 'what' and differ in what follows it: the bare purposive kusu, the bare copula ne, or both together.
Nakagawa reports "no clear meaning difference" among them .
The purposive linker kusu in its causal function is treated in .
'How many' and 'which' are prenominals: they precede and modify a head noun rather than standing alone.
hempak 'how many' further grounds hempakpe 'how many things', hempakiw 'how many people', and the intensive inehempak 'ever so many' .
The human-count suffix -iw and the thing-count suffix -pe are the same suffixes found in the numeral system; see .
Across Hokkaido, the Saru/Chitose hem-/hun- forms are replaced in most other varieties by an n-initial series.
The boundary follows the established dialect division between 日高西部 (Saru, Chitose, Mukawa) and the central and northern varieties ; .
The full dialect comparison, after Nakagawa's table 78, is as follows:

The most internally fragmented cell is 'where (to)': Shizunai and Tokachi use enon / onon, whose e-/o- elements may correspond to the 'head/tail' directional prefixes but whose -non remains unexplained .
The 'whose' or 'of which place' construction uses ney un even in h-series dialects, because the un there is the two-place relational verb 'belong to', not the allative case particle .
The relational-verb un is discussed alongside the possession system in .
The following pair from the アコㇿイタㇰ textbook illustrates the h/n split for 'who':

The Shizunai system as described by Refsing gives the most explicit formal statement of the demonstrative–interrogative–indefinite grid, aligning an anaphoric ne- series, proximal ta- series, distal to- series, interrogative ne- root, and indefinite …ka forms across person, place, and manner dimensions.
The overlap of the anaphoric ne, the interrogative ne- root, and the copula ne in the n-dialects may be "more than coincidence" ‹speculative›.
The demonstrative and anaphoric ne- system is treated in .
The internal structure of the hem-/hun- forms is not fully transparent in the accessible grammars.
Nakagawa notes that interrogatives are built on two roots (hem- and hun-) plus a third, geographically restricted root in mak- (makanak) .
The n-series form ney 'where/when (n-dialect)' is transparently segmentable: ne + hi (the formal noun 'place/time'), giving 'which place/time' .
The Shizunai place-form neyta adds the locative particle directly to this stem .

A bimorphemic analysis of the h-series has been proposed in the community: hunna 'who' = hun + na (a human-count suffix); hunak 'where' = hun + yak (the conditional yak); hempak 'how many' = hem + pak (the limitative postposition ); hempara 'when' = hem + pa + ara (nukopoli, , 2023-12-08) ‹contested›.

The decomposition is internally consistent with the two-root observation and would explain the h/n alternation as operating at root level; it remains unverified in the peer-reviewed literature, and the grammaticalization paths it requires are not reconstructed in the available sources.
The contracted Saru variants hnta and hinta (from hemanta) are spoken-register forms.
Both allow the existential question frame (hnta an? 'what is it?') and the copular why-frame (hnta ne? 'why?') .
hemanta also functions as an ordinary noun meaning roughly 'thing-of-unknown-sort', and in Chitose kor hemanta! serves as a term of abuse (lit. 'having a whatnot') .

The classical grammar of attests ne--root interrogative compounds — ne-kotan-un-pe 'person of which village', ne-moshir-un-pe 'of which land' — and the literary prenominal inki 'which' (inki nishpa 'which lord'), confirming the antiquity of the interrogative ne- element that the modern n-dialects preserve.
The 'when' form hempara is treated as original; the Tokachi and Bihoro n-series form nempara arose by analogical h- → n- replacement under pressure from the rest of the n-paradigm ‹speculative›.
The interrogative and indefinite ('some-', 'any-') functions are distributed across two form-sets in h-series dialects.

In Saru, the interrogative uses hem-/hun- forms while the indefinite uses the n-series: 'who?' = hunna but 'someone/anyone' = nen; 'what?' = hemanta but 'something/anything' = nep; 'where?' = hunak but 'somewhere' = ney .
The n-dialects have no analogous split: 'what?' and 'something' are both nep.
Two slots are identical for both functions in all dialects: 'how many' and 'which' .
The asymmetry is not absolute.

Residual mixing occurs in both directions: h-series forms can appear as indefinites in some Saru texts, and Horobetsu — which uses nep as its interrogative 'what' — uses hemanta as its indefinite, reversing the Saru pattern ‹corpus-suggested›.
These exceptions point to ongoing reorganisation rather than a categorical split.

Indefinite pro-forms combine with the focus/scalar particle =ka 'even, also' and the scalar concessive ne yakka 'even if': nep ka 'anything (at all)', nen ne yakka 'anyone (at all)', ney ta ka 'anywhere' .
The scalar semantics of =ka ('even X') combined with an indefinite root yields a free-choice reading; the particle itself belongs to the focus system described in .

Typologically, the pattern maps onto the cross-linguistic tendency — documented by — for interrogative and indefinite functions to be formally related but distinguished by particles or suppletive roots.
In Ainu the distinction in h-dialects is lexical (two root sets), with =ka overlaid on the indefinite root rather than on the interrogative ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Wh-words in Hokkaido Ainu are used in situ: they occupy the argument or adjunct position of the constituent they replace and do not move obligatorily to a clause-peripheral slot .
This follows from the nonconfigurational properties of the language discussed in , where nominal arguments are essentially free adjuncts and the verb indexes their referents independently.
A locative wh-word such as hunak un therefore remains in the goal position of a motion verb:
The clausal mechanisms that convert an in-situ wh-word into a matrix question — the existential frame an?, the question particle ya, and intonation — are treated in .
The wh-word itself takes no special morphology in the question context.
Wh-words embed freely in indirect questions.
The interrogative pro-form stays in situ within the embedded clause, which is then nominalized by the clause-final formal noun or the nominalizer p/pe.
The affiliative/possessed form is not triggered on the wh-word itself; it applies to the relational nouns that head the embedding.
This parallels the general nominalization syntax described in .

Independent personal pronouns — including the pro-forms built on the person-affix paradigm — are discussed separately in ; the present pro-forms are not personal pronouns but belong to the nominal and adverbial parts of speech catalogued above.
A small closed set of nouns in Hokkaido Ainu encodes the spatial or relational position of one entity with respect to another.
These nouns — , , , , , and others catalogued below — are called locative nouns (位置名詞) in the Japanese-medium descriptive tradition ; ; .
Three distributional properties define the class.

First, the members are obligatorily possessed: a relational noun cannot head a free-standing noun phrase in isolation; it must either be preceded by a noun phrase whose referent supplies the reference object, or it must carry a personal prefix directly to express whose spatial domain is at stake (§7 below; see ).
Second, Hokkaido Ainu case particles require a place-designating noun (〈場所〉) immediately before them ; ; relational nouns are the main device for building that slot from an ordinary common noun.

The canonical pattern is cise or ta 'at the house' (lit. house + place-of + at), and its extension to the other case particles (or un, or wa, or peka) constitutes the primary locative-case system, treated in .
Third, a relational noun appears in its possessed (affiliative) form when combined with a host noun: or → oro, ka → kasi (§3).
Whether the class is best analysed as a set of inalienably-possessed nouns or as a set of postpositions inflected for possession is the central analytical question of the chapter (§8).
The table below lists the core members with their concept form, possessed (long) form, spatial meaning, and a representative construction.
Possessed forms follow the locative-noun long-form system — the lexically specified suffixes -ke, -V, and -si (§ below) — rather than the common-noun affiliative pattern .
Nakagawa gives the long forms of or, ka, enka, sam, tum, and corpok directly; samake and the contracted tumke are also frequent in corpus text ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The forms given for os, pok, and kotor are not directly verified in the sources consulted ‹speculative›.

citations.pages: s.v. or, ka, sam, tum, corpok, soy, kotor

text: A few entries call for comment.

The pair ka / enka are often treated as co-members of the 'above' domain: ka encodes contact or near-contact with a supporting surface ('on top of, resting on'), while enka encodes vertical distance above without contact ('over, above').
The pair corpok / pok occupies a similar near-duplicate slot in the 'below' domain; the distributional boundary between them is not settled by the sources consulted ‹contested›.

The noun kotor appears reliably as a component of the compound tekkotor 'palm of the hand' (lit. hand + surface) , and the pattern suggests a class of vertical-surface spatial nouns; but its use as a free relational noun head (i.e.
X kotor ta 'at the face of X') is less thoroughly documented in the sources consulted.

The noun so appears in corpus narrative in the construction iwor so ka 'over the top of the hunting ground', where so (upper back area) combines with ka (top) — a stacking of two relational nouns into a single locative expression (see §4 below).
Its standalone affiliative form has not been identified in the sources consulted.
Two relational nouns — or and os — also appear in Nakagawa's catalogue of postpositional adverbs (後置副詞), the autonomous adverb class that does not require a 〈場所〉 host ; .
This dual membership is a structural fact at the heart of the noun-vs-adposition debate in §8.
The possessed forms in the table are built with a small suffix set — -ke, an echo or fixed vowel (-V), and -si — that is lexically specified per noun: Nakagawa's long form (長形) of the locative noun .
The system is separate from the common-noun affiliative suffixes, and Nakagawa hypothesises that one layer of common-noun possessive morphology was borrowed from it ‹speculative›.
-ke is the most frequent member, and several nouns combine two layers: kasi (ka + -si) is further extendable to kasike(he).
Consonant-final bases insert an echo vowel before -ke: sam-a-ke, tum-u-ke.

The contracted shapes without the echo vowel are frequent in text — tumke is much commoner in the corpus than tumuke (aynu tumke wa 'from among the Ainu', amam tumke ta 'among the grain'), and kaske stands beside kasike ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Three grammatical properties ride on the long form .

It can head a noun phrase alone, which the Type-1 basic form cannot; it is the form that carries the objective person prefixes (e=samake ta 'beside you'); and it accepts the further possessive extension -he (samakehe).

In running text the long form appears almost always in the layered locative frame, followed by a case particle: X samake ta, X tumke ta/wa, and temporal okake ta 'after that, afterwards', a high-frequency narrative connective ‹corpus-confirmed›.

This locational -ke is homophonous with two verbal suffixes — the anticausative -ke and the transitivizing -ke of the lexical valency pairs () — but distinct from both: it attaches only to the closed locative-noun class and yields a noun, never a verb.
The string orke carries two readings that have to be sorted contextually, and Tamura's Saru dictionary documents both .

In suptom orke 'the place around the middle of the trunk' and utar orkehe it is the ordinary long form of or, the same locative formation described above — the -he extension in the second confirms the analysis.
In the paired frame N orke … N orke the same string reads additively: anun orke apa orke nep uwehosi arikikpa 'outsiders and kin alike, all of them vie with each other in working hard'.
forms: anun orke apa orke nep uwehosi arikikpa

text: Corpus tokens divide the same way — tu kewtum orke re kewtum orke 'in two hearts, in three hearts' keeps the locative sense under the numerals ‹corpus-confirmed›.
forms: tu kewtum orke re kewtum orke

text: Relational nouns belong to the inalienable (obligatorily-possessed) noun class, alongside body parts, kinship terms, and part–whole relational stems.
Like those classes, they cannot appear as a syntactic head without an expressed or inferable possessor .
The morphology of this possession is the affiliative (所属形): in the construction [NOUN + relational-noun + case-particle], the relational noun takes its possessed form.
The phonological mechanism that produces or → oro, ka → kasi, sam → sami, and so on, is the echo-vowel or suffix-vowel process described in .
A diagnostically important minimal pair is provided by ni ka ta 'onto/on top of the tree' and cikuni kasi un 'toward the treetop' .
The first uses the concept (bare) form ka before the locative particle ta; the second uses the affiliative kasi before the allative un.

The distribution of concept vs affiliative form before different case particles for this noun parallels what Satō documents for or in Chitose: both forms are grammatical with a following locative noun, but the short-form fusion (or + ta → otta) is the unmarked spoken realization, while oro ta appears in more deliberate or expanded styles ‹corpus-suggested›.

A community discussion on samampa (nukopoli, 2024-11-26) analyses it as sam-am-pa 'lying on the side' — identifying sam 'side' as a productive base entering compound verb formation — and proposes that samama 'to place sideways' = sam-ama (Kayano's Saru dictionary) ‹speculative›.
This use of sam as an incorporated nominal base in complex verbs is a point of intersection with the noun-incorporation system (see ).

The canonical locative construction in Hokkaido Ainu is a three-member sequence: a reference-object noun phrase, followed by a relational noun in its affiliative or concept form, followed by a case particle.
Nakagawa labels the middle position the 〈場所〉 'place' slot — a morphosyntactic position that the locative, allative, ablative, and perlative particles all require ; .
Relational nouns are the primary filler of that slot for ordinary common nouns.
The particle-specific fusion of or merits particular attention.
When or immediately precedes the locative particle ta, the sequence contracts to otta: cise otta 'at the house', nupuri otta 'at/on the mountain'.
The long form oro ta remains uncontracted .
This fusion does not apply to or un, or wa, or or peka; those remain uncontracted in all varieties.
The construction extends straightforwardly to other relational nouns.
The same case-particle set attaches to ka, sam, soy, and the other members of the inventory:

Two relational nouns may stack in sequence when the spatial description requires a two-step reference: an outer reference object, then a spatial noun within it, then a second spatial noun closer to the target.

The corpus yields iwor so ka a=ehóyupu wa 'flew over the top of the hunting ground's upper part' (lit. hunting-ground + upper-back + top + 4.A=fly.around + CONJ) , where so 'upper-back area' specifies the subregion of iwor 'hunting ground', and ka then positions the protagonist above that subregion (, Kawagami Matsuko, uwepeker 民話8, aa-irc/006 line 52).
Such stacking is consistent with the head-initial, modifier-following structure of Ainu nominal possession ‹corpus-suggested›.

Among the relational nouns, or occupies a singular position: its meaning has bleached to the point where it functions as a general locative placeholder for any noun requiring the 〈場所〉 slot, not just for entities that constitute physical places.

Satō's dedicated Chitose study traces the drift of or from a concrete relational noun 'the place of X' toward a grammaticalizing locative morpheme that renders any nominal as a place-designating argument.
The bleaching is visible in combinations where the host noun is not inherently a physical location.

In tan KIKAY or ta a=ewkoytak hi an yakun 'if we had a conversation with this machine' (lit. this machine's-place at), (ex. 373, Saru; 田村 1984: 50), the host noun KIKAY (a recording machine) is an instrument, not a spatial locus; or ta constructs the 〈場所〉 argument that the particle ta requires, mapping the instrumental participant onto a locative frame.
forms: tan KIKAY or ta a=ewkoytak hi an yakun

text: The Chitose corpus adds many parallel instances where abstract events or instruments appear in the host-noun position .

Whether this drift constitutes the grammaticalization of or into a general locative case-marker, or whether it reflects a productive but still compositional use of the relational noun, is a point on which Satō and Nakagawa take partially different positions ‹contested›: Nakagawa treats the construction as productive composition (noun + spatial-noun + particle), while Satō's Chitose evidence shows or extending into contexts where the 'place of X' semantics is increasingly opaque, suggesting at least the beginning of a grammaticalization cline.
The issue connects directly to the noun-vs-adposition debate in §8, because an advanced-stage grammaticalized or would be functionally indistinguishable from a locative postposition.
Nakagawa distinguishes two sub-classes of locative noun in Hokkaido Ainu, a distinction also partly reflected in Satō .
The first-class locative nouns are those whose primary function is to supply the 〈場所〉 slot: they follow a host noun and directly host a case particle.
or, ka, sam, soy, and corpok are the clearest members.
The second-class members are those whose primary occurrence is in compound nouns and verb bases rather than in the free-standing [NOUN + relational-noun + case-particle] frame.

kotor 'surface' is the paradigm case: it appears reliably in the lexicalized compound tekkotor 'palm of the hand' ( + kotor) and has left traces in the archaic directional forms, but it is not a productive first-class head in the contemporary spoken register.

Similarly, tum 'interior/midst' appears in place-name formation (proposed: o-tum-nay 'head-interior-river' for the toponym Otomonai; nukopoli, 2026-01-22) ‹speculative› and in compound verbs (tumpu 'storehouse' = tum 'interior' + pu; antitwilight, 2024-11-16) ‹speculative›, but its distributional range in the first-class frame remains less thoroughly documented than that of or or ka.
The class boundary is not sharp, and intermediate members exist.
In the postpositional adverb system , os(i) 'after' appears as an autonomous postpositional adverb that does not require a 〈場所〉 host.

This dual membership — relational noun in one construction, postpositional adverb in another — is also observed for or itself: Nakagawa lists it in both noun paradigms and in the broader locative system as a particle-combining locative element.
The overlap between the two classes is structural evidence for the noun-vs-adposition debate (§8).

An archaic directional suffix -na is attested in frozen forms: setunna 'from the front' and kotunna 'from behind', analysed as setur-na and kotor-na respectively (antitwilight, 2026-06-09); compare also pokna 'below', which may preserve the same suffix on the relational noun pok.
This suffix is not a productive case particle in contemporary Hokkaido Ainu, and no primary-source grammar in the read set treats it as such ‹speculative›.

Its existence as a fossil form is consistent with the hypothesis that the relational-noun class is older than the current case-particle system and that some members grammaticalized into the particle system at an earlier stage.
The possessor of a relational noun is third person (zero-marked) when the reference object is supplied by the preceding host noun phrase.
But relational nouns can also be directly possessed by speech-act participants via the standard personal prefixes treated in and .
In that case, the relational noun itself — not the host noun — bears the person prefix:

The full person paradigm for or follows the ordinary nominal possession pattern: ku=or 'my place', e=or 'your place', or (zero) 'his/her/its/their place', ci=or (1PL.EXCL) 'our place', a=or (4th person) 'the protagonist's/their general place' .
The same paradigm applies to all other first-class relational nouns: ku=ka ta 'on top of me', e=sam ta 'beside you' ‹consensus›.

These forms appear in contexts where the locative relation targets a person rather than a physical landmark, and they are attested in body-part locatives and relational idioms (see for how this intersects with external possession).

A productive derived construction involves the verb eykaun 'to surpass/be superior to', analysed by nukopoli ( 2024-11-24) as ka un 'be at the top of (someone)' with an applicative or transitivizing suffix — effectively the relational noun ka with allative un grammaticalized as a comparative marker ‹speculative›.
Whether this represents a synchronically transparent construction or a frozen derivation is not settled by the sources consulted.
The central analytical question is whether relational nouns constitute a subclass of nouns or a subclass of postpositions.
The dispute turns on which grammatical properties are weighted most heavily, and different descriptive traditions have come down on different sides ‹contested›.

Evidence for the noun analysis. Relational nouns take person affixes in exactly the same slots and with exactly the same forms as other inalienably-possessed nouns (ku=or, ku=sam, ku=ka parallel ku=sapa 'my head', ku=tek 'my hand'); they appear in the possessed (affiliative) form under possession, following the same morphophonological rules as the inalienable class (; ).
They enter compound-noun and incorporated-noun formation as ordinary nominal bases (tekkotor, tumpu), which is diagnostic of noun status in Ainu (see ).
Nakagawa treats them as a noun subclass throughout.
The same analysis underlies Ijäs's pedagogical treatment , which presents the locative construction as a possessed-noun-plus-particle sequence.

Evidence for the adposition analysis. Functionally, relational nouns occupy the same distributional slot as adpositions: they appear between a nominal complement and a case particle, and they encode the same spatial relations that languages with postpositions typically encode with a postpositional head.
Several members of the class — notably os(i) 'after' — appear in Nakagawa's catalogue of postpositional adverbs (後置副詞) ; .

Satō's Chitose evidence for or shows the form extending beyond referential 'place of X' into a general locative-marking function, which is the expected trajectory of a grammaticalizing postposition, not of a lexical noun.

The pedagogical grammar by Ijäs places some members of the class in its postposition section alongside case particles — a pragmatic descriptive choice that reflects the adpositional function these forms serve for learners.

The most defensible synchronic position is that the class is in transition: the morphological behaviour (person affixes, affiliative alternation, incorporation) identifies the members as nouns, while their functional distribution (obligatory position between complement and particle, encoding spatial relations, extension to non-spatial contexts) pushes in the adposition direction.

A parallel situation is found in several languages of Mesoamerica, where the same class of inalienably-possessed nominal forms — often glossed as 'relational nouns' in the descriptive literature — occupies this intermediate position between noun and adposition .

In those typological terms, Hokkaido Ainu relational nouns are best labelled relational nouns rather than postpositions or adpositions: they are nominal in morphology and adpositional in function ‹contested›.

Whether first-class members like or and ka are more advanced on a grammaticalization cline toward postpositions than second-class members like kotor is a plausible hypothesis supported by Satō's work on or but not yet generalized across the full inventory ‹speculative›.
The syntactic behavior of relational-noun phrases in nonconfigurational and pronominal-argument contexts is taken up in and .
Hokkaido Ainu marks local relations — location, source, goal, and path — through two formally distinct classes.

Satō groups both under the label postpositions (後置詞) and draws a sharp internal split: case particles (格助詞) require a preceding locative nominal (a ⟨place⟩-type noun) and are bound to it; postpositional adverbs (後置副詞) are distributionally autonomous, take any preceding nominal, and several carry person prefixes of their own ; .
Ijäs 2023 presents the same two-class organization .

The structural pivot of the case-particle system is the locative noun (long form ), which converts a common noun into a ⟨place⟩-argument able to take a case particle: atuy or un 'to the sea' (atuy 'sea' + or 'place-of' + un allative).
Its syntax and possessed morphology are examined in ; the inalienability of locative nouns is set out in .
Nakagawa identifies six case particles for the Saru baseline :
The locative covers both existence-location (ta with an existential verb) and arrival goal (ta as the endpoint of a motion event), and also marks temporal reference-points :
The ablative marks the source of a motion event, not the path traversed.
Nakagawa draws this directly: going out through a door or window requires the postpositional adverb , not wa .
The temporal source form wano extends the same locative source semantics into the time domain:

The allative marks directed movement toward a goal, and the contrast with locative ta is a direction/arrival distinction: un indicates a direction-headed-toward while ta marks the completed arrival point.
Nakagawa illustrates with ni ka ta hemesu=an 'I climbed onto the tree' (arrival: ta) versus cikuni kasi un hemesu=an 'I climb toward the tree-top' (direction: un) :
The allative also appears as a case-frame on interrogative place-words: hunak un 'to where', hunak wa 'from where', hunak ta 'where (at)' — the three-case paradigm on the one place-root .
Interrogative pro-forms are examined in .
The perlative marks traversal of a spatially spread area.
It differs from the postpositional adverb kari in requiring a ⟨place⟩ head and in denoting a diffuse area rather than a single passage point :
The translative predicts conversion to a state or category and does not require a ⟨place⟩ head.
It also appears with numerals in copular predications (e.g., ren a=ne wa oka=an 'we lived, being three') :

The adnominal un forms a genitive construction linking a locative or place-name to a following noun, expressing origin or affiliation: kim un kamuy 'mountain deity (bear)', Sinutapka un kur 'person of Shinutapka' .
This un is pan-Hokkaido invariant across all dialects, which Nakagawa takes as evidence that it is etymologically distinct from the allative un, which varies dialectally .
The genitive construction is treated in detail in .
Nakagawa organizes the postpositional adverbs into two etymological strata .
The first, originally adverbial forms (本来型), includes , , , and .
The second, derived from transitive verbs (他動詞転換型), includes (instrumental), (comitative), (perlative), , (animate allative), and .
The verb-origin class retains the structural memory of its source: these forms take the transitive-object person prefix (en=akkari 'more than me', i=os 'after me') .
The contrast between case-particle peka and postpositional-adverb kari is a key diagnostic for the two-class split.

peka requires a ⟨place⟩-type noun (kim or peka 'through the mountains'); kari takes any nominal and does not require the locative noun or (ruyka kari 'across the bridge', puyar kari 'through the window') .
The test sentence from Satō also illustrates that kari heads a full motion event without any locative noun:
The limitative sets a terminal boundary — spatial or degree — on the action of its clause:
The instrumental is the standard tool-marking device, corresponding to Japanese で in this function.
The comitative is among the most frequent items in the corpus and may head an independent motion-clause constituent (macihi tura ku=ek 'I came with (my) wife').

The distinction between animate-goal eun and place-goal un mirrors Satō's minimal pair: Satporo un requires the place-name (*unarpe un is ill-formed), whereas unarpe eun 'to auntie' is well-formed because eun is a postpositional adverb .
The ⟨place⟩ requirement of the four local case particles is satisfied by a small closed class of locative nouns (位置名詞) that derive the internal spatial structure of a referent.
(long form ) is the most general: it maps any common noun to its associated location or interior.
Satō 2021 documents its distributional range in Chitose in detail .
The case particle ta fuses with basic or to give otta; the longer oro stays separate (oro ta) .

Other locative nouns include (upper surface: ni ka ta 'onto the tree'), (interior — this un is a locative noun distinct from both the allative particle and the adnominal particle), (exterior: cise soy ta 'outside the house'), , and .

These interact with the affiliative/concept-form morphology: a locative noun heading a possessed ⟨place⟩ phrase takes the affiliative suffix that marks inalienable possession, because locative nouns are inalienably related to their host noun .

A community discussion (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-11-09) highlights a distributional consequence of the ⟨place⟩ requirement: the existential verb requires a locative noun before the case particle (A B or ta an 'A exists at/in B'), while the two-argument verb (homophonous with the allative particle) takes a bare nominal (A B un 'A belongs to B').
This is corroborated by Nakagawa's analysis of adnominal un as etymologically a two-argument predicate rather than a case particle ; ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Whether ta / wa / un / peka constitute a local-case system or are better analyzed as postpositions turns on how one weighs three distributional facts against one morphophonological one.
The case-system argument rests on three properties ; .

First, the four particles form a closed paradigm organized around locative semantic primitives (at / from / toward / through) that parallels local-case inventories in languages with overt case morphology.
Second, the particles alternate on the single place-word hunak ('where') — hunak ta 'where-at', hunak wa 'from where', hunak un 'to where' — exactly as case suffixes do in case-marking languages.
Third, the allative particle shows regular dialectal allomorphy (un / en / (e)ne) that patterns as suppletive morphology rather than distinct lexical items.

The adposition argument notes that the particles remain phonologically independent words, never cliticize to their hosts, and that the ⟨place⟩ requirement is satisfied by a separate, grammatically active head noun (or) rather than by the noun itself taking an affix ; .

The case label adopted by Nakagawa and Satō is therefore a functional/semantic label, not a morphological one: these are postpositions that constitute a local-case subsystem by virtue of their paradigmatic organization and the ⟨place⟩ selection constraint ‹contested›.
Hokkaido Ainu has a substantial set of motion verbs that lexicalize direction, deictic orientation, and vertical or coastal dimension.
The most basic Saru–Chitose pair is (go, singular subject) and (go, in northern and eastern dialects); the suppletive plurals are and 's own plural form.
For 'come', the singular is with suppletive plural .

Beyond these general verbs, a lexical set encodes deictic path-direction: (move seaward / downhill / out to the open), (move inland / uphill), (enter an enclosed space), (ascend vertically), (descend), (go out/outside), and (go out to sea).
Each of these lexicalizes a specific path-direction in the verb stem itself.
Nakagawa 2024 treats these as a distinct lexical class on account of their suppletive number alternants and their complementary distribution with postpositional arguments .
A motion clause typically combines one of these path-encoding verbs with a postpositional phrase that specifies the Source (ablative wa) or Goal (allative un / locative ta):
Path through a specific route is marked by the postpositional adverb kari (for a single passage point or linear route) or the case particle peka (for a spread area).
When both a direction verb and a perlative phrase appear together, the verb encodes the terminal direction while the perlative phrase encodes the route:

The morphological alternation between the stem forms of direction verbs is itself a coding device for motion: nukopoli notes that motion verbs characteristically show a -n / -p stem alternation (san/sap, yan/yap, ahun/ahup, ran/rap, rikin/rikip), where -p is cognate with the formal noun pa, though the etymology of -n remains unsettled (nukopoli, 2026-05-18) ‹speculative›.
The causative of is uniquely rikinka; *rikipka is unattested, suggesting the -n stem is the causative base (nukopoli, 2026-04-27) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

Talmy's distinction between verb-framed languages (where Path is encoded in the main verb) and satellite-framed languages (where Path is in a satellite and Manner in the verb) provides a useful frame for locating the HA system .

The HA data are consistent with verb-framed organization at the lexical core — the path-direction verbs san, yan, ahun, rikin, and ran all lexicalize specific Path values in the verb stem — while the postpositional system adds goal/source precision through the un / wa / ta case particles and contributes a separate perlative specification through peka / kari.

What makes the Ainu system typologically mixed is that the perlative particles function as path-specifying satellites — they add information about the route that is not in the verb stem — while the goal and source particles function as standard local-case markers that any language, verb-framed or satellite-framed, may employ.

A manner verb like can occur with a perlative phrase (ne kenas or peka ekimne=an kor) in a way that resembles satellite framing, but the path-specialized verbs such as san and ahun carry Path in the verb itself.
forms: ne kenas or peka ekimne=an kor

Nakagawa traces the historical sequence as ne > ene > en > un, with the translative/copula ne the ultimate source .

The reanalysis of ne from a translative into an allative marker is plausible as a goal-marking grammaticalization, but the intermediate stages are not uniformly attested and the direction of the change has not been independently demonstrated ‹speculative›.
The adnominal un ('of, belonging to') does not participate in this variation: it is the same un in all dialects, including those that use en or ne for the allative.

Nakagawa takes this pan-HA uniformity as the strongest evidence that the two un's are etymologically distinct, with adnominal un deriving from the two-argument possession verb rather than from any locative source ‹consensus›.
Interrogative-strategy uses of the allative (ney un 'to where' in eastern dialects, as opposed to hunak un in western ones) are examined in .
Hokkaido Ainu numerals fall into three grammatical categories — numeral prenominals (数連体詞), numeral nouns (数名詞), and a counting-off form (数え上げ) — and the three are not interchangeable in syntax .

Underlying all three is a shared set of numeral roots from 1 to 10, with the integer 20 (hotne) serving as the base of a vigesimal counting system: even decades are formed multiplicatively from hotne, while the odd tens (30, 50, 70, 90) are built subtractively, expressing how many units fall short of the next even decade ; .

The vigesimal base sets Saru–Chitose Hokkaido Ainu apart from the surrounding Japanese decimal system and from several of its own dialects — Asahikawa and Sōya use a decimal base with the same root hot at the value of ten rather than twenty .
Sakhalin Ainu is also decimal.
A shift in modern usage away from the subtractive architecture and toward simpler additive or decimal expressions is documented by .

This chapter covers the numeral roots and their three form classes, the multiplicative and subtractive decade structure, the syntax of numeral phrases, the debate over classifier status, and the dialect geography of the base.

Ordinals, the interaction of numerals with quantifier syntax, and the day- and time-counting constructions are treated in the sibling chapter ; numeral phrases and the noun suffix -utar are set out in .
Each numeral value from 1 to 10, and 20, is represented in three paradigmatic shapes.
The prenominal precedes the noun directly; the numeral noun stands after the noun or alone; and the counting-off form is used for reckoning aloud in sequence ; .
The suffix -p (after vowel-final stems 1–5) and -pe (after consonant-final stems 6–10) are instances of the formal noun treated in .
The human counterparts -n and its suppletive partner -iw (6–10) are the same -n that appears in the interrogative nen 'who' and in hempak-iw 'how many people' — see .
The choice between -p and -n for human referents is weak: -p is described as "more brusque" but neither is ungrammatical with persons .

The community observation that the numeral-noun form rep cannot be placed before its noun — that 'three worlds' must be re mosir, not *rep mosir — is consistent with Nakagawa's syntactic description (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-09); .
A secondary '1' root ar- appears before certain nouns: ar-suy (also assuy) 'once', ar-itak 'one word' .
The same element appears in arwan (7) and in the iteratives arsuy, tusuy, resuy 'once, twice, three times' .
The etymology of roots 6–9 is historical, not synchronic.

Working from Chiri's finger-counting data and Patrie's comparative materials, Refsing analyses these as old "ten-minus" compounds: iwan (6) < i(ne)+wan "4+ten"; arwan (7) < ar+wan (where ar is glossed as an old '3' or old '1' — contested); tupesan (8) and sinepesan (9) as tu/sine+pesan, or in Patrie's reconstruction tu-upis/sine-upis, with upis an old '10' attested in Kuril Ainu .
These reconstructions are ‹speculative›; synchronically the forms are opaque roots.
The root hot (20) is analysed as 'a set' — a full complement of fingers and toes, the somatic basis commonly attributed to vigesimal systems .
The counting system above 10 operates in three zones: an additive zone for 11–29, a multiplicative zone for even decades, and a subtractive zone for odd decades ; .
11–19 are formed by adding a unit prenominal to the verb followed by wan '10': 11 = sine ikasma wan, 13 = re ikasma wan, 19 = sinepesan ikasma wan.
The construction frames each value as the amount by which the count surpasses the last decade — 'three exceeds ten' .
20 = hotne, the vigesimal base.
21–29 replace wan with hotne: sine ikasma hotne (21) through sinepesan ikasma hotne (29).
Even decades from 40 to 100 are multiplicative: the unit prenominal compounds directly with hotne, yielding tuhotne (2×20=40), rehotne (3×20=60), inehotne (4×20=80), and asiknehotne (5×20=100) .
The 100-value asiknehotnep is independently confirmed ‹corpus-confirmed›
(palestine_2026, aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-06-08).
Odd decades are subtractive.
The pattern is wan + the prefix e- + the next even decade: wan etuhotne = "ten toward forty" = 30; wan erehotne = 50; wan einehotne = 70; wan easiknehotne = 90.

The prefix e- marks the following even decade as the reference point from which ten units are counted off; this is the defining property that the literature labels vigesimal subtractive counting (二十進法; 下方算法) ; .

The community discussion of the subtractive pattern (aomidori_cs_, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-05-28) independently corroborates Nakagawa's 30 and 50 formulas; the same contributor extends the pattern analogically to propose expressions for negative quantities (*sine e-isam for −1, combining e- with isam 'be absent'), but that extension is a modern coinage ‹speculative› and lies outside the attested system .
In the counting-off form, the bare root hot replaces hotne: 20 = hot, 30 = wanpe etuhot, 40 = tuhot .
For composite numeral-noun phrases above 29, each component stands as an independent noun form: "31 things" is sinep ikasma wanpe etuhotnep; "11 loads" is sinep ikasma wan sike .

Nakagawa observes that composites above 10 "almost never appear in recorded classical texts"; the attested vigesimal compounds in the broader corpus are concentrated in modern アイヌタイムズ prose from the 1990s–2000s .

Prenominals precede the head noun directly, without an intervening classifier or particle; numeral nouns follow the head noun in apposition or stand alone; and the counting-off forms are used only for enumerating in sequence, without an NP head ; .
The error of placing the numeral-noun form before the noun — *sinep tuki for 'one cup' instead of sine tuki or tuki sinep — is explicitly flagged as a common learner mistake .

The [noun + postposed numeral-noun + verb] construction, as in pasuy sinep uk 'take one chopstick', is common and has been noted as productive — arguably more so than its Japanese near-counterpart (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-12); ‹corpus-suggested›.
Whether a modifier can intervene between a head noun and its following numeral-noun is undocumented: Satō notes that no such example appears in his data and flags the question as open ‹contested›.
A numeral noun combined with the copula ne — treated in — predicates a count or produces a count-adverbial.
The case particle ne here is the translative copula; the numeral noun takes its ordinary form:
A frozen copular numeral produces the adverb sinenne 'alone' (< sinen + ne), and the same pattern yields tup ne ukosaraye 'divide in two' .
When a count greater than one is specified with a prenominal, the head noun may take the associative plural suffix -utar: sine hekaci 'one child' but tu hekattar (< hekaci-utar) 'two children' .
The conditions for its omission versus realization, and its interaction with the transnumerality of Ainu nouns, are set out in .

Small, specified numbers (2, 3) take singular verb agreement; six or more, or unspecified plurals, take plural agreement (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-17, attributed to Satō) ‹corpus-suggested›; this is consistent with Refsing's numeral syntax data .
The person-number agreement system is described in .
Several numeral roots carry extended or bleached meanings in fixed constructions beyond their cardinal count function.
iwan (6) functions as an intensifier glossable as 'many' in oral literary registers and fixed expressions.
The expression iwan suy means 'many times', and the form noiwan is an intensified variant .
The pair tu / re in oral-literary formulaic contexts carries the sense 'many' rather than exactly 'two' or 'three': tu cup ka re cup 'many months', tu ray onkami / re ray onkami 'bow many times' .
forms: tu ray onkami / re ray onkami

text: By contrast, tutko rerko '2–3 days' genuinely denotes a short span .
Day-counting uses the combining form -ko: tutko '2 days', rerko '3 days', then ine rerko '4 days', asikne rerko '5 days'.
In the last two expressions rerko has bleached from 'three-day-span' to a general 'days' noun .
The animal count noun atuyta is lexically restricted to Saru/Chitose and denotes 10 head of animals in Saru but 20 head in Chitose — a lexical split internal to the same dialect cluster .
Whether -p/-pe and -n/-iw constitute numeral classifiers depends on the criterion applied.

Nakagawa's answer is unambiguous: Ainu has no numeral classifiers (助数詞) of the Sinitic type; quantification uses the prenominal plus noun directly, analogous to English counting, and the thing/person suffix pair is instead the native derivational contrast parallel to Japanese ひとつ/ひとり, a trait shared with the neighbouring Nivkh .
Refsing explicitly calls -p(e) and -n/-iw "a rudimentary system of 'classifiers' or 'counters'" and reserves 'numeral' for the bare stem .

The Handbook goes further, applying the label "word-classifiers" to to 'X days' and suy 'X times', and speculates about remnants of an earlier, more elaborate classifier system — though the passage is labelled as speculation in the source .

The disagreement reduces to a terminological question: Nakagawa's criterion requires Sinitic-style morphological obligatoriness and categorial specificity (absent in Ainu); Refsing's and the Handbook's criterion requires only semantic categorization in regular numeral co-occurrence (present in Ainu) ; ‹contested›.
The fuller treatment of the classifier debate, the status of to and suy, and the day-counting constructions are reserved for .
The vigesimal base is the defining property of the Saru–Chitose standard but is not pan-Hokkaido.
Two dialect areas use a decimal base, and in those the root hot takes the value ten rather than twenty.
Asahikawa is decimal above ten: sinehot = 10, tuhot = 20, rehot = 30, and so on.
The Sōya (宗谷) dialect similarly has wanhot = 100 (decimal 'ten-ten') .
Community records confirm that the collision between vigesimal and decimal speakers produced misunderstandings in commercial exchange ‹corpus-confirmed›
(nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-25; Deleted User, 2024-05-13).
The form for 100 varies markedly across Hokkaido.
Saru, Chitose, Horobetsu, and Nayoro use asiknehotne(p) (5×20); Yakumo and Obihiro use sineik; Bihoro uses ik; Sōya uses wanhot .
Sakhalin Ainu is decimal throughout .
The root for 10 is kunkutu, plausibly an Itelmen loan ‹speculative›
(antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-22), and 100 is sinetanku, from Tungusic tanku .
The Tungusic and Itelmen contact reflected in these forms has no counterpart in the Hokkaido system.
A directional shift in modern usage, from the subtractive architecture toward additive or decimal expressions, is documented by Ochiai .

The subtractive structure is complex to produce and rare in classical oral texts , and the pedagogical grammar of teaches both the vigesimal and a simplified decimal alternative, reflecting classroom practice.
The direction of change belongs to the sociolinguistics of the revitalization context; the attested classical system is as described above.
Hokkaido Ainu numerals appear in three formally distinct word-classes.
The numeral prenominal (数連体詞) is the bare cardinal stem that directly precedes a head noun: tu cip 'two boats', iwan kosonte 'six robes'.

The numeral noun (数名詞) is the cardinal stem carrying one of two suffixes — -p/-pe for non-human referents or -n/-iw for human referents — and it occupies a post-nominal appositional position: tuki sinep 'one cup (post-nominal)', tun katkemat 'two women'.
A third class, the counting-off form (数え上げ), is used in enumeration sequences as an interjection-like particle and is not treated here .
The present chapter covers the numeral noun suffixes and their syntax, the periphrastic ordinal strategies, quantifier float, and the universal and approximative quantifiers.
The cardinal system, the vigesimal arithmetic, and the 1–20 paradigm are treated in ; nominal -utar plurality and transnumerality in .

The thing-counting suffix derives from the formal noun (alternant pe) that also functions as the general thing-nominalizer treated in .
On the numeral stem it creates a counting noun whose referential domain is any non-human entity, though it can extend to humans in brusque register (see below).

The phonological conditioning is regular: the allomorph -p follows vowel-final stems (values 1–5: sine, tu, re, ine, asikne), and -pe follows consonant-final stems (values 6–10: iwan, arwan, tupesan, sinepesan, wan) ; .
The numeral noun carrying -p/-pe occupies the post-nominal appositional position — it follows the noun it quantifies.
This is in complementary distribution with the prenominal position of the bare stem.

The numeral noun follows:

Nakagawa characterises the -p/-n split as the native thing/person dichotomy — comparable to Japanese ひとつ vs ひとり and contrasting with Sinitic classifier systems that require an intervening counter word between any numeral and any noun.
The parallel with Nivkh, another non-Sinitic language of the region, is also noted .
The person-counting suffix parallels the thing-counting suffix in its allomorphy: -n after vowel-final stems (values 1–5) and -iw after consonant-final stems (values 6–10) .
The suffix -n/-iw is otherwise rare in the Hokkaido Ainu morphological inventory; its other occurrence is in the interrogative hempakiw 'how many people' (from hempak-iw) — see .
The primary domain of -n/-iw is human beings: tun katkemat 'two women', asiknen okkayo 'five men'.
Nakagawa notes that -p/-pe can also count human referents, but carries a brusquer register; in practice the distinction is weak and speakers vary .
The person-counting suffix extends to composite vigesimal numerals.
For 100 (= 5×20), the suffix attaches to the whole compound asiknehotne:
The numeral noun with -n/-iw also combines with the translative copula ne to form a predicative or adverbial phrase expressing numerical composition.
In this use the numeral noun functions without any overt head noun:
See also the parallel sinenne 'alone' derived by the same copular contraction, discussed in the ordinals section below.
Outside the -p/-pe and -n/-iw paradigm, two free nouns function as mensural elements when preceded by a numeral: and .
to 'day' follows a numeral prenominal to form a temporal span noun: sine to 'one day'.

For values 2 and 3, the idiomatic forms tutko '2 days' and rerko '3 days' are common; from value 4 onwards the additive pattern ine rerko '4 days', asikne rerko '5 days' shows that rerko has bleached from '3 days' to the general day-span slot .
suy 'time, turn' forms the iterative series.

The element for 'once' draws on the archaic root ar 'one' (also seen in ar-itak 'one word' and the counting-off base) rather than the regular prenominal sine: arsuy 'once', tusuy 'twice', resuy 'three times'.
Intensive reduplication with o- yields otusuy and oresuy 'over and over' ; .
The numeral 6 (iwan) has a secondary 'many' meaning in oral literary contexts; iwan suy therefore typically means 'many times' rather than a precise six:
Whether -p/-pe, -n/-iw, to, and suy constitute "numeral classifiers" is unresolved in the literature, partly because the disagreement is terminological ‹contested›.
Nakagawa argues that Hokkaido Ainu has no numeral classifiers (助数詞) in any meaningful sense.
Prenominal numerals attach directly to the noun without an intervening counting word — tu cip 'two boats', re nupuri 'three mountains' — just as English two ships does.
The -p vs -n contrast is the native thing/person dichotomy, found in many non-Sinitic numeral systems and present cross-linguistically without Sinitic influence .

The typology chapter of frames the picture differently: it refers to -p/-pe and -n/-iw as "counters" and to to and suy as "word-classifiers", speculating that these may be remnants of a formerly more elaborate noun-classifier system (Handbook 2022, epub — chapter and page are uncalibrated in the current reading).

Refsing takes a middle position, calling the suffixes "a rudimentary system of 'classifiers' or 'counters'" while reserving "numeral" for the bare prenominal stem and "number" for the stem plus counter .
The pivot of the disagreement is the definition of "classifier".
In the Sinitic sense a classifier is an obligatory mediating element: Mandarin requires 本 in 三本書 'three-CL-book'; no numeral can attach directly to the noun.
Hokkaido Ainu has no such requirement: the prenominal numeral combines with any noun without an intervening element.
On this definition — Nakagawa's — the suffixes are not classifiers because they are post-nominal, suffixal, and optional relative to the prenominal.
On Refsing's and the Handbook's definition they are, because they encode a semantic categorization of the counted entity.
Authors citing either view must specify which sense of "classifier" they intend.
None of the primary Hokkaido Ainu grammars — Nakagawa 2024 §17, Satō 2008 §33, Refsing 1986 §12.4, or Kindaichi and Chiri 1936 — describes a dedicated ordinal word-class or ordinal paradigm ; ; .
Ordinal meaning is expressed through several periphrastic strategies, two of which are independently attested in the grammars, while others are documented in community discussion ‹corpus-suggested›.
Two attested expressions involve a numeral noun combined with the translative copula ne.
The contraction of sinen ne 'being one person' to sinenne yields the lexicalized meaning 'alone, by oneself':
The same copular pattern with the thing-counting noun forms a partitive or distributive expression:
For 'first', the adverb fills the ordinal-adverbial slot.
The superlative phrase iyotta hoski (where intensifies ) expresses 'the very first, foremost'.

A community discussion notes that ordinals are generally avoided in Hokkaido Ainu — the expression sine to serves both 'one day' and 'the first day' — and that hoskino and iyotta hoski are the standard strategies for 'first'; for higher ordinals, one attested usage is the sequence sine kamuy, tu kamuy, re kamuy 'first, second, third (one)' with kamuy as a generic count noun, and the form iyeere-p has been reported for 'the third (thing)' (nukopoli, 2024-11-09, asserted) ‹speculative›.
forms: sine kamuy, tu kamuy, re kamuy

text: These community-attested strategies await systematic description in the primary grammars.
The iterative series arsuy 'once', tusuy 'twice', resuy 'three times' (§word-classifiers above) overlaps functionally with the ordinal domain when it tracks the sequence of occurrences.
The three numeral categories — prenominal, numeral noun, and pure noun predicate — occupy distinct syntactic positions with distinct meaning contributions ; .
The bare numeral stem precedes the head noun.

Other modifiers can intervene between the numeral and the noun without ungrammaticality: re ku=mataki 'my three younger sisters' (possessive prefix between numeral and noun), tu pon cep 'two small fish' (adjective between numeral and noun) .
The prenominal is the position available to all cardinal values, including composite vigesimal numerals.
The numeral noun (-p/-pe or -n/-iw) follows the noun it quantifies as an appositive count specification.
The position constraint is categorical: the numeral noun cannot precede the noun (*sinep tuki for 'one cup' is ungrammatical) .
The NP-internal appositive pattern is discussed alongside the possessor-appositive construction in .
Whether a modifier may intervene between the head noun and an appositional numeral noun — e.g.
noun + adjective + numeral.noun — is documented as an open research question: Satō reports no such example in his Chitose data and flags it explicitly ‹contested›.
Both numeral noun series can serve as predicates or standalone NP heads without a co-occurring noun.
The simplest predicative use places the numeral noun as the sole argument of an intransitive verb:
The translative copula ne turns the numeral noun into an adverbial predicate of composition or manner.
The person-counting series: ren a=ne wa oka=an 'we were three and lived' (§§person-counting above).
The thing-counting series: tup ne ukosaraye 'divide it in two' (§§ordinals above).
Both patterns use ne as a translative that equates the group or object with a numerical value — the same construction treated in the postpositions chapter .
The appositional numeral noun does not need to remain clause-adjacent to its head noun.

It can appear after the verb or in a position outside the canonical NP boundary — a distribution consistent with the broader pronominal-argument and non-configurational character of Hokkaido Ainu discussed in .
The pattern illustrated below has the object noun followed by the numeral noun and then the verb:
In this construction sinep is the appositional numeral noun counting the object pasuy, but the two are separated by the verb position.
Refsing's Shizunai data include the parallel a=kor mici akihi tun, ren an 'my father's brothers were two or three', where the numeral noun follows a relational noun phrase rather than a simple head .
forms: a=kor mici akihi tun, ren an

text: The noun–numeral.noun–verb pattern is documented as community-observed and structurally consistent with the primary sources ‹corpus-suggested›.

A numeral specifying a small count (2 or 3) typically co-occurs with the singular form of a noun that otherwise has a human-plural counterpart, while a large numeral (from 6 upwards), an indefinite quantity, or the quantifier inne 'many' co-occurs with the plural form.
Satō states the threshold explicitly (via community discussion attributed to him); the pattern also coheres with Refsing's data on the morphological forms involved:
(nukopoli, 2024-11-17, asserted, attributed to Satō); corroborated by ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Mass-like or uncountable referents stay in the singular regardless of quantity.

Under a specified numeral greater than 1, a human-denoting noun may take the associative-plural suffix -utar with phonologically conditioned allomorphy: sine hekaci 'one child' but tu hekattar 'two children' (< hekaci-utar, with assimilation) .
The full -utar paradigm and the transnumerality of bare nouns are treated in ; the verbal number interaction belongs to .
Several items outside the numeral paradigm proper function as universal or approximative quantifiers.
(variant obitta) is the universal quantifier 'all of, every'.

Its formal status is that of a postpositional adverb — it belongs to the class of originally adverbial postpositions — and it typically follows the noun phrase or clause it scopes over, distinguishing it positionally from the prenominal numeral.
The closely related epitta 'throughout, across the whole' has partly overlapping distribution.
(also inne ne 'being many') is the standard approximative 'many'.
It licenses the plural verb form and the plural -utar form of the noun in the same way as a large cardinal numeral (see §numeral–nominal number interactions above).
The numeral 6, iwan, has developed a secondary universal-like meaning in oral-literary register.

Fixed expressions including iwan suy 'many times', iwan kosonte 'many/six robes' (a gift-register formula), and the intensive noiwan (< no-iwan 'very many') all draw on this conventionalized 'many' reading .
These expressions are genre-marked and do not represent a productive grammaticalization of '6' as a plural marker in everyday speech ‹corpus-confirmed›.
is an approximative quantifier without a precise numerical value.
Its syntactic distribution parallels the prenominal numeral in modifier position, but it is not a numeral in the classifier-paradigm sense treated above.
Distributive plurality and the full three-way interaction among nominal -utar, verbal number, and quantifiers is systematically treated in .

The Hokkaido Ainu verb word is the head of its clause: every other constituent enters a grammatical or semantic relation with it, and it alone carries the bound indexes that identify the clause's core participants .

Satō describes the language as head-marking in the sense of , with the verb bearing the central information about which arguments fill its valence frame; external noun phrases may be absent, freely ordered, or arranged for discourse, while the indexes on the verb do the ordinary work of tracking who acts on whom .
Ijäs's classroom image of verb pockets, filled before and more obligatorily than free pronouns or full noun phrases, names the same head-marking fact for learners .

The personal-index architecture itself is the subject of ; this chapter sets out the verb word's morphological template and the order of its position classes, and routes the detail of each zone to the chapters that follow.
Several properties of the Ainu verb fix the boundaries of that template .
Tense is absent as an inflectional category: a bare verb form is read as past, present, or future from context, temporal adverbs, or discourse sequencing ; ; .

There is no separate adjective class; meanings rendered by English or Japanese adjectives are intransitive verbs, and a stative reading ordinarily carries an inchoative one — Ijäs presents hure as both 'be red' and 'become red', matching Nakagawa's poro 'be big; become big' and the imperative evidence Shibatani adduces for the verbal status of quality predicates ; ; .
Property predicates are treated as a verb subclass in and .
Person marking is obligatory while independent pronouns are optional, so the language is consistently pro-dropping and verb-final ; .

Tense, aspect, mood, evidentiality, and negation are assembled outside the lexical verb by auxiliaries, formal nouns, and particles that take an already person- and number-inflected verb as their input, and are treated in , , and the evidential and negation parts.
The verb word supplies the stem and its argument morphology; the larger predicate supplies the rest.
The finite verb word can be modelled as an ordered set of position classes.

The model is a descriptive abstraction over the recurrent linear positions of person indexes, valency-changing morphology, the lexical stem, stem-number morphology, derivational suffixes, and the outer plural markers.
Read from the outer left edge to the outer right edge, the zones are as follows.
Two ordering facts anchor the template.
The first is a side-switch by transitivity.

The first-plural-exclusive and fourth-person subjects appear as suffixes on an intransitive stem but as prefixes on a transitive one: inkar=an 'I/one looked' and arki=as 'we came' beside a=nukar 'I/one saw it' and ci=nukar 'we saw it' ; .
The second is the position of the two homophonous plural pa elements.

The Type-C plural suffix -pa is root-bound and stands inside the person suffix and inside the causative, whereas the outer plural element pa follows the whole person-inflected verb: iki-pa=an with the suffix before =an contrasts with iki=an pa with the clitic after it .
The relative order of these elements is the subject of and .
The template is partly positional and partly scope-driven.

Some ordering is fixed by position class, but the valency prefixes and suffixes stack in an order that tracks the order of derivation: a chain such as ruska 'be angry at' → ko-ruska → yay-ko-ruska → i-ruska raises and lowers valence step by step, each affix scoping over the stem already built ; .
Auxiliaries and light verbs such as ki 'do' and the abilitative easkay 'can' stand outside this word altogether, and are treated in and .
Transitivity is a formal property of the verb word, decided by structure and not by the meaning of the translation ; .
Two diagnostics define it.

A verb requires a fixed number of bare noun-phrase arguments — noun phrases without a case particle or postposition — and case-marked phrases are adverbial additions outside that count; one bare argument marks an intransitive verb, two or more a transitive verb .
An intransitive verb indexes only its subject (S), while a transitive verb indexes subject (A) and object (O) .

The surest operational test puts the verb in the first-person plural: an intransitive takes the suffix =as (exclusive) or =an (fourth person), a transitive the prefix ci= or a=, the other person cells being uninformative — a side-switch Satō calls irregular and still unexplained .
The minimal pair inkar 'look' and nukar 'see' shows why an English translation is an unreliable guide.
inkar is an intransitive activity of directing the gaze with no fixed object; nukar is transitive and takes a specified object.
A fourth-person subject therefore surfaces as the suffix =an after the intransitive stem and as the prefix a= before the transitive stem in one sentence :

Both arguments of a transitive verb are bare, and Ainu draws no formal distinction between a direct and an indirect object: what a Japanese translation marks as 〜を or 〜に is the same bare object in Ainu .

A three-place verb such as kore 'give' takes a subject and two bare objects, all omissible, yet only two participants can be indexed on the verb — the two-index cap holds even where the clause has three arguments ; .
When a non-third person is indexed it is the human recipient that the object affix tracks, a secundative pattern taken up in .

Ijäs's learner grammar reaches the same architecture through the contrast of verb pockets and external slots: the arguments are cross-referenced on the verb first, and a bare clause such as numan hekaci cep koyki presents both participants as bare noun phrases with an unmarked third-person verb .

Her further statement that the indirect object of a three-place clause stands between subject and object is a classroom simplification; the two objects and the subject of epakasnu 'teach' occur in several orders with one valence frame and no fixed position .
The argument count runs from zero to three, with a contested fourth.
