Nakagawa and Bugaeva and Kobayashi use the numeric labels 0-, 1-, 2-, and 3-argument verb precisely to keep the noun-phrase count apart from the person-affix fact of intransitive versus transitive; Satō, Tamura, and Ijäs keep the traditional intransitive/transitive/ditransitive terms ; ; .
The zero-place class is built from non-autonomous roots: weather and ambient predicates such as mean 'be cold' (< me- 'cold' + an 'exist') and sirpirka 'be fine weather' take no participant index .
Ijäs presents these as avalent verbs with the same examples, including the analysis of sir- 'surroundings' and a non-free me- 'cold' .

Where the contributing element is itself a free noun, the analysis is genuinely open: Ijäs treats apto as 'it rains' as a single avalent unit, but Nakagawa leaves it undecided, since apto 'rain' is an autonomous noun and the string may be a two-word clause ; ‹contested›.

The same root that gives a weather predicate often has an intransitive counterpart that does take a subject — climatic mean 'it is cold' beside experiential merayke 'feel cold' — a contrast Ijäs marks and Nakagawa lays out as a paired paradigm ; .
The copula ne shows that valence is not reducible to the number of person indexes.

It is two-place in the relation 'X is Y' and takes transitive-type subject marking, yet it admits no object index: okkayo ku=ne 'I am a man' is well formed while an object-indexed alternative is not ; .
The copula and predicate nominals are developed in .
Three-place verbs are mostly derived, by the applicative ko- or the causative -re, the one common base-form member being the locative o 'put X into a place' ; .
The valence classes, the small locative-object subclass, and ambitransitivity are the matter of .
The valency prefixes and the stem-internal suffixes are the positions that alter the argument count.
Their syntax and semantics belong to the voice part; in the template the relevant fact is the position each occupies and the direction in which it moves the count ; .

A reflexive or reciprocal prefix occupies the object position itself, so a subject index and an object index for the same participant never co-occur , and the antipassive i- absorbs the object of a transitive stem, as in ruska 'be angry at' → i-ruska 'be angry' ; .

The prefix e- is a standing warning against reading the template off shapes alone: it can be the second-person index, an applicative, or an affiliative nominal prefix, and only the valence computation and the surrounding morphology identify it in a given word .
The applicatives are developed in , the causatives in , , and , the detransitive in , the reflexives and reciprocal in , , and , and incorporation in .

Derivation that builds a verb stem without changing its valence — denominal and deverbal verb formation, and the adverb-forming -no that turns a property verb into an adverb (poro → poronno) — is treated in and .
The stem zone holds the lexical root together with any suppletive or suffixal singular/plural alternation.

Number in Hokkaido Ainu sits on the verb, not the noun: nouns are number-neutral and read as singular or plural by context — Ijäs notes that cep 'fish' may be either — while a minority of verbs have distinct singular and plural stems ; .

The alternation takes three shapes: outright suppletion (ek / arki 'come', an / oka 'exist'), the -n / -p pattern of directed-motion verbs (san / sap 'go down'), and the vowel-to--pa pattern of change-of-state transitives (tuye / tuypa 'cut') ; .
The two transitivity classes index plurality differently.
For intransitives the alternation is close to agreement with S: a plural subject normally selects the plural stem and a singular subject the singular stem .

For transitives the plural stem marks a plural object or a pluralized or repeated event, with the singular stem remaining the default even where the object is plural; Shibatani, following Durie, treats the alternation as a selectional restriction on the principally affected argument — S of an intransitive, O of a transitive — rather than as agreement ; ; .

Numerals and quantifiers show why the slot resists a simple agreement rule: a subject numerically specified as two, three, or sometimes four ordinarily takes a singular intransitive stem, against counterpatterns with iwan 'six' and with poronno 'many' that vary by dialect and speaker ‹contested›.
The full inventory, the corpus frequencies, and the agreement-versus-selection debate are the subject of , and the interaction with person of .
Four analytical questions bear on how the template is read, and none is settled.
The first is the mechanism behind the valence calculus.

Nakagawa's arity assigns every element — base verb, each derivational affix, each person index — a positive, negative, or zero value, the sum predicting the verb's remaining bare-noun-phrase positions .

Satō argues that a single arity value fails for the copula, for auxiliaries, and for ditransitives, and replaces it with three simultaneous layers — an invariant argument-slot count, a macrorole valency in the sense of that the person affixes index, and the morphological valency of the derived word — while flagging his own scheme as something still to be justified ; ‹contested›.
The template here records position and valence effect without committing to either mechanism.
The second question is the third-person zero.

Nakagawa assigns the third person no overt affix and no arity value, so that the calculus balances; Satō holds that a zero third-person affix is needed to explain the two-index cap and the impossibility of certain three-participant combinations ; ; ‹contested›.
The transitivity table above leaves the third-person cells empty and routes the analysis to .
The third question is the outer plural pa.

Nakagawa and the Handbook treat the postposed pa, eastern ci, and the Sakhalin cognate as a single clitic class distinct from the root-bound suffix; Satō's Chitose data make the clitic analysis doubtful, since postposed -an pa is rare and a speaker rejects *yaynu-as pa in favour of yaynupa-as ; ‹contested›.

The fourth question is the four-place class: Nakagawa lists causativized ditransitives such as omarere as four-place verbs, while Satō warns that the type is too marginal to support a regular category ; ‹contested›.
These debates leave the linear template stable while its interpretation is open.

Ainu has very few bare stems that serve as both intransitive and transitive without overt marking, with roski 'stand' effectively the sole instance, so valence alternation is almost always coded by the derivational positions catalogued above rather than by lability ; .
The valence classes and ambitransitivity are pursued in , and the productive derivation in .
Hokkaido Ainu classifies its verbs by the number and kind of core arguments each licenses, and the classification is decided by structure rather than by the meaning of a translation ; .
Two diagnostics fix a verb's class.

The first is the count of core arguments, where a core argument is a bare noun phrase carrying no postposition or case particle; a phrase marked by a local postposition is adverbial and can be added without altering the count, so that in cise or ta menoko hoku tura ipe 'in the house a woman ate with her husband' only menoko is an argument of ipe .
forms: cise or ta menoko hoku tura ipe

text: The second diagnostic is person marking: an intransitive verb indexes a single subject, while a transitive verb may index a subject and an object .
The indexing system that supports both diagnostics is the subject of , and the order of indexes inside the verb word of .
Three descriptive vocabularies coexist in current work and must be kept apart.

Nakagawa, with Bugaeva and Kobayashi, prefers numeric labels — 0-, 1-, 2-, and 3-argument verb — because the bare-noun-phrase count and the intransitive/transitive person-affix fact do not always line up and are best named separately; Satō, Tamura, and Ijäs retain the traditional terms intransitive, transitive, and ditransitive ; ; .

The abbreviations used here are structural labels and carry no claim about semantic agency: an intransitive verb may take an agent-like or an affected subject, and both receive the same subject index, a point developed in .

Ijäs's Lessons 2 and 3 introduce the same inventory for learners as avalent, intransitive, transitive, and ditransitive verbs, and present Hokkaido Ainu as a pro-drop, verb-final, head-marking language whose verb has argument "pockets" that are filled before, and more obligatorily than, any external noun-phrase "slot" .
That image renders head-marking in the sense of and matches Satō's argument-slot account of the same fact .

Two background conditions stated in the same lessons frame the classification: verb forms carry no tense inflection, and nouns are number-neutral unless plurality is supplied lexically or by context, so that cep 'fish' may be read as singular or plural ; ; .
Number enters the verbal system separately, through stem alternation and the plural elements treated in .
The person rows that make the intransitive/transitive contrast visible in surface form are the first-plural exclusive and the fourth (indefinite) person.
On an intransitive verb these appear as subject suffixes, =as and =an; on a transitive verb the corresponding subject markers are prefixes, ci= and a=.
Satō gives the operational test in these terms: put the verb in the first-person plural, and yields inkar=as while yields ci=nukar .
He notes that this side-switch is highly irregular and still without a convincing explanation .

The remaining rows are uninformative: the first singular uses the same prefix ku= for subject of either class, the second person is neutral across subject and object, and the third person has no overt segment in any role.
The pair inkar and nukar is the standard demonstration that a translation is an unreliable guide to class.
Both render English visual predicates, but inkar names an intransitive act of directing the gaze with no fixed object, whereas nukar takes a specified object.
In one clause chain the fourth person therefore surfaces as a suffix on the intransitive stem and as a prefix on the transitive stem .
Translation cannot decide class because the verb itself carries the argument structure.

Ijäs illustrates the ordinary transitive frame with a third-person subject and a third-person object: neither is segmentally marked, yet the two bare noun phrases fill the A and O positions of a two-place verb .

The verb word indexes at most one subject and one object — the two-index cap — even where a clause has more arguments than that, a limit that becomes load-bearing for three-place verbs and for the debates of the final section .
The zero-place class contains predicates with no grammatical subject and no object.

Most are ambient or weather expressions built on a bound element such as sir- 'surroundings' or a non-free root plus a verb: sirpirka 'be fine weather', sirkunne 'get dark', and mean 'be cold (weather)', the last analysable as me- 'cold' plus an 'exist' ; Shibatani analyses the type as subject incorporation .

Ijäs groups the same predicates as avalent and notes that descriptive meanings belong to the verbal system, since Hokkaido Ainu has no adjective class distinct from verbs and a stative verb such as hure 'be red' carries the inchoative reading 'become red' as well ; ; .

Where the contributing element is itself a free noun the analysis is open: Ijäs treats apto as 'it rains' as a single avalent unit, whereas Nakagawa leaves it undecided, since apto 'rain' is an autonomous noun and the string may be a two-word subject-plus-verb clause ; ‹contested›.
The boundary between zero-place and one-place verbs is sharpest in the temperature vocabulary.
Climate predicates take no person index; the felt-temperature counterparts take a subject.
One-place verbs cover agentive activities such as apkas 'walk' and ipe 'eat a meal', changes of state such as rewke 'bend', and properties such as pirka 'be good' and pewre 'be young'.

The single argument is grammatical and need not be a semantic agent: a patientive subject still takes the subject index, as in rittursere=an 'I am rolled by the waves' and ku=merayke 'I feel cold', where the affected participant is marked with the ordinary S set .
The active/unaccusative cut does resurface, but in derivation and incorporation rather than in the person paradigm, and it does not split the intransitive subject marking .
A two-place verb licenses a subject and a single object, both bare noun phrases, whatever the translation suggests about patient, goal, or other role.
Hokkaido Ainu draws no formal distinction between a direct and an indirect object: what a Japanese rendering marks with を or に is the same bare object in Ainu .
This is why cep ipe cannot mean 'eat fish': ipe is the intransitive 'eat a meal', and a specified food object requires a transitive such as e 'eat (something)' .
Several near-basic pairs show that close semantic correspondence does not entail formal identity; the most basic of them have to be learned as distinct stems ; .
The copula ne belongs with the two-place verbs in argument structure, relating a subject to a predicate nominal, and it takes transitive-type subject marking.
Its person behaviour is exceptional, however: it indexes only the subject and admits no object index, so that okkayo ku=ne 'I am a man' is well formed while an object-indexed *en=ne is not ; .
Predicate-nominal syntax is treated in , and the copula reappears in the final section as Satō's central case for distinguishing several measures of valence.
Three-place verbs license a subject and two bare objects, both omissible and without a fixed grammatical order between them.
With kore 'give', the theme and the recipient are both bare third-person phrases and only the subject is indexed below.
Almost all three-place verbs are derived, by an applicative such as ko- or the causative -re, the chief base-form member being the locative o 'put X into a place' ; .
Satō analyses the object index on kore as tracking the recipient, a secundative pattern, a point on which Bugaeva's account differs; the indexing options are set out in and ‹contested›.
Ijäs presents the ditransitive frame as subject, indirect object, and direct object, with the recipient placed before the theme .

Nakagawa's examples of epakasnu 'teach' show the two objects and the subject in several preverbal orders with one set of argument roles, so the recipient-before-theme sequence is a teaching convention rather than a grammatical requirement .
The productive operations that build and rearrange these frames are surveyed in .
A small closed class takes a place as a bare object, with no ta or or ta.

These locative-object verbs cut across the two- and three-place distinction: oma 'be in, enter a place', osma 'plunge into a place', and kus 'pass through a place' are two-place, while o 'put X into a place' is three-place and is the chief base-form ditransitive of the language .
The defining property is the absence of a local postposition, so that *cise or ta osma is ungrammatical against intransitive cise or ta ahun 'enter into the house', where ta is required .
The place noun within such a frame works like a covert case marker.

With omare 'put X into a place', ikayop omare is read as 'put the quiver somewhere', since a quiver is a theme, while ikayop or omare is read as 'put something into the quiver', with or supplying the locative object .
The applicative o- derives further locative-object verbs from non-locative bases, and the local-postposition system that these verbs bypass is treated in and .
Nakagawa generalizes valence into an arithmetic over the verb word.

Every element — the base verb, each derivational affix, an incorporated noun, and each person index — carries an arity value, and the sum predicts how many bare external arguments the surface predicate still licenses .

A base intransitive contributes +1, a base transitive +2, and a base ditransitive +3; applicatives and the productive causative add +1; a noun root or a concept-form prefix that fills an argument slot subtracts 1; a single person index subtracts 1 and a subject-plus-object pair subtracts 2.
The calculus earns its keep where one segment has several functions.

Built on intransitive itak 'speak' (+1), the applicative ko- gives ko-itak 'speak to' (+2), the subject index in ku=ko-itak brings the count back to +1, and the reflexive yay- in ku=yay-ko-itak fills the object position to leave 0, so that a further bare object is excluded .

The same arithmetic separates the three uses of prefixal e-: it must be the applicative (+1) in a=ureepunpa 'I kicked it up with my foot' for the count to admit a bare object, and the affiliative prefix (0) in a=koinawepunpa 'we offered inau' .
Satō credits this arity concept as Nakagawa's central theoretical contribution .
The valency-changing operations that feed the calculus — the applicatives, the causatives, the antipassive i-, and the reflexive and reciprocal prefixes — are catalogued in , , , , , and ; ; .
One commitment of the system bears directly on the debates below.

Third person contributes no affix and therefore no negative value; assigning −1 to an unpronounced third-person affix would throw off the arithmetic, so Nakagawa treats third person as having arity 0 .
Number morphology is likewise arity-neutral, while causatives and applicatives change the verb's class, so the verbal-number system can be kept apart from valence and is developed in .
Hokkaido Ainu has little productive ambitransitivity of the English type.

A single bare form serving as both intransitive and transitive is vanishingly rare; Satō's inventory of correspondence types yields effectively one identical-form pair, the plural roski 'stand' and 'stand something up'.

The other pairs show either partial derivational relatedness, as with transitive nunpa 'wring' beside intransitive inunpa, or no formal resemblance at all, as in the basic vocabulary of the preceding table .
Valence alternation is thus coded by derivation, incorporation, or a separate lexical stem rather than by lability.
What looks like lability is in most cases an uncoded alternation of semantic role within a fixed argument count.

Bugaeva and Kobayashi, after Kobayashi's work on valency, reduce the roles to agent, theme, and space-location, and observe that some intransitives admit either an agent or a theme as their single argument: as 'stand' takes a standing person or a standing tree, whereas apkas 'walk' is agentive only and tuy 'be cut' theme-like only .

The alternation becomes visible in causativization, where a role-flexible intransitive forms two causatives: the direct asi 'stand something up' for the theme reading and the indirect aste 'make someone stand' for the agent reading .
The same active/theme split governs which noun a verb can incorporate, a domain pursued in .
Verbal number gives a further reflex of the formal nature of transitivity.

The intransitive plural stem tracks the number of the subject and behaves much like agreement in Nakagawa's description, while the transitive plural stem tracks the plurality of the object or of the event, the singular remaining the default even when a plural object is overt; Shibatani, following Durie, treats the alternation as a selectional restriction on the principally affected argument — subject of an intransitive, object of a transitive ; ; .
A small set of cognition transitives is exceptional in that the plural stem tracks the subject instead, as in the plural understanding verb below.
What kind of valence the grammar should count is the central open question of this domain, and the two leading positions are to be held side by side rather than adjudicated.

Nakagawa's arity is a single surface-computable property: the value of the final form predicts how many bare noun phrases remain and how person indexes reduce that capacity, and it disambiguates homophonous prefixes, incorporated nouns, and person indexes in the same calculation .
Satō argues that one number collapses distinctions a head-marking language needs to keep, and proposes three valencies operating at once.

The first is the argument-slot count, an invariant abstract property of the lexical or derived verb, filled equally by a person affix, a nominal-derivational prefix, or an incorporated noun — so that incorporation is slot-filling and needs no head-movement analysis of the kind associated with .
The second is M-transitivity, the number of macroroles available for person indexing in the sense of , capped at two.
The third is morphological valency, the intransitive or transitive behaviour of the final form .

The copula displays all three: its argument-slot count is two, but the predicate-nominal term is not a referential undergoer, so its M-transitivity is one and it takes no object index, while its morphological valency is transitive, as the incorporating nispa a=ne 'I am a master' shows.
This derives the excluded *en=ne from a principle .
Satō notes that his own scheme is complex and remains to be justified ‹contested›.
Two narrower disputes follow from the same divide.

Nakagawa records a marginal four-place category from causativized ditransitives such as epakasnure 'make someone teach someone something', korere, and a textual omarere 'made someone put something into something' .
Satō declines to raise so rare a configuration to a regular class, given that the ordinary three-place verb already exceeds the two-index cap and is syntactically special on its own ‹contested›.
The second dispute is the third-person zero.

Nakagawa's arity excludes any third-person affix, while Satō holds that a zero third-person affix is required to explain why a verb cannot host three person indexes — why, for instance, *en-e-raykere 'he makes me kill you' is impossible, the two overt affixes having already filled the cap with no room for the third-person causer ; ; ‹contested›.
Ijäs's zero sign for the unmarked third person is compatible with either side if it is read as the absence of an overt segment .
The observable diagnostics remain bare-noun-phrase valence, person-index behaviour, and derivational morphology, and these are stable across the analyses.

Arity serves as the working calculation for stem formation and argument realization; Satō's three-valency account is the reference wherever the copula, the ditransitives, incorporation, or the zero-affix question make a single count inadequate.
The realization of overt and omitted arguments continues in , and the voice operations that alter these frames in .
A small, high-frequency class of Hokkaido Ainu verbs distinguishes a singular from a plural stem.

The contrast is carried by the verb: ordinary nouns are number-neutral, and the plurality of a participant is read from context, quantification, or human collectives such as , while the verb itself is the only locus at which number is grammaticalized ; ; ; .
The nominal side of that division belongs with , the position of the stem and the plural elements within the verb word with , and the consequences for the personal indexes with .
Transitivity fixes which argument the plural stem tracks.

An intransitive verb indexes the number of S, its sole argument, and the relation is close to agreement: a plural subject index and a plural subject phrase take the plural stem, a singular one the singular stem.

A transitive verb indexes the plurality of O, or of the action construed through O, independently of subject number; the singular stem is the default and surfaces even with an overtly plural object ; .
Following Durie, Shibatani states the cross-class generalization as selection of the principally affected argument — S of an intransitive, O of a transitive — rather than as agreement .

Nakagawa accepts the S/O split but reads the intransitive side as agreement-like and reserves the selectional, marked character for the transitive side, so the agreement-versus-selection question is best left open ‹contested›.
In Corbett's typology of number the category is verbal number proper: a value on the predicate keyed to participant or event plurality, set apart from the agreement number of a nominal controller .

The pattern is cross-linguistically uncommon, and Nakagawa places Ainu among the few languages of northern Eurasia that carry it, with the isolates Ket and Burushaski; even within Ainu the opposition reaches a minority of the verbal lexicon ; ‹consensus›.
Ijäs's learner grammar states the same architecture for the classroom: nouns do not inflect for number, and a subset of verbs have distinct singular and plural forms, set out in her Lesson 9 .
Her example sentences are constructed teaching material rather than corpus attestations.
Type A is total stem alternation: the singular and plural members are lexically distinct.
The class is small and centres on basic existence, posture, and motion verbs, with a handful of transitives of handling and affected change ; .
Dialect membership is part of each entry.

Saru, Chitose, Mukawa, and Shizunai have oka beside okay elsewhere; Saru and Chitose have arpa for 'go' where other dialects often use oman; and Tokachi has no singular partner to ronno 'kill', so it treats that verb as number-invariant .
The transitive rows are the reason a simple subject-agreement rule fails.

A plural object index or a plural object phrase does not force the plural stem: Nakagawa's a=eci=rayke 'I kill you (pl)' keeps singular rayke under an overtly plural object, and one narrator tells the same hunting formula with singular rayke and with plural ronnu for the same event .
Satō reaches the same conclusion, that the conditions on the transitive plural stem remain partly obscure ‹contested›.
A few transitive pairs depart from the O-locus: eram(u)an / eramuoka 'understand', attested as a pair only in Saru, Chitose, and Shizunai, tracks the number of the subject.
A surface-string count over the aligned corpus points in the same direction without giving a grammatically disambiguated figure.
In every pair the singular member outnumbers the plural, most sharply in transitive rayke / ronnu, consistent with the singular as the default.

The figures are tokens of the written surface string, and homophonous an, oka, and ek — which also serve as existential, auxiliary, and other functions — inflate the existential and motion rows ‹corpus-suggested›.
Two further patterns have a segmentable exponent and a wider, though still lexically bounded, membership.
Type B alternates a final -n in the singular with -p in the plural, and is confined to intransitives of directed motion.
The matching transitives are derived with singular -ke (or -ka) and plural -te, and the number relation runs off the moving participant, with rikinka an exception to the -ke shape .
Type C replaces a stem-final vowel with -pa.
It is the most populous class and consists mainly of transitives denoting a change of state in the object; many pair with a same-root intransitive whose S corresponds to the transitive O ; .

The change-of-object semantics is a strong tendency with lexical exceptions: piru / pirpa 'wipe', suwe / supa 'boil', and ani / anpa 'hold, carry' impose no change on the object and have no intransitive partner .

When a derivational prefix si-, he-, or ho- builds an intransitive on a Type-C transitive, the alternation is preserved and the derived verb agrees with its subject: situri / siturpa 'stretch' (< turi / turpa 'stretch something'), hopuni / hopunpa 'rise, get up', hoyupu / hoyuppa 'run' .
Derived transitives inherit the number relation of the base that supplies their affected participant.

A transitive built on an intransitive keeps subject-type agreement, as with hosippa 'return.PL' (< ho-sipi); a causative in -re tracks the causee, which is the original intransitive subject, so hopunire is used for sending off one slain bear and hopunpare for three wolves .

The Type-C suffix -pa is therefore a stem-forming, root-bound suffix, the pa1 of the Handbook account, and is kept apart from the outer plural clitic pa2 treated next; its place in the verb word is set out in , and the derivation in .
Plurality is also marked outside the stem.
Western Hokkaido — Saru, Chitose, Ishikari — uses the postverbal element pa2; eastern Hokkaido uses ci; and Sakhalin has =hci / =ahci, the three in rough complementary distribution ; .
Reduplication occupies the same descriptive neighbourhood but ordinarily contributes iterative, continuative, or intensive lexical aspect, and stays outside the number category proper .
The diagnostic that separates the root-bound suffix pa1 from the clitic pa2 in Saru is position.

The outer plural element primarily indexes participant plurality, especially of the agent, which is the device behind one cross-linguistically unusual property of Ainu: plural-marked transitives can co-occur with a plural transitive subject, as in i=res-pa 'they raised me' .

The eastern ci behaves the same way and gives the inside/outside test directly: in Horobetsu it is a fossilized suffix inside the person clitic (iki-ci=as), while in Shizunai it is a productive auxiliary outside it (hotke=an ci 'we slept') .
The interaction of these elements with the second-person-plural index is taken up in .
The status of pa2 is disputed.

Nakagawa and the Handbook treat it, eastern ci, and Sakhalin hci as a single clitic class distinct from the stem suffix, on the positional evidence above, with Sakaguchi reaching the same conclusion for hci ; .
Satō's Chitose data make the clitic analysis less secure there: =an pa is rare, a consultant rejected *yaynu-as pa in favour of the bound yaynupa-as, and okaypa is marginal ‹contested›.

The descriptive generalization is consistent: the postverbal marker supplies plurality where the stem does not, and adds emphatic or event-plural force where the stem already carries number; Nakagawa reads forms such as kuspare and korpare as evidence that pa2 is drifting toward affixhood.
The Sakhalin marker serves as a contrast.

Murasaki analysed -hci as a third-person plural affix, but its optionality and its appearance with non-third-person reference led Nakagawa to class it with optional plural markers rather than person indexes ; .
It can over-mark a stem that is already suppletively plural.
Two environments separate semantic number from stem number.

A semantically singular referent takes the plural stem in the polite imperative: a bare singular stem commands one addressee (ek! 'come!'), but the polite imperative in yan requires the plural stem even for one addressee, so arki yan is well formed and *ek yan is not .

The honorific fourth person used for a single respected addressee, and in many dialects a single story protagonist in the fourth person, likewise take the plural stem; these are person-system effects, routed to , , and .
The reverse mismatch is a semantically plural subject specified by a numeral, which ordinarily takes the singular intransitive stem.
Tamura's rule of thumb, reported through Nakagawa, is that two, three, and sometimes four favour the singular .

The threshold is not firm: the culturally salient iwan 'six' often takes the singular as well, and the quantifier poronno 'many' favours the plural yet is recorded with singular predicates by both Nakagawa and Satō, so no predictive rule covers the full range of numeral, quantifier, dialect, and stance ; ‹contested›.
The quantifier syntax itself belongs with .
Hokkaido Ainu has a small set of high-frequency verbs whose lexical meanings are bleached in particular constructions while their ordinary verbal morphology remains visible.

The central member is , a transitive verb that supplies a verbal host for a preceding event expression; the same support pattern appears in clausal negation, clause linkage under negation, and some pro-verbal uses where the lexical content is recovered from context.
The copula and the existential also serve as supports, especially in predicate-nominal, evidential, existential, and aspectual frames ; .
The shared condition is structural: the support verb supplies the finite predicate position, so person marking, negation, and clause-linking material attach to a verb word of the kind described in .
The inventory rests on the same valence diagnostics as ordinary verbs.
Intransitives take S markers, transitives take A/O architecture, and the side-switching first-plural and fourth-person forms provide the clearest test ; .

Nakagawa's arity calculus counts person indexes, derivational prefixes, noun incorporation, and base verbs in a single computation; Satō separates argument slots, macrorole transitivity, and morphological valence, using ne as a central case where two argument slots coexist with only one indexable macrorole ; ‹contested›.
The support verbs preserve ordinary head-marking morphology even where their lexical semantics is weak.
The clearest grammaticalized use of ki is the periphrastic negative frame V (ka) somo ki.
The notional predicate precedes the negative adverb somo, optionally followed by the focus/additive particle ka; ki supplies the finite verbal head that somo negates.

In Bugaeva's formulation, the preceding notional verb functions as an object-like complement of ki; Nakagawa describes the same configuration as a use of the formal verb ki that verb-phrasifies the preceding material ; .
The person index belongs to the notional predicate; ki itself is unindexed in the periphrasis.
The direct frame somo V places the negator before the whole person-marked verb and does not split a person prefix from the stem ; .
Nakagawa finds no clear semantic difference between the two arrangements, and Satō notes that ordinary verbal negation very often uses the periphrastic pattern ; .
The internal constituency of somo ki is disputed.
Bugaeva and Nakagawa keep the compositional analysis in which ki is the formal verb and the preceding predicate is its complement ; .
Satō, in the Chitose description reported by Takahashi, treats somo ki as a single auxiliary; Takahashi leaves the historical path open ; ‹contested›.
The disagreement bears on constituency while both analyses place the construction in the same post-predicate slot.
The distribution and scope of the negator are developed in .
Outside negation, ki verbalizes event-denoting material and can stand where English translations reach for 'do'.
The complement may be a predicate stem, an event nominal, or a nominalized clause, and its transitive subject is marked by the A-set, as expected for a transitive verb.
This use provides the bridge between ordinary lexical ki and the negative support frame: both build a finite predicate out of material whose own syntax is already present.
The positive frame V ka ki also belongs here.
Nakagawa cites ipe ka a=ki and rok=an ka ki in comparing post-predicate and preverbal negative patterns, and treats the event before ka ki as the complement verbalized by ki .
These examples license a restricted pro-verb analysis: ki can carry the finite morphology for an event already specified by an adjacent complement ‹consensus›.
They do not demonstrate an unrestricted substitute for a missing verb phrase; broader VP-substitution uses would require a separate corpus study ‹corpus-suggested›.
The variant iki is clearest in template diagnostics.

The plural suffix -pa and the outer plural element pa form a minimal ordering pair with this verb: iki-pa=an has root-bound -pa inside the fourth-person subject suffix, while iki=an pa has the clitic after the person-inflected word .

That ordering pair shows why support verbs still count as verbs: they take the ordinary person and number morphology when they function as the predicate of a clause, even where their lexical content is bleached.
A negated action predicate normally links to a following clause with no, yielding the common 'without doing X' reading.
Nakagawa and Satō state the rule that stative predicates and negated action predicates take no, with wa excluded from this environment ; .
The result is a three-level stack: ki supplies the predicate of the negated clause, somo negates it, and no links the whole to the following clause.
The same architecture appears below formal-noun nominalization and evidential predicates.
A negated verb phrase can stand inside the proposition headed by the possessed formal noun ruwe; ne then predicates the nominalized proposition.
The negation is internal to the nominalized clause, while the copular evidential frame scopes over it .
This ordering is a useful boundary test.
In … somo ki ruwe ne the proposition is negated and the evidential remains outside the scope of negation.
When somo falls on the copula of the formal-noun predicate, as in ruwe somo ne, the result is a high-scope rhetorical or convictional frame, a reading outside ordinary propositional negation .
The details of that outer frame are routed to and .
For the linking inventory see .
The copula ne is formally transitive in valence classification, yet only its subject is indexed.

Nakagawa gives okkayo ku=ne 'I am a man' with a transitive-type subject prefix and rejects object indexing on the predicate complement ; Shibatani likewise describes the copula as taking transitive subject morphology .

Satō's three-valency analysis accounts for the pattern by separating the two-place predicate relation from indexable macroroles: the predicate nominal is a complement of the copular relation, while only the subject is available for person indexing ‹contested›.
Because ne is the ordinary support for predicate nominals, the negative frame of copular clauses is NP (ka) somo ne.
Satō notes that ne ka somo ki, expected if the copula simply fed the ordinary somo ki frame, is almost unattested .
The copular construction keeps its own negation architecture, detailed in and .
The evidential example below combines both support verbs in a single sentence.
Ne predicates a zero-place weather verb in the first clause, while ki hosts the support negation in the second.
The layering makes it a useful diagnostic for the whole support system.
The existential an remains an intransitive verb when it predicates existence or location, and it enters support constructions from that source.
One pathway is lexical compounding into zero-place ambient predicates.
Nakagawa derives mean 'be cold (weather)' from a non-free root me- plus an; such predicates take no person index because no subject slot remains .
Shibatani analyses these as subject-incorporation, and Ijäs teaches them as avalent weather verbs ; .

Where the first element is a free noun, the boundary is unsettled: Ijäs treats apto as 'it rains' as an avalent unit, while Nakagawa leaves the analysis open because apto is an autonomous noun ‹contested›

The v0/vi pairing in this table is directly grounded in Nakagawa's analysis: the sir- prefix and the me- root are non-autonomous elements that fuse with an into a zero-place compound, whereas the felt-temperature verbs take a subject marked by the ordinary S-set ‹consensus›.
A second pathway keeps an as an overt support verb.
Existential and locational clauses are described in ; aspectual frames such as kor an and wa an are treated in .

In evidential constructions, the alternation between copular ne and existential an contributes to the direct/indirect opposition of formal-noun predicates, with siri an and related forms routed to the evidential chapters.
These support uses preserve the intransitive origin of an while extending it into TAM and information-source constructions ‹consensus›

Ijäs's treatment foregrounds the learner's problem: Ainu negation and auxiliary-like meanings are built with independent verbs, so the person marker stays with the predicate that supplies the argument frame.
Her rule that somo precedes the verb and cannot split a person marker from its stem matches Satō's and Nakagawa's description ‹consensus›

Her identification of ki as a dummy 'do' verb that fills the required verb position because somo cannot stand as the predicate of a clause also matches the compositional account in Bugaeva and Nakagawa ‹consensus›
Two Ijäs claims carry caveats.
Her suggestion that postverbal ka somo ki reflects Japanese influence on word order is not supported by the read Hokkaido grammars and should be attributed to Ijäs alone ‹speculative›

Her presentation of lexical negative verbs as blocking somo plus an affirmative counterpart also states a tendency too strongly; the primary sources describe lexicalized negative predicates and preferences, while coexistence with somo is independently attested in some environments ‹contested›
The support-verb system is outside the verb word proper, whose person indexes, valency prefixes, incorporated nouns, and stem-internal suffixes are ordered in .
Valency-changing derivation — applicative, causative, antipassive — changes the argument frame of the lexical stem; ki, ne, and an provide a higher predicate host above the already-built stem.
The lexical semantics of the copula and existential are treated in and .
The degree of grammaticalization differs across the three verbs.

Somo ki may be analysed as a compositional support-verb construction or as a single auxiliary; kor an and wa an behave aspectually while still showing clause-chain morphology; ne is a verb-like copula whose object indexing is blocked.

These disagreements affect analysis, not the descriptive ordering: person-marked lexical predicate first, support predicate above or after it, and clause-level operators outside that support layer ‹contested›.
Hokkaido Ainu derives verbal stems from nominal and verbal sources through mechanisms that must be distinguished from the valency and voice operations treated in the chapters routed from .
Valency operations — applicatives, causatives, antipassive, reflexive, and reciprocal — alter the verb's external argument count in a principled and largely productive way.
The processes documented below either place a base into an argument class without changing that count, or build a new stem whose argument class is determined by the source.

They include the combination of bound nominal roots with verbal heads, the copula and the transitive verb as routes for nominal predication, adverbial prefixes, and the deverbal stem modifications that alter lexical aspect or number without altering argument structure.

The architecture is head-marking in the sense of : a derived stem must enter one of the four argument-count classes — zero-place ambient predicates, one-place intransitives, two-place transitives, or three-place verbs with two bare objects — and the person-index set then diagnoses the class of the result.
Nakagawa assigns every formative a numerical arity value so that the derived form's external argument capacity is computable from the visible morphology .

Satō accepts the same head-marking premise but separates three simultaneously active valency dimensions: an invariant argument-slot count, macrorole transitivity, and the morphological class of the derived form; the copula and three-place verbs motivate the split .
The two accounts are presented together where they produce the same classification and distinguished where they diverge ‹contested›.

For data modelling, it is useful to visualize an Ainu stem the way Japanese grammars visualize intransitive–transitive pairs: the stem may branch into a direct transitive, a productive causative, an anticausative, an autocausative, a reflexive, and an antipassive.
The branches are not symmetric and should not be assigned one flat tag.
Bugaeva's 2025 analysis is especially important here: -ke is the primary anticausative marker, while verbal si- is mainly autocausative and only secondarily anticausative .
The most clearly documented denominal verbs in the Hokkaido evidence are ambient zero-place predicates built from bound nominal roots.
Nakagawa classifies (< + ), (< me- 'coldness root' + ), (< + ), , and as zero-place verbs: they take neither a subject nor an object, and therefore no person index appears on them .

Shibatani describes the same ambient and weather predicates as a form of subject incorporation, with the nominal element supplying the domain that an ordinary intransitive would predicate of an external subject .
The fuller treatment of the incorporative analysis is in .
The autonomy of the source noun determines whether the string constitutes a single word or a two-word sequence.
The roots sir- and me- cannot stand as ordinary nouns in the relevant predicates — *sir anak pirka and *me ka an are ungrammatical — so sirpirka and mean are single zero-place verbs.
The noun , by contrast, is free, and Nakagawa leaves apto as 'it rains' undecided between a zero-place compound and a two-word noun-plus-verb clause ‹contested›.
The same bound-vs-free diagnostic applies to other weather-like expressions.
A set of temperature terms shows the zero-place and one-place contrast side by side.
The zero-place member describes the ambient climate and carries no person index; the one-place member describes a felt bodily state and carries the intransitive subject index.
Property predicates — forms such as and — are intransitive verbs with no separate adjective class; a stative reading ordinarily carries an inchoative one as well ; .
Their clausal behaviour is treated as a subclass in and .
The denominal ambient predicates above are their zero-place counterpart: the nominal root takes the same finite-verb template but licenses no external argument.
The copula is the primary path from a nominal expression to a finite predicate.
A noun or noun phrase precedes ne as a predicate nominal, and the result is a two-place construction with a subject and a predicate nominal argument.

Nakagawa classifies ne as a two-place verb, yet it admits only the subject person index: the object-indexed form *en=ne is excluded in his diagnostic example, while the subject takes the transitive-subject prefix set ; .
Satō uses this pattern to motivate the separation of three valency dimensions.

The argument-slot count of ne is two, since the construction predicates a class or identity; its macrorole transitivity is one, since the predicate nominal is not a referential undergoer and therefore licenses no object affix; its morphological valency is transitive, which explains the transitive-subject-prefix pattern.
Lexicalized denominal compounds such as nispa a=ne 'I am a master' and inne 'be numerous' (< ir-ne) follow the same transitive-prefix pattern ‹contested›.
Nakagawa's surface observation that ne never takes an object index and Satō's principled account of why it does not are two descriptions of the same morphological fact.
Because Ainu property verbs carry an inchoative reading alongside their stative one, a noun plus ne can similarly express both 'be X' and, in the appropriate aspectual context, 'become X'.

A productive denominal suffix -ne detached from the copular construction has no independent support in the available evidence; lexicalized forms such as inne are best analysed as the copula incorporated into a compound stem rather than as the output of an autonomous verbalizing suffix ‹corpus-suggested›.
The syntax and semantics of predicate-nominal constructions are treated in .
The transitive verb supplies a second denominal route.
A noun or nominalized expression may function as the object of kar, and frequent collocations may lexicalize as single verb stems.
The synchronic default is that kar is an independent lexical transitive verb.

Nakagawa's example tanpe kar pe en=ne, cited to show the copula's blocked object index, shows kar functioning as the verb of a relative clause 'the one who made this'; it takes ordinary transitive morphology and is clearly separate from ne .
Horobetsu kar-ici 'make, do' — with the eastern plural suffix ci inside the person index — is a verbal-number fact about the stem itself, not evidence for a productive denominal verbalizer .
A transparent N kar sequence is therefore a two-word clause with kar as its verb.

A single derived verb stem arises only where morphological diagnostics confirm it: fixed wordhood, phonological fusion, or person and number morphology showing that the nominal element has been incorporated into the verb word rather than occupying an external object slot.
Nakagawa applies the same bound-vs-free diagnostic to the weather predicates: bound roots such as me- and sir- support a single-word analysis, while free nouns leave the boundary unsettled .
Without those independent tests, the default analysis of N kar is a two-word clause ‹corpus-suggested›.
The light-verb and pro-verb uses of kar, including its behaviour with incorporated objects, are treated in and .
Several deverbal processes change the shape or the lexical-aspect profile of a verb stem without altering its argument frame.

Nakagawa assigns arity 0 to adverbial prefixes such as ar- 'completely' and ru- 'slightly': they modify the degree or thoroughness of the denoted event and leave the external argument count unchanged .
Their position in the verb template and their interaction with person indexing are set out in .
Reduplication adds iterativity, continuity, or intensity without altering the argument count.

Nakagawa distinguishes root reduplication, partial-stem reduplication, and full-stem reduplication: yields tutturi (root-reduplicated, marking repeated action), turiri (partial, marking result-state persistence), and turituri (full, marking sustained repetition).
He treats reduplication as encoding lexical aspect rather than verbal number, though the two interact at the surface ; .
The Type-C vowel-replacement alternation creates plural stems from singular ones without changing argument count: / , / .
Nakagawa assigns arity 0 to the suffix -pa in this pattern, so the plural stem enters the same argument class as the singular source .
The full verbal-number system — Types A (suppletive), B (-n/-p), and C (-V/-pa), the auxiliary pa, and the relationship between subject vs object plurality and stem choice — is treated in .
Derived intransitives formed by prefixes such as si-, he-, and ho- on transitive bases inherit the verbal-number type of their source.
Nakagawa lists si-turi / si-turpa 'stretch (intr)', ho-puni / ho-punpa 'get up, fly up', and ho-yupu / ho-yuppa 'run' as derived intransitives that still undergo the Type-C alternation .
Number agreement in these forms follows the subject — the single argument of the intransitive — because the prefix has converted the transitive base to an intransitive.
The argument class of the output, not the source, determines the number-agreement target .
The prefixes themselves, insofar as they create anticausative or middle-like readings, are treated in the voice chapters via .
Hokkaido Ainu has almost no productive lability: a single stem serving as both intransitive and transitive is extremely rare.
Satō reports only as the standard case of a form that fills both slots, and he presents it as an exception rather than a productive pattern .
The near-absence of lability means that most intransitive–transitive correspondences are lexical pairs, partial derivations, or suppletive-looking forms that require separate learning ; .
Three formal correspondence types occur.
First, identical surface forms: only roski.

Second, partial formal similarity, as in (vt) and (vi), where the intransitive member is analyzable as the antipassive prefix i- attached to the transitive base, though the pair has lexicalized to distinct meanings .
Third, no formal similarity at all — suppletive-looking pairs of basic vocabulary where the relationship between the two stems is not synchronically derivational .
Selected pairs of the third type are listed below.
The class membership of a form is diagnosed formally, not semantically.
A vi takes the suffixal fourth-person subject marker (=an) and the suffixal first-person-plural exclusive marker (=as); a vt takes the corresponding prefixal forms (a=, ci=).
The contrast between inkar and nukar — glossed by the same Japanese verb 見る — appears within a single sentence:
Bugaeva and Kobayashi identify a related pattern of uncoded role alternation.
Certain one-place verbs may take either an agent-like or a theme-like subject without any change in form: can express both 'stand there (agent subject)' and 'stand upright (theme subject)'.
The alternation becomes visible under causativization — an agent subject yields the indirect 'make sb stand' formation, a theme subject the direct 'stand sth up' formation .
That distinction intersects with the transitivity-pair suffix system, where the inventory of -V, -ke, and -ka formations and their productivity are treated in detail.
Productive valency-changing operations form a separate system whose paradigms are documented in the voice and valency chapters.

Applicatives e-, ko-, and o- add or promote an object and raise the verb's arity by one; the productive causatives -re, -e, and -te add a causer argument; antipassive i- absorbs the object and yields an intransitive; reflexives yay- / si- and reciprocal u- fill the object slot internally so that a subject and an object of the same person are not both indexed by person affixes ; .
Their paradigms are in , , , , , and .
The homophony of the prefix e- shows why holding these categories apart matters.

In one derived verb it is the applicative with arity +1 (adding an object); in another it is the affiliative nominal prefix with arity 0 (contributing a body-part relation); in another it is a second-person object index with arity −1.

Nakagawa's worked examples a=ureepunpa 'I kicked it up with my foot' (applicative, arity +1) and a=koinawepunpa 'we offered inau' (affiliative, arity 0) are distinguished only by the arity computation, since the resulting argument count differs .
The affiliative nominal prefix is defined in .
Locative-object verbs form a small class whose distinguishing property is that their object is a bare place expression.
Nakagawa lists , , and as two-place verbs of this type.
The single base-form three-place verb in his inventory is ; derived three-place locative-object verbs such as , , and are formed by applicative or causative processes from non-locative bases .

The derivational chain that Satō documents on the base illustrates the regularity of the full valency system: applicative ko- raises the base to a three-place verb (ko-ruska); reflexive yay- reduces it (yay-ko-ruska); antipassive i- yields a one-place intransitive (i-ruska); applicative ko- re-applies (ko-i-ruska); and causative -re raises that in turn (i-ruska-re, ko-i-ruska-re, and further) ‹consensus›.
Each step alters the verb's argument class by a calculable amount; the individual formatives are treated in the chapters named above.
Ijäs's Basic Lessons 2 and 3 supply a pedagogical framing of the same system.
Her zero-place, one-place, two-place, and three-place classes correspond to Nakagawa's N-place inventory, Satō's argument-slot count, and the Handbook valency chapter ; ; .

Her "pockets" image — person markers fill positions on the verb itself before and more obligatorily than free noun phrases — is a learner-facing rendering of head-marking, and is especially close to Satō's argument-slot language .
Her statements that bare verb forms carry no tense and that nouns are number-neutral agree with all primary sources ; .
Her Lesson 2 zero-place weather verbs match Nakagawa's zero-place category and correctly include the inchoative reading of descriptive predicates such as .

One qualification on her treatment: she presents apto as alongside the bound-root zero-place forms, but is a free noun and Nakagawa leaves the word-boundary status of the expression unresolved ‹contested›.
Two Ijäs simplifications require a caveat from the primary sources.

Third person is segmentally zero in all attested forms, and her explicit Ø- notation is descriptively harmless; the theoretical status of that zero is nonetheless disputed, with Nakagawa treating it as the absence of an affix and Satō positing a zero third-person affix to preserve the two-index cap ; ; ‹contested›.

Her presentation of the indirect object of a three-place verb in a fixed position between subject and direct object reflects a teaching default; Nakagawa's examples with show that the two objects and the subject are freely ordered by discourse conditions ‹consensus›.
Her forward reference to verbs with distinct singular and plural stems belongs with ; her adverbial -no examples with .
Neither stem alternation nor the adverbializer alters the argument structure of the base.
The form no converts a predicate into an adverbial constituent.
At the word level it appears as a suffix on a descriptive intransitive stem — moyre-no 'slowly', tunas-no 'quickly' — and the output is a manner or degree adverb.

At the predicate level it follows a saturated finite predicate phrase, especially a stative predicate or a negated action predicate, and links that predicate as an adverbial circumstance to the following one.
The two uses share a form; the boundary between suffix and post-predicate particle is difficult to draw exactly.

Nakagawa finds a particle analysis cleaner for the finite-predicate cases but observes that it cannot account for the frozen quantity adverb poronno 'many, much', whose status as a single, semantically distinct word is well established ‹contested›.
Property meanings belong to the intransitive verb in Ainu.
Forms such as and are predicates, and a stative reading ordinarily carries an inchoative one alongside it ; ; .
The adverbializer takes such a predicate as its input.
The position of adverbial material relative to valency and person morphology is set out in ; the broader status of property predicates is treated in .
Descriptive intransitive stems form manner and degree adverbs by suffixation with -no.
Ijäs gives the learner formulation: yields moyre-no 'slowly' .
Shibatani's example illustrates the pattern in a full utterance: tunas-no, from , modifies the property predicate , which in the imperative carries its inchoative reading .
The lexicalized quantity forms poronno and ponno are morphophonologically distinct from the transparent derivation.
Ijäs explicitly records poronno as the correct output and excludes the regularized *porono ‹consensus›.

The quantity meaning of poronno brings it into contact with verbal number: subjects modified by poronno may co-occur with either plural or singular intransitive stems without a mechanical agreement rule ; ‹contested›.
That interaction is treated in .
Derived adverbs occupy no argument slot and leave the valence of the modified predicate unchanged.
Nakagawa's arity table assigns arity 0 to adverbial prefixes such as ar- 'completely' and ru- 'slightly', which occupy the same valence-neutral zone in the verb word .
The suffix -no belongs with that side of the template.
The valence-changing morphology that contrasts with this neutral zone is surveyed in .
When no follows a saturated predicate phrase, it links that predicate as an adverbial state or manner to the following predicate.

Nakagawa places it in the temporal-succession connective group alongside wa and kor, but with a narrower aspectual profile: wa links predicates whose first element delivers a result-state, kor marks concurrent action, and no is conditioned on a stative first predicate or a negated action predicate .
Refsing's Shizunai data show the same adverbializing value in that dialect, where the particle follows a prohibitive predicate to supply the attendant negative state for the polite imperative .
The negative construction is the dominant use.

The frame somo … ki no — negating a predicate with the standard negative support verb ki 'do' and then adverbializing the result with no — yields the 'without doing' reading and is near-obligatory in that function; substituting wa or kor is unexpected in negated contexts ‹consensus›.
The support construction somo … ki itself is treated in .
Ijäs identifies the same two uses of no and presents a further conditioning factor: she describes it as the choice when the linked clauses share a subject, with wa favoured when they do not .

The primary grammars derive the no/wa alternation from aspectual and polarity properties of the first predicate — stative or negated predicates take no — and Refsing's Shizunai conjunctionalizer treatment is consistent with that account ; ; ‹contested›.

Subject continuity is frequent in negated contexts because a manner condition is naturally predicated of the same participant as the following event; the grammars do not extend this tendency to a grammatical rule.
The connective inventory and the position of no in the wider temporal-succession system are treated in ; the syntax of manner and degree adverbial subordination is in .
Hokkaido Ainu marks person on the finite verb.
An intransitive predicate indexes its single argument; a transitive predicate indexes the combination of its subject and its object.

Independent pronouns — kani ‘I’, eani ‘you’, coka ‘we (excluding you)’, asinuma ‘the fourth-person self’ — are available for emphasis or contrast and are used more sparingly than their Japanese counterparts, while the verbal index carries the ordinary work of tracking arguments ; .

Satō describes the pattern as head-marking in the sense of : the verb, the head of its clause, bears the central information about which participants fill its valence frame, and a transitive verb may host both a subject index and an object index .

Nakagawa recognises four formal persons, numbered 1 to 4, each with a singular and a plural, and treats the numerals as form-classes detached from any fixed speaker-or-addressee value; the mapping between form and reference is many-to-one .

The fourth person is the limiting case: it is a single form-set into which everything that persons 1 to 3 cannot express is gathered, so that the referential range of those three is narrowed in turn .
Terminology for this set is unsettled.

Nakagawa calls it the fourth person; Tamura divides the same Saru forms into separate persons — the inclusive, the quotative, the second-person honorific, and the indefinite — counting eleven persons in all; Bugaeva uses “indefinite” and reanalyses the quotation use as logophoric; Satō treats the forms as polysemous; and Takahashi, working on Tokachi, adopts “inclusive person” as the label that unifies the otherwise disparate uses ; ; ; ; ; ‹contested›.
The form-label “fourth” or “indefinite” is used here; its referential functions are set out in the indefinite/fourth-person chapter and the honorific and logophoric chapter.
The person indexes divide into three role sets.
S is the sole argument of an intransitive verb, A the subject of a transitive verb, and O its object.
Nakagawa presents these as separate intransitive-subject, transitive-subject, and object tables, and Bugaeva’s southern Hokkaido table gives the same Saru–Chitose paradigm in S/A/O terms ; .
The three-way distinction is load-bearing: two persons keep distinct forms for all three roles, one opposes an S=A pair to O, and two collapse the roles entirely.
The rows below give the architectural cell values for the standard Saru–Chitose baseline; allomorphy, dialect microvariation, and the person-combination rules belong to the chapters that follow.
The first singular is the one nominative–accusative cell: ku= serves both S and A, opposed to the object en= ; .
Its forms, together with the second singular, are treated in .
The second-person cells are neutral, e= and eci= spanning A, S, and O alike.
The third person is unmarked.

Whether the blank reflects a zero affix or the absence of any third-person exponent is disputed: Satō argues that a zero third-person affix is required by the cap of two indexes per verb and by the ungrammaticality of three-index combinations, against an analysis that recognises no third-person affix at all ; ; ‹contested›.
The architectural asymmetry of the paradigm is the side of the verb on which the subject index appears.
First singular and second person are prefixal, or zero, in both subject roles.
First plural exclusive and the fourth person switch sides by transitivity: ci= and a= stand before a transitive stem as A, while =as and =an follow an intransitive stem as S.
This side-encoding is the morphological basis on which Bugaeva calls these two rows tripartite ; ; .
The object counterparts of these two sets, un= and i=, are prefixal, so each set keeps its three roles formally distinct in both shape and position.
The fourth-person object i= indexes, among other referents, the narrator’s own in oral narrative :

The choice of a= over an= for the fourth-person A is itself dialectal: Saru and the western dialects use a=, while Tokachi, Ishikari, Shiranuka, and Samani favour an= under conditions that vary by locality, and Nakagawa takes an= to be the older form .
The boundary symbols used throughout the grammar follow a working convention: = writes the personal-index boundary and - the boundary of derivational and number morphology.
The convention is deliberately neutral, because the sources disagree about the morphological status of the individual indexes.

Bugaeva, on prosodic and separability grounds, distinguishes word-like =an and =as, clitic-like a= and eci=, and fuller prefixes such as ku=, en=, and i= that shift the accent kernel; Nakagawa writes the whole set with = for convenience yet flags the unusual autonomy of =an, which can be separated from its verb; Sakaguchi’s explicit clitic/affix criteria, developed for Sakhalin material, likewise rank fourth-person =an as the most autonomous subject marker ; ; ‹contested›.
The ordering and boundary diagnostics are pursued in .
Second person collapses the role distinction: e= marks 2SG as A, S, and O, and eci= does the same for 2PL.

The same eci= additionally serves as the portmanteau exponent for a first-person A acting on a second-person O, covering 1SG→2SG, 1SG→2PL, 1PL.EXCL→2SG, and 1PL.EXCL→2PL with a single prefix in place of a sequence of first- and second-person indexes ; ; ; .
The surrounding clause resolves the resulting ambiguity, and the cell is developed in .
The mirror configuration is less regular.

Most dialectal paradigms express 2→1 with a second-person A index followed by the first-person object form, but Saru and Chitose drop the expected second-person subject and use bare en= for 2SG→1SG, Chitose extending the bare form to 2PL→1SG as well ; .
A verb admits at most one subject index and one object index, and no third argument is ever indexed.
The cap shapes ditransitive marking.

With verbs such as kore ‘give’ the object index falls on the human recipient while the theme stays a bare noun phrase, a secundative pattern that Satō takes as further evidence for a zero third-person affix; Nakagawa describes the same three-place verbs through valence, with two bare object phrases and neither obligatorily indexed when both are third person ; ; ; ‹contested›.
Object indexing and the three-place verbs are treated in .
The person paradigm intersects with number at two layers.
The first plural row is exclusive: ci=, =as, and un= exclude the addressee, while addressee-inclusive ‘we’ belongs to the fourth person.
Tokachi confirms the same division, an exclusive first-plural series beside an inclusive fourth-person series whose forms take a plural verb even when the referent is single ; ; ; .
The exclusive paradigm is developed in .
Verb number is its own system.

Hokkaido uses suppletive singular/plural stems — ek / arki ‘come’, arpa / paye ‘go’ — alongside a root-attaching plural suffix -pa and, in Saru, Chitose, and Ishikari, an outer plural pa that sits outside the person index.
The minimal pair iki=an pa and iki-pa=an places the outer pa after the fourth-person suffix and the stem-forming suffix -pa before it ; ; .

The Sakhalin verbal plural =hci and its relatives attach outside the person-inflected verb; their classification as number rather than third-person marking is a point on which Nakagawa and Sakaguchi converge against earlier descriptions ; ; .
Person–number agreement is taken up in .
Several fourth-person uses select plural morphology for a single referent.
Honorific address to one esteemed person and the inclusive ‘you and I’ take the fourth-person form with a plural stem, as does much narrative first-person use outside Saru and Chitose ; .

The whole semantic range of the fourth person — inclusive first plural, honorific second person, impersonal agent-defocusing, narrative first person, and logophoric reference inside a quotation — rests on this one form-set.

The old account of an “elevated” literary person distinct from an everyday one is contested: Nakagawa assigns the narrative use to viewpoint and text type, Satō derives it from a first-person-plural strategy, and Bugaeva analyses the quotation use as logophoric and finds it outside folklore as well ; ; ; ‹contested›.

The fourth-person object i= must be kept apart from the homophonous detransitivising prefix i- ‘something’, whose origin is itself debated ; the detransitiviser belongs to the valency system and is treated under the antipassive.

Read person by person, the system is mixed in morphological alignment: 1SG is nominative–accusative with S=A≠O, the second and third persons are neutral with S=A=O, and the first plural exclusive and the fourth person are tripartite with S≠A≠O.
Bugaeva’s analysis of Hokkaido Ainu rests directly on the S/A/O paradigm and on the side-encoding of ci=/=as and a=/=an, and she characterises the language as mixed but basically tripartite ; .

The person indexes do not split the intransitive subject by agentivity: agentive and patientive intransitives take the same S set once valence is fixed, so the agreement paradigm is not split-intransitive in the morphological sense .
The split that the literature pursues under that name surfaces in verb classes, noun incorporation, and valency-changing morphology, and is treated in .

The competing system-wide analyses — tripartite, hierarchical, inverse — are sharpened by Sakhalin work: Dal Corso rejects a tripartite component for Sakhalin in favour of a mixed nominative–neutral–inverse account, while warning that the diachrony may not carry over to Hokkaido ‹contested›.
The Hokkaido paradigm above supplies the empirical base for .
The personal indexes occupy the outer argument-marking layer of the verb.

Subject and object indexes precede the stem in transitives, while the intransitive S forms =as and =an follow it; derivational material — applicatives, causatives, the reflexive, the reciprocal, the antipassive i-, and the stem-forming plural -pa — sits closer to the root, and a reflexive or reciprocal fills the object slot rather than co-occurring with an object index for the same participant ; ; .
The full ordering of these positions is the subject of .
In the Hokkaido Ainu person paradigm, the first- and second-person singular cells are distinguished by whether the language maintains or collapses the S/A/O contrast within the row.
First singular keeps two distinct forms: ku= for the single argument of an intransitive verb (S) and for the transitive subject (A), and en= for the object (O).
Second singular has one form, e=, in all three roles.
In alignment terms, the 1SG row is nominative–accusative (S=A≠O) and the 2SG row is neutral (S=A=O) ; ; ; ; .

The architecture of the complete paradigm — including the side-encoding of the first plural exclusive and the fourth person, the two-index cap on the verb, and the boundary-notation convention — is set out in .
The present chapter treats the 1SG and 2SG rows in detail.
The free pronouns kani and eani are optional emphatic or contrastive expressions; ordinary finite clauses carry the person information on the verb alone.
Their etymology — kani from the 1SG prefix plus an existential base; eani invariant across the surveyed Hokkaido dialects — and their distribution relative to the verbal index are treated in ; .
The prefix ku= indexes 1SG in both the intransitive-subject and the transitive-subject roles; the two uses share a single form.
This identity of S and A, set against the distinct object en=, is the formal basis for describing the 1SG row as nominative–accusative ; .
In Saru, Chitose, and Mukawa, ku= reduces to k= before stems beginning in a, u, e, or o: ek 'come' yields k=ek, and eramuan 'understand' and eunkeray 'receive' appear as k=eramuan and k=eunkeray.
Nakagawa writes the Hidaka-western and Chitose convention as k(u)=, recording the same alternation; the notation reflects phonological context, not two morphologically separate forms ; .

Bugaeva classifies ku= as a full prefix: it is inseparable from the stem and shifts the accent kernel, properties that set it apart from the more autonomous intransitive-subject suffixes =an and =as, which can be separated from the verb by intervening words and form their own prosodic units .
Nakagawa writes all personal indexes with = as a practical orthographic convention, noting the symbol carries no claim about clitic status .
Satō and Tamura write these forms with a hyphen; the learner grammar of Ijäs does likewise, stating the hyphen is a teaching convention rather than a pronunciation symbol .

Sakaguchi's explicit clitic/affix criteria — developed primarily for Sakhalin material, and applied to Hokkaido only by extension — place root-bound personal indexes in the prefixal class and rank =an/=as as the most autonomous subject markers; on these diagnostics, ku= would belong to the fully prefixal end ‹contested›.
The ordering diagnostics are developed in .

Ijäs introduces ku= early as the obligatory subject marker on both transitive and intransitive verbs, presenting it before the optional independent pronoun and treating the pronoun as emphatic or clarifying rather than grammatically required .
This is consistent with the head-marking account of the Ainu verb given by Satō and with the typological framework of .

An idiosyncratic note in Ijäs's phonetic guidance specifies that initial i retains the fuller form and that careful Saru speech may realise the u vowel before other vowels; these are L2-oriented observations about pronunciation and do not affect the morphological alternation .
The object counterpart of 1SG is en=.

It indexes a first-person singular participant in the O role: the patient of a monotransitive verb or, with three-place verbs such as kore 'give' and epakasnu 'teach', the human recipient rather than the theme ; ; ; .
The secundative object-indexing pattern — recipient indexed, theme left as a bare noun phrase — is developed in .
A syncretism affects en= in the Saru and Chitose combination tables.
Across most Hokkaido dialects, a second-person subject acting on a 1SG object surfaces as a second-person A exponent followed by en= — e=en= for 2SG→1SG or eci=en= for 2PL→1SG.
In Saru and Chitose, the expected second-person A exponent is absent, and bare en= covers the 2SG→1SG cell; Chitose extends the same bare form to 2PL→1SG.
The bare en= form is therefore shared between the 3→1SG and 2→1SG cells in these dialects, and the subject is recovered from discourse or from an overt pronoun ; ‹contested›.
The full dialect-by-dialect combination table, and the parallel 1→2 portmanteau eci=, are treated in .

Ijäs presents the bare-en= situation to learners as a predictable rule: when the 1SG participant is in O position and the subject is second or third person, the verb shows only en=, with the subject inferred from context .
The constructed example below illustrates the Saru/Chitose 2SG→1SG reading.
In the literary and oral-narrative register, the 2→1SG configuration maps to i=, the fourth-person object index, with the subject again unexpressed .
That use belongs to the functional range of the fourth person and is treated in .
The 2SG index e= is neutral across argument roles: one form marks 2SG.S, 2SG.A, and 2SG.O alike.
This pattern is shared by the 2PL form eci=, so neither the singular nor the plural second-person index distinguishes subject from object ; ; .

On an intransitive verb, e= marks 2SG.S; on a transitive verb with a third-person counterpart, e= may mark either 2SG.A or 2SG.O, and the role is supplied by the co-occurring indexes and by discourse.
The role ambiguity of e= on a transitive verb is inherent to the neutral row.

In a clause such as kanpisos e=kore, the prefix may signal either 2SG.A (the addressee gives the book to someone) or 2SG.O (someone gives the book to the addressee), depending on which participant is third person; the gloss assigned in interlinear analysis follows what the discourse establishes.
Ijäs flags this ambiguity explicitly in her fifth lesson as a diagnostic for learners .
When a 1SG or 1PL.EXCL subject acts on a second-person object, the portmanteau eci= replaces any sequence of separate first- and second-person indexes.
All four 1→2 combinations — 1SG→2SG, 1SG→2PL, 1PL.EXCL→2SG, 1PL.EXCL→2PL — surface as eci=, so that forms such as *ku=e= and *ci=e= do not occur ; ; ; .
The portmanteau's double role — 1→2 combination exponent and 2PL index for S, A, and O — is treated in .
Second-person neutrality is the consensus descriptive position for Hokkaido Ainu ; ; .

Its diachronic status is more open: most treatments assume an earlier S/A≠O distinction was lost, while Satō's reported 2024 position treats neutrality as original — a strategy of empathy or deferred agency never preceded by a subject/object split ‹contested›.
The alignment-level debate and the competing system-wide accounts are taken up in .

The first-person plural of Hokkaido Ainu is exclusively exclusive: ci= as the transitive subject (A), =as as the intransitive subject (S), and un= as the object (O) always refer to a group from which the addressee is absent.
Nakagawa, Tamura, Satō, and Bugaeva converge on this characterisation without qualification ; ; ; .
The free pronoun for this row is Saru coka, with dialectal counterparts Tokachi ciokay and ciutari.

Both the Saru and Tokachi forms are built on the transitive-subject prefix ci= followed by the plural existential oka(y) 'there are', nominalized — so coka(y) is, in origin, 'those who exist as ci=-ers' ; .
The three-cell paradigm, set within the full person architecture, is introduced in .
The table below places the exclusive row beside the fourth-person/indefinite row, whose first function is the inclusive 'we'.
The contrast between the two rows is the structural basis of clusivity in Hokkaido Ainu.
Before a vowel-initial stem, ci= reduces to c=, parallel to the reduction of first-singular ku= to k= in the same phonological context ; .
The exclusive first plural is one of two tripartite rows in the Hokkaido paradigm: all three role exponents differ in form and position.
ci= precedes a transitive stem as A; =as follows an intransitive stem as S; and un= again precedes a transitive stem as O.
The S/A side-switch — prefix for A, suffix for S — is the morphological basis on which Bugaeva assigns this row a tripartite classification ; ; .

The Tokachi example below shows both subject functions within a single clause chain: the exclusive group is the A of the transitive verb o 'board' and, in the same utterance, the S of the intransitive plural motion verb arki 'come'.
The object prefix un= occupies the normal O-prefix slot of the transitive verb alongside a distinct subject index.
In the Saru example below, the transitive agent is an indefinite/impersonal fourth person indexed by a=, while the exclusive group stands as object, indexed by un=.
