un= is formally separate from the fourth-person object i=: the two prefixes belong to different paradigm rows and index different participants.

Their historical relationship — including whether Hokkaido un= and the Sakhalin counterpart in= are cognates of the exclusive O or of the indefinite O — is part of the broader alignment debate and is pursued in ‹contested›.
The semantic domain 'we' is distributed across two formal rows.
The exclusive forms ci=/=as/un= index a speaker-only group; addressee-inclusive 'we' falls to the fourth-person row a=/=an/i=.

Nakagawa identifies inclusive 'we' as the first of five referential values of the fourth person; Tamura treats the same morphology as an inclusive first plural in her eleven-person Saru analysis; and Bugaeva places the inclusive value at the centre of the indefinite paradigm ; ; ; .

Tamura notes that coka is the genuine plural of kani 'I', while aoka would more accurately be described as a speaker-plus-addressee category — though she retains the label 'inclusive first plural' for it .
The exclusive row carries no inclusive value in any Hokkaido description consulted.
The complete morphology and the non-inclusive uses of a=/=an/i= belong to and .
Terminological disagreement over the fourth-person row does not affect the clusivity fact.

Nakagawa's 'fourth person' is a formal class label; Tamura distinguishes several persons whose morphology is neutralised; Bugaeva's 'indefinite' groups inclusive, honorific, logophoric, and impersonal functions; and Takahashi, on Tokachi, adopts 'inclusive person' as a unifying functional term, arguing that the participant structure of the inclusive gives a principled account of all the disparate uses ; ; ; ‹contested›.
Across these analyses, addressee-inclusive 'we' takes the fourth-person forms.
Takahashi's Tokachi description provides the most explicit formulation of the exclusive/inclusive opposition for a single Hokkaido dialect.
The exclusive side has ci-, -as, and un-, with free pronouns ciokay and ciutari; the inclusive side has a-/an-, -an, and i-, with anokay and anutari .
Takahashi's hyphens for personal markers are a source-internal convention; they correspond to the =-notation for personal indexes used here.

Takahashi also notes that the inclusive row selects plural verb morphology even when the referent is a single additional person: a sole addressee triggers plural stem agreement on an inclusive-marked verb .

Nakagawa documents the same pattern for the fourth-person honorific and hortative uses — one esteemed individual addressed with a plural stem — and for the narrator in most dialects outside Saru and Chitose .
The person-number agreement consequences and the conditioning of plural stems are developed in and .
In oral-narrative texts, the exclusive series serves a genre-specific narrator function.
In kamuy yukar, the divine protagonist uses ci=/=as/un= as self-reference, distinguishing the kamuy narrator's speech from the human first-person voice of uwepeker, which uses the fourth person .
Whether this pattern derives from an original first-person plural strategy or a register-internal specialisation is debated ; ‹contested›.
These narrative and logophoric dimensions are treated in and .
Sakhalin Ainu presents a different configuration.

Sakaguchi reports that the ci=-series functions as a grammatically plural encoding of the first singular, while the fourth-person an=-series covers both first singular and first plural without an exclusive/inclusive split of the Hokkaido type ‹SA›.
The = boundary on personal indexes and the - boundary on derivational and number morphology are descriptive conventions, not a uniform claim about morphological status.

Bugaeva distinguishes three grades for the Hokkaido indexes, using prosodic autonomy and separability as diagnostics: =as and =an are word-like (they may be separated from the stem by intervening material and have autonomous prosodic weight); a= and eci= are clitic-like; and ku=, ci=, en=, and un= are fuller prefixes that shift the accent kernel .

Sakaguchi's explicit diagnostics, formulated for Sakhalin material, classify -as as root-attaching (affixal) and fourth-person =an as autonomous (clitic-like) — reversing Bugaeva's ranking for =as — while both agree that =an is the most autonomous of the subject indexes ‹contested›.
Nakagawa writes all person indexes with = as a convenience notation, explicitly disavowing any clitic claim .
The ordering diagnostics and the clitic/affix boundary question are pursued in .
Ijäs's learner grammar writes the exclusive markers as ci-, -as, and un-, with hyphens used as a teaching convention rather than a phonological boundary symbol .

The attested example below from the Ainu Times newspaper shows all three exclusive exponents in a single sentence: the A prefix ci=, the S suffix =as (twice), and the plural existential okay hosting that suffix.
The prefix eci= occupies two cells in the Hokkaido Ainu personal-index system.
As the second-person plural index it marks the agent, subject, or object of a predicate whose addressee participant is plural, in parallel with the second-person singular e=.

As the portmanteau for first-to-second combinations it simultaneously indexes the subject and the object when a first-person agent — singular or exclusive plural — acts on a second-person object, singular or plural.
The two functions share a single surface form, producing a syncretism that surrounding context consistently resolves ; ; .
The full S/A/O paradigm and its alignment patterns are set out in .
The present chapter develops the two functions of eci=, the syncretism between them, and the interaction with Hokkaido plural marking.
Adjacent paradigm material belongs to for e= and en=, to for the two-index cap and ditransitive object choice, and to for plural agreement.

Both e= and eci= carry no subject–object distinction: the same form appears whether the addressee is the agent of a transitive verb, the sole argument of an intransitive verb, or the object of a transitive verb with a third-person agent ; ; .
Tamura's formulation is explicit: the second-person affix marks the subject and the object without distinction .

The S=A=O patterning places second person in the neutral column of the mixed alignment system, alongside the zero third person, and against the nominative–accusative 1SG and the tripartite 1PL.EXCL and fourth person ‹consensus›.
Nakagawa's combination tables record eci= as the 2PL index in Saru, Chitose, Horobetsu, and Shizunai, while Ishikari and Tokachi also show es= in the second-plural row .
Where a dialect supplies es=, it fills the same neutral paradigm cell with the same functional range.
When a first-person agent acts on a second-person object, eci= indexes the complete local-person relation.
The four subject/object number combinations — 1SG acting on 2SG, 1SG acting on 2PL, 1PL.EXCL acting on 2SG, and 1PL.EXCL acting on 2PL — all receive the same prefix.
The stacked sequences *ku=e=, *ku=eci=, *ci=e=, and *ci=eci= are unattested and ungrammatical.

Bugaeva enumerates all four covered combinations explicitly; Nakagawa's Saru combination table places eci= in every 1→2 cell; Tamura's earlier Saru analysis already treats the form as the second-person affix used in the first-to-second-person relation ; ; ; ‹consensus›.
The portmanteau character of the 1→2 form is confirmed by the contrast with the 1→4 combination.
Nakagawa's Saru combination table records eci=i= when the agent is first person and the object is fourth person: the agent index eci= and the fourth-person object i= appear as separate prefixes .

The 1→2 cells merge the two slots into one, in keeping with the two-index cap: a verb carries at most one agent index and one object index, and the portmanteau satisfies both positions simultaneously.
The cap and its consequences for three-argument verbs are treated in .
A verb beginning with eci= is formally ambiguous among 2PL.S, 2PL.A, 2PL.O, and the 1→2 portmanteau.
Several cues resolve the ambiguity.
On an intransitive predicate, which has no object slot, the form can only be 2PL.S.
On a transitive predicate with an overt third-person subject noun phrase, the 2PL.O reading is forced; with an overt third-person object, the 2PL.A reading holds.
The portmanteau reading arises on a transitive predicate whose agent is a locally tracked first-person participant.

Ainu discourse tracks participants across turns through the bound indexes and does not regularly deploy independent pronouns for reference maintenance; the free forms eani (2SG) and ecioka (2PL) add emphasis or mark contrast rather than supplying a referent from scratch ; .
The 2→1 configuration presents an asymmetry in Saru and Chitose.

Where other Hokkaido dialects form 2SG→1SG by combining a second-person agent index with the first-person object en=, Saru uses bare en= alone, suppressing the expected *e=en=; Chitose extends this to 2PL→1SG, making *eci=en= ungrammatical in that variety as well ; .
The full 2→1 paradigm and its dialect variation are developed in .
The 2PL value carried by eci= is participant-number indexing and is independent of verbal number.

Hokkaido Ainu expresses verbal plurality through three further devices: suppletive stem alternations such as arpa / paye 'go', a root-attaching suffix -pa, and — in Saru, Chitose, and Ishikari — an outer plural auxiliary that follows the fully person-inflected verb ; ; .
Each device occupies a distinct structural position and can co-occur with eci=.

Nakagawa's minimal pair illustrates the ordering diagnostic for the outer auxiliary versus the stem suffix: iki=an pa has the outer pa following the fourth-person suffix, while iki-pa=an has the stem suffix -pa inside the person marker .

Sakaguchi formalises the criterion — a marker that attaches to the fully person-inflected form is a clitic rather than an affix — for Sakhalin Ainu; the most directly relevant Hokkaido evidence is the Saru/Chitose/Ishikari outer pa ‹contested›.
Person–number agreement and the selection of plural stems are treated in .
The online learner grammar by Ijäs introduces e= in Lesson 2 as the second-person singular index on intransitive verbs; the plural counterpart is deferred .
Lesson 5 then presents eci= as the marker for a first-person singular agent acting on a second-person singular object, and e= as the second-person singular object form with a third-person agent .

Her pedagogical scope covers one number combination of the portmanteau; the reference sources extend eci= to all four first-to-second-person subject/object number combinations and additionally treat it as the full 2PL index across A, S, and O ‹consensus›.

Ijäs notes that second-person neutrality creates an interpretive ambiguity: a predicate carrying e= alongside a third-person participant can be read with the addressee as either agent or object unless additional context fixes the role .
The observation matches the structural picture: predicate valence and the state of participant tracking supply what the person index alone leaves open.
This grammar writes the personal indexes with =, including e= and eci=.
The symbol is a house convention for the personal-index boundary and makes no claim about morphological status.
Nakagawa writes all person markers with = for convenience, explicitly noting that the symbol is unrelated to phonological or syllabic structure .

Bugaeva assigns graduated status on prosodic and separability grounds: eci= is clitic-like — inseparable from the stem and not shifting the accent kernel — while ku=, ci=, e=, en=, un=, and i= are full prefixes that do shift it ‹contested›.
Ijäs writes e- and eci- with a hyphen and notes that equal signs are also in common use ; the forms in this chapter are normalized accordingly.
The morphological boundary status of the Hokkaido personal indexes is treated in .
A monotransitive verb indexes its object with the O column of the personal-index paradigm.

In the standard Saru–Chitose baseline, that column contains en= for 1SG.O, un= for 1PL.EXCL.O, e= for 2SG.O, eci= for 2PL.O, a zero exponent for third person, and i= for the fourth/indefinite person ; ; .

The three-set S/A/O paradigm and its cell-by-cell alignment are set out in ; this chapter examines each O form in its monotransitive function, its morphological and positional properties, and the allomorphic contrasts that arise in specific combinations.

A finite verb carries at most one subject index and one object index; a third argument — such as the theme in a ditransitive clause — is never additionally person-indexed and surfaces as a bare noun phrase ; .

The object index occupies the prefixal argument-marking layer immediately before the lexical stem, alongside the transitive subject index; derivational material — applicatives, the causative, the antipassive, the reflexive, and the root-attaching plural -pa — sits closer to the stem.
The full template is treated in .

Ijäs's Lesson 5 introduces the O set through an "object markers" frame: the English object pronoun corresponds to a verbal prefix on the Ainu finite verb, so that "me" and "you" map onto en= and e= respectively .
Her pedagogical notation uses hyphens throughout; the convention in this grammar is that = marks the personal-index boundary and - is reserved for derivational and stem-number morphology.
The prefix en= indexes a first-person singular object.

Its S/A counterpart ku= covers both intransitive subject and transitive subject functions; the opposition ku= (S=A) versus en= (O) is the one nominative–accusative cell in the Hokkaido Ainu paradigm ; ; ; .
The full 1SG row and the morphological properties of ku= are developed in .
The combination 2A→1SG.O takes a dialect-specific shape.
Most Hokkaido dialects form it with a second-person A prefix followed by en=: the expected sequences are e=en= (2SG.A→1SG.O) and eci=en= (2PL.A→1SG.O).

Saru and Chitose drop the second-person A prefix and use bare en= for 2SG→1SG; Chitose extends the bare form to 2PL→1SG as well, so that the same surface prefix covers both 3→1SG and, in those dialects, 2→1SG — subject identification falls to discourse context or overt noun phrases ; ‹consensus›.

An oral-literary parallel uses i= where the colloquial register uses en=: in the elegant register the 2SG subject is again unexpressed, and i= appears as the first-person object prefix in the 2SG→1SG configuration .
The literary referential range of i= is part of the fourth-person narrative system, developed in .
The prefix un= indexes a first-person plural exclusive object.
It belongs to the tripartite 1PL.EXCL row alongside ci= (A) and =as (S), all three formally distinct ; ; .
The row is exclusive throughout: un= marks a speaker-group object that excludes the addressee, while addressee-inclusive 'us' is indexed in the object position by the fourth-person prefix i=.
Tokachi confirms the same exclusive–inclusive split, with un= systematically opposed to the fourth-person object ‹consensus›.
The full exclusive paradigm and the clusivity opposition are developed in .
Second-person indexes are role-neutral: e= marks 2SG as A, S, or O, and eci= does the same for 2PL, with no dedicated object form for either ; ; .

The role of e= in a transitive clause follows from discourse: a form such as e=kore may be read as 2SG.A acting on a zero-indexed third-person O, or as a zero-indexed third-person A acting on a 2SG.O, with overt noun phrases or context resolving the ambiguity.
Ijäs notes this as one of the practically challenging features of the O set for learners of Saru .

The form eci= additionally serves as the portmanteau exponent for a first-person A acting on a second-person O: the four combinations 1SG.A→2SG.O, 1SG.A→2PL.O, 1PL.EXCL.A→2SG.O, and 1PL.EXCL.A→2PL.O all surface as bare eci=, without a separate first-person subject prefix ; ; ; .
The portmanteau and its consequences for the combination paradigm are developed in .
The prefix i= is the O member of the fourth-person tripartite row, alongside a= (or dialectally an=) as A and =an as S.

Nakagawa lists five referential uses for the form-set — inclusive first-plural, second-person honorific, impersonal or agent-defocusing, oral-narrative protagonist, and logophoric reference in reported speech; Bugaeva covers the same range under "indefinite", reanalysing the quotation use as logophoric; Tamura distributes the functions across analytically separate persons ; ; ‹contested›.
The full referential paradigm of the form-set is treated in ; the concern here is i= as the object prefix common to all of those contexts.
The prefix i= is homophonous with the detransitivising prefix i-, which derives intransitive predicates from transitives — as in beside transitive .

The two items belong to different grammatical layers: the object marker i= is a personal index in the paradigm, while the detransitivising i- belongs to valency-changing morphology and patterns with the reflexive and the reciprocal ; .

Their historical relationship is debated: the older analysis derives the antipassive from the fourth-person object marker; Bugaeva reverses the direction; Nam proposes a common source in the generic noun *hi/*ihi 'thing, place, time' ‹contested›.
The detransitivising prefix is treated in .
Third-person objects carry no overt index.

With a first- or second-person subject, the visible personal prefix is the A form alone — ku=, ci=, e=, eci=, or a=; with third-person subject and object alike, the finite verb carries no overt person prefix ; .
Whether the absence of a third-person index reflects a zero affix or the simple absence of any third-person exponent is contested.

Nakagawa treats third person as lacking an affix; Satō argues that a zero third-person affix must be posited to sustain the two-index cap — the ungrammaticality of sequences such as *Ø=en=e=kore 'one makes me give you' follows if both subject and object slots are already occupied by zero, blocking a third index ; ; ‹contested›.
The alignment implications of the zero versus absent-exponent analysis are pursued in .

Three verbal indexes make up the Hokkaido Ainu form-set called the fourth person by Nakagawa, the indefinite by Bugaeva, and the inclusive person by Takahashi: a= or dialectally an= as the subject of a transitive verb (A role), =an as the subject of an intransitive verb (S), and i= as the object (O).
The full S/A/O architecture of all four persons is laid out in ; this chapter covers the internal paradigm and the referential values licensed by the row.
The row is parallel in structure to the first plural exclusive ci= / =as / un=: both keep distinct forms for all three roles.
The S/A distinction is expressed by the side of attachment — a transitivity-conditioned position switch absent from the first singular and the second person.
That asymmetry is the morphological basis on which Bugaeva calls these two rows tripartite ; ; .
The subject index selects its position by transitivity.
With an intransitive predicate, the fourth-person subject appears as the suffix =an; with a transitive predicate, the same referent is indexed by the prefix a=.
The following sentence contains both on adjacent predicates of different transitivity ; .
In Saru and the dialects to the west, a= is the regular transitive-subject form.

Elsewhere the longer allomorph an= appears in varying distributions: Tokachi uses an= before vowel-initial stems without first-syllable accent and a= elsewhere; Ishikari and Samani favour an=; Shiranuka mostly has an= with a= chiefly before ; Shizunai shows no such split.
Even Saru, Chitose, and Horobetsu preserve an= in verse formulae, and Nakagawa regards an= as historically prior ‹speculative›.
The Hokkaido-wide quantitative distribution of the two allomorphs is incompletely documented ‹corpus-suggested›.

The clitic-or-affix status of =an and a= is contested: Bugaeva treats =an as word-like and a= as clitic-like on the basis of prosodic independence and separability; Nakagawa writes all person indexes with = as a convenient notation and separately documents the high autonomy of =an; Sakaguchi's formal clitic criterion — developed on Sakhalin evidence — converges on the same autonomy ranking for the fourth-person S form ; ; ‹contested›.
Ordering and wordhood diagnostics are treated in .
The plural auxiliary pa of Saru, Chitose, and Ishikari positions itself outside the person index (stem=an pa), while the stem-forming plural suffix -pa sits inside (stem-pa=an).
Nakagawa's minimal pair from Saru makes the contrast explicit ; :

Nakagawa lists five referential values for the same formal row — addressee-inclusive first plural, honorific second person, indefinite or impersonal human agent, the narrator or protagonist of oral narrative, and the quoted speaker inside reported speech — stressing that no single meaning covers all five .

Tamura distributes the same Saru forms across several distinct persons in her eleven-person system; Bugaeva uses the cover label "indefinite" and reanalyses the quotation use as logophoric; Satō treats the forms as polysemous; Takahashi's Tokachi account adopts "inclusive person", arguing that the inclusive value is primary and the other uses follow from it ; ; ; ; ‹contested›.
The inclusive value fills the gap left by the first plural exclusive.
The set ci= / =as / un= excludes the addressee; addressee-inclusive 'we' therefore requires the fourth-person row ; ; .
Tokachi preserves the same clusivity split, and Takahashi observes that the inclusive/fourth-person series triggers plural verb forms even where the referent would otherwise be singular .
In its impersonal or generic value, a= indexes an unspecified human agent on a transitive predicate.
The patient remains in the O role; the verb retains transitive valence; an explicit agent-like participant may appear in a source phrase headed by or wa 'from'.

Japanese translations routinely render the construction with a passive, but Ainu has no subject-promoting passive morphology: the agent does not receive subject marking, and the patient is not promoted to a nominative argument ; ; .
Ijäs's learner grammar illustrates the same generic-human value, glossing a=nu as 'people hear (it)' in a lesson on perceptible sounds .
Her notation uses a hyphen where this chapter writes =; that reflects a pedagogical convention carrying no claim about clitic or affix status.
The generic-agent prefix combines with the nominalizer p ~ pe to yield participant nominalizations of the type a=e-p 'food' (literally 'what people eat').
The following example shows a=e p in a headless relative construction:
The morphology and arity diagnostics of p ~ pe are developed in .
The object index i= belongs to the same paradigmatic row as a= and =an.
In narrative and address it indexes the fourth-person argument as patient, recipient, or undergoer — the narrator's 'me' or the honored person as object .
The prefix i= is phonologically identical to the detransitivising prefix i- 'something/someone', which incorporates a generic object and reduces the verb's transitivity.

The two are notated differently — = for the person index, - for the derivational prefix — and they differ syntactically: the person index occupies the O slot of an already-transitive stem, while the antipassive derives an intransitive stem from a transitive base.
Tamura already keeps the two apart on functional grounds; their diachronic relationship is disputed.

Older accounts derive the detransitive prefix from the fourth-person object; Bugaeva argues in the opposite direction, connecting the antipassive to O-incorporation of a generic noun; Nam proposes a generic-noun source *hi/*ihi 'thing, place' for the detransitive prefix directly ; ; ‹contested›.
The detransitive prefix and its morphology are treated in .
Honorific use applies the fourth-person row to an esteemed addressee.

Nakagawa describes women addressing adult men and humans addressing kamuy in prayer; Tamura documents the same politeness value for Saru; Satō groups it with the literary-person system of oral performance ; ; .
The verb takes a plural stem even for a single referent, a number agreement conditioned by register rather than by the count of persons.
In oral narrative the protagonist's first person is expressed by the same row.

In Saru and Chitose a singular narrator may appear with singular verb stems and the pronoun asinuma; Horobetsu and Shizunai display opposite mismatches between verb number and the available pronouns .

Nakagawa treats the narrative use as the indefinite person applied to an unanchored referent; Satō argues the literary self-reference derives from a first-person strategy and cannot be collapsed into the indefinite; Bugaeva, finding comparable uses in non-folklore Asahikawa texts, removes the dependence on an elegant register entirely ; ; ‹contested›.

The fifth use — the quoted speaker's self-reference inside a reported-speech clause — is analysed by Bugaeva as logophoric: the fourth-person row tracks the discourse-source of the embedded proposition, functioning as a participant-tracking device independent of literary genre ; ; .
The social and discourse dimensions of the honorific and logophoric values are developed in and .
The competing labels encode different analytical choices.
Nakagawa's "fourth person" positions the row as a formal residual class within a four-person paradigm, gathering everything that persons one to three cannot express .

Tamura's Saru analysis distributes the same forms across the inclusive, two quotative persons, the honorific second, and the indefinite, treating the labels as functionally distinct values rather than a single form-class .
Bugaeva's "indefinite (IND)" foregrounds the generic and inclusive core; the quotation use is relabelled logophoric, a move supported by its occurrence outside the narrative register ; .
Takahashi's "inclusive person" gives the Tokachi system a unified participant label, arguing that the inclusive function is primary ‹contested›.

Dal Corso applies the label "fourth person" to the cognate Sakhalin AN-series by word form, while his diachronic reanalysis — which rejects the tripartite component for Sakhalin and treats the cognate system as mixed nominative–neutral–inverse — is explicitly cautioned as inapplicable to Hokkaido ; ‹contested›.
For Hokkaido, the tripartite characterization of a= / =an / i= — formalized in Bugaeva's mixed-alignment account and adopted in the architecture chapter — remains the standard analysis .

The honorific and logophoric values of the fourth person belong to the same formal row as its inclusive and indefinite uses: the transitive-subject prefix a= (dialectally an=), the intransitive-subject suffix =an, and the object prefix i=.
The S/A/O architecture of this tripartite row and its agent-defocusing function are set out in and .

The present chapter treats two discourse-anchored functions: respectful address to a socially elevated second person, and self-reference by a narrated protagonist or by a speaker whose words are embedded inside a quotation ; ; .

Nakagawa subsumes all these values under a single fourth-person label; Tamura's Saru analysis separates the honorific second person and the quotative first person as distinct categories; Bugaeva's cover term is indefinite, with the quotation use reanalysed as logophoric; Satō discusses the literary and quotative functions under the literary-person problem without positing a fourth-person label; Takahashi, working on Tokachi, uses "inclusive person" for the same form range ; ; ; ; ; ; ‹contested›.
The fourth-person row indexes a second person of elevated social standing.

Nakagawa cites two primary contexts: a woman addressing an adult man, and any speaker addressing a kamuy in prayer; in both, the verb takes fourth-person morphology and a plural stem even when the addressee is singular ; .
Tamura's Saru account places the same frame alongside contexts of esteem toward an adult .
The plural-stem requirement in this single-referent frame is grammatically obligatory for the honorific use.
The same constraint — one referent triggering plural verbal morphology — operates across the honorific, inclusive, and narrative fourth-person functions .
Person–number interactions in the verbal system are treated in .
The syntax of prayer address to a kamuy and the attendant ritual formulas are developed in .

Ijäs's online pedagogical grammar documents several present-day address strategies for L2 learners, including plural-stem imperatives with the final particle as a routine polite request, and the use of and as address terms for non-relatives .
The following constructed example illustrates the plural-stem polite imperative, a strategy structurally distinct from the fourth-person S suffix =an used in the honorific paradigm:
In Hokkaido oral narrative, the protagonist's self-reference is expressed by the fourth-person row.
The verb takes fourth-person morphology, and Japanese translations of the same passages render the protagonist with first-person pronouns, because the referent is the narrated self .
Satō discusses this under the literary-person problem; Bugaeva places it alongside the logophoric use ; ; .
All three grammatical roles are attested.
The following Saru example shows the intransitive-subject suffix and the possessive prefix together:
Saru and Chitose permit a singular narrator to appear with a singular verb stem, as in the example above.

Dialect variation is substantial: in Horobetsu, the verb may carry a singular fourth-person index while the only available free pronoun is the plural aokay; in Shizunai, the free pronouns distinguish singular anani from plural anoka, but the verb is consistently plural ‹contested›.
These opposite mismatches between pronoun number and verbal number across the dialect area indicate that the number dimension of the narrator form diverged from a common source.
The object prefix i= indexes the narrator as patient or recipient alongside a= and =an.
A single predicate can carry both the agent-defocusing a= and the narrator-object i=:
The distinction between the fourth-person object prefix i= and the antipassive detransitiviser i- 'something' requires attention to syntactic context.
The antipassive is treated in .
Earlier analyses distinguished a "literary" person (雅語の人称) from an "everyday" person (日常語の人称), treating the narrative fourth-person as a register marker.

Nakagawa rejects this bifurcation: prose tales (uwepeker) use fourth-person marking for the protagonist even though their register is conversational, while prayers (inonno itak), though formally elevated, use first-person ku= for the praying speaker.
The controlling factor is discourse role: a character's story-internal self-representation takes the fourth person; a speaker's real-world first-person address takes ku= .
Satō advances three objections to reducing the literary person to the indefinite .
First, Ainu speakers and translators consistently interpret the narrative form with first-person reference.

Second, the indefinite in its agent-defocusing function is referent-non-specific and incompatible with an overt free pronoun; yet narrators use asinuma alongside fourth-person verbal morphology, indicating referential specificity.
Third, kamuy-yukar texts from Horobetsu use the first-plural exclusive row ci=/=as/un= as the divine narrator's person — a fact that resists derivation from an indefinite base .

Nakagawa counters that most texts mix the first-plural exclusive and the fourth person, and that the uniformly first-plural presentation of Chiri Yukie's 1923 神謡集 is likely an editorial regularisation, since Kanari Matsu's tellings of the same material show mixed usage.
The divine narrator pattern and its genre context are examined in .
Bugaeva's approach sidesteps the origin question by relocating the quotation-internal use to logophoricity and documenting it in non-folklore Asahikawa reported-speech data ; .
Since the form appears wherever a discourse source refers to itself — in oral literature and in everyday reported speech alike — a register-based account cannot be primary.
The three analyses agree on the empirical core while diverging on grammatical category and diachronic origin ‹contested›.
When a third party's speech is embedded after the quotative complementizer , that speaker's self-reference appears as fourth-person morphology in place of ordinary first-person ku= or ci=.

Tamura had already treated this as a "quotative first person" in Saru; Bugaeva reanalyses it as logophoricity in the typological sense, where a dedicated form tracks the self of the source of a reported utterance ; ; .
The logophoric analysis receives support from non-folklore contexts.
Bugaeva's Asahikawa data show the same pattern in everyday reported speech, severing the connection to elevated register .

Nikitina and Bugaeva develop the syntactic argument further, proposing that logophoric reported speech in Ainu is a structurally distinct category, neither indirect speech nor ordinary direct speech .
The dialectal scope remains uneven: Nakagawa confirms the phenomenon for Saru and Chitose, while its extension to other dialects is less well documented ‹contested›.
The free pronoun asinuma (< a= + sinuma 'oneself') is the fourth-person singular self-referential pronoun.

Bugaeva notes that the consultant Ito Oda consistently glossed asinuma as Japanese 自分 'oneself', never as 私 'I', which is consistent with a logophoric interpretation: the pronoun tracks the perspective of the contextually salient discourse source rather than fixing the speaker of the utterance .
The morphology of the logophoric use is identical to that of the honorific and narrative uses: a=, =an, and i= serve all three.

Disambiguation depends on discourse frame — quotative embedding, story narration, or respectful address — together with the number of the verb stem and the presence of the free pronoun asinuma or its plural counterpart aoka.
The clusivity contrast between the exclusive ci=/=as/un= and the fourth person is developed in .
The sekor construction and the syntax of quotative complementation are treated in .
The extended analysis of logophoric narration and reported discourse is in .
The cell values of the personal-index paradigm — which forms exist and what morphological alignment each person row exhibits — are established in .

This chapter examines how those indexes are ordered on the verb word: which positions they occupy relative to the stem, how that ordering relates to valency-changing morphology, and what the positional difference between subject prefixes and subject suffixes entails for the verb's internal structure.
The chapter covers the personal-affix layer of the verb; the full verb word template, including TAM, negation, and nominalization layers, is treated in .
The table is a positional map, not a template in which every slot must be filled.
Most verb forms contain only the stem and one index; a verb with a third-person subject and third-person object shows no overt personal material.

The outer number layer is relevant here because it supplies an ordering diagnostic for the right edge: material that follows a fully person-inflected form belongs outside the personal-affix template, even where earlier descriptions treated comparable segments as person markers ; ; .

When a transitive verb is inflected for a non-third subject, the A index occupies the leftmost position in the word: 1SG ku=, 1PL.EXCL ci=, 4th/indefinite a= or an=, 2SG e=, and 2PL eci= all stand before the stem.
Object indexes are prefixal across all persons: 1SG en=, 1PL.EXCL un=, 4th i=, and 2SG/2PL e=/eci= stand before the stem when overt ; .
The left personal layer is outside the valency-prefix layer.
Applicatives ko-, e-, and o-, the reflexive and reciprocal prefixes yay-, si-, and u-, and the detransitivising prefix i- all attach closer to the root than any personal index.

The detransitivising i- must be kept apart from the homophonous 4th-person object prefix i=: the two occupy different positions, carry different boundary symbols, and have distinct etymological histories; the detransitiviser is treated in .
Valency morphology derives a transitive or intransitive base from the root, and the personal indexes appear outside that derived base, indexing its arguments ; ; .
The 4th-person A prefix shows a dialectal split within the left personal layer.
Saru and the western dialects use a= exclusively; Tokachi, Ishikari, Shiranuka, and Samani favour an= under locally varying conditions, and Nakagawa takes an= to be the older form .
Both shapes occupy the same left-edge position ‹consensus›.
Two subject indexes appear at the right edge of the inflected verb: 1PL.EXCL =as and 4th/indefinite =an.
Both mark S on intransitive verbs and follow any stem-internal suffix.
Their transitive-subject counterparts, ci= and a=/an=, stand in the left personal layer.

This side-switch — suffix on an intransitive S, prefix on a transitive A — is the positional basis on which Bugaeva calls these two rows tripartite: each keeps A, S, and O formally and positionally distinct ; ; .
All other persons keep their subject index on the left.
First singular ku= marks both S and A as a prefix, opposed to the object en=.
Second-person e= and eci= are neutral — the same form serves A, S, and O — and always prefixal.
Third person is zero in all roles.
The portmanteau function of eci= for a first-person A acting on a second-person O is a separate rule and is developed in .
The right personal layer is the exclusive domain of the two side-switching rows ‹consensus›.
Valency-changing material and the stem-forming plural occupy positions between the root and any right-edge person suffix.
The causatives -re, -e, and -ka, and the stem-forming plural -pa, all follow the root and precede =as or =an.
A causativised intransitive, for example, yields a derived stem to which the right-edge person suffix then attaches: the personal layer is outside the valency layer in both directions ; .
The clearest ordering diagnostic for the right edge comes from Nakagawa's minimal pair with iki 'do'.
Hokkaido has a stem-forming plural suffix -pa that attaches to the root, and in Saru, Chitose, and Ishikari an outer plural auxiliary pa that follows the person-inflected form.
The pair contrasts their positions directly:
Sakaguchi formalises the inside/outside distinction as a clitic diagnostic: a marker is a clitic when it attaches to the fully person-inflected form, an affix when it attaches to the root.
He applies this to Sakhalin Ainu, where the verbal plural =hci appears outside the inflected verb and the root-attaching plural suffix -pa inside it .
His criterion bears on the Hokkaido outer pa by extension from a Sakhalin-focused analysis ‹contested›.
The verbal number system, the pa/ci auxiliary alternation across dialects, and the interaction with suppletive stems are treated in and .
A finite verb hosts at most one subject index and one object index.
No additional personal prefix or suffix is possible regardless of how many semantic participants the predicate involves.
The restriction is most visible in three-place predicates: with kore 'give', recipient and theme cannot each receive an overt index.
When both are third person, neither is indexed and both surface as bare noun phrases ; .
When a non-third participant is present with a three-place predicate, the object index is assigned to the human recipient.

Satō analyses this as a secundative pattern, treating the recipient as the selected undergoer of the indexing slot; Nakagawa frames the same verbs as three-place predicates with two bare object phrases that may occur in varying word order, and neither obligatorily indexed when both are third person ; ; ; ‹contested›.
Object-indexing rules and the recipient-vs-theme selection are developed in .
The ceiling also determines how reflexive and reciprocal derivations interact with personal marking.

Once yay-, si-, or u- occupies the internal argument position as part of a derived stem, the verb is indexed according to its derived valence; a separate object index for the same participant would exceed the cap and is ungrammatical ; .

Satō uses this two-index restriction to argue that a zero third-person index must be posited in the paradigm, so that the cap is stateable uniformly, in disagreement with Nakagawa's earlier position that third person has no affix ; ; ‹contested›.
The boundary symbol = used throughout this grammar at personal-index junctions is a notational convenience, not a settled morphological claim.
Nakagawa employs = for all person markers as a convenience mark explicitly decoupled from phonology and syllable structure .
Tamura and Satō write the same markers with hyphens.
Bugaeva grades the indexes into three classes on prosodic and separability grounds :
Nakagawa arrives at a comparable assessment of =an through a different route.

His 分離人称 (separated-person) data show =an detached from its verb by the additive particle ka or the topic marker anak — a separability property he characterises as clitic or 倚辞 status, possibly tracing the form to the existential verb an 'exist' :
Sakaguchi's 2024 thesis on Sakhalin Ainu draws a formal distinction between affix boundaries (-, root-attaching) and clitic boundaries (=, attaching to the fully person-inflected form).

Under his analysis the 4th-person =an/an= is classified as highly autonomous and clitic-like, while 1PL.EXCL -as is treated as a root-attaching affix — a verdict that parts from Bugaeva, who places =as in the same word-like class as =an ; ‹contested›.

Sakaguchi's systematic diagnostics were developed for Sakhalin material; the only explicitly Hokkaido application in that work is the clitic status of the outer verbal plural pa in Saru, Chitose, and Ishikari, derived from Nakagawa's inside/outside ordering criterion.

A dedicated clitic/affix study of Hokkaido person-marking at comparable rigour has not been produced; the Hokkaido boundary gradation rests on Bugaeva's prosodic classification and Nakagawa's separability data ‹contested›.
The boundary analysis is taken further in .

Ijäs's online pedagogical grammar presents the same left-right ordering for L2 learners, grouping person indexes as the verb's obligatory argument positions and treating noun phrases as optional outer constituents .
The framing correctly reflects the head-marking character of the system: the verb carries the obligatory participant indexes while the independent pronouns are optional ; .
Her examples are constructed teaching forms, not corpus attestations, and she writes personal-index boundaries with hyphens as a pedagogical convention.
Two features of the Ijäs presentation are pedagogical conventions rather than grammatical generalisations.

Her word-order guidance for ditransitives treats the indirect object as occupying a fixed position between subject and direct object — a useful classroom rule that does not correspond to a syntactic constraint; Nakagawa's data on three-place predicates allow the two bare object phrases to appear in varying orders .

The zero-marking of third-person transitive arguments in her examples is factually accurate but theoretically neutral: it is compatible with Nakagawa's position that there is no third-person affix and with Satō's posit of a zero index required by the two-index ceiling ; ; ‹contested›.
Person and number meet in Hokkaido Ainu at two formally distinct layers.

Within the personal-affix paradigm, number is built into specific person rows: the first plural exclusive series (ci=/=as/un=), second plural eci=, and the fourth-person series, whose number behavior is reference-dependent rather than form-fixed.

Verbal number forms a second layer, realized through suppletive singular/plural stem alternations and through two homophonous formatives: a root-attaching plural suffix -pa and an outer plural auxiliary or element pa that follows the person-inflected verb ; ; .
The person inventory is set out in ; the stem alternations in ; the exclusive row and clusivity in ; and the full range of fourth-person functions in .
Corbett's distinction between the indexing of participant number and the marking of event or action number maps onto these two layers.
Intransitive plural marking in Hokkaido is agreement-like: the number of S determines both the stem choice and the S-affix form.
Transitive plural marking is oriented primarily to the object or to the action, bringing it closer to event-number marking in Corbett's terms .
With intransitive verbs the plural stem — whether suppletive (ek/arki 'come', arpa/paye 'go', an/oka(y) 'exist') or suffixal (V/-pa pairs such as rewe/rew-pa) — agrees with S.
The 1PL.EXCL suffix =as and a plural fourth-person suffix =an both obligatorily co-occur with a plural intransitive stem; a singular S affix selects the singular stem ; .
With transitive verbs the picture diverges.
Plural marking is tied primarily to the plurality of O or of the action; a first- or fourth-person plural A prefix (ci=, a=) does not by itself reliably trigger the plural stem or outer pa.
Nakagawa characterises intransitive plural as agreement-like and transitive plural as action- or object-oriented and often optional ; .
Ijäs's learner grammar states the same split: intransitive plural follows S, transitive plural ordinarily follows O or the action .

The corpus shows verb-specific and dialect-variable departures from any simple threshold, and Nakagawa's discussion of numerals and quantifiers treats the co-occurrence with plural morphology as complex and speaker-variable .
Nakagawa distinguishes the two pa elements by their position relative to the person-inflected form.
Stem-forming -pa builds the plural member of a V/-pa pair and attaches to the root, inside any person marker or causative suffix.
Outer pa follows the fully person-inflected verb, outside any person affix, and marks participant or event plurality .

Sakaguchi applies a formal positional criterion — a clitic (接語) attaches to the person-inflected form rather than to the root — and concludes that the Saru, Chitose, and Ishikari outer element is a clitic, distinct from the root-attaching suffix .
The hypothesis that outer pa is a later western Hokkaido development that displaced an earlier pan-Ainu outer (h)ci is argued in ‹contested›.
The minimal pair demonstrating the position contrast uses the fourth-person intransitive suffix =an.
When outer pa is used, it follows =an; when stem-forming -pa is used, it precedes =an.
Outer pa can repeat across conjoined predicates in a clause chain because its scope is over the person-inflected predicate, not over the root.
The inner suffix -pa belongs to the stem and contributes its number reading at the lexical level.
The two may co-occur on the same verb — a V/-pa stem combined with outer pa — and both combine with causative suffixes while maintaining their respective attachment sites .
The fourth-person series triggers plural verbal morphology in four of its five uses, regardless of the actual referent count.
Nakagawa enumerates five functions at 2024: 174–179; the number behavior follows from the function ; ; .
Inclusive first plural (use ①, 'you and I') always takes the plural verb stem, since the referent is inherently multiple ; .
In Tokachi, the inclusive series consistently co-occurs with plural verb forms even when referring to a pair, and this co-selection is obligatory .
Honorific second-person address (use ②) requires the plural verb stem for a single addressee, as a form of social amplification ; .
The mismatch between grammatically plural morphology and a singular referent is systematic and socially conditioned.
Indefinite/impersonal use (use ③) — the equivalent of French on or German man — also takes the plural verb stem, with an unspecified agent defocused from the event ; ; .
Narrative first-person use (use ④) is where dialectal variation is sharpest.
In Saru and Chitose, a single protagonist may appear with the singular verb stem.
Horobetsu also permits singular stems for a singular narrator, though the only available free pronoun is the formally plural aokay.
Shizunai shows the opposite configuration: the verb is consistently plural regardless of narrator number, while the pronouns distinguish anani (singular) from anoka (plural) .

The crossed mismatches — singular verb with plural pronoun in Horobetsu, plural verb with singular pronoun in Shizunai — confirm that the fourth-person form-set is not simply a plural of the first person, and they supply evidence for the historically composite character of the series ‹consensus›.
Shizunai uses an outer ci where Saru, Chitose, and Ishikari use outer pa.
The position is the same: Shizunai ci follows the person-inflected form, outside =an, in exactly the outer-plural slot .
Horobetsu presents a formally different element.

Its -ci suffix appears fossilized in items such as iki-ci and kar-ici, and the diagnostic ordering places it inside the person marker (iki-ci=as), with the derivational layer rather than the outer plural slot.
The Horobetsu form therefore behaves like a root-level suffix, not like the outer elements of Shizunai or Saru .
The Sakhalin form =(a)hci (Aniwa Bay =(a)hsi) was described by Murasaki as an optional third-person plural marker .

Nakagawa disputes the classification: the element is non-obligatory and appears with subjects of all persons, placing it with the outer-auxiliary set rather than with person-agreement affixes ‹contested›.

Sakaguchi applies formal positional diagnostics and arrives at the same result: =hci attaches to the person-inflected verb, can follow an auxiliary, and precedes a nominalizer — the signature of a clitic over the person-inflected form, not a root-level agreement suffix .
Baek adds that Sakhalin -(a)hci extends to the nominal domain, a trait shared with Uilta and Nivkh in the Sakhalin area and absent from Hokkaido .
The result for Hokkaido is that no dialect has a productive third-person plural agreement suffix.

Plural participant reference is encoded at the verbal-number layer — suppletive stems, inner -pa, outer pa or ci — and through the number mismatches of the fourth-person row, not through an additional person-affix position .
The plural exponents occupy different layers of the verb and can therefore accumulate within a single predicate.
A V/-pa stem encodes plural at the root level; outer pa can follow the person-inflected form of that same stem to mark additional participant or event plurality at the outer layer.
Similarly, a V/-pa stem combines with causative morphology before the person affix while outer pa appears outside.
In clause chains, outer pa may repeat on successive predicates because its scope is over the person-inflected predicate rather than the clause sequence as a unit .
Plural accumulation does not affect the cap on person affixes.
A finite verb carries at most one subject index and one object index, and no third argument is indexed by person.

In ditransitives such as kore 'give', plural morphology can co-occur with the ordinary object-indexing pattern in which the object affix tracks the human recipient while the theme remains an unindexed bare noun phrase ; .
The two-affix cap and the ditransitive pattern are treated in and .
A split-intransitive, or active–stative, alignment divides intransitive subjects into two agreement classes: subjects that pattern with transitive A, and subjects that pattern with transitive O.
The conditioning factor is typically control, volition, or affectedness ; .
The Hokkaido Ainu finite person-index system makes no such division.

A predicate's transitivity class — zero-place, one-place, two-place, or three-place — fixes which indexes appear on the verb; within the one-place class, no further agentivity distinction feeds the morphology ; .

The morphological architecture, including the full S/A/O paradigm and the side-encoding that makes the 1PL.EXCL and fourth-person rows tripartite, is described in the personal-affix architecture chapter.
This chapter addresses the narrower diagnostic: whether the intransitive S column itself splits by agentivity.

It also explains where an active-looking division genuinely occurs — in lexical classification, incorporation diagnostics, and valency-changing morphology — and why that domain does not constitute an agreement-level split ‹consensus›.
Nakagawa's valence chapter gives the decisive test.
Hokkaido intransitive verbs with an acting, controlling subject and intransitive verbs whose sole argument is a patient, experiencer, or affected entity alike take the intransitive S forms.
Agentive intransitives and patientive ones are both one-place verbs; the personal-index system responds to the valence count, not to the semantic role .

His own examples pair a zero-place ambient predicate — which bears no person index at all — with an experiential predicate whose sole argument is an affected experiencer indexed by the fourth-person S suffix =an, the same suffix an agentive subject of the same person would carry.
A force-of-nature predicate provides the same diagnostic from a different angle.
In , the wave element is incorporated into the stem and the human undergoer is the sole grammatical subject.
That undergoer is indexed by =an; the fourth-person object form i= does not appear.
A patient-like meaning does not move the index toward the O set .
The first singular supplies a complementary diagnostic.
The 1SG row is nominative-accusative: ku= serves as both A and S, opposed to the object en= ; .
A 1SG agentive intransitive and a 1SG experiential intransitive look identical in their person index; the object form en= appears only when the participant is the O of a transitive verb.
The identity belongs to the 1SG row of the paradigm and is not tracking control ‹consensus›.
Connected uwepeker narration supplies the fourth-person complement from attested speech.

The motion verb arpa 'go' — an agentive, controllable intransitive — carries the same fourth-person S suffix =an as the experiential and patientive predicates above: in uwepeker telling the narrator-protagonist's person is routed through the fourth-person series, and the S set assigned to the verb is unchanged by the agentive semantics.
Within the intransitive class, a semantically motivated distinction is widely recognized.

Intransitive verbs whose subject is a semantic agent — labelled Sa — behave differently from those whose subject is a semantic patient or undergoer (So) with respect to certain derivational and syntactic operations ; .
In Hokkaido Ainu the distinction operates at the lexical and derivational level; it does not feed finite person-index assignment.
The clearest evidence for an Sa/So cut comes from noun incorporation.

The accessible Shibatani source is the 1988 conference abstract, which states that the incorporable nominal is the patient subject of an intransitive clause and the object of a transitive clause — an unaccusative framing stated in terms of semantic role and grammatical relation .
The abstract contains no alignment-type term.

A broader active-alignment characterisation sometimes associated with cannot be attributed on the basis of the pages read; that book could not be independently consulted for this grammar ‹speculative›.
The noun-incorporation domain, including the patient-subject diagnostic, is developed in noun incorporation.
The Sa/So distinction is therefore a valence and lexical-class diagnostic, not an agreement-level split.
A patientive intransitive subject is eligible for certain derivational processes — notably the unaccusative-style incorporation Shibatani describes — that agentive subjects are not.
Once the predicate's transitivity class is fixed, its sole argument takes the S set regardless of whether that argument is an agent, experiencer, or undergoer.
Valency-changing morphology moves predicates across transitivity classes before person indexing is assigned.

The antipassive or indefinite-object prefix detransitivises a transitive verb whose object is indefinite or backgrounded; the resulting predicate is intransitive, and its sole argument — which is an agent — takes the S set, formally identical to that of any intransitive experiencer ; .
Reflexive yay- and reciprocal u- fill the object position and reduce transitivity in the same way.
Applicatives and causatives add object positions, moving a predicate from intransitive to transitive class ; .

The antipassive i- is the case most directly relevant to the split-S question, because applying it to a semantically transitive stem produces an intransitive whose subject is an agent yet whose S index is formally identical to that of an intransitive experiencer.

The prefix must also be distinguished from the fourth-person object pronoun i=, which is an O-form of the indefinite/fourth series alongside A-form a= and S-form =an; the two are kept apart by the transitivity class of their host, not by the meaning of the argument ; .
The antipassive and its origin debate are treated in the detransitive i-.
The boundary between zero-place and one-place predicates marks the outer limit of S-set assignment.
Ambient weather predicates such as and are zero-place: they index no participant .
Felt-temperature predicates such as and are one-place and carry a person index on their experiencer subject.
The zero-place/one-place boundary separates argument-free from argument-bearing predicates; it is a valence distinction, not an agentivity one.

Ijäs treats weather expressions as avalent and places ambient forms in that category; Nakagawa agrees on the category but leaves apto as 'rain falls' analytically uncertain, since apto 'rain' is an autonomous noun that can function as a subject in other constructions ; ‹contested›.
Property-concept predicates — , , and related items — are one-place intransitives in the baseline Hokkaido analysis.
Ijäs notes that descriptive verbs also carry inchoative readings, so a single lexeme spans a stative and its onset without changing the person index.
Both uses index the sole argument as S.
Their predication syntax is treated in .
The corpus confirms the zero-place pattern for apto as.

In the following attested sentence the verb as 'fall (of rain)' carries no person index whatsoever: the noun apto 'rain' appears as an overt subject-like NP, but the predicate is morphologically bare, exactly as the zero-place analysis predicts.
Ijäs's learner grammar organises valence through the metaphor of verbal "pockets": the verb carries participant information obligatorily, while external noun phrases are optional cross-references.
Analytically this is the head-marking architecture of , used also by Satō .

Her Lesson 2 states that intransitive verbs take one argument and Lesson 3 that transitives take two; these arity classes align with Nakagawa's zero/one/two/three-place distinctions and Satō's valence discussion ; ; .
Two Ijäs formulations that bear on the split-S question carry caveats.

Her Lesson 9 account of i- as an antipassive filling the object position with a generic 'thing/place' meaning aligns in substance with the Bugaeva line; Satō uses a derivational-prefix label without the term 'antipassive' ; ; ‹contested›.

Her Lesson 3 formulation that the indirect object falls between subject and object in ditransitives is a pedagogical word-order simplification; Nakagawa's ditransitive examples show no fixed order for the two non-subject noun phrases ; ‹contested›.
For Hokkaido person indexing, the secure description is mixed morphological alignment by person row, with no productive split-S agreement.
Bugaeva's formulation remains the standard account: neutral alignment in second and third person, nominative-accusative in 1SG, and tripartite in 1PL.EXCL and the indefinite/fourth person ; .
Nakagawa's valence chapter blocks an agentivity-conditioned reading of the S column .
Satō frames the same system as head-marking and argues for a zero third-person affix on the basis of the two-index cap and ditransitive restrictions; Nakagawa denies a third-person exponent.
That dispute affects the model of the zero row but produces no active/stative split among the overt S forms ; ; ‹contested›.
Sakhalin work sharpens the typological contrast.
Dal Corso rejects a tripartite component for ‹SA›
Sakhalin, proposing a mixed nominative-neutral-inverse analysis, and explicitly cautions that his diachrony and hierarchical account may not apply to Hokkaido ‹contested›.
The tripartite, hierarchical, and inverse positions are weighed against one another in ; the Sakhalin contrast leaves the Hokkaido picture intact.
The productive-split question has one remaining open edge.
The literature does not yet provide a verb-by-verb inventory of whether any Hokkaido intransitive verb alternates between A-like and O-like S marking according to control or discourse construal.
Such an inventory would require a raw-token study across the corpus; the normalised frequency layer strips personal-affix clitics and cannot supply per-affix counts for individual S forms.

No example in the material consulted shows an intransitive undergoer indexed by the object forms en=, un=, or i=; the available evidence supports the uniform-S generalization as the correct synchronic description ‹speculative›.
Hokkaido Ainu encodes the S/A/O distinction through person indexes that appear on the finite verb — head-marking in the sense of .

The architecture of the four formal persons and the combination rules are set out in ; the present chapter evaluates the typological labels that have been applied to the paradigm and assesses how far hierarchical and inverse analyses bear on the Hokkaido data.
The split-intransitive question — whether the S position subdivides by agentivity — belongs to .
Free-NP realization and the relationship between indexing and nominal argument structure are taken up in .
Reading the person-indexing paradigm cell by cell, the morphological alignment is mixed.
The standard Saru–Chitose forms, cited directly in Bugaeva, Nakagawa, Tamura, and Satō, yield four distinct row patterns ; ; ; .

Bugaeva's characterisation follows from the table: 1SG is nominative–accusative (S=A, distinct from O); second and third person are neutral (all three roles carry the same form); the first plural exclusive and the indefinite/fourth-person rows are tripartite, because each uses a distinct form for S, A, and O.
She summarises the language as "mixed (but basically tripartite)" ; .

The tripartite character of those two rows rests on a positional split: the 1PL.EXCL A form ci= and the fourth-person A form a= are prefixes on the transitive stem, while the S counterparts =as and =an are suffixes on the intransitive stem; the O forms un= and i= are prefixal but formally distinct from both ; .
The Tokachi example places the 1PL.EXCL A and S exponents within a single clause chain ‹consensus›:

The fourth-person O prefix i= indexes the undergoer in oral narrative — including the narrating protagonist — and together with a= for A and =an for S makes the tripartite character of that row verifiable in a single utterance :

Bugaeva's three-way gradation of the indexes by prosodic and separability tests — word-like =an and =as, clitic-like a= and eci=, full prefixes such as ku= and en= — and Nakagawa's independent identification of =an as separable from the verb by particles reflect a cline of morphological tightness that is orthogonal to the alignment classification ; ; ‹contested›.
The ordering diagnostics belong to .

The literature assigns different labels because it addresses different questions: synchronic Hokkaido exponence, historical reconstruction, Sakhalin comparison, and the referential structure of the fourth-person set.
The table below collects the principal positions; attributions via Dal Corso are second-hand for this grammar.
Dal Corso's mixed nominative–neutral–inverse account is formulated for ‹SA›
Sakhalin.

He dismisses the tripartite component for Sakhalin by arguing that the S and A forms sharing common origin belong to a nominative sub-system rather than tripartite cells, while the fourth-person or participant-referentiality-mismatch dimension is analysed as inverse .
He is explicit that this diachrony may not extend to Ainu as a whole and that the hierarchical analysis may not apply to Hokkaido ‹contested›.
The Hokkaido description accordingly retains Bugaeva's cell-based tripartite label for the two rows in which S, A, and O carry distinct forms and distinct sides of attachment.
An "active" or split-intransitive characterisation of Ainu person marking appears in the secondary literature and is commonly attributed to Shibatani.

The text accessible for this grammar is the 1988 LSJ abstract, which treats noun incorporation and argues that the incorporable nominal corresponds to the patient subject of an intransitive clause or to a transitive object — explicitly invoking an unaccusative analysis .

The abstract assigns no alignment label to the person-indexing paradigm, In the 1990 monograph Shibatani does operate with an active/inactive classification of intransitives — his applicative discussion tests Baker's claim that no inactive intransitive clause feeds applicative formation, and falsifies it with Ainu data — but that is a verb-class distinction inside the incorporation argument, not an alignment label assigned to the person-indexing paradigm ‹contested›.
The person-indexing paradigm itself does not partition the intransitive subject by agentivity.
Agentive intransitives and patientive or change-of-state intransitives take the same S-form set once the verb is intransitive; the conditioning factor is valency, not semantic role .
Satō's 2025 characterisation places Ainu with head-marking languages in the sense of and develops the argument-indexing system without assigning an alignment label ‹speculative›.
The split that the literature pursues under the active or split-intransitive name surfaces in verb classes, incorporation, and valency-changing morphology, and is treated in .

Two aspects of the paradigm are better described in hierarchical or referential terms than in a flat S/A/O frame: the speech-act-participant combination cells and the referential range of the fourth-person set.

The second-plural prefix eci= serves as the portmanteau for all combinations in which a first-person A acts on a second-person O — 1SG.A→2SG.O, 1SG.A→2PL.O, 1PL.EXCL.A→2SG.O, and 1PL.EXCL.A→2PL.O — using a single prefix where a sequence of first- and second-person indexes might be expected ; ; ; .
The cell and its ambiguity with the plain 2PL marker are developed in .
The 2→1 direction is irregular in a different way.

Most dialectal combination tables carry a second-person A index followed by the first-person object form, but Saru and Chitose suppress the expected second-person subject prefix and use bare en= for 2SG→1SG; Chitose extends the bare form to 2PL→1SG as well ; .
The fourth-person set adds a second hierarchical dimension through its referential range.

Five uses cluster in the same form-set: the inclusive first plural, the honorific address to a respected second person, the indefinite or agent-defocused transitive subject, the narrative first person in oral literature, and logophoric reference inside a quotation ; ; .
The honorific use brings the hierarchy most plainly into view: one addressee is indexed with the fourth-person suffix on a plural verb stem.
The fourth-person A prefix defocuses the transitive agent while the patient remains the grammatical object; Ainu has no subject-promoting passive.
The same prefix participates in the indefinite construction that Japanese or English translations often render passively ; ; .

Bugaeva analyses the inclusive and quotation uses as unified by a logophoric function: the set organises participant reference from a discourse perspective, with the singular pronoun asinuma glossed by native speakers as 'oneself' rather than 'I' ; .
Dal Corso's participant-referentiality-mismatch framing for ‹SA›
Sakhalin treats the same dimension as a referential hierarchy of speech-act participants, but explicitly limits that analysis to Sakhalin data ‹contested›.

The Hokkaido evidence supports a synthesis: person indexing is row-wise mixed in morphological alignment, while the fourth-person set and the eci= portmanteau and 2→1 irregular cells display a referential-participant hierarchy overlaid on the S/A/O frame.
This overlay does not replace the tripartite exponence of the 1PL.EXCL and fourth-person rows; both dimensions are operative in the same paradigm ‹speculative›.

The basis is the five-use analysis of the fourth person and the combination data cited here (; ; ); the synthesis is offered as an integrative label for an existing pattern, not as a new theoretical commitment.
The third-person row is formally uniform — Ø for A, S, and O — but the interpretation is contested.
Nakagawa treats third person as the absence of any affix: a bare noun phrase satisfies the verb's valency position without triggering a marker .

Satō argues for a zero third-person affix, required to account for the cap of two personal indexes per verb and the ungrammaticality of three-index combinations in causative and ditransitive configurations ; .
Bugaeva's paradigm table writes Ø in the third row, describing the surface form without adjudicating between the two analyses ‹contested›.

Ijäs's learner grammar presents the same operational generalization for L2 learners: a finite verb obligatorily indexes its non-third participants while third-person arguments surface as bare noun phrases .
Her presentation is compatible with both sides of the zero-versus-absent debate.
Ijäs's fixed-order statement for ditransitives — indirect object between subject and object — is a teaching simplification.
Nakagawa's three-place-verb examples show that the two object phrases and the subject are not locked in a single linear order ; .
The ditransitive evidence bears directly on alignment.
Satō argues that the object index in three-place verbs such as kore 'give' ordinarily identifies the human recipient while the theme stays unindexed — a secundative pattern in the indexing slot ; .
Nakagawa describes the same verbs through valency, with two bare object phrases when both are third person .

Both accounts converge on the generalization that a verb hosts at most one subject index and one object index; the difference is whether the unfilled third-person position contains a zero marker ‹contested›.
The full object-indexing system and its relationship to valency classes are treated in .
The most defensible synchronic label for Hokkaido Ainu person-indexing is person-conditioned mixed morphological alignment.

Row by row: 1SG is nominative–accusative (S=A≠O), second and third persons are neutral (S=A=O), and the 1PL.EXCL and fourth-person rows are tripartite (S≠A≠O, with side of attachment realising the S/A distinction) ‹consensus›.

A language-level label such as active, ergative, or inverse characterises at most one row accurately: the active label is unverified for the agreement paradigm ; the ergative analysis is a diachronic reconstruction for Proto-Ainu; and the inverse label is Dal Corso's analysis of ‹SA›
Sakhalin, explicitly limited by its author to that variety .
Above the row-wise pattern, a hierarchical overlay is operative in the fourth-person set and in the eci= portmanteau and 2→1 irregular cells.
This overlay encodes referential distinctions — inclusive versus exclusive, honorific versus plain, logophoric versus direct report — that fall outside the binary S/A/O frame.

The overlay is grounded in the five-use analysis of the fourth person and the combination data cited above, and is presented as an integrative account of the competing labels rather than a new theoretical proposal ‹speculative›.
Several questions remain open.

Whether the positional contrast that grounds the tripartite label (prefix for A, suffix for S) warrants a tripartite classification or is better captured diachronically, as Dal Corso proposes for ‹SA›, is a live disagreement ‹contested›.

The origin of second-person neutrality — whether it reflects an original non-distinction or a lost S/A≠O pattern — is unresolved; Satō (2024, as reported by Dal Corso) argues for the original account, while most earlier work assumes a later merger ‹contested›.
The zero-versus-absent debate for third person remains open between Nakagawa and Satō ‹contested›.
Hokkaido Ainu reworks the argument frame of the verb through a dense layer of derivational morphology.

Nakagawa presents the system as an arithmetic over the verb word: every derivational element carries an arity value, the derived verb’s argument capacity is the sum of those values, and the person indexes fill whatever argument positions remain .

The Handbook covers the same ground as verbal valency and voice — the applicatives, the causatives, the reciprocal, the reflexive, the antipassive, the middle, and a set of valency-neutral alternations .
Noun incorporation belongs to this architecture as well, since an incorporated nominal satisfies an argument slot inside the verb word and is diagnosed by the position of person marking ; .
The diagnostic substrate is the transitivity system of and the four-person paradigm of .
A derived intransitive takes the suffixal S indexes =as (first-plural exclusive) and =an (fourth); a derived transitive takes the prefixal A indexes ci= and a= ; .
Placing a verb in the first-person plural is therefore the one operative test of its derived transitivity.
Satō’s pair pukusa a=ta ‘we dig ’ beside pukusa-ta=an makes the point: incorporating the object intransitivizes the verb, and the fourth-person S suffix =an becomes available .
A verb hosts at most two person affixes, one subject and one object, so every operation works under a two-slot ceiling ; .
Ijäs’s learner image of argument “pockets” on the verb beside external “slots” renders the same head-marking intuition ; her terms are pedagogical and her example sentences constructed ‹consensus›.
The working inventory for the part is given below.
The values in the first column are arity effects in Nakagawa’s sense, and they predict the person-marking diagnostics used by Satō and the Handbook.
Several surface strings recur across rows, so the arity and the host verb class settle how a given occurrence is glossed.
Each operation is developed in its own chapter, listed in the final column.
The inventory also marks the homophony hazards that run through the part.
Applicative e- and o- add an object; affiliative e- and o- fill a part slot while keeping a possessor; second-person e= is a person index.
The prefix ci- may be the middle, while ci= is the first-plural-exclusive A index.
The suffix -kar transitivizes on an intransitive base, while a homophonous -kar on transitives is a verse-filler with no arity effect .
None of these can be glossed without first reading off the arity.
The productive causative is one suffix with three principal allomorphs: -re after a vowel or glide, -te after most consonants, and -e after r ; .
It raises arity by one.

On an intransitive base the original S becomes the object of the causative verb; on a transitive base the result is a double-object verb, and double causatives are admitted as well, both of which are taken up in .

The suffix covers coercive and permissive causation alike, and Bugaeva’s Saru sample shows it as the productive default, taking in many direct-causative uses that older descriptions assigned to non-productive transitivizing suffixes .
The older, less productive direct-causative suffixes -V, -ke, and -ka build many valency pairs and are split out into .

Bugaeva analyzes most of this morphology as direct causative in function, where Nakagawa keeps the forming suffixes, the productive causative, and the special motion-verb causatives distinct by their distribution ; ‹contested›.
The indefinite causative -yar, which adds a causer while leaving the causee unexpressed and unindexed, is valency-neutral and is treated separately in .

Ijäs’s Lesson 9 statement that -re “turns intransitive verbs into transitive verbs” gives the right entry intuition but states no allomorphy and conflates causation with transitivization ; ‹consensus›.
The applicatives e-, ko-, and o- add a non-agent participant to the object set, turning an intransitive into a transitive and a transitive into a double-object verb ; .

Their applied objects range well beyond a narrow instrumental or benefactive: Bugaeva’s role tables cover content, theme-patient, instrument, location, range, addressee, goal, comitative, benefactive, malefactive, recipient, source, and purpose .
The three prefixes, the diagnostics, and the older 充当相 and case-relation-prefix labels they displace are set out in , with the individual prefixes in , , and .
The prefix i- fills the object position of a transitive verb with a generic ‘thing’ or ‘someone’ and intransitivizes it, so that yields i-huraye ‘do the washing’ and yields i-ku ‘drink alcohol’ .
Its label divides the literature.
Bugaeva analyzes it as an antipassive on syntactic, semantic, and discourse grounds, and Nakagawa adopts the term after her; Ijäs follows the same usage in Lesson 9.
Satō’s textbook treats the identical prefix as a derivational i- ‘people, someone’ and uses no antipassive label ; ; ; ‹contested›.

Its origin is a separate dispute: the older line relates it to the fourth-person object index i=; Bugaeva derives the antipassive from incorporation of a generic noun and then the pronoun from the antipassive; Nam reconstructs the source as *hi or *ihi ‘thing, place, time’, the generic noun he also ties to the nominalizer and the possessed suffix ‹contested›.
Ijäs’s further suggestion that isam ‘not exist’ contains this i- over a lost *sam is idiosyncratic and unverified.
The reflexives yay- and si- both mean ‘self’ and both reduce arity by filling the object slot .
Their division of labour is among the most disputed points in Ainu derivation.

Earlier accounts split them by intentionality or by an agentive against a patientive self; Satō’s Chitose analysis, adopted by Nakagawa and the Handbook, separates direct self-involvement, marked by yay-, from indirect involvement or dependence on another participant, marked by si-, so that yay-rayke ‘commit suicide’ stands against si-rayke ‘be ruined by ill fortune’ ; ; ‹contested›.
The two prefixes are treated in , and the possessive use of the same morphology, where si- supplies a subject-coreferent possessor to an incorporated noun, in .
Reciprocal u- fills the object slot with reciprocal participants and yields an intransitive verb with a plural subject.
Its readings reach past ‘each other’: u-tures-kor means ‘have a sister, be siblings’ and u-mina-re ‘laugh together’, with no causative-reciprocal sense ; .
Ijäs’s Lesson 9 gloss ‘mutually, each other’ captures the core reciprocal ‹consensus›.
The valency-neutral sociative uko- / uwe-, built from u- plus an applicative, is taken up with the reciprocal in .

The middle ci- presents an event from its affected side and yields an intransitive: gives ci-cari ‘be scattered’, with the affected noun as subject, against a=cari, which keeps that noun as the object of a transitive clause with an indefinite agent ; the Handbook glosses this ci- object-resultative .
It is normally restricted to third-person participants, which keeps it apart from the first-plural-exclusive index ci=.
Hokkaido Ainu has no subject-promoting passive.
