The work of a passive is carried by the fourth, indefinite transitive subject a=, dialectally an=: the agent is defocused while the patient stays the object of a transitive verb, and a demoted agent may appear in an or wa ‘from’ phrase ; .
Satō’s subjecthood test confirms the structure: a ‘want to be loved’ clause cannot treat the patient as an intransitive subject and instead requires a nominalized, object-marked frame ‹consensus›.
The middle, the anticausative patterns that overlap it, and the boundary with this indefinite-agent construction are pursued in .
Noun incorporation forms one verb word from a nominal stem and a verb ; .
The wordhood diagnostic is again the outer position of the person index.

With a phrasal object the index sits on the verb, cep ku=koyki ‘I catch fish’; under incorporation it precedes the whole noun-verb complex, ku=cep-koyki ‘I fish-catch’; and with a fourth-person subject the test is decisive, because the intransitive suffix =an cannot attach to a transitive verb ; .
Object incorporation is the unmarked, lexical type and the overwhelming majority in Satō’s Chitose count; it answers to Mithun’s Type I compounding ; ; .
Subject incorporation is marked and divides into natural-force and possessor-requiring subtypes, the latter stranding a possessor that the subject recovers — the material of .
Oblique nouns do not incorporate directly: an instrument or a location first becomes an object through e-, ko-, or o-, and only the derived object incorporates ; , the feeding relation pursued in .
The status of incorporation is contested.

Shibatani argues that a purely grammatical-relation account and a purely semantic-role account each fall short, and that Ainu incorporation must reference both the incorporated noun’s low agentivity and its grammatical position ; .

Satō revises the unaccusative account because transitive natural-force subjects also incorporate, and takes low agentivity as the defining property, ranking the four types by a markedness calculus ; .

Bugaeva places Ainu among the polysynthetic languages in Baker’s sense while recording where it departs from the Mohawk prototype — its word order, its in-situ wh, and its unrestricted morphological causatives ; ‹contested›.
These questions are developed in and .
The valency prefixes sit inside the person-index layer and before the root, while the causative suffixes follow the stem and its forming material.

Nakagawa’s position table gives the order as person index, nominal or applicative prefix, root, forming and plural suffix, causative suffix, and suffixal person index , the template developed in and .
Because the person index is the outermost shell, any element standing outside it begins a new word, which is the same fact that underlies the incorporation diagnostic above.
Stacking is extensive and bounded by the template.
A single verb may carry up to two applicatives, two causatives, two incorporated objects, and a lexical prefix, alongside a reciprocal, reflexive, or antipassive and the agreement indexes .

The Handbook’s yay-ipe-e-ko-sunke ‘eat meagre meals’ shows the converse, a three-object applicative frame re-intransitivized by incorporating one object and reflexivizing another .

Valency morphology also interacts with verbal number, since what a plural stem or the plural -pa tracks depends on transitivity: an intransitive plural tracks subject number, a transitive plural tracks object or event number ; ‹consensus›.
That system belongs to and , and a valency operation can shift which participant a plural form tracks.
Hokkaido Ainu marks causation with a small set of verb-final suffixes.
The productive majority is one underlying form realized as three phonologically conditioned allomorphs: -re after a vowel or the glides y, w; -te after any consonant other than r; and -e after r ; .

In Nakagawa's arity calculus it carries the value +1: the original subject of the base verb is reassigned to the object position of the derived verb, and a new causer participant fills the subject position .

Three further suffix types occupy the same post-stem slot: the forming suffixes -V and -ke that build transitivity pairs, the direct-causative / transitivizer -ka, and the valency-neutral indefinite causative -yar / -ar.
The indefinite causative, which leaves the causee unexpressed and unindexed, is treated in ; the forming suffixes and -ka are covered in .
Causee marking, the double-object frame, and double causatives are developed in .
The present chapter concerns -re / -te / -e alone: their allomorphy, their arity effect, the productive versus non-productive split, and the direct/indirect and coercive/permissive distinctions.
The three surface forms are phonologically predictable from the stem-final segment ; ; .
Tamura's Saru dictionary and Bugaeva's 387-verb Saru/HSW corpus sample converge on the same conditioning environments.

Satō's Chitose textbook gives the same three allomorphs with the qualification "大体 by stem-final sound, but with exceptions", acknowledging a residue of forms that resist the phonological prediction .
One phonological property separates the productive suffix from the non-productive cluster: it does not shift the pitch-accent kernel of the stem — kú-re and sinót-te, not *ku-ré or *sinot-té .

The analysis of siknu-re 'keep alive' — intransitive plus -re — is corroborated in community linguistic discussion (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2026): the vowel-final stem takes the predicted allomorph without irregularity ‹corpus-confirmed›.

A related community observation notes that lexicalized forms such as iyairaykere ({'i=yairayke-re, lit. 'makes people grateful') and irankarapte ({'i=rankarap-te, lit. 'makes people greet') may carry an "obligatory" or "deserving-of" reading, analogous to participial active/passive contrasts in other languages (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024) ‹speculative›.
The allomorphic conditioning in these forms follows the regular pattern; the proposed extended reading of the construction is not confirmed in the primary literature.

On an intransitive base the productive causative yields a transitive verb: the base's sole argument (S) is reassigned to the object position (O), and the new causer argument fills the subject position (A).
The person-marking diagnostics of confirm the output class: a derived transitive takes the prefixal A indexes, while the base intransitive takes suffixal S indexes.
Nakagawa positions the causative suffix after the forming and plural material and before the outer person index, placing it in the penultimate layer of the verb-word template .
The base-and-derived pair for makes the argument-frame shift visible.
In the base clause matkaci 'girl' is the intransitive subject; in the causative clause she is the object (causee), while the causer hapo 'mother' takes the subject position:
When the causee is cross-referenced on the verb by a person index, the argument reassignment is morphologically explicit.
Where the first person is the intransitive subject (ku=sinot 'I play'), causativization realigns the same participant as the object en=:

On a transitive base, the productive causative yields a double-object verb (vd): the original A becomes the O causee, the original O is retained as an inner object, and the new causer is the derived A.

The attested form a=e=tuy-e-re 'I made you cut (the grapevines)' — tuy-e 'cut' [vt] with -re added — carries two simultaneous person indexes and is cited by Bugaeva and Kobayashi as evidence that causativization of transitives is both licensed and productive .
Double causatives — the productive suffix added to an already causativized base — are also attested, yielding a four-place verb; the attested kor-e-re 'cause to give' is one such form .
Both the double-object frame and double causatives are treated in .
Bugaeva's 387-verb Saru/HSW corpus sample provides the most comprehensive quantitative treatment of the suffix inventory .
The four suffix types divide by count, base-class, and causation type:
At 190 tokens, the productive suffix outnumbers the three non-productive types combined and is the only one that covers both direct and indirect causation from both vi and vt bases .
It also attaches freely to derived stems — those prefixed by applicatives or reciprocal u- — while the non-productive suffixes do not .
This combinatorial range marks it as the productive default of Hokkaido Ainu causation ‹consensus›.
Nakagawa separates the forming suffixes -V and -ke as 形成接尾辞 ('forming suffixes') building lexical transitivity pairs, distinct in status from the grammatical causative .
Bugaeva's analysis subsumes even these under 'direct causative', treating the entire cluster as a valency-increasing operator set with differing scopes ; .
The classification of the forming suffixes as lexical versus grammatical causatives is ‹contested›; the relevant forms are developed in .
When the base intransitive has an agentive subject, the productive causative yields an indirect causative: the causee acts on its own in response to the causer's enabling, permission, or direction.
When the base is stative or non-agentive, the direct reading predominates, with the causee as a highly affected non-volitional patient .
The non-productive suffixes are limited to the direct reading; the productive suffix spans both.
An earlier analysis by Fukuda (Tamura) restricted the productive suffix to coercive causation; Bugaeva corrects this, citing Satō 2008, and documents permissive readings from corpus data .

A verb of ingestion such as → e-re carries both coercive ('feed a child') and permissive ('let an adult eat') readings contextually, following the crosslinguistic pattern for ingestive verbs observed by Shibatani and Pardeshi (cited in ).
Satō 2008 lesson 30 presents the same coercive/permissive ambiguity and derives it from the same form .

Ijäs's Lesson 9 formulation that -re "simply turns intransitive verbs into transitive verbs" is a workable approximation for the basic indirect causative; it omits the allomorphic detail, the permissive reading, the causativization of transitives, and the direct-causative uses ‹consensus›.

A subset of singular motion verbs takes -ke as their primary causative suffix, and Nakagawa documents a semantic split within this class: when a non-volitional object (cargo, luggage) is caused to move, the suffix -ke is standard; when a volitional person is caused to move, the productive -te is used instead .

The -ke / productive-suffix alternation applies to (ran-ke for objects, ran-te for persons) and (yan-ke for objects) .

The verb takes -ka (rikin-ka) in most dialects; its reduplicated plural allomorph rikip does not feed a causative *rikip-ka, the causative being formed on the singular stem only (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2026) ‹corpus-confirmed›, consistent with the motion-verb causative paradigm documented by Nakagawa .
One restriction spans all causative suffix types: zero-place meteorological verbs resist any causativization, because there is no subject argument to reassign to the object position.
sir-pirka 'the weather is good' has no causative *sirpirka-re ; .
Among the non-productive suffixes, -ke additionally requires a one-argument base; the productive suffix and -ka accept both one- and two-argument bases .
The productive suffix is encroaching on -ka territory across Hokkaido dialects, with the shift most advanced in Saru and the southwest.
Many verbs that take -ka in northeastern Hokkaido appear with -re/-te/-e in Saru; intra-dialectal doublets such as nam-te ~ nam-ka in Saru document the change in progress ; .
Sakhalin varieties (‹SA›) preserve -ka more broadly .
The -ka suffix straddles the transitivizer and direct-causative functions in a way the productive suffix does not.
Satō 2008 flags some -ke and -e forms as bleached transitivizations — san → san-ke 'put out a fine', where no causer argument is introduced — distinct from the grammatical causative .
The productive suffix is unambiguously causative in function ‹consensus›.

In the Horobetsu dialect, Takahashi documents an extension of the productive causative suffix into a switch-reference function: in coordinated clauses it marks that the subject of the following predicate differs from that of the preceding one (different subject), while in subordinated clauses it marks same-subject continuity .
The attested Horobetsu forms — é-re 'make eat', kasuy-re 'make help', cis-te 'make cry', wen-te 'make bad' — show the same allomorphic distribution as Saru and Chitose .

Whether the switch-reference function is an independent grammaticalization or a secondary extension of the causative meaning is not settled in the accessible sources; no equivalent use is documented for Saru or Chitose ‹contested›.
Three morphological mechanisms build transitive verb forms from intransitive bases in Hokkaido Ainu, all operating within the arity calculus set out in .

The oldest layer consists of stem-specific forming suffixes — a vowel suffix -V or the suffix -ke — that produce lexically listed transitivity pairs; these are non-productive and the intransitive and transitive members are recorded as separate dictionary entries .

A second suffix, -ka, overlaps in function with the forming suffixes but extends to stative and property bases and to derived stems, placing it on the boundary between the forming-suffix category and the productive direct causative; the literature has not settled its classification ; ‹contested›.

The third mechanism, the transitivizer -kar, productively adds an object to any intransitive base (arity +1) and must be distinguished from two surface-identical strings: a verse-filler -kar appended to transitives with no arity effect, and the verb that appears as the head of incorporated-object constructions such as cise-kar 'build a house' .
The productive indirect causative -re/-te/-e, which supplies the default transitivizing strategy and gradually displaces -ka in the more southerly dialects, is treated separately in .
The valency classes and the transitivity test that diagnoses derived verb type are discussed in .
Nakagawa's paradigm tables 表38 and 表39 set out two structural patterns .
In the first, the intransitive is the bare root and the transitive adds a final vowel (a suffix -V that assimilates to the stem shape).
In the second, the intransitive already carries -ke and the transitive replaces it with the vowel suffix.
For the motion-verb class the pattern reverses: the bare root is intransitive and -ke marks the transitive.
Table 1 samples all three patterns, ending with the -ka pair discussed in the following section.
Bugaeva's 387-verb Saru sample counts 111 verbs with -V and 9 with -ke, classifying all as direct causatives on semantic grounds .
The -V set is closed and non-productive; no new pairs of this type are formed, and the members are listed separately in the dictionaries .
The three motion verbs that take -ke as their transitive suffix (ran, ahun, yan) have plural counterparts formed with the productive suffix -te instead .
Among the motion-verb set, takes -ka as its transitive suffix in most Hokkaido dialects.

Nakagawa's 表43 also lists a further set of verbs to which -ka attaches without belonging to the motion-verb class: , , , and several dialect-restricted forms (teyne in Ishikari; een in Yakumo, Saru, and Bihoro).
The distribution across this second group is a lexical property of the individual verbs, not a regional feature .

In Saru, the pair nam-te ~ nam-ka 'make cold' shows intra-dialectal competition between the productive suffix -te and -ka on the same base ; the analytical implications are taken up in the debate section below.

Cross-dialectally, -ka covers a broader verb class in northeastern Hokkaido; the replacement of -ka by -re/-te/-e is most advanced in Saru, as Bugaeva's sample of 38 -ka verbs against 190 -re/-e/-te verbs shows .

The semantic boundary between the forming-suffix causatives and the productive -te/-re is visible on verbs that admit both: for , ahun-ke encodes direct causation with a non-agentive, inanimate causee (putting luggage inside), while ahun-te or ahun-re is used when the causee is an agentive human brought inside .
The parallel holds for -ka: it signals that the causee is treated as a highly affected patient (direct causation), contrasting with the indirect or permissive readings accessible to -re/-te/-e .
The suffix -ka also attaches outside the indirect reflexive prefix si- to produce a 'pretend to' reading.

Satō (2007) analyses this construction within his account of si- as marking indirect self-involvement: a pretense is only effective through others' perception, which is precisely the situation the indirect reflexive encodes .
The suffix -kar productively transitivizes intransitive verbs (arity +1): → ; → ; → .
Its productivity range is wider than that of -ka: no restriction to a semantic class or phonological stem shape applies, and derived forms can be created from any intransitive base.
Three surface-identical strings require disambiguation through the arity computation .
First, the transitivizer -kar itself, raising arity by one on an intransitive base.

Second, a homophonous verse-filler -kar that appends to transitive stems with no arity change and no semantic contribution — a poetic register device extending syllable count: kocari (a three-place verb) remains three-place as kocari-kar.

Third, the verb kar 'make, do' that appears as the head of incorporated-object constructions: in cise-kar 'build a house', the noun cise 'house' fills the object slot of the two-place verb kar, and the arity is that of kar itself .

Community observation identifies a productive 'treat-verb' pattern within the third type: forms such as nimaw-e-kar 'treat a wound with medicinal bark', osoro-kar 'wipe', and sikaye-kar 'hammer in a peg' each incorporate an instrument or body-part noun into kar 'do' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024).
These are incorporated-object constructions and belong to the account in , not to the transitivizer suffix ‹corpus-suggested›.
Nakagawa treats the forming suffixes (-V, -ke) as 形成接尾辞 listed in 表38–39, a distinct category from the causative suffixes of 表41–43, which include -re/-te/-e, -ke for motion verbs, and -ka .
The category distinction rests on closed membership and the absence of productive alternation: the -V and -ke pairs are dictionary-listed lexical alternants.
Bugaeva (2014: 129–130, 143) unifies -V, -ke, and -ka as direct causatives, opposing them as a group to the indirect causative -re/-te/-e by the non-agentive, highly-affected causee they encode.
The 387-verb Saru count — 111 verbs under -V, 9 under -ke, 38 under -ka — establishes the proportions but does not settle the morphological-status question independently .
Kobayashi (2015: 33) adduces evidence for separating -ka from the most lexicalized forming suffixes.

Two properties distinguish it: intra-dialectal alternation with -re/-e/-te (the nam-te ~ nam-ka Saru pair noted above), and attachment to derived stems — ar-us-tek-ka 'annihilate' and ipe-rusuy-ka 'make hungry' both show -ka appended to a multi-morpheme derived stem, a combinatorial freedom the closed -V and -ke forming suffixes do not share .
The si-…-ka 'pretend' construction described above provides a further case: -ka attaches outside the reflexive prefix si-, which has already reconfigured the argument frame.

Satō (2008: 235–238) includes -ka in the causative allomorphy list alongside -re, -te, -ke, and -e, stating that it tends to follow stems in m or y — "大体 as a tendency, with exceptions." The qualifier matters: a pure phonological allomorph would show regular conditioning; the exceptions reflect a lexical residue that fits neither a clean allomorphy account nor a uniform forming-suffix categorisation.

Satō also notes that some -ke and -e forms are bleached transitivizers with no causative semantics (san-ke 'put out a fine' from san 'go out'), which aligns with Nakagawa's forming-suffix category and places the productive/lexical boundary inside, not between, these suffixes .

Ijäs's Lesson 9 states that -re 'turns intransitive verbs into transitive verbs', which captures the right intuition for the valency-increasing set as a whole but supplies no allomorphy and does not distinguish -ka, -ke, or the lexical forming-suffix pairs as separate sub-types ‹consensus›
(the source gives no allomorphy detail).

The verb belongs to a class of Hokkaido Ainu motion-verb intransitives showing a -n/-p stem alternation in reduplication and some plural contexts, paralleling san/sap, yan/yap, and ahun/ahup (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2026) ‹speculative›.
In reduplication contexts rikin alternates with rikip.
When -ka attaches, only rikin-ka is attested; the form *rikip-ka is absent from the corpus (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2026) ‹corpus-suggested›.
The distribution shows that -ka targets the citation form of the stem — the singular -n variant — not the alternate -p shape that arises in reduplicated environments.
The attachment point is the lexical base, prior to any stem alternation, a property shared by other causative suffixes that affix to the verb stem before verbal-number morphology applies.
This behavior is consistent with Kobayashi's evidence that -ka operates at the same morphological level as the productive causative rather than with the most lexicalized forming suffixes .
The diachronic account of the -V and -ke/-ka pairs as anticausatives in origin is explored in .
The middle and anticausative patterns that overlap synchronically with the transitivity pairs are treated in , and deverbal derivation more broadly in .
The productive causative suffix -re/-te/-e raises arity by one.

Applied to an intransitive base it creates a two-place transitive; applied to a transitive base it creates a three-place ditransitive; applied a second time to a derived causative stem it produces a four-place verb.

The chapter follows the causee — the participant who is made or permitted to act — through each of these steps: its expression as the O of a derived transitive, the priority it takes over the theme when both objects compete for the single O-index slot, and the behaviour of double causatives under the two-slot ceiling.
The allomorphy and the productive versus non-productive distribution of causative morphology are developed in .
The indefinite causative -yar/-ar, which adds a causer while leaving the causee both unexpressed and unindexed, is treated in .
When -re/-te/-e derives a transitive verb from an intransitive base, the former intransitive subject becomes the O of the causative verb.
Person marking shows this shift directly.

The intransitive takes the first-person A prefix ku=; once the causative -te is added, that same participant reappears as the first-person object en=, and the new causer — hapo 'mother' — occupies the A position, unmarked because third-person A is zero .
The causee bears no case particle.
Ainu objects are invariably unmarked, so the causee surfaces as a bare NP alongside any O-set affix that cross-references it, in exactly the same way the patient of any transitive does ; .

The same principle carries into the three-place frame that arises when a transitive base is causativized: the marking type does not change, only the number of competitors for the single O-index slot increases.
When -re/-te/-e applies to a transitive verb (arity +2), the result has arity +3.
The new causer fills the A position, the original transitive subject (now the causee) fills one O position, and the original patient or theme fills a second O position.

Bugaeva (2014: 142) characterizes the causee in this frame as an unmarked direct object in a double-object construction, parallel in its coding to a recipient in an applicative-derived ditransitive ; .
A corpus example from the Saru texts in the Nakagawa archive illustrates all three participants at once.
The base verb is , the transitivized member of the tuy/tuy-e pair; adding the causative -re raises arity to three.
The causer is indexed by a= (fourth person, functioning as narrative first person), the causee 'you' by e= (2SG.O), and the theme appears as a bare NP without any person affix on the verb:

In the three-place causative frame two objects compete for the single O-slot.
The attested indexing pattern, exemplified by a=e=tuy-e-re, gives the O-slot to the causee and leaves the theme as a bare NP.

This outcome places Ainu causative ditransitives in the secundative column of ditransitive indexing typology (see ): the causee, as derived O, patterns with the O of a monotransitive verb for person-marking purposes, rather than the original patient claiming that slot ; .
The pattern mirrors what applies in applicative-derived ditransitives, where the applied object — not the original patient — is indexed in the O-position ‹corpus-suggested›.
Whether the reverse indexing (theme indexed, causee as bare NP) ever occurs is not settled in the sources consulted ‹speculative›.
A lexicalized sub-pattern involves the fourth-person object affix i= serving as an indefinite causee.

Forms such as iyairaykere and irankarapte have been proposed by nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, November 2024) as i= + stem + -re/-te, glossable as 'cause people/someone to be grateful' and 'cause people/someone to greet' respectively.
On this reading i= occupies the O-slot as an indefinite causee, and some lexicalized tokens drift toward an adjectival-modal reading analogous to English excit-ing alongside excit-ed.
The analysis is not yet verified against the corpus and Nakagawa's (2024) treatment of these forms has been judged insufficiently detailed by the same discussant ‹contested›.

If the i=-causee reading is correct, causee expression in the productive causative system presents a three-way gradient: a specific causee (named NP plus O-set affix on the verb) → an indefinite causee (i=-affix, cross-referenced but unspecified) → an unindexed causee (-yar, not cross-referenced at all).

The antipassive prefix i- can similarly fill the causee slot with a generic object when applied to a causative-derived stem — Bugaeva's examples i-newsar-ka 'amuse people' and i-oripak-ka 'make people feel humble', reported via the Handbook — and forms a related but distinct indefinite-causee strategy ‹corpus-suggested›.
The productive suffix applies iteratively.
A derived causative stem may itself serve as the input to a second causativization, and the allomorphy rules apply at each step.
After the vowel-final first causative -e (the allomorph after r), the second causative surfaces as -re (the allomorph after a vowel), producing the sequence -e-re ; .

The first causative suffix -e (after r) yields (+3): the giver is the new A, and the original possessor becomes a causee-beneficiary in the O position.
A second -re yields kor-e-re (have-caus-caus, +4): an outer causer now makes the giver give.
Bugaeva (2014: 142–143) records kor-e-re as attested once in her 387-verb Saru sample .

The base is a locative verb; is its three-place causative; omare-re is the double causative with four participants .
An attested token of this very double causative appears in the Biratori uwepeker narratives.
In the sentence below the outer causer is indexed by the fourth-person A prefix a= on omarere; the verb carries no further person index, illustrating the two-slot ceiling in a live four-place frame.
The two-slot ceiling limits what can be cross-referenced in any four-place frame.
Of four participants, only the outer causer (A-slot) and the immediate causee (O-slot) can be indexed by person affixes on the verb; the remaining objects must be expressed as overt bare NPs.
The asymmetry between a morphologically productive stacking operation and its restricted expressibility in person marking explains the marginal corpus status of double causatives.

Bugaeva and Kobayashi observe that the licensing of double-object frames and double causatives in Ainu is cross-linguistically unusual, most languages blocking iterative morphological causativization ‹corpus-suggested›.

The causative sits within a broader combinability system in which two applicatives, two causatives, two incorporated objects, reflexive, and agreement indexes can co-occur on a single verb — surveyed in ; .
The two-slot ceiling is the shared operational bound across all combinations ; .
Kobayashi's argument-structure analysis is relevant background here.

She separates causative derivation — which always adds an agent-like participant, displacing the original subject to O — from applicative derivation, which adds a non-agent participant to the object set.
The distinction predicts which slot a new participant targets and clarifies when applicative and causative are alternatives for expanding the argument frame ; .
The non-causative side is taken up in .

Takahashi (2017) reports that in Horobetsu the causative suffix acquires an additional switch-reference function in clause linkage: in coordinate chains it marks a different subject in the following clause; in subordinate chains it marks the same subject.

This function is not attested in descriptions of Saru or Chitose and does not bear directly on causee marking, but it shows the causative suffix to be morphologically multifunctional in at least one dialect ‹corpus-suggested›.
For the non-productive lexical causatives (-V, -ke, -ka) and their relationship to transitivity pairs, see ; for the arity classes themselves, .
Hokkaido Ainu derives causative verbs by two principal suffix types that differ in their effect on the argument frame.
The productive causative -re/-te/-e, treated in , raises verb arity by one: a new causer takes the subject position and the original subject is demoted to object.

The suffix -yar, and its allomorph -ar, introduces a causer as the new subject but suppresses the causee entirely — the party that carries out the caused action is neither expressed as a separate argument nor cross-referenced on the verb, so the net argument count of the derived form equals that of its base ; ; .
Nakagawa's label for this type is 不定使役 'indefinite causative' ; the Handbook chapter on verbal valency places it among the valency-neutral alternations alongside the sociative uko-/uwe- .
The broader arity calculus that frames all valency operations is set out in the overview chapter; causee marking and double causatives are in .
A causative suffix that leaves argument count unchanged is typologically unusual ; .

Within the arity system the outcome is coherent: -yar encodes a new causal event while the causee is structurally absorbed, in the same way that noun incorporation satisfies an argument slot from inside the verb word without expanding external valency .
The suffix surfaces as -yar after a vowel or a glide and as -ar after other consonants ; .
The conditioning environment mirrors that of the productive causative, where vowel- and glide-final stems take -re, most consonant-final stems take -te, and r-final stems take -e .
The canonical -yar form is → nu-yar 'make someone unspecified hear something, tell'.

The allomorph -ar would surface on consonant-final bases such as a hypothetical sinot-ar 'have someone play'; the allomorphy is stated in the Handbook but no consonant-final form is attested in the read corpus sources ‹corpus-suggested›.
Nakagawa's slot table places -yar/-ar in the causative suffix position, after the stem and any forming material and before the suffixal person index .
Any suffixal person index on the derived form marks the new causer-subject, not the suppressed causee.
The causee — the party who carries out the caused action — is structurally absent from the derived verb: no person index cross-references it and no bare NP expresses it as a core argument.
Satō states that the suffix cannot license a separate causee NP; Kobayashi's valency study describes the type as 不定使役 with the causee role suppressed and valency unchanged ; .

This separates -yar from the productive causative, which expresses the causee as a direct object, cross-references it with a person index, and produces a double-object frame when the base is already transitive .
When a speaker wishes to indicate the implied original agent despite its exclusion from the verb's argument frame, the postpositions or peka, or un, or eun supply a peripheral adjunct slot.
Nakagawa's Saru examples (exx. 961–963) include nispa or peka a=korar 'marry off to a rich man', where or peka specifies the intended recipient without making that recipient a core verbal argument .
The same option appears in oral narrative, where a deity named in an eun phrase receives the message conveyed by nu-yar while the verb itself indexes no causee .
Three semantic characterisations appear in or near the literature, and the sources consulted converge only on the structural valency facts while leaving the label question open ; ‹contested›.
The indefinite-causation reading — the causer causes an event but the party who performs it is unspecified (誰にでも 'to whoever') — is the characterisation that Nakagawa and the Handbook share ; .
It fits the most frequent attested form: nu-yar functions as the regular verb for public announcement or reporting, a speech act whose point is precisely that the recipient class is left open.
The permissive reading surfaces in contexts of polite or deferential causation, where the causer enables an action that the unnamed causee has reason or inclination to perform.
Bugaeva and Kobayashi note that a host may say ipe-yar=an ro 'let's have the guest eat' rather than naming the guest as a direct causee, producing a softer formulation ; .

Bugaeva's Saru study shows that the productive -re/-te/-e also covers permissive causation alongside coercive causation, and that ingestive verbs like 'eat' and 'drink' take both readings with that suffix .

The structural property of -yar — suppression of the causee — is what distinguishes it from -re/-te/-e in permissive contexts; the permissive vs coercive axis alone does not predict the choice between the two suffix types.
The label sociative causative — marking the causer's participation together with or on behalf of others — has been mentioned in connection with -yar alongside the indefinite and permissive labels.
The sources consulted do not adjudicate between the three characterisations.
Bugaeva's 2014 causative study, the most comprehensive treatment of Ainu causative morphology available, explicitly excludes -yar for reasons of space .
The data for this table come from , , and .
The pair nu-re / nu-yar makes the contrast explicit.

The productive causative nu-re 'make someone hear something' is a three-place verb: the causer is subject, the causee occupies one object slot and receives a person index, and the content heard fills the second object slot.
The indefinite causative nu-yar keeps the two-place frame of the base : the causer is subject, the content is the sole object, and the recipient is absent from the verb's morphosyntax .
Frequency data from the Hokkaido corpus show the suffix active in only a small set of forms.
The token ipeyar returns approximately 2 hits (rank 14,619), making it marginal; nuyar is more frequent but the absolute total remains small ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The distribution reflects lexicalized or semi-lexicalized combinations rather than productive attachment across the verb lexicon .
nu-yar's higher frequency follows from its speech-act function.

The indefinite-causee structure is suited to public announcement: a causer who makes something known without restricting who will receive the information has systematic recourse to this form wherever the open recipient set is the point.
The permissive-polite use — ipe-yar=an ro 'let's have the guest eat' — is attested but at low frequency ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Ijäs's learner grammar does not treat -yar; Lesson 9 on special verb forms discusses the causative, reciprocal, and antipassive but covers only -re among the causative types .
Several questions are unanswered in the sources consulted.
Bugaeva's 387-verb Saru causative study — the most comprehensive available — excludes -yar for reasons of space .

No source in the present corpus offers a distributional account of which verb classes the suffix selects, what semantic or pragmatic factors predict the choice between -yar and -re/-te/-e on the same base, or how the suffix patterns dialectally outside Saru.
The structural facts — arity 0, causee unexpressed, or peka/or un/eun adjunct option for the implied agent — are consistent across the four sources that address the suffix ; ; ; .
The semantic label — whether indefinite, permissive, or sociative causation best characterises the suffix — remains open ‹contested›.

One diachronic proposal treats -yar as descending from a pronominal-causative construction *i=a-de, with regular intervocalic *d > r; the zero-valency outcome would follow from the prior grammaticalization of the indefinite causee pronoun into the verb complex, parallel to how the meaning of i=…-re semantically overlaps with that of -yar (; antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, 26 May 2026) ‹speculative›.
No peer-reviewed source develops this account.

The three prefixes , , and are valency-increasing derivational morphemes that promote a semantically peripheral participant to the status of a direct object, in the sense established for applicative constructions cross-linguistically ; ; .

In Ainu, object status means appearing as a bare noun phrase in the argument frame of a transitive or ditransitive verb; there is no case marking by which objecthood can be read off the noun itself, so the test is transitivity and the agreement prefix the verb licenses ; .

Each of the three applicatives raises arity by one: an intransitive base (vi, one argument) becomes a transitive (vt, two arguments), and a transitive base becomes a ditransitive (vd, three arguments) ; .

The person-marking diagnostics of the valency system expose this arity shift: a derived intransitive takes the suffixal S indexes =as and =an, while a derived transitive or ditransitive takes the prefixal A indexes ci= and a= ; .
The applied object's semantic range is broader than the canonical benefactive or instrumental applicative found in many languages.

Bugaeva's corpus study of Chitose and Saru applicatives maps the three prefixes onto instruments, locations, goals, comitatives, benefactives, malefactives, recipients, sources, themes, content, causes, paths, and purposes .

Nakagawa's heading 充当接頭辞 gives the core paraphrases as 〜について・〜で以て・〜〈場所〉で (about / by means of / at a place) for e-, and 〜に向かって・〜とともに (toward / together with) for ko-, with o- restricted to 〜〈場所〉へ (toward a place) ; .
The sources do not slice this space identically.
Satō's summary groups 手段・着点・場所 (means, goal, location) under e- and o- together and gives ko- as 方向・手段 (direction, means) — extending the instrumental sense to ko- as well .
Bugaeva's corpus tables place Means-Instrument with e- (13% of its uses) and record no instrument class for ko- ; the divergence is one of classification granularity rather than of data.

The lexical frequency order is ko- > e- > o- .
o- is rare in prose and confined largely to verse; Satō similarly marks it uncommon in his pedagogical treatment ; .
Bugaeva's (2006) role classification of the Chitose/Saru corpus sample yields two findings that bear on typological interpretation .
First, the most frequent role added by e- is Content (39%), followed by Theme-Patient (17%); only at third place do instrument and locative roles appear.

Second, 75–96% of e- applied objects across roles derive from intransitive bases, meaning the applicative is introducing a new core object rather than re-encoding a participant that already had an object-like coding .
These figures reflect a typological property: most Ainu applicatives are obligatory rather than promotional.

In the canonical promotional type, an oblique participant has a postpositional paraphrase that the applicative replaces optionally; in Ainu, the majority of applied objects — especially the Content class of e- — have no independent postpositional frame, so the applicative construction is the only coding available.
Bugaeva calls the Content-adding use of e- the most productive class and 'very typical in its atypicality' precisely because it sits outside the promotional prototype ; .
The cross-linguistic placement of Ainu in applicative typology, drawing on Bugaeva's 2010 comparative study, is taken up in the per-prefix chapters.

For ko-, Addressee (20%), Goal (19%), Comitative (18%), and Benefactive (18%) together account for three-quarters of applied-object tokens; Source and Recipient each contribute 5%, with the remainder across Cause, Range, and Location .
The o- distribution is narrowest: locative roles (Goal-into-place 57%, Location 29%, Source/Theme 14%) cover all attested instances, all paraphrasable by ta / un 'at/to' .
The role percentages are from a single corpus sample and serve as approximations; no pan-Hokkaido frequency study has been conducted ‹corpus-suggested›.
Nakagawa distinguishes four subtypes of e- by the relationship between the applied object and its postpositional paraphrase, where one exists .
The classification is reproduced here because it identifies which uses are promotional (subtypes 1–2) and which are obligatory (subtypes 3–4); full analysis and corpus examples are in .
Subtype (3) is where e- functions as a non-causative transitivizer adding a core Theme or Content object with no other syntactic route.
The derivation → e-ikka 'steal something (vt)' → ko-e-ikka 'steal something from someone (vd)' illustrates the Content-adding step followed by a second applicative layer .

A community-proposed etymology for illustrates the Content / Theme-adding function in a compound form: the verb may derive from e- applicativizing the locative predicate ka un 'be above' → eykaun 'surpass something', with a parallel -u transitivizer yielding the doublet kaunu (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024) .
The proposal is consistent with the range of e-'s Content / Theme uses, but the lexical history has not been established in the peer-reviewed literature ‹speculative›.
ko- covers the roles associated with an animate or non-spatial goal: Addressee, Goal, Comitative, Benefactive, Malefactive, Recipient, and Source are all represented in Bugaeva's sample ; .
The diagnostic contrast with o- is the type of goal argument: ko- preferentially takes person or animal goals, while o- is restricted to place nouns ; .

A community-proposed analysis of illustrates a less common behavior: the form ku=sir-ko-peker may represent ko- inserted inside the compound intransitive sir-peker 'the sky brightens', with the applied object (first person 'I') raised to subject of the whole derived verb, yielding 'I pass the night' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024) .
This object-to-subject raising analysis is not directly addressed in the accessible peer-reviewed sources and is offered as a community-proposed reading of an opaque form ‹speculative›.
Two applicatives may combine on a single verb.
The most attested pairing is ko-e- or e-ko-, where each prefix encodes an independent applied object: e-ko-isoytak 'tell stories about something (e-) to someone (ko-)'.

Bugaeva and Kobayashi report no visible semantic difference between the two prefix orders in this combination, and Nakagawa gives e-yay-e-isoytak as a further expansion that inserts the reflexive yay- between the two applicatives, treating the whole as one word ; .

The arity ceiling on double applicatives follows from the two-person-affix cap: a verb may carry at most one subject index and one object index, so a third applied object is unindexable without compensatory intransitivization ; .

The Handbook illustrates the compensatory strategy in yay-ipe-e-ko-sunke 'eat meagre meals', where three applied-object positions are successively reduced — one object incorporated (ipe 'food'), one reflexivized (yay-) .
The full range of applicative–reflexive and applicative–causative stacking is in .

Across the lexicon, the applicatives are pervasive: Bugaeva estimates roughly one-third of all verbs are applicative-derived, amounting to up to 7% of the entire Ainu lexicon, and characterizes them as 'productive, ubiquitous, and versatile' .

The prefixes attach to almost every verb class, with the exception of meteorological, bodily-process, and certain change-of-state verbs at one extreme of the transitivity hierarchy and effective-action verbs at the other .
Ijäs's learner grammar surveys transitive and derived forms but does not extend to the applicative prefixes in the banked lessons; the pedagogical description is in Satō's Lesson 31 ; .
A further structural consequence of the applicative system is its role in enabling noun incorporation.
Oblique nouns — instruments and locations — cannot incorporate directly: an applicative must first promote them to object status, and only the derived object then incorporates into the verb word ; .

A verb-noun sequence bearing an applicative prefix is therefore a reliable sign that incorporation has occurred: o-tumi-osma (with o-) is unambiguously incorporated, while bare tumi osma is ambiguous .

When incorporation takes place, the applicative carries the postpositional meaning that would otherwise be expressed by a separate postposition: at-e-uk 'catch with a net' (= at ani uk), pira-ko-hokus-te 'fall toward a cliff' (= pira or un hokuste) .

Shibatani (1990) demonstrates that Baker's Case-theoretic prediction — that unaccusative bases are blocked from applicative formation — is falsified in Ainu, which does applicativize unaccusatives ; .
Kaiser (1998) examines the morphological properties of this interaction in detail ; the treatment is continued in and .
Three surface forms shared with the applicative prefixes carry different arity values and require disambiguation by context and argument counting.

Applicative e- (+1) has two homophonous companions: the affiliative e- 'the head/end of' (arity 0), which fills a part slot on the object while requiring a separate possessor, leaving net arity unchanged; and the second-person subject index e=, a person affix rather than a derivational prefix ; .
The lexical body-region prefix he- 'head' (arity −1) provides a further contrast, filling the object slot with the subject's own head region.
The Chitose pair he-puni 'lift one's own head (vi, −1)' against e-puni 'lift someone's head (vt, +1)' separates applicative from lexical prefix by the person-suffix test .
Applicative o- (+1) has a parallel affiliative twin o- 'the bottom/base of' (arity 0).
None of these can be glossed without first computing the arity.
The full homophony set is in ; the affiliative morphology is in .
The applicative category was recognized early in Ainu grammaticology.
Kindaichi and Chiri (1936) named it 充当相 (applicative voice); Nakagawa notes alongside it Chiri's earlier label 格の関係を表わす接頭辞 (prefixes expressing case relations) ; .

The typological rarity of productive applicatives as a grammatical system in Eurasian languages — closest parallels in certain Caucasian languages and Burushaski — was already remarked upon in this early literature and confirmed by Bugaeva's later cross-linguistic survey ; .
The modern English term 'applicative' and the object-promotion analysis of e-, ko-, and o- are established in Bugaeva (2006, 2010) and consolidated in the Handbook ; ; .
Nakagawa's own term 充当接頭辞 follows the same analysis .

Baker's (1988) P-incorporation theory treats applicative formation as preposition/postposition incorporation into the verb, promoting its complement to object; Shibatani (1990) applies this framing to the Ainu data, and its most direct analytical consequence is the feeding-relation account above ; .

The older 'case-relation prefix' terminology and the 'preverb' framing encountered for cognate categories in some other languages do not figure as active analytical positions in the recent Ainu literature: Bugaeva (2006), the Handbook, Nakagawa (2024), and Satō (2008) adopt the applicative analysis consistently, and the terminological variation reflects a historical shift in descriptive vocabulary rather than a substantive analytical disagreement among the current sources ; ‹consensus›.
The prefix e- belongs to the applicative series together with and .
An overview of all three and their place in the valency architecture is given in .

Its function is to add one participant to the verb's argument set: an intransitive becomes transitive and a transitive becomes a double-object verb, consistently raising arity by one regardless of the semantic role of the added argument ; .
The valency-class diagnostic of confirms the change: after e- attaches to an intransitive, the verb takes the prefixal agent indexes ci= and a= and resists the intransitive S suffixes .
Positionally, e- occupies the slot between the outer person prefix and the root: person — applicative — root — forming-suffix — causative-suffix — suffixal-person .

The prefix and root together form a single accentual unit; Nakagawa analyses the applicative-plus-verb sequence as one word for prosodic purposes, a pattern the community archive documents with forms such as kotán → ekótanne (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024) ; ‹consensus›.

Among the three applicatives, ko- is the most frequent, followed by e- and then o-; by Bugaeva's estimate, applicative-derived verbs account for roughly one-third of all Ainu verbs and up to seven percent of the total lexicon .
The instrument sub-type (see §2 below) offers the most direct illustration of the +1 arity effect.
The verb is transitive in its base form and takes one object (the thing cut); e-tuye raises it to a three-place verb whose new object position is occupied by the cutting instrument.

The derivational chain → e-ikka 'steal something' → ko-e-ikka 'steal something from someone' illustrates successive applicativization: each step adds one argument .

Bugaeva draws a typological inference from these data: most Ainu e- applicatives are the only grammatical means of expressing a given participant relation, so they are obligatory in the sense that the cross-linguistic option of an adpositional alternative simply does not exist .
The Peterson typology of applicative constructions provides the comparative frame for this characterization .

A periphrastic pattern complementary to the morphological applicative exists for the instrumental reading: the construction ani X p ('the thing with which one does X') expresses instrumentality as a nominalization rather than through the e- prefix — for example, ani e=kanpinuye p 'a thing with which one writes' (= pencil) or ani humi a=aste p 'a thing with which one produces sound' (= musical instrument; nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2026) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The two constructions serve different functions: the morphological applicative frames the instrument inside the verbal predicate; the ani ... p nominalization names the instrument as a noun.

Three homophonous prefixes occupy the same surface slot and require the arity computation for disambiguation: the applicative e- (+1), the affiliative e- 'head of' (0), which fills a body-part position while retaining its own possessor, and the second-person agent index e= (a person index, effective −1 on the available slots) ; .
The minimal contrast between the applicative and the affiliative — he-puni 'lift one's own head' versus e-puni 'lift someone's head' — is set out in .
Many verbs carry a lexicalized e- whose applicative analysis is opaque in current usage.
A community-proposed decomposition treats as applicative e- applied to kaun derived from the postpositional phrase ka un 'be on top of' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024) ‹speculative›.
The etymology is semantically motivated but cannot be verified against the diachronic record from the sources consulted; synchronically, eykaun functions as a transitive base.

The analytical question of whether some e- forms are better described as lexical preverbs (case-relation prefixes) than as applicatives in the cross-linguistic sense is not engaged by the principal sources consulted.

Bugaeva treats all three markers as applicatives throughout and positions the older labels — 充当相 (Kindaichi and Chiri 1936) and case-prefix 格の関係を表わす接頭辞 (Chiri 1942) — as historical precursors rather than competing analyses ; .
Baker's incorporation analysis, which treats applicative formation as P-incorporation in the syntax, is the nearest theoretical alternative present in the literature consulted ; ‹contested›.
A dedicated assessment appears in .
e- stacks freely with ko- in both orders, ko-e- and e-ko-, with no documented meaning difference between the two sequences on the same verb type.
In , e- contributes the Content applied object (the stories told) and ko- the Addressee (the person addressed) ; .
The ordering constraints on stacked applicatives and their interaction with reflexive and reciprocal morphology are developed in .
e- may apply to a verb that has already been antipassivized with , restoring transitivity while the antipassive's absorbed participant remains unexpressed.
The compound illustrates this: i-kasuy 'do helping' is intransitive (the beneficiaries absorbed by i-), and e- re-applicativizes it to take a Content object encoding the nature of the help.
The +1 arity effect of e- also opens the path to oblique noun incorporation.

Instruments, locations, and purpose arguments cannot incorporate directly, because they are adjuncts, not core arguments; once e- promotes them to object status, the derived object becomes incorporable.
Shibatani formulates the dependency as a general condition: oblique incorporation in Ainu is invariably mediated by a prior applicative ; .
The incorporated forms at-e-uk 'catch with a net' (instrument; cf.
at ani uk) and turepta-e-arpa 'go to dig lily-bulbs' (purpose) both rest on the same e- applicativization illustrated above.
Kaiser's analysis of the applicative-incorporation interaction provides a formal account of the feeding relation .
The incorporation patterns that result are treated in and .
The prefix adds a participant — typically a goal, recipient, addressee, or comitative partner — to the argument frame of the verb as a new core object, raising arity by one ; .
On a one-place intransitive base the derived verb is transitive; on a two-place transitive the result is a three-place double-object verb.

The applied object enters the object slot and may be cross-referenced by the object-series person prefix — the operative arity diagnostic described in the valency overview and grounded in the applicative system.
Among the three applicative prefixes of Hokkaido Ainu, ko- is the most frequent.

Bugaeva's Saru and Chitose corpus places the order ko- > e- > o- by token frequency; taken together, applicative verbs account for roughly one-third of all verbs and up to seven percent of the entire Ainu lexicon .

Nakagawa characterizes the applied object as 〜に向かって (directed toward) or 〜とともに (together with), two senses that correspond to the Goal / Addressee cluster and the Comitative cluster in Bugaeva's role classification .
