Each percentage is the share of ko- tokens in which the applied object bears that role; the intr/tr column records the proportion derived from an intransitive vs transitive base verb.
The four largest categories — Addressee, Goal, Comitative, and Benefactive — account for roughly three-quarters of all uses.
All four share a common structural denominator: the applied object is an entity the action is directed toward or performed alongside.

For the Comitative role, where the postposition tura 'together with' offers a paraphrase, the applicative construction promotes the companion to the object slot and makes it indexable by the object person-prefix .
For most other roles no regular oblique paraphrase exists and the applicative is the only means of encoding the relationship.

The Recipient and Source categories (5% each) stand out for their predominantly transitive base verbs (66%), a profile consistent with transfer and extraction verbs rather than the one-place motion verbs that feed the Goal uses (95% intransitive base) .

A lexical instance of the Source use is ko-nu 'hear/ask something from someone', where ko- adds the Source participant to two-place nu 'hear', alongside the oblique alternatives wa (ablative) and eun .
With motion verbs, ko- licenses the physical or spatial goal as the new core object.
yields (example above) and yields ; in both cases the base intransitive takes S-series suffixes while the derived transitive takes A-series prefixes.
With speech and emotion verbs the applied object is an Addressee — the person to whom an utterance or attitude is directed.
The pair versus makes the semantic split explicit: ko- takes the human target of the gratitude (Addressee), e- takes the content — the thing one is thankful for — both with the same base ; .
The Saru corpus attests ko-yayirayke with a person-deity as applied object:
When the applied object is a comitative participant — one who acts jointly with the subject — ko- corresponds to the postpositional adjunct tura 'together with'.
The applicative construction promotes the companion to an indexable object position, which the adjunct cannot do.
This function interacts productively with noun incorporation: when the comitative applied object is incorporated, it merges with ko- inside the verb word, and the verb returns to intransitive arity.
Nakagawa gives a Chitose example in which two comitative participants are incorporated in parallel constructions:
Benefactive uses (18%) cover contexts in which the applied object's interests are served by the action, with an approximately even split across intransitive and transitive base verbs.

At their boundary the Malefactive category (6%) shades into adversative uses: the applied object is the entity against whose interest the action runs, most commonly derived from intransitive bases (86%), consistent with the pattern of adding a new human object to a one-place activity verb .

Both ko- and can encode a directional Goal, and the primary distributional division concerns the applied object's reference type: o- takes place nouns, ko- takes persons, animals, and more abstract directional targets .
Nakagawa provides a near-minimal pair with the same intransitive base :

The o- applicative is restricted to place-denoting applied objects; ko- extends to persons and, as the opening kohopuni example shows, to spatial targets that function as directional goals without being named place nouns in the strict sense (kanto kotor 'sky-vicinity').
The o- applicative is considerably rarer across Hokkaido dialects and is largely confined to verse register ; its distribution and relationship to the spatial noun o(r)- are treated in .
Because ko- raises arity by one, it feeds and is fed by other valency operations in a regular derivational calculus.

The chain built on illustrates eight consecutive derivations: ruska (vt, +2) → ko-ruska (vd, +3; adds a person-target of anger) → yay-ko-ruska (vt, +2; reflexive fills the object slot) → i-ruska (vi, +1; antipassive) → ko-i-ruska (vt, +2; ko- re-applicativizes the antipassivized verb) → si-ko-i-ruska (vi, +1) → i-ruska-re (vt) → ko-i-ruska-re (vd) (citing ).

The step i-ruska → ko-i-ruska is particularly revealing: ko- restores a goal participant that the antipassive i- had absorbed, returning the verb to transitive; the A-series prefix confirms the derived transitivity:
ko- also stacks with the e- applicative.

When both prefixes appear on the same verb, e- adds its Content or Instrument applied object and ko- adds its Addressee or Recipient applied object; the orders ko-e- and e-ko- are both attested with no reported semantic difference ; .
The speech verb is the standard illustration: e-ko-isoytak is a three-place frame in which e- encodes the topic narrated and ko- the listener:

A sequential applicativisation of the same type underlies : base ikka 'steal (vi)' → e-ikka 'steal something (vt, e- adds the stolen item)' → ko-e-ikka 'steal something from someone (vd, ko- adds the Source)' .
Here the ko- applied object bears the Source role (the person stolen from), one of the Table 1 categories in which the transitive base (64%) predominates, as this chain confirms.
The learner grammar of includes ekoyayirayke among its ditransitive examples (Lesson 3).
The form parses as e-ko-yay-irayke: e- adds the thing one is grateful for, ko- adds the person being thanked, and yay- is the direct-reflexive prefix on the base irayke 'thank'.

Ijäs's VD label captures the three-place output but does not expose the derivational layering; her example sentences are constructed and the morphological decomposition is spelled out here following .
For the i--containing members of the chain, see .
Many verb stems containing ko- have undergone lexicalization, with internal structure that ranges from fully transparent to opaque.

The form has been proposed as ko- + sirepa, where sirepa itself decomposes as sir-epa (environment + e-applicative + root pa 'go'), giving an original sense of directed motion toward one's surroundings (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-14) ‹contested›.

The Chitose compound kotan-kosirepa=an 'one arrives at the village' incorporates kotan 'village' as the ko- applied object; the fourth-person S-series suffix =an proves that the incorporation has reduced arity back to one place.

The phrasal counterpart kotan a=kosirepa keeps kotan as a separate transitive object under the A-series prefix a=, and together the two forms supply the person-affix word-hood diagnostic (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-14) ‹contested›.

A community-proposed etymology identifies as ko- + pan, with pan a deverbal form of pa 'mouth'; the semantic drift toward 'distasteful, taboo' is then tied to the later ko-kopan and the related sir-pan (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-11) ‹speculative›.
The synchronic meaning of kopan 'dislike' does not transparently reflect the proposed compositional structure, and the analysis remains unverified against the primary lexicographic literature.
A grammatically more consequential pattern involves ko- appearing within a natural-force verb stem.

The Chitose form ku=sir-ko-peker 'I stayed up until dawn' has been parsed as an instance of ko- interpolated into the otherwise closed sir-peker compound (weather-brighten), with its applied object (the speaker, indexed by ku=) raised to clause subject (nukopoli, citing Satō, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-05) ‹contested›.
Parallel formations maw-ko-wen and kur-ko-tunas are proposed under the same structural type.

If the analysis is correct, ko- here operates inside a lexicalized natural-force compound rather than prefixing to it as a whole — a pattern that would distinguish this use from ordinary derivational stacking and that is not addressed in the primary grammatical literature.
The prefix belongs to the applicative series together with and ; an overview of all three and their place in the arity calculus is given in .

Its function is to promote a place-denoting noun into the verb's argument set as a direct object, raising arity by one: a base intransitive becomes transitive and a base transitive becomes a ditransitive ; .
The applied object of o- is always a spatial noun — a goal, a location, or a source — never an animate participant, which separates it from ko- ; .
Bugaeva's corpus study of the Chitose and Saru dialects supplies a role breakdown for the applied objects of o- .
All three categories resolve to postpositional expressions in ta 'at/to' or or un 'into', making o- the only applicative whose applied object is consistently paraphrasable by a locative postposition.
The intr-base column records how many forms in each role class derive from an intransitive base.
The role figures are drawn from a single Chitose/Saru corpus sample; no pan-Hokkaido frequency study has been conducted ‹corpus-suggested›.

They are consistent with the claim, made by Nakagawa on the basis of text distributions, that o- is the rarest of the three applicatives and occurs predominantly in verse rather than prose or conversational registers ; .
Bugaeva's lexical frequency order is ko- > e- > o- .

The register observation is older than either treatment: Fukuda already set o- aside as frequent in 伝承文学や歌 (oral literature and song) but rare in conversation, surviving there only in a handful of 化石化した形式 (fossilized forms) .

The Source row of the table has lexicographic backing in Nakagawa's own dictionary: the entry for the prefix gives 〜〈場所〉へ・〜〈場所〉に・〜〈場所〉から (to / at / from a place), interchangeable with the postposition un .

The ablative から sense is thus registered by Nakagawa himself, against the narrower goal-and-location-only formulation that Bugaeva reports from his earlier work ; the place restriction is unaffected — all three senses take place nouns only.
The restriction of o-'s applied object to place nouns gives rise to a minimal contrast with ko- that is most sharply illustrated by the two applicatives on the same base verb.
With , the difference in applied object type triggers the choice of prefix: the place goal takes o-, the animate goal takes ko- ; .
The full minimal pair and its analytical discussion are in .
The same pattern holds for other motion verbs.
Adding o- to yields o-arpa 'go to [a place]', a derived transitive whose place-goal applied object is paraphrasable as X or un arpa 'go toward X (a place)' or X ta arpa 'go to X' .
The prefixal A index confirms the arity shift to transitive:

Within the attested inventory, a set of motion-verb derivatives stand as effectively lexicalized transitive verbs: , , and are all derived by o- applicativization of the corresponding intransitive base and carry a stable spatial-goal reading.

Their frequency in verse texts is higher than the productive applicative uses; Nakagawa's observation that o- is a 'mostly verse' prefix reflects this asymmetry rather than a blanket restriction on productive application .
A community-proposed morphological analysis illustrates the o- prefix in a lexicalized nominal form.

The noun is analyzed as a=o-ipe-p, in which the fourth-person agent a=, the applicative o-, the verb , and the agent nominalizer -p combine to yield 'the thing one eats from / into which one eats' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, December 2024) .
In this reading, o- promotes the container from a locative adjunct to the direct object of ipe, and the whole applicative clause is then nominalized to name the vessel.

Tamura's Saru dictionary enters aoypep 'food vessel' without morphological decomposition ; the proposed analysis is consistent with the semantic range of o- but is not established in the peer-reviewed sources ‹contested›.
Three distinct elements share the surface form o- and require the arity computation for disambiguation.
The applicative prefix o- adds one argument (arity +1).
The affiliative o- 'the bottom/base of' (arity 0) fills a body-part slot while retaining its own possessor, leaving net valency unchanged; the full homophony set is discussed in .

The third element is the lexical verb , which is already a two-argument form in its base: the theme (the thing moved or placed) fills the A index position and the destination place fills the O index position .

Ijäs describes o / oma as a 'special locative-transitive' in which the subject is the thing placed and the object is the place, and identifies the causative form as the means of adding an external putter to the argument frame ‹consensus›.

Nakagawa's analysis agrees: omare (= oma-re) is a three-argument ditransitive derived from the two-argument base by the productive causative suffix -re, which promotes the theme argument to object and introduces the agent as the new subject .
The corpus attests the base verb o with a place-denoting direct object:
A community-proposed etymology treats the alternant as oma-n, where -n is an intransitivizing suffix parallel to other motion-verb formations (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, May 2026) .
The proposal connects oman to the base form o and is consistent with the known -n / -p alternations on motion verbs, but it has not been assessed in the peer-reviewed literature ‹speculative›.

The practical disambiguation test is the arity read-off: if an intransitive base acquires a prefixal A index after a preceding o--shaped element, the element is the applicative (+1); if the verb is already two-argument in its base form and the o-initial sequence is the whole predicate, the element is the verb root; if arity is unchanged and the associated noun is a possessively construed body-part, the element is the affiliative (0) ; .
Oblique place nouns cannot incorporate into the verb word directly; an applicative must first promote them to object status, and the derived object then becomes incorporable.
For spatial goals and locations, o- performs this promotion.

Shibatani's word-hood test shows the result: o-tumi-osma is unambiguously one incorporated word, because the applicative prefix could not attach to a bare noun, while tumi osma 'the war began' is structurally ambiguous between a phrasal and an incorporated reading .
The Mirror Principle ordering places the applicative inside and the incorporated noun outside, mirroring the syntactic derivation .
The interaction between applicatives and noun incorporation is developed in and in .

A set of spatial verbs that independently select a place noun as a core object — including and — presents cases where the applicative and causative morphology interact with the verb's spatial argument structure.

Kobayashi (2020) examines these interactions for otke and kamu specifically and argues that the argument-structural properties of the place-denoting participant determine which valency-increasing operation is available .
These verbs and the broader spatial valency alternations are taken up in .
Two feeding relations connect the applicative prefixes to other grammatical operations of the verb word.

Oblique nominals — instrumentals, locatives, goals, purpose arguments — cannot incorporate directly into the verb; an applicative prefix must first promote the oblique to core-object status, after which incorporation can proceed ; ; .

Bare obliques are equally inaccessible to the prenominal gap strategy that Hokkaido Ainu uses in relative clauses; applicative promotion again opens the relativization path by moving the nominal to the direct-object tier of the accessibility hierarchy ; ; .
Both relations turn on the same structural shift: from a postposition-marked peripheral role to an unmarked core object whose position is targetable by later grammatical operations ‹speculative›.
This synthesis — grounded in the convergent evidence of Shibatani (1990), Nakagawa (2024), Kaiser (1998), and Dal Corso (2020) on the promotion logic — is a proposal original to this grammar.

The chapter also treats applicative stacking — the co-occurrence of two applicative prefixes on one verb — together with the two feeding relations, since stacking creates the complex valency frames in which both paths may apply simultaneously.
The individual prefixes , , and are treated in , , and the system as a whole in .
Up to two applicative prefixes appear on one verb simultaneously, each raising arity by one ; .
The most productive double-applicative patterns pair e- (Content, Instrument, Location, Purpose) with ko- (Addressee, Goal, Comitative), in either order — e-ko- or ko-e-.
Bugaeva and Kobayashi report no visible semantic difference between the two orders; in both, e- contributes a Content or Instrument object and ko- an Addressee or Goal ‹contested›.
Nakagawa places applicative prefixes in the single slot immediately inside the person index and before the root, so whether order encodes any semantic scope remains open ‹speculative›.
With , the double applicative yields a three-place frame — an Addressee (ko-) and a Content argument (e-) alongside the base Agent:

The example documented by Shibatani — attributed to Chiri (1936: 169) — combines two applicatives with one reflexive proper, one reflexive-possessive prefix, an adverbial element, and an incorporated object on a single root:

Bugaeva and Kobayashi's second example demonstrates re-intransitivization through stacking: a frame extended by two applicatives is collapsed back to bivalent by incorporating one applied object and reflexivizing the other :
A text-attested case of comitative incorporation via ko- is visible in the following Chitose passage, where the comitative objects are incorporated in sequence with their respective verbs:
The wordhood diagnostic in establishes that only core objects — nominals that stand in the argument position targeted by the outermost person index — can incorporate into the verb word.
A nominal held in a postpositional phrase (, , ) has no such position and cannot incorporate.
The applicative removes the postposition and assigns the nominal core-object status; incorporation then proceeds.
Nakagawa gives three parallel derivations :
The same three-step derivation is spelled out in Shibatani's analysis of a comitative-instrument example :
The affix order in Stage 3 instantiates Baker's Mirror Principle : the morphological order mirrors the syntactic derivation because applicative formation precedes incorporation.

Shibatani extends this logic to a wordhood diagnostic: the presence of an applicative prefix on a noun-verb sequence that is otherwise ambiguous between NI and a phrasal reading resolves it unambiguously as incorporation .
The form tumi osma 'war began' is ambiguous, but o-tumi-osma with the locative applicative o- is unambiguously an incorporated word.

Several forms in Chiri (1936: 93) place the incorporated noun before rather than after the applicative — o-ni-pici alternating with ni o-pici 'fall from a tree' — in apparent violation of mirror ordering.
Shibatani calls this a "minor irregularity" without resolving it ‹corpus-suggested›.
Baker's Case-theoretic prediction that applicative formation (P-incorporation) should be impossible on unaccusative bases is falsified by Ainu ; ; .
Verbs such as mokor 'sleep' freely combine with e- (mokor a=e-wen 'I missed sleeping'; sake a=e-niste 'I am strong at wine'), contrary to Case-theory's expectation ‹contested›.

The implication for the feeding chain is that an oblique associated with an intransitive base can be promoted and subsequently incorporated or relativized by the same mechanism as one associated with a transitive base.
Hokkaido Ainu relative clauses are prenominal and gap-based: the modifying clause precedes the head noun and leaves a null gap in the position the head noun would otherwise occupy within the clause.
Subject and direct-object gaps are both accessible to this strategy ‹corpus-confirmed›; see for the full construction.

A nominal in an oblique role — held by a postposition — lies outside the reach of gap-formation: Ainu has no mechanism for stranding a postposition in situ while extracting its complement as a relative-clause head ; .
Applicative promotion removes the postposition and places the nominal at the direct-object tier, where gap-formation is licensed.
The applied object then stands in a relativization-accessible position, and a prenominal relative clause can be formed with that applied object as its head ; .
The following constructed example illustrates the pattern, based on the instrument applicative e-tuye attested in Nakagawa 2024: 194 (ex. 173):
The same promotion operates with ko-.
A Goal or Addressee that would appear with un 'to' or tura 'with' can head a relative clause built on a ko--derived predicate.

Dal Corso documents the construction for Southern Hokkaido texts and finds that applied objects — regardless of which prefix produced them — pattern identically to base transitive objects in gap-formation ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The Keenan–Comrie hierarchy frames the typological significance: Subject > Direct Object > Indirect Object > Oblique > Genitive > Comparee .
Hokkaido Ainu relativization is robustly accessible at Subject and Direct Object; bare Oblique is inaccessible; the applicative closes the gap by importing the oblique into the Direct Object tier.

Kaiser (1998) demonstrates that the resulting applied object is treated as a morphosyntactic direct object in the relative clause — there is no distinct 'applied-object relativization' mechanism separate from ordinary object relativization .
The synthesis that a single structural promotion underlies both the NI-feeding and the relativization-feeding paths is a proposal original to this grammar ‹speculative›.
What grammatical relation the promoted nominal bears — and therefore where it sits on the accessibility hierarchy — is contested between two broad analytical traditions .
A relational account assigns the promoted nominal the relation of direct object from the moment of applicative formation.
The applied object inherits full direct-object properties, including gap-licensability and incorporability, and stands at the Object tier of the hierarchy.

The primary supporting evidence is morphosyntactic: Ainu marks no case distinction between the base Patient-object and the applied object of a ditransitive — both appear as bare NPs, both are cross-referenced by the single O-index on the verb ; .
Without a formal difference between the two objects, assigning them to distinct tiers of the hierarchy lacks morphosyntactic grounding.
Baker's (1988) head-movement account treats the applicative as P-incorporation: the postposition moves into the verb, leaving its complement in a derived specifier position.
The applied object's accessibility to gap-formation and incorporation would then be a secondary consequence of that specifier position — not a primitive direct-object property .

Shibatani identifies the applicativization of intransitive bases in Ainu as a direct refutation: Baker's Case-theory predicts this should be impossible, yet it is productive in Hokkaido Ainu ; ‹contested›.
A community observation reported in the aynu-corpora Discord is consistent with the relational account.

The verb sir-ko-peker 'spend the night' — where ko- interrupts the derivationally closed stem sir-peker — has been analysed (attributed to Satō, reported by nukopoli, 2024-12-05 ) as a construction in which the ko--object is promoted to the grammatical subject of the whole predicate: ku=sir-ko-peker 'I spend the night' has the experiencer — originally the applied object — in the subject index position.
Parallel forms maw-ko-wen and kur-ko-tunas are noted in the same discussion.

If the ko--object can reach the subject position in closed-stem environments, promotion to direct object in open-stem environments is the weaker operation — collateral support for the relational account ‹contested›.
For double-applicative verbs, both applied objects are morphosyntactically equivalent (bare NPs, single O-index), and both are in principle accessible to gap-formation or incorporation individually.
Whether both can independently head distinct relative clauses within a complex sentence has not been investigated in the sources consulted ‹speculative›.
The verb word accommodates at most two person indexes — one A-type and one O-type — so the ceiling on simultaneously indexed participants is two, regardless of how many applicatives stack ; ; .
Extra applied objects must be reabsorbed by reflexivization ( / ), incorporation, or antipassivization before the verb is finalized.
The yay-ipe-e-ko-sunke example above instantiates two reabsorption strategies on one verb.

Bugaeva's (2014 abstract) characterization of Ainu as polysynthetic in Baker's sense — with the caveat that it departs from the Mohawk prototype in word order, in-situ wh, and unrestricted morphological causatives — places this stacking capacity in typological perspective .
The feeding chain can extend across multiple derivational steps.

Antipassive i- reduces a transitive to intransitive by absorbing the object slot with a generic argument; re-adding an applicative restores transitive valency with a new object, which is then accessible to further incorporation or relativization by the same logic as any other applied object ; :

The chained sequence — applicative, then antipassive, then re-applicativization, then relativization or incorporation — is bounded only by the template order (person index | nominal/applicative | root | forming suffix | causative | person index; ) and the two-slot ceiling.

Each step in the chain either adds a slot (applicative, causative) or removes one (antipassive, reflexive, incorporation), and the feeding paths are open whenever the net result is a nominal standing at the direct-object tier ‹contested›.

Ijäs's Basic Lessons 3 and 9 do not cover applicative stacking or the feeding relations; the lessons treat i- and -re as independent operations without addressing their combination with applicatives or with relativization .

The learner grammar's entry point — applicatives as independent valency-raisers — is the correct starting place, with the stacking behavior and its downstream interactions belonging to advanced grammar.
The prefix occupies the object position of a transitive verb with a semantically generic 'thing, someone, people', reducing the verb's arity by one and rendering it intransitive.
In Nakagawa's arity calculus the operation is a standard −1 step: a two-place transitive yields a one-place intransitive, and a three-place ditransitive yields a two-place transitive ; .
The resulting intransitive takes suffixal S indexes — =as (1PL.EXCL.S) and =an (4.S) — where the base transitive had taken prefixal A indexes such as ci= and a=.
This person-affix shift is the single operative diagnostic for the detransitivization ; .
The place of the operation in the wider valency system is set out in .
The prefix sits immediately before the verb root, inside the person-index layer.

Under Nakagawa's position-class template it occupies the same slot as the other valency-decreasing prefixes yay-, si-, and u-, and it combines freely with applicatives outside it and causative suffixes after the stem: ko-i-ruska (APPL-ANTIP-be.angry at), a re-transitivized applicative of the antipassive i-ruska 'be angry', is well-formed, and so is the further reflexivized si-ko-i-ruska .

The derivational chain ruska (vt) → i-ruska (vi) → ko-i-ruska (vt) → si-ko-i-ruska (vi) → i-ruska-re (vt, 'make sb angry') → ko-i-ruska-re (vd) shows that i- is not a terminal derivation but a mid-chain element and that the arity bookkeeping remains coherent at every step .
In the corpus, iruska 'be angry' appears 655 times (rank 264), making it among the most frequent antipassive derivatives ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The antipassive is productive across a restricted range of semantic classes.

Bugaeva, working from Nakagawa's corpus, identifies 48 verbal lexemes that form antipassive derivatives, concentrated in Perception/Cognition, Ingesting, Interaction, Communication, Grooming, and Traditional-Activity verbs .

Absent from the set are Creation, Transformation, and Contact-by-Impact verbs — a distribution consistent with the typological generalization that antipassives in non-ergative languages preferentially target low-transitivity predicates ‹contested›.
Many antipassive derivatives have lexicalized to a fixed, conventionalized object reading.

i-ku no longer simply means 'drink something' but specifically 'drink alcohol' — a euphemistic narrowing noted by Nakagawa as 婉曲 (indirect expression) — while i-omante and i-carpa are restricted to ritual contexts ; .

At the extreme of lexicalization the morphological boundary is no longer transparent: inkar 'gaze' (< i-nukar) and ipe 'food; eat a meal' (< i-e) have undergone phonological fusion and are synchronically nominal or verbal roots in their own right .

Bugaeva and Kobayashi further report that i- is fossilized residually on the adverb i-mak 'behind' and the particle i-y-os(no) 'afterward, later', where the original Patient-incorporating reading is entirely opaque .

The discourse motivation for the antipassive parallels what Bugaeva identifies typologically: i- is preferred when discourse focus falls on the Agent or the activity as a whole rather than on a specific, individuated Patient .

Bugaeva also notes that the prefix can antipassivize a Recipient or a direct Causee, as in i-newsar-ka 'amuse people' and i-oripak-ka 'make people feel humble' — an antipassivization of the causee rare across languages .
The functional description is uncontroversial; the grammatical label is not.

The traditional analysis, associated with Tamura and reported through Bugaeva and Kobayashi, treats i- as a generalised object marker — a derivational prefix introducing an unspecified object 'someone, thing' — without applying the voice category antipassive .
Satō's textbook grammar follows this line, describing the identical prefix as derivational i- '人を' (people-as-object) and listing no antipassive in its voice inventory .
On this account i- is a lexical derivational element that selects a generic reading rather than a voice morpheme that restructures argument relations.

Bugaeva's antipassive reanalysis argues from three converging criteria that i- meets the typological definition of an antipassive: it systematically demotes the Patient/Theme/Recipient from a core object position; its output always carries an unspecified or generic object reading; and it is discourse-conditioned, appearing precisely where the speaker defocuses the Patient to foreground the Agent or the activity ; .
Nakagawa endorses this reanalysis, noting that the term 逆受動態 (antipassive) has become standard in recent work following Bugaeva, and adopts it while acknowledging the derivational tradition .

Ijäs's learner grammar also uses the antipassive label; her characterization — the prefix 'takes the place of the object and fills it with a generic meaning of thing/place' — renders Bugaeva's substance accurately ‹contested›.

The two positions share substantial common ground: both agree that the prefix occupies the object position, that its semantic contribution is generic and unspecified, and that the verb becomes intransitive by the person-affix test.
The disagreement is whether this slot-filling constitutes a grammaticalized voice alternation or a lexical derivation that happens to intransitivize.
The width of the prefix's semantic scope — extending to Recipient and Causee demotion, not only Patient — and its discourse conditioning give the antipassive account stronger typological grounding.
This chapter adopts Bugaeva's label while registering Tamura's and Satō's derivational reading as the earlier, still-maintained alternative ‹contested›.
Two surface strings i- must be kept distinct.
The antipassive prefix i- is a derivational element in the slot immediately before the verb root; the fourth-person object marker i= is a person index belonging to the transitive object paradigm.
Both are segmentally identical, and both can appear on the same verb surface, but their distributional profiles diverge ; .
The antipassive prefix satisfies the object slot derivationally and renders the verb intransitive: the derived verb takes S suffixes and cannot simultaneously host a separate object marker.
The fourth-person marker, by contrast, leaves the verb transitive and is cross-referenced by a prefixal A index alongside the i= object marker.

A minimal diagnostic: i-nu=an (ANTIP-hear=4.S) is intransitive, proven by the suffixal =an; while a=i=nu (4.A=4.O=hear) is transitive and the i= there is the object marker, not the antipassive prefix .
The arity computation — the same instrument that distinguishes applicative e- from affiliative e- and from the second-person marker e= — is the sole disambiguating tool in both cases .

The antipassive instantiates an S=A alternation: the Agent argument of the transitive base surfaces as the sole argument of the antipassive intransitive, cross-referenced by the same person indexes that mark the transitive A.

The alternation is illustrated by Bugaeva and Kobayashi's minimal pair: nea kamuy a=ri 'I skin that bear' (transitive, specific Patient) versus i-ri=an '(I will) skin the catch' (antipassive, Patient removed from the frame) .
In the antipassive the prefixal a= is absent because there is no object slot to fill; the suffixal =an carries logophoric first-person-singular reference in the narrative context.

The 1PL.EXCL intransitive suffix =as cannot attach to a transitive verb, so its presence on i-nu=as and i-ku=as 'we drank (alcohol)' unambiguously proves the intransitive status of these antipassive derivatives .

The latter form is attested in a Saru oral narrative (Tamura 1993[1979]: 6, cited via Bugaeva 2021: 219 in Nam 2021: 62) and constitutes the core corpus evidence that the Person-Affix test extends to real discourse contexts, not only constructed elicitation.
The antipassive can be re-applicativized: the applicative prefix e- reintroduces a content or instrument object to the now-intransitive stem, raising arity by one and yielding a transitive again.
The result is that e- and i- cancel each other's arity effects while changing the type of object expressed:

This pattern, where an applicative overlays an antipassive to shift the object type without restoring the suppressed Patient, is productive and has a direct structural parallel in the re-applicativization of other arity-decreasing prefixes.
The derivational chain through ruska documented in traces the same logic: the arity decrements and increments compose arithmetically, and each step is attested in the corpus.
Three accounts of the historical source of antipassive i- are in active competition, and none is settled in the sources consulted directly for this grammar.
The dispute turns on the direction of the relationship between the antipassive prefix and the fourth-person object marker i=, and on what the ultimate etymon of both might be.

The traditional view, associated with Kindaichi, Tamura, and Shibatani and reported through Nam, derives the antipassive from the bound fourth-person pronoun: the clitic was grammaticalized into a derivational voice prefix as its object-demoting function became conventionalized ‹contested›.
Bugaeva reverses the direction.

In her 2021 analysis the antipassive i- arose from object-incorporation of a generic noun 'thing / place / time', in the same way that the body-part prefixes he- 'head' and ho- 'bottom' arose from incorporated body-part nouns.

Once the incorporated generic noun grammaticalized into a Patient-demoting voice morpheme, the antipassive form — superficially resembling the pronoun — extended to unspecified speech-act participants, and this extension gave rise to the person index i=.
The antipassive thus preceded the pronoun ; ‹contested›.
Nam's 2021 reconstruction agrees with Bugaeva that the antipassive is older than the pronoun but proposes a different etymon.

Drawing on the parallel between the antipassive prefix, the clause-final nominalizer -i (< *ihi), and the possessed suffix -hV/-VhV, he reconstructs the source as Proto-Ainu *hi / *ihi 'thing, place, time'.

The initial consonant was lost through the accumulated phonological effect of a long incorporation history: incorporated noun-stems that are word-initial rarely follow a vowel, which would have preserved the h, and word-initial *h was subsequently lost in that position.
Cross-linguistic parallels include Winnebago wa- and Bantawa kha, both generic-noun-origin antipassive markers ‹contested›.
A single fossilized form bears directly on all three positions.

The transitive verb has been analyzed as i-kV-ka (ANTIP-steal-CAUS), a frozen antipassive re-transitivized by the direct causative suffix -ka, synchronically opaque but historically preserving the derivational layer.
This analysis is attributed to Bugaeva (2010) by nukopoli in the aynu-corpora Discord community (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2026-05-19) ; .
Since Bugaeva (2010) is not consulted directly for this grammar, and since the competing segmentation ik-ka vs.
i-kV-ka cannot be decided from the surface form alone, the fossil analysis is graded ‹contested›.
Vovin's competing reconstruction of Proto-Ainu *ihka for the same root implies no antipassive layer (reported via the same Discord discussion).

If the Bugaeva/community segmentation is correct, ikka parallels the lexicalized antipassives inkar and ipe at a deeper historical stratum where the causative has since merged with the root ‹speculative›.

The width of the antipassive's semantic scope — extending to non-human objects and to ritual 'thing/place' readings (i-omante, i-mak 'behind') — fits the generic-noun hypothesis better than the pronoun-first account, since a grammaticalized human pronoun would be expected to bias the antipassive toward human Patients rather than generating the observed range ‹speculative›.
The residual-distribution evidence and Nam's phonological argument converge on this conclusion.

The middle prefix ci-, treated in full in , likewise reduces arity by one but from the affected side: it presents an event as experienced by the Patient rather than suppressing the Patient from the frame.

The paired minimal set in Nakagawa is: a=cari 'I scatter (something)' (transitive, Patient as object, agent indefinite) versus ci-cari 'it is scattered' (middle, affected noun as sole subject, agent absent) .
Both operators are arity −1, but i- foregrounds the Agent as S while leaving the Patient unindexed, while ci- foregrounds the Patient as S while leaving the Agent unindexed.
The two are therefore the A-perspective and P-perspective members of a single arity layer, and the Handbook glosses the latter object-resultative (RES) where this chapter's analysis uses ANTIP .

A community-proposed analysis identifies a productive series of middle-voice derivatives in which ci- takes a transitive or causative base and produces an intransitive middle/anticausative: cikarkarpe 'made thing', copirasa 'spread (intr)', ceosmare 'rush forward' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2023-12-08) .
This extends the picture in and is graded ‹contested› pending systematic corpus verification.

The ci-/i- split documented here aligns with the reflexive split treated in and : multiple arity-decreasing operations target different argument roles, and the arity calculus in provides the unifying framework.
The prefix fills the object position of a transitive verb with a participant coreferential with the subject, reducing arity by one and converting the base transitive to an intransitive ; .

Placed in the first-person plural, a verb bearing yay- takes the intransitive S-suffixes =as (exclusive) or =an (fourth-person) rather than the transitive A-prefixes — the person-affix test of the derivation described in ; .
A sister prefix occupies the same template slot and carries the same arity value; its own distribution and the two prefixes' contrast are treated below and in .

Nakagawa lists yay- among the 名詞的接頭辞 (nominal prefixes) of the verb-derivation chapter alongside si-, the reciprocal , the antipassive , and the lexical body-region prefixes /, all of them arity −1 and all filling the object slot from the inside of the verb word .

Ijäs's learner lessons (L3 and L9) do not cover the reflexive prefixes, as she addresses them in later material .
yay- is nearly unrestricted in base selection: it attaches to transitives and ditransitives of any semantic class, and to derived transitives (causativized or applicativized stems) .
The prefix also attaches to nominals, where arity is unchanged because a noun carries no object slot to absorb — the reading is then possessive, 'one's own': (yay- + ) is a representative form .

A productive subtype is the quasi-possessive reflexive : where an incorporated body-part noun is interpreted as belonging to the subject, yay- supplies the possessor rather than filling the object slot directly.
In (literally 'do about one's own mouth'), is incorporated as the object of , while yay- identifies the subject as the possessor of that mouth.
The arity is still reduced by one because the incorporated noun absorbs the object slot; the reflexive element determines whose body part is implicated.
This intersects with the object-incorporation system treated in .
The accent of yay- is stable: the prefix carries primary stress as yáy- regardless of the following segment, unless lexicalization has displaced it .

Forms such as yáyesiru confirm that the accent falls on yáy even before a vowel-initial stem; this accent pattern is corroborated by community corpus observation (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024, ) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

si- is more restricted than yay- in base selection, and when both co-occur the ordering is fixed: yay-si-turi-re 'lay oneself down stretching' places yay- outside si-, while the reverse *si-yay- is unattested .
Nakagawa infers that si- sits closer to the root, behaving more like a forming element than an independent prefix.
Three semantic fields attract yay- most productively.
Body-treatment and grooming verbs form the first: builds on , the same verb that underlies and related compounds (see ).

Community corpus work independently documents -kar as productive for 'handle/treat' operations — nimawe-kar (treat with a bark compress), osoro-kar — making yay-kara 'treat oneself' the expected reflexive of that class (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024, ) ‹corpus-suggested›.
A rolling-about verb in the Saru narrative corpus shows causative stacking on a grooming-motion base:

A community decomposition of yayhonokka 'educate, discipline' as yay-ho-nok-ka (REFL-bottom.body.region-CAUS) would show yay- stacking over the body-region prefix ho- and a causative suffix, with cross-dialectal support from Saru and Shizunai forms (ku=yayhonokka; ci=honokka; taan hanokka) (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2026, ) ‹contested›.
The decomposition has not been verified against the analytic literature.
Emotion and mental-state verbs make up a second field.
Ainu transitive verbs of feeling take a stimulus as their object; yay- reflexivizes that position, yielding an intransitive of self-directed affect.

The minimal pair yay-rayke 'commit suicide' vs si-rayke 'be destroyed by misfortune', both from , shows how the same base divides between the two prefixes; the opposition is examined in the yay-/si- section below .
Self-transformation verbs form the third class.

The functional boundary between yay- and si- has produced several accounts that remain in tension ; ; .
The four most developed positions are set out in the table below; the sources for the first two and third are cited second-hand through the works that survey them.

For the grammar's glossing practice, Bugaeva's 2025 diachronic formulation is the most useful high-level distinction: yay- is REFL proper, while verbal si- has shifted along the common path from reflexive to autocausative and only secondarily to anticausative.
The older direct/indirect terminology remains important for explaining individual examples, but it is no longer the primary glossing distinction used in the morpheme database .
Satō's direct/indirect account, developed for Chitose, is adopted by Nakagawa and the Handbook as the current best analysis ‹contested›
It holds that yay- marks an action the subject performs directly on itself, without requiring any mediating agent or social condition.

si- marks a situation where the subject's involvement is indirect: the outcome is achieved through another participant's action, through circumstances beyond the subject's control, or through a state that holds only because others perceive it as holding.
The canonical Chitose minimal pair is yay-pusu 'pop up by swimming (volitionally)' vs si-pusu 'float of itself (spontaneously)', both from .
The si- form applies to a physical property of spruce:
The si- class also covers a productive 'pretend' construction: si-mokor-e 'feign sleep', si-kamuy-ne-re 'pretend to be a deity', si-ranpewtek-ka 'pretend to know nothing' ; .
In each case the subject's performed state depends on how others perceive her — a condition that cannot hold without an audience, hence the indirect marking:

From Nakagawa, a parallel emotional pair: yay-rayke 'commit suicide' (direct, deliberate self-directed action) vs si-rayke 'be destroyed, come to ruin (by misfortune)' (the outcome is brought about by external forces) .
Bugaeva and Kobayashi add yay-etaye 'draw oneself out (actively)' vs si-etaye 'withdraw, pull oneself back in (in response to something)' .
The Shizunai corpus supplies an attested instance of si-etaye where the withdrawal is triggered by being seen:
Satō himself notes that the direct/indirect analysis has not reached consensus (定説ではない) ; .
The earlier intentional/unintentional framing (Kindaichi, Tamura) remains in pedagogical use ‹contested›.

A community reformulation characterizes yay- as 'by one's own power' (reflexive) and si- as 'happens to / gets through others' (anticausative), with yaykaopiwki 'save oneself by one's own action' cited as a diagnostic (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024, ) ‹contested›.
This formulation is consistent with Satō's account while aligning the si- end with anticausative typology.

The hypothesis that the two prefixes represent historically distinct voice categories rather than two subtypes of reflexive (aomidori_cs_, aynu-corpora Discord 2023, ) ‹speculative› — no diachronic evidence bearing on a pre-reflexive function of either prefix has been identified in the sources consulted for this grammar.

Bugaeva and Kobayashi note that no other reported language encodes the distinction between dependence-on-others vs absence-of-such-dependence through a pair of reflexive prefixes, making the Ainu opposition typologically unusual .

The full treatment of si- — including its unaccusative uses, its possessive-reflexive function with incorporated body-part nouns (si-etu-uyna 'hold one's own nose'), and the pretend-to constructions — is in .
yay- combines freely with the applicative prefixes e-, ko-, and o- (see ).

Since an applicative raises arity by one (+1) and yay- lowers it by one (−1), their combination on a transitive base preserves the original transitivity while shifting which object position holds the reflexive participant.
On a base that already has an outer applicative-object, yay- fills the inner original-object slot with 'self'; the outer applicative slot remains available for an external NP.

The combination ko-yay-irayke 'be grateful to someone for something one has experienced oneself' is attested in the Saru narrative corpus — here ko- promotes the deity as the addressee-goal, and yay- fills the inner object of with the subject:

The derivational chain through demonstrates the calculus across further steps: ruska (vt) → ko-ruska (vd, 'be angry toward') → yay-ko-ruska (vt, 'be angry at oneself') → i-ruska (vi, 'be angry', object defocused) — each step changes arity by exactly one unit ; ‹consensus›.
The antipassive i- in the same chain is treated in .

The verb template places reflexive and applicative prefixes inside the person-index layer and outside the root: person-index — reflexive/applicative — root — forming-suffix — causative — person-index .
Two reflexive prefixes and two applicatives can co-occur on a single root, as in the word a=e-yay-ko-tuyma-si-ram-suy-pa discussed in ; .

A community-proposed decomposition of yaykipniwkes as yay-ki-p-niwkes — with ki 'do' as a light verb and niwkes as the state predicate (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024, ) ‹contested› — illustrates the opaque prefix stacking that occurs in this zone; the analysis awaits verification against primary morphological descriptions.
The reciprocal u-, which parallels yay- in its arity value while filling both S and O slots simultaneously, is in .
The prefix has to be glossed by construction.

On verbs, Bugaeva's 2025 analysis treats it as historically reflexive but synchronically chiefly autocausative (AUTOC: self-induced motion or change), with a secondary/emerging anticausative (ANTIC) use; where the object slot remains genuinely self-coreferent, as in the 'pretend to' construction with the causatives -re/-ka, the gloss stays REFL.
In Nakagawa's arity calculus and in Satō's direct/indirect account, it still reduces the external argument frame by one and shifts the resulting verb to the intransitive S-index set.
On nouns and incorporated nominals, however, si- is REFL.POSS: it marks the noun as belonging to the clause subject, as in si-ram 'one's own heart' ; ; .
is more restricted in distribution than : the latter attaches to transitives, intransitives, and nouns alike (with arity 0 on nouns, as in ), whereas is productive only on transitive bases .

Beyond the basic reflexive reading it also functions as a reflexive-possessive, marking the subject-coreferent possessor of an incorporated nominal, and it enters a 'pretend to' construction when combined with the causative suffixes -re and -ka ; .
The meaning that underlies all three uses is the same: the subject's involvement passes through another participant or external circumstance rather than arising from direct self-initiated action.
Four analyses of the yay-/si- contrast are on record, all working from the same minimal pairs.
The classic pair is → 'pop up by swimming (volitionally)' versus 'float up of itself', attributed to Kindaichi (1931: 149, reported by ) and .
Nakagawa adds → 'commit suicide' versus 'be ruined by ill fortune' .
The direct/indirect analysis (line four) is the framework Nakagawa (2024: 189) and the Handbook adopt as the current working account ‹contested›.

Satō (2007: ≈31–38) builds it from three paradigm cases: 'have oneself tattooed' (traditional Ainu tattooing required another person to do the work); 'have others help oneself' (the help comes from outside); and 'pretend not to know' (the pretence succeeds only if another observer believes it).
In each case the subject's reflexive involvement is mediated by another party's action or perception.
Satō himself qualifies the account as not yet established (定説ではない) .
None of the earlier analyses is fully discredited.
The intentionality framing (Kindaichi, Tamura) captures the spontaneous reading of but not the pretend-to construction, where the subject acts with full intent.
The agentive/patientive framing (Kirikae 1994: 316, reported by ) separates the forms at the thematic role level, but feigning sleep — — is agentive and falls outside the patientive characterisation.

The argument-structural restriction that Kobayashi (2008: 140) derives — occupies Theme or Patient but never causee — correctly excludes causee arguments but does not explain the opposition between and , where both occupy a Theme role .

The Handbook extends the empirical base with two additional minimal pairs: versus — where the latter signals a shedding of human clothes driven by the subject's transformation into bird form, an outward change not self-initiated — and 'draw oneself out' versus 'withdraw, pull back in response to another's approach' .

A discussion on the aynu-corpora Discord (nukopoli, , 2024) labels the contrast as anticausative () versus reflexive proper (), on the grounds that marks 'something that happens to the subject through another force' and marks 'the subject acting on itself directly'.
The labelling is consistent with the Satō analysis and invokes an explicit anticausative category ‹contested›.
A separate thread (aomidori_cs_, , 2023) proposed that one prefix may originally have encoded a voice distinct from reflexive proper, without adducing corroborating evidence ‹speculative›.
When a transitive verb incorporates a body-part or closely possessed nominal, can mark that nominal as belonging to the subject — the reflexive-possessive function.
The example cited by the Handbook is 'hold one's nose', where supplies the possessor 'one's own' for the incorporated noun and is thereby intransitivized .

The parallel -possessive — 'feed oneself', literally 'do to one's own mouth' — shows that both prefixes can supply the possessor of an incorporated nominal, with the yay-/si- distinction projecting onto the possessive domain in the same way it does onto the reflexive .

The reflexive-possessive reading also surfaces obligatorily in locative contexts: when a locative nominal's possessor is coreferential with the clause subject, (or the applicative construction built around it) is required, and substituting a non-coreferential possessor yields a distinct, non-reflexive reading .
In arity terms the function remains −1: the incorporated nominal fills one argument slot, fills that nominal's possessor internally, and one external argument is removed.

The parallel in noun incorporation is the possessor-requiring subject type, where the stranded possessor receives a reflexive interpretation by recovery from the clause subject — the 'reflexive interpretation rescue' in Satō's markedness calculus, treated in .
The reciprocal construction uses the same word-internal possession pattern with u-.
Forms such as u-tek-kisma ‘shake hands’, u-oruspe-nu ‘discuss things’, and u-itak-nu ‘agree; obey’ are treated together with the reflexive patterns in .
The shared structure is a possessor prefix followed by a bare incorporated noun and its verbal host.
combined with a causative suffix yields a 'pretend to V' reading.
Nakagawa (2024: 189) gives three examples with the productive suffix -re: 'feign sleep', 'pretend to be a kamuy', and 'act childishly'.
With the direct-causative -ka, Satō (2007: ≈36) gives 'pretend not to know'.
In each instance the state or appearance is externally attributed: sleep must be witnessed to be believed, kamuy status requires another to be deceived, ignorance requires an observer to accept it.
The 'pretend to' reading is therefore a direct realisation of the indirect-reflexive semantics of in a context of social inference.
The construction is limited to verbs of state or appearance assignable by an external observer; verbs of direct physical action or creation do not enter it .
In the slot ordering summarised in , precedes the root and any incorporated nominal but follows the applicative prefixes.
The ordering constraint with is decisive: yay-si- is attested — Nakagawa (2024: 189) cites 'lay oneself down while stretching' — while the reverse *si-yay- is not .
This places closer to the root, in a position Nakagawa compares to forming affixes.

The derivation chain illustrates the ordering across the arity calculus: the ditransitive ko-i-ruska yields the intransitive si-ko-i-ruska when is prefixed — it absorbs the applicative complex's object slot while remaining to its left ; .

In the polysynthetic example discussed in — a=e-yay-ko-tuyma-si-ram-suy-pa — a second sits immediately before the incorporated noun in the reflexive-possessive reading ('one's own heart'), while occupies the outer layer at the applicative boundary.
The yay-outer / si-inner hierarchy is visible in a single stacked verb form ; .
The prefix is a valency-decreasing derivational morpheme with arity −1: it fills the object slot of a transitive verb with a mutual or collective participant, detransitivizing the verb ; .
The derived verb always takes a plural or collective subject — only two or more participants can stand in a mutual relation.

The person-marking diagnostic (the operative test of derived transitivity set out in ) confirms the intransitivization: a verb that takes the prefixal A-indexes a= or ci= shifts to the suffixal S-indexes =an or =as after u- ; .

The slot u- occupies is the same nominal/applicative position as the reflexive prefix , , and the antipassive ; these prefixes all decrease or rearrange valency, but their semantic domains differ — self-directed action, autocausative/anticausative/reflexive or reflexive-possessive marking, object defocusing, and mutual participation, respectively.

The prefix is highly productive: it attaches to base transitive verbs, to applicative-prefixed stems, and to causativized forms, with the arity calculus predicting the transitivity of each output (see ).

A further complication is that u- covers not only canonical bilateral reciprocal meaning ('each other') but also joint or associative participation ('together'), and the two readings are not always distinguishable without context.
In its canonical use, u- expresses mutual action: each participant in the plural subject simultaneously acts on and is acted on by the others.
The paradigm pair (transitive) → (intransitive), and → , illustrates the productive base pattern .
u- also operates on ditransitive (three-argument) bases.
When the Addressee or Recipient of a ditransitive is the argument filled by the mutual relation, the construction is termed indirect reciprocal .

Several forms with u- do not yield a strictly bilateral 'each other' reading.
Here u- signals joint involvement or a two-party social relation without requiring symmetric action between every pair of participants .
The clearest instance is , which incorporates the noun and the verb .
The surface subject may be syntactically singular — a young man described in terms of having a sister — yet the verb carries u- because the sibling relation inherently involves two parties:

Similarly, does not mean 'make each other laugh' but 'all laugh together' — a sociative reading arising from the arity calculus: u- (−1) prefixed to the already-causativized intransitive mina-re (arity 2) yields net arity 1 (intransitive), encoding collective action rather than imposing a new causer slot .
This u- + causative-on-intransitive path to a sociative reading is treated further in below.
Bugaeva and Kobayashi identify five constructional types for u- reciprocals, organized by the nature of the mutual relation and the morphosyntactic base :
The quasi-possessive type distributes each participant's possessed noun across the group: u-tek-kisma 'shake hands' (lit. 'shake each other's hand') and u-oruspe-nu are further instances .
For the parallel reflexive construction in which a possessed noun is incorporated with yay- or si-, see .
The term quasi-possessive reciprocal describes a reciprocal relation located inside an incorporated nominal.
Its structure is [u-Npossessed]-V: u- supplies the possessor of the noun, and the resulting u-N unit is incorporated into the verb.
The participants therefore act upon one another through a relationally possessed entity such as words, stories, strength, or hands ; .
This constituency explains the arity effect.
The incorporated noun fills the Theme position of the transitive verb, while u- identifies the noun’s possessor reciprocally with the plural or collective subject.
The whole complex has one syntactic argument and behaves as an intransitive predicate.
The bracketing for u-itak-nu is therefore [[u-itak]-nu]: first ‘one another’s words’, then ‘hear those words’.
This analysis gives each morpheme one role and directly derives the attested intransitive behavior.
Possession elsewhere in Ainu commonly uses a person prefix together with an affiliative form of the noun.
For example, the concept form tek ‘hand’ has the affiliative forms tek-e and tek-e-he, as in ku=tekehe ‘my hand’ .
Noun incorporation uses the bare concept stem: u-tek-kisma contains tek.
Its possessor is still recoverable because u- stands immediately before the noun inside the verbal word.
See for the free nominal paradigm and for the general incorporation pattern.
This is especially transparent with nouns whose interpretation invites a possessor.
A hand, a person’s words, and a person’s inner state naturally raise the question ‘whose?’.

The word-internal prefixes answer it: u- distributes possessors across participants, yay- links the possessor to an intentional subject, and possessive si- links it to the subject in the lexical patterns that select si-.
The bare noun remains inside the predicate, so no separate possessed noun phrase is required.
The reflexive examples show the same architectural principle.
In yay-par-oyki and si-etu-uyna, the prefix possesses an incorporated body-part noun .

Dal Corso identifies the same construction in Sakhalin yay-cise-koro ‘have one’s own house’ and reports cise ‘house’, kotan ‘village’, cara ‘mouth’, and ram ‘soul’ as recurrent incorporated nouns in Piłsudski’s corpus .
In si-hum-nu-yar, si-hum is ‘one’s own sound’, nu is ‘hear’, and -yar introduces an indefinite hearer .
The larger si-ram family lexicalizes mental activity through movements of one’s own ram ‘heart/mind’; its applicative stacks are analyzed in and .
The lexical development of u-itak-nu begins with an ordinary social event: participants hear and accept words belonging to one another.
Mutual uptake supports the reading ‘agree’, while successful uptake of another person’s direction supports ‘obey’.
Tamura defines uitaknu as ‘listen to what each other says; agree/obey’ and explicitly segments it as u-itak-nu .
Bugaeva’s Sakhalin example above independently confirms the obedience reading .
Mandarin tīnghuà is defined as ‘comply’ .
Turkish dictionaries give söz dinlemek as an equivalent of ‘obey’ , and Dehkhoda groups Persian حرف‌شنوی with obedience and submission .
A corpus study of Biblical Hebrew finds that the valency pattern שמע בקול regularly triggers ‘obey’ .
These parallels establish a recurrent semantic mapping HEAR WORDS/VOICE → HEED → OBEY.
They explain the motivation of the Ainu social meaning and carry no claim of common origin or borrowing.
The title of Batchelor’s 1897 New Testament contains Aeuitaknup ‘covenant, promise, testament’ .
Batchelor’s 1903 standalone grammar documents the contemporary descriptive framework ; his 1905 dictionary supplies the lexical definition ‘a covenant; a promise’ and Japanese 誓約、ケイヤク .
Tajima gives the full morphological analysis a=e-u-itak-nu-p and translates its nominal core as ‘that one another’s words are heard’ .
The internal derivation proceeds in three layers.
First, u-itak denotes ‘one another’s words’.
Second, [[u-itak]-nu] denotes mutual hearing or acceptance and has the lexical reading ‘agree/obey’.
Third, the applicative e-, fourth-person A marker a=, and nominalizer -p form the title noun.
Tajima’s 1992 terminology calls a- passive; this grammar uses the fourth-person analysis developed in later Ainu descriptions.
The quasi-possessive constituency of u-itak-nu remains the same under either account.

The arity of the base verb and the order of operations determine which reading obtains; surface form alone is insufficient ‹corpus-suggested›.

Plain applies only reciprocal u-, so 2 − 1 = 1 and the result is intransitive.
In , sociative uko- combines ko- (+1) with u- (−1), for a net change of 0; 2 + 0 = 2, and the result remains transitive :
uko- is commoner than uwe- in Saru texts, reflecting the higher productivity of ko- as an applicative .

The two are partially interchangeable in derivationally transparent forms (uko-yaykopuntek ~ uwe-yaykopuntek 'rejoice together'), but ko-'s comitative and goal-directed semantics give it the advantage where joint orientation toward shared participants is foregrounded .
For the full applicative semantics of ko- and e-, see ; for their stacking with other prefixes, .
Among the arity-decreasing voice prefixes, presents an event from the affected side and yields an intransitive verb whose sole argument is the entity undergoing the action .
Nakagawa labels the output 中動態 (middle voice) and gives the underlying semantics as "expressing, from the affected side, an action one thing performs on another" .
The Handbook glosses the same prefix object-resultative (RES), emphasising the affected argument's endpoint state .
Both labels address the same morphosyntactic fact: the base transitive loses its agent position, arity drops by one, and the base object surfaces as the intransitive subject.
The terminological difference between "middle" and "object-resultative" is not analytical ‹contested›.
The prefix reduces arity by exactly one.
(transitive, +2) gives ci-cari 'be scattered' (intransitive, +1); (transitive) gives ci-sina 'be tied'.

The prefixed form takes suffixal S-argument indexes (fourth-person =an, first-plural exclusive =as) in place of the A-argument prefixes of the transitive base — the standard transitivity diagnostic of .
