Typologically, middle voice marks spontaneous, patient-initiated, or affectee-oriented events across many of the world's languages — the semantic space where a passive would otherwise be expected but no agent is expressed .

In Hokkaido Ainu, ci- occupies that niche: the source event is agentive (someone scatters, someone ties), but the prefix profiles its outcome from the affected participant's perspective, suppressing the agent position entirely.
The middle prefix ci- is restricted to third-person subjects.

The form *ku=ci-montapire ('I was informed') is ungrammatical; a first-person affected participant instead requires the indefinite-agent construction with objective cross-referencing: a=en=montapire 'the indefinite agent informed me as object' .
This restriction distinguishes ci- sharply from the reflexive and the antipassive , which are available across persons.

The prefix is homophonous with the first-person plural exclusive A-index ci=, and both reduce arity by one — the index by filling the subject slot with a specific 1PL.EXCL argument, the middle by suppressing the agent entirely.
Nakagawa treats them as "probably related but synchronically distinct" and notes a shared phonological behaviour: before a, e, o the i drops, yielding surface ca-, ce-, co- (ci-opirasa → copirasa) .
Disambiguation in context relies on person morphology and arity: a middle verb takes suffixal S-indexes, while a first-plural A-prefix takes the O-indexes typical of transitives.
Several ci- forms have lexicalized as uninflected bases.
The noun — 'thing that is hunted' — freezes the middle of , no longer perceived as a productive derivational composite by speakers .
Lexicalized middles of this type document the prefix's historical productivity; the set of active, synchronically transparent pairs is smaller.

Discussion in the aynu-corpora Discord has proposed that ci- functions as a systematically productive middle/anticausative across a wider set of lexemes than the published literature has catalogued (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023–2024) .

The proposal analyses several opaque-looking forms as transparent middle derivations: copirasa 'spread out, widen (intr)' as ci=opirasa (from transitive ); ceosmare 'dash forward, plunge in' as ci=e-osma-re (from an applicative-causative 'cause to thrust into'); and cikarkarpe as ci=kar-kar-pe 'things being made' ‹contested›.
The same line of analysis was applied to ci-koykarkar.

On this reading the ci- in hattoho ci-koykarkar is the middle prefix, yielding a passive-like meaning 'restrictions are imposed on [us]', rather than the first-plural A-index ci=, which would give 'we impose restrictions together' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024) ‹contested›.
The disambiguation requires pragmatic and discourse context; surface form alone does not decide it.

These community analyses are leads rather than established findings: they extend the attested middle use productively to forms the peer-reviewed descriptive literature has not formally analysed under this label.

The core claim — that ci- is a productive middle prefix — is supported by Nakagawa and the Handbook; the community contribution is the extension to a broader set of lexemes and the identification of middle ci- in forms previously treated as first-plural-exclusive or as unanalysed compounds.

A further diachronic hypothesis that ci- derives from an earlier passive-like *ti, distinct in origin from the person index, was proposed but disputed on phonological grounds — the affricate [t͡s] realised as c also appears in non-palatalizing environments, casting doubt on a straightforward palatalization account (nukopoli and aomidori, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023) ‹speculative›.
The reflexive prefix covers a semantic domain that overlaps partially with the middle.

Under Satō's analysis, adopted by Nakagawa and the Handbook, si- marks the subject's indirect involvement — through another agent, through circumstance, or through a force outside the subject's direct control ; ; .

The minimal pair yay-pusu 'float up volitionally (by swimming)' against si-pusu 'float up of itself' illustrates the anticausative semantics of si-: the event is profiled as spontaneous, with an affected participant rising without an expressed agent .
Similarly, the transitive yields si-turi 'stretch, lie down (of itself)', which Tamura analyses as a pure intransitivizing derivation .
Kobayashi groups such pairs under "anticausativization" — a transitivity alternation in which the causer is suppressed and the event presented as spontaneous .
The morphological and person-marking properties of ci- and si- remain distinct despite the semantic overlap.

ci- suppresses the agent position entirely and is restricted to third-person contexts; si- fills the object slot with a self-participant coreferent with the clause subject and is available across all persons.
Spontaneous or agent-backgrounded events with a first- or second-person participant therefore surface with si-, not ci-.
The full treatment of the yay- / si- opposition belongs to and ; the present section records only the semantic intersection with the anticausative domain.

Bugaeva's diachronic study of anticausatives in Ainu concentrates on two markers: the primary anticausative / intransitivizing suffix -ke, and si-, whose path is REFLEXIVE > AUTOCAUSATIVE > ANTICAUSATIVE .
The inchoative-causative interface — where a stem such as / pairs a spontaneous intransitive with a transitive — is treated in .

The prefix ci- is therefore best kept as a separate MID/RES resultative prefix: it suppresses an agent and profiles an affected result, but it is not the same historical problem as Bugaeva's si- anticausative path.
Two lexical prefixes of noun origin, he- 'head, tip' and ho- 'base, bottom', also reduce arity by one by filling the object slot with the subject's own body-region ; .
(transitive) yields he-puni 'raise one's head' (intransitive) and ho-puni 'get up, fly up' (intransitive); yields he-kiru 'turn around'; yields ho-tuye 'shout' (semantically opaque) .

These prefixes are the arity-decreasing (−1) counterparts of the homophonous affiliative e- 'head of' and o- 'base of', which are arity-neutral (0) and fill a slot while requiring their own possessor.
The minimal pair makes the arity contrast concrete: he-puni is intransitive and takes S-indexes, while affiliative e-puni 'raise the head/end of something (belonging to someone)' remains transitive .

Bugaeva and Kobayashi group he- and ho- together with the ci- middle under the object-resultative heading, noting that they "function similarly to O-incorporation" — a body-region semantics fills the object slot and makes the verb intransitive .
Many surface forms are semantically opaque: ho-tuye 'shout' transparently contains tuye 'cut' with ho- 'base', yet the compositional meaning is not recoverable .

When a transitive event is presented with an unspecified or backgrounded agent, Hokkaido Ainu uses the fourth/indefinite person prefix — or the dialectal variant an= in Ishikari and some other varieties — as the agent argument of the transitive verb.
The patient stays in object position; no promotion to subject occurs.
The construction is valency-neutral: the verb retains its transitive argument frame, with the indefinite agent filling the A slot and the patient cross-referenced as O ; .
A demoted agent is expressed with the postpositional phrase or(o) wa 'from', taking the NP that would normally appear as the transitive subject .
The construction is frequent with unintended or inanimate causers and in polite speech where direct naming of the agent is avoided.
The full morphology, referential range, and dialect distribution of the fourth/indefinite person are treated in .
Satō's subjecthood diagnostic makes the non-promotion of the patient explicit.
If the patient were a true intransitive subject, a 'want to be loved' predicate should take bare with subjective marking.
Instead the construction requires the nominalizer hi together with objective cross-referencing on the verb :

The distinction between the ci- middle and the a= construction also emerges clearly here: in a ci- clause the affected participant surfaces as the intransitive subject and no agent may be expressed at all; in the a= clause the patient is syntactically the object, an agent may appear in or wa, and the verb is transitive by all formal tests .
Hokkaido Ainu has no subject-promoting passive ; .
Nakagawa states it directly: それにあたるものはアイヌ語には無い 'there is nothing in Ainu that corresponds to it' .
The two constructions that carry the functional load a passive would otherwise bear are structurally distinct from each other and from any classic subject-promoting passive.
The ci- middle moves the base object into subject position — in that respect it is the nearest Ainu analogue to a valency-decreasing passive — but it categorically blocks agent expression .
A classic passive combines patient-as-subject with an optional by-phrase; no Ainu construction combines these two properties.

Nakagawa adds that the middle has a verse-register periphrastic use with the causative — ci-ra-na-ran-ke (from , stretched to five syllables) — where meaning is unchanged; this verse device is not available for the a= construction .
The Handbook labels the a= / an= construction a "valency-neutral impersonal passive" to capture its agent-defocusing function, while recognizing that it lacks subject promotion ‹contested›.
Satō's preferred formulation — "a half-active, very peculiar passive structure" — likewise foregrounds the mismatch with cross-linguistic passive prototypes ‹contested›.
Neither label implies that the construction is a passive in the structural sense; both describe the same functional fact from different angles.
The functional distribution that results follows from the structural properties.
For third-person affected participants where no agent is at issue, ci- presents the event from the affected side, and the patient-as-subject reading is the natural one.
For first- or second-person patients, or wherever the agent may need to be expressed, a= / an= is used instead, with the patient retaining object status and the verb its transitive morphology .
A by-phrase that co-occurs with patient-as-subject is unattested in the Hokkaido corpus ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Ijäs's learner grammar does not treat the passive question or the ci- middle .
The nominalizer hi that anchors Satō's subjecthood diagnostic connects this discussion to the nominalization system of .
The antipassive i-, which defocuses the object from the subject's side, is the mirror-image operation and is treated in .
The productive causative -re / -te / -e, which introduces an agent argument rather than suppressing one, is in .

Object noun incorporation takes a nominal stem and absorbs it into a transitive verb as its Patient argument, producing a single verb word that expresses subject, incorporated object, and predicate together ; .
In Nakagawa's arity calculus the transitive host carries arity +2 — one slot for a subject argument, one for an object argument.
The incorporated noun fills the object slot at arity −1, and the resulting compound has arity +1: an intransitive verb .
and yield cep-koyki 'fish-catch': the nominal is inside the verb word and the object argument position is saturated.
The criterion for wordhood is the outer position of the person index ; .
With a phrasal object the index attaches to the verb alone: cep ku=koyki has the 1SG prefix on koyki, with cep as a separate noun phrase.
Under incorporation the index precedes the entire noun-verb complex: ku=cep-koyki 'I fish-catch'.
With 4th-person marking the diagnostic is decisive: cep-koyki=an can only be one intransitive word, because the transitive root koyki cannot host the intransitive S suffix =an on its own .

The overview of the valency system in introduces this diagnostic; the present chapter develops object-type incorporation specifically: the detransitivizing morphology, the semantic vocabulary of incorporated nouns, and the typological position of Hokkaido Ainu Object NI.
Incorporating the object reduces the verb's argument count by one and shifts its person marking from the transitive to the intransitive paradigm.
Satō's minimal pair makes the shift visible : the transitive pukusa a=ta carries the 4th-person A prefix a=, which marks an indefinite transitive agent.
Once is incorporated, the predicate becomes intransitive pukusa-ta=an, bearing instead the 4th-person S suffix =an.
The suffix =an is impossible on a transitive verb: a transitive verb with an indefinite 4th-person agent must carry the A prefix a= ; .
It therefore serves as the definitive morphological test for intransitivity after Object NI.

The same alternation appears with : the incorporated intransitive is kinakar=an, while the phrasal construction gives the transitive kina a=kar with the A prefix; this pair is consistent with the analysis in and has been independently noted in community discussion (thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024 ) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The same intransitivization is attested across the Saru oral corpus.
Kawakami Matsuko uses cep-koyki=an repeatedly in narrative; the 4th-person S suffix =an appears on what is otherwise the transitive root koyki :
The person-marking shift is the sole morphological trace of Object NI.
There is no overt incorporation morpheme, no case suffix on the noun stem, and no change to TAM morphology ; .
The incorporated noun leaves no external argument slot: the Patient NP can no longer appear in the clause as a co-referential noun phrase.
The two-affix ceiling — at most one subject index and one object index on any verb — bounds the system: Object NI uses up the object slot, leaving only the subject slot available ; .
Satō classifies Hokkaido Ainu noun incorporation into four types by the grammatical relation of the incorporated noun to the base verb ; ; .
The distribution below comes from a count of 517 NI tokens in the Chitose-dialect speech of the narrator 白沢ナベ ; .
No pan-Hokkaido NI-type frequency study has been published; the percentages are Chitose-specific and derive from a single narrator's corpus ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Object NI accounts for nearly seven eighths of all incorporation tokens.

Its alignment with Mithun's Type I — lexical compounding in which the incorporated noun names a general activity type rather than a specific referent — is consistent with the Chitose data, though the theoretical status of Ainu NI more broadly is a live debate ; ; .
The three subject-NI subtypes, including the possessor-stranding construction that is typologically the most marked, are treated in .

Ijäs's Lesson 3 introduces the two-argument transitive frame with the constructed example numan hekaci cep koyki 'the boy caught some fish' , the phrasal form of the root that appears incorporated as cep-koyki above.
Her lesson does not treat incorporation; the contrast between the phrasal and the incorporated frame is developed here ‹consensus›.
Satō's Chitose count yields a breakdown of the semantic domains from which Object NI compounds draw their incorporated nouns :

The space category reflects the frequency of spatial compounds in which a location noun functions as the direct Patient of the incorporating verb: these are Object NI, with the locative noun already in the object grammatical relation.
Oblique incorporations — instruments and locatives that were first promoted to object position by an applicative before incorporating — are a distinct construction treated in ; .
Body-part compounds cluster around perception and contact verbs; plant, tool, and fire nouns reflect the subsistence activities that are most elaborated in Ainu oral narrative.
The following Chitose example illustrates the tool / house type, with absorbed into :

Satō's corpus attests several NI↔phrase near-pairs — apa asi / apa-asi 'close the door', cep koyki / cep-koyki, wakka ta / wakka-ta — but these alternations are few and not systematically productive; most Object NI compounds have no attested phrasal counterpart ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The phrasal side of the apa asi pair is attested as a straightforward transitive predicate:
The incorporated noun must be semantically unbounded: a generic, non-referring stem ; .
A common noun such as cep 'fish' incorporates freely into cep-koyki 'fish-catch'.
A specific proper noun cannot: *Sikotpet-tomotuye 'cross the Shikotsu river' is ungrammatical because a river name is an inherently referring expression ; .
Ainu Object NI groups with Mithun's Type I — lexical compounding in which the incorporated noun names the type of object typically affected rather than a referential argument ; ; .

Nakagawa places the same character in a distributional frame: NI compounds are commoner in verse than in ordinary prose or conversation, and they represent a lexicalized stratum of the verb vocabulary rather than a productive derivational slot .

Whether Ainu NI is best analysed as purely lexical, as Baker's syntactic head-movement, or as a hybrid that must reference both grammatical relations and semantic roles as Shibatani proposes is a dispute the sources consulted do not resolve; it is taken up in ; ; ‹contested›.
A small set of verbs permits simultaneous incorporation of two nominal stems, producing rare three-element compounds.
Nakagawa cites cep-ya-o-kuta 'dump fish onto the shore' — incorporands cep 'fish' and ya 'shore', mediated by the applicative o- — and itak-mak-kus-te 'use hidden words' as attested cases .
The general limit is one incorporated noun per verb , and these forms are marginal in the corpus ‹corpus-suggested›.

NI compounds that have lost any productive phrasal alternant are synchronically lexicalized denominal verbs; the derivational pathway that produces them connects to the broader denominal processes treated in .

A diachronic line also links Object NI to the antipassive prefix : Bugaeva proposes that i- arose from grammaticalization of O-incorporation of a generic noun, with the 4th-person pronoun i= derived secondarily from the antipassive , while Nam reconstructs the source as a distinct generic-noun stem ; the dispute belongs to ‹contested›.

Where Object NI is blocked — most critically at the possessor-requiring type (impossible because an inflectional possessor makes the incorporated noun specific, and no reflexive rescue is available) — the function passes to quasi-incorporation (QI), a tight phrasal unit that is idiomatic but not yet a single verb word ; .
The QI construction and the markedness calculus governing the NI–QI division are developed in .
Object incorporation accounts for the overwhelming majority of Ainu noun incorporation, but the language also incorporates subjects.

Satō's Chitose count places subject incorporation at about 14% of all incorporation tokens, divided into three functional subtypes that differ in which noun is incorporated, what happens to the verb's valency, and whether an external possessor must be retained ; .
These figures come from the corpus of the late Shirasawa Nabe (Chitose) and reflect one idiolect; no pan-Hokkaido NI-type frequency study has been published ‹corpus-suggested›.

The wordhood diagnostic is the same as for object incorporation: because the person index is the outermost element of the verb word, an incorporated noun must sit inside it, and a fourth-person S suffix on a normally transitive base is decisive proof of intransitivisation ; .
The broader valency architecture is in , and object incorporation in .
The incorporated noun in this subtype is not a full lexical noun but a bound stem denoting a natural force or ambient condition.
Two such stems are attested in Hokkaido: and ; .

Neither appears as an independent subject noun alongside the same predicate — the phrasal counterpart does not exist — which distinguishes this subtype sharply from object incorporation, where phrasal and incorporated forms often alternate .

Nakagawa groups these predicates among the zero-place verbs of the verb-class system; their person-prefix behaviour confirms that status, since the zero-arity result takes no person affixes in its basic meteorological use .
The weather stem combines with stative predicates to form a set of meteorological expressions: , , , , and similar.
The corpus count for sirpirka stands at 147 tokens (rank 873), confirming its standing as the most frequent member of the set ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The cold stem functions identically: me-an 'it is cold' incorporates me as the subject of the existential an, again without an independent-noun counterpart .
Nakagawa's subclassification requires that the incorporated noun appear in its concept form (裸形), as opposed to the possessed form that characterises the possessor-requiring subtype below .
The two forms — concept and possessed — are treated in .
The second intransitive subtype incorporates a body-part or relational noun that grammatically requires a possessor.
Because the incorporated noun carries its possessive morphology into the verb word, that possessor must surface as an external argument — the phenomenon Satō terms possessor stranding ; .
This corresponds to Mithun's Type II: the construction rearranges grammatical relations rather than merely lexically compounding ; .
The mechanism is this: a stative intransitive verb whose S argument is a body-part noun takes that noun in its possessed form (所属形) and incorporates it.

The possessed form grammatically encodes that the noun belongs to someone; that possessor must therefore be supplied from outside the incorporated complex, and it is promoted to the S of the whole predicate.
Overall arity does not decrease: the promoted possessor fills exactly the slot that the incorporated noun's argument position vacated ; .

The possessed-form noun appearing as an incorporated subject is itself the structural signature of this type and distinguishes it from the natural-force type, where the incorporand is in concept form.
A further example shows the possessor-stranding structure in context: Satō's Chitose Appendix (iii) gives ku=ram-u-tuy wa ku=si-y-etu-esikari 'I was startled and grabbed at my own nose' .
The first clause incorporates in its possessed form as the subject of u-tuy (RECP-cut, intransitive); the possessor of the heart, the speaker, surfaces as S indexed by ku=.
The second clause uses the indirect reflexive si- as the quasi-possessive of the incorporated — a pattern treated in .

What licenses the stranded possessor is a reflexive interpretation: the possessor must be understood as coreferential with the subject of the predication — that is, the body-part is read as belonging reflexively to whoever occupies S.
Satō formalizes this as a reflexive-interpretation rescue that offsets most of the markedness penalty that stranding would otherwise attract ; .
Satō ranks all incorporation subtypes by a constraint-and-rescue scoring system, where each restriction adds penalty points and each licensing factor subtracts them ; .
Penalty values differ between the 2022 Handbook chapter and the 2016 paper (alternative scores in parentheses), but the rank order and frequency proportions are identical.
The Backgrounding rescue applies to natural-force and body-part nouns because their low referential salience makes incorporation semantically unobtrusive.

The Reflexive rescue applies only where the stranded possessor is coreferential with the predicate's subject — possible for subject-incorporated body-parts (possessor = experiencer = S) but not for possessed object nouns, because the inflectional possessor i= there makes the noun definite and blocks any reflexive reading .
The final row exposes the systematic gap: possessor-requiring object NI is ungrammatical because no available rescue reduces the net penalty sufficiently.
The slot is instead filled by quasi-incorporation — Satō's third verb class of idiomatic tight phrasal constructions such as par oyki 'feed' and aske uk 'invite' — treated in .
Shibatani observed that Ainu subjects do not incorporate freely: only the patient-subject of an intransitive — not the agent — incorporates, and he proposed that this tracks unaccusativity ; .
On that account, the incorporable subjects are those that originate as the underlying object of an unaccusative base, while agents of unergative predicates cannot incorporate.

Satō accepts the empirical restriction but rejects unaccusativity as the defining criterion, on the grounds that the natural-force transitive subtype — in which the original A of a transitive predicate incorporates — cannot be captured by the unaccusative account ; .
The property that covers all subtypes is low degree of agentivity: a noun is incorporable as subject when it denotes a force or body-part acting without volition, intention, or independent agency.
Waves, rain, wind, cold, and body-parts all meet this criterion; human or animal agents do not.
Unaccusativity then becomes a sufficient condition for incorporability — all unaccusative subjects qualify — but not a necessary one ‹contested›.

The connection to the split-intransitive alignment is direct: the distinction between patient-like and agent-like S arguments is already grammaticalized in Hokkaido Ainu person marking, and the class of incorporable subjects maps onto the patient-like side of that split.
The theoretical debate between the unaccusativity account and the low-agentivity account is not settled in the sources surveyed here ‹contested›.
The rarest subtype incorporates the subject of a transitive verb.

The incorporated noun is always a natural-force concept — wave, rain, snow, wind, light, deity — and must appear in concept form, not possessed form, which is the same morphological criterion that applies in the natural-force intransitive subtype ; .

The structural result is passive-like: the incorporated noun was the A of the transitive base; after incorporation the arity drops by one and the former O surfaces as the new S, taking S person suffixes.
The intransitive suffix =an (fourth-person S) on the derived verb is the diagnostic .
The attested incorporands for this subtype include , , , , , , , , and .
All denote ambient natural forces with minimal agentivity.
Satō notes that this subtype is "probably impossible in many languages", which makes it one of the more typologically distinctive features of Ainu noun incorporation .
The zero-argument meteorological predicates built on sir- can host the applicative ko-, which adds a beneficiary or experiencer and promotes it to the verb's sole indexed argument.
Forms like sir-ko-kunne 'it darkens for X / night falls for X' and ku=sir-ko-peker 'the weather brightens for me / I experience daybreak' are current in Chitose and Saru .

A community-proposed analysis (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-12-05) reads ku=sir-ko-peker as follows: the base meteorological verb sirpeker 'the weather brightens' is a closed stem in which sir- is already incorporated; the applicative ko- inserts into this closed stem between the incorporated noun and the root rather than attaching to the outside of the compound.
The ko- object — the experiencer — is then promoted to the overall subject, indexed by ku=.
Parallel structures proposed in the same discussion include maw-ko-wen 'the mist becomes bad for X' and kur-ko-tunas 'it becomes cold for someone' ‹contested›.
A related morphological observation from the same source concerns ordering.
The attested form is sir-ko-kunne, not the hypothetical *ko-sir-kunne.

This ordering — where the incorporated subject sir- precedes the applicative ko- — is consistent with subject incorporation occupying the pre-applicative, pre-root slot of the verb template, not a position inside the applicative layer, and is proposed as evidence that subject incorporation is structurally distinct from other prefix types ‹contested›.
The verb-word template is treated in , and the feeding relation between applicatives and incorporation in .

The basic architecture of noun incorporation in Hokkaido Ainu is the person-affix diagnostic: when a nominal stem merges with a verb, the person index moves to precede the entire noun-verb complex, making the incorporation a one-word structure ; .
Object (patient) and patient-like subject incorporation — the overwhelming majority — follow this path directly.

The route for oblique participants is different: an instrument, a location, a source, a purpose, or a comitative argument cannot incorporate until an applicative prefix has first promoted it to core-object status ; ; .

The further details of how applicatives stack and feed relativization belong to ; the present chapter develops the oblique-to-incorporated derivation itself and the theoretical debate over what that derivation implies.
Shibatani (1990: 67) traces the derivation through three steps, illustrated with the verb .
In the source phrase, the comitative participant pone tura ('bone' + comitative postposition tura 'with') is a peripheral argument: nea cep pone tura a=kuykuy 'I bit the fish with its bones'.
The applicative promotes pone to an additional core object, dropping the postposition and yielding the intermediate nea cep pone a=ko-kuykuy.
The newly created object then incorporates: the person prefix a= moves outside the whole complex.
Two properties of the result bear on the theoretical debate in §.

First, the affix ordering is not arbitrary: the incorporated noun sits outside the applicative, which sits inside the verb root — the order applicative-inside / incorporated-noun-outside mirrors the derivational history, consistent with what Baker (1988) terms the Mirror Principle ; .
Second, the entire sequence remains a single verb word, because no person index intervenes between the incorporated noun and the root.
examines the applicative–incorporation interaction in Ainu systematically; the constraints she identifies align with the analysis in Shibatani (1990) and Nakagawa (2024: 484).

Each postposition or case relation that can be expressed obliquely has a corresponding applicative encoding the same relation as a core object, and only through that applicative can the noun incorporate.
Nakagawa (2024: 484) summarises the pairings; the table below assembles them alongside the relevant applicative prefix and an incorporated-form gloss.

The applicative is restricted to place nouns and is rare in prose ; Shibatani (1990: 63) notes that the sequence o-tumi-osma, with the applicative, is unambiguously incorporated, whereas bare tumi osma is ambiguous between a phrase and a compound in third-person contexts (see §).
A corpus example illustrates the comitative feed in a running text.
Nakagawa (2024: 198) cites a Chitose narration in which two coordinate clauses apply ko- to the comitative participants and , incorporating both into the verb :

Once the oblique has been applicativized and then incorporated, the resulting verb word is structurally identical to an ordinary object-incorporated compound; the derivational history is preserved only in the affix order (applicative inside the noun) and in meaning.
treats the applicative–incorporation interaction as a single system on these grounds.
Adverbs incorporate directly into the verb without any applicative prerequisite.
The mechanism drops the adverbial suffix -no from the basic adverb form and places the adverb stem immediately before the verb root ; .
The minimal pair for illustrates the contrast:
A noun and an adverb may co-incorporate — Shibatani (1990: 72) cites kiraw-riki-kur-roski 'raise the horns high', with the noun kiraw 'horn' and the adverb riki 'high, up' both inside one verb word.
The one-noun-at-a-time limit is the productive norm: Shibatani (1990: 72) states that two independently incorporable nouns cannot ordinarily stack.

Nakagawa (2024: 488) records rare exceptions (cep-ya-o-kuta 'dump fish onto the shore', itak-mak-kus-te 'use hidden words'), which he places at the lexicalized fringe of the system rather than as evidence for productive double-NI.

The quasi-incorporation strategy discussed in § is a separate, structurally different response to the ceiling on NI — it handles cases where NI is grammatically blocked, not cases where noun stacking would otherwise be possible.
Ainu noun incorporation has attracted theoretical attention because it sits uncomfortably within any single prior account.

Shibatani (1988: 210–211) reviewed three frameworks at the 1988 LSJ annual meeting — Relational Grammar, Mithun's semantic account, and Baker's syntactic derivation — finding each insufficient on its own; the 1988 source is a one-page abstract, and the extended discussion appears in Shibatani (1990: 60–73).
Subsequent contributions from Satō and Bugaeva have refined the picture further.
The positions are catalogued below with evidence grades.
Baker's Case-theoretic prediction affords the clearest empirical test the debate contains.
Baker (1988) derives from Case theory that unaccusative clauses cannot undergo applicative or P-incorporation, because the internal argument already fills the available Case position .
Ainu falsifies this directly: applicatives attach freely to unaccusative bases, yielding objects that can then incorporate.
Shibatani (1990: 66) cites mokor a=e-wen 'I missed sleeping' and sake a=e-niste 'I am strong at wine', both with e- on an unaccusative base, as the falsifying data ‹contested›.
This result disfavours the specific Case-theoretic derivation without settling whether an alternative syntactic mechanism or a lexicalist account better describes the system.
Shibatani's hybrid position requires reference to both the semantic role (low agentivity) and the grammatical position (derived or original object) of the incorporated element.

Satō (2008: 226; 2022, §1) revises the semantic-role component: natural-force transitive subjects also incorporate (Type IV, 1.7% of Chitose tokens), so 'Patient' and 'unaccusative subject' are both too narrow.

The correct generalisation is the incorporated noun's low degree of agentivity — a property shared by patients, natural forces, and possessed body-parts — and no other currently defined property predicts all four types jointly .
Shibatani's grammatical-relation requirement (object or patient-subject, including applicative-derived objects) survives the revision intact.

Community discussion in the aynu-corpora Discord has noted that Ainu has very few pure-noun endocentric or exocentric compounds — constructions built solely from two nouns without a verbal head — with nominal formation concentrated on verb stems (antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, June 2026; ) ‹contested›.

Taken at face value, this would contrast Ainu with the kind of free lexical noun-noun compounding that Mithun (1984) treats as the prototype of Type I NI , lending support to treating Ainu NI as morphologically integrated into the verbal system.
The observation is a community-proposed lead and has not been submitted to systematic quantification across the corpus.
A related terminological divide runs through the valency literature and is relevant to the syntactic-vs-lexicalist question.
The prefix is analysed as an antipassive on syntactic, semantic, and discourse grounds by Bugaeva (2021), and labelled accordingly by Nakagawa (2024: 190–192) and Ijäs (Lesson 9) ; .
Satō (2008: 232–233) treats the same prefix as a derivational marker 'people, someone' without invoking the antipassive category ‹contested›.
The antipassive analysis presupposes a syntactic operation demoting a grammatical object; the derivational analysis is compatible with a fully lexicalist account of the same data.
The origin dispute and fuller analysis are in .
Satō (2016: 88; 2022, §5) assigns a markedness penalty to each NI type by summing restriction factors and subtracting rescue factors.

The penalty scores differ between the 2016 article and the 2022 Handbook chapter in their absolute values, but the rank order and the Chitose frequencies — drawn from the late Shirasawa Nabe's corpus, a single narrator — are identical across both sources.
The table records both sets of scores; Satō (2022, §5.7) himself describes them as "tentatively defined" ; .
Restriction factors: Subject NI [+10], Possessor Stranding [+15 in Satō 2022 / +10 in Satō 2016], Ambiguity [+4 in 2022 / +7 in 2016].
Rescue factors: Backgrounding [−5 in 2022 / −8 in 2016], Reflexive interpretation [−14 in 2022 / −9 in 2016].
The absolute values are tentative; the stable result is the rank order and the zero-frequency gap at the bottom ‹corpus-suggested›.

The systematic zero at the foot of the table arises because the inflectional possessor that body-part nouns require makes the incorporated noun definite and thereby removes the reflexive-rescue option.

Satō (2022, §4) illustrates the ungrammatical gap with *a=i-par-oyki 'I am fed by others' (lit. 'fed at the mouth'): i= would supply the possessor for , but i= on an object creates a definite, non-reflexive reading that blocks the rescue .

This gap is filled by what Satō terms quasi-incorporation (QI) — [O V] units that are tight, idiomatic, and non-compositional in meaning but remain transitive: the person index for the main object sits outside the QI complex as a whole, whereas in true NI the person index precedes the incorporated noun and the result is intransitive ; .
Nakagawa (2024: 494–498) calls the same items 連動詞 (serial verbs / third-class verbs).
The chapter lists the QI inventory in full; the example below shows the transitive structure that distinguishes it from NI:

The NI⊃QI accessibility hierarchy that Satō (2016: 88–92; 2022, §6) derives runs: Object NI > Natural-force intransitive subject NI > Possessor-requiring intransitive subject NI > Natural-force transitive subject NI > Possessor-requiring Object NI — with NI covering the left-hand, accessible portion and QI taking over once NI is structurally or semantically blocked.
The hierarchy extends Mithun's four-type scale into the QI domain and provides a unified account of why certain noun-verb collocations lexicalize as NI while others lexicalize as QI ; .
A register asymmetry runs across the whole system.
Nakagawa (2024: 480) notes that incorporation is commoner in verse than in prose or conversation; Ainu rarely incorporates two nouns into one verb.

The verse preference is consistent with observations in Mithun (1984) that NI often develops in rhetorically dense contexts , though the Ainu data do not support a diachronic claim about direction of change ‹speculative›.
The person-affix test that defines incorporation fails for third-person contexts.

Hokkaido Ainu marks third-person A and O with a zero morph: a sequence like cep koyki has no surface index to place inside or outside, so the test cannot determine whether the sequence is a phrasal cep koyki or an incorporated cep-koyki ; .
For any incorporable pair with two third-person arguments, lexicographic representation and interlinear glossing must choose between the two analyses without a decisive test.
Two secondary diagnostics are sometimes invoked but neither is conclusive in the general case.
Accent and intonation might separate a compound from a phrase, but Nakagawa (2024: 482) states that no firm basis for an accentual test has been established.

A derivational prefix on the nominal-verbal sequence (e.g. an applicative over the whole pair) proves one-word status when attested, since derivational morphology cannot straddle two separate words; but the prefixed form and the bare form are distinct constructions and the diagnostic applies only where the prefixed form independently exists.
The open-class-verb cases — apto as 'rain fell', upas as, rera as — are formally undecidable in the third person, and Nakagawa (2024: 493–494) leaves their word-boundary status open.
Where the fourth person replaces the third, the test is again decisive.
The fourth-person subject suffix =an is licensed only on intransitives; its presence on a noun-verb sequence is unambiguous evidence of incorporation and intransitivization.

This diagnostic has been observed in community practice with the pair kinakar=an (incorporated, intransitive) beside kina a=kar (phrasal, transitive with the fourth-person A prefix a=) for the colocation of and (thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord, December 2024; ).
The observation directly corroborates Nakagawa (2024: 482–483) and Satō (2022, §2) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

The undecidability of third-person cases does not affect the theoretical positions catalogued in § — the incorporated forms with first- and fourth-person agreement supply sufficient data for the relevant contrasts — but it does place a ceiling on frequency counts derived from surface strings.

The Chitose percentages in § are from one narrator; comparable counts for Saru or Horobetsu are not available because the undecidability of third-person tokens in other narrators' texts makes systematic NI frequency comparison across dialects intractable at present ‹speculative›.

The typological comparison — Mithun's four-type hierarchy applied to Ainu — is introduced in ; subject incorporation and possessor-stranding data are developed in ; the transitivity diagnostics that ground the person-affix test in the wider grammar belong to .
A verb stem may carry, immediately before its root, a second, non-head verb stem that reads as a manner: , .
The mechanism is the one Shibatani sets out for what he calls adverb incorporation: the adverbial suffix -no drops, and the bare stem sits against the verb root, inside the person index ; .
The minimal pair on shows the one-word result:
The person-index test that identifies noun incorporation (§) carries over: an index before the whole stem, not between modifier and root, marks the sequence as a single verb.
This chapter takes the manner variety on its own terms, because what fills the modifier slot turns out not to be an adverb.
Ainu has no adjective or adverb class distinct from the verb: property concepts are stative intransitive verbs — , , ; .
The adverb pirka-no is derived from that verb by -no.
In the incorporated construction it is the bare verb stem pirka, not the adverb pirka-no, that joins the head — the same -no-drop Shibatani describes.
The element inside the word is therefore a verb, and the label "adverb" tracks the English gloss rather than the Ainu category ‹speculative›.
The modifier need not even be intransitive.
is a transitive verb (Batchelor's tomtere 'to adorn'), and is transitive, yet both compound before with the same manner reading and the same effect on argument structure — none.
A stative pirka and a transitive tomte behave alike here, which is expected of non-head verbs in a compound and not of a lexical adverb ‹speculative›.
Because the modifier adds no participant, the head keeps its frame.

pirka-resu stays a two-place transitive: the manner verb's own single argument is identified with the head's subject, in the manner of a depictive secondary predicate, and contributes a relation rather than an argument (arity +0).
The valency layer records this as a manner_compound operation that adds an internal, non-surface slot; see .
The rearing verbs of the Chitose and Saru corpora give the clearest paradigm.
Nakagawa lists both compounds as headwords, each analysed as manner + resu: from pirka 'good', from tomte 'finely' .
Narration routinely runs the two as a couplet:
A single word can stack both manner verbs: .
Whether it brackets as [[pirka-tomte]-resu] or [pirka-[tomte-resu]] is not settled by the few attested tokens ‹corpus-suggested›.
The manner verbs sit apart from the valency-changing operations, and the two combine on one stem.
The instrument applicative promotes the means a child is raised on to a core object, giving a three-place stem eresu '…を〜で育てる':
Applied to the doubled manner stem, the same applicative yields epirkatomteresu, which Yoshikawa's Saru valency list places among the verbs of long-term action and glosses '…を〜で大事に育てる' :
The split is the point: pirkatomteresu is two-place and epirkatomteresu three-place, and the difference is carried entirely by e-.
The manner verbs modify the event; the applicative rearranges the arguments.
A noun and a manner verb may incorporate together.
Shibatani cites kiraw-riki-kur-roski 'raise the horns high', with the noun kiraw 'horn' and the element riki 'high, up' both inside one verb .

Where the modifier is a spatial word with no verbal source, like riki, the adverb analysis may hold; the productive manner class built on property verbs is the part this chapter reanalyses ‹speculative›.
The manner verb also composes below the applicatives in the long pondering verbs.

In eyaykotuymasiramsuypa 'ponder deeply about', the core is the noun-incorporation siram-suypa 'sway one's mind'; — a stative verb, glossed here 'deeply' — adds a manner over that core (+0), and only then do the applicative ko-, the reflexive yay-, and the applicative e- stack outward .
The database keeps tuyma here as the stative verb rather than a separate adverb entry, so the manner reading follows from its non-head position, not from a change of class.
Incorporation theory is built around the noun.

Mithun's four-type developmental scale is a typology of noun incorporation, and its implicational steps concern patients and case, not manner modifiers ; the syntactic (Baker) and lexicalist (Rosen) accounts likewise take N-into-V as the object of study ; ; . "Adverb incorporation" is named in passing rather than established as a category parallel to noun incorporation ‹contested›.
Read as verb-verb compounding, the Ainu pattern has clearer relatives.

A non-head predicate expressing manner or result inside one verbal word is the shape of the Chinese resultative verb compound (养好 'raise-good'); Ainu reverses that order, with the manner verb before the lexical head ‹speculative›.

Bound evaluative morphology of the Inuit type — Inuktitut -tsiaq- 'well' — translates alike but differs in kind: the postbase is bound from the lexicon, not a free verb drawn into the word, so Eskimologists treat it as derivation rather than incorporation .
Chukchi incorporates degree and quantity stems on a comparable path , and Gunwinyguan verbs admit adverbial as well as nominal incorporation ‹contested›.

The evaluative counterpart of the manner construction is not compounding at all but the applicative on the property verb: e-pirka 'be good with respect to X' keeps pirka as the head and adds the ground as an argument, the way Japanese 住みよい 'good to live in' makes the property word the head and the verb its ground.
Manner pirka-resu does the reverse: the action verb is the head and the property verb the modifier.
One asks how the event proceeds, the other whether a participant is suited to an activity, and Ainu marks the split by which element heads the word ‹speculative›.
Hokkaido Ainu is verb-final.
Every non-verbal element of the clause — nominals, adverbials, negators, subordinate clauses — precedes the verb phrase, and the verb phrase occupies the rightmost position in the sentence.
This verb-finality holds without exception: no grammatical process moves a finite verb to a non-final position .

The same head-final logic ramifies down into the noun phrase — modifiers, relative clauses, and property verbs precede the head noun — and upward into clause-level relations — subordinate clauses precede main clauses, and markers that relate an NP to the predicate follow the NP as postpositions.
Bugaeva gives the canonical summary: "the basic constituent order in Ainu is SV/AOV.
Modifiers are prepositive, and subordinate clauses come before main clauses.
All particles are postpositional.
Topical NPs tend to come first" .
The deep typological fact behind these orders is head-marking.

Satō frames the profile through Nichols's head-marking / dependent-marking distinction: the verb, as clausal head, bears obligatory person-indexing suffixes and prefixes that already satisfy all argument slots; overt NPs are accordingly optional, and when present they are appositional to those indexes rather than positional carriers of grammatical role .

The surface resemblance to Japanese — both verb-final, both postpositional — therefore conceals a fundamental typological difference: Japanese is dependent-marking, with case particles on the NP encoding grammatical relations; Ainu is head-marking, with person markers on the verb doing that work ; .
For the person-indexing apparatus that underpins this system, see .

For the question of whether optional and freely ordered overt NPs license a nonconfigurational / pronominal-argument analysis of Ainu, and for the Ainu-internal counter-evidence from the 〈location〉-noun class, see and .
For the overall typological placement of Hokkaido Ainu, see .
Nakagawa (2024: 361, §10.1) schematizes the Ainu sentence as a left-to-right sequence:
[adverbials 0…x] [NPs 0…n] [verb phrase (n)] [(evidential frame)] (sentence-final particle)
Within the preverbal field, "there is no fixed rule for the order of NP–NP and NP–adverbial; both need only be before the verb phrase" .
An evidential frame (ruwe ne, hawe ne, and the rest: see ) attaches to the right of the verb phrase; clause-linking particles (wa, hine: see ) extend further right.
Only a connective that introduces the next sentence sits outside the sentence boundary.
Head-finality applies at every level of structure.

notes one structural feature that sits awkwardly with the "ideal SOV" characterization: Ainu is simultaneously verb-final and heavily prefixing, with person-marking affixes, applicative prefixes, and incorporated nouns attaching to the left of the verb root.
In the Greenbergian correlates of SOV order, postpositions, Rel–N, and Gen–N are harmonic, but prefixing morphology is not .

The prefixing pattern follows directly from head-marking: the clausal head hosts its argument indexes and derivational material to the left of the root, independently of the clause's surface word order ‹contested›.
Whether the ordering of agent (A) and object (O) NPs among the preverbal positions is grammatically fixed is the central word-order debate in Ainu studies.
Two readings of the same data have been sustained in the literature.

Shibatani (1990: 22) argues that word order encodes grammatical role: "Since there are no case inflections on nouns, word order plays as important a role as in English in determining the grammatical functions of certain nouns." He presents the following pair as a minimal role-contrast ‹contested›:

Nakagawa counters with the observation that the same speaker, in the same session, produces three distinct orderings of the three arguments of the four-place verb epakasnu 'teach', all describing the same scene: 'my wife taught our daughter women's work' ; reproduced in English in :
A further ordering (DO – A – IO) appears in a Saru instance by the same speaker .

Nakagawa concludes that "which one is the subject cannot be grammatically determined" from word order or NP morphology; common sense — the plausibility that a wife teaches a daughter, not the reverse — is what rules out the inverted reading .
Bugaeva independently states the same finding: Ainu "does not show the syntactic relations subject and object either by case marking or by word order" ‹contested›.
Satō (2008: 2) holds a middle ground: roles are signalled by "語順 or 文脈 (word order or context)", allowing that either mechanism may operate without assigning priority to either.

Refsing's Shizunai data present a third position , §2.4, reporting Chiri (1936: 167): a default SOV order when both subject and object are full NPs, with systematic deviation to O–S–V when the subject is a prefixal person marker (the object NP then precedes the prefix-bearing verb).
Three-place clauses show "flexible" ordering, with IO before DO as the most frequent pattern when the subject is a prefix (§13.4.3).
These regularities match Nakagawa's Chitose data as statistical tendencies, not as categorical rules ‹contested›.

The zero-marking of third-person arguments — the bare verb stem simultaneously serves as the third-person and citation form — means that when both A and O are third persons, no index disambiguates the roles, and interpretation falls entirely to common sense or to the 〈location〉-noun class of one of the NPs .

The third person bears no overt affix in the standard Saru–Chitose paradigm; a possessive construction already concedes that third-person indexing is zero-marked (nukopoli, 2024-12-25, asserted, consistent with ).
See for the fourth-person form-set and its contrast with the zero-marked third person; for the free pronouns.
All prenominal modification is head-final: property verbs, relative clauses, demonstratives, genitives, and numerals all precede the head noun.

The two N + N types differ in syntactic status.
When both nouns are in the concept (non-possessed) form, the construction is a compound and the two elements cannot be separated: *sar tanne cironnup 'tail that-long fox' is ungrammatical.

When the first noun is in the concept form and the second is in the possessed (affiliative) form, the construction is an appositive possessor–possessee pair — two NPs — and the possessor can be displaced by relativization or topicalization: saraha tanne cironnup 'the tail that is long (of the fox)' is well formed .
This appositive possession structure, where the possessee is obligatorily head-marked and the possessor NP is optionally present or absent, is discussed in cross-linguistic perspective by .

Numerals occupy two alternative slots: a numeral-adnoun precedes the noun (Num–N, e.g., sine aynu 'one person') and a numeral-noun follows it (N–Num, e.g., ponmenoko sinep 'one young woman'); the two patterns are largely interchangeable for common numerals .

Core arguments — the S/A subject and the O object — are never marked by a postposition or case particle; their roles are encoded by person-marking on the verb ; .
Postpositions mark only adjunct and oblique relations: locative, ablative, goal, instrumental, and comitative.
All follow their NP, consistently maintaining the N–Postp order.
Nakagawa (2024: 386–389, §10.6) and Bugaeva (2012: 476) distinguish two morphological classes.
Postpositional adverbs can stand alone without a preceding NP and some can take person affixes; many derive from verbs still undergoing grammaticalization, such as (from 'hold') and .
Postpositional particles (格助詞) cannot stand alone, cannot be person-indexed, and function as purely relational markers: the locative and , the ablative , and the perlative belong to this class.
The translative particle (homophonous with the copula) marks the NP-as-role ('as', 'in the role of').
The classes overlap in translation; the diagnostic is whether the element can form an adverbial phrase independently .
Full treatment is in .
The standard sentential negator and the prohibitive appear before the verb phrase.
This is preverbal placement but not a special word-order fact: both are adverbs and take no person marker, so their preverbal position follows the general Adv–V rule directly ; .
Scope interactions of somo with TAM, evidentiality, and evidential-outer-frame negation (ruwe somo ne) are treated in .
The preverbal field as a whole is freely ordered with respect to adjuncts and oblique phrases.
Time adverbials, manner adverbs, and postpositional phrases can appear in any sequence before the verb phrase.
Refsing (§2.4) declines to formulate a rule for adjunct ordering in Shizunai, finding it "very free" .
Topical NPs gravitate to sentence-initial position regardless of grammatical role, and they are often — though not obligatorily — overtly marked by the topic particle :

Community discussion confirms that anak/anakne is used more sparingly than Japanese は: a referent already established in discourse need not be re-marked, and the particle carries the weight of '～に関しては (as regards ~)' rather than a routine topic reset (nukopoli, 2024-11-09, asserted, consistent with ).

Certain adjunct-ordering details show sensitivity to language-contact pressure.
The traditional sequence ani patek (instrumental ani before the focus adverb patek 'only') is in retreat in modern use in favour of the reversed patek ani.

Community analysis argues that patek is an adverb and cannot be nominalized as Japanese だけ can, so placing it first — matching Japanese particle ordering — represents Japanese-influenced reordering (nukopoli, 2024-12-16, proposed ‹contested›).
Questions do not disturb the basic constituent order.
Content-question words — , , — remain in situ at the position of the corresponding non-question constituent; there is no wh-movement to a pre-clausal position .
Polar questions are signalled by the sentence-final particle ya or by rising intonation.
The full interrogative system is in .
