The predicate in Hokkaido Ainu carries obligatory person indexes that identify its core arguments: the sole argument S of an intransitive verb, and the agent A and patient O of a transitive verb.
Overt noun phrases for those same roles are optional and, when present, stand in apposition to the index already on the verb rather than filling a case-marked argument slot.
The result is a head-marking language in the sense of : the predicate head encodes grammatical relations, and the dependent nominal does not.
develops the contrast with dependent-marking languages such as Japanese, where the argument NP bears obligatory case particles.
states the profile concisely: Ainu is agglutinating, polysynthetic, and head-marking, with verb-final constituent order and a mixed (basically tripartite) morphological alignment.
This chapter asks how S, A, and O are realised at the clause level: through bound indexes, through optional overt NPs, or through null.
The person-affix paradigm itself — its cells, allomorphy, and the S/A/O distinctions — belongs to and the chapters that follow it.
Morphological alignment is pursued in .
Pragmatic word order and topic fronting are treated in and .
Reference tracking across clauses — zero anaphora, the fourth person in narrative, the absence of switch-reference morphology — is taken up in .
Person indexes are not optional agreement controllers: they are the grammatical realisation of the argument itself.
A finite verb without any overt NP is a complete, well-formed sentence.
The intransitive with its first-singular prefix is self-sufficient as a one-word utterance:

states the principle directly: "grammatical relations (subject and object) … are not obligatory elements in Ainu; rather it is the personal affixes that are obligatory for the predicates." formulates the same point as pro-drop with obligatory indexing: the language drops its overt NPs freely because the index already encodes the referent.
A fuller transitive clause shows the same structure: without the NP cep 'fish', a=koyki 'catch' is a grammatically complete predication indexing a fourth-person agent and a third-person patient.

Independent personal pronouns — kani 'I', eani 'you' — are available for emphasis or contrast but are used more sparingly than their Japanese counterparts, since the verbal index already does the referential work ; .
They are a distinct word class from the bound indexes and are treated in .
An attested uwepeker line shows the division of labour directly.

The contrastive pronoun eani 'you' is fronted and topicalised for the moment of identification, while the verbal indexes already encode both participants — a=kor 'I have' and e=ne 'you are' — so the pronoun adds emphasis without carrying referential work of its own:
When an overt NP does appear for a core role, its structural position relative to the verb is not that of a case-flagged argument filling a valency slot.

, working within Role and Reference Grammar, places the person index as the PRO inside the clausal CORE — the actual argument — and positions the co-referential NP outside the CORE as an optional, non-obligatory element.

The Lakhota-parallel structure he gives for cep a=koyki has the same logical structure (LS) whether the NP is present or absent; the NP adds lexical specification without changing the underlying argument count.
An immediate formal consequence is that no case particle marks the S/A/O distinction on the NP itself.
Ainu carries no markers corresponding to Japanese が or を for core roles ; ; .
Two NPs in the same clause — say, an agent and a patient — bear no formal distinction between them on the nominal.
Role is readable from the verbal index and from contextual plausibility; a consequence explored in is that the preverbal NPs may appear in any sequence.

The same appositive status holds for possessor NPs: the possessee is obligatorily head-marked by a person prefix, so "pronominal possessor NPs are normally not used and even nominal possessor NPs may easily be omitted if contextually recoverable" .

captures the same pattern pedagogically, describing the verb as having obligatory "pockets" for its arguments and the overt NP as redundant: "you would need to convey the same information twice but that would be very uneconomical."

"It is not necessary in Ainu for a noun phrase that is clear from the context to appear in a sentence, and such a noun phrase is not even represented by a pronoun; even if a verb takes two objects, it is normal for only one of them to be present" — (ch.14, before ex.75).

formalises this in the sentence template: a NP "need not be present in the sentence as long as it can be supplied meaningfully from context." The missing argument is read as a zero anaphor — not a phonologically null pronoun alongside the index, but the index itself satisfying the valency slot with no additional NP exponency.
A particularly clear case arises with three-place verbs.
A verb hosts at most one subject index and one object index (; ), so the third argument of a ditransitive — typically the theme — is never indexed and appears only as an optional bare NP or is null.
Its reference remains unambiguous: "verbal valency guarantees the interpretation of anaphoric reference without any personal affix" .
The following clause is the second in a two-sentence passage; the preceding clause establishes the theme (a sweet).
The second clause drops it entirely, leaving only the human recipient and the first-singular agent overt or indexed:
The third person is zero-marked throughout the paradigm: the bare verb stem without any affix expresses a third-person argument.
argues that recognising a possessive prefix a= (fourth person) already commits the analyst to a zero third-person affix in the slot that a= contrasts with.
describes the same paradigm without explicitly positing a zero affix ‹contested›; the status of the zero is examined in .

A community observation corroborates the zero-3rd-person analysis: "the bare verb form = 3SG = citation/dictionary form" and "using a possessive already concedes a zero 3rd person" (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-25, asserted) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
provides the master inventory of how a core argument can be realised in a head-marking Ainu clause.
The five modes are not mutually exclusive — noun incorporation combines bound morphology with what would otherwise be an NP slot — but they represent the primary structural options:

draws a theoretical conclusion from this inventory: because argument fulfilment is "sometimes by syntactic means and sometimes by morphological means," the syntax/morphology boundary "is blurred in Ainu," a consequence of its head-marking character.
Mode 4 in particular — the theme as bare NP without an index — "partly shows a dependent-marking characteristic" while remaining under head-marking control.

further uses the attested A-incorporation pattern (ku=koy-yanke 'the waves wash me ashore') to argue against Baker's () syntactic head-movement theory of incorporation: since the person index already anchors the argument inside the verb, incorporation need not be derived by NP movement.

Whether overt NPs that co-occur with verbal indexes should be analysed as true arguments of the verb or as appositives to pronominal arguments already residing on the verb is an open analytical question that the literature on Ainu explicitly engages ‹contested›.

The pronominal-argument position (associated with Jelinek 1984 and Baker 1988/1996, as framed in ch.1 §4.3) holds that in head-marking languages the bound indexes are the clause's actual arguments and co-referential NPs are mere appositives that lexically qualify them — adjuncts, not arguments.

Applied to Ainu, this analysis predicts that an overt NP should be freely omissible (attested), freely ordered (attested), uncased (attested), and potentially discontinuous (attested for floating quantifiers; ).
As a theoretical classification it would place Ainu in the nonconfigurational company of Mohawk or Lakhota.
The full battery of diagnostics is examined in .
(ch.1 §4.3) names and entertains the pronominal-argument position but does not adopt it for Ainu.

Her preferred account, aligned with Mithun (2003, cited in Bugaeva 2022 ch.1 §4.3), is shared argumenthood: bound pronouns and coreferential NPs jointly share argumenthood, neither alone being the sole argument.

The Ainu-specific evidence she marshals is the location-class noun (see §6 below): when both A and O are third-person and therefore zero-indexed, what disambiguates the two roles is the semantic class of one of the NPs — specifically whether it is a locative-type noun.
If NPs were pure appositives with no grammatical traction, their semantic class would have no leverage on role assignment; the fact that it does points toward retained argumenthood.

, working in Role and Reference Grammar, gives a third structural description: the person index is the PRO inside the clausal CORE, and the co-referential NP sits outside the CORE — architecturally close to the pronominal-argument analysis but without endorsing the PAH label or a nonconfigurational classification.
Satō does not invoke Jelinek's Pronominal Argument Hypothesis or describe Ainu as nonconfigurational; the account is head-marking with an optional external appositive.
The current consensus is partial.
That Ainu is head-marking, pro-drop, without core case, and with freely ordered optional overt NPs is uncontested.

Whether those NPs are appositive adjuncts to pronominal arguments (Jelinek/Baker line) or share argumenthood with the indexes (Mithun/Bugaeva line) is contested, and no Ainu specialist has published a dedicated pronominal-argument study; the framing reaches Ainu only through Bugaeva's and Satō's typological treatments, and Bugaeva's own preferred position argues against the pure appositive reading.
The chapter-length treatment is in .
When both the agent and the patient of a transitive clause are third person — zero-indexed, no case marking, no fixed order — the verbal indexes supply nothing to distinguish agent from patient.
This is the empirical gap at the centre of Bugaeva's counter-argument to the pure appositive analysis.
(ch.14) documents the resolution: what disambiguates the roles is the location-class status of a noun.
Locative relational nouns such as , , and — attached after an NP — mark that NP as a Location argument, leaving the other NP unambiguously as the theme or patient.
The disambiguation is lexical and semantic, not morphological: it depends on the inherent or augmented location-class status of one NP, not on a separate case affix.

As (ch.1 §4.4) notes, the mechanism is "particularly relevant when one of the arguments is omitted" — when the non-location NP is null, the locative NP's class alone tells the listener what role the missing argument fills.

The contrast with Nivkh is instructive: Nivkh also lacks case on S/O but fixes the object immediately preverbal and signals it by a consonant mutation; Ainu uses neither device, relying on indexing and the location class instead .
The locative noun system and its postpositional extensions are treated in and .

Because arguments are indexed on the verb and overt NPs are optional, participant continuity across a narrative rests primarily on zero anaphora plus the verbal indexes themselves; pronouns are not routinely redeployed to maintain reference.
Overt NP re-mention is reserved for (re)introduction, contrast, or scene change (ch.14); .
The fourth person does additional tracking work in narrative.

In oral texts it marks the protagonist's or quoted speaker's first person as distinct from both the plain third-person cast and the narrating speaker's first singular, functioning as an obviative-like "other first person" ; .

An observed instance: in an uwepeker telling, the narrator alternates a= and ku= to keep the in-story protagonist's speech separate from the narrator's own voice (thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-07-04, asserted) .
This alternation is consistent with 's logophoric analysis of the fourth-person quotation use and with 's narrative first-person account.

The fourth person's full referential range and its interaction with topic-marking are treated in , , and ; the wider reference-tracking apparatus — zero anaphora, clause chaining, and the absence of morphological switch-reference — is taken up in and .
Hokkaido Ainu combines two properties whose joint presence creates genuine analytical tension.
The finite verb is clause-final without exception, and every phrase type is head-final: modifier precedes head, postposition follows noun, subordinate clause precedes main clause ; .

At the same time, within the preverbal field the relative order of noun phrases is controlled by information structure rather than grammatical function: the same three-argument verb epakasnu 'teach' is attested with its arguments in at least four different preverbal sequences in natural speech from a single speaker, and no case particle indicates which NP is subject and which is object ; .

What fixes grammatical roles is the verb's obligatory person-index system: bound argument-marking affixes appear on every finite predicate, and an overt NP is structurally optional — an elaboration on a participant already indexed, not a required structural position ; .

These properties place Ainu in the cross-linguistic neighbourhood of head-marking languages such as Mohawk and Lakhota, whose argument NPs have been analysed as adjuncts to pronominal argument positions inside the verb — the Pronominal-Argument Hypothesis (PAH) as reviewed by .

Whether that analysis extends to Ainu is a question the accessible literature addresses but does not settle; the present chapter sets out the evidence, the competing positions, and what Ainu unambiguously does and does not exhibit.
The verb-finality rule and the head-final NP structure are treated in ; the person-affix paradigm, alignment typology, and ditransitive indexing cap belong to and its sibling chapters.
A finite verb in Ainu marks its arguments by means of bound person prefixes and, for some persons, suffixes; these affixes are obligatory on every predicate.
Satō, following the head-marking framework of , describes the verb as the clausal head that bears the central information about which participants fill its valence frame .
A finite verb alone, with no overt NPs at all, is a complete and grammatical clause:
When an overt NP does appear, its relationship to the verb is appositional rather than structurally necessary.
In Role and Reference Grammar terms, Satō places the person prefix (PRO) inside the CORE as the actual argument, with any co-occurring NP outside the CORE as an optional, non-obligatory adjunct .
This is the Lakhota-type structure: "the same logical structure gives rise to morphologically different structures" depending on how many overt NPs are supplied .
The overt object NP in the following example holds precisely that adjunct status:
Personal pronouns, being informationally redundant with the person index, are used only for emphasis or contrast and are rarer in Ainu than their Japanese counterparts ; .
The independent pronoun kani 'I' can co-occur with ku=mina 'I laughed', but without kani the clause still indexes a specific first-person singular subject; the pronoun is emphatic, not anaphoric .

The possessor NP stands in the same appositional relationship to the possessed noun: the possessee is obligatorily head-marked by an agreement prefix, so the possessor NP is normally omitted and expressed only when referentially new or contrastive .

The community observation that the bare verb form with no person affix is the third-person form and the citation form of the verb — with the zero-marking implicitly conceding a zero third-person affix — is consistent with Satō's formal argument that such a zero is required by the two-affix cap on finite verbs (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-25, asserted; ) ‹contested›.
This debate is developed in .
With intransitive predicates the single preverbal NP is unambiguously the S argument.
With transitives, the evidence is divided, and the ordering question is the analytical crux of this chapter.
Shibatani uses the following minimal pair to argue that linear position determines grammatical function:
Both NPs are third person, zero-marked; role assignment differs only by position.

Shibatani concludes that word order "plays as important a role as in English in determining the grammatical functions of certain nouns" , allowing object-first order only when context or semantics rules out an incorrect reading.
Satō's introductory description is comparably cautious: the role of an NP is "shown by word order or context" .

The pedagogical grammar of likewise describes Ainu as SOV and explains apparent flexibility by appeal to the zero third-person marker, such that "if we put the linguists' zero mark (Ø) in our example sentence … the word order indeed is correct." This framing is pedagogically effective but does not engage the evidence for genuine order freedom.
That evidence comes from Nakagawa's Chitose data.

Three utterances by the same speaker describing the same scene place the three arguments of epakasnu 'teach' in three different preverbal sequences, all translating as 'my wife taught our daughter women's work' ; reproduced in English at :
A fourth order (DO – A – IO) is attested in a Saru text .

Nakagawa's conclusion is explicit: "since the noun phrase itself carries no indicator of which is subject and which is object, which one is the subject cannot be grammatically determined"; the disambiguation rests on "common sense" and knowledge of the scene, not on syntactic position .
Bugaeva, drawing on the same data, states that Ainu "does not show its subject and object either by case marking or by word order" .

This is the ‹contested› heart of the question: whether role is fixed by first-noun default (Shibatani, Satō 2008) or is genuinely free and recoverable only via person-indexing and real-world plausibility (Nakagawa, Bugaeva).

No corpus-level count of A-before-O versus O-before-A frequencies in transitive clauses exists in the literature consulted; the Nakagawa triple is the strongest available evidence, but it derives from one speaker in one session ‹contested›.
The topic particle anak(ne) in example 702 is a distinct confound: when a NP is overtly marked as topic it tends to come first regardless of grammatical role ; .
The fuller treatment of topicalization and left-dislocation belongs to and .

The community observation that anak/anakne is used with far less frequency than Japanese は, carrying approximately the weight of 'as regards' rather than a default topic marker, is consistent with the descriptive literature's picture of a device that marks rather than requires left-periphery position (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-09, asserted; ; cf.
) ‹corpus-suggested›.

A separate class of word-order evidence comes from right-dislocation: some Ainu texts place the subject or object NP after the verb, attached via the light verb ki 'do', providing participant specification after the predicate has already established the referential relations .
This discourse-level device is a processing-driven supplement to verb-final order, not a grammaticalized alternative to it.
Null arguments are the default state of Ainu syntax.
A verb's person affixes index every participant, so overt NPs appear only when they carry additional discourse work — introducing a referent, contrasting it, or marking it as topic.
Nakagawa formalizes this in his sentence template: a NP "need not be present in the sentence as long as it can be supplied meaningfully from context, and the sentence still stands" .

Satō, framing the same observation under head-marking, writes that "grammatical relations (subject and object) … are not obligatory elements in Ainu; rather it is the personal affixes that are obligatory for the predicates" .
When a participant is contextually available, the standard strategy is zero anaphora: the missing argument triggers no overt substitute, not even an independent pronoun.

Bugaeva illustrates this for a demoted oblique: in itanki huraye hine (itanki) ani Ø=i=ko-i-puni 'she washed a bowl and served me food with (that bowl)', the second mention of the bowl "can easily be omitted and the sentence would trigger a zero-anaphora interpretation 'holding (that bowl)'" .

Ditransitives extend the same pattern: the language's two-affix cap means a third argument cannot be indexed, so it is expressed as a bare NP whose reference is guaranteed by verbal valency rather than by its own person marking .
The cap is treated in and the object-indexing chapters.
The following attested clause illustrates how overt possessed-NPs in narrative serve to reintroduce participants rather than maintain ongoing reference.
Both NPs name the narrator's parents, which context would have made recoverable, but appear here to foreground the two co-subjects of the embedding:
Reference continuity in oral narrative depends primarily on the unbroken chain of person affixes across linked clauses, not on overt NP repetition.
Re-introduction by NP marks a scene change or new referential ground, a function treated in the reference-tracking chapter ().
A standard diagnostic for nonconfigurationality is the permissibility of discontinuous NPs: two parts of one noun phrase separated by material that is not part of that phrase.

Nakagawa provides an attested Saru instance in which the head noun toma 'mat' and its numeral sinep 'one' are separated by the focus particle ka 'even', yet the predicate isam 'be absent' is an intransitive verb requiring exactly one S argument:

Nakagawa frames this via verbal arity rather than via the nonconfigurationality literature, but structurally it instantiates what that literature treats as quantifier float: the numeral has drifted from its host noun into a position that an independent argument would occupy.

The community observation that the pattern N + adverbial-numeral + V (pasuy sinep uk 'takes one chopstick') is "perfectly normal, maybe more frequent than in Japanese" is consistent with quantifier float being productive in Ainu, though frequency claims remain unverified (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-12, proposed; ) ‹corpus-suggested›.
The NP-internal ordering of head and numeral is treated in .
The standard diagnostics for nonconfigurationality, as applied to Ainu in and , pattern as follows:
Six of the seven diagnostics are positive.
The seventh — rigid verb-finality — is a counter-signal.
In the best-described nonconfigurational languages (Warlpiri, Jiwarli), the verb can appear in any position among the free NPs.
Ainu's verb-finality is absolute: every adverbial, every NP, every negative somo precedes the verb phrase, but the verb phrase itself does not move.
Nichols notes that head-marking languages achieve word-order freedom through either verb-initial or verb-final strategies with equal ease ; Ainu takes the verb-final option.
Its preverbal field is pragmatically ordered but bounded by the clause edge.
The combination — verb-final, head-marking, caseless core arguments, free preverbal NP order — is typologically rare.

Nakagawa observes that languages with SOV order that mark neither subject nor object by case nor by fixed position "are probably relatively rare"; he cites Nivkh as the nearest geographic neighbour and notes that Nivkh compensates with obligatory immediately-preverbal object position plus a consonant-mutation dependency, while Ainu does neither .

The Pronominal-Argument Hypothesis holds that in head-marking languages the bound affixes are the actual grammatical arguments and the free NPs are adjuncts — lexical specifications of what the pronominal arguments refer to, with no direct argument status of their own.
This position is associated with the work of Jelinek and of Baker, as reviewed in and in .
The logical consequence for syntax is that there are no argument positions for NPs to fill, which is why they can appear discontinuously and in any order: they are not in the phrase structure at all.
Ainu's profile — obligatory affixes, optional NPs, free preverbal order, null anaphora, discontinuous NPs, no case — fits this description wherever the accessible data bear on it ‹contested›.
Bugaeva presents the hypothesis explicitly and then argues against the pure appositive reading for Ainu:
"There remains an important theoretical issue of whether NPs in head-marking languages are arguments or clause constituents of any kind at all.

A number of researchers consider them mere appositives that lexically specify or qualify the actual arguments, which are on the verb. … However, a more widely accepted view is that argumenthood is shared between bound pronouns and coreferential NPs.
As to Ainu, the latter view seems to fit better because there is an extra <location> elaboration on the noun …"
The Ainu-specific counter-argument turns on a subset of nouns with inherent locative semantics.

When two third-person arguments of a three-place verb are both zero-marked, the locative-noun class — nouns such as or 'place (of)', sam 'near', ka 'above', corpok 'below', as well as the category of place-role nouns (kim 'mountain-area', pis 'beach-area') — distinguishes the Location argument from the Theme.

Nakagawa's Chitose example [ci a=e-p] [saranip or] oma-re 'she put the cooked food into the basket' shows the mechanism: the NP saranip or (basket + locative or) is unambiguously the Goal because it contains a locative noun, leaving the other NP as Theme; without or, the two basket-and-food NPs would be ambiguous .
Bugaeva reads this as evidence that the noun carries grammatically relevant information about its own argument role, which a purely appositive / PAH NP would not need to do .
The counter-argument has two acknowledged limits.

First, it applies only when one argument is a Location: in the many transitive clauses where neither argument is locative — including the kamuy aynu rayke pair — the disambiguation rests on plausibility and world knowledge, not on lexical noun class.
Nakagawa is explicit that in those cases it falls back on "common sense" .
Second, the argument rests on a small number of illustrative examples and has not been tested against a quantified corpus of three-argument clauses with two zero-marked third-person NPs ‹contested›.

Satō's analysis, using Role and Reference Grammar, reaches a structurally PAH-like result — person affixes fill the argument positions inside the CORE, NPs sit outside it as optional adjuncts — but within a framework that does not endorse the PAH label, and it explicitly rejects the head-movement analysis of as unable to handle the attested subject incorporation in Ainu (koy-yanke 'the waves wash [me] ashore', where the A argument is incorporated into the verb) ; .
Noun incorporation and its implications for argument structure are the subject of and .

The three positions — PAH-type (NPs as adjuncts, affixes as sole arguments), shared argumenthood (Bugaeva), and RRG-structural (Satō) — produce near-identical empirical predictions for the phenomena described in this chapter; they differ in theoretical commitments about what counts as an argument.
No Ainu specialist has published a study dedicated to the PAH or the nonconfigurationality hypothesis as such; the framing reaches Ainu through Bugaeva's and Satō's typological discussions.
Chapter authors should present the classification as a live framing question rather than an established result ‹contested›.
Several properties typical of the best-described nonconfigurational languages are absent from or unattested in Hokkaido Ainu, and these absences limit the scope of any nonconfigurationality claim.
No morphological switch-reference. Warlpiri and many Australian languages deploy dedicated same-subject / different-subject morphology on non-finite verb forms (converbs).
Ainu has no converbs and no morphological switch-reference (; ).

Reference continuity across linked clauses is maintained by the obligatory person affixes on each finite predicate, by zero anaphora, and by the fourth-person logophoric device — functional substitutes, not formal equivalents of switch-reference morphology .

No wh-movement. Content-question words remain in situ: hunna 'who', hemanta 'what', hunak 'where' occupy the same position they would hold in a corresponding declarative, with no movement to a left-peripheral question position .
This is consistent with a head-marking typology but is shared with many language types that are not nonconfigurational.
Verb-finality is rigid. Unlike Warlpiri, where the finite verb participates in the general NP-scrambling freedom, the Ainu verb does not leave clause-final position.

This is the one reliable constituent-order fact: every preverbal element — NPs, adverbials, negative somo, topic-marked constituents — is ordered by discourse and pragmatics, but the verb-phrase occupies clause-final position without exception ; .
The verb-final constraint is the one point on which all sources, across the dispute about whether order is otherwise free, agree.
No dedicated person-tracking morphology on the NP. Case suffixes on NPs exist only for obliques (postpositional adverbs and case particles); core S/A/O NPs are bare.
There is no obviation morphology on the NP, no "obviative" nominal suffix marking a secondary third-person referent.

The fourth-person prefix set on the verb does analogous work for first- and fourth-person participants in discourse, but it is verbal morphology, not nominal, and it targets person, not rank-in-discourse ‹contested›
Reference continuity in Ainu oral narrative is maintained primarily by the verbal person-index system combined with zero anaphora.
A participant introduced by an overt NP in one clause is reidentified in later clauses by the recurrence of the same person index on the finite predicate, with no overt NP required.
Re-mention by NP signals reintroduction, scene change, or contrastive foregrounding — not ordinary anaphoric continuity.
The fourth-person form-set () performs additional tracking work in oral narrative.
It marks the protagonist's viewpoint and first-person reference inside the reported world, distinct from both the narrating speaker's first person (ku=) and the unmarked third (zero).

In performance, narrators alternate a= (fourth-person agent) and ku= (first-singular agent) to distinguish the in-story protagonist's speech from the narrator speaking as herself; this alternation has been observed in attested uwepeker performance (thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-07-04, asserted; ; consistent with ) ‹corpus-suggested›.
The logophoric analysis of the fourth-person narration device is in .
For clauses with two zero-marked third-person arguments, the locative-noun class provides a lexical disambiguation device.
When one argument is a locative noun or a noun modified by a locative element (or, sam, etc.), it is unambiguously the Location argument, leaving the other NP as Theme or Patient .
Outside that subset, disambiguation rests on plausibility.

Ainu therefore substitutes a combination of person-index transparency, lexical semantics, and discourse context for the case-marking and fixed-position strategies that other SOV languages use to track grammatical role across clauses .

Verbal number contributes independently in some environments: the transitive plural stems mark object plurality — rayke → ronnu 'kill' — an ergative-like S≈O≠A pattern in the number system that disambiguates S and O for zero-marked third persons when the count of participants differs (consistent with the community observation by nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-12, asserted; ).
The fuller treatment of verbal number as a grammatical resource is in and .

Clause-linkage particles pattern with participant continuity statistically but not morphologically: wa correlates with same-subject sequences in Refsing's Shizunai count, but the correlation is not grammatically enforced and carries no formal same-subject / different-subject encoding .
This is treated in full in and .
Hokkaido Ainu has essentially no verbless predication at the structural level.

As Nakagawa states in the Handbook chapter on parts of speech, "the element that occupies the predicate position in Ainu is invariably a verb phrase and the head of the verb phrase is a verb or an auxiliary verb" .
A bare nominal or oblique phrase cannot stand as the main predicate of a sentence.

What looks verbless in discourse is always one of four things: an ambient verb with an incorporated nominal root and no overt subject; an insubordinated formal-noun clause reduced to its nominalizer; a vocative or exclamative fragment that is not a predication at all; or genuine ellipsis of a recoverable predicate under discourse conditions that license it.
These are the phenomena organized in this chapter.
The three productive structural predicate types — copular, existential/locational, and property-concept — are treated in , , and respectively; the present chapter maps their borders.

The nearest Ainu equivalent to an 'impersonal' or 'ambient' clause is the zero-place verb (完全動詞), in which a nominal root is incorporated into an existential or posture verb to form a word that predicates an ambient state with no subject slot and no person indexing ; ; .
The most transparent example is , etymologically + the existential — 'coldness exists' — which Shibatani explicitly analyses as noun incorporation .
The same root combines with property verbs to make weather predicates: (= ⁠-), (= ⁠-), (= ⁠-).
The posture verb forms the parallel 'voice' ambient: (= ⁠-).
The grammar-diagnostic pair is the contrast between a 0-place ambient and a 1-place experiential verb with the same root.
'the weather is cold' takes no person affix and no subject, while 'feel cold' takes the standard intransitive subject index:

The parallel 0-place / 1-place split holds for hawas 'there is a sound' vs 'X says'; a single nominal root surfaces in both, but the 0-place member predicates an ambient event in the scene, while the 1-place member requires an indexed agent-experiencer .
The zero-place class is small and largely lexicalized (weather, atmospheric light, acoustic ambiance); productivity is limited .
The noun-incorporation mechanism that creates them is treated in ; the existential an in the aspect-auxiliary role is treated in .
There is no clause type in Hokkaido Ainu in which a bare oblique phrase — a postpositional phrase, a locational NP, a temporal adverb — functions as the predicate of a main clause.
Nakagawa's clause-constituent analysis (§10.1) treats adverbs, case-marked NPs, and postpositional adverbs uniformly as adjuncts on the verb phrase, never predicate heads .

Refsing states the complementary positive requirement: locational and existential meanings are expressed with the existential verb, not with a bare PP — she lists no 'locational copula' type separate from an/oka(y) in the Shizunai grammar .

The practical consequence is that a Japanese-style bare 'topic–locative' sentence (トキヨには大きな家が多い) is dispreferred in Ainu: the intransitive existential an cannot take a bare second NP because it is strictly one-argument.
The natural pattern marks the location as an oblique with or ta 'in the place of' (or bare ta), leaving the existential as the predicate head .

The community discussion of this constraint, confirmed against Satō's account, gives the rule concisely: an is intransitive, so the frame is A B or ta an 'A is at B', while the transitive licenses a bare nominal complement A B un without or ta (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-09, confirmed against ) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Because obliques never head a predicate, a phrase like kotan ta 'in the village' requires an or oka to form a complete predication: kotan ta an 'is in the village', not bare *kotan ta.
This parallels the constraint that the copula ne is needed for predicate-nominal clauses (a Japanese-style bare-nominal predicate is also excluded).
In both cases the verbal head is obligatory, and what reads as a 'nominal predicate' or 'locational predicate' in English always has a verb beneath it.
The copular frame A B ne serves not only to classify (see for its full paradigm) but also to label and name referents in discourse.

The specificational pattern — where a nominalized clause is the subject and a name or title is the complement — is particularly frequent in naming contexts and in traditional oral narrative when a deity or character is formally introduced.
Nakagawa's example of this frame comes from the formal-noun-headed subject:

In this pattern the formal noun hawe 'voice, utterance' functions as the possessed-form nominalizer that packages the quotative clause as a referential NP, and the copula ne predicates identity between the subject and the named referent.
This is not a separate construction from the ordinary copular clause; it is the same frame with a nominalized complement.
The formal nouns that head these nominalized clauses are defined in ; the quotative particle sekor belongs to the quotative complementation chapter.

The sekor a=ye hawe ne frame is also the canonical 'it is called X' formula for introducing traditional names of places, deities, and artefacts in oral narrative, functioning as a specificational-naming copular in the context of cultural transmission.
The constituent structure — [[sekor a=ye] hawe] ne — keeps the copula ne as the single predicate head; there is no head-stacking and no verbless portion.

The copula's person marking follows the standard transitive-subject set on the nominative argument (see the person-marking architecture chapter); the absence of an object person index on ne, despite its two-place semantics, is the diagnostic idiosyncrasy noted by Nakagawa: the complement NP takes no object affix on the copula .
Nakagawa 2024 lays out a four-member paradigm for the sentence-final formal-noun frame, in which the choice of predicate after the nominalizer encodes illocutionary force .

The declarative and content-question members take the copula ne and the existential an respectively (treated in the evidential chapters for , , , and ); what concerns this chapter is the reduction of that frame to a bare formal noun — without either ne or an — which functions as a polar question or exclamative:

The bare-nominalizer polar question is an instance of insubordination: a nominalized clause that would ordinarily be embedded under the copula or existential stands instead as a main clause, retaining the illocutionary force of a question or exclamation from prosodic and contextual cues rather than from any grammatical marker.
The sentence e=eraman hawe? 'you understood?' is a polar question in Saru without the following ne or an .
The same shape can function as an exclamative — expressing surprise or emphatic assertion — again distinguished from the declarative only by intonation.
Nakagawa notes the Saru reinforced form ruwe he an? (with the particle he and the existential) as a more explicit polar-question variant .
The affirmative-answer member NMLZ + un likewise reduces the declarative frame by replacing the copula with the final particle un, forming a minimally marked confirmation.
The formal-noun head is retained, making the affirmative answer morphologically kin to the declarative without being one:
An additional bare-predicate use of isam functions as the full predicate of a content question in the corpus.
Nakagawa's example shows isam, isam? 'it's gone, gone?' functioning as the rhetorical pivot of a question where the missing entity is already established in discourse:
These fragment-like patterns are not structurally verbless: the formal noun is nominalized from a full clause and the bare-NMLZ frame still has a verbal predicate implicit in the nominalization.
Predicationally, the clause is complete; it is only the final copula or existential that is elided under the reduced illocutionary frames.
This is therefore ellipsis at the right edge of the clause, conditioned by illocutionary force, rather than an absence of predication.
The full treatment of the evidential paradigm and its illocutionary differentiation is in ; sentence-final particles that interact with these frames are treated in .
In response to a content question the standard strategy is to repeat the relevant verb phrase, matching the morphology of the questioned predicate.

There are no dedicated 'yes' and 'no' words in the affirmation/negation sense that English uses for all questions (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-04, asserted; reported across multiple dialects; confirmed against the affirmative-frame ruwe un of Nakagawa 2024: 396) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
For polar questions (yes/no questions), there is notable dialect variation.

In the Saru dialect the answer pattern mirrors Japanese: the respondent targets the propositional content of the question and affirms or denies it ('no, I am not going' in reply to 'are you not going?').

In other dialects — attested for Yakumo, Horobetsu, Tokachi, Bibai, Asahikawa, and Sōya among others — the respondent avoids a simple yes/no particle altogether and instead repeats the relevant verb phrase.

To a negative polar question like somo e=oman ya? 'are you not going?', a speaker from these dialects would reply with the verb alone, such as somo ku=oman 'I am not going' or ku=oman kus ne 'I am going (because)', rather than with an affirmation or denial particle (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-04, asserted ✔; reported across eight dialect localities: Yakumo, Horobetsu, Saru, Tokachi, Bibai, Asahikawa, Nayoro, and Sōya) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

The forms e, ho, and m that superficially resemble affirmation/agreement particles are response-to-call utterances, used when a speaker is addressed by name or summoned — not as affirmations of propositional content (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-04, asserted ✔) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
They are treated under .

The minimal answer clause is therefore a predicate-only utterance: the subject is entirely omitted and the verb phrase — including any person indexes that anchor the participants — is the complete response.
This is predicate ellipsis (the subject NP and topic marker are recoverable from the question), not absence of predication.
Interrogative strategies and the full polar-question morphosyntax are treated in .
Direct address in Hokkaido Ainu uses bare nominal forms — personal names, kin terms, or title nouns — with no predicate.
These are not propositions and not even elliptical predications; they are illocutionary acts of calling or summoning a participant.
Their grammatical content is entirely addressee-targeting: the utterance indexes who is being addressed, not what is being said about them.

In that sense vocative fragments are structurally parallel to the response-to-call particles above — both are non-propositional speech acts that lack a predicate by virtue of their illocutionary type, not by virtue of any structural anomaly.

Kin terms used in vocative address may appear in the plain uninflected (non-possessed) form rather than the possessed/affiliative form that the same term would take when used referentially inside a clause, since the affiliative suffix presupposes a possessor argument that is not relevant in a direct address.
The illocutionary inventory of Hokkaido Ainu, including the interaction of address, register, and honorific speech, is the subject of and .

One productive minor construction builds on the copula by adding the conditional particle : the frame [Subject] [Complement] ne yakun expresses a condition on class membership or identity — 'if (S) is (C), then …' ; .

Ijäs treats the construction as a standard conditional antecedent in her pedagogical grammar, noting that the copula in the conditional takes the same transitive-subject person indexes as in the declarative .

In the factual sense the construction is just a copular clause with yakun in the conditional-particle slot that the clause-linkage system places at the right edge of a dependent clause (see for the full conditional system).
The frame is especially frequent in discourse framing, where a speaker conditionally asserts the identity of a referent as a premise for what follows.
The negative counterpart places the standard copula negator before ne: X ka somo ne yakun 'if (S) is not (C)' (see for the ka somo ne copula negation pattern, and for the existential counterpart).
The person-marking behaviour is the same as in the declarative copular clause, including the idiosyncrasy whereby the copula takes no object-person affix even though it is semantically two-place .

One micro-fact about ne in the ka somo ne negation frame and sporadically in other contexts is that the copula appears without a subject affix — the person marking is absent in a way not predicted by the zero-marking of third person (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-25, speculative; "reason unclear") ‹speculative›.
This is an open gap in the description: no read primary source addresses the pattern systematically, and no structural account of the affix loss has been proposed.
It may reflect the frozen or idiom-like status of the ka somo ne string, but this remains without structural support.

The copula also participates in the inchoative 'become' reading when followed by the existential an (the ne an sequence discussed by community members as the Ainu equivalent of Japanese 〜になる) (thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-13, proposed; consistent with Refsing 1986: 145 and Nakagawa 2024: 118–119) ‹contested›.
That inchoative construction is the interface between the copula and the TAM system and is treated in and .
Across the constructions in this chapter, a common thread is the conditions under which the predicate — or its final element — is absent from the surface string.
Three environments license predicate-omission or predicate-reduction in Hokkaido Ainu:

Illocutionary reduction (formal-noun fragments, §above): the copula or existential that ordinarily closes the formal-noun frame is elided when the illocutionary force is polar-interrogative or exclamative.
The nominalizer is retained; only the predicate over it is absent.
The licensing condition is a specific illocutionary type, not a general ellipsis rule.

Discourse-anaphoric ellipsis (elliptical answers, §above): in responses to polar and content questions, the subject NP and topic material are omitted under identity with the antecedent question; what remains is the predicate alone (or predicate + negator).
This is VP-only predication, not verblessness.
Non-propositional use (vocatives, address particles): the utterance is not a predication at all, so no predicate is expected.
These are illocutionary primitives, outside the scope of clausal syntax.

In none of these environments does an oblique phrase, a bare noun, or a bare adjective function as a predicate head — the environment in which Japanese and many SOV languages routinely omit the copula in informal speech has no structural counterpart in Hokkaido Ainu.
The copula ne and the existential an/oka are obligatory in their respective predication environments and cannot be structurally omitted to yield a bare-nominal or bare-locative predicate ; ; .
The discourse conditions that govern when topic NPs and subject indices may be absent — a separate phenomenon — are treated in , , and .
ranks as the second most frequent token in the Hokkaido corpus of nearly 1.6 million running words, behind only the existential .
The count conflates several homophones — the predicate-nominal copula, a mutative case postposition, and anaphoric/interrogative roots — but the copular use accounts for a substantial share.
Predicate-nominal clauses are accordingly among the most pervasive structures in the language.
When the predicate of a finite clause is a noun phrase, the copula ne must appear after it.
Without ne, a sequence of two noun phrases does not constitute a grammatical clause; the element occupying the predicate position in Ainu is always a verbal head .

This sets the construction apart from the other two major non-dynamic predicate types: the existential an / oka(y), which handle existential and locational predication, and the property-concept verbs (pirka 'be good', poro 'be big'), which predicate directly without any copula.
The distribution is determined by argument structure: ne is required when and only when the predicate is a nominal ; .
Ijäs's pedagogical grammar covers the copula in its treatment of basic clause types .
The predicate-nominal clause has the shape [Subject] [Complement-NP] ne.
The complement takes no case marker and immediately precedes the copula.
Satō isolates the three-constituent structure as 主語 + 補語 + 指定詞 ne :
The complement may be a bare noun, a noun modified by an adnominalised verb, or itself a nominalised clause .
Refsing states that ne "cannot form a sentence by itself" and "always needs a nominal complement" .

Nakagawa's constituent parse of a copular sentence — [Adverbial][Complement-NP][ne VP][ruwe ne clause-final] — confirms that the copula heads the verb phrase with everything to its left serving as complement or adverbial .
ne takes the transitive-subject (A) person affixes and never the object (O) affixes.
The three primary sources state the same morphological fact in different analytical terms.
Nakagawa classes it as a 2-place verb (2項動詞), sub-typed コピュラ .
Satō treats it as a distinct subclass 指定詞 (designative), separated from ordinary transitives because it inflects and negates differently .
Shibatani characterises it as taking "the same personal affixes as do transitive verbs" on the grounds that it requires a complement to be semantically complete .
Refsing and Tamura file it as a fourth verbal subclass, the copula .

For the earlier tradition, Kindaichi called it an "incomplete intransitive" glossed 'become', and neither Kindaichi nor Chiri applied the concept of copula to it — Tamura first identified it as such, as Refsing documents ; ‹contested›.
All analyses agree on the morphological reflex: the 1SG prefix on ne is ku= (A set), not en= (O set).
Nakagawa's minimal pair establishes the constraint directly.
okkayo ku=ne 'I am a man' is grammatical; the restructured *tanpe kar pe en=ne, which places the object prefix en= on the copula, is ungrammatical.
The intended reading ('it is me who made this') requires a different clause: kani tanpe ku=kar .
The complement noun phrase receives no person prefix; only the subject position does.
The person paradigm is set out in .
The copula does not supplete for number: a single form ne serves both singular and plural subjects .
This distinguishes it sharply from the existential an (sg) / oka(y) (pl), which shows obligatory number suppletion tracking the subject ; .
Number suppletion in the existential is treated in ; the claim that the copula suppletively has a plural form is addressed in §Competing analyses below.
Refsing describes the copula as covering "the equative and attributive meanings of the copula" without filling existential or locative roles ; .
The attested uses fall into three functional types.

The sources consulted do not apply the Higgins four-way classificational/specificational/identificational grid; the following typology is editorial synthesis from the attested data, not a claim drawn from any single source ‹speculative›.
Classificational (class-membership): the subject is assigned to a category; the complement is non-referential, denoting a kind.
This is the default and most frequent use ; :
Equative / identificational: both subject and complement are referential noun phrases placed in an identity relation :
Specificational / naming: the subject is a nominalised clause and the complement supplies the label.
The formal-noun evidential constructions (hawe ne, ruwe ne) are structurally of this type — the formal noun nominalises a clause and ne predicates the result.
A naming instance at Nakagawa 2024: 392 exemplifies the pattern: tap a=ye katu Piratur sekor a=ye hawe ne 'the way it is now said is "Piratur"' .
forms: tap a=ye katu Piratur sekor a=ye hawe ne

text: Whether Hokkaido Ainu morphosyntactically distinguishes specificational from identificational readings is not addressed by any read source ‹speculative›.
ne carries no morphological mark for change of state: it covers both 'be X' and 'become X', a duality shared by other Ainu verbs including the existential an .
The same sentence Tan-kur poro nispa ne can mean 'this person is a great chief' or 'this person became a great chief'; context determines the reading :
The stative/inchoative range does not extend to property-concept verbs: *hure ne 'become red' and *poro ne 'become big' are ungrammatical.
Property words already predicate inchoatively without a copula; inserting ne after them is the classic learner error .
See and .
Between two nouns, ne establishes identity or class membership within the noun phrase — what Refsing classes as an attributive postposition alongside un and kor :
A third Refsing example: sapa ne kur 'chief' (lit. 'person who is a head') .
The construction is the attributive counterpart of the predicative copular clause; ne is the same item in an NP-internal position.
For the concept-form and possessed morphology of noun heads in such compounds, see and .
The inchoative 'become' reading of ne grammaticalises further into a mutative/translative case postposition marking the result of a change, glossed transl:
Refsing notes that the dynamic 'become' use is the same ne that functions elsewhere as the copula, now in a result-marking role .

A community discussion (thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-11-13) characterises this as 転成格 '〜に（なる）' (mutative case) and observes that ~ne an — mutative ne plus the existential an — corresponds transparently to 'become X', while ~ne kor is awkward because Japanese 'に持つ' ('hold as') is not a natural expression ‹contested›.
The grammaticalization pathway from 'be' to a translative/result marker is cross-linguistically well attested .
The conjunctive particle hine (< hi + ne) is a further grammaticalised descendant; see .
Copular predicates are negated by the idiom X ka somo ne: the scalar particle ka 'even' and the negative adverb somo are inserted between the complement and the copula.
The alternative *ne ka somo ki does not occur ; :

This pattern sets the copula apart from property-concept verbs, which use standard clausal negation (somo V / V ka somo ki), and from the existential, which is negated by the suppletive lexical negative isam:
Full treatments are in and .
One under-described feature is that ne in ka somo ne frequently carries no subject-person prefix — and this prefix-drop also occurs, less regularly, outside negation.
No read grammar catalogues the behaviour; Satō 2008: 22 attests the idiom without commenting on its person-marking pattern.
A community observation (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-25) flags it as a genuine micro-gap in the description, noting only that the reason is unclear ‹speculative›.
The interaction of copula negation with TAM and the formal-noun tail is treated in .

At the right edge of a clause, ne closes the formal-noun evidential construction: a clause is nominalised by one of four bound formal nouns (ruwe, siri, hawe, humi), and the result is predicated with the copula.
Structurally this is the predicate-nominal clause described above, with a nominalised-clause subject.
The copula here is systematically opposed to the existential an: formal-noun + ne marks the declarative; formal-noun + an marks the content question :

The construction further cannot modify a common noun (*pirka ruwe ne kewtum is ungrammatical), and its interaction with clause-linking material is ordered — kusu ne ruwe ne is well-formed but *ruwe ne kusu ne is not .
A community discussion (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-09) confirms both constraints .
The formal nouns that make the construction possible are defined in ; the evidential system as a whole is in ; and ruwe ne specifically in .
Four analytical disputes run through the literature and bear directly on how ne is characterised.
Copula vs. 2-place verb vs. special subclass. The positions are surveyed in §Person marking and verbal status above ‹contested›.
Practically, all analyses converge on the same morphological facts: A-set prefixes only, no O prefix, no sentence-final use without a complement.

The terminological disagreement — whether to call ne a copula subtype of the verb, a distinct 指定詞, or simply a transitive-type verb — has no consequence for the glossing conventions used in this grammar (which follow in treating it as a 2-place verb sub-typed COP).

Copula vs. existential — separation or overlap. Refsing states the division most clearly: ne covers equative and attributive meanings while an / oka covers existential and locative ones, with no overlap .
Nakagawa and Satō maintain the same two-way partition: ne is 2-place, an is 1-place ; .

Shibatani, by contrast, files the locational clause ku-kor kotan ta oray-as 'we were in my village' under "Copular sentences" and labels oray a "plural suppletive copula form" — conflating the existential plural with the copula ‹contested›.

The form oray does not appear in the Hokkaido corpus as a copula and is unattested in that function in any other read source ‹corpus-suggested›; the Shibatani example is most plausibly an existential locational clause.

Number invariance of the copula. On the Nakagawa/Refsing account, the copula shows no number suppletion — one form ne for both singular and plural subjects — in contrast to the existential pair an / oka(y) .
The only apparent counterevidence is Shibatani's oray, dismissed under the preceding point ‹consensus›.
Classificational/specificational typology. The sources consulted use "equative" and "attributive/class-membership" as the descriptive labels for the semantic range of ne ; .
No source applies the Higgins-style four-way grid to Ainu, and no read source tests whether Hokkaido Ainu morphosyntactically distinguishes a specificational from an identificational reading.
The three-way table in §Semantic readings is editorial synthesis ‹speculative›.
The pronominal-argument question. Whether the overt complement NP is a syntactic argument or an adjunct on a pronominal-argument head is unresolved.

Refsing's observation that ne "always needs a nominal complement" and "cannot form a sentence by itself" points toward argument status, but because the complement is never person-indexed, it occupies the same formally indeterminate position as other non-pronominalised objects in a head-marking language .
The broader question is pursued in ‹contested›.
The intransitive verbs (singular) and / (plural) are the existential and locational predicates of Hokkaido Ainu.

Both animate and inanimate subjects appear with them: a single verb covers the domain that Japanese divides between いる (animate) and ある (inanimate), so that 'there is a big house' and 'a person is there' are expressed by the same predicate ; ; .

Placed against the typology of intransitive predication , the construction is an existential-locational predicate: it asserts that something exists or is found at a location, with the location expressed as an oblique.

The stative reading 'exist, be located, live' alternates with an inchoative one: paykar an 'spring comes / it becomes spring' and kunneywa an 'it becomes morning' show the onset-of-existence value ; .
The same static–inchoative duality holds for the copula ne and for property-concept verbs; neither is morphologically marked for the change reading.
The division of labour between the copula and the existential is treated in .
By raw corpus frequency, an ranks first in the approximately 1.57 million–token Hokkaido corpus (86,986 occurrences) and oka twenty-third (9,637).

Both figures fold in the fourth-person intransitive suffix =an and the aspect-auxiliary uses treated elsewhere, so they are upper bounds on the existential predicate proper; even so, the rank signals how load-bearing this predicate type is ‹corpus-confirmed›.
an is strictly intransitive: it takes one NP argument (the entity that exists or is located) and no second bare NP.
A location is expressed as an oblique, canonically the locative postpositional phrase N or ta (or bare N ta), not as a second NP argument.

Satō's diagnostic makes this concrete: a sentence modelled on a Japanese double-NP structure, *Tokiyo anakne poro cise poronno an ('Tokyo big-houses many exist', treating Tokyo as a bare NP co-argument), is disfavoured; the grammatical form marks the location overtly — Tokiyo ot ta anakne poro cise poronno an 'in Tokyo there are many big houses' .
forms: Tokiyo ot ta anakne poro cise poronno an

text: The community formulation of the same rule is direct: an is intransitive, so *A B an is ill-formed; 'A is at B' is A B or ta an.
The transitive locational verb works differently — because it takes the location as its object, A B un is well-formed ; nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024 ‹consensus›.
The locative noun in or ta is the possessed / affiliative form of the spatial root o 'place', expressing 'the place of —'.
The detailed distribution of or vs bare ta in locational constructions is documented for the Chitose dialect by .
The existential verb is one of the canonical suppletive number pairs in Hokkaido Ainu , a pattern documented cross-linguistically in .
The singular stem an is uniform across all dialects.

The plural stem varies: oka is the prevalent form in Saru, Chitose, Shizunai, and Mukawa; okay prevails in other dialects and, even within oka-dialects, appears before the nominalizer pe / p (thus okay pe, not *oka pe) .
The plural stem is controlled by subject number in straightforward cases: a singular subject nominal licenses an, a plural nominal licenses oka.
The full agreement mechanics are treated in .
The fourth-person (honorific / narrative / inclusive) paradigm introduces a mismatch between referential and grammatical number.
When the intransitive fourth-person suffix =an is attached, the existential stem is obligatorily the plural oka — even when the argument is referentially singular.

The phrase sinen ne oka=an 'I am living alone' (with sinen ne 'being only one, alone') illustrates this directly: a singular first-person narrator uses the plural stem because the fourth-person suffix requires it.
Outside the Saru–Chitose core area, this singular-referent / plural-stem pattern is, if anything, the pan-Hokkaido norm ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The fourth-person paradigm and its number behavior are treated in and .
The negative existential is the suppletive lexical negative of an / oka(y): it occupies the same argument slot and takes person affixes normally (e=isam 'you are not there / you are absent') ; .
Its historical depth is notable: isam 'ない' appears in the 1630 Matsumae no Kotoba wordlist, among the earliest documentary records of the language.
The full treatment of existential negation, including the wa isam completive ('V and be gone'), is in ; the standard clausal negation somo is in .
The parallel negative for the possessive predicate kor 'have' is the transitive , which takes the possessor as its subject and the lacked item as its object: tamasay ka sak 'has no necklace even'.
This LACK/HAVE pairing parallels the EXIST/ISAM pairing and shows the same suppletive negation strategy across the non-dynamic predicate system.
Beyond its core existential and locational function, an enters several grammaticalized constructions that are cross-referenced here but treated in full elsewhere.
Combining an with a preceding conjunctive particle yields the existential-type aspect periphrases: V wa an (resultative/continuative, '〜ている'), V kor an (progressive), V kane an, and V hine an.

Yoshikawa documents these for the Saru and Chitose dialects and notes that an in these constructions retains its concrete existential value — it requires a personal affix and participates in subject-number agreement, distinguishing it from a fully grammaticalized auxiliary ; .
The negative counterpart wa isam (completive, '〜てしまう') presses the negative existential isam into the same periphrastic slot.
The full paradigm of existential-type aspect forms is in ; the TAM overview is in .

Closely related is the stative-possessive kor wa an ('have-and-be', expressing resultant or persistent possession), where the possessive verb kor is followed by resultative wa an; this sits at the possession–aspect interface and is treated in .
The zero-valency ambient predicate 'the weather is cold' is transparently analysable as me 'cold' + an 'exist' — literally 'coldness exists' ; .
It belongs to a class of ambient meteorological predicates formed by incorporating an environmental noun into an or a similar root (sirpirka 'the weather is good', from sir- 'scene/land' + pirka).
These are full verbs: the appearance of subjectlessness follows from noun incorporation, not from the absence of a predicate.
The one-place vs zero-place contrast — zero-place mean 'the weather is cold' vs one-place merayke=an 'I feel cold' — is developed in .
In the sentence-final evidential construction, the copula ne and the existential an alternate by illocutionary force.

A formal noun (possessed-form nominalizer) followed by the copula yields a declarative — ruwe ne, hawe ne, siri ne, humi ne — while the same formal noun followed by the existential forms a content question: ruwe an?, hawe an?, and so on .
The copula↔existential opposition is thus grammaticalized into a mood distinction at the right periphery of the clause.
The full evidential-frame paradigm is in ; the inferential ruwe ne is treated in detail in , and the TAM and negation behavior of these frames is in .

The existential an (sg) / okay (pl) and the negative isam also appear in a BE-type predicative possession construction, restricted to affiliative-form inalienable nouns (body-part and kinship terms in their possessed morphology): a=yupi an 'I have an elder brother' (literally 'my-elder-brother exists'), a=po-ho ka an 'I even have a son' .
This is structurally the same existential an serving a possessive reading by virtue of the affiliative-form subject.

The HAVE-type kor construction handles the majority of predicative possession; a community-proposed restriction — that inanimate possessors cannot take kor and are paraphrased with the existential instead — is a sharpening of the BE/HAVE split that awaits systematic corpus documentation ; nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024 ‹contested›.
The full analysis of BE-type vs HAVE-type possession, the kor wa an stative-persistence construction, and the role of the affiliative form are in and .
Hokkaido Ainu encodes predicative possession — 'X has Y' at the clause level — through two verb-based strategies.
The dominant one deploys the transitive verb , which takes the possessor as its subject (A argument) and the possessed entity as its object: kasa ku=kor 'I have an umbrella'.

The second strategy, confined to a closed class of affiliative body-part and kinship nouns, places the possessed noun in its affiliative (possessed) form and predicates it with the intransitive existential verb (singular) or (plural): a=yup-i an 'one has an elder brother'.

A third pattern, kor wa an, combines possession with the resultative auxiliary to encode stative or resultant possession; it belongs to the intersection of predicative possession and the aspect system treated in .

Adnominal possession — the ku=kor cise genitive-like construction, the affiliative double-marking pattern, and the appositive construction — is covered in and ; the present chapter treats only predicative (clause-final, copula-free) possession constructions.

Typologically, the two-strategy system places Hokkaido Ainu in the mixed HAVE/BE category of : the HAVE strategy with a dedicated transitive verb covers the great majority of cases, while the BE strategy — here the existential an — is confined to the inalienable domain ‹corpus-suggested›.
Huber's corpus study finds that over 80% of predicative possession clauses employ the HAVE-type construction .
The pedagogical grammar of likewise introduces kor as the canonical possession verb.
The verb is a two-place transitive verb (2項動詞) with the possessor as its A argument and the possessed entity as its O argument .
It takes the standard S/A/O personal-affix paradigm described in : the possessor is indexed by the A-series (transitive subject) prefixes, while a third-person possessed noun carries no person index.

Refsing analyses kor as an "attributive postposition" when it appears inside a noun phrase (ku=kor cise 'my house') and as a predicative verb when it closes a clause ; Nakagawa treats both uses as the same transitive verb .
One caution on homonymy: kor also functions as the conjunctive particle 'while', marking simultaneous or background events in a clause chain.
The two uses are distinguished by their syntactic position — predicative kor is clause-final, conjunctive kor occurs between two verbal clauses — and are treated separately in .
The corpus rank-5 frequency of 30,389 tokens for kor folds both functions together ‹corpus-suggested›.
As a transitive verb, kor takes the A-series prefix for the possessor and no prefix for a third-person possessed NP.
The table shows the possessor-A cells for the standard Saru–Chitose baseline ; the 1SG cell is attested, the remaining cells are illustrative (constructed from the paradigm):
The 1SG prefix ku= and the 2SG prefix e= are the same A-series forms they carry on any transitive verb.
The 1PL.EXCL prefix ci= is the standard tripartite-cell A form.
In adnominal use the same prefixes appear within the noun phrase: a=kor kamuy 'the god who holds the sea' (cf.

No published primary source states a categorical animacy ban on kor, but community intuition reported in discussion (nukopoli, , 2024-11-10) holds that an inanimate subject cannot serve as the possessor of kor: 'a religion has three books' is judged ungrammatical with kor and is instead paraphrased with the existential — … sekor a=ye re kampisos an 'there exist three books called …'.

This pattern is consistent with the cross-linguistic HAVE(animate)/BE(existential) split documented by and with Huber's finding that inanimate-possession contexts shift toward the existential strategy ‹contested›.
A second strategy is restricted to nouns that carry an affiliative (possessed) form — primarily body-part and kinship nouns.
The possessed noun appears in its affiliative form (root plus suffix -i, -he, -ke, etc.), and the possessor is encoded by the appropriate person prefix on that noun itself.
The predicate is then the intransitive existential verb (singular) or (plural), making the literal structure 'one's X exists' :
This is the same existential an that appears in bare existential and locational clauses (see ), here pressed into possessive service by the inherent person prefix on the possessed noun itself.
Because the possessor is already encoded on the noun, no additional verbal person marking is needed: the construction is entirely intransitive from the verb's perspective.
The number suppletion an (sg) / okay~oka (pl) tracks the number of the possessed entity, following the same agreement pattern as in all other existential clauses .
The kinship and honorific dimensions of this construction — including which kin terms carry affiliative forms — are developed in ; the morphophonology of the affiliative suffix itself is in .

The periphrasis kor wa an — possessive verb kor + conjunctive wa + existential an — encodes stative or resultant possession: the possessor is in a persisting state of holding something as the result of a prior obtaining event.
This pattern is an instance of the wider resultative V wa an construction analysed in ; in the possession domain it specifies that a possession relation has been established and continues to hold.
The pattern extends to incorporated nominals, where a body-part or object noun is fused into kor as a compound before the resultative tail:

The same frame with the 4th-person intransitive suffix =an — a=kohon-kor wa an=an 'was pregnant with (lit. hold-belly-have, one-exists)' (川上まつ子, 民話23 [aa-irc/023#74]) — shows noun incorporation, possessive predication, resultative aspect, and 4th-person marking interacting in a single verb complex.
The incorporation and valency dimensions are treated in .
The two possession strategies negate by different means, each recruiting a suppletive lexical negative rather than ordinary clausal negation .
For the HAVE-type, the transitive verb takes the same A/O argument frame as kor: the possessor is the subject and the lacked entity is the object .
Ordinary clausal negation somo kor is also possible but less frequent than the suppletive sak (see ):

For the BE-type, the negative existential — the suppletive lexical negative of an/okay — follows directly from the structure: if the possessed noun in affiliative form fails to exist, the possessor lacks it.
The possessive reading ('has no X') is thus the automatic negative of 'X exists (as one's possession)'.
The full description of isam is in .

The asymmetry — both possession strategies using suppletive, lexical negatives rather than the plain somo operator — parallels the negation of the copula (ka somo ne) and of the existential (isam) documented in .
The interaction of these negators with TAM, evidential tails, and scope is treated there.
The choice between HAVE-type and BE-type tracks the semantic relationship between possessor and possessed.
Alienable possession — objects, tools, animals, goods — takes kor exclusively.

Inalienable possession, where the possessed entity (body part or kinship relation) is inherently indexed to a possessor through the affiliative morphology, admits the BE-type construction in addition to kor ; .
The BE-type is further restricted to those inalienable nouns that actually carry an affiliative suffix form (see and for the full taxonomy).
Typologically, this profile maps onto the mixed HAVE/BE type in : a language with a dedicated transitive HAVE verb as the default and an existential BE construction for inalienable possession.

The inalienable-domain restriction of the BE type is expected under the cross-linguistic generalisation that languages permitting both strategies tend to use the existential for possession relations that are encoded also in the morphology of the possessed noun itself ‹consensus›.

A diachronic note: an early modern source (もしほ草, ca. 1806) records possessive expressions where kor is absent and the possessor is instead encoded by a person prefix on an existential verb — ci=oro okay kotan 'our village' (lit. 'our-in existing village'), ci=okay cas 'our castle' — suggesting that kor had not yet grammaticalized as the dominant possessive predicate in that textual register.
This may reflect an earlier stage in which various existential strategies were available before kor extended its possessive scope (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-11-23) ‹speculative›.

The current dominance of kor (>80% of predicative possession in Huber's data ) would then represent the outcome of that grammaticalization trajectory, though the textual evidence is thin and the comparison of registers is uncontrolled.
Property-concept words — , , , , , , , , and their class-mates — occupy the predicate slot of a simple clause without a copula.
The clause cape pon 'the cat is small' is structurally parallel to cape hoyupu 'the cat ran': in both, a bare intransitive verb is the entire predicate ; .
This behavior reflects a categorical fact: Hokkaido Ainu has no dedicated adjective word class ‹consensus›.
What English and Japanese encode in a distinct adjective category is covered in Ainu by a set of intransitive stative verbs.

The three-criterion argument — morphological identity with intransitive verbs, structural parallelism in the prenominal slot, and evidential compatibility — is set out in ; the present chapter treats the predication patterns that the analysis implies.

Because property words are verbs, they take subject-agreement affixes, combine with the standard clausal negation morphology, and take the evidential tail ruwe ne exactly as any other predicate does ; .
A learner who writes *pirka ne for '(it) is good' has imported a copula requirement that the grammar does not impose .
The copula ne is restricted to predicate-nominal clauses (see ) and cannot combine with a property verb.
Property verbs take the intransitive subject (S) person affixes — the same set that marks the sole argument of action verbs — following the paradigm described in .
The prefix ku= marks first-singular S on any intransitive stem, whether it denotes motion, existence, or a property:
The full intransitive paradigm applies without adjustment.

No object affix can appear: property verbs are strictly intransitive and take no object slot.

A member of the aynu-corpora community observed that the zero-marked (3rd-person) form of pirka shifts contextually toward 'that's fine / it's OK' when no overt subject is present, while person-marked forms like e=pirka read as a direct evaluation of the indexed person ('you are beautiful, in good shape') (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, November 2024) ‹contested›.
Property verbs appear in two syntactic positions: as bare predicates heading the main clause, and as prenominal modifiers preceding a noun head.
The morphological form is identical in both — a fact recognized since ‹consensus›.
In predicative position the property verb alone constitutes the predicate:
In attributive position the same verb precedes the noun head with no morphological change — no suffix, no linker, no case marker.
This is structurally parallel to a prenominal relative clause in Ainu, where the predicate verb likewise immediately precedes the head noun ; see :

The prenominal slot admits person-marked property verbs: ku=pewre or ta in the example above reads as 'in the time of my being young', a headless relative clause with the property verb predicated of the implicit head .
This confirms that the prenominal position is a syntactic slot that verbs occupy, not a morphologically distinct adjectival form.
Like other Ainu verbs, property-concept words encode both the state ('be X') and its onset ('become X') without distinct forms; context determines the reading ; .
