The inchoative reading is contextual, not morphological.
It follows that the copula ne cannot be inserted to force an inchoative: *poro ne for 'become big' is ungrammatical in Hokkaido Ainu .
Where the copula does appear after an inchoative-type expression (as in nispa ne 'become a chief'), the complement is a nominal, not a property verb.
The copula's own stative–inchoative duality belongs to the predicate-nominal system treated in .

A community discussion noted that both ne an and pirka an carry 'become' readings, raising the question whether the existential an contributes an inchoative-aspect value in such environments (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, November 2024) ‹speculative›.
The aspectual uses of an as a periphrastic auxiliary are set out in .

Property verbs follow the standard clausal negation strategies of intransitive verbs: the negator somo precedes the verb (somo V), or the frame V ka somo ki is used for contrastive or emphatic negation ; :
These patterns contrast with the dedicated frames required by the copula and the existential ; .
The copula requires X ka somo ne (the negator placed before ne itself), and the existential an recruits its suppletive negative isam 'not exist'.
The property verb is the only non-dynamic predicate type that takes ordinary clausal negation, a direct reflex of its status as an ordinary intransitive verb.
The full scope of negation across predicate types is treated in and .
Property verbs carry no inherent comparative or degree morphology.
Degree is expressed by adverbs that precede the property verb without triggering any change to its form .
The most frequently recruited degree adverbs are , , , and .

The prefix si- combines directly with the verb root for intensification: si-poro 'really big' .
Property verbs also generate manner adverbs for other predicates through the suffix -no: yields tunasno 'fast(ly)', yields moyreno 'slowly' .
The derived adverb quantifies the manner of the event described by the main predicate and is not itself a predicate.

The comparative construction (akkari 'surpassing, more than') and the full adverb system are treated in ; the sources consulted do not provide a systematic degree–comparison paradigm for property verbs, and the gap is noted there.
A small set of property verbs — including , , and — can follow a main predicate as a post-verbal auxiliary expressing the pace or adequacy of the denoted event :

The classical treatment in (§§129, 189–193) recognized that property words inflect for person just as verbs do, yet nonetheless posited a separate 形容詞 'adjective' class defined by its dual attributive–predicative distribution.
Kindaichi conceded the instability of the boundary directly: "the difference between a verb and an adjective is razor-thin" (動詞と形容詞の差は紙一重; §129).
His own person-inflection tables for 形容詞 reproduce the intransitive S paradigm without modification — the concession is already implicit in the paradigm.
Chiri's reanalysis (, summarized in ) proposed the 用詞 category — a class of stative verbs covering property meanings — and collapsed the distinction.

All subsequent major grammars of Hokkaido Ainu adopt that position: classifies property words as a semantically defined subclass of verbs without a distinct morphosyntactic status; notes that property words take "the same personal affixes" as intransitive verbs; places them within his four-verb-type classification as a stative subtype; and provides the most detailed argument, covering all three diagnostic dimensions ‹consensus›.

In terms of the cross-linguistic typology of intransitive predication , Hokkaido Ainu is an unambiguous case of the verbal-property type: the coding of property meanings through intransitive verbs extends without exception to every diagnostic — morphological marking, syntactic distribution, TAM compatibility, and negation strategy.
One genuinely open question concerns the interaction of property predication with the evidential system.

Takahashi's study of Tokachi Ainu shows that individual-level (permanent) property predicates select the trace nominalizer ru rather than the visual nominalizer sir, because the visual form is restricted to stage-level (transient) predicates .

This predication-type constraint operates on individual-level vs. stage-level readings across the verb inventory and is not specific to property words, but it shows that the ontological character of property predicates is grammatically active in Ainu.
The interaction of property predicates with the evidential paradigm is treated in and .

All three non-dynamic predicate types that occupy the predicate slot in a Hokkaido Ainu simple clause — the copula ne, the existential an (sg) / oka(y) (pl), and property-concept verbs — are verbs, and TAM and negation attach to them through the same clausal mechanisms that operate on action verbs ; .
The full TAM and aspect system is described in ; the evidential formal-noun frame in ; the person-marking that each predicate type takes in .

This chapter maps the interface: where each predicate type departs from the verbal default in its negation strategy, how the perfect auxiliary a attaches, how the inchoative reading arises without any dedicated morphology, and how the ne / an alternation at the clause edge encodes illocutionary force on non-dynamic predicates.
The three predicate types diverge most sharply in their negation strategies.
The copula ne has a dedicated frame, X ka somo ne, that inserts the focus particle ka and the negator somo between the predicate complement and the copula.
The existential draws on the suppletive lexical negative isam.
Property-concept verbs, being ordinary intransitive stative verbs, take the standard clausal negation described in .
Possessive similarly has the suppletive negative ; that construction is treated in .

Typologically, the distribution maps onto the hierarchy of non-dynamic predication that identifies: equative/classificatory (copula ne), locational/existential (an/oka(y)), and attributive (property verbs) each carry a distinct negation exponent.

The recourse to dedicated negative lexemes for the existential and possessive types, alongside a frame strategy for the copula, is consistent with the cross-linguistic pattern whereby existential and possessive predicates frequently recruit non-standard negation ‹consensus›.
The standard negation of a predicate-nominal clause is X ka somo ne, where the focus particle ka 'even/also' and the negator somo insert between the complement nominal and the copula ; :
The alternative frame *ne ka somo ki — negating ne via the standard verbal pattern V ka somo ki — is ungrammatical ; .

Both Satō and Nakagawa treat this as the defining idiosyncrasy that sets the copula apart from ordinary verbs: its negation is expressed by modifying the complement position, not by post-verbal negation of the verb itself.
In the affirmative, the copula takes the transitive-subject person set — okkayo ku=ne 'I am a man' — because it is analysed as a 2-place verb with a nominal complement ; .

In the ka somo ne frame, the copula frequently carries no overt subject affix; this person-marking loss in the negated copular frame is noted but not explained by any read primary source ‹speculative›
(nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2023; ).

The observation is consistent with the third-person zero realisation that ne shows in affirmative clauses with 3rd-person subjects, but its extension to other persons in the negative frame is a genuine micro-gap.
Person marking on the copula is set out in and .

Separate from inner-scope ka somo ne, the construction ruwe somo ne is an outer rhetorical frame in which somo ne scopes over the evidential formal noun ruwe rather than over the complement of the copula; it is treated in .

The perfect/perfective auxiliary a attaches to the copula in the same position as to any verb — after the finite verb and before any following formal-noun evidential tail — and yields a completed or previously-true copular state:

All three non-dynamic predicate types share a static ⇄ inchoative duality that is read off context without dedicated morphology: ne covers both 'be X' and 'become X', an/oka(y) both 'exist' and 'appear/come into being', and property verbs both 'be big' and 'grow big' ; ; .

The sequence [complement] ne + existential an /oka=an makes the inchoative reading salient — a community member notes that ~ne an corresponds to Japanese 〜になる 'become', while ~ne kor is not idiomatic ‹contested›
(thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord 2024; ).
This is consistent with the general dynamic reading that an lends to a preceding predicate in the aspect periphrasis (cf.
V wa an resultative); the aspect-auxiliary use of the existential is treated in .
The ne / an alternation at the right clause edge is grammaticalized into an illocutionary distinction.
With the formal-noun evidential frame, the copula ne closes the declarative and the existential an closes the content question, while the bare formal noun marks polar questions and exclamations .
The pattern holds identically for non-dynamic predicates and verbal predicates:
The ordering constraint confirms the clause's layered structure: the formal noun and its predicate sit outside inner-clause TAM material.

The form kusu ne ruwe ne 'because (it is a fact that)' is well-formed, but *ruwe ne kusu ne is not, because a further ne-predication cannot embed over an already-closed evidential — confirmed against the primary source by a community member (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024; ).
The possessed form morphology of the formal nouns (ru-we, haw-e, sir-i, hum-i) and the full evidential paradigm are treated in and ; the interrogative system is treated in .
The existential an (sg) and oka(y) (pl) do not take the somo frame as their primary negation.
The lexical verb is the suppletive negative partner of the existential pair ; .

isam is an intransitive verb that takes person affixes normally: e=isam 'you are gone/absent'.
Historical depth confirms its stability: the form isam 'ない' is attested in the 1630 Matsumae no koto wordlist, making the negative existential one of the oldest recorded Ainu predicate forms.
The etymological decomposition of isam as i- (antipassive) + root *sam is ‹speculative› and is proposed independently by and by (lesson 9); see for fuller discussion.
The somo an construction is available as an alternative where a denial reading is required rather than the lexical 'absence' meaning:
The existential negative also feeds the aspect system.
V wa isam expresses that a state of affairs has become absent as the result of the preceding event — roughly equivalent to Japanese 〜てしまう 'V and it's gone' .
This mirrors the resultative V wa an (〜ている), in which the existential carries the positive persistent state.
Both the aspect periphrasis and the number suppletion of an/oka(y) are treated in ; the full locational and existential semantics in .

Property-concept verbs (, , , , and their class) are intransitive stative verbs and take the standard negation that any intransitive verb takes: pre-verbal somo V, or the post-verbal frame V ka somo ki :

The divergence between property-verb negation (somo V / V ka somo ki) and copula negation (X ka somo ne) is the direct morphosyntactic reflex of the difference in predicate class: the copula is a special 2-place verb with an idiosyncratic negation frame, while property verbs are ordinary intransitives ; .

The error of inserting the copula after a property word — *pirka ne 'be-good COP' — is flagged by Nakagawa as the characteristic learner mistake, and its ungrammaticality confirms that the ka somo ne frame is copula-specific and does not extend to the property-verb predicate type .
The word-class argument for property verbs as intransitive verbs is made in .

When a non-dynamic predicate is closed by the formal-noun evidential frame, negation sits inside the evidential: the predicate is negated before the formal noun, and the ruwe ne (or other formal-noun + copula) remains outside the scope of negation, predicating the negated content as recognised fact.
For copular predicates under ruwe ne, the expected sequence is [complement] ka somo ne ruwe ne: the ka somo ne frame negates the copular predication, and the evidential closes over it.

The layering is confirmed by the same ordering constraint noted above: kusu ne ruwe ne is licit because kusu ne is inner-clause intentional material, but *ruwe ne kusu ne is not, because the evidential cannot be embedded under a further copular predication .
The interaction of negation and polarity items within the evidential scope is treated in ; the structure of the evidential frame in .
The nominalizer p ~ pe turns a finite clause into a noun phrase.

It is a member of the closed class of formal nouns — light, weakly autonomous nouns placed after another element to build an NP — and it supplies a generic nominal head meaning, in its concrete uses, ‘the one who’ or ‘the thing that’.

Hokkaido Ainu has no participial or otherwise non-finite verb form for this work: the verb inside the nominalized phrase keeps its ordinary person marking, polarity, number, and clause-internal morphology, and subordination is signalled by the following formal noun rather than by any change in the verb ; ; .
The allomorphy is phonologically conditioned: the short form -p follows a stem-final vowel, and -pe follows a stem-final consonant.
The same split holds whether the host is a single stative stem (poro-p ‘the big one’, pon-pe ‘the small one’) or a full clause (a=e p ‘what one eats’, okay pe ‘what one carries’) ; ; .
Satō records a sandhi variant pa at the junction of p and a following conjunctive wa .
The form spans lexical derivation and syntax without a break.

Shibatani describes -p(e) as deriving a noun for a person or thing characterized by the verb, as in pirka-p ‘good thing’ and ray-pe ‘the dead’, and as a productive phrasal and clausal nominalizer besides .

In Bugaeva's areal account of nominalization, Hokkaido expresses clausal nominalization through a nominalizing word placed after the clause, the type [(np…) V p/pe], a stage from which lexical items such as have crystallized; the Sakhalin varieties extended the same system to possessed verbal forms .

Among the formal nouns, p ~ pe keeps a ‘thing/person’ profile beside the maximally abstract hi and the sensory-evidential heads ruwe, siri, hawe, and humi, whose inventory and possessed morphology are set out in and whose clause-final evidential use is treated in .
In its participant reading, p ~ pe is a generic head whose referent is fixed by the argument structure of the clause before it.
The clause contains a gap, and the role of that gap — agent, patient, or an oblique participant — is recovered from the verb's valence and from any postposition left in place ; .
This is the headless edge of the relative-clause system: where an ordinary relative clause precedes a lexical head noun, p ~ pe supplies the head itself.
The gap strategy, the accessibility hierarchy, and the postposition-retention facts are developed in , and the place of the headless type within the wider typology of noun-modifying clauses in .
Lexicalized items preserve the syntax at word scale.
is a=e-p, ‘thing one eats’, with the fourth-person transitive prefix and the nominalizer .

Nakagawa's contrast between the synthesized a=e-suke-p ‘kitchen utensil’ and the compound sukemakiri ‘kitchen knife’ shows the diagnostic: the relative-clause nominalization keeps the applicative e- that licenses the instrument it names, whereas a compound leaves the relation between its two nouns grammatically unspecified .
The lexicalized inventory is treated in .
An oblique participant is nominalized the same way, with the governing postposition retained inside the clause so that the relation between head and predicate stays overt.
With an instrument the postposition ani ‘with’ remains, and p names the instrument ; ; .

Ijäs teaches the same rule for relative clauses generally: the modifying verb phrase precedes the head, there is no relative pronoun, and an oblique head keeps the postposition fronted within the clause .
Her examples are constructed teaching material and align with Nakagawa, Satō, and Bugaeva.

When the clause before it is already saturated — every argument the verbs require is present — p ~ pe nominalizes the event or fact as a whole and serves as a complementizer rather than a participant head.

Nakagawa treats some formal nouns, p ~ pe among them, as filling this complementizing role; Satō draws the line explicitly between a nominalizer (名詞化辞) that turns a whole content clause into a noun phrase and a formal noun that heads a relative clause, the first allowing no reconstruction of an underlying sentence ; .
In this use p ~ pe stands beside the other complementizing formal nouns — abstract hi and the sensory heads — which differ in the construal they impose.

The complement-taking predicates and the control and raising diagnostics are treated in ; the future-oriented sequence kuni p in ; the quotative complementizer sekor and the indirect-speech markers in ; and the clause-final evidential reflexes of the sensory heads in the inferential ruwe ne.
Nakagawa's valence arithmetic keeps the participant and complementizer uses from collapsing into one reading.

A formal noun has arity −1, on a par with hi and uske; a clause that still requires a participant has positive arity, and the formal noun fills the open slot, giving a relative-clause NP; a clause of arity 0 is complete, and the formal noun nominalizes the whole of it, giving an event or fact nominal .
The surface string [clause] p/pe is identical in both; the grammatical relation differs.

The descriptions agree on the substance — p ~ pe builds lexical, phrasal, and clausal nominals, heads a generic participant in a relative clause, and nominalizes a saturated clause as an event or fact — and differ on the labels.

Shibatani and Refsing use ‘nominalizer’ broadly; Satō separates the whole-clause nominalizer from the relative-clause-heading formal noun; Nakagawa makes the formal noun a word class and the complementizer a syntactic role available to some of its members; Bugaeva treats these light bound nouns as the generic heads of gapped relative clauses ; ; ; ; ‹contested›.
The constituency of the nominalized clause plus a following copula — the frame [clause] p/pe ne — is the deeper disagreement, and it is the same one that runs through the evidential system.

One line analyses the structure as biclausal, a formal or possessed noun heading the preceding clause and closed by the copula; another holds that the erstwhile noun is grammaticalizing toward a monoclausal complex predicate.
No source read here offers a constituency proof that decides between them ; ; ; ‹contested›.
Ijäs's observations on relative clauses fit this system, with two cautions.

Her report that the subject of a ditransitive resists being the head matches Bugaeva's finding that no example of an A-of-three-place-verb head is attested; the construction is an attested gap rather than a settled ungrammaticality ‹corpus-confirmed›.

Her difficulty in finding ablative wa(no) ‘from which’ or mutative ne ‘as which’ as relative-clause heads is shared by the sources read here, so the forms she suggests for them are left aside rather than presented as established ‹corpus-suggested›

The same nominalizer feeds clause linkage at the far end of the cline: a bleached p ~ pe works as an adversative conjunction ‘though, and yet’, no longer an argument of the following clause, and the Horobetsu nominalizers grammaticalize a step further into adverbial-clause markers ; .
Token frequency confirms that pe is common but cannot measure this construction directly.

The corpus word-frequency table returns 13,249 tokens of pe (rank 15), a figure that folds together the formal noun, the numeral counter -pe, and lexical pe ‘water’, while the short allomorph p is obscured by segmentation.
A per-function count would require construction-level annotation ‹corpus-suggested›.
Hokkaido Ainu forms nominalized clauses by placing a formal noun after a finite predicate.
The verb retains its ordinary person marking; the formal noun supplies the nominal head and converts the preceding material into an NP.

The class is closed and its members differ in the semantic profile they impose — 'thing', 'person', 'place', 'appearance', 'voice', and so on — and in whether they function as relative-clause heads, complementizers, or both ; ; .
The allomorphs ~ , their participant-nominalization and complementizer functions, and the arity diagnostic that distinguishes the two readings are treated in .
The gap strategy, accessibility hierarchy, and postposition stranding that characterize all relative clauses are covered in .
The clause-final evidential uses of , , , and are treated in .

The present chapter addresses the morphological contrast between the concept form and the affiliative (possessed) form of these nouns, the semantic profiles that govern head-selection across the formal-noun inventory, in its several uses, the sensory-noun formal nouns as non-evidential perception-complement heads, and the cline from clausal nominalization to lexicalized noun.
Each formal noun has two shapes described in .
The bare concept form (概念形) is the citation form of the noun, autonomous in a sentence.

The affiliative form, or possessed form (所属形), marks the noun as belonging to an antecedent; it is the shape in which the sensory-noun formal nouns appear in their evidential and perception-complement uses.
For the four sensory nouns the two forms are distinguished by a possessive suffix :

Satō observes that a noun in its possessed form presupposes an antecedent — something it belongs to — so that placing a sensory noun in this form after a finite clause grammatically encodes that the described situation is already held as given by the speaker .
This presupposition distinguishes evidential ruwe ('the trace of —', implicating a recognized antecedent event) from lexical ru ('a track').

Dialect evidence reinforces the contrast: southern Hokkaido (Saru, Chitose) uses the possessed forms in the clause-final evidential frame, while Tokachi and Ishikari close the clause with the bare concept forms ru, sir, haw, hum ; .
All formal nouns have arity −1, which allows them to terminate a relative clause (closing an arity ≥+1 gap) or a saturated complement clause (arity 0) alike .
The table below covers those relevant to nominalization; the full catalogue with arity derivations appears in .
The pair usi / uske are dialectally distributed: uske is attested in Saru, Chitose, and Shizunai; the forms usi and usike are more widely spread across Hokkaido .
Both head relative clauses without requiring the relational noun or that movement-case postpositions need before locative complements .

Shibatani lists the nominalizers -p(e), -i, -ike, and -kur as productive phrasal and clausal nominalizating suffixes in classical/yukar Ainu , corresponding to the word-class of formal nouns in Nakagawa's synchronic description .
The formal-noun head selected for a nominalized clause is determined primarily by the semantic category of the reference being expressed.

p ~ pe and hi cover the widest range but along different dimensions: p ~ pe profiles a concrete entity — a thing or person that can be encountered or handled — while hi is maximally abstract, covering fact, time, and place readings alike ; .
Where the referent is specifically a person and an honorific register is required, kur (from ) is used; utar extends this person head to a group.
The place nouns usi(ke) and uske head nominalizations that refer to a location or time without the concrete/abstract ambiguity of hi.
Satō's diagnostic sharpens the contrast between the relative-clause use and the complementizer use for any formal noun.
A formal noun functioning as a relative-clause head heads a clause from which a participant has been gapped; the original sentence can be reconstructed by reinserting that participant.
A formal noun functioning as a complementizer nominalizes the whole clause as a proposition, and no such reconstruction is possible .

Both p ~ pe and hi fill either role depending on the arity of the clause they follow; the sensory-noun heads serve both functions as well, though their complement use is semantically restricted to perception contexts.
Person formal noun kur produces nominalizations whose referent is a specific individual.
In classical and epic texts these regularly lexicalize: kotan kor-kur 'chief' (lit. 'person who has a village'), ray-kur 'the dead' (lit. 'person(s) who die') .

Compound nominalizations of this type remain analytically transparent even after lexicalization, illustrating the continuity between productive RC nominalization and the lexicalized stratum treated in the final section.
is the most abstract formal noun in the inventory; its gloss covers 'thing, matter, fact', 'time when', and 'place where'.
After a consonant it surfaces as -i — as in the lexicalized ape-o-i 'hearth', treated in the next section ; .
In the 'thing/fact' and 'time' readings, hi nominalizes a saturated clause (arity 0) and functions as a complementizer.
The nominalized clause may serve as the grammatical subject of a matrix predicate:
Or as the object of a complement-taking predicate.
In the following example, hi appears twice: as the object-head of a=ye 'say' (arity +1, 'what to say') and of a=kar 'do' (arity +1, 'what to do').
In each case the clause before hi has an open slot, so hi fills the head rather than the complementizer role:
The 'place' reading calls for a different structure: the governing postposition is retained inside the relative clause, marking hi as the locative head (arity +1 because the location slot is gapped):
With the time and abstract-fact readings, the clause is saturated and hi nominalizes it whole.
The postposition that follows hi is not part of the RC but a postposition governing the entire nominalized clause:
Nakagawa frames the place/non-place split as a tendency.

The 'place' reading is more concrete and closer to an ordinary noun, so the grammatical relation requires overt expression; the 'time/fact' reading is abstract and freely nominalizes the whole clause.
Okuda (1989), quoted and refined by , first systematized this contrast.

An attested exception — seta utar osoma hi 'the dogs' privy', from 知里幸恵's kamuy yukar collection (Horobetsu), which uses a 'place' reading without a retained postposition — shows the constraint does not hold categorically ‹corpus-suggested›.
The locative formal nouns usi and uske offer an alternative to hi for the 'place' reading.
Because they are inherently locative, they require no retained movement-case postposition.
The directional postposition eun 'toward' is instead retained for the oblique head:

Ijäs observes that usi-headed compound nouns — such as ipeusi 'restaurant' (lit. 'eating-place') — are historical RC nominalizations, and that usi-words require no relational noun or before movement-case postpositions ‹consensus›.
A locative relative clause with a plain common noun head does require the relational noun:

Apart from their clause-final evidential function (treated in and the inferential ruwe ne), the possessed-form sensory nouns ruwe, siri, hawe, and humi function as nominal heads of complement clauses whose matrix predicate is a perception or cognition verb.
In this intra-sentence use, the matrix verb follows the formal noun rather than closing the clause .

Each formal noun is selected by a specific subset of perception predicates: nukar 'see' takes siri (the visual scene) or hi (an abstract perceived content); nu 'hear, ask about' takes hawe (verbal content), humi (a non-verbal sensation), or hi; cognition predicates eramiskari 'not know' and eraman 'understand' take hi or p ~ pe .
The complement-taking predicates and the structural properties of these complements are treated in .

Within the visual domain, Satō distinguishes the two available heads: siri applies to an action or situation in progress at reference time — a scene being witnessed — while ruwe applies to an already-existing state or non-progressive action asserted as recognized fact .
In the following example the speaker uses siri to frame the visible absence of large trees as the scene that prompted anger:

The shift from this intra-sentence perception complement (matrix verb follows siri) to the clause-final evidential frame (copula ne follows) instantiates Bugaeva's Stage II grammaticalization path: the nominal head that was an argument of a perception predicate becomes the terminal element of an evidential construction .
The two uses remain synchronically productive and distinct; the evidential use is the more grammaticalized endpoint ‹consensus›.

The constituency of the whole construction — whether it is biclausal (a possessed noun heading the preceding finite clause, closed by the copula) or is grammaticalizing toward a monoclausal complex predicate — is unsettled.
The biclausal analysis is held by Tamura, Okuda, and Satō, and is endorsed by Nakagawa under the label 補文標識 'complementizer' ; .

Bugaeva argues that the erstwhile nouns are considerably grammaticalized and the construction is moving toward a monoclausal complex predicate, supported by the fact that the formal noun no longer heads a full NP (*pirka ruwe ne kewtum is ungrammatical — no determiner or attributive modifier can attach) ; ‹contested›.
A relative-clause NP of the form [(NP…) V nmz] can crystallize into a single lexical noun when the constituent parts are reproduced as a unit with a conventional, fixed meaning.

Bugaeva traces a grammaticalization cline from productive RC nominalization to lexicalized noun in the Hokkaido data, placing Hokkaido at Stage II of a broader areal typology (Stage I = zero-nominalization; Stage II = nominalizing word; Stage III–IV in Sakhalin = possessed verbal forms) .
The lexicalized products are morphologically transparent but synchronically function as ordinary nouns.
Two items illustrate the pattern with allomorphs of different formal nouns:

The allomorph split across these two items reflects the same head-selection principle visible in productive clausal nominalizations: -p ~ -pe yields a concrete entity ('thing killed', 'thing cooked'), while -i (allomorph of hi) yields a location ('place where fire enters').
The semantic specialization survives lexicalization.
A relative-clause NP and a compound noun are superficially similar — both consist of a predicate-like element preceding a noun — but the arity test separates them .

The compound tureptani 'uba-lily digging-stick' juxtaposes turep 'uba-lily' and tani 'digging-stick' without marking the semantic relation between them; the RC reading 'the stick with which that woman dug uba-lilies' requires the instrumental postposition ani 'with' to be retained inside the clause, making the instrument role explicit:

The diagnostic generalizes: in an RC nominalization the semantic relation between the formal-noun head and the predicate is grammatically specified — via a retained postposition, the verb's argument structure, or an applicative prefix.
In a compound noun, that relation is implicit.
Lexicalized RC nominalizations such as ci=ronnu-p and ape-o-i were once transparent RC structures; the grammatical marking has become inert but remains recoverable from the morphology.

Ijäs's observation that usi-words such as ipeusi 'restaurant' ('eating-place') descend historically from RC structures aligns with Bugaeva's Stage II account and with Shibatani's finding that -p(e), -i, -ike, and -kur function as both phrasal and lexical nominalizers ; ; ‹consensus›.
The productive and lexical levels are not sharply bounded; what counts as a new RC formation versus a lexicalized item depends on the frequency and semantic conventionalization of the combination.

The Hokkaido Ainu relative clause is prenominal and head-final: the modifying clause precedes its head noun, there is no relative pronoun, and the relativized participant is simply absent from the clause — a zero gap ; ; ; .
Stative property verbs modify a following noun directly and without any special marking: hure suwop 'red box'.

Any verb, stative or dynamic, can head the modifying clause; the verb inside the RC carries the same person prefixes, number-sensitive suppletion (singular vs plural ), polarity, and clause-internal morphology as it would in a main clause ; .
Subordination is signalled by the structural position of the clause before its head, not by any morphological change to the verb ; .

This architecture — a full finite clause immediately before its head — is shared by the headless relative (where a formal noun such as ~ supplies the head) and the complement clause (where a formal noun nominalizes a saturated clause).
The boundary between these constructions is governed by Nakagawa's valency (arity) principle, discussed in the following section and with worked examples in the chapter on the nominalizer p~pe.
The headless variant is treated in ; lexicalized RC-headed nominalizations such as in .
Nakagawa's arity accounting provides the formal test that separates the relative clause from the complement clause.
Each verb contributes a positive arity value equal to the number of NP arguments it requires; each NP present inside the clause subtracts one; a formal noun has arity −1.

When the summed arity of the embedded clause plus its formal-noun head is still positive (≥ +1), one argument slot remains unfilled — that is the gap — and the whole unit functions as a relative clause.
When the arity reaches zero, the clause is saturated and the formal noun nominalizes the whole clause as a complement .
The surface string [clause] p/pe is identical in the relative and the complementizer readings; only the arity count distinguishes them.
Satō's rule of thumb for the same distinction is whether the original sentence from which the head noun was extracted can be reconstructed: for a relative clause it can, for a nominalizer it cannot .
The gap is a zero element: no pronoun, resumptive or otherwise, marks the relativized position inside the RC ; .

When the head noun fills a core argument position (S or O) in the embedded clause, this gap is sufficient, because the verb's argument structure and the remaining NPs identify the role of the missing participant.

When the head fills an oblique position — instrumental, comitative, locative, dative — the postposition that governs that oblique remains inside the RC, moved to a position at or near the left edge of the embedded clause.
This retained postposition is what marks the semantic role of the gapped head when that role is not recoverable from the verb's argument structure alone ; .
The practical consequence is that a postposition's presence inside an RC signals an oblique head.
Conversely, removing the postposition collapses the arity to zero and makes the relative-clause reading unavailable.

Nakagawa's minimal pair makes this visible: nea menoko ani turepta ni is grammatical as an instrumental RC ('the stick with which that woman dug uba-lilies'), but the postposition-free string *nea menoko turepta ni has no gap and cannot relativize the instrument .
Only postpositions that are capable of appearing independently with a zero-anaphoric NP in a main clause — , , , — undergo this retention directly.

For locative and allative postpositions that require a case-marking particle (ta, un), the relational noun must be inserted before the particle; it serves as the NP host for the postposition and as the covert correlate of the gapped head ; ; .

An inalienable possessor can be relativized.
The possessed noun inside the RC retains its possessive suffix, which serves as the morphological trace of the possessor-possessee relation; the head noun fills the gapped possessor position ; .

Alienable possession in Hokkaido Ainu is itself expressed by a gapped prenominal relative clause: ku=kor cep 'my fish' is literally '[the fish that I have]', with as the transitive verb and ku= as the 1SG agent ; .
Extracting a possessor from this structure would require relativization from inside a relative clause — an island constraint — and the construction is accordingly unavailable ‹consensus›.
Direct relativization of the standard of comparison is not attested.

What Bugaeva documents is a degree-adjunct workaround: a clause of the type 'a rich man [to whose degree of wealth no rich man exists]' places the degree comparison inside the RC as a modifier on the head, rather than gapping the standard participant from a transitive clause :
Whether this is a grammaticalized equivalent to comparison-standard relativization or a pragmatic repair is not settled ‹corpus-suggested›.
Heads corresponding to ablative wa(no) 'from which' and mutative ne 'as which' are absent from Bugaeva's inventory of retainable postpositions and are not attested in any source read here .
Ijäs reports the same absence and explicitly withholds constructed examples for these positions .
They are not presented as established ‹corpus-suggested›.

The bound noun supplies a generic semantic category — person, people, thing, place — while the RC clause provides all the identifying content.
When the formal noun is p~pe, the construction shades into the headless relative.

Her core grammatical claims — prenominal head-final order, absence of a relative pronoun, gap strategy for core arguments, postposition retention for obliques (including the oro-insertion rule for locatives/allatives) — align precisely with the primary sources ‹consensus›.
Her demonstration that ku=kor cep 'my fish' is itself a relative clause ('the fish that I have') follows the Handbook's alienable-possession analysis ‹consensus›.

And her identification of the ditransitive subject as a problematic head position matches Bugaeva's "no examples attested so far" ; she is consistent in flagging it as an open question rather than asserting ungrammaticality ‹corpus-confirmed›
(as gap).
Two of her claims need a hedge.

Her report that the ordering of multiple stative modifiers is free (poro retar seta ~ retar poro seta 'big red dog, red big dog') is her own inference from the absence of counter-examples; she acknowledges this explicitly.
Modifier stacking is attested — Shibatani gives ampene pirka sukup aynu from yukar data — but a free-order generalization across dialects exceeds what the sources establish ‹corpus-suggested›.

Her inability to locate attested examples of ablative wa(no) or mutative ne as RC heads is shared by all sources read here; the forms she cautiously suggests for these positions should not be treated as established ‹corpus-suggested›.
All major descriptive accounts converge on the externally-headed, prenominal gap strategy: , , , , and all describe the construction in these terms.
The differences among them are terminological — Refsing calls the process "adnominalization", Nakagawa uses "関係文", Bugaeva "gapped prenominal relative clause" — rather than empirical.

Dal Corso 2020 proposes that certain southern Hokkaido indirect-evidential constructions (siri ki, hawe as, humi as) show a layout reminiscent of internally-headed relative clauses, instantiated through what he calls classificatory noun incorporation .

This proposal covers the indirect-evidential constructions specifically; it has not been adopted by Bugaeva, Satō, or Nakagawa; and its claim of classificatory NI remains unconfirmed in the wider literature ‹contested›.
The relativization system described in this chapter is the externally-headed construction; the IHRC/CNI question bears on the evidential construction and is addressed in .
Three gaps in the accessible evidence remain open.

First, whether the ditransitive subject position is grammatically excluded or merely unattested is not decided: the absence is systematic — reported independently by Bugaeva 2015: 48 and by Ijäs — but no source provides a grammaticality judgment supported by speaker elicitation ‹contested›.
Second, ablative and mutative RC heads are unconfirmed in any source read here ‹corpus-suggested›.
Third, the accessibility-hierarchy findings rest primarily on Saru and Chitose data ; whether all Hokkaido dialects relativize the same positions has not been systematically tested ‹speculative›.

Hokkaido Ainu builds noun-modifying clauses prenominally: a finite verb phrase precedes a head noun with no relative pronoun and no change to the verb's morphology; the relativized argument's role is recovered from a gap in argument structure and from any postpositions retained inside the clause ; ; .

When no lexical noun is available or intended as the head, a member of the closed class of formal nouns fills that role, supplying a generic semantic type — 'person', 'thing', 'people', 'place', 'time' — while the clause itself names the referent.
In continuous Hokkaido Ainu text these formal-noun heads appear more often than common-noun heads in relativization contexts .
Two further analytical questions organize the later sections.

The first is whether any Hokkaido Ainu constructions approach the internally-headed pattern of noun modification — in which the notional head is expressed inside the modifying clause rather than outside it — and whether that pattern involves a form of noun incorporation.
Dal Corso raises this for southern Hokkaido Ainu indirect evidential constructions and proposes a classificatory-incorporation analysis .

The second is whether the perception-complement constructions built with possessed sensory formal nouns are biclausal — an external formal noun heading a relative clause — or whether they have grammaticalized toward monoclausal complex predicates.
Both questions remain contested in the literature ‹contested›.

The ~ formal noun in its RC-head and complementizer uses is treated in ; the gap strategy, the accessibility hierarchy, and postposition stranding in ; lexicalized forms that crystallized from headless relative clauses in ; and the evidential clause-final uses of the sensory formal nouns in and in .
The formal nouns that serve as generic heads form a compact, closed set.

Nakagawa lists them as a distinct word class defined by weak lexical autonomy — they follow another element to build an NP — and shows that they carry arity −1, on a par with common nouns in their citation form .
This arity value allows a formal noun to fill the open argument slot of a clause with total arity ≥ +1 and produce a headless relative-clause nominal .

Among person-type heads, p ~ pe is maximally generic and extends to human referents with a pejorative or collective edge in those contexts; kur (< ) selects specifically for a personal referent and carries a polite register.
Shibatani describes -kur as a phrasal nominalizing suffix in Classical/yukar Ainu, productive alongside -p(e) :
The utar head provides person semantics with plurality.
Bugaeva's accessibility-hierarchy study records it as a headless head for clauses with a plural human referent:
The p ~ pe formal noun extends to human agents when context provides that reading.
Bugaeva attests a pair of parallel headless nominals whose open argument is the subject of a motion verb:
The argument positions available to headless nominalizations are the same as those available in externally-headed relative clauses.

Under the noun-phrase accessibility hierarchy of , Hokkaido Ainu relativizes subjects, agents, objects, and a range of obliques through the gap strategy; the alienable possessor and the standard of comparison resist this because of island constraints and the absence of an accessible comparee position respectively .
These exclusions carry through to the headless type: there is no headless relativization of an alienable possessor or a comparison standard in Bugaeva's data.
For oblique participants, the governing postposition stays inside the relative clause when the head is a formal noun, as it would with a common-noun head.
The place-type formal noun usi ~ uske heads clauses with a locative, dative, or directional gap:
Nakagawa's arity accounting governs the boundary between a headless relative-clause nominal and the complementizer use of the same formal noun.
When the clause preceding p ~ pe or hi is already saturated (arity 0), the formal noun nominalizes the event or fact as a whole rather than filling a participant gap .
The complementizer use is treated in and for p ~ pe specifically in .

Shibatani identifies a distinct pattern in Classical/yukar Ainu that he calls the appositive construction: a clause followed by a bare sensory noun in its concept form — without the possessive suffix — where the noun names the perceptual character of the event described by the clause :

In the standard description of the Saru/Chitose perception-complement construction, the sensory noun carries the possessive suffix — haw-e 'the voice of—', sir-i 'the appearance of—', hum-i 'the sensation of—' — and the suffix cross-references the preceding finite clause as the implicit possessor ; .

On that analysis the construction is an externally-headed formal-noun relative clause: the head carries arity −1, the possessed suffix makes the semantic link between head and clause overt, and the possessed formal noun is then an argument of the matrix perception verb or the copula.

Bugaeva's relativization study and Dal Corso's subsequent work both observe a distributional difference when the sensory noun appears in its bare (non-possessed) form alongside an existential or posture verb: hum as 'there is a sensation of', siri an 'there is an appearance of' ; .
In this variant the possessed link that sustains the external-RC analysis is absent.

Bugaeva reads the distribution as showing characteristics of a general noun-modifying clause construction (GNMCC) — a type in which a nominal element classifies the clause referent from inside rather than standing as an external head:
The possessed and non-possessed variants have different distributional profiles: the possessed head functions as an argument of a matrix perception verb (e.g.
, ), while the bare-noun variant appears as a predication in its own right, typically clause-final.

Whether the distributional difference warrants a distinct structural analysis — GNMCC versus external RC — or reflects a stage of bleaching along the same grammaticalization cline is not settled by the sources accessible here ‹corpus-suggested›.
Dal Corso develops the GNMCC observation into a formal structural claim specific to the indirect evidential constructions of southern Hokkaido Ainu.

He argues that siri ki, siri an, hawe as, and humi as are instances of internally-headed relative clauses (IHRCs) in which the sensory noun is incorporated into the event clause as a classifier rather than serving as an external head .

The proposal comprises two components: (i) an IHRC claim — the notional head is expressed inside the modifying clause — and (ii) a classificatory noun incorporation (CNI) claim — the mechanism is a type of noun incorporation in which the incorporated noun classifies the event described by the clause .
The argument turns on the contrast between direct and indirect evidential pairs.

The direct forms (siri ne, hawe ne, humi ne) carry the possessive suffix and close with the copula ne; the possessive suffix cross-references the preceding clause as the possessor, sustaining an external-RC analysis.

The indirect forms replace ne with existential or posture verbs (an, as, ki), and the sensory noun appears without possessive morphology; Dal Corso reads the absence of possessive marking as a diagnostic that the sensory noun is incorporated into the clause as a classifier rather than standing as an external head outside it .
The analysis has not been adopted by Bugaeva, Satō, or Nakagawa in their accounts of Hokkaido Ainu ‹contested›.

Bugaeva's relativization study treats the same perception complements as noun-complement structures where the possessed nominal head cross-references the clause as a whole, and characterizes the non-possessive variant as an emerging GNMCC pattern rather than a settled IHRC structure .
Nakagawa and Satō describe the sensory formal nouns as complementizers of the perception domain without positing an IHRC subcase ; .

The CNI claim further intersects with the broader question of what constitutes noun incorporation in a language where the nominalization-to-lexicalization cline already accounts for many apparent incorporation effects; the incorporation dimension is taken up in .

The wider biclausal-versus-monoclausal question — whether [clause] ruwe ne, [clause] hawe ne, and their kin are biclausal (an external formal noun heading the preceding clause, the copula predicating the result: ; ) or are grammaticalizing toward monoclausal complex predicates (; ) — is addressed with its evidence in and .
No constituency proof in the sources available here settles the question ‹contested›.
Headless relative clauses sit at one end of a cline whose other end is a lexical noun.
Bugaeva documents a set of Hokkaido Ainu nouns that crystallized historically from [VP]–p or [VP]–i nominalizations :

These forms illustrate Bugaeva's Stage II of Hokkaido Ainu nominalization development: a nominalizing word follows a full finite clause and the result gradually freezes into a noun, the clause eventually compressing into a stem .
The productive synchronic counterpart is the headless RC with ~ ; the line between productive construction and lexicalized noun is determined by morphological productivity .

Nakagawa's diagnostic distinguishes an active relative-clause nominalization from a compound noun: the nominalization retains the postposition or applicative that marks the head's semantic role inside the clause, while a compound leaves the relation between its members lexically implicit.
The contrast with instruments is sharpest: a=e-suke-p 'kitchen utensil' retains the applicative e- that licenses the instrument, whereas the plain compound sukemakiri 'kitchen knife' does not .
The lexicalized inventory is treated in .

Ijäs observes that place nouns such as derive historically from headless relative clauses with as the head, and that lexicalized usi-type nouns need no accompanying relational noun when used synchronically, unlike the productive headless-RC construction ; .
The observation fits Bugaeva's Stage-II account and the productive/fossilized distinction Nakagawa draws .
Dal Corso's CNI proposal connects the cline back to the IHRC discussion.

If the bare sensory noun in the indirect evidential constructions is an incorporated classifier, it occupies an inside-clause position analogous to the nominalizing element in the lexicalization cline, rather than the external-head position of the possessed formal noun.

The proposal would extend the incorporation-nominalization interface already visible in the lexicalized nouns above to a productive grammatical construction, making classificatory incorporation a third strategy alongside externally-headed and headless relative clauses.

Whether this extension is warranted by the southern Hokkaido data, or whether the indirect evidential constructions are better handled as partial grammaticalization of the external-RC pattern, is among the questions Dal Corso raises without fully settling ‹contested›.
Hokkaido Ainu reports speech and thought by placing the invariable particle sekor at the right edge of the quoted string, before the matrix verb of saying or thinking.

This mechanism occupies a distinct slot in Refsing's four-way clause-embedding typology: conjunctionalization, nominalization, quotationalization, and adnominalization — with quotationalization, realized by sekor (and its variant ari), forming a separate category from the nominalized-complementizer system .

The nominalized complementizers — kuni, kunak, yak, kusu — that Nakagawa treats in his indirect-speech section operate through the formal-noun nominalizing machinery described in and ; sekor does not nominalize — it quotes directly .
The matrix verbs that take sekor overlap substantially with those that select the indirect-speech markers: , , , and .
The choice between the quotative and the nominalizing complementizers encodes the direct-vs-indirect distinction and controls the person-marking pattern in the embedded clause ; .
How the formal-noun class that enables nominalized complementation is constituted is set out in .
sekor is morphologically invariant: it carries no person affixes, no TAM morphology, and no allomorphic alternation conditioned by the shape of the preceding clause.
Its canonical position is immediately after the last element of the quoted string and before the matrix verb: [quoted clause] sekor [matrix verb].

Refsing identifies a variant ari with the same quotative function in the Shizunai dialect; both are treated as "quotationalizers" forming a class distinct from the nominalized-complementizer inventory .
The quoted clause preserves all features of a main clause: person affixes, polarity, TAM markers, and clause-internal particles are intact inside the quotation.

Sentence-final particles (na, wa, etc.) may appear within the quoted string but not between sekor and the matrix verb — a distributional restriction shared with the indirect-speech markers, whose embedded clauses also exclude final particles .
The clearest evidence for the sekor vs indirect-complementizer distinction is person marking.
Under sekor, the original speaker's person forms are preserved unchanged inside the quote.
Under kuni, kunak, and yak, the embedded clause's person is adjusted to the reporting narrator's viewpoint: an original first person shifts to the fourth, the indefinite/logophoric person .
The indirect-speech markers also differ among themselves in the temporal or semantic value they impose on the embedded proposition ; .
The person contrast between sekor and kuni is illustrated by the following pair.
The proposition 'I will return' appears first as a direct quotation (constructed), then under the indirect-speech complementizer kuni (attested in Nakagawa's grammar):
The temporal contrast between kunak (future proposition, reported as ongoing) and yak (past or general proposition) runs in parallel within the indirect system.
Satō's kunak example combines the indirect-speech marker with the ongoing-aspect phrase kor an:
The directive use of kuni — 'tell X to do Y' — appears frequently in folktale dialogue and marks the complement as a directed action rather than a proposition:
The purposive and deontic extensions of kuni beyond the reported-speech domain are treated in .
The formal noun hawe — possessed form of , 'the voice/report of' — extends the quotative architecture in two directions.
As a bare complementizer it nominalizes a speech event and supplies it as the perceptual object of verbs like : the complement clause becomes "the voice/talk of" the event .

Combined with the copula, hawe ne forms the reportative evidential frame; when sekor precedes it, the compound sekor hawe ne attributes a quoted proposition to an unspecified external source ‹corpus-suggested›:

The clause-final reportative evidential hawe ne standing alone — where it marks information acquired through speech without framing an embedded quotation — is treated in , and the four-way evidential paradigm to which it belongs in .
is the most frequent speech verb in narrative dialogue — narrators routinely use it to introduce character utterances — while appears predominantly in indirect-speech and complementizer frames.
Both appear after sekor and both select kuni/kunak for indirect complements ; .
A stable semantic or register distinction between the two verbs in quotative syntax is not established in the sources consulted ‹corpus-suggested›.
Person adjustment in the indirect-speech complementizer frames reflects what Bugaeva identifies as logophoricity in Southern Hokkaido Ainu.
The fourth-person markers a=/ci= on transitives and =an on intransitives replace an original first person in the embedded clause, reanchoring it to the reporting narrator's viewpoint.
Nakagawa formulates this as a categorical rule: under the indirect-speech markers, "final particles cannot be embedded; the speaker's-viewpoint person shifts 1→3/4" .

Bugaeva's study of reported discourse and logophoricity in Southern Hokkaido Ainu provides the analytical framework: the fourth person here is not a simple third-person referential shift but a logophoric device, indexing the embedded protagonist — the original speaker or thinker — whose perspective the narrator temporarily adopts .

The surface form is identical to the generic/indefinite fourth person (also a=/=an); the logophoric reading is determined by the presence of a complementizer frame and by contextual co-reference with the matrix subject ‹contested›.
The full fourth-person paradigm and its logophoric distribution across narrative genres are treated in and .

Nikitina and Bugaeva develop a stronger claim: the construction is better characterized as logophoric speech rather than indirect speech in the conventional theoretical sense, because the person system encodes the narrator's perspective adoption, not a syntactic binding of the embedded subject to a matrix controller .
The discourse contexts — first-person narration in uwepeker and yukar — where this perspective adoption is most systematic are examined in ‹contested›.
Under sekor direct quotation, no person shift applies: the original speaker's person forms are preserved inside the quote, and the logophoric reanchoring does not arise in the embedded clause.
This is the morphological correlate of the direct/indirect boundary: sekor preserves the perspective of the original utterance; the indirect-speech markers reanchor it to the narrator's viewpoint ; .
The descriptions converge on the categorical point.
Refsing separates quotationalization from nominalization as coordinate clause-embedding types, placing sekor/ari outside the nominalizer class .

Nakagawa's §18.2, which treats the indirect-speech markers extensively as nominalization-based complementizers that take a nominal-object slot, is consistent with keeping sekor as a non-nominalizing quotative; his account of the person shift and the final-particle ban applies to kuni/kunak/yak and not to sekor .
Shibatani, whose treatment foregrounds the formal-noun complementizer system, does not single out a quotative particle in the dialect data he covers .
Three questions remain open in the sources consulted.

First, the geographical and register distribution of sekor vs ari across Hokkaido dialects is documented only by Refsing's Shizunai attestation of both ; whether ari carries any semantic or pragmatic distinction from sekor or is a register/lexical variant is not established ‹speculative›.

Second, the grammaticalization status of the compound sekor hawe ne frame is not settled: whether the sequence is transparently compositional (quotative + reportative evidential) or a lexicalized reportative formula cannot be decided from the sources read here ‹speculative›.

Third, the logophoricity analysis of Nikitina and Bugaeva awaits corpus-level testing at construction level; whether the person-shift pattern under kunak/yak distributes differently from the generic fourth-person use is not settled by evidence in the sources consulted ‹contested›.

Ijäs's pedagogical grammar covers relative clauses and the formal-noun nominalizer system in Lesson 11 — the material banked for this grammar's nominalization domain — but her treatment of direct and indirect speech falls in a separate lesson not yet incorporated here .
No Ijäs claims on sekor or quotative framing are available for grading here.

Clausal complements in Hokkaido Ainu are formed through the same nominalization strategy that builds relative-clause NPs: a finite, person-marked clause is followed by a formal noun or complementizer that turns the whole into a nominal argument of a higher predicate.
The verb inside the embedded clause keeps its ordinary person affixes, polarity, and aspect morphology; no non-finite or participial form exists ; .
What separates a complement clause from a relative clause is a single structural condition, the arity of the embedded clause, treated in the section that follows.

The inventory of complementizers includes the abstract formal noun , the sensory possessive forms , , and , the concrete nominalizer ~ , and the irrealis complementizer , together with a set of indirect-speech markers treated in .

Their grammaticalization from lexical nouns and their role in evidential clause-final constructions are set out in and ; ~ as a headless relative-clause nominalizer is treated in , which cross-references the present chapter for the complementizer use.
Nakagawa's arity (アリティ) accounting provides the structural boundary between a relative clause and a complement clause.
Every NP in the clause contributes −1 to a running count; every argument slot required by the verb contributes +1.
A formal noun itself has arity −1.
When the clause before a formal noun has total arity ≥ +1, a participant slot remains open and the formal noun fills it as the head of a relative-clause NP.
When the clause already has arity 0 — every argument slot is satisfied — the formal noun nominalizes the whole clause as an event or fact; this is the complement reading .

Satō's formulation of the same distinction is categorical: a nominalizer (名詞化辞) nominalizes a whole content clause and allows no reconstruction of an underlying sentence, whereas a formal noun (形式名詞) heading a relative clause can be so reconstructed .
Nakagawa prefers to treat the formal nouns as a word class and the complementizer function as a syntactic role available to some members of that class .
The same surface string [clause] hi or [clause] p is parsed differently depending on which reading the arity yields; examples below illustrate both.
The following illustrates the complement reading of hi.
The embedded clause hekattar tura sinot=an has arity 0: sinot 'play' is an intransitive verb (+1) whose S slot is satisfied by the fourth-person suffix =an (−1), leaving no gap.
hi therefore nominalizes the whole clause as a fact:
The matrix predicates that select a nominalized complement fall into three semantic groups: cognition, perception, and speech/directive.

A verb's argument structure places an upper bound on the number of person affixes it can carry — typically one for the agent (A) and one for the object (O); the complement clause then occupies the single object slot .
This is directly related to the two-affix cap on the verb template.
The list above is drawn from Nakagawa and Satō and is not exhaustive ; .

The complementizer preferences are typical but not always categorical: ramu, for instance, co-occurs with kuni for future and wished content, with yak for past or ongoing content, and with the sensory heads sir-i and hum-i when thought involves a quasi-perceptual quality ‹corpus-suggested›.
The formal noun is the maximally abstract complementizer.

Satō describes it as carrying "almost no concrete meaning" and functioning to nominalize the entire clause before it ; Nakagawa calls it a 補文標識 (complementizer) when its preceding clause has arity 0 .
In this role it appears most frequently as the object of cognition predicates such as eramiskari 'not understand' and kopan 'refuse':
A nominalized clause headed by hi can also serve as the grammatical subject of a stative predication.
Bugaeva cites (after Tamura) a clausal-subject construction in which a coordinated VP is nominalized by hi and predicated as 'best':

The Okuda–Nakagawa analysis of hi distinguishes a 'place where' reading (arity ≥ +1, RC head, requires a case postposition such as oro ta) from a 'time/thing/fact' reading (arity 0, complementizer, no postposition required) .
This distinction is a tendency, not absolute: the Horobetsu example seta utar osoma hi 'the dogs' privy' (literally 'the place dogs defecate') lacks oro ta yet takes the 'place' reading ‹contested›.
The 'place' analysis rests on Okuda (1989), read only second-hand via Nakagawa here.

The four possessed-form nominalizers ru-we, sir-i, haw-e, and hum-i function primarily as clause-final evidential heads (treated in and ), but Satō shows that three of them — sir-i, haw-e, and hum-i — also nominalize embedded clauses as perception-object NPs under nukar 'see' and nu 'hear/ask', with a semantic specialization: sir-i marks an event in progress at reference time (visual perception), haw-e a speech event heard, and hum-i a non-visual sensation ; .
In this use the possessed-form nominalizer takes a saturated clause as its implicit possessor: the 'appearance/voice/feeling of [the embedded event]'.
The whole [clause] sir-i or [clause] haw-e then fills the O slot of the perception verb:

Nakagawa observes that these four evidential nominalizers constitute "one type of complementizer" alongside the non-evidential complementizers; the clause-final 文末句 use (where they are closed by the copula ne or existential an) is the same construction extended to main-clause predication .
The Dal Corso debate about whether these structures are biclausal or partially grammaticalized monoclausal predicates applies equally here and is taken up in the constituency section below.

The complementizer nominalizes the preceding clause and expresses content that is future-oriented, inferred, desired, or directed: what the matrix subject says must happen, thinks should happen, or intends to happen .
Nakagawa classifies kuni as a conjunction with formal-noun-like use (接続助詞の形式名詞的な用法); Bugaeva analyses the complex kuni-p as deontic 'what should be' .
The purpose and adverbial uses of kuni are treated in ; the focus here is on the complement-of-speech and complement-of-cognition uses.
With ye 'say', kuni marks a directive or an anticipated future event reported in speech:
With ramu 'think', kuni expresses a wished or expected state of affairs:
The combination kuni p forms a deontic or purposive nominal .
The embedded clause is nominalized by kuni and then a second formal noun p further nominalizes the resulting complex as 'a thing one should / will do':

The corpus count of kuni is 6,362 tokens (rank 38), a figure that conflates the complementizer, purposive, and adverbial uses; no per-function count is derivable from word-frequency data alone ‹corpus-suggested›.
Beyond kuni, four elements function as complementizers in indirect speech and thought contexts, each encoding a different epistemic or temporal profile ; :
A shared diagnostic: all of these elements nominalize the preceding VP and make it the object of the matrix transitive.
The form yakne is not an indirect-speech marker — it is a conditional conjunction, distinct from the complementizer yak .
Final particles of the type used in main clauses cannot appear inside these embedded complements, and person marking shifts from the original speaker's viewpoint to the narrator's .
The kunak and yak complementizers, and the quotative sekor, are treated in detail in .
The embedded question complementizer ya introduces content questions and polar questions as the object of cognition predicates such as eramiskari 'not know'.
Nakagawa distinguishes the polar-question use ('whether') from the content-question use ('what/where/when'), both employing ya .
A small residue of complement constructions in the corpus involves no overt nominalizer: the embedded clause appears without a following formal noun, directly as the argument of the matrix predicate.
Bugaeva identifies this as Stage I of her diachronic typology of Ainu nominalization — the oldest stratum, in which a bare finite clause functions nominally without a nominalizing word .
Refsing similarly notes cases in Shizunai Ainu that she tentatively treats as "ellipsis of the nominalizer" .
The construction is residual in the Hokkaido attested record and not systematically documented for modern Saru or Chitose ‹corpus-suggested›.
Its relationship to compounding and to the lexicalized nominalization cline (where p ~ pe has contracted into lexical items such as ) is treated in and .

Because complement clauses in Hokkaido Ainu are finite and carry their own person morphology, the embedded subject is always expressible: the verb inside the complement bears its own person affixes independently of the matrix clause.
No PRO or empty-category mechanism is posited in the sources consulted, and no formal control or raising analysis of HA complements appears in the literature surveyed here.
Nevertheless, patterns of participant identity are observable.

With cognition predicates (ramu, eramiskari), the person marking of the embedded clause in the corpus tends to match the matrix subject: the one who thinks or fails to understand is also the agent of the thought or the one about whom the proposition holds.

The examples above show this — ku=ramu 'I think' with an embedded clause about a state of affairs the speaker cares about, a=eramiskari 'one does not understand' with an embedded clause about what that same person ought to say or do.
The regularity, however, follows from the semantics of cognition verbs, not from a grammatical control mechanism, and divergent persons are possible where the content demands it ‹corpus-suggested›.

With the directive use of ye + kuni, the pattern runs in the opposite direction: the matrix subject (the one who speaks) addresses the matrix object (the addressee), and the embedded clause's agent is typically that addressee, not the speaker.

The corpus example from Kawakami Matsuko above — 'when I told them to enter' — shows the fourth-person speaker (a=ye) directing a different group (the addressees) toward an action (ahun 'enter') whose agent goes unmarked in the embedded clause because it is recoverable from discourse ‹corpus-suggested›.
The indirect-speech analysis that best captures this is given in Nakagawa's treatment of indirect speech perspective shifts .

The term raising (movement of an embedded subject to a matrix position) has no attestation in the analytical literature on Hokkaido Ainu clausal complementation, and the available data supply no diagnostic that would motivate such an analysis.
The embedded clause remains a nominalized finite clause whose internal arguments are expressed by the embedded verb's own person affixes ‹speculative›.

Whether the structure [clause] NMLZ ne is biclausal or a grammaticalizing monoclausal complex predicate is a live debate that cuts across complement clauses, evidential constructions, and the formal noun system generally.
The two positions are:
The biclausal external-RC analysis treats the nominalized clause as a full NP whose head is a possessed formal noun.
The copula ne then closes the outer predication.
Tamura, Okuda, and Satō take this position ; .
The grammaticalization-to-monoclausal analysis holds that the erstwhile noun is considerably bleached and the construction is moving toward a complex predicate.

The diagnostic is that a fully lexical noun can take demonstratives and attributive modifiers (pirka menoko 'a beautiful woman'), whereas the evidential formal noun cannot: *pirka ruwe ne kewtum is ungrammatical ; .
No read source provides a constituency proof — a bracket test or movement diagnostic — that decides between these ‹contested›.
The same unresolved question is noted in the dedicated treatments of ruwe ne in and of p ~ pe in .

For the complement constructions treated in this chapter, the practical consequence is that the formal nouns function synchronically as clause-final markers that package a finite clause as a nominal argument.

The diachronic source in lexical nouns remains transparent (Bugaeva's nominalization-cline stages, ), and partial grammaticalization explains why the same forms build RC heads, complement clauses, evidential assertions, and — at the furthest end of the cline — conjunctions and adverbial-clause markers ; .

Ijäs's pedagogical grammar introduces relative clauses and notes that formal nouns such as uske 'place/time' are best understood as nouns that have historically originated from relative-clause constructions, without committing to a formal analysis of the biclausal-vs-monoclausal debate .
This aligns with the historical-cline view and is graded as consistent with the consensus on diachrony ‹consensus›.
The particle kuni nominalizes a finite VP into a nominal whose content is irrealis, prospective, or deontic — what the reporting subject expects, wishes, or presents as obligatory.
It is a member of the small set of complementizers that take a saturated VP and make it the argument of a transitive matrix predicate, forming what Nakagawa calls the indirect-speech (間接話法) system .
The complementizer yak marks the retrospective or ongoing counterpart; hi and p ~ pe nominalize without a temporal restriction ; .
The closed class of formal nouns that includes p ~ pe is defined there; the arity arithmetic that separates complementizer from relative-clause use is developed in .
Three construction types exploit kuni.
Before or , it nominalizes a VP expressing what the reporting subject says will happen, believes should happen, or directs someone to do.
Before the formal noun , it yields a purposive or deontic nominal (kuni p).
And before the copula directly, Classical Ainu data show an expectative predication meaning 'it must be that' or 'in order that' (kuni ne) .
These three are treated in the sections below.
Corpus search returns 6,113 tokens of kuni (rank 36), a figure that conflates the complementizer with any phonologically identical material and gives an upper bound on the construction's frequency.
The matrix verbs that select kuni are and .
Each member of the indirect-speech complementizer set marks the temporal or epistemic stance the reporting subject takes toward the reported content.
kuni occupies the prospective end of the system: the embedded VP describes what will, should, or is wished to come about .
Two syntactic properties hold across all four members.
Final particles of the main-clause type (na, ya, etc.) cannot appear inside the embedded clause; they are anchored to the speaker's own utterance, not to the reported one.
And the referential perspective inside the embedded clause shifts from the speaker's to the reporting subject's: a first-person speaker becomes third or fourth person as the locus of predication .

These properties confirm that each complementizer heads a nominal object: even yak, originally a conditional conjunctive, cannot be followed directly by an intransitive verb (*yak hawean 'that someone spoke' is ungrammatical as a standalone), because as a nominal it must be the transitive verb's object .
ramu 'think' selects the same kuni complement when the thinker's belief is prospective or deontic.

The distinction between kuni and kunak within the prospective subsystem is the most discussed.

Nakagawa assigns the directive reading exclusively to kuni: a command or instruction reported under ye takes kuni; the two forms are not freely interchangeable even in purely inferred contexts ‹corpus-suggested›.
The kuni / yak contrast is cleaner: the pair divides prospective from retrospective content, mirroring a tense–modality divide in the reported proposition.

When kuni is followed by the formal noun p (allomorph pe after a consonant-final stem), the compound nominalizes the preceding VP and yields two related readings depending on how the head is construed: a purposive nominal 'thing to V / what is to be done', and a deontic or propositional nominal 'what will / must happen'.
Both are well attested in the Saru corpus.
The purposive reading is clearest when kuni p denotes objects or activities defined by their intended function.
