The deontic or propositional reading appears when kuni p is itself predicated.

Combination with the copula and the inferential formal noun ruwe yields the frame [VP] kuni p ne ruwe ne, which presents the VP-content as inevitable or obligatory and asserts it as established fact (see ):
The four main patterns built on kuni, ranging from indirect speech through purposive nominal to the full epistemic deontic frame, are summarized in the following table ; :
The p of kuni p is the same formal noun treated in .
Its arity (−1) closes a purposive clause with an open participant slot (purposive nominal reading) or nominalizes a saturated irrealis clause as a whole (deontic reading).
The complement-taking predicates that select these nominals are discussed in ; the overlap with the deontic modal domain in .
Shibatani groups kuni followed directly by the copula ne alongside the other formal-noun-plus-copula modal expressions (ruwe ne, siri ne, hawe ne, humi ne) under the label "expectative mood".
The form yields two readings in his Classical Ainu data: an epistemic 'it must be that [VP]' and a purposive 'in order that [VP]' .
On this account, kuni itself functions as a formal-noun-like head nominalizing the preceding VP; the copula predicates that nominalization.
The two readings correspond directly to the deontic and purposive readings of kuni p ne, where the additional formal noun p is present between kuni and the copula.
Whether bare kuni ne and kuni p ne are diachronically related variants or a single construction with optionally present p is not settled by the sources read here ‹speculative›.
Shibatani's data are from Classical epic Ainu (yukar traditions of the Itadori and Ishikari areas).
No read source provides modern Saru or Chitose corpus examples of bare kuni ne without the intervening p; the banked Saru corpus examples above all show the kuni p ne form.
Nakagawa's grammar, based on modern Saru and Chitose, records kuni p ne ruwe ne as the productive frame .

The formal-noun-plus-copula paradigm underlying both constructions connects kuni to the evidential system: Nakagawa observes that clause-final evidential phrases (ruwe ne, siri ne, etc.) constitute one type of complementizer applied to a main clause, and kuni participates in the same nominal architecture .
The full paradigm is set out in .
Purpose clauses built on kuni in adverbial position are treated in .
Two analyses of kuni appear in the literature and make different predictions about its internal structure.

Nakagawa treats it as a conjunctive particle (接続助詞) with formal-noun-like behavior (形式名詞的な用法) — a free form that nominalizes the preceding VP and feeds it to a transitive matrix predicate, on the same footing as yak and kunak .
On this analysis, kuni p is a sequence of two free forms: the particle kuni followed by the formal noun p.

Bugaeva's morphological analysis decomposes kuni-p as kun-i-p — an obligation-related root kun- (semantics uncertain), a possessive suffix -i, and the nominalizer -p — yielding a deontic head meaning 'the thing that must be done', without necessarily treating kuni and p as syntactically separate ‹contested›.
The lexical source of the root kun- remains unverified.

The broader constituency question — whether kuni p ne ruwe ne is biclausal (a nominalizing particle and formal noun heading the preceding clause, closed by the copula) or is grammaticalizing toward a monoclausal complex predicate — runs parallel to the same debate for the evidential frame ruwe ne, discussed in and .
No read source provides a constituency test that decides between them for the kuni construction specifically ‹contested›

Shibatani's Classical data add a historical dimension: his "expectative mood" label groups kuni ne with the possessed sensory-noun heads, suggesting the formal-noun-like behavior Nakagawa observes reflects a partly grammaticalized noun origin — the same diachronic cline by which ruwe, siri, and hawe moved from sensory nouns to nominalization heads ‹speculative›.
Hokkaido Ainu has no grammatical tense.

Past, present, and future reference are never read off the shape of the finite verb; the categories the verb does engage are aspect, mood, modality, and evidentiality, and even these are optional rather than obligatory inflections ; ; .

Takahashi states the point for the modern reference literature: aspect and evidentiality are not obligatory grammatical categories in Ainu, and the perfective/imperfective opposition is not fixed either lexically or grammatically ; .

The grammatical work that other languages assign to tense and bound aspect is carried here by periphrastic complex predicates: a second finite verb, an existential verb, or the copula follows the lexical verb and supplies the temporal, aspectual, or modal value.
In the terms of aspectual typology and the grammaticalization of tense–aspect–mood, the system uses optional analytic operators where an inflecting language would use bound morphology ; .
The time-reference system itself is treated in ; this chapter maps the forms that supply aspectual, modal, and illocutionary values and routes each to its detail chapter.
Whether a tenseless predicate has a preferred temporal translation was debated through the twentieth century.

Kindaichi held that Ainu makes no temporal distinction yet renders everything as past, the moment of speech being too fleeting to fix; Chiri narrowed the past reading to non-stative predicates, leaving statives to translate as a Japanese -te iru present; and Refsing argued that a language without the category of tense does not order events on a linear timeline at all, so that no past translation is more correct than a present one ; ‹contested›.

The descriptive consensus that displaced these positions is the one stated above: there are no pure tense markers, and a bare finite verb takes whatever English tense its event type and discourse setting require .
Three constructional frames carry almost all of this load, distinguished by their shape and by which verb hosts the person index.
The distinction is diagnostic: in the auxiliary frame only the lexical verb is indexed, whereas in the pair-verb frame both predicates can be, because each remains a finite verb in its own right ; .
One principle organizes the pair-verb frame: a verb phrase has exactly one person-bearing main verb.
In ku=tere wa k=an 'I am waiting', the existential verb an 'exist' carries the same ku= as the lexical tere 'wait', so the string is two clauses linked by wa rather than a single inflected predicate.

Nakagawa accordingly treats kor an and wa an not as aspect proper but as forms that express aspect-like meaning, and Yoshikawa develops the same point under the cover term "existential aspectual forms": the existential an here is less grammaticalized than Japanese iru/aru and keeps its concrete existential sense ; ‹contested›.

The lexical material of these frames comes from the suppletive singular/plural verb pairs that Ijäs's Lesson 9 catalogues as special verb forms — a/rok 'sit', an/oka 'exist', ek/arki 'come', arpa/paye 'go' ; .

Two of these pairs feed the TAM system directly: a/rok grammaticalizes into the perfective/anterior auxiliary, and an/oka into the existential-aspect frames, the number of the auxiliary tracking the number of the subject ; ‹consensus›.
Temporal location is recovered from four overt resources.

Time adverbs such as numan 'yesterday' and nisatta 'tomorrow' place the event directly; prospective and necessity forms such as kusu ne, oasi 'surely will', and etokus 'be about to' yield future readings; the situational evidential siri anchors a visible ongoing scene in the present; and completion forms such as a, nisa, and wa isam support past translation .
Each yields a temporal reading only relative to the moment of utterance, and context can override the default.
The same prospective frame surfaces in the grammars as intention, scheduled future, and, with a second-person subject, near-command.

Ijäs glosses it 'be going to, intend to, plan to', matching Nakagawa and Satō, but her pedagogical orthography writes kusune as one word; the analysis followed here is the conjunction kusu plus the copula ne, with the one-word spelling kept as a teaching convention and carrying no separate morphological claim ; ; .
Before any periphrasis applies, each verb carries an inherent aspectual character that conditions which frame it enters.

Nakagawa divides the lexicon into action, change, and stative verbs, a division that aligns with the actional classes Takahashi and Yoshikawa use; derivational Aktionsart suffixes on (often onomatopoeic) roots, such as -kosanu 'happen once, briefly' or -natara 'persist', add a lexically restricted second layer ; ; .
A stative verb can also be read as the change into its state, so the same lexeme may shift class: poro is 'be big' or 'become big', and the choice of aspect frame turns on that reading .
The progressive kor an joins a lexical verb, the simultaneous conjunctive kor 'while', and the existential an (plural oka).
With action verbs it marks an action in progress; with change verbs it marks the process leading into the change; and it covers habitual and repeated situations as well ; ; .
Because the construction is a clause chain, the lexical verb and an share the subject index:
The resultative wa an joins a lexical verb, the sequential conjunctive wa, and the existential verb, and denotes the state that exists after a change ; ; .

Satō draws the selectional line sharply: an action verb leaves no direct result for wa an to predicate, so action perfects fall to the auxiliary a instead, and only change and stative verbs enter wa an ; .
Perception and cognition verbs such as nukar 'see' and eramuan 'understand' take either frame, and how the contrast should be stated is unsettled.

Nakagawa's 1981 account separates nukar kor an from nukar wa an by active observation against passive coming-into-view; Satō rejects activeness as primary and derives the contrast from continuation of action against continuation of result, treating any activeness as a contextual by-product.
Nakagawa concedes the matter needs further discussion ; ‹contested›.

A dialect-specific restriction compounds the picture: in Tokachi, kor an does not co-occur with a first-person subject, the progressive of a first-person subject using kan an instead; no equivalent is reported for the southern dialects ‹contested›.
Several dialectal continuatives occupy the same field.
Saru and Chitose kane an adds a noteworthy-situation nuance, while Shizunai and Samani use it as a plain merger of kor an and wa an; Tokachi and Ishikari have kan an, and Tokachi tek an ; .
Yoshikawa groups these with wa an and kor an as existential aspectual forms — forms that may express aspectual meanings without being grammatical aspect .
The full treatment of the progressive and resultative belongs to , the appearance-based and merged continuatives to , and the iterative and habitual periphery to .
The auxiliary a (plural rok), grammaticalized from the verb a/rok 'sit', is the most disputed member of the system, and the disagreement is substantive rather than terminological.

The Kindaichi–Tamura tradition reads it as perfective or past; Bugaeva and Satō read an actional perfect that, on Satō's account, cannot combine with a negative and so leaves the stative perfect to wa an; Nakagawa, following Yoshikawa, denies it is tense or aspect at all, taking it to mark an event set in contrast to a following one; and Yoshikawa's handbook chapter analyses it as perfective with a direct-evidential, witnessed-reminiscence component ; ; ; ‹contested›.
The admirative aan (plural rokoka) forms a tidy paradigm against a.

It signals that, at some reference point, the speaker recognizes after the fact what an earlier situation was, often with surprise; Yoshikawa analyses it as perfect plus indirect evidentiality, with mirativity as an extension, where a is perfective plus direct evidentiality, the two echoing the direct/indirect past of Classical Japanese ki and keri ; .
The plural rok-oka is the strongest internal argument that aan is the auxiliary a plus existential an, since it pairs the plural of a with the plural of an.

The singular surface forms vary by locality — anan in Chitose, awan in Horobetsu and Tokachi, haw'an in Shizunai — and Yoshikawa grants that some invite alternative segmentations, so the unified a + an etymology rests on the plural rather than on every singular form ; ‹contested›.
Completion has a wider periphery than a.

The recent perfect nisa marks an event just finished, and the completive pair verbs wa isam and wa okere carry the lexical traces of isam 'be absent' and okere 'finish', patterning with clause linkage because both members can stay person-bearing predicates ; .

Ijäs's Lesson 9 records a repeated a ... a pattern as prolonged continuity; this is the reduplicated perfective with an iterative value, and the full account of a, its reduplication, and aan is given in ; ‹corpus-confirmed›.

Modality is distributed across the auxiliary, transitive-verb-auxiliary, and final-particle layers, with epistemic, ability, deontic, and desiderative values occupying different positions in the clause ; .
Epistemic nankor marks probability or conjecture, and with a second-person subject and final na it softens into expectation or command .

Ijäs gives the same range — 'must have' on a past event, 'probably' on a future one — and adds an etymology from a verb 'be trustworthy'; no source read for this account confirms that derivation, and it is best left as her own suggestion ‹speculative›.
Ability is expressed through the transitive-verb-auxiliary group, whose negative is lexical rather than built with somo.

easkay gives general ability, eaykap the broad inability (lack of skill or of circumstance), and koyaykus the specifically circumstantial inability; the scalar ka 'even' may intervene, especially under negation.
Ijäs treats easkay and eaykap correctly as a lexical positive–negative pair ; ‹consensus›.

Deontic necessity and permission draw on several sources: the auxiliary easirki expresses obligation, kuni an expectation or 'should', and conditional predicates such as yak pirka 'should', yak wen 'should not', and yakka pirka 'may' express advice and permission .
The full inventory belongs to , the ability auxiliaries to , and the epistemic and desiderative forms to .
The direct imperative to a singular addressee is the bare verb with no second-person subject prefix; object prefixes may remain, and adding a second-person subject affix is ungrammatical.
A plural or polite addressee takes final yan, number-sensitive verbs using the plural stem, and the softener hani or a benefactive wa kore 'do for (me)' turns the command into a request .
Ijäs's command lesson matches these points and warns explicitly against the second-person subject affix ‹consensus›.
Prohibition is formed by a preverbal prohibitive adverb, most often Saru and Chitose iteki, with dialect variants itekke, etekke, and ecikki.
The adverb precedes both imperatives and indirect command forms such as kusu ne na and nankor na .
The hortative uses the final particles ro, rok, or no, distributed by dialect, after a fourth-person verb.
This is the main directive environment in which the fourth person expresses an addressee-inclusive 'we' .
Imperative and prohibitive are developed in , the hortative and optative in , and the person base in .
TAM and evidentiality are adjacent systems because several aspect forms carry evidential or mirative values.
The perfective a has been analysed as direct evidential, aan as indirect-evidential and mirative, and the situational siri frame anchors a visible ongoing event in present time ; .
The formal-noun evidential system — ruwe ne, siri ne, hawe ne, humi ne — is treated in , with the central member in the inferential ruwe ne.
Scope ordering keeps the two systems distinct.

The evidential predicate sits above clause-internal aspect and modality but below the clause linkers, so kusu ne ruwe ne is well formed while *ruwe ne kusu ne is not, and negation goes inside the frame, as in … somo ki ruwe ne 'it is a fact that one does not …' .
In the ability domain negation is lexicalized as eaykap or koyaykus, and prohibition uses the iteki adverbs, so both belong to the negation system as well as to mood.
Clause linkage supplies the connective material of the periphrastic frames.
The sequential wa that chains events appears in wa an, wa isam, and wa okere, and the simultaneous kor of adverbial clauses appears in kor an.

When the second predicate keeps its person marking and verbal properties, the construction retains the shape of a linked predication, which is why the existential-aspect frames stand between aspect and clause chaining.
The linking grammar these forms recruit is set out in sequential wa and simultaneous kor.
Hokkaido Ainu has no grammatical tense.
No alternation in verb form encodes whether an event precedes, coincides with, or follows the moment of speech.
Nakagawa states the finding plainly: past, present, and future reference "cannot be expressed by any change of verb form, and normally need not be" .
Bugaeva draws the same conclusion twice: "there are no pure tense markers" and the verb "may be marked for aspect, modality, and evidentiality" .

Takahashi adds that even aspect and evidentiality are not obligatory grammatical categories in Ainu ; Yoshikawa reports that a clear perfective–imperfective opposition is absent both lexically and grammatically .
A finite verb, unmarked for any of these, yields whatever temporal interpretation its event type and discourse context allow.
Nakagawa draws a typological parallel with Mandarin Chinese, which likewise recovers temporal reference from adverbs, aspect particles, and contextual position rather than from verb inflection .
The grammatical categories the Hokkaido Ainu verb does engage — aspect, mood, modality, and evidentiality — form a periphrastic system of complex predicates whose architecture is mapped in .
The present chapter focuses on the theoretical status of the tense absence and the mechanisms through which temporal reference is achieved in its place.

Whether Ainu is best described as radically tenseless, as implicitly past, or as encoding a covert two-way tense opposition through the auxiliary was debated across most of the twentieth century and remains contested at one point.
Four positions have been held.
Kindaichi's claim that Ainu "expresses everything in the past" rested on the observation that finite forms in oral narrative translate with past-tense equivalents.
This describes a discourse default of the narrative register: events are ordered against a temporal frame set at the opening, so a bare verb reads as past by pragmatic inference, not by inflection.

Chiri's refinement — that the past reading is obligatory only for predicates denoting change or action, while stative predicates prefer a present-progressive translation — anticipates the modern aspectual classification (treated in ) but treats a discourse-aspectual tendency as a grammatical rule.

Refsing's position is the sharpest departure: a language without the category of tense has no grammatical linear time ordering and so admits no preferred translation tense; calling the past "more proper" misapplies a European temporal grid to a system that lacks the category altogether ‹contested›.
The auxiliary (plural ) is the form closest to a tense marker, and its analysis is genuinely unsettled .
Kindaichi and Tamura read it as past, which would produce a covert two-way opposition: marked a = past, unmarked = non-past.
Bugaeva and Satō treat it as an actional perfect — a past event with present relevance — which yields a past reading but is not a tense category ; .

Nakagawa, following Yoshikawa's reanalysis, denies that a encodes tense or aspect at all, taking it to mark an event set in contrast to what follows rather than to locate that event in past time ; ‹contested›.
The full debate is developed in ; what this chapter records is that even the form most likely to encode tense is not analysed as a tense marker by the modern descriptive consensus.
When explicit temporal location is required, the primary device is a free temporal adverb.
and are the basic past- and future-anchoring items; comparable expressions specify this morning, last year, and other reference points .
The adverb occurs freely in clause-initial or preverbal position, and the bare verb it modifies requires no additional tense marking.
Temporal information is distributed across the clause: the adverb locates the event, and the verb contributes its aspectual character.
In narrative, discourse position does the anchoring work that temporal adverbs do in speech.

A story-world frame established at the opening locates subsequent bare verbs as past without any overt marker; transitions in scene or topic are often marked by the completive a, which places the preceding event in the background before the shift ; .

This relative, discourse-anchored time reference — where temporal interpretation tracks a reference point established in prior context rather than the absolute speech moment — is the dominant mode of temporal location in Hokkaido Ainu .
Three of the four overt strategies for temporal location recruit grammatical forms whose primary value is aspectual, modal, or evidential; the temporal reading is an inference .

The situational evidential siri anchors a visible, ongoing event in the present: a clause closed by siri ne profiles an event the speaker observes unfolding at the moment of speech ; its own description belongs to .
The progressive and resultative do not specify tense, but in narrative context they deliver recognizable temporal orientations.
kor an presents an action as ongoing within the story frame and so reads as past from the perspective of the outside hearer; wa an presents the state left after a change and reads similarly.
The example below illustrates both the progressive and the bare existential in a narrative setting where the past reading is entirely a function of discourse context.

The completion forms — a/rok, the recent perfect , and the pair verbs wa isam and wa okere — carry the strongest past-temporal implicature, because a completed event is canonically prior to the speech moment.

Nakagawa notes the limit explicitly: these forms yield a temporal reading "only relative to the utterance moment" and "are not, in themselves, tense forms"; context can override the default past reading .
A past English gloss for a bare verb or a kor an clause renders the discourse context, not a grammatical tense feature.
Future reference draws on modal forms rather than a future tense.
The prospective–intentive marks the speaker's intention or a scheduled event; marks an event as certainly forthcoming; indicates imminence; and marks incipient preparation ; .
Each carries its modal value — intention, scheduled certainty, imminence — and the future temporal reading follows as pragmatic inference.

Ijäs's pedagogical grammar covers the same set under 'be going to, intend to, plan to', correctly grouping them as modal rather than tense, and observes that nankor with a future-oriented proposition yields a probability reading .
The nisatta … nankor example above illustrates the modal–adverb combination that together delivers an unambiguous future reading without any future tense marker.
The segmentation of kusu ne as the conjunction kusu plus the copula ne — rather than a single morpheme — is followed here in preference to the one-word pedagogical spelling kusune ; ; .

Tenseless languages — in which tense is not a grammaticalized, obligatory category of the verb — are well attested cross-linguistically, and the universality of tense is not confirmed by the typological record.

Bybee, Perkins, and Pagliuca, surveying tense, aspect, and modality across 76 languages, find that many languages mark temporal reference optionally or through aspect alone, encoding it in the same formal position as mood and evidentiality rather than through a dedicated tense paradigm .
Comrie's foundational account of aspect explicitly separates the aspectual category from tense precisely because many languages grammaticalize the former without the latter .
Hokkaido Ainu falls in this class: its verb's grammatical categories are aspect, modality, and evidentiality, none of which is tense.

Within the typological space of tenseless systems, Ainu's aspect-prominent profile is characteristic: the verb's grammatical distinctions map onto aspectual, modal, and evidential values, and temporal reference is delegated to peripheral adverbs and contextual inference.

The grammaticalization sources of the aspect forms — the existential feeding the progressive and resultative frames, the posture verb feeding the perfective auxiliary — are intransitive verbs that carry no tense meaning and acquire none through grammaticalization.
The system as a whole confirms that the absence of tense is a primary fact about the language rather than a surface disguise for a covert category ; ; .
Two periphrastic constructions recruit the existential verbs an (singular) and oka / okay (plural) as the second predicate in a clause chain.
The simultaneous frame V kor an marks an action or change in progress and habitual situations; the sequential frame V wa an marks the state that persists after a change has been completed ; ; .
Both constructions belong to the pair-verb frame: each predicate retains its own person marking and its status as a finite verb.

This finite independence is the diagnostic that distinguishes them from fully grammaticalized aspect suffixes, and it is the basis on which Nakagawa treats kor an and wa an as forms that express aspect-like meaning rather than as grammatical aspect proper .

Yoshikawa develops the same point under the cover term existential aspectual forms (存在型アスペクト形式): an here is less grammaticalized than Japanese いる/ある, retaining its concrete existential sense, and the cline from lexical existential to aspectual auxiliary has advanced without reaching obligatory inflectional morphology ; ‹contested›.
The locational and existential uses of an and oka are covered in .
The suppletive SG/PL alternation underlying the pair belongs to .
The conjunctive particles kor 'while' and wa 'and then' are analysed in their wider clause-linking roles in and .
The merged and extended continuatives kane an, kan an, tek an, and hine an belong to , and the actional-perfect auxiliary a/rok to .
an and oka form one of the suppletive singular/plural verb pairs that the Hokkaido verb system maintains: the singular stem is an, the plural oka (realized as okay in many phonological environments).
The two are in strict complementary distribution by the number of the controlling argument ; ; ‹consensus›.
In the aspectual periphrases this suppletion carries over directly: the auxiliary tracks the same argument that would trigger the choice between the lexical forms.
For kor an and the standard intransitive pattern of wa an, that argument is the shared subject; in the transitive object-agreement pattern of wa an, it is the object.

The preserved SG/PL alternation is consistent with the partial-grammaticalization assessment shared by Nakagawa, Yoshikawa, and Bugaeva: a fully fused aspect suffix typically loses lexical alternations of this kind.
Ijäs catalogues an/oka as one of several suppletive pairs — alongside a/rok 'sit', ek/arki 'come', and arpa/paye 'go' — whose number suppletion extends into grammaticalized contexts ; ‹consensus›.
The construction V kor an (plural: V kor oka) joins the lexical verb to the simultaneous conjunctive particle kor 'while' and the existential verb.
With action verbs — activities without an inherent change of state (apkas 'walk', mina 'laugh', sinot 'play') — the construction marks the action as in progress at the reference time.

With change verbs — predicates whose completion involves a change of state or location (as 'stand up', hacir 'fall', ek 'come') — it marks the process leading toward the change, not the resulting state, which is the domain of wa an ; ; .

The construction also covers habitual and repeated situations — the type that Japanese translates with 〜している in iterative contexts — and with change verbs approaching their culmination, an inceptive reading ('it is getting light'; Saru epuykehe tane sipuske kor oka 'the buds are now about to open') ; ; .
When the subject is plural, an is replaced by oka.

Because kor an is a chain of two finite clauses, the lexical verb and the existential each take a person index independently, and both must agree with the shared subject.
The co-indexation is the clearest diagnostic of the pair-verb structure: in the example above, the fourth-person suffix =an appears on both sinot and the existential.
The same holds with overt second-person prefixes:
In Tokachi, kor an cannot co-occur with a first-person subject.
The progressive of a first-person event uses kan an instead: ku=nukar kan ku=an 'I am watching it' is grammatical where *ku=nukar kor ku=an is not.

Takahashi proposes that Tokachi kor an carries an observational component — presenting an event as witnessed by the speaker — that is incompatible with the speaker being the agent performing the action ‹contested›.
The restriction is specific to Tokachi; no equivalent is reported for Saru, Chitose, or the remaining Hokkaido varieties.
The distribution of kan an is covered in .
The construction V wa an (plural: V wa oka) joins the lexical verb to the sequential conjunctive particle wa and the existential verb, denoting the state that exists after the completion of a change.
The canonical environment is a change verb: the nearest Japanese equivalents are 〜ている in its result-state reading and 〜てある ; ; ; .
The motion verb ek provides the clearest minimal pair, because it enters both frames with distinct readings:
Stative verbs enter wa an under their inchoative reading.
The verb 'be big / become big', read as 'become big', takes wa an to describe the reached state: poro wa an 'has grown / is now big' .

Action verbs — activities without an inherent endpoint — are excluded, since they leave no stable result for the existential to predicate: *tapkar wa an (from ) and *uenewsar wa an are ungrammatical .
Their completion falls to the auxiliary a, treated in .

Satō extends the action-verb exclusion into a complementary-distribution claim: the actional perfect — completion of an action, without implying a residual state — belongs exclusively to the auxiliary a, while wa an covers only stative perfects (a result state persists) ; ‹corpus-suggested›.
Bugaeva concurs that a separate auxiliary-based construction handles the actional perfect .
Nakagawa draws attention to mokor wa an 'is asleep' as a case where Ainu forces a choice that Japanese leaves ambiguous.
The verb is construed as a change of state — the act of falling asleep — rather than as an ongoing activity, so the result state (being asleep) is what wa an predicates.
A progressive reading under kor an is unavailable for this verb .

Japanese 眠っている is ambiguous between the progressive and the resultative; West Japanese dialects resolve the same ambiguity formally, with -shiyoru (progressive) and -shitoru (resultative), paralleling the Ainu distinction.
As in kor an, both predicates in the chain carry independent person marking.
For wa an, however, the controller of the existential depends on transitivity and which argument holds the resultant state ; :
In (a) and (b), both predicates bear the same person index, exactly as in kor an.

In (c) — the construction closest to Japanese 〜てある — the agent's action is complete and what persists is the object in its new state; the existential an appears bare when the object is third-person or inanimate, because no explicit person prefix is required ; ; .
Verbs of perception and cognition — , , and — take either construction, and the contrast between nukar kor an and nukar wa an is the main analytical locus of debate within this domain.

Nakagawa's 1981 analysis attributed the distinction to the degree of active involvement of the perceiver: nukar kor an is active, deliberate looking, while nukar wa an is a passive coming-into-view of a scene .
Satō (2006) challenges this characterization.

In his account the primary contrast is between continuation of the perceiving action and continuation of the post-acquisition knowledge state: nukar kor an = 'is in the act of looking' and nukar wa an = 'has seen it and now holds that knowledge'.
Any impression of deliberateness is a contextual by-product of the action/result distinction rather than its basis ; .
Nakagawa concedes in the 2024 edition that the question warrants further investigation ‹contested›.

Yoshikawa adds a structural caution: for these verbs, the line between "continuation of an aspectual relation" and "a coincidental co-occurrence of two situations" is genuinely unclear, and the ambiguity is part of the broader argument that these constructions occupy a gradient between clause chaining and grammaticalized aspect ‹contested›.
The cross-linguistic grammaticalization of an existential or locative verb into a progressive or resultative auxiliary is well-attested typologically ; .
Hokkaido Ainu represents a mid-stage on that cline.
Three properties mark the constructions as only partially grammaticalized ‹consensus›:
First, the source verb is morphologically and syntactically present — both predicates remain independently finite and indexed.
Second, the suppletive number alternation an/oka is preserved, a property typically lost when aspect auxiliaries fuse into bound morphemes.

Third, aspect is not an obligatory grammatical category in Ainu: the constructions can be omitted without ungrammaticality, unlike the obligatory aspect marking of heavily aspect-marking languages ; .

In Bugaeva's typology of Ainu periphrastic frames, the pair-verb construction is distinguished from the auxiliary-verb frame (hosting a, nankor, rusuy, and their kin) precisely by this double indexation: in the auxiliary frame only the main verb is person-marked, while in the pair-verb frame both predicates are .
Several Hokkaido varieties deploy additional forms that overlap with or extend the kor an/wa an field.

Yoshikawa groups kor an, wa an, kane an, and hine an under the cover term existential aspectual forms, all tracing to the same grammaticalization source in the lexical existential an, with individual varieties positioned at different points along the cline ; .

In Saru and Chitose, kane an covers both progressive and resultative readings and adds a noteworthy-situation nuance that the simpler pair lacks; in Shizunai and Samani it serves as a plain, unmarked equivalent of either construction.
Tokachi and Ishikari have kan an — leaning progressive in Tokachi, resultative in Ishikari — and Tokachi additionally uses tek an for the resultative of change verbs ; .
The full dialect survey belongs to .
One community observation notes a correspondence between Hokkaido wa an and a Sakhalin form hemaka in cross-variety word lists (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, December 2024) ‹speculative›.
The sources consulted for this grammar do not address this correspondence, and its functional equivalence requires independent verification in the Sakhalin grammatical literature.
Two auxiliaries of anterior or perfective value form a closely related pair in the Hokkaido Ainu auxiliary system: (singular) and (plural).

Both are grammaticalized forms of the suppletive intransitive verb pair a / rok 'sit (SG/PL)', and they retain the number-sensitivity of that source pair: a appears when the clause subject is singular, rok when it is plural ; ; .

Ijäs's Lesson 9 catalogues the a / rok suppletive pair as a morphological special form alongside ek / arki 'come' and an / oka 'exist', without connecting the pair directly to the grammaticalized auxiliary .
The suppletive pair and its role in verbal number are treated in .
Structurally, a and rok belong to the auxiliary-verb frame: the shape is V AUX, with no conjunctive particle between the lexical verb and the auxiliary.
Person marking falls on the preceding lexical verb; the auxiliary carries none.

This single-indexed structure sets the construction apart from the pair-verb frames (kor an, wa an), where each predicate bears its own person index because each constitutes a finite clause in its own right ; .
The overall periphrastic architecture is set out in ; the existential-aspect pair verbs in .
When the subject is plural, rok replaces a.

What a marks is genuinely disputed, and the five positions in circulation represent substantive rather than merely terminological disagreements ; ; ‹contested›.
The perfective / past and perfect readings (positions 1 and 2) capture the most frequent translation equivalence.

Their limitation surfaces in what Yoshikawa calls "exceptional a": time-invariant constants and self-evident truths on which a appears but a past reading is unmotivated, pointing toward a non-temporal account .
The actional-perfect restriction (position 3) carries the sharpest distributional claim.
Satō argues that a marks a completed action as still affecting the current situation, and negating the action removes that link; hence a cannot scope over a negated predicate.
The stative or resultative perfect — 'V-ed (and is still in that state)' — is expressed by wa an instead ; .
The stative-resultative frame is treated in .
The background-event analysis (position 4), following Yoshikawa 2015, draws on discourse distribution.
Clause-final a recurrently precedes a reversal connector — korka 'but/although', sequential wa, or the nominalizer p in an adversative frame — marking the preceding event as contrasted background.
Nakagawa takes this as evidence that a is primarily discourse-structural, and any past-tense reading a contextual by-product ‹contested›.

Yoshikawa's 2022 Handbook analysis (position 5) integrates the distributional and discourse observations: a combines perfective aspect with direct evidentiality and witnessed-reminiscence modal value.
The "exceptional a" on time-invariant truths is reanalysed as direct evidentiality marking the speaker's certain knowledge.

Yoshikawa explicitly acknowledges that the analysis rests heavily on fourth-person narrative data, with few third-person-subject examples, and he marks the evidential dimension as warranting further investigation ‹contested›.

Positions 4 and 5 are partly complementary: the background-event account is a synchronic-discourse claim about the typical environments of a, while the direct-evidential account is a semantic one about its grammatical value.
An event marked as the speaker's directly witnessed background is precisely the configuration that both accounts predict ; ‹speculative›.
Cutting across the semantic debate, there is broad agreement on a's function as a narrative scene-shift signal.
The pattern [event] a p (perfective + nominalizer) or [event] a korka recurrently marks the point at which the scene, topic, or acting participant changes ; .
The genre-level distribution of a across narrative, ceremonial, and conversational texts is treated in ; the temporal reference context in .
The auxiliary may reduplicate to express an iterative or prolonged-continuity reading — 'went on V-ing, V-ed over and over'.
The pattern repeats the verb-plus-auxiliary unit: V a V a (singular) or V rok V rok (plural).
With a fourth-person subject, the person index may stand alone in the second occurrence (=an a =an a), abbreviating the repeated verb base ; .
Bugaeva labels the pattern "emphatic continuative" .

Ijäs records an a … a pattern glossed 'verb and verb (prolonged continuity)' but does not connect it to the auxiliary ; the connection is established by Nakagawa's glossed corpus examples ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The iterative and habitual periphery shared with other aspect forms is treated in .
The auxiliary marks an event as just completed — closer to a terminative or hot-news perfect than the general anterior value of a, and rendered in Japanese as '〜てしまった' with a freshness nuance ; .
Like a, nisa belongs to the auxiliary-verb frame and takes no person marking; unlike a it shows no number alternation.
The two forms overlap in signalling a past event but differ in aspectual profile: nisa foregrounds the just-completed endpoint, while a in its primary use foregrounds the contrast with what follows.
Alongside a / rok stands the auxiliary (singular) and (plural), combining perfect aspect with indirect evidentiality and a mirative (after-the-fact surprise) value.
All major analyses decompose the form as a (perfective auxiliary) + an (existential 'exist') ; ; .
The strongest morphological argument is the plural: rok-oka(y) pairs the plural of a with the plural of an, exactly as [a+an] predicts .

Yoshikawa grants that several singular dialect forms admit competing segmentations — anan (Chitose) invites [an+an], while haw'an / awan (Shizunai, Tokachi, Horobetsu) invite [haw+an] — so the unified etymology rests on the plural form rather than on every singular surface shape ‹contested›.

Nakagawa characterizes the core meaning as: at some reference point, the speaker realizes what an earlier situation actually was — rendered in Japanese as '〜だったのだなあ' ('so that's what it was!') .
Chiri's earlier formulation emphasizes the affective dimension: surprise at an unexpected fact or result .

Yoshikawa integrates both under perfect aspect plus indirect evidentiality, with mirativity as a contextual extension: the speaker asserts a past event known only via inference or retrospective access, and the unexpected discovery of that fact yields the surprise reading ; .
The Horobetsu dialect form awan carries the same value:
Yoshikawa's most productive contribution is treating a and aan as a paradigmatic pair along two simultaneous parameters ; :

The structural parallel between a+an and Classical Japanese き+あり > けり provides an independent argument for the [a+an] etymology: both pairs decompose the indirect-past into a direct-past base plus an existential, and both the direct and indirect members share a perfective component ; .
The same direct / indirect past opposition is cross-linguistically attested and is placed in typological perspective by ‹contested›.
The grammaticalization source a / rok 'sit' fits a cross-linguistic cline in which posture verbs grammaticalize into aspect markers via a resultant-state intermediate .
The path 'sit (in the position resulting from settling)' > 'be in a completed-state position' > anterior / perfective auxiliary is typologically plausible ‹speculative›.
The broader diachronic framing of the Hokkaido TAM system is in .

A frequent narrative pattern places aan immediately before the inferential evidential ruwe ne: the speaker first signals an after-the-fact discovery (aan), then packages that discovery as established knowledge (ruwe ne).

Hirosawa analyses the sequence as a territory-of-information shift: aan places the content outside the speaker's territory (the surprising, indirectly-accessed event), while ruwe ne reclaims it inside as fact the speaker now owns .
Both corpus examples in the preceding section — oripak kamuy poho a=ne aan ruwe ne and mokor=an aan ruwe ne — show this stacking.

Four constructions complement the progressive kor an and the resultative wa an described in : the appearance-based continuative built on siran (sir-an, 'appearance-exist'); the merged durative kane an; the resultative variant hine an; and the Tokachi–Ishikari pair kan an / tek an.
Each recruits the existential verb as its second predicate.

Yoshikawa groups all of them with kor an and wa an under the cover term 「存在型アスペクト」, existential aspectual forms — constructions that may express aspectual meanings without constituting a grammatical aspect category in the strict sense ; .

None of them is distributed uniformly across dialects, and the forms centred on the sensory noun straddle the boundary between the aspect system and the nominalization-plus-copula evidential paradigm treated in .
The noun is the source both of the evidential formal noun sir-i and of the existential-aspectual predicate sir-an 'appearance-exist'.

As the second predicate in a pair-verb chain, sir-an replaces the plain existential an and adds a perceptual dimension: the state or action named by the first verb is not merely ongoing but visibly so, its appearance persisting for the observer ; .
Nakagawa frames this function as the third of four temporal-reference strategies available in the tenseless system.

Where a time adverb places an event on the timeline and a prospective form such as kusu ne points to the future, clause-final siri anchors an action unfolding visibly in front of the speaker — 「現在まさに目の前で行われている行為」 .
The form is not a tense marker; the present-ongoing temporal reading follows from the evidential value, because if the speaker is currently perceiving the event, the event is current.

Structurally, sir-an occupies the position of the existential in the pair-verb frame: a lexical verb is linked to it by a simultaneous conjunction, most commonly kor, the same conjunction that builds kor an.
The resulting contrast is between V kor an (action in progress) and V kor sir-an (action in progress, visibly apparent).
Person agreement follows the pair-verb pattern: both the lexical verb and the existential component of sir-an carry the subject index .

In attested usage, sir-an frequently appears embedded before the inferential evidential ruwe ne, forming a double-evidential stack: the visual state is packaged as an ongoing scene and then reframed as an established fact.

Dal Corso reads sir-an in this position as the indirect visual evidential in his eight-form system, the form that applies when the scene is accessible but the speaker treats the evidence as somewhat less immediately processed than under the direct-perception siri ne .
The overlap between the continuative reading of siran and the evidential functions of siri ne and siri an is a recognized analytical difficulty.
Nakagawa treats the present-ongoing reading under temporal-reference strategy 3 without assigning it to the aspect system proper .

Yoshikawa, whose existential aspectual forms group includes kor an, wa an, kane an, and hine an, does not list siran among them; the progressive reading is a pragmatic inference from the evidential value rather than an independent category .

Dal Corso reads siri an as one of eight evidential forms — the indirect visual counterpart to the direct-perception siri ne — organized by the parameters of source reliability and event accessibility .
These framings are not contradictory; they describe the same construction from different angles.
The present chapter treats siran / siri ne as a form that licenses a continuative reading through its evidential value, while locating it primarily in the evidential paradigm.
The direct-perception evidential siri ne and the indirect visual siri an receive their full treatment in .

The stacking pattern kor an siri ne — attested in Nakagawa's corpus of Saru Ainu — supplies the most transparent diagnostics: the progressive marks the action as in progress, the situational evidential marks the speaker as currently witnessing it, and the scope order (aspect inside, evidential outside) is fixed .

When sir-an fills the existential slot itself, the visual dimension is encoded in the existential predicate rather than in a separate closing evidential, and the form sits at the intersection of the two systems ‹contested›.
kane an is a pair verb of the same structural type as kor an and wa an: a lexical verb is linked to the existential an by the simultaneous conjunction kane.

Its aspectual behaviour differs in that it is unconstrained by verb class: it accepts action verbs (progressive reading) and change-of-state verbs (resultative reading) equally, merging the two values into a single durative continuative ; ; .
Chiri's classic label for it is 持続態 durative, set against 進行態 progressive (kor an) and 完了態 perfective (wa isam / wa okere) in his three-way aspect classification ; .
The dialectal picture divides into two patterns.
In Saru and Chitose, kane an is marked: alongside its durative value it carries a nuance of remarkable or unexpected situation.

This nuance connects it to the standalone auxiliary kane (Nakagawa 2024: 309–310 table 74), which Tamura characterizes as marking an unanticipated action or state and Satō as encoding degree — a semantic base that grammaticalizes toward simultaneity in some contexts ; .
In Shizunai and Samani, kane an carries no such nuance and functions as the plain imperfective, replacing both kor an and wa an without selectional constraint on verb class ; ‹contested›.
The aspect-neutral character of kane an in Saru is visible within a single clause chain: the form can take a resultative reading on one conjunct and a progressive reading on the next.

Person agreement follows the pair-verb pattern: both the lexical verb and an carry the subject index, and the plural existential oka replaces an with a plural subject (kane oka), parallel to kor oka and wa oka .

hine an uses the sequential-temporal conjunction hine in the existential-aspectual construction and functions as a resultative like wa an: the conjunction encodes that the situation has come to obtain as a result of the lexical verb's action.
Yoshikawa lists it among the Saru–Chitose existential aspectual forms; Chiri's gloss '…hine an = be …-ing' applies the durative label to it ; .
kan an is the Tokachi and Ishikari counterpart of Saru–Chitose kane an: it merges progressive and resultative values into a single durative continuative.
The form's aspectual centre of gravity differs between the two dialects: Tokachi usage leans progressive, Ishikari usage leans resultative ; .
tek an (Tokachi) covers the resultative of change verbs, corresponding to Saru wa an in selectional behaviour.

Nakagawa traces a connection to the Saru auxiliary tek 'do briefly / suddenly', which shows how the same root grammaticalizes along different paths in different dialect communities — as a momentary-action auxiliary in Saru, as a resultative pair-verb connector in Tokachi ‹speculative›.
Tokachi presents a distributional constraint on kor an that elevates kan an into a distinct functional role.
In Tokachi, kor an cannot take a first-person subject: where another dialect would say ku=nukar kor ku=an 'I am watching', Tokachi requires ku=nukar kan ku=an with kan an.

Takahashi's hypothesis is that kor an encodes the speaker's observation of an event, a meaning that clashes with a first-person subject who is themselves the agent; the construction is therefore confined to second- and third-person subjects in this dialect.
No equivalent restriction has been documented for Saru, Chitose, or any other Hokkaido variety ‹contested›.

Takahashi invokes a cross-linguistic parallel with Shuri Ryūkyūan, where the progressive equivalent likewise bars first-person agents; the Tokachi restriction is thus positioned as an instance of a typologically attested pattern rather than an isolated anomaly .

The further question — whether the restriction reflects a residual connection between kor an and the visual-evidential domain, such that first-person use is blocked because first persons cannot be their own external observers — remains open in the sources ‹speculative›.

All the forms in this chapter share a grammaticalization path: a conjunction (kane, hine, kan, tek) or a sensory noun (sir) links a lexical verb to the existential an, and the compound develops an ongoing-state reading from the literal meaning 'the state of V-ing exists' .

This is the same path as kor an and wa an in ; the cross-dialect variation concerns which conjunction is recruited and whether the result merges or maintains the progressive / resultative distinction.

Yoshikawa's assessment is that none of these forms has reached obligatory grammatical aspect: the existential an retains semantic content, person marking is overt on both predicates, and the construction is optional.
They are 'forms that may express aspectual meanings but are not grammatical aspectual forms' .
The cross-dialectal evidence supports this.

The Shizunai–Samani kane an, which has lost the remarkable-situation nuance retained in Saru and Chitose, appears to be at a more advanced stage: the form is more bleached, its selectional freedom more complete.
Different dialect communities have therefore travelled different distances along a single grammaticalization trajectory ‹corpus-suggested›.
