text: Nakagawa tabulates the evidential values .

The regular possessed forms of the source nouns may carry an additional ending — ruwe(he), humi(hi) — but the evidential formal nouns block this extension: *ruwehe and *humihi are ungrammatical in the evidential function .
Whether the concept form (sir, haw) and the corresponding possessed form carry a usage or nuance difference is explicitly left unresolved in Tamura's dictionary ‹speculative›.

The possessed morphology is significant in its own right: a noun in its possessed form grammatically presupposes an antecedent, so these nominalizers formally encode that the speaker already has the relevant situation in hand .
Mapped onto Aikhenvald's evidential typology , the Ainu system belongs to the C1 type: visual, non-visual sensory, inferred, and reported sources of information are grammatically distinguished ; .

The type is realized analytically through a nominalization-plus-copula construction, not through dedicated verbal affixes — this makes Ainu a textbook case of the nominalization-based evidential strategy ; ‹consensus›.
The cell assignments are approximate.
ruwe ne covers the inferred cell (information from reasoning or assimilated knowledge), siri ne the visual cell, humi ne the non-visual sensory cell, and hawe ne the reported cell.
The boundary between the visual (siri) and the knowledge-from-trace (ruwe) cells is contested in the recent literature and is discussed in the ruwe ne chapter ; ‹contested›.
Dal Corso's morphosyntactic account resolves the four formal nouns into an eight-form system organized by two parameters: source reliability (REL) and event accessibility (ACCES) .

The four direct forms use the copula ne (internal, speaker-anchored perspective); the four indirect forms replace it with the existential an, the action verb ki, or the posture verb as (external perspective; 2018: 313–314).
Source reliability is not epistemic modality: it specifies the psychophysical or cognitive channel of acquisition and says nothing about the speaker's degree of certainty .

The underlying sense hierarchy runs Sight > Smell/Taste–Touch > Hearing, yielding a coarser visual/non-visual split: ruwe ne and siri ne are the higher-reliability direct members, humi ne and hawe ne the lower .
A structural asymmetry distinguishes the ru-series: in Saru, Chitose, and Biratori the trace-noun enters only direct evidentiality, and there is no indirect *ru an counterpart to siri an .
The hawe as indirect form has, moreover, nearly fully specialized as a reportative — for quotation when the source is overt and for hearsay when it is absent — while humi as is never reportative .
The per-form indirect semantics are treated in , , and .
ruwe ne dominates the paradigm quantitatively.

In Dal Corso's Hokkaido reference texts it accounts for 1508 of 2232 evidential tokens — roughly two thirds of all eight forms, and more than five times the next most frequent form (hawe ne, 298 tokens) .
The asymmetry is independently noted by Tamura and by Yoshikawa: ruwe ne outstrips the other forms in oral-narrative (口承文芸) registers, where it functions as the default frame-text predicate .

Community discussion characterizes ruwe ne in the same terms — frequent especially in oral narratives and legends, functioning like Japanese のだ to close narrative segments and mark topic shifts (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-09) .

These counts derive from Dal Corso's specific reference texts (Kayano, Tamura, Nakagawa, Bugaeva), not from the full Hokkaido corpus, and should be treated as indicative of the skew rather than as absolute proportions ‹corpus-suggested›.
The dominance of ruwe ne is consistent with its status as the unmarked, most grammaticalized member of the paradigm.
The genre distribution of evidential usage across narrative registers is treated in .
Four analytical traditions describe the same construction from different angles, and they partially conflict.
The oldest is the mood (法) tradition.
Kindaichi identified seven distinctive moods in Ainu; within that taxonomy siri is the 見説法 (seeing-speech mood), hawe the 聞説法, humi the 感説法, and ruwe the 確説法 / 事実法 ; .
The mood label captures the speaker-oriented, assertive character of these forms but does not isolate their source semantics.
The modern evidentiality framing, now standard in the descriptive literature, places the system in the typological framework of information-source encoding .
It is adopted by Takahashi , Dal Corso , Nakagawa , and Hirosawa .
Dal Corso's is the most detailed morphosyntactic account (§Direct and indirect evidentiality above).

The predication-type framing (Takahashi 2013) adds a dimension orthogonal to source channel: in Tokachi, the visual nominalizer sir is restricted to stage-level (transient, scene-describing) predication, and individual-level (permanent) properties take ru regardless of the information channel .
The ontological type of the predicate thus independently constrains the available evidential ‹consensus›.
The information-structure framing is Hirosawa's (2026).
He argues that ruwe ne additionally marks discourse-new information, parallel to Japanese のだ, and unconditionally declares the content to lie inside the speaker's territory of information .
Dal Corso explicitly argues that the territory-of-information account is inapplicable to Hokkaido direct evidentiality .
These two recent treatments disagree on the right framework for ruwe ne ‹contested›.

Community discussion, summarizing Yoshikawa (2020), characterizes ruwe ne as semantically unmarked relative to the other forms — lacking their specific evidentiary highlighting — and as functioning to close a narrative segment and transition to the next (場面転換・統括), consistent with Hirosawa's analysis (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-03-17) ; this observation is treated here as corroboration of the literature rather than an independent authority.
Ijäs's pedagogical grammar presents the system under the evidentiality framing without adopting any of the specific theoretical positions above .
The pedagogical description aligns with the standard evidential account and is useful for language learners but does not adjudicate the analytical disputes.
All four formal nouns participate in a shared set of clause-final frames that vary the following element and the sentence type.
Nakagawa arranges these into a paradigm of four patterns :
The bare polar-question frame is an instance of insubordination — a once-embedded nominalized clause promoted to main-clause use .

Negation operates inside the evidential scope: the predicate is negated with somo before the formal noun, while the formal noun remains outside the scope of negation (…somo ki ruwe ne 'it is a fact that [one does not …]') .
The interrogative frames are treated in ; the existential frame in the existential an chapter.
The constituent nominalized by the formal noun is a finite, clause-sized predication.

It carries its own person marking, verb suppletion (singular ek vs. plural arki 'come'), aspectual auxiliaries, perfective a, and negation; the evidential formal noun scopes over that whole TAM-marked clause .

The layering is transparent from ordering: the formal noun may be followed by aspectual material (a, nankor), final particles (na, wa), and clause-linkers (hine, kusu), but the intentive kusu ne ('intends to') cannot follow the evidential: kusu ne ruwe ne is well-formed but *ruwe ne kusu ne is not .
The evidential thus sits above clause-internal aspect but below clause-linkers and intentive modality.
Community discussion independently observes that this ordering follows from the clause hierarchy placing the evidential inside modality operators (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-09) .

Dal Corso ties the copula vs. existential/posture-verb choice to perspective: the copula ne expresses an internal, speaker-anchored viewpoint and hosts the direct forms; an, as, and ki express an external viewpoint and host the indirect forms .

A structural polysemy follows for siri an: it is three-way ambiguous between the interrogative existential frame, the indirect visual evidential, and an aspectual resultative-progressive — a polysemy treated in and .
The interaction of the evidential with the wider clause-final TAM and negation apparatus is treated in and .
In Tokachi the choice among the formal nouns is constrained not only by information source but also by the ontological type of the predicate.

Takahashi's Tokachi study shows that the visual nominalizer sir is restricted to stage-level (transient, scene-describing) predication; for individual-level (permanent property) predicates — even those known by sight — Tokachi uses ru, which is unmarked for information type .
Of the four, only sir carries this restriction; hum, haw, and ru function at both predication levels.
Takahashi parallels the constraint with the ban on individual-level complements of English perception verbs; in Ainu the restriction surfaces on the nominalizer rather than on a matrix verb.
This finding sets bounds on any pure source-channel account of the formal-noun choice: the grammar of predication independently constrains the available evidential ‹consensus›.
Its implications for the ruwe ne / siri ne boundary are discussed in the ruwe ne chapter.
The formal nouns are partially, not fully, grammaticalized from their source nouns.

The diachronic path is already stated in the early grammars: the source nouns function first as lexical nouns, then as clause-nominalizing heads in embedded complements, then as clause-final evidential sentence-enders ; .
At each stage the lexical semantics of the source noun remains visible, but the syntactic freedoms of a full noun are progressively lost.
The evidential formal nouns admit no demonstrative or attributive modifier of their own, cannot head an ordinary common-noun relative clause, and are fixed in linear position ; .

Dal Corso stresses that the degree of grammaticalization varies across the system: ruwe ne is the most grammaticalized of the four Hokkaido direct forms, with the Sakhalin particle manu at the far end of the cline as a fully fused suffix .
The Sakhalin nominalization innovations and their contrast with Hokkaido are set out in .
The path from noun to nominalizer to clause-final particle belongs to the wider nominalization-grammaticalization cline treated in .
The semantic organization of the system — four channels, direct vs. indirect — is consistent across Hokkaido; its morphosyntactic realization varies.
Four dialect-level patterns stand out.
Saru, Chitose, Biratori (the core of Dal Corso's data) use the possessed forms ruwe / siri / hawe / humi and maintain the eight-form direct/indirect system .
Tokachi (and frequently Ishikari) close the clause with the bare concept forms ru / sir / haw / hum rather than the possessed forms ; .
Allomorphs sin (for sir) and aw (for haw) are attested .
Horobetsu grammaticalizes the possessed-form nominalizers a step further into adverbial-clause markers and conjunction-like particles — a use not reported for well-described Saru .

Kindaichi and Chiri had already noted the nominalizers in conjunction-like uses; Takahashi shows Horobetsu has systematized this extension, bringing evidentiality into the set of categories expressed in adverbial clauses alongside aspect and modality — an instance of 'versatile nominalization' ‹corpus-suggested›.
Asahikawa and Shiranuka show an inferential ru an, with the trace-noun entering the indirect frame in apparent complementary distribution with the siri an of the southern dialects .
This is the one Hokkaido context where ru forms indirect evidentiality; the distribution is flagged by Dal Corso as requiring a wider-dialect study ‹corpus-suggested›.
Dialect coverage is solid for Saru/Chitose/Biratori and Tokachi; thin or second-hand for Ishikari, Asahikawa, Shiranuka, and Shizunai.
The dialect classification is set out in the dialectology chapters; the TAM-evidential variation across registers is in .
Two evidential expressions may stack in one clause; this is more frequent in Hokkaido than in Sakhalin .
Two constructions recur.

In the first, a character's indirect source is placed within the narrator's ruwe ne, yielding both the character's subjective source and the narrator's assertion of the event as traditional knowledge:
In the second pattern, ruwe ne reinforces a lower-reliability direct form, boosting epistemic commitment: attested hawe ne nankor ruwe ne 'maybe my god secretly let me know' .
Other attested combinations include hawe as ruwe ne, siri ki siri ne, siri an ruwe ne, and humi ne humi as .
The consistent outer position of ruwe ne in stacked constructions supports its analysis as the epistemic-incorporation operator of the paradigm, a role discussed in .
The four formal nouns do not themselves encode mirativity (意外性).

Dal Corso finds no evidence that the Hokkaido evidential paradigm systematically generates mirative readings; this contrasts with Sakhalin, where personal-knowledge evidentials can trigger mirative interpretations through a deictic-gap mechanism .
In Hokkaido, mirative value attaches instead to the perfective auxiliary aan and to anan .
Yoshikawa argues that aan signals indirect evidentiality plus mirativity (reported via ) ‹speculative›
(Yoshikawa 2018 cited second-hand).
The two mechanisms can co-occur.

When aan places information outside the speaker's expected knowledge and ruwe ne follows, the sequence expresses surprise then reclamation: the speaker marks the event as unexpected (aan) and then declares it recognized fact (ruwe ne).
Hirosawa parallels this with Japanese みたいな + のだ .
The full treatment of the evidential-to-mirative interface, evidential scope, and the cline from formal-noun evidentials to sentence-final particles is in .
Hokkaido Ainu marks the speaker's source of information periphrastically: a finite clause is nominalized by a bound formal noun and the result is predicated with the copula ne.
The language has no dedicated evidential verbal affix.
Four formal nouns build the core paradigm, each the possessed form of a sensory noun: ruwe (< ), siri (< ), hawe (< ), and humi (< ) ; .
Mapped onto the typology of , the system is of the C1 type — visual, non-visual sensory, inferred, and reported — realized analytically, through a native nominalization-plus-copula construction ; .

The architecture common to all four terms is set out in ; the present chapter treats the central member ruwe ne, and its siblings in the situational evidential, the reportative, and the sensory evidential.
The closed class of formal nouns that makes the construction possible is defined in .

Dal Corso resolves these four direct terms into an eight-form system whose indirect counterparts replace the copula with the existential an, the verb ki ‘do’, or as ‘stand’, organized by two parameters, source reliability and event accessibility; within it ruwe ne is the highest-reliability direct form, and the trace-noun ru forms direct evidentiality alone — the southern dialects have no indirect *ru-counterpart to siri an .
ruwe ne also dominates the paradigm quantitatively.
In Dal Corso's Hokkaido reference texts it supplies 1508 of 2232 evidential tokens — roughly two thirds of the eight-form system, and far ahead of hawe ne, siri ne, and humi ne .
The present Hokkaido corpus of 167,890 sentences makes the skew sharper.

A string search returns 16,350 tokens of ruwe ne beside 796 hawe ne, 607 siri ne, and 200 humi ne among the direct forms, and 304 siri an, 395 hawe as, 210 humi as, and 218 siri ki among the indirect: some 86% of the eight forms together, and about 91% of the four direct ones (the two corpora are compared below).
The string count folds in the homophonous lexical noun ruwe and the reduced final particle, so 86% is an upper bound on the evidential proper.
The asymmetry is far too large to follow from that conflation, and it confirms the descriptive consensus that ruwe ne is the unmarked, most grammaticalized term of the four ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The head ruwe is the possessed form of the noun .

In Tamura's Saru dictionary the ordinary possessed form is ruwe(he) ‘the track that — passed along, the path made by —’s passing’, and the evidential formal noun is analysed as ru-e, the noun plus a possessive ending .
For glossing this is decisive: the morpheme is the possessed ru-we, ‘the trace of —’, whose implicit possessor is the event described by the nominalized clause.
The same possessed-noun pattern underlies sir-i, haw-e, and hum-i .

A subtle point distinguishes the evidential from the full noun: the lexical possessed forms may carry an extra ending (ruwehe, humihi), whereas the evidential formal nouns block it (*ruwehe is ungrammatical as the evidential) .
The construction is therefore a copular predication over a nominalized clause — [clause] ruwe ‘the trace/fact that [clause]’, closed by the copula ne treated in .
It is not, however, an ordinary relative-clause head plus a copula.

The head has lost the syntax of a free noun: it admits no demonstrative or attributive modifier of its own (contrast a true lexical head such as pirka menoko ‘a beautiful woman’), it cannot head a common noun (*pirka ruwe ne kewtum), and it is fixed in linear position — kusu ne ruwe ne is well formed but *ruwe ne kusu ne is not ; .

The accurate synchronic label is thus a partially grammaticalized formal-noun evidential, intermediate between a fused verbal suffix and a fully lexical noun, and it is best analysed alongside the formal-noun nominalization treated in and the general clausal nominalizers of ‹consensus›.
Four framings of ruwe ne compete, and they are best read as describing one form from different angles.
The oldest, the mood tradition, classed ruwe as the 確説法/事実法 ‘assertive / fact mood’, with Chiri deriving it diachronically from ‘there is a trace of X’ to ‘there is the fact of X’ ; .

The evidential framing, now standard, retains a source semantics: Nakagawa defines ruwe ne as marking that the speaker recognizes the clause content as fact , and Dal Corso treats it as a direct evidential of reasoning or knowledge (glossed dir.rsn / dir.knw), the highest-reliability direct source.

This reliability is a matter of source, not of epistemic modality: it names the psychophysical or cognitive channel of acquisition and says nothing about the speaker's degree of certainty, and the original stimulus is typically backgrounded once the information has been assimilated into personal knowledge .
Satō's question data refine what that channel is.

Among the four nominalizers, ruwe applies where the relevant content is an abstract state of affairs, recognized only indirectly through the exercise of understanding — the domain left once hawe takes an utterance, siri a visible ongoing scene, and humi a sensation .

He further notes that the very fact that these nominalizers stand in the possessed form presupposes an antecedent — a possessed noun needs something to belong to — so the form grammatically encodes that the speaker already has the relevant situation in hand .
The diagnostic case is a predicate whose truth no sense can deliver:
The fourth framing is Hirosawa's, who relocates ruwe ne into information structure.

He argues it marks discourse-new information much as Japanese のだ does, and more generally declares the content to lie inside the speaker's territory of information (情報のなわ張り); since ruwe references processed knowledge (知識), this reconciles its two apparently opposite uses — introducing brand-new information and ‘summing up’ (前方統括) information already developed in the discourse .
The self-identification below involves no inference and no perceptual source at all; the sea-god simply supplies his identity to the protagonists as new information:

The same mechanism lets a narrator assert events of the story world that she could not have witnessed, presenting them under ruwe ne as traditional, shared knowledge — the use that makes it the default predicate of the narrative frame-text ; :

These accounts are not interchangeable, and at one point they genuinely conflict: Hirosawa builds his analysis on territory-of-information, whereas Dal Corso explicitly argues that the territory-of-information theory is inapplicable to Hokkaido direct evidentiality ; ‹contested›.

The synthesis adopted here is that ruwe ne grammatically encodes epistemic incorporation: the clause is predicated as a possessed trace (ru-we, ‘the trace of —’) whose possessor is the described event, so that the proposition is offered as content already taken into the speaker's knowledge and thereby made assertable.

This single device derives both Dal Corso's observation that the stimulus is backgrounded once information enters personal knowledge and Hirosawa's that the form marks new information and claims it for the speaker's territory: incorporation is exactly what lets a freshly perceived, inferred, remembered, or just-narrated state of affairs be presented as a fact the speaker now owns.

The possessed morphology — which, as Satō notes, presupposes an antecedent — is the formal anchor of this account, and it explains why the older ‘fact mood’ label, the modern source label, and the discourse-new label each capture a true facet of the same form ‹speculative›.
The hardest boundary in the system is between ruwe ne and siri ne, because both can rest on what the speaker sees.

Dal Corso states plainly that a sense-channel hierarchy does not predict the split: if both are ‘visual’, it fails to say why Ainu so often chooses the trace-form where sight is available, and he leaves the question open, suspecting a driver beyond elicitation .

Hirosawa's response is to separate raw sight from processed knowledge — siri profiles the visible situation, ruwe the knowledge the situation yields — but he offers this as an explicit hypothesis (仮説), not a settled result ‹contested›.
The double-evidential distribution gives a positive argument that resolves part of the puzzle.
When two evidentials stack, the indirect visual siri an is reinforced specifically by ruwe ne, and not by siri ne .

Were ruwe and siri two co-equal visual channels this would be unmotivated; it follows naturally if ruwe is not a fourth sense parallel to sight, sound, and speech, but a higher knowledge-from-trace operator that ratifies the output of another evidential as established fact.

On this reading Dal Corso's unresolved ‘why ruwe and not siri when sight is available’ and Takahashi's Tokachi finding that individual-level — cognitively stable — properties take ru while transient scenes take sir become two faces of one contrast: siri profiles the accessible appearance, and ruwe the cognized fact extracted from it ‹speculative›.

The boundary with hawe is similarly non-rigid — Hirosawa cites near-identical sentences alternating hawe ne and ruwe ne, which fits a form that can absorb information of any original channel once it has become knowledge .
ruwe heads a small family of sentence-final frames that vary the following predicate and particle.

Nakagawa arranges them into a paradigm shared by all four formal nouns: NMLZ + ne declarative, NMLZ + an content question (with a question word), bare NMLZ polar question and exclamation, and NMLZ + un affirmative answer .
The bare polar reduction is an instance of insubordination — a once-dependent nominalized clause used as a main clause — analysed for the Tokachi cognate by .
These interrogative uses belong with the wider interrogative system in , and the existential frame with the existential an.
The content question replaces the copula with the existential and is opened by a question word, the formal noun staying in place:

Negation belongs inside the evidential: the proposition is denied by negating the verb before the formal noun (the pattern … somo ki ruwe ne ‘it is a fact that [one does not …]’), which leaves ruwe ne itself outside the scope of negation.
The rhetorical ruwe somo ne is a separate outer frame, a high-scope convictional construction distinct from this inner propositional negation .
The interaction of the evidential with the sentence-final negation and TAM apparatus on a copular predicate is treated in .
The constituent before ruwe ne is a finite, clause-sized predication.

It carries its own person marking, number-sensitive verb choice (singular ek vs. suppletive plural arki ‘come’, so íne nispa ek ruwe ne ‘four men came’), aspect and perfective auxiliaries, and negation; the evidential then scopes over that whole TAM-marked clause .
This is also why ruwe ne can close a non-verbal predicate, as in the copular kamuy a=ne … ruwe ne example above.

Ordering confirms the layering: the evidential may be followed by aspectual and clausal material (a, nankor, na, wa, hine, kusu), and it sits above clause-internal aspect but below the clause-linkers, so kusu ne ruwe ne is grammatical and *ruwe ne kusu ne is not .

Dal Corso ties the choice of post-nominal predicate to perspective: the copula ne expresses an internal (speaker-anchored) viewpoint and so hosts the direct forms, while the existential and posture/action verbs an, as, and ki express an external viewpoint and host the indirect forms .
For ruwe the paradigm is asymmetrical — in the southern dialects there is no indirect *ru form — so ruwe ne functions as the direct, personal-knowledge anchor of the whole system .

What the accessible sources do not settle is the formal size of the nominalized clause: that it is finite is clear from its TAM and person marking, but no read source provides a constituency account that would decide between a finite nominalization, a nominalized predicate phrase, and a construction-specific evidential projection ‹speculative›.
The complementation side of the same formal-noun strategy — ruwe and hi clauses under perception and cognition verbs — is taken up in .
Takahashi's Tokachi study adds a factor outside the reach of both the mood tradition and a pure source typology.
In Tokachi the visual nominalizer sir is restricted to imperfective, stage-level (transient) predication: it presents a passing scene.
For an individual-level (permanent) property — even one known by sight — Tokachi instead uses ru, which is unmarked for information type.
Of the four, only sir carries this restriction; hum, haw, and ru work at both levels .
The constraint surfaces on the nominalizer itself, which Takahashi parallels with the ban on individual-level complements of English perception verbs.
For the present form this matters in two ways.

First, the ru domain is broader than ‘inference’ narrowly understood: it is the unmarked choice where sir is blocked by predication type, which is consistent with the knowledge-from-trace reading developed above.

Second, it shows the Hokkaido system to be organized partly by the ontology of the predicate — eventive, stage-level, individual-level — alongside source of information; this does not overturn Dal Corso's reliability/accessibility account but bounds its domain, marking where the grammar of predication independently constrains the available evidential ‹consensus›.
ruwe ne is often rendered ‘it turned out that …’ in surprising contexts, but the surprise is not contributed by ruwe.
Mirativity in Hokkaido Ainu is carried mainly by the perfective auxiliary aan and by anan; ruwe ne then packages the resulting proposition as fact .

Dal Corso is explicit that Hokkaido shows no evidence of the evidential paradigm itself systematically generating mirative meanings — so mirativity may co-occur with ruwe ne but is not its value ‹contested›.
The system-level treatment of the evidential-to-mirative interface, evidential stacking, and the cline to sentence-final particles is given in .
Double evidentiality, more frequent in Hokkaido than Sakhalin, confirms the special standing of ruwe ne argued for above.

Two patterns recur: a character's indirect source layered under the narrator's ruwe ne as shared knowledge (… hawe as ruwe ne), and ruwe ne reinforcing a low-reliability direct form (… hawe ne nankor ruwe ne) .
In both, ruwe ne is the member that can ratify an already evidentially marked proposition as established fact, behaving as a knowledge operator that scopes over the other evidentials.

The diachronic path is transparent and is stated already in the earliest grammars: the noun ru ‘track, path’ > the possessed formal noun ru-we ‘the trace of —’ > the clause-final evidential [clause] ruwe ne, part of the larger cline by which sir, hum, haw, and ru all move from sensory nouns to nominalizers to evidentials ; .

Dal Corso stresses that the result is only partially grammaticalized — the lexical source stays visible and the choice of post-nominal predicate still matters — so grammaticalization here is a matter of degree ; .

The endpoint of that cline is reached unevenly across Hokkaido, and the differences are morphosyntactic: a single semantic field realized by varied forms, which cautions against writing one morphology for all of Hokkaido ‹contested›:
Saru, Chitose, Biratori — the southern core of Dal Corso's data — keep the possessed forms ruwe / siri / hawe / humi and the eight-form direct/indirect system .
Tokachi (and frequently Ishikari) close the clause with the bare concept forms ru / sir / haw / hum instead of the possessed forms ; .
Horobetsu grammaticalizes the possessed-form nominalizers a step further, into adverbial-clause and conjunction-like markers — a ‘versatile nominalization’ use not reported for well-described Saru .

Asahikawa and Shiranuka have an inferential ru an, apparently in complementary distribution with the siri an of the south — a genuine exception to the generalization that ru forms direct evidentiality alone .
The Sakhalin reflex. The Sakhalin varieties split the trace-form where the southern Hokkaido system has a single member.

Beside the copular ruwehe ne(e) they carry an existential ruwehe ʔan, and the two divide one inferential field by reliability: the existential encodes inference from a less-processed visual stimulus, the copular form inference from a stimulus already worked through, the more reliable of the pair .

Southern Hokkaido has only ruwe ne and admits no existential *ruwe an; the ru an of Asahikawa and Shiranuka is the one Hokkaido locus where the trace-noun enters the existential frame, and Dal Corso reads it as the Hokkaido counterpart of Sakhalin ruwehe ʔan .
The split sits within a wider reorganization of nominalization in the Sakhalin variety .
The formal noun siri — the possessed form of — is the direct visual evidential of Hokkaido Ainu.
Combined with the copula ne it yields the declarative frame siri ne, glossed dir.vis by Dal Corso: a direct evidential whose information source is a situation accessible to sight .
The full four-term paradigm and its nominalization-plus-copula architecture are set out in ; the present chapter treats siri ne and its indirect siblings siri an and siri ki.
The reasoning-based term ruwe ne is treated in ; the non-visual sensory term in .
Within the reliability hierarchy, siri ne occupies the second position, below ruwe ne (knowledge/reasoning) and above humi ne and hawe ne .

In Dal Corso's Hokkaido reference texts it supplies 149 tokens (6.68% of all evidential forms), against 1508 (67.56%) for ruwe ne; its indirect counterparts siri an (59 tokens, 2.64%) and siri ki (42 tokens, 1.88%) are less frequent still .

Unlike , whose evidential reflexes are confined to direct evidentiality in the southern dialects, enters both direct and indirect evidentiality, yielding the three-member subfamily set out in the table below.
The source noun covers a semantic cluster of visible and spatial referents: land, mountain, island, 'that area', and the observable appearance or state of something .

The noun's polysemy — 'ground, surface, countenance, sheath' — noted by community analysts as unusually broad (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2023) ‹corpus-confirmed› is consistent with Tamura's dictionary entry and with its distribution across compounds, place names, and weather predicates.
The possessed form is sir-i, 'the appearance of —', which serves as the evidential formal noun .
Tamura notes explicitly that whether the concept form sir and the possessed form siri carry a usage or nuance distinction in the evidential function is unknown ‹speculative›.
The blocking of the extra syllable that suppresses *ruwehe and *humihi in evidential function does not apply here: siri already coincides with the regular possessed form .

As a free noun, has low currency in Saru and Chitose — it appears mainly word-internally in weather and light-condition compounds (sir-pirka 'good weather', sir-kunne 'be dark', sir-peker 'be bright / dawn') and in place names such as Poro-sir (Horoshiri, 'big mountain') .
The weather-compound use is the synchronic residue of the noun's meteorological-and-landscape origin and reinforces the evidential's visual-situational semantics.
On the continuative and aspectual forms built on — including siran / siri=an 'pass (of time)' — see .
The earliest grammarians classified siri ne as the 見説法, the 'sight-report mood': it asserts what the speaker directly observes.
Chiri glosses it as "saying 'such-and-such is / has just happened' about a fact before one's eyes" ; .

The modern evidential framing preserves the core: Nakagawa defines siri ne as marking that the speaker's judgment rests on visual information , and Tamura gives it as 'used for conditions that can be seen' .
Satō's question data refine the characterization: when the interrogative frame uses siri, the content nominalized is a process ongoing before the eyes — not a completed event or stable property .

Dal Corso's dir.vis gloss captures the same range: the copula ne signals an internal, speaker-anchored perspective on a visually accessed event, distinguishing siri ne from the external-perspective indirect forms .
Two extensions of the basic visual reading arise in the corpus.

Hirosawa cites an example in which siri ne predicates a future event not yet observed — a punishment that will happen — showing that the form can range over a situationally entailed, not merely currently perceived, state of affairs ‹corpus-suggested›.

And Dal Corso's dir.vis subsumes both ongoing direct perception and cases where visible evidence yields a near-certain situational inference; both are direct in the sense that the copula perspective is the speaker's own .
The contrast with ruwe ne on the same visual base is the hardest boundary in the system.
Dal Corso leaves it explicitly unresolved: a sense-channel hierarchy fails to predict the choice, and he suspects a driver beyond elicitation .
Hirosawa's hypothesis — that siri profiles the raw visible appearance while ruwe profiles the knowledge extracted from it — is offered as a hypothesis (仮説), not a settled result ‹contested›.
The double-evidential evidence bearing on the split is set out in the section on double evidentiality below.
siri an is three-way ambiguous.
The three readings are formally identical but contextually distinguished:
Interrogative frame: siri (formal noun) + the existential an replacing the copula, forming a content question.
The Kanazawa 1898 example Tokyo un paye=an siri an? 'Did you go to Tokyo?' illustrates this use ; .
This is the interrogative-frame counterpart of declarative siri ne, parallel to ruwe an and hawe an in the same paradigm; see .

Indirect visual / reasoning evidential (ind.rsn): an evidential with external, non-copular perspective, reporting an event visually or situationally accessible but not directly witnessed by the current speaker.

Dal Corso places this reading higher in reliability than siri ki and notes that it systematically pairs with ruwe ne in double-evidential constructions — discussed in the section on double evidentiality below .
Aspectual resultative / progressive: a periphrastic aspect form semantically close to wa an / kor an, expressing an unspecified or vaguely defined condition ; .
In this use siri an functions as a lexical predicate ('be like, appear, pass of time') and is not an evidential.
The aspectual and continuative uses, including siran, are treated in ; the existential an itself in the existential and aspectual an.

The three-way ambiguity is described functionally in the sources consulted but lacks a unified syntactic account; Satō 2013's analysis of siri an as a polysemous aspectual-modal-evidential in Chitose is cited by Dal Corso but was not consulted directly ‹speculative›.
Discourse context and the presence or absence of a question word are the primary practical diagnostics.
siri ki (also contracted sirki) is the unambiguous indirect-visual form.

Dal Corso glosses it ind.vis: an event visible in a distanced way or from a source other than the current speaker, the verb ki 'do' placing it in the external-perspective set alongside humi as and hawe as .
A Kayano (Biratori) narrative instance has a character's skilled cooking assessed by a bystander under sirki, expressing surprised indirect-visual perception .
siri participates in the four-slot illocutionary paradigm shared by all formal nouns :
A notably absent frame is the affirmative-answer construction: unlike ruwe un, there is no attested *siri un — the un-answer is restricted to ruwe in the sources consulted ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The polar-question reduction — bare siri without a following predicate — is an instance of insubordination: a nominalized clause pressed into main-clause function.
Takahashi analyses the Tokachi cognate pattern as 脱従属節化 .
Negation operates inside the evidential, the verb negated before siri ne and the evidential scoping over the resulting proposition .
Takahashi's Tokachi study (consultant: Sawai Tomeno, Honbetsu) establishes that the visual nominalizer is restricted to stage-level (imperfective, transient) predication.
A passing scene — someone in the act of fleeing — takes the Tokachi cognate sin (concept-form allomorph of sir): kira sin ne nankor '(she) seems to be fleeing' (Takahashi 2013, ex. 5).
An individual-level (permanent) property, even one visually accessible, takes ru instead — the unmarked member that imposes no predication-type restriction .
Among the four Tokachi nominalizers, only sir carries this restriction; hum, haw, and ru operate at both predication levels ‹consensus›.

Takahashi draws a parallel with the English perception-verb constraint on individual-level complements: a stage-/individual-level distinction that in English appears on the complement-type of the matrix verb, but in Ainu appears on the nominalizer itself .
The constraint corroborates siri ne's characterization as inherently tied to observable, imperfective situations.
Satō's Chitose evidence points the same direction: in interrogatives, siri selects for processes ongoing before the eyes, not for stable properties .
Whether the Tokachi restriction is a local grammaticalization feature or a pan-Hokkaido tendency described only piecemeal in the southern sources remains unresolved ‹speculative›.
The complementary distribution with ru / ruwe is examined in .

Double evidentiality — two formal nouns stacked in the same clause — is more frequent in Hokkaido Ainu than in Sakhalin Ainu, and the siri-family forms participate in it in a diagnostically consistent pattern .

When siri an (indirect visual) occurs in a double-evidential construction, its reinforcing partner is invariably ruwe ne, never siri ne — as in the smoke-rising example (supuya at kor sir-an ruwe ne anan, Nakagawa text, Dal Corso ex. 268) .
forms: supuya at kor sir-an ruwe ne anan

text: The pattern is systematic: siri ki siri ne is also attested (Dal Corso exx. 267, 274), while combinations such as *siri an siri ne are not reported .
This distribution provides a reliability argument for the ruwe ne / siri ne split.
If the two were merely co-equal visual channels, there would be no structural reason for the indirect visual form to seek out ruwe ne specifically as its ratifying partner.

The systematicity of the pairing suggests that ruwe ne functions as a knowledge operator that can ratify the output of a lower-reliability evidential as established fact, while siri ne — as a scene-level visual evidential — cannot fill that ratifying role ‹contested›.
Dal Corso leaves the exact semantic driver open ; the full argument is developed in .

The diachronic path parallels those of the other formal nouns (see ): the noun yields the possessed formal noun sir-i 'the appearance of —', which grammaticalizes as the clause-final evidential [clause] siri ne ; .
The grammaticalization is partial: the lexical source remains transparent in weather compounds, and the choice of post-nominal predicate (ne vs an vs ki) continues to carry evidential weight .
The meteorological transparency is most visible in the compound predicates built on : sir-pirka 'good weather', sir-kunne 'be dark / nightfall', sir-peker 'be bright / dawn'.
These incorporate sir as a weather-subject noun and are lexicalized verb compounds, not evidential constructions.
The evidential and the weather-noun use are synchronic relatives on a shared stem, one grammaticalized into the clause-final paradigm, the other retained as a productive lexical pattern.
Dialect microvariation runs parallel to what was observed for ruwe ne:
Tokachi uses the bare concept form sin (allomorph of sir) in clause-final position — not the possessed siri — and applies the stage-level restriction discussed above ; .
Horobetsu grammaticalizes siri a step further, into adverbial-clause and conjunction-like markers — a 'versatile nominalization' use not reported for well-described Saru.
The earliest attestation is Chiri's adversative construction (ci-sautar-i sinki siri suke ki wa … 'my sisters, though tired, cooked…') .
forms: ci-sautar-i sinki siri suke ki wa …

text: Asahikawa and Shiranuka use ru an in the inferential function that siri an fills in the southern dialects — an apparent complementary distribution that complicates pan-Hokkaido generalizations .
hawe ne is the reportative member of the Hokkaido Ainu evidential paradigm.

Like its three siblings it consists of a formal noun in the possessed form followed by the copula : where ruwe ne signals a fact recognized through knowledge or reasoning, siri ne a directly visible situation, and humi ne a non-visual sensation, hawe ne signals that the information was acquired verbally — through hearing someone speak, receiving a report, or encountering hearsay.
The architecture common to all four is set out in ; the other three evidentials are treated in the inferential ruwe ne, the situational siri ne, and the sensory humi ne.

In Dal Corso's eight-form analysis, hawe ne is the direct evidential of hearing (DIR.HRN), the lowest-reliability direct form in the paradigm; its indirect counterpart is hawe as (IND.HRN), treated in §hawe as below .

In Dal Corso's reference texts, hawe ne accounts for 298 of 2232 evidential tokens (13.35%), and hawe as for a further 94 (4.21%), making the two hawe-forms together the second most frequent pair after ruwe ne .
The source noun is .

Tamura's Saru dictionary defines haw as '(人間・動物の)声、(バイオリンなどの)音' — the voice of a human or animal and the sound of certain instruments; general inanimate sounds such as a drum are expressed instead with the separate noun .
The ordinary possessed form is hawehe 'the voice of —'.

The evidential formal noun is hawe = haw-e, the voice noun plus its possessive suffix, but like the other formal nouns of the evidential paradigm it blocks the additional possessive extension: the form with a further -he is ungrammatical as the evidential (*hawehe) ; .
Glossing it as voice-POSS tracks this morphological origin.
The lexical noun remains productive alongside the formal noun.

The community notes the prohibitive construction iteki e=hawe aste 'do not raise your voice' — where e=hawe is the second-person possessed form of haw and is the lexical verb — as evidence that the person-marked lexical noun is still active, distinct from the evidential formal noun which takes no person prefix (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2025-12-03) ‹contested›.

A related observation: sekor haw=an '(one) says thus' and sekor isoytak '(one) narrates thus' are both attested as quotative expressions, differing in whether a general act of speaking or more formal narrating is meant (thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord, 2025-06-03) ‹corpus-suggested›.
In sekor haw=an the verb haw=an is the lexical 'to speak / give voice', not the formal noun; the two functions of the root coexist.

Chiri described the diachronic shift as running from 'there is a voice/rumor of X' (「云々の声がある」「云々の噂がある」) to the hearsay assertive (cited via ), following the same cline documented for all four evidentials: sensory noun > possessed formal noun > clause-final evidential .
Nakagawa defines hawe ne as indicating that the speaker judges from information received verbally (言葉で聞いた情報から判断していること) .
Three overlapping functions are documented in the sources.
The core use is the direct report: the speaker heard a specific person say something, and hawe ne encodes that hearing as the information source.
Tamura describes this as '誰かが言ったことに基づいて述べる; 他人の発言の紹介、自分の発言の さらなる説明' — presenting what someone said, or elaborating on one's own earlier statement (cited via ).
The second function is hearsay: the information reaches the speaker through general social knowledge or rumor rather than from a named interlocutor.

The example in Hirosawa (2026: 71, ex. 3), where a narrator attributes a plague to a divine figure's anger on the basis of circulating report rather than personal reasoning, illustrates this function; the example is drawn from Tamura 1988 audio materials (narrator Wateke, Saru) .

Third, Nakagawa notes for Chitose that hawe ne may mark the speaker's own statement, as in the framing expression hawe ne yakun 'if that is the case / given those words' (cited via ) ‹corpus-suggested›.
In this use, the form makes explicit the verbal nature of what was just said.
Dal Corso places hawe ne at the lowest-reliability position of the four direct evidentials, reflecting the sense hierarchy sight > touch/taste/smell > hearing.

Source reliability in his framework is a property of the acquisition channel, not a claim about epistemic certainty — hawe ne specifies how the information was obtained without committing the speaker to a degree of confidence in its truth ‹consensus›.

Hirosawa (2026: 81) observes that near-identical sentences can alternate hawe ne and ruwe ne — one version presenting the proposition as heard speech, the other as assimilated knowledge — without a sharp semantic break ; .
The boundary between the two forms is gradient rather than categorical ‹contested›.
The most prominent environment for hawe ne in the Saru and Chitose corpus is the quotative frame built with the complementizer .
A clause of quoted content is followed by sekor and a speaking verb, with hawe ne at the clause edge:
[quoted content] sekor [verb of saying] hawe ne
forms: [quoted content] sekor [verb of saying] hawe ne

text: sekor marks the boundary of the quoted content; the speaking verb specifies the act of utterance; hawe ne then asserts that the speaker's information derives from hearing.
The full analysis of sekor and direct speech framing is in .
The use of reported-speech frames in oral literature is described further in .

The community has proposed that Saru sekor is analytically se + kor 'saying while holding', and that ari / ani — the equivalent in other dialects — preserves an older quotative form, with sekor a Saru-centred innovation (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-09; 2024-12-06) ‹contested›.
These etymological questions belong to ; the relevant point here is that the sekor … hawe ne combination is the canonical reported-speech construction in the Saru/Chitose corpus ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The indirect counterpart of hawe ne is hawe as (phonologically hawas), formed by replacing the copula ne with the posture verb , the same auxiliary used in humi as.
The table below summarizes the two hawe-forms along Dal Corso's organizing parameters .

hawe as has specialized so thoroughly as a reportative that it is the only indirect form with a robust hearsay reading: humi as is consistently inferential and never reportative, while hawe as handles both the quotative use (overt speaker named) and the hearsay use (source diffuse or absent) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
As a lexical item, hawe as means 'a voice is heard; someone speaks; a sound resounds' — the compositional reading of 'voice stands' .
The evidential is an extension of this lexical meaning, and in some corpus occurrences the boundary between a literal sound event and a reportative attribution is genuinely ambiguous ‹speculative›.

The four formal nouns share a paradigm of clause-final frames; Nakagawa arranges them as: NMLZ + ne declarative, NMLZ + an content question (with a question word), bare NMLZ polar question and exclamation, and NMLZ + un affirmative answer .
The hawe column is as follows.

The polar reduction hawe! follows the insubordination pattern documented for the other bare-nominalizer forms: a once-dependent nominalized clause used as a main clause to express surprise or strong emotion at the reported content ; .
Interrogative frames in the wider system are treated in .
The hawe ta an? variant with an inserted ta is dialectally restricted, attested in Shizunai and Horobetsu and apparently absent from Saru/Chitose .
Whether ta here is the locative/temporal postposition or a separate interrogative element is not settled in the accessible sources ‹speculative›.
The clause dominated by hawe ne is a fully finite predication: it carries its own person marking, aspect, and perfective auxiliaries.
hawe ne scopes over the entire TAM-marked clause, and negation belongs inside the evidential (… somo ki hawe ne 'it is said that [one] does not …'), not on hawe ne itself .

Post-evidential material — the perfective a, final particles, conjunctions, and nominalizers — may follow hawe ne, exactly as for ruwe ne; the evidential sits above clause-internal aspect but below clause-linkers.

The ordering restriction — hawe ne kusu is grammatical while *kusu hawe ne is not in this meaning — confirms that the evidential sits at the outer edge of the VP and inside the scope of clause-linkers, the same layering found for ruwe ne ‹consensus›.
What accessible sources do not yet settle is the precise constituency status of hawe ne within the nominalized projection ‹speculative›.
hawe as and hawe ne both enter double-evidential constructions with ruwe ne.
The most frequent pattern is … hawe as ruwe ne, where a character's indirect verbal source is layered under the narrator's ruwe ne, which presents the event as traditional shared knowledge .
A second pattern, … hawe ne nankor ruwe ne, uses ruwe ne as an epistemic reinforcer on a lower-reliability direct form .
In both, the outer ruwe ne can ratify an already evidentially marked proposition as established fact; it behaves as a knowledge operator that scopes over the other evidential.
The wider picture of evidential stacking is in .

In narrative texts hawe ne marks the narrator's explicit attribution of a proposition to a verbal source, contrasting with the narrative default ruwe ne, which presents events as traditionally known facts.
The genre-level distribution of the evidential forms is treated in .

The shift from sensory noun to formal noun is transparent and is noted in the earliest grammars: haw 'voice' > haw-e (possessed) 'the voice of —' > hawe ne 'it is said that …', parallel to the evolution of sir, hum, and ru ; ; .

Dal Corso's general assessment applies: the grammaticalization is partial — the lexical source noun is still visible in the blocking of -he, and the lexical verb haw as 'a voice sounds' remains active — so the shift is a matter of degree rather than categorical completion ‹consensus›.
Dialect realization of the reportative evidential varies in the same way as the other three forms:
Saru, Chitose, Biratori — the possessed form hawe in the full eight-form direct/indirect system .

Tokachi (and frequently Ishikari) — the bare concept form haw closes the clause rather than the possessed hawe; aw is an attested Tokachi allomorph; iruska haw ne 'was angry (reportedly)' exemplifies the pattern ; .

Horobetsu — the possessed-form nominalizer hawe grammaticalizes a step further into adverbial-clause and conjunctive-particle uses not reported for well-described Saru, extending the 'versatile nominalization' cline .

The dialect geography of the quotative particle that co-occurs with hawe ne mirrors this variation: Saru and Chitose use sekor while other dialects use ari / ani, a distribution that community discussion has analyzed as a Saru-centred innovation against a more widely preserved older form (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-06) ‹contested›.
The full dialect picture of the quotative is described in .

Among the four direct evidential forms of Hokkaido Ainu, humi ne marks that the speaker's information derives from a non-visual sensory source: a physical sound, a smell or taste, a touch or bodily sensation, or an internal impression that is neither visible nor verbally reported.
The construction — a nominalized clause headed by a formal noun and closed by the copula ne — is common to all four terms and is described in .
The other three direct forms are treated in the inferential ruwe ne, the situational siri ne, and the reportative hawe ne.
Dal Corso's morphosyntactic account arranges the four direct forms along a source-reliability scale: ruwe ne > siri ne > humi ne > hawe ne.

Source reliability in this account designates the psychophysical channel of acquisition, not a degree of epistemic certainty: a speaker using humi ne specifies non-visual sensory access, not a lower confidence in the proposition .
The visual/non-visual macrodivision groups ruwe ne and siri ne on the visual side and humi ne and hawe ne on the non-visual .
Mapped onto the typology of , the system is C1-type (visual, non-visual sensory, inferred, reported) .
humi ne is among the less frequent members of the paradigm.
In Dal Corso's Hokkaido reference texts it supplies 45 of 2232 evidential tokens (2.02%), with its indirect counterpart humi as adding a further 37 (1.66%) .
Both counts place the sensory evidential as the third-most frequent direct form and second-to-last in the full eight-form system ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The formal noun humi is the possessed (affiliative) form of the noun .
Tamura's Saru dictionary records hum (ordinary possessed form humi(hi)) with the primary senses 音・感じ 'sound; feeling/sensation' .

The same source noun underlies the lexical predicate humas (hum-as 'to sound, there is a noise'), where is the posture-verb element that also appears in hawe as and in other transient-state predicates such as apto as 'it rains' and rera as 'the wind blows' .

As a formal noun in the evidential function, humi blocks the additional possessive ending that the full lexical possessed form may carry: the regular possessed noun is humi(hi), but evidential *humihi is ungrammatical — the same blocking that disallows *ruwehe for the inferential ; .

This restriction, shared by all four formal nouns and discussed in , is a diagnostic of partial grammaticalization: the form has shed ordinary head-noun syntax without yet becoming a bound morpheme ‹consensus›.
The standard gloss is sound/feeling-poss: the morpheme is hum-i (base plus possessive suffix), whose implicit possessor is the nominalized clause.
The scope of hum sets it apart from the adjacent source noun .
Tamura is explicit: inanimate and non-vocal sounds — a drum, ambient noise, a sound with no identified speaker — take hum, while human and animal voice takes haw .
This lexical distinction is grammaticalized in the evidential pair: humi ne for non-verbal sensory access, hawe ne for verbal report and hearsay.
The construction is a copular predication over a nominalized clause — [clause] humi 'the sound/feeling that [clause]', closed by the copula ne (treated in ).
The traditional label for this form is Kindaichi's 感説法 'feeling-mood', characterizing it as expressing 'it feels like … / it seems like …' in the modality of uncertain sensory judgment ; .
The modern evidential framing retains the source semantics.
Tamura specifies humi ne as appropriate for hearing, touch, and bodily or emotional feeling .
Nakagawa's Chitose dictionary extends the domain to 音・匂い・味・体感・直感 — sounds, smells, tastes, bodily sensations, and intuitions obtained through any means except sight and verbal report ; .
His 2024 grammar gives the standard definition: humi ne marks that the speaker's judgment rests on sensation other than sight and language .
Satō's question paradigm assigns 感覚・物音 'sensation, physical sound' to the humi domain .
Dal Corso glosses the form dir.flt (direct evidential, feeling) and lists the covered channels as hearing, smell, touch, taste, and an internal 'sixth sense' .
He documents a recurring sensor-stimulus mismatch: the evidential derives historically from the noun meaning 'sound, feeling', yet it licenses gustatory and other non-auditory stimuli .
