The boundary with siri ne is explicit in the definition: siri encodes a directly visible situation or appearance, while humi covers any percept not accessed through sight.

The boundary with hawe ne runs along the verbal/non-verbal divide: hawe (from ) encodes information obtained from words — spoken, reported, or overheard — whereas humi covers physical sounds and bodily perceptions that are not themselves linguistic utterances .
humi participates in the shared clause-final frame paradigm documented by Nakagawa and summarized in .
The interrogative frames are treated in .
The bare exclamatory humi! is the most distinctive member.
It packages an immediate sensory reaction — most frequently gustatory or thermal — as its own utterance, without the copula:

Negation follows the pattern shared by all four evidentials: the proposition is denied within the embedded clause (the pattern …somo ki humi ne 'there is no feeling that [one does …]'), with humi ne remaining outside the scope of negation.
The fixed expression humi ka isam expresses the complete absence of the relevant non-visual percept.
The interaction of the evidential with the wider TAM and negation apparatus is treated in .

The indirect sensory evidential humi as replaces the copula ne with the posture verb , shifting the evidential reading from direct to more distanced sensory access: the speaker has sensory grounds but presents them as slightly removed or inferential .
Dal Corso glosses it ind.flt (indirect evidential, feeling).
The opposition copula ne (internal, direct) vs posture/existential verb (external, indirect) runs across all four formal nouns and is set out in .
A functional asymmetry distinguishes humi as from its verbal-source counterpart.
hawe as has largely specialized as a reportative — encoding hearsay when the source is absent and quotation when it is overt .
humi as retains its sensory basis throughout: it is consistently inferential from a non-verbal sensory impression and is never reportative ‹corpus-confirmed›.
As a lexical predicate, humas (hum-as) means 'to make a sound, to resound' .
The physical-sound use is the most frequent in the corpus:
Like the other formal nouns, humi enters double-evidential constructions in which two evidentials stack within a single clause .
The combination humi ne humi as stacks the direct and indirect sensory evidentials on the same non-visual channel:
This pattern differs from the double-evidential constructions in , where ruwe ne ratifies an indirect form from a distinct channel as established knowledge.
In humi ne + humi as, the same sensory channel provides both layers; the two evidentials together convey a closely felt percept reported with residual uncertainty .
The constituent nominalized by humi is a full finite clause carrying its own person marking, aspect, and negation, over which the evidential then scopes.
The scope properties are shared across all four formal nouns and are set out in ; nothing in the structure of humi ne alters that general picture.
Mirativity is carried in Hokkaido Ainu by the auxiliaries aan / awan and by anan, not by the formal-noun evidentials themselves ; .
Chiri's freezing example above, rupus humi ne awan, shows the admirative tail awan occupying the post-evidential slot: the surprised-retrospective reading comes from awan, not from humi ne itself.
The full treatment of mirativity and its interaction with the evidential system is in .
The grammaticalization path parallels that of the three sibling formal nouns.
The noun grammaticalized first into the possessed nominal hum-i, and from there into a clause-final formal noun whose implicit possessor is the nominalized event rather than a personal possessor ; .

The overall cline — sensory noun > possessed formal noun > evidential — is shared by sir, haw, and ru and places the Ainu system within the nominalization-based evidential strategy discussed by ; the path is set out for the full paradigm in .
Dal Corso's account of the degree of grammaticalization applies to humi as to the others: partial, with residual nominal behaviour visible in the possessive blocking .
Dialect variation in the realization of humi follows the system-wide patterns:
Saru, Chitose, Biratori — the core of Dal Corso's data — use the possessed form humi throughout, with the direct/indirect split humi ne / humi as .
Tokachi (and frequently Ishikari) close the clause with the bare concept form hum rather than the possessed humi; the declarative frame attested by Takahashi appears as … ran hum ne awan ; .

Horobetsu grammaticalizes the possessed-form nominalizers a step further into adverbial-clause markers and conjunctive-particle uses not attested in well-described Saru — an instance of what Takahashi calls 'versatile nominalization' .
Ijäs's pedagogical grammar treats humi ne under the evidential framing without adjudicating the analytical disputes discussed in .
The genre patterning of humi ne within narrative texts and its distribution relative to ruwe ne across frame-text, reported inner experience, and direct speech are taken up in .

Three properties of the Hokkaido Ainu evidential system are treated here because they apply across all four formal-noun evidentials rather than belonging to any single term: the expression of mirativity and its structural separation from the evidential nominalizers; the scope of the evidential predicate over the TAM-marked clause it closes; and the grammaticalization cline by which ordinary sensory nouns become clause-final formal-noun evidentials.
Double-evidential stacking is treated alongside grammaticalization because it reveals the hierarchical position that ruwe ne has reached on that cline.
The individual evidentials are described in , , , , and .
Surprise at the content of a proposition — mirativity — is not encoded by any of the four formal-noun evidentials.
The mirative value in the Hokkaido corpus attaches instead to the perfective auxiliary and to the related form .
states this explicitly: Hokkaido Ainu shows no systematic evidence that the evidential paradigm itself generates mirative meanings, in contrast to some Sakhalin configurations.
The mirative reading arises from aan/anan, not from the choice of evidential nominalizer.

argues that aan encodes not just mirativity but also indirect evidentiality — placing the information at a remove from the speaker's direct epistemic access — and that the two meanings are inseparable in this auxiliary ‹contested›.
, working from a different theoretical framing, finds no grounds for aligning aan with the indirect evidential paradigm and treats its mirative effect as pragmatic.
The debate turns on sources consulted second-hand; Yoshikawa's two studies are cited here via .
What the accessible sources agree on is the descriptive fact: aan/anan is the element that contributes mirativity ‹corpus-suggested›.
Within a clause the two elements can divide the semantic labour.

(ex. 33) analyses a Saru narrative example in which aan places content outside the speaker's prior epistemic territory — the structural basis of the surprise — while a following ruwe ne reclaims that same content as established fact, producing the 'it turned out that…' reading.
Hirosawa reads the sequence as a territory-conflict pattern parallel to Japanese みたい followed by のだ: outward epistemic displacement, then incorporation ‹contested›.
The same anan follows double-evidential constructions when a mirative reading accompanies an indirect evidential stacked under ruwe ne:

An early attestation of the mirative tail with the non-visual sensory evidential is preserved in : rupus humi ne awan 'it had completely hardened and frozen', where the past-mirative tail awan (a form historically related to or identical with aan) follows humi ne.

This pattern — any of the four direct evidentials followed by a mirative tail — recurs in the corpus, confirming that mirativity is an independent layer above the evidential rather than a property of any particular nominalizer.
The pedagogical grammar presents the evidential nominalizers alongside perfective and mirative auxiliaries without foregrounding the structural distinction between them.
The primary analyses ; agree that this distinction is grammatically real, even where they diverge on the semantics of aan itself.
All four formal-noun evidentials share the same scope geometry: the evidential predicate (formal noun + copula or existential verb) closes a fully finite, TAM-marked clause.

The constituent before the evidential carries its own person marking, suppletive number alternations, aspect and perfective auxiliaries, and propositional negation; the evidential then takes scope over the entire embedded clause ; .

Propositional negation — the denial of the embedded proposition — is expressed by negating the verb before the formal noun; the pattern …somo ki ruwe ne predicates the negative proposition as a recognized fact, with ruwe ne outside the scope of somo.
The same holds for all four siblings: …somo ki siri ne, …somo ki hawe ne, …somo ki humi ne.
The outer rhetorical frame ruwe somo ne is categorically different — it negates the evidential predication as a whole — and is discussed in .
The ordering of the evidential with respect to other clause-level material follows a fixed hierarchy.

For ruwe ne, the clause-linkers wa, hine, akusu, kusu, and nominal heads hi, p all follow the evidential; the purposive modal kusu ne takes the evidential as its complement (kusu ne ruwe ne is grammatical) but cannot follow it (*ruwe ne kusu ne is ungrammatical) .

The community discussion at aynu-corpora Discord (nukopoli, 2024-11-09) restates this as a layer-hierarchy principle — modal heads sit above the evidential, taking it as complement rather than the reverse — a formulation corroborated by Nakagawa's paradigm data ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The evidential therefore occupies a position above clause-internal aspect but below the clause-linking and modal projections that take a finite clause as their argument.
Person and number agreement inside the evidential clause is independent of anything outside it.
Suppletive verbal number alternations are resolved inside the evidential: the contrast íne nispa ek ruwe ne (singular ek 'come') vs.
íne nispa arki ruwe ne (plural arki) turns on agreement within the embedded clause.
The formal noun and copula carry no agreement of their own .
The formal status of the nominalized clause embedded under the evidential is not settled in the sources consulted directly for this grammar.
Its finiteness is evident from its TAM and person marking.

observes that the copula ne of the direct forms expresses an internal, speaker-anchored viewpoint while the existential and posture verbs of the indirect forms express an external perspective, but stops short of a formal constituency analysis.
Whether the embedded constituent constitutes a full finite nominalization, a predicate-phrase nominalization, or a construction-specific projection remains ‹speculative›.
The general nominalization strategy underlying the construction is treated in and ; the perfective auxiliary that may follow the evidential is treated in .

The four formal-noun evidentials derive from the possessed forms of ordinary sensory nouns: the path-noun yields the possessed form ru-we 'the trace of —', the appearance-noun yields sir-i, the voice-noun yields haw-e, and the sound/feeling-noun yields hum-i.

The shift from sensory noun to clause-final marker was recognized in the earliest grammatical descriptions and is confirmed morphologically by Tamura's dictionary entries and Chiri's etymology: ruwe derives from 'there is a trace of X', shifted to 'there is the fact of X' ; .
On the typological framework of , the Ainu evidentials represent an intermediate point on the layered cline from lexical noun to grammatical marker.

stresses that the result remains only partially grammaticalized: source-noun semantics are still active in the synchronic distribution (each form retaining a distinct sensory channel), the post-nominal predicate choice still matters for the direct/indirect distinction, and the formal nouns have lost full noun-phrase syntax — they admit no demonstrative or attributive modifier, block the extra possessive ending (*ruwehe, *humihi as evidentials), and are fixed in linear position .
The Ainu system as a whole is a graded category; no Hokkaido form approaches the full grammaticalization of the Sakhalin particle manu ‹consensus›.
Within Hokkaido, the grammaticalization has advanced differently across dialects.
Three stages are directly attested in the sources, yielding an intra-areal cline ‹speculative›:

In Stage I dialects the bare concept form closes the clause where Saru uses the possessed form: Tokachi iruska haw ne 'she was angry', tuk ru ne 'it emerged', alongside Saru iruska hawe ne and tuk ruwe ne ; .
The allomorphs sin (for sir) and aw (for haw) are Tokachi-specific .
Stage I and Stage II represent a morphological difference — concept form vs. possessed form — rather than a semantic one; the four-way source distinction is present at both stages.
Stage III, the Horobetsu development, takes the possessed-form nominalizer a step further.
documents uses in which the nominalizers function not as complement-clause heads but as adverbial-clause markers — subordinating-conjunction-like elements — without a following copula.
The adversative use is the clearest instance:

notes that this versatile adverbial use is anticipated in Kindaichi & Chiri's 1936 description of nominalizers as conjunctive particles , suggesting the Stage III path is of some age within Horobetsu rather than a recent innovation.
Takahashi connects this to what Noonan termed 'versatile nominalization' — a nominalization strategy that extends across both complement-clause and adverbial-clause functions.
One dialect fact complicates a simple Stage I → II reading of the cline.
In Asahikawa and Shiranuka the trace-form ru enters the existential frame as an inferential (ru an), apparently in complementary distribution with the siri an of the southern dialects .

This gives ru an indirect-evidential function that the southern varieties lack for this stem; it may reflect convergence toward the Sakhalin existential pattern (ruwehe ʔan), but the sources are thin and Dal Corso flags the comparison as requiring a wider-dialect study ‹speculative›.
The grammaticalization trajectory also bears on the frequency asymmetry within the direct paradigm.

characterizes ruwe ne as semantically unmarked among the four direct forms, capable of summarizing and marking scene transitions much as Japanese のだ does — a discourse function consistent with its being the most grammaticalized direct member .

The community discussion at aynu-corpora Discord (nukopoli, 2024-03-17) summarizes the same Yoshikawa 2020 characterization and notes the high frequency of ruwe ne in narrative and its summative/transitional function, a point corroborated by Dal Corso's corpus counts ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Genre-specific evidential patterning is treated in .
Double evidentials — two formal-noun evidential constructions stacked within a single clause — are more frequent in Hokkaido than in Sakhalin .
documents three functional types from the Kayano, Tamura, Nakagawa, and Bugaeva corpora:
In Type A the outer ruwe ne functions as a ratifier.

An indirect form — typically hawe as (reportative indirect) or siri an (visual indirect) — presents the content from a character's perspective, and ruwe ne closes the utterance from the narrator's perspective as traditional, shared knowledge .
Attested Type A combinations include hawe as ruwe ne, siri an ruwe ne, and siri ki siri ne .
The outer form in Types A and B is systematically ruwe ne and not siri ne, hawe ne, or humi ne.

This asymmetry supports the analysis developed in : ruwe ne functions as an epistemic incorporation operator — a form that can ratify any already-evidentially-marked proposition as established knowledge — rather than as a fourth parallel sensory channel.

Among the direct members it is the one whose source-noun semantics ('the trace of —') has bleached sufficiently to generalize across all sources of evidence once they have been assimilated by the speaker.
Type B uses ruwe ne as an epistemic upgrade.
A direct evidential of relatively lower reliability is reinforced by a final ruwe ne asserting the speaker's overall confidence in the proposition.

(ex. 276) cites a narrator's utterance of the form hawe ne nankor ruwe ne — the modal nankor 'probably' attached to hawe ne is then closed by ruwe ne, which does not eliminate the uncertainty introduced by nankor but frames the compound as an incorporated fact from the speaker's perspective.
This use is consistent with ruwe ne's position at the top of the source-reliability hierarchy in Dal Corso's analysis.
Type C, same-stem iteration, occurs in narrative contexts where the speaker presents both a subjective sensation and its arising as separate evidential moments:
adds a distributional argument bearing on the siri forms.
When the indirect visual siri an appears in a double-evidential construction, the ratifying outer form is consistently ruwe ne and never siri ne.

Were the two simply co-equal visual channels, this selection would be unmotivated; it follows naturally if ruwe ne occupies a higher position in the evidential hierarchy, one at which its source-noun meaning has bleached enough to allow ratification of any other evidential type.
The distributional gap that Dal Corso's sense-hierarchy account left open is therefore partially resolved by the double-evidential distribution itself ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The stacking found in mirative contexts (§2 above) should be distinguished from double-evidential stacking.

In siri an ruwe ne anan, the final anan is a mirative auxiliary, not a third formal-noun evidential; the stacking is between two evidential predicates and a mirative auxiliary in sequence, not among three co-equal evidential forms.

Conflating the two construction types would obscure the structural difference between the evidential system (formal noun + copula or existential verb) and the mirative system (a perfective auxiliary above the evidential layer) ; .
Standard clausal negation in Hokkaido Ainu is carried by the free adverb , placed before the predicate phrase.
The verb itself takes no negative inflection; the language has no negative conjugation comparable to the Japanese verb-final suffix ない ; ; .

Nakagawa is explicit that the preverbal position is not a negation-specific rule: somo is an adverb, and the general principle that a modifier precedes the phrase it modifies puts it, like any other preverbal adverb, in front of the verb .
The negator can also stand alone as a one-word reply, somo ‘no, that is not so’ .
The table separates standard negation from the lexical and directive systems that also yield negative meanings, and the split has syntactic consequences.
A clause built on or contains a negative predicate that indexes its arguments in the ordinary way; a clause with somo keeps the positive predicate and places a negative adverb in its scope.

Satō formalises the division by predicate type: a verbal clause is negated as [subject] V (ka) somo ki or with preverbal somo directly before the verb, while a copular clause is negated as [subject] [complement] (ka) somo ne, with the negator before the copula ne .
Ijäs presents the same architecture for learners: copular ‘A is not B’ is A B somo ne, agreeing with Satō’s paradigm and Nakagawa’s ordering description ; ; .
With a verbal predicate, somo stands immediately before the person-marked verb.

Satō states the adjacency as a rule: the negator precedes the verb, and the personal index is part of the verb form, so the negator cannot intervene between the index and its stem — somo ku=arpa ‘I do not go’, never *ku=somo=arpa ; .
Ijäs gives learners the same warning against splitting the personal affix from its stem with the negator .
For an ordinary verb the bare frame somo V is grammatical but, by Satō’s report, used less often than the ka somo ki periphrasis of the next section .
A modal or other postverbal element follows the verb in its normal place, with the negator still at the front of the predicate:

Standard negation here is symmetric in the sense of the typology of negation: the affirmative and negative declarative clauses differ only by the added negative morpheme, with no separate negative verb form or special negative agreement ; .
Takahashi’s Tokachi weather predicate gives the minimal pair, the affirmative ruyanpe ruy ‘it rained’ differing from its negation by somo alone:
Preverbal somo also negates the existential-locational predicate , where the positive verb stays available alongside the suppletive negative existential isam.

Ijäs draws a semantic line between the two — isam for outright absence or disappearance, somo an where the ‘live, be located’ reading of an is to be preserved — but the exact split is her own formulation and is not stated in those terms by the read grammars ‹contested›
The privative paradigm and possessive uses of isam are treated in .
The second verbal frame places the notional predicate before somo ki, with optional ka between them: V (ka) somo ki.

Bugaeva gives the compositional analysis: it is the verb that somo formally negates, while the notional verb functions as an object-like complement of ki; the notional verb keeps its person marking and ki carries none .
Nakagawa treats the same string as one use of the formal verb ki, which supplies a verbal host so that conjunctions and clause-final material can attach .
Ijäs’s pedagogical account agrees, describing ki as a dummy ‘do’ verb filling the slot that somo cannot occupy on its own .

Against this, Satō’s description of Chitose, as reported by Takahashi, analyses somo ki as a single auxiliary rather than as ki negated over a complement; the internal constituency of the periphrasis is therefore genuinely disputed ‹contested›
Refsing records the construction for Shizunai as well .

Nakagawa finds no clear semantic contrast between the preverbal frame and the somo ki frame, and likewise no special meaning in the presence or absence of ka ; Ijäs treats the longer construction as broadly exchangeable with plain somo .
When ka is present it brackets the notional predicate as the focused complement of ki:
Ijäs additionally suggests that the postverbal ka somo ki arose as a calque on Japanese verb-final negation, with preverbal somo as the older Ainu pattern.

No read Hokkaido source supports a contact origin, and Dal Corso’s diachronic account of Ainu negation derives the periphrastic forms internally, so the contact hypothesis is best left as her own conjecture ‹speculative›
A predicate-nominal clause is negated by placing somo before the copula ne, optionally with ka: NP (ka) somo ne ; .

Satō notes that the alternative ne ka somo ki, expected if ne is fed through the ordinary somo ki frame as a verb, is scarcely attested; the productive negator of the copular clause is somo ne or ka somo ne .
The particle ka in ka somo ki and ka somo ne is the ordinary additive and focus particle ‘also, even, at all’, here attached to the negated constituent.
Nakagawa observes that negative clauses favour ka — adding focus to the element whose absence is asserted sharpens the negation — while its presence carries no meaning of its own .

Satō isolates a distinct ‘negative particle’ ka, left untranslated in his paradigms, while granting that it is hard to separate strictly from the additive particle; for Bugaeva, following Tamura, the same ka focuses the complement with a nuance of unexpectedness ; .
The divergence is one of analysis and terminology over a single form ‹contested›.
Ijäs presents ka somo ne as the more emphatic equative negation, glossing ka ‘also, even, at all’ .

The same ka builds the negative-polarity indefinites nep ka ‘anything, and under negation nothing’ and nen ka ‘anyone, no one’, whose licensing depends on the scope of the negator over the whole clause; that interaction is treated in .

A clause closed by a formal noun plus ne — the evidential frames ruwe ne, hawe ne, siri ne, humi ne — is negated by negating the verb phrase inside the nominalization, leaving the evidential frame itself in place.
Nakagawa states the rule directly: the negative counterpart of such a clause makes the verb phrase before the formal noun negative, so the negation scopes below the evidential .

A surface-similar sequence in which the negator falls on the copula of the evidential, ruwe somo ne, is not ordinary clausal negation but a rhetorical or convictional construction, close to ‘was it not the case that …?’ .
The contrast — propositional negation inside the evidential against the high-scope rhetorical frame on the copula — belongs with the evidential paradigm in .

In main declarative clauses, verbal and copular alike, somo negation is symmetric: the negative clause retains the predicate architecture of the affirmative and adds the negative adverb before the predicate ; .
Subordinate clauses behave differently.

Hokkaido temporal adverbial clauses link with several conjunctive particles — wa for a successive event, no for a stative one — but a negated adverbial clause selects only no, and the successive wa is blocked .
The restriction is uncontroversial as a fact ‹consensus›; its explanation is the live contribution.

Following Tamura’s analysis that the negation of an action is construed as a static state rather than as an event, Takahashi and the Handbook treat the no-only pattern as an asymmetry driven by aspect, with the choice of linker depending on polarity ; .
Nakagawa’s account of no gives the same conditioning from the affirmative side: no links a preceding phrase that is stative, negative in meaning, or an action verb accompanied by a negative element .
Whether the dependency is best modelled as aspect government, as reduced transitivity, or pragmatically remains open in the literature ‹contested›.
Several negative meanings adjacent to somo have their own predicate architecture.

The negative existential isam and the privative express absence and lack with ordinary verbal syntax; the ability and cognition negatives eaykap, koyaykus, eramiskari, and erampewtek form a lexical-negative class; and the prohibitive belongs to directive mood ; .
These are routed to , , and .

Ijäs’s claim that the existence of a lexical negative normally bars somo plus the corresponding positive verb states the tendency too strongly: Dal Corso records southern Hokkaido somo kor ‘not have’ beside privative sak, and the read grammars describe lexicalized meanings and preferences rather than categorical blocking ‹contested›

Dal Corso’s Sakhalin-focused comparative work links somo and isam to an older negative-existential root *sam, deriving somo from a form like *samno and isam from antipassive i- on that root; Ijäs reaches the same speculation for isam, marking it as conjectural ; .
The read Hokkaido grammars state no such etymology, so the shared-root proposal stands as a specific historical hypothesis, not as settled synchronic analysis ‹speculative›.
The standard negator varies dialectally.

somo covers most of Hokkaido; the eastern Pacific coast and parts of the east use other free negators in the same structural slot, and the eastern dialects also have a rare suffix -ko that derives a rhetorical negative adverb from a stative intransitive — a genuinely morphological negative in an otherwise periphrastic system ; ; .
The microdistribution is assembled from scattered dialect reports rather than from a full conditioning study, and no rule is given for which negator a transitional locality selects ‹contested›
The wider dialect classification is treated in .
Hokkaido Ainu negates existence and possession with verbs whose meaning already contains the negation, leaving the preverbal adverb somo absent.
The negative existential is , the lexical counterpart of the positive existentials (singular) and oka(y) (plural); the privative is the lexical counterpart of ; .
Because the negative resides in the verb, the predicate indexes its arguments in the ordinary way and no adverbial negator is added.
The standard somo strategy is treated in , the positive existential and locational predicates in , and predicative possession with kor in .

isam and sak belong to a wider class of lexical negatives that also includes eaykap ‘cannot’, eramiskari ‘never, not know by experience’, and erampewtek ‘not understand’, all of which carry negative polarity as part of their lexical content ; .
The ability and cognition members of that class are treated in ; the present chapter takes the existential and possessive members.
Ijäs groups the same items as ‘lexically negated verbs’, pairing an/oka with isam and kor with sak .
isam is a one-place intransitive verb.

It takes the entity whose absence is asserted as its sole argument and indexes it with the ordinary intransitive person set — ku=isam ‘I am gone/absent’, e=isam ‘you are gone’ — while a third-person subject is zero-marked.
Dal Corso notes that isam is the only intransitive member of the lexical-negative class .
Its single argument slot serves as a constituency diagnostic: a clause containing two independent noun phrases cannot be a simple isam predication, since the verb supplies only one position .
The Handbook flags one isam clause whose lack of an overt personal affix it finds unexpected, against the normal pattern in which the verb does index its subject .

isam licenses the same ka-indefinite polarity items that occur under somo: nep ka ‘anything’ reads ‘nothing’ in its scope, and the additive ka may be repeated across several indefinites for an exhaustive ‘nothing at all’ .
The indefinite series and the scope of negation over it are set out in .
Two values of isam should be kept apart.

The existential value ‘there is none’ denies presence in a place or discourse domain; the change-of-state value ‘be gone’ presents absence as the result of a disappearance, and extends to a person’s death or absence .

The second value survives in the auxiliary wa isam, where a verb phrase linked by wa leads to a state in which the relevant participant or result has disappeared, the source of renderings such as ‘V away’ or ‘end up gone’ .
Its aspectual placement among the wa-auxiliaries is taken up in .
The lexical isam does not displace the positive existential an/oka.
An existential or locational predicate may still be negated analytically by placing somo before an, as with any verbal predicate ; .
The sources consulted agree that isam is the lexical negative of the existential, but they do not quantify when a speaker selects lexical isam over analytic somo an.

Ijäs proposes a semantic division: isam denotes complete absence or disappearance, while somo an is used where an keeps its broader value ‘live, be located’, and can additionally mark an absurd or impossible existence .

The division is plausible, since an independently covers existence, location, and residence and positive predicates are negatable by somo; the precise split is her pedagogical formulation and is not stated in those terms by Nakagawa, Satō, or Bugaeva ‹speculative›.
The somo an side of the contrast is treated in .
The same caution applies to the blocking rule.
Ijäs presents isam and sak as the normal negatives wherever such a paired verb exists, so that somo plus the positive counterpart is ‘not usually possible’ .

Dal Corso reports southern Hokkaido somo kor ‘not have’ beside sak, with a pragmatic difference supplied by Nakagawa , and Bugaeva characterizes these verbs only as containing negation in their meaning, not as barring somo .
The evidence supports a lexical preference; a categorical ban overstates the distribution ‹contested›.
Possessive negation is distributed over two related constructions.
Where the missing entity is profiled as absent from a possessor’s sphere, an existential isam clause expresses ‘there is no X (for Y)’.
Where the possessor is the subject of a privative predicate, the verb is sak.
Bugaeva identifies sak as the lexical negative of kor ‘have’ , and Ijäs gives the same pair .
For positive predicative possession and the nominal affiliative alternatives to kor, see and the possessed form.

sak is transitive: the possessor is its subject and the lacked thing its object, so a nominalized ona sak pe is ‘father-lack NMLZ’, hence ‘one who has no father’, with the lacked kin term as the complement of sak .
The privative base also enters lexical compounds, such as the tabooed snake-name sak-somo-ay-ep recorded by Nakagawa .
The no of the constructed example reflects a general linkage pattern: negative and negative-meaning predicates favour the stative adverbial linker no over successive wa.
Takahashi gives Tokachi evidence that negated subordinate clauses select no, and Nakagawa states the rule for stative, negative-meaning, or overtly negated verb phrases ; .
Ijäs extends the observation to lexical negatives such as sak and isam .
The symmetric/asymmetric typology behind the no-only restriction is set out in .
Dal Corso’s comparative account of Ainu negation is anchored in a Sakhalin study but makes a specific Hokkaido-facing proposal.

He reconstructs a negative-existential root *sam and analyses Hokkaido isam as the antipassive prefix i- on that transitive root, with antipassivization yielding the intransitive ‘not exist’; the standard negator somo is derived in the same account from *samno through final stress and an a/o change .
On this reconstruction a single source *sam underlies both the surviving negative existential isam and the general clausal negator somo.
The read Hokkaido reference grammars present no such etymology, so the shared-root analysis is a diachronic hypothesis rather than a synchronic fact about Hokkaido clauses ‹speculative›.
Ijäs independently reaches essentially the same segmentation, i- plus a lost transitive sam* ‘something is not located’, and explicitly labels it speculation .
The convergence of her lesson note with Dal Corso’s philological argument raises the point from an isolated pedagogical guess to a live scholarly proposal.
It remains a proposal: for ordinary clause grammar isam behaves as a single intransitive negative existential, with no productive alternation involving a free sam root ‹speculative›.

The reconstruction situates Ainu within two diachronic models that Dal Corso applies to it: the Givón negative cycle, by which a negator is periodically renewed, and the Negative Existential Cycle, by which a negative existential predicate develops into a general clausal negator and may leave existential traces in the result ; ; .
The cycle would explain why a negative existential and a standard negator are diachronically connected in one account while occupying distinct synchronic constructions.
Its application to Hokkaido is a historical hypothesis, not a synchronic generalization ‹speculative›: in the present-day grammar isam is a verb, and somo the preverbal negative adverb of .
Most clauses in Hokkaido Ainu are negated analytically, by the preverbal adverb placed before the predicate (treated in ).

A small set of verbs negates differently: the negation is part of the verb's lexical meaning, so the negative clause is built on a verb distinct from its affirmative counterpart rather than on somo plus the positive verb.
The members that express ability and cognition are the most clearly auxiliary-like part of this set — , , , , and .
Nakagawa lists them among the 他動詞起源の助動詞 ‘auxiliaries of transitive origin’ (his Table 75); Bugaeva describes the same forms as verbs that contain negation as part of their meaning ; .
The existential and privative members of the wider lexical-negative class, isam ‘not exist’ and sak ‘lack’, are treated in .

The negatives are well represented in the aligned Hokkaido corpus: eaykap occurs 1,082 times, eramiskari 464, erampewtek 454, niwkes 177, and koyaykus 154, against affirmative easkay 1,324 and amkir 143.

These are lemma-level token totals, normalized across dialects with personal affixes stripped, so they measure the salience of each item rather than the rate of any one construction; on that measure the class belongs to the core grammar of negation and not to an incidental lexical field ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The ability pair is morphologically transparent.
Easkay is e-askay, the applicative e- on askay ‘be skilled’, and eaykap is e-aykap, the same prefix on aykap ‘be unskilful’ ; ; .
The negation therefore resides in the root: askay and aykap are themselves a lexical antonym pair ‘skilled’ versus ‘unskilful’, differentiated by s ~ y and not by a productive negating morpheme.
The applicative e- supplies the slot for the thing or event one is or is not able to do, which is what makes both verbs transitive and lets them take a clause as their object.
The cognition negatives are lexicalized as wholes.

Eramiskari stands as the negative of amkir, and erampewtek as the negative of eraman / eramuan; Tamura classes all four as transitive verbs and tags eramiskari and erampewtek explicitly as 否定動詞 ‘negative verbs’ .

The two negatives share the element eram(u)- ‘mind, understanding’ with their affirmative counterparts, but neither segments into a recognizable negator, and the accessible grammars do not analyse them further.

Koyaykus and niwkes are likewise treated as unanalyzed units; koyaykus attaches as a whole after a verb, as in the dictionary forms mokor koyaykus ‘be unable to sleep’ and hunara koyaykus ‘be unable to find’ .
The cognition negatives carry minor dialect variants.
Saru has eramiskari, with eramuskari recorded for a single Nibutani speaker and eramuskare in Ishikari; erampewtek appears as erampetek elsewhere ; .

Because they are transitive in origin, these predicates can stand as the main verb of their clause, indexing an experiencer or agent as subject and taking the event as object, or they can follow another verb as an auxiliary.

In the auxiliary use the lexical verb keeps its personal marking and the negative auxiliary adds none, exactly as the formal verb does in the somo ki periphrasis: the negation sits in the auxiliary, while person stays on the predicate it scopes over .
The transitive origin remains active: the auxiliary may instead carry its own personal prefix, with the preceding clause as its object.
In the next example the indefinite person a= attaches to eaykap, not to the verb paye ‘go’, so that eaykap predicates ‘one cannot [go further upstream]’.
The auxiliary may be preceded by the particle , in the frame V ka eaykap (also V ka eramiskari), with no clear difference in meaning from the plain frame.
Nakagawa notes that this ka slot is available to the transitive-origin auxiliaries but is lacking for the native auxiliaries, which makes it a diagnostic of the class .
The strengthening that Ijäs assigns to the slot pedagogically is the ordinary scalar contribution of ka, not a separate negative morphology .
The shared post-verbal slot identifies these predicates with the auxiliary zone rather than with immediately preverbal somo.

Satō treats eaykap as an auxiliary occupying the same position as somo ki; the difference is that somo ki negates through the formal verb ki, whereas eaykap and its peers are themselves the negative predicate, so somo is not added to them ; .
Eaykap is the broad negative of easkay.
Nakagawa defines its range as inability in a wide sense, covering both a lack of capacity and a situation that does not permit the event, and Tamura adds the further reading ‘be poor at’ ; .
The modal semantics of the easkay / eaykap pair as a category of ability and possibility are developed in .
Koyaykus narrows the same space to circumstantial inability: the subject cannot do the event because the situation or the moment is against it, rather than for want of skill.
Tamura draws the contrast directly — koyaykus for what outside factors prevent, eaykap for what is beyond one's ability or generally impossible ; .
Niwkes is more specific again, ‘be unable to carry an action through to completion’ .
The lexicon of ability pairs it with eaykap as a doublet, the two glossed together as ‘cannot do’ and ‘cannot manage’ .

The articulation of the field has a consequence for glossing: a negative ability clause is rarely a bare ‘not able’, since the predicate chosen also classifies where the impossibility comes from ‹consensus›.
The cognition negatives split a domain that English often keeps together.
The pair amkir / eramiskari concerns knowledge by acquaintance or experience.
As a main verb eramiskari is ‘not know, not recognize’; after a verb phrase it gives an experiential negative, ‘have never V-ed’ ; .
The pair eraman / eramuan versus erampewtek concerns understanding and knowing how.
As a main verb erampewtek is ‘not understand, not know’; after a verb phrase it means that the subject does not know how to carry the event out, and so cannot ; .
Tamura keeps the two cognition negatives apart by source of knowledge: failure to recognize a person or thing is eramiskari, while failure to understand or to have the knowledge is erampewtek .
Ijäs's pedagogical contrast between experiential knowledge and understanding follows this same source split ‹consensus›.
Two facts show that the lexical negatives do not stand in complementary distribution with standard negation.
First, although somo is not added to the lexical negative itself, it freely negates a different predicate in the same clause:
Second, the lexical negative may sit inside a clause whose outer frame is itself negative.

In Nakagawa's example the experiential negative a=eramiskari falls within the proposition, while the rhetorical ru-we somo ne is the outer conviction frame of the evidential, not a second analytic negation of eramiskari .
The layering of negation with the formal-noun evidentials is treated in .
Whether the lexical negative outright blocks standard negation of the corresponding positive verb is a genuine question.
Ijäs states the rule categorically: where a lexical negative exists, somo plus the positive verb is not normally possible, so that one says k=erampewtek and not *somo k=eraman .
For at least one pair this is borne out by a primary source: Tamura's entry for amkir states that negation with somo is not formed, and the negative verb eramiskari is used instead .
The generalization does not hold across the whole class, however.

Dal Corso records southern Hokkaido somo kor ‘not have’ beside privative sak, with a distinct pragmatic value, and Bugaeva describes these verbs only as containing negation in their meaning, not as barring somo ; .

The blocking is best stated as graded: near-obligatory for the cognition pair amkir / eramiskari, a strong preference for the ability verbs, but not a categorical rule, so that Ijäs's blanket statement overstates it ‹contested›.
The lexical negatives license the same polarity-sensitive environment as somo and isam.

Nakagawa groups the ka-indefinites such as nep ka ‘anything, and under negation nothing’ with eaykap alongside the standard and existential negators ; the licensing and scope of these items are treated in .

In clause linkage they pattern with negative predicates: Takahashi shows that a negated subordinate clause selects the stative linker no rather than successive wa, and the lexical-negative auxiliaries take no in the same way, even without somo ; ‹consensus›.
The class is narrow, and an ordinary antonym is not a member of it.
Ijäs lists lexical opposites such as eese ‘agree’ / kopan ‘refuse’ and pa ‘find’ / turaynu ‘lose’, which remain ordinary verbs and take somo in the normal way .

The source check treats this as plausible but not separately verified for every pair, so the grammatical generalization is confined to the well-described negatives in the table above ‹corpus-suggested›.
The secure baseline for the class is the Saru description of Nakagawa and Tamura, with Ishikari and Tokachi variants where the examples mark them.
Takahashi documents the Tokachi auxiliary use of the experiential negative:
Refsing's Shizunai description confirms that eaykap and somo ki both occur in Shizunai, but the available text for the relevant pages is too damaged to support Shizunai-specific claims .

Dal Corso's history of Sakhalin negation bears on the class only diachronically: his proposal that negative-existential material underlies wider Ainu negation helps explain why the lexical negatives and standard somo form one connected domain, but the ability and cognition predicates described here are analysed from Hokkaido sources, and that history remains a hypothesis rather than a settled Hokkaido-internal fact ‹speculative›.
Hokkaido Ainu builds its principal indefinite series by adding the additive focus particle ka to an interrogative pro-form: nep ‘what’, nen ‘who’, hunak / ney ‘where’, and hempara ‘when’.

Outside the scope of negation the resulting forms are existential — nep ka ‘something, anything’, nen ka ‘someone, anyone’; within the scope of a negative predicate the same forms are read ‘nothing’ and ‘no one’ .
The two readings are values of a single form, fixed by the polarity of the clause that contains it.

The series is of the cross-linguistically common type whose members derive from interrogatives and spread across a graded set of functions — specific and non-specific existential, question, conditional, and negation .

In Ainu the negation function is morphologically continuous with the existential one: there is no separate negative pronoun, and the ‘nothing’ / ‘no one’ reading arises only when the existential indefinite falls under a negator.
The affirmative existential use is attested for all four bases and is especially frequent in interrogative and inferential frames, where nen ka introduces a non-specific ‘someone’:
The morphology of the bases and the wider set of interrogative-derived forms belong with ; the particle ka as additive and scalar focus belongs with .
The question pursued here is how these forms are licensed under negation, and where the licensing negation takes scope.
The standard negator itself is described in .
Any negative predicate in the clause licenses the indefinite series.
Three licensers recur: standard somo negation, whether preverbal somo V or the periphrasis V (ka) somo ki with the formal verb ; the negative existential ; and the negative ability verb .
In the periphrasis the notional predicate and its complement stand before somo ki, and the polarity item falls inside the complement that somo negates ; .
Preverbal somo licenses the same series.
In the topical dictionary nep ka ‘anything’ falls under somo in a polar question:
The negative existential isam licenses the series without somo; its privative and possessive uses are treated in .
With nen ka the result is ‘no one’, the negative counterpart of the existential ‘someone’ in (1):
The negative ability verb eaykap — one of the lexical negatives treated in — licenses the series in the same way, here on both the body-part object and the notional predicate:
The dialectal negators that replace somo in the same structural slot license the same forms.
Nakagawa's eastern-Hidaka example uses henne, and his Shiranuka example the dialectal negator omo with the focus variant kay for ka .

The generalization across these licensers is a scope condition, not a property of the indefinite itself: a clause contains one negative predicate, and the interrogative-plus-ka phrase receives a negative interpretation when it falls within that predicate's scope ‹consensus›.

The system therefore has no negative pronouns of the English nothing kind, which carry their own negation and can negate a clause unaided; the Ainu forms are read negatively only in concert with an overt negator ‹corpus-suggested›.
The particle ka does two jobs in these clauses.
It builds the indefinite (nep ka ‘anything’), and it focuses the constituent that is negated (… ka somo ki, … ka somo ne).
The two often co-occur, so that a single clause carries ka twice, once on the indefinite and once on the focused predicate:
Whether ka is present or absent carries no meaning of its own; negative clauses simply favour it, because focusing the constituent whose absence is asserted sharpens the denial .
Three analyses of this ka compete.
Satō isolates a distinct ‘negative particle’ ka, left untranslated in his paradigms, while granting that it is hard to separate strictly from the ordinary additive particle .
Nakagawa and Bugaeva keep it continuous with additive and scalar focus ‘also, even, at all’, the latter adding, after Tamura, a nuance of unexpectedness ; .
Ijäs presents the longer construction as emphatic and broadly exchangeable with plain somo, glossing ka ‘also, even, at all’ .
The disagreement is over how many homophonous particles to recognize for a single surface form ‹contested›.
The copular negation NP (ka) somo ne uses the same focus particle with the copula ne as its host, and Ijäs treats ka somo ne as the more emphatic way of saying ‘A is not B’ ; :
A small set of scalar items reinforces the negative reading by naming the low endpoint of the relevant scale.
Numeral-based sinep ka ‘even one’ gives ‘not even one’ under a negator; oar ‘completely’ sharpens absence to ‘absolutely none’; poka and ponno ka add a minimal-degree ‘even a little’ .
None of these changes the formal licenser; the scalar additive poka under preverbal somo is illustrated in .
Exhaustive negation over a list is built by repeating the negated predicate, not by a dedicated quantifier.
Nakagawa's clause denies each member of the series in turn:
The Handbook restates the same pattern with the coordinated somo ipe somo wakka ku no an ‘neither eating nor drinking’, after Takahashi's analysis of negated subordinate clauses ; .
forms: somo ipe somo wakka ku no an

text: Constructed teaching examples in Ijäs use the same scalar logic, placing oar under somo for ‘completely not, absolutely not’; these illustrate an attested pattern but are not corpus evidence .

A dedicated free-choice paradigm — a distinct ‘anything whatever’ or ‘whoever’ series set apart from the existential one — is not described in the sources consulted; the scalar minimizers carry the ‘even the least’ load that free-choice items carry elsewhere ‹speculative›.

The licensing condition is a scope condition: the indefinite is interpreted within the scope of the negative predicate of its clause, and the negator's scope is the whole verb phrase that contains the indefinite ‹corpus-suggested›.
The clearest scope evidence comes from the interaction with the nominalization-plus-copula evidential.

A clause closed by a formal noun plus ne is negated by negating the verb phrase inside the nominalization; the negator and the indefinite it licenses sit in the embedded proposition, and the evidential frame stays outside the negation .
The mirror-image order locates the boundary.

With ruwe somo ne the negator falls on the copula of the formal-noun predicate, and the clause is no longer plain propositional negation but a rhetorical or convictional assertion, close to ‘was it not the case that …?’ .
This high-scope copular negation does not license the indefinite series; the polarity items nep ka and sinep ka are licensed only in the lower, negated proposition.
The evidential's own negation belongs with the nonverbal-predicate apparatus of , and the inferential frame itself with .

Within the embedded proposition the placement of somo can in principle leave the scope underdetermined — whether it negates the notional verb or only the existential that hosts the evidential — and Dal Corso's evidentiality study reports both readings for the relevant configurations .
The read Hokkaido grammars describe the scope facts but settle no constituency analysis that would adjudicate such ambiguities ‹contested›.

The sources settle the basic pattern: interrogative-plus-ka forms are existential outside negation and negative within it, and they are licensed alike by standard somo, by dialectal negators such as henne and omo, and by lexical negatives such as isam and eaykap ‹consensus›.

They do not provide a quantified corpus study of the individual indefinite types, or a formal account of the scope ambiguities in evidential and nominalized clauses; the corpus tools available here count lemmas, not the multi-word [interrogative] ka … somo configurations, so no per-construction frequency is asserted ‹corpus-suggested›.
The remaining analytic boundary is with ordinary focus.

Because the same ka marks addition, scalar focus, and the indefinite series, a single negative clause routinely shows the particle twice — once forming an indefinite, once focusing the negated predicate — and the grammars agree on the surface distribution while disagreeing on how many particles to posit ‹contested›.
The general account of the particle, including its positive uses, is the necessary counterpart, given with the focus and additive particle.
The prohibitive is the negative member of the directive system.
A command not to act is formed with a prohibitive adverb in front of the predicate, most often in the Saru and Chitose dialects, answering to an English negative imperative.
Nakagawa groups iteki and its dialect counterparts as 禁止の語句 ‘prohibition words’, and Bugaeva glosses the construction as proh before the verb ; .
In the aligned Hokkaido corpus iteki is the frequent, default form, with 1278 tokens ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The propositional negator denies a declarative clause; the prohibitive adverb withdraws a directive addressed to the hearer.
In the typology of standard negation, which is defined over declarative verbal main clauses, the prohibitive falls outside the core and into the separate domain of the negative imperative .
The two systems are formally distinct and can co-occur (below).
The affirmative imperative and the politeness morphology that the prohibitive shares with it are set out in ; hortative and optative directives in .
The bare prohibitive places iteki at the left edge of the predicate phrase, ahead of the whole verb phrase rather than immediately before the verb:
The prohibitive adverb has several Hokkaido shapes.
Nakagawa reports iteki for Saru, Chitose, Horobetsu, and Abuta; itekke for Shizunai, Samani, and Tokachi; etekke for Shiranuka, Bihoro, and Tokachi; and eciki or ecikki for Ishikari .
The forms differ regionally and carry no reported difference in meaning; Tokachi appears for both itekke and etekke in the source.
The distribution rests on one witness form per locality and is best read as indicative rather than as a closed conditioning map ‹consensus›.

Nakagawa states the positional rule more loosely for the prohibitive than for somo: iteki and its counterparts may stand anywhere before the verb, whereas somo is in principle directly before the verb form ; .
The latitude follows from function.
Standard negation supplies polarity to a finite verb; the prohibitive adverb contributes directive force to the predicate phrase as a whole, and so occupies its left edge.
In the bare prohibitive the addressee is the understood S or A argument and the verb carries no subject index.
An object may still be indexed on the verb, as in iteki e yan ‘do not eat it’, where the directive subject is unexpressed and the third-person object is borne by the verb .
The person-marking facts thus run parallel to the affirmative imperative.
The prohibitive shares the politeness scale of the affirmative imperative.
A plain verb is the most direct command; iteki followed by yan with a plural verb stem addresses a plural or respected hearer; iteki with hani softens the directive ; ; .
Beyond the bare imperative stem, iteki takes a verb that keeps its person affix.
This is regular when a prohibited predicate is linked by no ‘without V-ing’ to a following directive, so that the prohibitive adverb scopes over a fully person-marked clause .
The no linkage ties the prohibitive to the asymmetry of negated subordinate clauses.

Takahashi shows for Tokachi that a negated temporal or manner clause selects no and blocks the successive wa, because a negated action is construed as the static state of the action not taking place .
Nakagawa gives the same conditioning from the affirmative side: no links a preceding phrase that is stative, negative in meaning, or an action verb accompanied by a negative element .
A prohibitive-headed clause is one such environment; the symmetry of main-clause negation and the subordinate asymmetry are set out in .
Ijäs formulates the classroom rule as ‘do Y without doing X’: the prohibited predicate is linked with no and the following predicate carries the positive directive .
Her further suggestion, that a wa linker would let the prohibition continue across the next predicate, is offered without a supporting Hokkaido example and is left open ‹speculative›.
Iteki feeds the same clause-final directive frames as the affirmative command.
Nakagawa lists iteki … yak pirka na, iteki … kusu ne na, iteki … p ne na, and iteki … nankor na .
Negative directive force is therefore compatible with conditional, intentive, nominalized, and modalized packaging.
The conditional element yak underlies two adjacent constructions that must be kept apart.
In the directive frame iteki … yak pirka na the conditional yak ‘if’ combines with pirka ‘be good’ to deliver a command.

The concessive yakka ‘even if’ instead builds the permission frame yakka pirka ‘it is all right even if’, and a permission is negated by the propositional somo, giving ‘you need not V’ rather than a command.
The division follows the boundary between propositional negation and negative directive force; the illustrating sentence is constructed in Ijäs’s pedagogical text .
Iteki and somo are not in complementary distribution.
Nakagawa’s iteki pasirota somo eci=ki nankor na carries both the prohibitive adverb and the propositional negator in one clause .
forms: iteki pasirota somo eci=ki nankor na

text: The prohibitive directs the addressee away from an action; the periphrastic somo ki adds clausal negation of the embedded proposition.
Each layer contributes its own value, which is why iteki cannot be reduced to an allomorph of the standard negator.
Hokkaido Ainu has a set of warning adverbs adjacent to the prohibitive: ika, ikiya, ikia(n)kunak, inkian, and the elevated ikineypeka .

They express a cautionary ‘lest, be careful not to’ value, and the verb after them takes ordinary subject person marking, which separates the construction from the bare imperative even where the discourse force approaches a prohibition.
The apprehensive warns that an unwanted event may occur; the prohibitive commands the addressee not to act.
Where iteki mokor says ‘do not sleep’, an ikiya clause with a person-marked predicate cautions against an outcome outside the addressee’s direct control .
Hokkaido Ainu builds complex sentences by chaining fully finite clauses.

Each linked predicate keeps the ordinary verbal morphology of its own clause — person indexing, polarity, plural stem choice, aspectual auxiliaries, and any clause-final evidential or nominalizer — and the link between clauses is carried by a separate post-predicate particle such as wa, hine, akusu, kor, kusu, or yakun.

There is no finite/non-finite split in the verb and no converb series: the Ainu verb does not oppose a sentence-final form to a special linking form, so a Japanese rendering in 〜て gives no warrant for a converb analysis .
The typological profile of the language states the same fact directly — Ainu has no participles, converbs, or other standard non-finite forms .
The connectives are therefore particles that join finite clauses, glossed here as conj and not as verbal suffixes.
The particle is looser than a verbal suffix in prosody as well as in structure.

Nakagawa, reporting Tamura, notes that a speaker may close the first clause with full sentence-final intonation, pause, and only then produce the connective and the clause that follows it; on this account the connective belongs to neither of the clauses it joins .
Refsing records the same delayed continuation for Shizunai, where a pause may fall between the verb expression and the conjunctionalizer .

This autonomy feeds a genuine disagreement over constituency: Nakagawa declines to posit a clause (節) unit or a main-versus-subordinate division for Ainu, holding that the apparatus cannot be carried over from Japanese or English unchanged, while Refsing and the Handbook describe the same surface domain with terms such as conjunctionalizer, adverbial-clause marker, and subordinate clause ; ; ‹contested›.
Two word-classes do the linking work, and keeping them apart resolves most of the descriptive clutter.

The post-predicate conjunctive particle (接続助詞) is bound to the predicate it closes; a clause-initial connective adverb such as orowa(no) ‘and then’ or rapok(ke) ‘meanwhile’ is free and can stack after a conjunctive particle.

Refsing makes this the organizing cut of her chapter, between bound conjunctionalizers and free conjunctions; Nakagawa keeps only the particles as a 助詞 class and folds the free connectives into the adverb phrase ; .
Several of the particles are segmentally identical to material from other classes, and the grammar resolves the clash by word-class and position rather than by form.

Wa is the sequential linker, the ablative case particle, and a sentence-final emphatic; kor is a linker and the transitive verb ‘have’; kusu is a causal/purpose linker, a free ‘therefore’, and part of the intention auxiliary kusu ne; no is a linker and the adverb-forming suffix -no ; .

Nakagawa organizes the Saru-based conjunctive particles into seven semantic groups — temporal succession, unfolding event, condition, adversative, concession, cause/purpose, and conjecture/manner — together with a parallel-listing use .

Refsing's Shizunai grammar reaches a near-identical seven-way taxonomy, with local realignments: Shizunai uses kane for the simultaneity that Saru marks with kor, and konno for an inevitable-consequence conditional where Saru again uses kor .
The detailed treatment of each domain belongs to the chapters routed below; this chapter sets out the system and the boundaries between them.
Whole-corpus word-form counts confirm that these items carry the descriptive load, with the homonym caveat kept in view.

In the aligned Hokkaido corpus wa (≈50,600), kor (≈29,300), and kusu (≈16,000) are among the commonest words, but those totals fold in the ablative and final-particle wa, the verb kor ‘have’, and the future kusu ne, and so overstate the connective.
The cleaner items, where few homonyms intrude, still show the shape of the system ‹corpus-suggested›:
The inventory spans a continuum rather than a clean coordinate/subordinate dichotomy.

At one edge, hine enumerates events in temporal order and takes no stance on how they are related; at the other, the complementizing uses of sekor, kuni, kunak, yak, and kusu place an entire clause under a verb of speech, thought, or command .

Most linkage falls between the poles: the medial clause stays finite and keeps its own argument indexes while the chain is read as one larger episode, the configuration that the coordination–subordination typology of treats as cosubordination.
Wa binds more tightly.
In Tamura's characterization, as transmitted by Nakagawa, wa gathers two situations into one coherent event; Nakagawa divides its readings into result-state, manner or method, and cause-and-effect .

Satō gives the same three-way description and supplies the diagnostic that separates Ainu wa from a same-subject converb: the two clauses it joins may have different subjects, which a Japanese 〜て clause cannot .
Akusu and awa sit at a third point: a realized first event is followed by a discovered, witnessed, or newly unfolding second one, with the causal connection left open.
Nakagawa treats the two as semantically equivalent and conditioned by register and dialect — Saru prose favours akusu, Saru verse and several other varieties favour awa .
Satō describes the domain as factual condition and ties awa to oral literature .

Hokkaido Ainu tracks participants across a chain through the obligatory person indexes on each finite verb and through discourse expectation; it has no same-subject/different-subject converb morphology .
The connectives carry only statistical tendencies.

Refsing finds that the predicates joined by wa share a subject in about ninety percent of her Shizunai material, yet Satō shows the preference is not a constraint, since wa tolerates different subjects ; .
The result is a same-subject-preferring chainer with no dedicated morphology.
The no/wa choice is derived from the first predicate rather than from coreference.
Nakagawa and Satō tie no to the aspect and polarity of that predicate: stative predicates and negated action predicates take no, with the high-frequency reading ‘without doing X’ under negation ; .

Ijäs offers the learner's heuristic that no marks a same-subject negated clause and wa a different-subject one; that framing is hers, and the primary grammars condition the choice on polarity and aspect, not on subject identity ‹contested›
The nearest approach to a switch-reference device is discourse-structural.

The Handbook's descriptive grammar reports that the sequence of a perfective a auxiliary and a connective such as korka, wa, or connective p tends to fall where the scene, topic, or actor of a narrative changes, the perfective marking a situation as completed and cut off from the present ‹speculative›.
The exact author and page of that passage have not been confirmed against the print edition, and the device is a clause-chaining boundary marker, not grammaticalized switch-reference.

Whether the sequential connectives hine and akusu encode subject continuity in a switch-reference-like opposition or instead encode discourse (un)expectedness is the central open question of the domain ‹contested›; it is adjudicated against a corpus count of subject continuity in , and the reference-tracking toolkit as a whole is drawn together in .
The conditional system is organized by realis status and, distinctively, by the sentence type of the matrix clause.

Satō's dedicated study finds that Ainu conditionals are mood-constrained but do not privilege the epistemic mood the way Japanese conditionals do: the language has no conditional restricted to truth-judgement, yet it has conditionals that require an imperative or interrogative matrix .

Yakun is the broadest member, attested with declarative, interrogative, imperative, and volitional or conjectural matrices, and so it bears most of the translator's load across Japanese レバ, タラ, and ナラ ; .

Yak attaches to law-like or warning premises and clusters with an evaluative pirka ‘good’ or wen ‘bad’; ciki and conditional kor are the mood-bound members, ciki introducing a premise for a command or question and kor the general-causation conditional that elsewhere requires a wh-interrogative matrix ; .
Concession and counter-expectation sit alongside the conditionals.

Yakka ‘even if, even though’ states that the matrix holds whatever the event of the marked clause, and in the frames yakka pirka / yakka wen it grants or withholds permission; korka ‘but’, transparently plus , marks counter-expectation ; .
Ijäs banks the same set for the learner, and her listing construction illustrates the concessive cleanly:
Cause and purpose are centred on kusu.
Plain kusu gives the purpose of the following event, especially with motion verbs, or its reason; wa kusu and hi kusu are reason-only forms that present the first event as actual ; ; .
The same segmental material enters the intention auxiliary kusu ne, the copula taking no person index, so the detail chapter separates clause-linking kusu from future and intention syntax .
Conjunctive particles attach outside the clause-final evidential frame.

A clause may close on a nominalizer-plus-copula evidential such as ruwe ne or hawe ne and then take a linker, giving attested orders ruwe ne akusu, hawe ne yakun, and hawe ne kusu; the evidential sits above clause-internal aspect but below the connective, so kusu ne ruwe ne is well formed while *ruwe ne kusu ne is not .
The general order for a linked clause is thus predicate – evidential – connective.
The inferential value is treated in and the system as a whole in .
Satō notes one cross-linguistically marked interaction at this seam: akusu can follow a ruwe ne tail, where the Japanese factual と/たら rejects a preceding のだ .
Several connectives are formal nouns pressed into linking service, and the same set runs a grammaticalization cline.

A formal noun can be a relative-clause head that fills an argument gap, a complement marker that nominalizes a saturated clause, or a connective that is neither subject nor object of the following clause; Nakagawa distinguishes the three by the argument structure around the marker, and places connective p, pe, and hike ‘but, and’ at the connective end of the cline .
This links clause combining to nominalization, treated in and .
Sekor is the bridge into reported speech.

In Saru and Chitose it frames a direct quote with a verb of speaking or thinking, names entities in the pattern X sekor a=ye ‘call it X’, and frames cries and mimetic sound, its history transparent in ‘say’ plus ‘while’ ; .

It is also the one connective that triggers person reassignment: a third party's quoted first person is expressed by fourth-person forms while the narrator's own quoted speech keeps the first person, the mechanism behind the fourth-person voice of oral narrative, which Bugaeva reanalyses as logophoricity ; .
The interaction belongs with and is developed in .
The inventory is dialectally uneven, with Saru and Chitose the best-described baseline in Nakagawa and Satō and Shizunai a full reference grammar in Refsing.
Shizunai realigns two cells: kane marks the simultaneity that Saru assigns to kor, and konno the conditional/consequential function ; .
Tek is the clearest micro-debate.
It is not a connective in Saru or Chitose, where it is an auxiliary, yet in most other dialects it links clauses with an ‘immediately upon X’ sense.

Nakagawa's synthesis is geographical: western dialects near Saru carry the short-duration restriction, while eastern descriptions dispute whether short duration belongs to the meaning at all, and one analysis makes its core function parallel listing ‹contested›.

A related open question is whether the bare verb-plus-verb sequences of Tokachi, Ishikari, and Shiranuka — where Saru requires an intervening connective — constitute a serial verb construction ‹contested›.
Sakhalin supplies a contrast at the edge of the system, where sa kusu covers the continuation and result-state range that Hokkaido splits between kor and wa, rather than marking cause or purpose .

The foundational descriptive source for the whole domain, Tamura's Saru study of the connective particles, could be reached only through Nakagawa and Refsing; the classic characterization of wa as fusing two events into one, and the formulation that the connective belongs to neither clause, both rest on that intermediated witness ‹speculative›.
The Handbook's claims on negation asymmetry and on the perfective a scene-switch device await verification against the print edition ‹speculative›.

The quantitative base is also thin: the available corpus figures are homonym-mixed word-form counts, and the per-function rates that would settle how often connective wa differs from the ablative, or how far hine and akusu correlate with subject continuity, belong to and ‹corpus-suggested›.
The particle is the most versatile and most frequent of Hokkaido Ainu's conjunctive particles.
Its core function, in Tamura's formulation as transmitted by Nakagawa, is to gather two events E1 and E2 into one coherent action and present them as a single sentence-unit .
Where hine merely lists events in temporal order, wa asserts a closer bond: the first event supplies the result-state, the manner, or the cause that licenses the second.

The three semantic readings share the surface form and overlap in natural speech; the context, the verb's aktionsart, and the presence of reinforcing adverbs (such as the sequence-marker orowa(no)) determine which reading is primary in any given clause pair ; .
The system as a whole is laid out in ; the present chapter treats wa and its culminative companion ayne specifically.
Satō identifies three uses of wa: sequential continuation (often reinforced by orowa 'and then'), cause-to-effect (reinforced by kusu 'therefore'), and attendant circumstance or manner .

Nakagawa adds a unifying temporal criterion: the first VP must be at its result-state stage — the action has concluded and that result-state frames E2 — rather than ongoing (simultaneity, kor) or stative-negated (absence of change, no) .
The minimal triad comes from Nakagawa's analysis of the Saru particle system ; for kor and no see .

Nakagawa also notes that the result-state account alone does not predict every wa collocation: the fixed phrase apkas wa arpa 'walk-and-go' shows wa marking walking as the route or method of going, even though the walking partly overlaps the going.
Tamura's integration criterion (via Nakagawa) accommodates this under a "state/method/reason" cluster that subsumes all three readings .
