In Refsing's Shizunai material, approximately ninety percent of the clause pairs joined by wa share a subject .
The preference reflects the particle's integration semantics: if E1 is the manner or prior stage of E2, the same actor typically performs both.
Yet the preference is not a syntactic rule.

Satō shows that the two clauses joined by wa may have different subjects — unlike Japanese 〜て, which requires coreference — and that fact bears on its analysis as a conjunctive particle rather than a same-subject converb ; .
Reference tracking across a wa chain rests on the obligatory person indices that each finite verb carries independently.

The statistical same-subject preference, combined with the absence of a formal constraint, places wa in the configuration that the cosubordination typology of describes — finite clause-chaining without converb morphology and without a grammaticalized same/different-subject opposition.
The comparison with hine and akusu, and the broader question of whether any Hokkaido particle encodes subject continuity in a switch-reference-like way, belong to .
Hokkaido Ainu prose narrative strings several wa-linked clauses into a single chain.
Each medial predicate closes on its own person indexing followed by wa, before the chain continues to the next step.
The result presents a process as an integrated sequence of stages:
The free connective adverb orowa(no) 'and then, from there after' can follow a wa-marked clause to make the sequential boundary more prominent ; .
This stacking — connective particle before, connective adverb after — is one of the clearest diagnostics separating the two word classes.
The treatment of orowa(no) as a discourse boundary marker belongs to .
The particle closes a stretch of sustained effort and points to the eventual outcome.
Where wa integrates events step by step, ayne marks the endpoint of a duration — a process that went on and finally yielded a result ; .
Refsing notes a nuance of impatient delay ('and then at last') absent from the neutral chainer hine .

The most characteristic environment is the intensifier pattern V a V a ayne, in which the perfective auxiliary a reduplicates the verb to signal repeated iteration before the particle closes the stretch:
The particle easir 'only then, at that point' frequently follows ayne to mark the delay before the outcome ; .

The pattern wa…wa…ayne is common in narrative: a run of wa-chained steps leads up to a final ayne that marks the point of resolution, as in the manner example above (corpokke a=eapkas wa arpa=an ayne).
The etymology is transparent: durative auxiliary a plus the neutral chainer hine, grammaticalized into a separate particle (Chiri 1936; Tamura, via ).
Tokachi uses ahinne (occasionally ainne), and some Tokachi varieties such as Honbetsu lack the form altogether, distributing its function across hine and wa .
With a negated preceding clause, ayne shifts to a 'before having V-ed' reading (negated-protraction), attested in Chitose .
Wa is the conjunctive particle most recruited as the pivot of Ainu's periphrastic aspect constructions .

The result-state reading extends naturally into a family of analytic forms in which the result-state of a closed event is overlaid by an existential or auxiliary verb, yielding a resultative, a terminative, a prospective, an attemptive, or a benefactive nuance.
Nakagawa's §15 (pp. 452–455) lists the principal forms; the full aspectual analysis belongs to .

The resultative wa an — where the preceding verb closes on its result-state and the existential an predicates that state as ongoing — produces a modifier-head construction interpretable as a resultative relative clause:
The terminative wa isam foregrounds completion rather than persistence:

In all these constructions wa is the conjunctive particle, the same item that links finite clauses in the sequential reading; the boundary with the connective use is syntactic (an auxiliary follows immediately and predicates only aspect) rather than formal.
The perfective auxiliary a that often precedes wa in scene-switch positions adds a further layer, completing the situation before the chain continues; that interaction is treated in .
When wa immediately follows a stem ending in -n or -m, the initial w- assimilates to the preceding nasal and the particle surfaces as [ma].
Refsing documents the alternation for Shizunai , and Nakagawa writes the allomorph phonetically in his transcriptions: the resultative an wa an appears as an ma an .

The pattern is phonological and pan-dialectal at the segment level ‹corpus-confirmed›: the standard romanized orthography retains wa throughout to represent the underlying form, while katakana transcription writes マ in the relevant environment, reflecting the surface pronunciation (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024; ).
The same assimilation applies before any stem ending in a nasal, including an 'be/exist', oman 'go (honorific)', and verbs whose final syllable carries -n.
The allomorph is predictably conditioned; no separate particle ma exists alongside wa.
The form wa covers at least three distinct grammatical entries, kept apart by position and syntactic host rather than by form ; .
The connective wa always follows a finite verbal predicate and always opens a following clause; it never occurs clause-initially.
The ablative wa(no) attaches to a nominal and typically co-occurs with a spatial or temporal noun (cf.
orowa = or + wa 'from that place').
The sentence-final emphatic is isolable at the end of a complete utterance.

In natural text the three are rarely ambiguous; glossing discipline requires keeping them distinct, since the particle counts for the sequential wa are inflated by ablative and final-particle tokens in any raw word-form search ‹corpus-suggested›.
Two conjunctive particles anchor this chapter.
closes a finite clause and places it before the next in temporal order, without committing to any causal, manner, or integrative relation between the two events.
closes a realized first event and opens the clause in which a consequence is encountered or witnessed.

Both are bound, post-predicate particles — not verbal suffixes, not converbs — and both join fully finite clauses that carry their own person indexing, polarity, aspect, and any evidential tail, in the pattern established for the whole inventory in .

The typological question they raise — whether their distribution tracks same-subject versus different-subject reference in the manner of switch-reference morphology — runs through the descriptive literature on Ainu clause-linking.

The evidence supports a discourse-semantic account rather than a grammaticalized subject-tracking one: neither particle carries a same-subject or different-subject feature, and the observed correlations with subject continuity follow from the particles' discourse-semantic roles rather than from an independent reference-tracking function.
places two events in temporal sequence and takes no stance on how they are related.
Nakagawa's characterization is precise: hine "lists events in time order" without any commitment to causal, manner, or purpose connection .

The bond is therefore looser than , which fuses two acts into one coherent event — presenting the first as the method, result-state, or cause of the second — and looser than , which signals a discovered or witnessed consequence ; ; .
In Saru and Chitose prose, hine is the dominant chainer for the stock opening that establishes the narrator's household before the story begins.
The formula … an hine oka=an — one or more existence clauses strung together and closed by the plural existential 'we lived on' — recurs with minimal variation across the genre.
The pattern is so regular that Refsing identifies hine as more frequent in folk tales than in colloquial speech :
Corpus texts show the same frame pivoting into the episode proper via the formula oka=an pe ne hike 'and we lived on, and …', where the formal-noun connective opens the narrative event:
The particle derives from the nominalizer plus the copula : hi + ne > hine (Tamura 1972b: 158, via ; Kindaichi 1960: 193, via ).
The source material is reached here through intermediaries; the etymology is reported, not independently verified.
It aligns with a wider pattern in which nominalization-plus-copula material grammaticalizes into clause-linkers, visible also in the evidential system (see ).
Phonologically, word-initial h is regularly dropped in normal-speed speech, and the resulting vowel i fuses with a preceding final consonant: ek hine 'came-and' → [ekine]; a=ne hine → [aneine].
Ishikari, where initial h is generally absent, writes the form ine.
In rapid speech the vowel itself may elide to bare [ne] ; .
Dialect distribution is uneven.
Tokachi uses hinne (e.g.
Honbetsu) and hine in alternation; Shiranuka and Kushiro write ine; Honbetsu lacks both forms entirely, the chaining function falling to other resources.
In Shiranuka, frequency is lower than wa and tek combined .

The whole-corpus count of approximately 14,368 tokens — the highest-frequency temporal-sequence particle with few competing homonyms — is a usable signal of the particle's prominence, with the usual caveat that Hokkaido and Sakhalin varieties are not separated in the aggregated count ‹corpus-suggested›.
and belong to Nakagawa's group-② 'unfolding event' (事態の展開) connectives, alongside and .

Their core function is to present a completed first event followed by a second event that comes to the participant's attention — "the anterior event actually happened, and then coincidentally (偶発的に) the posterior event occurred" .
Satō classes the construction as a factual condition (事実的条件): the protasis is realized rather than hypothetical, and the apodosis reports the encountered consequence ; .
The discovery flavor of akusu — English 'whereupon', 'and then (I found/saw that)' — is not a causal claim.

Nakagawa makes this explicit: the causal connection between E1 and E2 is irrelevant to the particle; what it marks is that E2 comes to the attention of a participant after E1 is complete, whatever the causal structure may be :
Akusu attaches after a clause-final evidential tail — confirming the ordering [VP]–evidential–connective established for the system as a whole.
When the first clause closes on ruwe ne, the anterior event is presented as an established fact before the discovery linker opens the next clause:
Akusu and awa are semantically equivalent; no descriptive source establishes any difference in meaning.

Their distribution is conditioned by register and dialect: in Saru, prose texts favour akusu while verse texts heavily favour awa; Horobetsu and Ishikari use awa regardless of register; Shizunai and Tokachi use akusu .
Satō's characterization of awa as the oral-literature (口承文芸) variant aligns with the verse skew in Saru ‹consensus›:
The Horobetsu verse preference is attested directly in Chiri Yukie's kamuy yukar: the discovery linker awa closes the first clause and the narrator encounters an empty scene:

The etymology of akusu as a (perfective auxiliary) + kusu (consequential) is supported by Refsing and is consistent with the particle's semantics — a completed event (a: 'situation done and closed') from which a consequence follows (kusu) .
The second morpheme of awa has not been identified with confidence .
Shizunai uses the phonologically reduced form akus (word-final vowel devoicing and deletion) .
The Shizunai corpus shows the reduced form in a typical discovery junction — the heard sound completes the first clause, and the silence that follows is the encountered consequence:
Whole-corpus word-form counts register approximately 3,861 tokens for akusu and 2,071 for awa.
Both are among the cleaner particle counts with few homonyms, and the ratio is consistent with a mixed-register corpus containing proportionally more prose than verse ‹corpus-suggested›.
Per-function counts that would separate Hokkaido from Sakhalin are not available from the current search tools.
Switch-reference — dedicated morphological marking on clause-linkers that co-indexes subject continuity between clauses — is absent from Hokkaido Ainu.
The language has no converbs, no non-finite verb forms, and no SS/DS feature on any conjunctive particle ; .

What can be asked is whether the choice among particles statistically or semantically correlates with subject continuity, and whether any such correlation is grammaticalized or follows from the particles' discourse-semantic content.
The one quantified figure in the literature is Refsing's Shizunai count: approximately ninety per cent of the predicate pairs joined by wa share a subject .
No comparable count exists for hine or akusu in any Hokkaido variety; the quantitative base is a single informant's Shizunai material.

The ninety-per-cent figure is consistent with a preference but demonstrably not with a constraint: Satō shows that wa tolerates different-subject junctions without any change in form, as in the child-throws-stone / barrel-falls example where the thrower and the barrel are different participants — a junction Japanese 〜て cannot make .
No primary grammar states a same-subject requirement for hine, and its neutral-listing semantics entails no such restriction ; .

The simultaneity particle provides a direct test: it takes different-subject complements without restriction, as in Saru ku=horipi kor en=nukar 'she looked at me while I danced' , corroborated by an oral-literature example in Satō .
Shizunai kane "generally" takes same-subject complements but exceptions are attested .
Across the particle inventory, any same-subject preference is a graded tendency, not a binary SS/DS grammatical feature.
Ijäs offers the pedagogical heuristic that negated clauses take no when the two predicates share a subject and wa when they do not .
Nakagawa and Satō derive the no/wa choice from the aspect and polarity of the first predicate — stative and negated action predicates take no — rather than from subject identity ; .
The Ijäs framing is noted because it has entered pedagogical circulation ‹contested›; the primary descriptive sources do not support it.
Nakagawa's and Satō's analyses locate the hine / akusu contrast in event structure and narrative stance, not in subject continuity.
The neutral temporal enumerator hine naturally chains a single protagonist's sequential acts — producing a predominance of same-subject pairs without encoding subject identity.

The discovery connective akusu marks that the narrator encounters or witnesses the second event after the first is complete, a framing that often foregrounds a new or unexpected participant and thereby produces an apparent different-subject tendency.
The observed SS/DS distributions are statistical consequences of discourse function, not evidence for a grammaticalized opposition ; ‹consensus›
(for the basic semantic descriptions).
The nearest structural analogue to a switch-reference signal is discourse-organizational rather than morphological.

The Handbook's descriptive grammar notes a tendency for the sequence of the perfective auxiliary followed by a connective such as , , or the formal-noun connective to fall at transitions of scene, topic, or acting participant in narrative ‹speculative›.
The perfective marks the anterior situation as completed and cut off from the present; an adverb of time typically follows to open the new episode.
The printed location of this observation has not been confirmed against the Handbook print edition, so the claim is treated as speculative.
The device is a clause-chaining boundary convention.
No morpheme on the connective particle encodes subject identity; the signal comes from the co-occurrence of the perfective auxiliary with a particular linker at a discourse transition.
Subject identity across a chain is tracked by the obligatory person affixes on each finite predicate, the mechanism drawn together in .
The competing positions, arranged by evidence grade:
The ‹speculative› synthesis draws on what each source establishes independently.
Hine neutrally chains events along a single narrative strand — which by default is the protagonist's sequential acts — hence the same-subject predominance without a grammatical constraint.

Akusu frames the second event as encountered or discovered after the first is complete, a perspective that frequently involves a new or surprising participant and thereby shows an apparent different-subject lean.
Neither particle requires a particular subject configuration; the SS/DS distributions reflect the default narrative configuration of each connective's domain.
A corpus annotation of subject continuity across hine and akusu junctions in Saru text would supply the empirical test ‹speculative›.
Conjunctive particles attach outside the clause-final evidential frame.
The ordering [VP]–evidential–connective, established for the system as a whole in , means that akusu can follow a ruwe ne tail, yielding … ruwe ne akusu ….
The evidential sits above clause-internal aspect but below the clause-linker, so kusu ne ruwe ne is grammatical and *ruwe ne kusu ne is not .
Satō identifies a typologically notable property of this interface.

Japanese factual conditional と / たら cannot follow a preceding のだ, yet Ainu places no such constraint on the ruwe ne akusu sequence: the first event is presented as knowledge-established fact and the discovery linker then opens the encountered consequence .
The construction presents the two layers as separately stackable because they occupy distinct positions in the clausal hierarchy.

A member of the aynu-corpora Discord community corroborates both the frequency and the discourse function of this sequence. nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2024) observes that ruwe ne is associated with scene transition and summary framing in prose narrative, and that ruwe ne akusu functions as a compound of that discourse anchoring with the discovery connective ‹speculative› — corroborated by .
The observation is consistent with the evidential+linker ordering described by Nakagawa and with the ruwe ne system set out in .
The particles described above rest primarily on Saru and Chitose attestation.
Several dialect-specific details bear on the comparison.
Shizunai uses akus (the word-final vowel devoiced and deleted) for the same discovery function .
Horobetsu and Ishikari favour awa regardless of register, while prose-oriented Shizunai and Tokachi use akusu as the default .
The category is stable across the dialect continuum; phonological shape and genre weighting shift, not the underlying semantic function.
Tokachi uses hinne alongside hine for neutral chaining; Honbetsu Tokachi shows neither form.
These micro-variations caution against projecting Saru frequency data onto the dialect cluster as a whole .
The full topology of the conjunctive-particle system across Hokkaido dialects is surveyed in ; the conditional and concessive members of the system are treated in .

The foundational Saru description of the conjunctive particles, Tamura's 1972 study of the 〜して constructions (Tamura 1972b), is the primary source for nearly every claim about hine in the grammars consulted here, but it was not read directly — all attributed page numbers reach it through and ‹speculative›
(the page attributions are second-hand).

The quantitative base is thin: Refsing's ninety-per-cent same-subject count for wa in Shizunai is the only published figure; no per-function counts for hine or akusu in any Hokkaido variety exist in the accessible literature.
The whole-corpus totals — approximately 14,368 for hine, 3,861 for akusu, 2,071 for awa — are homonym-mixed, Hokkaido-and-Sakhalin combined, and carry no subject-continuity annotation.

Whether akusu junctions show measurably lower same-subject rates than hine junctions — the empirical test of the ‹speculative› synthesis — remains open and requires bespoke corpus annotation over a tagged Saru text.
The reference-tracking apparatus as a whole is drawn together in ; narrative cohesion and tail-head linkage are treated in .

The conjunctive particle joins two finite clauses in Hokkaido Ainu and carries two distinct linking readings: a simultaneous reading ('while, as, at the same time as') and a habitual/factual conditional reading ('whenever, when habitually').
The same segment is also the transitive verb 'have, possess', creating a three-way collision of forms that both Nakagawa and Ijäs flag explicitly ; .

Word-class and linear position resolve the collision: the conjunctive particle follows a finite predicate and precedes the next clause; the possession verb carries its own person-index prefixes directly (ku=kor 'I have it', a=kor huci 'one's grandmother').
As a conjunctive particle, kor belongs to the bound post-predicate class (接続助詞) inventoried in .

Whole-corpus token counts place kor at approximately 29,300 occurrences (rank 5 in the aligned Hokkaido corpus), but that figure conflates the possession verb, the simultaneous particle, and the conditional reading, so the raw total is an upper bound on any single function ‹corpus-suggested›
The simultaneous reading of kor signals that two events or states co-occur: the first predicate is ongoing while the second takes place, or both proceed together.
Nakagawa's primary gloss is Japanese 〜しながら ; Satō gives the same value for Chitose .
Among the temporal-succession connectives of Saru, kor occupies a phase-specific slot.
Nakagawa draws a three-way contrast according to the temporal phase of the first predicate :

Nakagawa notes that the phase account alone does not explain every distribution: the fixed collocation apkas wa arpa 'walk and go' resists *apkas kor arpa, suggesting that additional manner or cause semantics govern some wa collocations (Tamura 1972b: 152, via ).
The no particle and its negation distribution are treated in ; sequential wa belongs to .

The simultaneous kor carries no same-subject requirement.
Unlike Japanese 〜ながら, which requires coreferential subjects in both clauses, Ainu kor permits the two linked predicates to have different subjects.

Satō demonstrates this with an example where the speaking subjects (mother and father) are distinct from the entity that acts in the matrix clause ; Ijäs makes the same observation, citing a Tamura example where the dancer and the looker are different persons :
Reference tracking across the chain relies on the obligatory person-index prefixes on each finite predicate.
Ainu has no morphological switch-reference — no dedicated same-subject or different-subject converb morphology — as established in and examined in .

For the Shizunai cognate kane, Refsing observes a statistical tendency toward same-subject co-occurrence in her materials, with documented exceptions ; no equivalent quantitative statement has been made for Saru kor ‹corpus-suggested›.

When the simultaneous kor is followed immediately by the existential verb an (singular) or oka (plural), the combination functions as the Ainu progressive: the event of the first predicate is in progress at the time of reference.
Nakagawa gives the paradigmatic Saru form and glosses it 歩いている 'is walking' :
The progressive contrasts directly with the resultative-perfect wa an: where wa presents a result-state following completion of an action, kor an presents the action as still unfolding.
This contrast follows directly from the temporal-phase distinction in the table above.

The full distributional and frequency evidence for the kor an progressive, its contrast with wa an, and the eight-form aspectual paradigm as a whole are developed in , which draws on Satō's dedicated Chitose aspect study .
The TAM system is surveyed in .
The cognate kane an continuative of Shizunai and the related siran forms are treated in .
The second conjunctive reading of kor expresses general causation or habitual recurrence: whenever E1 obtains, E2 follows as a general truth or matter of routine.
Satō characterizes this as 一般的因果関係 ; Nakagawa glosses it 〜すると（たびに） and gives as a stock example sironuman kor cikap utar iwak 'when it gets dark the birds go home' .
The relationship is a general truth or a habitual pattern across occasions.

Satō's study of Ainu conditionals identifies a mood constraint on this reading: with a declarative matrix clause, the habitual kor expresses a general truth; for a one-off individual event it is restricted to wh-interrogative matrix clauses .
The contrast with the hypothetical conditional yakun is stark: yakun applies to one-time premises and takes any matrix mood, making it the broadest member of the system.
The full conditional paradigm, mood constraints, and Satō's cross-linguistic comparison are set out in .

The two linking functions that Saru assigns to a single kor are distributed across separate particles in other Hokkaido varieties.
Shizunai presents the clearest formal split:

In Shizunai, Refsing describes kane as the 'contemporal' conjunctionalizer — 'at the same time as' — and assigns konno to a separate 'sequential' slot covering inevitable consequence, closer to what Saru expresses with the habitual conditional kor .
Nakagawa traces the Saru/Shizunai particle split to Tamura 1972b: 148 .

The reduced Horobetsu/Kushiro form ko reflects the regular reduction of word-final r attested in other Hokkaido environments (e.g.
kur 'person' → ku) and noted from 切替 2003: 313 by Nakagawa .
The Shizunai kane an continuative and its relationship to the siran family of forms are taken up in .
Two high-frequency conjunctive particles are built on kor and inherit its temporal semantics transparently.
, the adversative conjunctive particle, is formed as kor 'when' + ka 'even' = 'even when (X, nevertheless Y)' ; .
The etymology is stated consistently across Nakagawa, Satō, and Ijäs and is uncontested.
Adversative korka is treated in .

, the quotative complementizer, is analysed as se 'say, make a sound' + kor 'while' = 'while saying / while making the sound of …', with the simultaneous value of kor still transparent in the etymology ; .
Community analysis corroborates this parsing as an asserted, well-grounded etymology (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024 ).

A further community-proposed analysis holds that sekor is a specifically Saru innovation and that the pan-dialectal ari/ani represents the older form — a hypothesis put forward by nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2024 ) ‹contested›; the primary grammars read for this chapter do not settle the dialectal priority question.
The framing function, person-switch mechanism, and dialect distribution of sekor are developed in .
Hokkaido Ainu marks hypothetical, temporal, and concessive relationships between clauses through post-predicate particles attached after the full finite predicate of the antecedent clause.

Each linked predicate is fully finite — it carries its own person indexing, polarity, aspect, and any clause-final evidential — and the particle follows, belonging to neither of the two clauses it joins ; .

The principal members of the conditional–concessive subsystem are: yakun (hypothetical conditional), and yakne (evaluative and oral-literary conditionals), ciki / cik (mood-restricted conditional), kor in its conditional use (habitual or temporal), yakka (concessive and permissive), and korka (adversative).
Two dimensions organize the system: the realis status of the antecedent clause, and the sentence type the particle requires or permits in the matrix clause.

Satō's dedicated study of Chitose conditional expressions finds that Ainu conditionals impose no restriction tied to epistemic-judgement mood, yet they do impose restrictions linked to directive and interrogative illocution — a distributional pattern not predicted by hierarchies of conditionality derived from Japanese .

These particles are conjunctive particles (接続助詞) in Nakagawa's classification: post-predicate, bound forms distinct from the free connective adverbs such as orowa 'and then' and rapokke 'meanwhile', which can stack after them .
The architecture of the whole clause-linking inventory is set out in ; cause and purpose particles are treated in , and the complementizer uses of kuni, yak, and kusu in indirect speech belong to .

Yakun is the broadest and most frequent of the conditional particles, attested in Saru and Chitose with declarative, imperative, interrogative, and conjectural matrix clauses alike; Satō's study finds no mood restriction on it ; .
Its semantic scope covers the hypothetical one-off conditional: the protasis states a premise and the matrix presents its consequence.
Japanese distributes comparable functions across three conditional forms (レバ, タラ, ナラ); Ainu lays them largely on yakun, so a Japanese rendering must disambiguate by context .
The etymology is transparent: conditional plus the allative/attributive postposition , a segmentation reported for Shizunai by Refsing and supported by morpheme decomposition .

The particle can also head a sentence independently, with the anaphoric reading 'in that case, then', a free-standing use that marks its partial grammaticalization beyond the strictly bound conditional ; .

Refsing notes a 'when'-nuance in Shizunai realis contexts, where yakun attaches after an event already in progress or completed, yielding something closer to 'when X happened, Y followed' ‹corpus-suggested›.
The protasis of a yakun conditional may carry its own evidential tail before the particle, since the verified ordering is [VP] – evidential – connective.
The sequence hawe ne yakun 'if (it is said that) X' presents the protasis as reported hearsay before conditionalizing it; ruwe ne yakun presents it as established fact .
The interface with the evidential system is discussed in the final section of this chapter.
Where yakun handles one-off hypotheticals, yak marks a habitual or law-like premise whose consequence the speaker evaluates.
Its hallmark is a strong tendency to be followed by the evaluative predicates or , or by a directive expression; it carries a warning nuance when the evaluation is negative ; ; .

The idiomatic frame yak pirka 'it would be good if one did X' functions as mild advice or prescription ('one should X'); its negative counterpart yak wen 'it would be bad if one did X' conveys prohibition or warning ('one must not X') .
Both frames can be reinforced by anak / anakne, easir 'only then', or tasi .
These obligation frames differ from the permissive frames yakka pirka / yakka wen built on the concessive particle, treated below.

In the Ishikari dialect the sequence yak easir (conditional yak plus easir 'only then') extends the evaluative conditional into an explicit obligation construction — 'it is only fitting if one does X' — moving from evaluation toward necessity ‹contested›; the analysis is proposed in community discussion and awaits corroboration from a primary grammar of Ishikari (nukopoli, 2026).

Yakne functions similarly to yak but is associated with prayer and oral-literary register; yakne pirka is extremely rare and the form appears mainly in the fixed phrase wa ne yakne (sequential wa plus copula ne plus conditional yakne), concentrated in kamuy yukar and prayer texts .

Ciki (Shizunai, Samani, and Tokachi cik) presents a premise for which the speaker issues a command or asks a question; the particle consequently requires an imperative or interrogative matrix clause and is ill-formed with a declarative ; ; .
This places ciki at the opposite end of the mood-freedom scale from yakun.
The stock formula opening instructions and demonstrations illustrates the imperative use:

Refsing characterizes Shizunai cik as carrying an assumption: the speaker takes the protasis to be true or imminent and issues a directive or question on that basis, distinguishing it from the purely hypothetical yakun .

In the Horobetsu and Chitose dialects, ciki overlaps in use with the sequential-discovery particle akusu — it can mark factual discovery ('did X, and then found Y') — a temporal reading absent from the mood-restricted Saru form ‹contested›.
The etymology of ciki is not settled by the primary grammars.

A community-proposed segmentation reads the particle as ci (a continuative or plural auxiliary attested in most dialects outside Saru and Chitose) plus ki 'do', making the conditional a lexicalized construction; the primary sources treat the form as an unanalyzed particle ‹contested›
(nukopoli, 2024).

A diachronic connection between the conditional ciki and the homophonous adverb ciki 'now' — pointing to a grammaticalization path from 'now (if …)' toward the conditional–admonitive — is advanced in community discussion but likewise awaits support from primary sources ‹speculative›
(antitwilight, 2024).
The particle carries two distinct conjunctive uses — simultaneity ('〜しながら') and a habitual or general-causation conditional ('〜するたびに / 〜すると') — that are sometimes indistinguishable in context ; .
The simultaneity use is treated in ; the present section concerns the conditional reading.
In the conditional use, kor encodes general causation or a recurrent event: 'whenever X, Y'.
This differs from yakun (one-off hypothetical) in that the protasis describes something that holds repeatedly or as a general law.
Satō finds that conditional kor takes a declarative matrix in general-causation statements; for a one-off individual event the particle is restricted to wh-interrogative matrices .
The Shizunai equivalents are konno / koonno, and those of Horobetsu, Shiranuka, and Kushiro are ko, all serving the conditional function that Saru assigns to kor ; .

A formal-noun tail pe ne / p ne frequently closes the matrix of a kor conditional, yielding the reading 'it is the sort of thing that happens when X' and underlining the habitual or general-truth character of the pattern .
This is an instance of the nominalizer p functioning as a connective after a saturated clause; the formal-noun continuum is treated in .
Satō's study, based on Chitose data with consultant Shirasawa Nabe, produces the following typological finding: Ainu conditionals are mood-constrained but not in the way Japanese conditionals are.

Japanese conditionals tend to be organized around epistemic-judgement mood; Ainu conditionals impose no such restriction on yakun, yet they restrict ciki to imperative or interrogative matrices and restrict conditional kor to declarative (for general truths) or wh-interrogative (for individual events) .
The table below summarizes the five particles Satō compares; the factual conditionals akusu and awa are included for completeness and are treated in detail in .

Satō frames the finding against Japanese typology: Japanese has no conditional restricted to imperative or interrogative matrices, whereas Ainu has two (ciki and conditional kor); Japanese has conditionals restricted to epistemic-judgement mood, while Ainu has none.
Whether this constitutes evidence against a universal conceptual hierarchy of conditionality is an open question ‹contested›
Yakka 'even if, even though' is the concessive particle.

Corpus counts place it at roughly 7,500 tokens in the aligned Hokkaido corpus, the highest among the conditional–concessive particles and a signal of its frequency in narrative and daily speech alike .
The etymology is transparent: conditional plus scalar , literally 'even if', the same analysis given for Shizunai by Refsing .
Dialect variants yakkay (Tokachi, Shiranuka) and yakkayki (Kushiro verse) carry an emphatic or rhythmic suffix found also on korkay .
Nakagawa distinguishes two readings by the temporal orientation of the protasis.
With a future or hypothetical protasis, yakka yields a suppositional concessive: 'whatever happens with X, Y holds'.
With a past protasis the reading shifts toward adversative: 'though X occurred, Y is/was so' .

The idiomatic frames yakka pirka and yakka wen are the primary permissive and non-permissive constructions of Hokkaido Ainu.
Yakka pirka licenses an action for the addressee ('you may X'); yakka wen withholds that license ('you may not X') ; .
These differ structurally and semantically from the obligation frames yak pirka / yak wen, which prescribe or prohibit an action as a habitual norm rather than granting or denying a right.
The permissive and deontic dimensions of the conditional system connect to the broader modal apparatus in and to the imperative constructions of .

A distinct use builds a parallel-listing construction from the pattern [NP] ne yakka [NP] ne yakka …, surveying nominal alternatives under the concessive and asserting that the main clause holds regardless of which alternative obtains ('whether X or Y, both X and Y') .
Korka 'but, however' marks the matrix clause as counter to the expectation raised by the preceding clause.
Corpus frequency of roughly 3,700 tokens confirms its steady use across oral literature and modern prose .

The etymology is the same construction-type as yakka: conditional plus scalar — literally 'even when' — pointing to an original conditional reading that has shifted entirely toward counter-expectation ; .
The dialect variant korkay (Samani, Tokachi, Shiranuka, Kushiro) carries the same emphatic suffix found in yakkay .
Hikeka (Ishikari ikeka; Shiranuka and Kushiro ikekay) occupies overlapping semantic space.
Some analysts classify it under concession (譲歩) rather than adversative (逆接), but its distribution in attested texts is largely interchangeable with korka ; ‹contested›.
Etymologically it is the loose-link formal noun plus , a formation parallel to the kor + ka source of korka.
The conditional and concessive particles of this chapter attach outside the clause-final evidential frame.

The ordering [finite VP] – evidential nominalizer – connective is verified: hawe ne yakun 'if (it is reported that) X', ruwe ne akusu 'and (as established fact) Y was then discovered', and ruwe ne korka 'though X is the case' are all attested .
The evidential sits above clause-internal aspect but below the connective: kusu ne ruwe ne is well-formed while *ruwe ne kusu ne is not, confirming that the connective scopes over the evidential .
The evidential paradigm is treated in .

A cross-linguistically notable asymmetry at this seam was identified by Satō: the factual conditional akusu can follow a ruwe ne tail — the functional equivalent of Japanese のだ — whereas the Japanese factual conditional と / たら rejects a preceding のだ.

Ainu thus allows [clause — established fact — discovery-link], while Japanese does not; this difference argues that the interaction of evidentiality with clause-linking is organized differently in the two languages .

The deontic constructions built on the conditional system — yak pirka / yak wen (obligation and prohibition) and yakka pirka / yakka wen (permission and non-permission) — intersect with the modal and epistemic system of and with the imperative and prohibitive constructions of .

Among Hokkaido Ainu's conjunctive particles, kusu stands out as the only member whose primary meaning spans two semantic relations: it marks the preceding clause as either the reason or cause of the following event, or the purpose or aim toward which the following clause's action is directed.
Nakagawa assigns it, together with wa kusu and hi kusu, to group ⑥ (原因・目的, 'cause/purpose') of his seven-way semantic taxonomy of conjunctive particles .
Refsing places the same particle under her "Consequential" grouping alongside kunine and na for Shizunai .
Satō treats it in the section adjacent to korka 'but', contrasting purposive and causal readings .
The three sources agree on the central fact: the single particle kusu covers both cause and purpose, and the reading is determined by context.
Two reason-only compound particles restrict the semantic range.
Wa kusu foregrounds a completed event as the cause of the main clause; the sequential wa signals that the preceding event actually took place.
Hi kusu is the formal-noun construction hi ('the fact/time of') + kusu and similarly carries reason only ; .
The three particles and their properties are given in the table below.
The final vowel of kusu is frequently devoiced in running speech, yielding the variant kus; this is a phonological process, not a distinct lexeme.
The segmentally identical material also enters the intentive auxiliary kusu ne 'be going to; intend to' and the indirect-speech complementizer use treated in .
The inventory context for kusu is established in the clause-linkage overview.
When kusu marks purpose, the preceding clause describes the goal or aim of the action in the following clause, and the following clause is typically a motion verb.
This distributional tendency is strong and is explicitly noted by Nakagawa .
The purpose-marked clause occupies the adverbial slot of a prospective complement: the event it describes has not yet occurred at the time of the motion.
The purposive reading is available whenever the following clause describes a transition, displacement, or initiation rather than a completed past event.

For purpose complements governed by a transitive verb of thinking, saying, or wanting, the complementizer takes over the embedding role; the boundary between adverbial kusu and complementizing kuni is treated in .
A rarer purpose-adverbial, kunine (kuni + copula ne), is attested in Satō and Refsing but is less productive than plain kusu in this function ; .
The reason/cause reading of kusu treats the preceding clause as the motivation, antecedent condition, or cause of the following one.
The preceding clause typically describes a state of affairs that holds or held at the time the speaker asserts the consequent.
The following example shows kusu after a desiderative clause: the speaker's desire to pursue is the stated reason for preparing the boat.
When the cause is a realized state of affairs, the same kusu applies.
In the following example a formal-noun predicate (p ne) closes the cause clause before kusu introduces the consequence.
Refsing documents the same structure in Shizunai: kusu introducing a consequence after a stative cause clause ('yesterday since the weather was fine, the three of us strolled over the mountain') .

The cause-clause predicate type (desiderative, formal-noun, stative) does not by itself determine the choice of kusu; the cause reading is the more accessible one wherever the preceding clause describes a completed or persistent state.
A conjunctive particle attaches outside the clause-final evidential frame.
When a cause clause closes on an evidential nominalizer such as ruwe ne or hawe ne, kusu follows the evidential rather than intervening between the verb and it.
Nakagawa states the ordering for all linkers: predicate – evidential – connective .
The following attested example from Kawakami Matsuko's Saru oral narrative shows the reportative evidential haw-e ne followed directly by kusu.
The ordering constraint has a corollary for the intentive auxiliary.

When causal kusu follows a ruwe ne evidential, the string ruwe ne kusu is well formed and frequently attested; however, the intentive kusu ne requires an opposite arrangement — kusu ne ruwe ne — and is not licensed after ruwe ne, making *ruwe ne kusu ne ungrammatical .

Nukopoli characterized this as a scope hierarchy in which the intentive modal must scope outside the evidential, and the characterization is corroborated by the published account (, nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024).
The evidential system and its interaction with clause-linking material is treated in the ruwe ne chapter.
The compound wa kusu restricts the meaning to cause and reason, excluding the purpose reading.
The sequential particle wa signals that the preceding event is completed and its result-state is in force; kusu then marks that actualized event as the cause of the main clause ; .
Because the preceding event must be actualized for wa to apply, a future or hypothetical purpose clause — which by definition has not yet occurred — is incompatible with wa kusu.
The following constructed example illustrates the compound.

Satō cites an adversative frame in Chitose where wa kusu occurs inside a sentence headed by korka 'but': the speaker wanted to go to town but the addressee's arrival (e=ek wa kusu) caused the cancellation .
The construction is well represented in colloquial speech across Hokkaido.
Hi kusu is a distinct compound: the formal noun nominalizes the preceding clause ('the fact that …'), and kusu marks it as cause.
The result closely parallels plain kusu in meaning — reason only — but the formal-noun nominalizer adds a more explicit factual presupposition.
Nakagawa confirms the reason-only reading and notes that hi kusu is common in Saru and Chitose but rare and dialectally variable outside those varieties .
Refsing identifies a set of lexicalized compounds built on kusu/kus in Shizunai: nekusu 'therefore', wakusu 'so that', and the interrogative nepkus 'why' .
These frozen compounds represent the end-point of lexicalization within the same grammaticalization pathway that gives rise to the free conjunctive use described in the next section.
An ordinary conjunctive particle is bound to the predicate it closes and does not head a sentence.

Kusu is exceptional: it can appear sentence-initially as a free connective adverb meaning 'therefore; that is why' (Japanese そのために), straddling the boundary between conjunctive particle and conjunction .
This free use is noted in the clause-linkage overview; see the particle/adverb distinction.
In this position, kusu links a preceding discourse unit to the following clause as its consequence or result, functioning as a clause-level connective adverb rather than a post-predicate particle.
Refsing's lexicalized Shizunai compound nekusu 'therefore' carries the same discourse function in more grammaticalized form .

In contemporary teaching Ainu and learner speech the partially translated form sorekusu — Japanese それ 'that' plus Ainu kusu — occupies the same slot as a sentence opener meaning 'that is why; therefore' (, thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord 2025) ‹contested›.

The classical Hokkaido equivalent is the sentence-initial free kusu documented by Nakagawa, or its Shizunai counterpart nekusu; sorekusu is a revitalization-context form that integrates the Japanese demonstrative as a topic antecedent.
When kusu is followed by the copula with no person-marking affix, the combination grammaticalizes toward an auxiliary meaning 'be going to; intend to' — the intentive or prospective ; .

The absence of person marking on ne is the diagnostic: ordinary copular predicates carry person indexes, but in kusu ne the copula is a grammaticalized element of the complex, and person is already encoded on the preceding verb.
Ijäs teaches the phonologically reduced form kusne alongside the fuller kusu ne, reflecting reduction in everyday speech .
The construction's semantics spans intentionality, prospective aspect (an event about to occur), and future-oriented modality.
Nakagawa places kusu ne in the 意志・必然 (volition/necessity) section of his auxiliary inventory .

Nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2024) characterizes kusu ne as covering both intentionality and tense, analogous to English will; this is a community-proposed extension of the description that available published sources do not fully adjudicate () ‹speculative›.
The modal and deontic extensions — in particular the 'must, should' readings — are treated in , and the construction's place in the broader TAM system in .
Refsing additionally reports a Shizunai intentional construction kusu ki, where the generic verb replaces the copula .
This is a dialect-specific instantiation of the same purposive-to-intentive grammaticalization path ‹corpus-suggested›.

Several factors favour the purpose reading of bare kusu: a motion or initiation verb in the main clause, a prospective or unrealized event in the marked clause, and a goal-oriented relationship between the actor of the marked clause and the actor of the main clause.
Factors favouring the cause reading include completed or stative predicates in the marked clause, an evidential tail before kusu, and a disjoint event-time relationship between the two clauses.
Satō makes the clearest separation: he treats kusu after a formal-noun predicate as cause, and in proximity to a motion verb as purpose .
Nakagawa gives both readings under a single entry and notes the motion-verb clustering for purpose .
Ijäs, following Nakagawa, presents the gloss 'because / so / in order to' as a single continuum and identifies motion-verb clustering as the most reliable purpose-cue in text .
The polysemy itself is uncontroversial across sources; what the accessible sources do not provide is a formal-syntactic account that would predict the reading from structure alone ‹speculative›.
Within Hokkaido, the distribution of the three particles is uneven.
Hi kusu is confirmed for Saru and Chitose; Nakagawa flags it as rare and dialectally variable outside those varieties .
For Shizunai, Refsing's grammar documents kusu in all the functions described here and adds the lexicalized compounds .
The Sakhalin varieties present a typologically notable divergence.

In Sakhalin Ainu, kusu does not mark cause or purpose but instead covers the action-continuation and result-state range that Hokkaido splits between kor (simultaneous action) and wa (result-state after completion) .
The Sakhalin particle is therefore a false cognate for Hokkaido purposes: segmentally identical but functionally divergent.
This contrast is summarized in and is relevant to .

The conjunctive-particle inventory of Hokkaido Ainu (surveyed in ) contains three sets of items whose semantics cluster around manner, state, and degree rather than temporal sequence, conditionality, or causation.

This chapter treats all three: the conjunctive particle in its stative and negated-manner uses; the group ⑦ simile and evidential-inference particles , , , and ; and degree and extent clauses built around the postposition .

The chapter is bounded on two sides: the manner-adverb-deriving suffix -no that attaches to stative verb roots to form adverbs such as belongs to the word-formation domain and is treated in ; the conditional and concessive particles, though partially manner-like in their semantics, are documented in .

The conjunctive particle no occupies the same post-predicate slot as wa and hine (see ), but its distribution is conditioned by the aspectual and polar character of the clause it closes rather than by temporal semantics.
Nakagawa states the conditioning directly: no appears when the preceding predicate is either stative, expressing a persistent condition, or an action verb under negation .
Satō identifies the high-frequency pattern as the 'without doing X' reading after negation: in somo … no … constructions the choice of no over wa or kor is near-obligatory .
Refsing reports the same distributional pattern for Shizunai, where no on a stative predicate yields an adverbial-adjunct reading 'in the state of X' .
The particle no is segmentally identical to the manner-adverb suffix -no that derives adverbs from stative verb roots (see ), and the two overlap where the host is a stative property verb.

The string pirka no arpa 'went well' admits either the particle analysis — a stative-predicate clause [pirka] followed by the connective — or the suffix analysis, where pirkano 'well' is a derived adverb modifying the motion verb.

Nakagawa notes that the particle analysis is more transparent for productive negation patterns such as k=eyam no 'without hesitating', but that frozen adverbs such as poronno 'a lot' — from , which does not mean 'big-ly' in compositional terms — resist it; he concludes that a sharp line cannot be drawn between the particle and the suffix .

Ijäs presents no for the learner alongside the claim that it tends to mark a same-subject context while wa marks a different-subject one; that framing is Ijäs's own and is not supported by the primary grammars, which derive the distribution from polarity and aspect ‹contested›
That debate is adjudicated in the overview chapter.
Nakagawa places a cluster of four particles in group ⑦ of his semantic taxonomy, labelled 推量・様態 'conjecture/manner'.

All four follow a finite predicate in the standard post-predicate position, but they encode the speaker's epistemic stance toward the preceding clause — either as a comparison against something the speaker knows to be false (simile) or as an inference drawn from available evidence.

The distinction matters for translation and for analysis: pekor likens the main-clause state of affairs to a counterfactual standard, while noyne and kotom present a genuine inference the speaker holds about what is actually the case .
These particles overlap with the broader evidential system; their relation to the nominalizing evidentials is taken up in and .
Sources: ; .

The pekor cluster. Pekor and its dialectal allomorphs pokor and pokon liken the main-clause situation to the preceding clause while presupposing that the preceding clause is false or counter-to-fact from the speaker's viewpoint .

The intensified apekor (allomorphs apokon) strengthens this to utter impossibility: Nakagawa's illustration is a figure in narrative so large that two or three men stacked on one another would match the comparison, a physically impossible standard .
A segmentally related postpositional pair — nepkor / nepkon 'like (a noun)' — takes a nominal host and is distinct from the clause-final particle both in its host category and in its position .
Noyne and kotom. Where pekor introduces a counterfactual standard, noyne and kotom present what the speaker genuinely infers.

Noyne is the everyday-speech variant, attested in Saru, Chitose, Horobetsu, and Shizunai; kotom(no) carries a literary register and is commonly found with judgment verbs such as a=esanniyo 'I judged/surmised' .
Recurring collocation frames for noyne include noyne ramu / yaynu 'think that', noyne humas 'feel as if', and noyne siran 'look as if' .
Both noyne and kotom sit at the boundary of the evidential system in .

Their collocational frames — noyne siran 'look as if', noyne humas 'feel as if' — parallel the situational evidential siri ne (visible scenes) and the non-visual humi ne (sensations), but the two systems differ structurally: noyne and kotom are conjunctive particles and do not take the copula ne ‹consensus›.

Refsing's Shizunai grammar classifies pokon 'pretence' and kotom 'seeming' together as "nominalizers of appearance" in her §14.12 conjunctionalization taxonomy, and lists alongside them a "comparative" formal noun koraci .

These subclass labels are specific to Refsing's Shizunai analysis and are not foregrounded in Saru or Chitose descriptions; the extent to which koraci is productive in other Hokkaido dialects is not established in the accessible sources ‹speculative›.
The postposition heads a range of extent and degree constructions in Hokkaido Ainu.
Its core use is spatial or temporal — 'up to the house', 'until now' — but the same form extends to degree: 'to the extent/degree of X'.

Nakagawa lists pakno in the postposition inventory without assigning it a special comparative status; the degree reading follows from the general extent semantics applied to a property or state rather than a location or time point .
In the clause-linkage domain the most grammatically productive role of pakno is in comparison frames.
Bugaeva documents a prenominal relative-clause strategy in which pakno marks the standard against which a property of the head noun is measured.

Because direct relativization of a standard of comparison — the head noun filling a gap in a comparative clause — is not attested, Ainu instead embeds a degree-adjunct clause prenominally: the construction '[to whose extent no rich man exists] rich man' places the comparison standard inside the relative clause as a degree adjunct rather than gapping the standard as an argument .
The full relativization mechanism behind this construction is treated in .

Bugaeva identifies the type as an "equivalent of the standard-of-comparison relativization" — a degree-adjunct workaround rather than a grammaticalized comparative morpheme — and leaves open whether it constitutes a productive strategy or a pragmatic repair ‹corpus-suggested›
A further degree/comparison use surfaces in Satō's description of kane.

Alongside its core function as a simultaneity particle in non-Saru/Chitose dialects (see ), Satō records a reading glossed '〜ほどに' 'to the degree/extent that' — a degree-comparison value of the same form .
The extent to which this degree use is distinct from the simultaneity value, and how it distributes across dialects, is not settled in the available sources ‹speculative›.
Oral narrative in Hokkaido Ainu — both prose tales (uwepeker) and verse epics (kamuy yukar / yukar) — is built from extended chains of fully finite clauses linked by post-predicate particles.
The inventory of those particles and the structural principle of finite-clause chaining are set out in .

The present chapter focuses on the devices through which those chains produce discourse cohesion over longer stretches: the recapitulative (tail-head) repetition of a preceding verb at a chain juncture, the recapitulative formal-noun frame pe ne hike, the pattern by which the evidential ruwe ne plus a connective marks the close of a narrative episode, and the free discourse connective (no) that links sentences across episode boundaries.
The distribution of cohesion devices is genre-sensitive.
is the unmarked clause-chaining particle in prose uwepeker and is more frequent in folk tales than in colloquial speech ; .

The discovery connective characterises verse narration in Saru, while its prose counterpart dominates in uwepeker and in several eastern dialects; the distribution is treated in and the broader genre system in ; .
The table below summarises the genre and dialect profile of the main cohesion devices.
Among the conjunctive particles, is the one most characteristic of oral narrative prose.

Nakagawa identifies it as the particle of pure temporal enumeration: it lists events in sequence without taking a stance on how those events are causally or aspectually related, and it occurs heavily in the opening segments of prose tales, where the narrator sketches the circumstances of the story world .
Refsing corroborates the genre bias for Shizunai: hine is more frequent in folk tales than in everyday speech .

The looser bond of hine relative to — which integrates two acts into one coherent event — makes it the preferred chainer when the narrator wants to preserve the distinctness of each action; the structural contrast is treated in .
The stock opening of a Saru uwepeker exploits this characteristic directly.
The formula presents the narrator's family setting through a chain of bare existential predicates joined by hine, arriving at the existential =an that marks the narrative present:
The same particle sustains longer chains through the body of a narrative.
Multi-clause hine chains serve a pacing function: each clause delivers one distinct action, and the chain as a whole presents those actions as a continuous, unified segment.

The prosodic autonomy of hine — a speaker may close the preceding clause with full sentence-final intonation, pause, and only then produce the particle and the following clause — allows the narrator to control pacing: each hine juncture is a potential breathing point in the performance ; .

This prosodic flexibility, shared across the bound conjunctive particles but exploited most visibly by hine in multi-clause narrative chains, allows extended episodes to be calibrated to the speed and emphasis the narrator wants in the moment.

Tail-head linkage is the pattern in which the last predicate of one clause (the tail) is repeated as the first predicate of the following clause (the head), creating a recapitulative bridge across the juncture.
In Hokkaido Ainu oral verse the pattern concentrates at junctures, where the tail verb is resumed in the next clause either in the same form or with a complement marker such as .
The bridging connective between tail and head is awa in Saru verse, akusu in Saru prose and in several eastern dialects ; .
The following verse couplet, transmitted via Nakagawa from 金田一 (1931b), shows the pattern at its clearest:
The repetition is structural, not merely stylistic.

By re-opening the new clause with the same verb that closed the previous one, the narrator first names the action, then suspends it across the juncture to frame the unimaginable object, and finally resumes the same verb as an embedded complement under a=ramu rok 'had thought'.
The awa connective marks the whole as a discovery event: a looking that encountered something unforeseen.

This suspension effect — forcing the listener to hold the verb in suspension during the inter-clausal parenthetical and only then receive its complement — is a resource of oral poetics in Saru verse ‹corpus-suggested›.

In prose uwepeker, the same recapitulative function falls to akusu rather than awa, and the bridged predicate need not be restated verbatim: a demonstrative or anaphoric phrase may stand for the recapitulated content.

The awa / akusu register split reflects the broader genre-dialect conditioning documented in : awa is the expected discovery connective in Saru verse and dominates in 幌別 and 石狩 prose; akusu is the regular form in Saru prose, 静内, and 十勝 .
A second recapitulative device operates at the level of a whole clause chain rather than a single verb.
After a hine-chain narrates the opening circumstances, the chain frequently closes on the structure pe ne hike — the formal noun predicated by the copula followed by the connective .
The pe ne nominalizes the entire preceding chain as a fact ('it was the case that …'), and hike then pivots to the next narrative segment.
The construction packages everything narrated up to that point as settled background and opens the narrative onto the first complication of the story proper.
The formal-noun grammaticalization cline that underlies this use — relative-head → complement-marker → connective — is treated in .
The pattern recurs across Saru uwepeker openings.
The two examples below are from corpus narrations by the same Saru narrator; they share the closing pe ne hike but embed different chain lengths before it.

The recurrence of the … hine oka=an pe ne hike closure across multiple narrations by the same speaker, and its attestation for other Saru narrators, supports treating it as a formulaic frame rather than a freely variable construction.
Corpus evidence places the frame consistently at opening boundaries; it is not a device attested with the same density mid-narrative ‹corpus-suggested›.
The evidential serves a narrative cohesion function beyond its evidential semantics: in oral narration it regularly marks the close of a narrative episode before a connective opens the next one.

Dal Corso identifies ruwe ne as the default predicate of the narrative frame-text in Saru Hokkaido narrations — the form through which the narrator presents story-world propositions as established, known facts — and traces its dominance in the paradigm partly to this function .
The evidential architecture underlying that use is treated in .

Community observation from the aynu-corpora Discord corroborates and extends this picture: nukopoli notes that ruwe ne is especially frequent in folktales and legends, that it functions for scene transitions and summaries analogously to Japanese のだ, and that the sequence ruwe ne akusu is a common narrative collocation (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024; ) ‹corpus-suggested›.

This is consistent with Dal Corso's finding and with the observation by Satō that akusu can attach after a ruwe ne tail — a combination that would be anomalous in Japanese, where the factual と/たら conditionals reject a preceding のだ .

The scope ordering is fixed: the evidential sits above clause-internal aspect but below the connective, giving the narrative formula [VP] – ruwe ne – connective, where the connective can be akusu (discovery pivot), p or hike (loose or adversative link), or korka (counter-expectation) .

The Handbook's descriptive grammar reports that the sequence perfective a plus a connective such as korka, wa, or nominal p tends to fall at points where the scene, topic, or actor of a narrative changes ‹speculative›
(the chapter-and-page attribution is unconfirmed).
