The ruwe ne a p formula functions as the episode-boundary counterpart of the pe ne hike opening frame.
Where pe ne hike closes a background-setting chain and pivots forward, the ruwe ne a p / ruwe ne akusu cluster closes a completed narrative segment and marks entry into a new situation.
Both depend on the grammaticalization of formal nouns (pe, p) from relative-head through complement-marker to connective use, as described in .
Inter-sentential cohesion — the link between sentences that stand as separate prosodic and information units — is carried by free connective adverbs rather than by the bound post-predicate particles.
The most frequent in oral narrative is (no), derived from the locative noun or 'place, location' plus the ablative wa 'from', with the compositional meaning 'from there onward'.
Related forms include ora and oraun .
Ijäs notes orowa as a sequence-emphasiser that can follow wa in a compound linking phrase .

What distinguishes these free connectives from the bound particles is their syntactic freedom: they can begin a new sentence, they need no host predicate, and they can stack after a bound particle rather than replacing it.

Nakagawa draws the organizing cut between bound 接続助詞 (conjunctive particles) and free 副詞句 (connective adverb phrases), placing orowa(no), ora, and rapok(ke)(ta) 'meanwhile' in the second class ; Refsing makes the same cut for Shizunai between bound conjunctionalizers and free conjunctions .

For narrative cohesion, this syntactic freedom makes orowa(no) the appropriate device when the narrator wants to jump across a topic or scene boundary — where a bound particle like hine would imply continuity within the same participant chain — and to re-orient the listener from one starting point to a new one.

Hokkaido Ainu has no morphological switch-reference system: there are no dedicated same-subject or different-subject verb forms, and no converb series whose morphology encodes participant continuity .
Reference tracking across a clause chain therefore rests on the obligatory person indexes on each finite verb and on the statistical preferences associated with each connective.
The general treatment of this mechanism belongs in ; the points specific to narrative chains are as follows.
Within a hine-chain, the participant set established in the opening frame tends to persist across junctures.

For wa, Refsing finds that the predicates it joins share a subject in approximately ninety percent of her Shizunai material, making it a same-subject-preferring chainer without a same-subject requirement .

Hine is structurally looser — it separates events rather than integrating them as one coherent act — and within an extended narrative segment the participant set introduced at the opening tends to carry through its junctures ‹corpus-suggested›.

The person indexes on each finite verb make any departure from that continuity visible: a shift from fourth-person a= / =an to first-person ku= inside a chain signals a shift of narrated perspective, most commonly into a direct-speech quotation or a moment of vivid self-identification within the story.

Discovery connectives — awa and akusu — regularly accommodate reference changes across the junctures they bridge, since their semantics (the first event is completed and a new, often unexpected situation is encountered) naturally accompanies a shift in the narrated actor or scene.

At the macro level of episodes, the ruwe ne a p / ruwe ne akusu boundary markers identified in the preceding section tend in corpus narrative to coincide with just those points where the actor or scene changes ‹speculative›
(the chapter-and-page attribution is unconfirmed).
The interaction of the evidential system with narrative genre is pursued further in .

Reference tracking in Hokkaido Ainu discourse rests on a cluster of mechanisms that work in concert: obligatory verbal person indices, pervasive zero anaphora, the referential properties of the fourth-person form-set, the lexical class of location nouns, and constructional signals of topic continuity and scene transition.
There is no morphological switch-reference system.

The bound person indices do not encode same-subject versus different-subject across clause junctions, and the clause-linking particles carry no built-in reference-change signal; participant continuity is inferred from index identity and from discourse structure, not marked by a dedicated morpheme ; .

The formal person paradigm, the S/A/O sets, and the fourth-person cell are treated in ; the semantics of the fourth-person form-set in and ; clause-chaining and the wa/hine relationship in ; topicalization and anakne in ; logophoric narration and reported speech in .
Because every finite verb obligatorily indexes its arguments through bound person markers, an overt NP is an optional supplement to the cross-reference already present on the verb.

An NP recoverable from context is simply absent, with no pronoun in its place: "it is not necessary in Ainu for a noun phrase that is clear from the context to appear in a sentence, and such a noun phrase is not even represented by a pronoun" ; .

The result is that participant continuity across a narrative is maintained principally through the identity of the person indices across successive verbs, not through a chain of co-referring pronouns.

Even when the person indices cannot identify an argument — specifically, when a three-place (ditransitive) verb's two-affix cap leaves the theme unindexed — the verb's valency guarantees the anaphoric reading without any overt NP or pronoun.
The theme of kore 'give' is zero in the following pair of sentences; its reference to the sweet just mentioned is resolved by the verb's own argument-structure requirement :
Overt NP mention is reserved for participant (re)introduction, contrast, or a shift in discourse topic.
When an NP does appear alongside a person index, it stands in an appositional relation to that index: the index constitutes the argument; the NP specifies or highlights it ; .
The NP's position within the preverbal field is set by pragmatic prominence; argument realization and appositional NPs are treated in and .

The fourth-person form-set — intransitive subject suffix =an, transitive subject prefix a= (dialectally an= in Tokachi and Ishikari), and object prefix i= — does substantial reference-tracking work in oral narrative genres.

Its functions in this domain fall into two related types: narrating the story-world protagonist's actions (narrative first person), and marking the reported speaker's first person inside a quotation (logophoric use).
Both are documented principally for Saru and Chitose ; .

In kamuy yukar (divine verse) and uwepeker (prose tales) narrated in the first person, the protagonist-narrator who is the hero of the story uses the fourth-person set rather than the everyday first-person ku=/=an/en=.

Nakagawa analyses this as a viewpoint distinction tied to text type: the protagonist inhabits the story world and addresses it from within, and the fourth-person form signals that inner-story perspective to the audience .

Satō derives the same usage from a first-person-plural origin: the fourth-person form encompasses the narrator and any hearer who identifies with the protagonist, making it an inclusive strategy ; ‹contested›.

The tracking function is real regardless of which analysis is adopted: wherever a narrator reserves a=/=an/i= for the hero's actions and ku=/en= for her own narrating voice, the two form-sets constitute a formal contrast between two discourse roles.
A community-observed instance corroborates the formal contrast in an attested narration.

In an uwepeker told by Sadamo, the narrator alternates a= for the story-internal protagonist's speech and ku= for her own voice as the framing narrator — the two person form-sets tracking two distinct discourse roles simultaneously (thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-07-04, asserted; ) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Within a direct quotation, the reported speaker's first person is indexed by the fourth-person set rather than by ku=.
Bugaeva analyses this as a logophoric function: the form marks the participant whose speech or thought is being reported, who is not identical to the narrating speaker at the time of utterance ; .

The switch from ku= to a=/=an at a quotation boundary is therefore a reference-change signal — "speaker in quote ≠ narrating speaker" — even though it is realized through the person paradigm rather than through a quotative morpheme.
This use is attested for Saru and Chitose and is treated fully in .

The fourth person has been described as "obviative-like," and the functional analogy has substance: like an obviative, it marks a participant (the story-internal first person) as formally distinct from both the ordinary third person and the plain first person, functioning as "the other first person" in the narrative .
The analogy does not constitute a category equivalence ‹contested›.

Algonquian obviation is a grammaticalized noun-phrase category that applies systematically to any third-person participant ranked below the proximate in a referential hierarchy, independent of text type; the Ainu fourth person applies to a specific set of referential roles — the narrative protagonist, the honorific addressee, the inclusive referent, the reported speaker — without encoding a proximate/obviative hierarchy on nouns or noun phrases.
The form-set belongs to the person paradigm; its reference-tracking properties are a consequence of those referential roles, not of an independent grammaticalized tracking category.
Characterizing the fourth person as a switch-reference device is less apt still ‹contested›.
Switch-reference systems mark whether the subject of a dependent clause is co-referential with the subject of the adjacent main clause, typically by morphology on the clause-linking element.
The Ainu fourth person is marked on the finite verb itself, not on a connective; it does not encode a same-subject versus different-subject opposition across clause junctions.
The apparent reference-change at a quotation boundary follows from the logophoric function analyzed by Bugaeva , not from switch-reference morphology.
The clause-linkage chapters provide the detailed comparison: see and .
When two third-person participants share the same zero marking, the lexical class of location nouns provides a means of role assignment.
Nouns designating places or spatial relations — or 'inside/place', ka 'above', sam 'near', corpok 'below', and others — are semantically constrained to the Location argument of a predicate.
When one participant is or includes a location noun, it is unambiguously the Location role, and the other must be theme or patient.
Role is resolved without case marking or fixed word order ; .

The attested test case from Nakagawa's Handbook chapter is the contrast between saranip or oma-re 'put into the basket' (where or flags the goal) and the ambiguous saranip oma-re without it, where the basket could be either theme or goal .

Bugaeva takes the location class as evidence that argumenthood is shared between the bound person index and the coreferential NP, since only a semantically contrastive NP can bear this tracking weight .

The mechanism is a lexical resource, not a grammatical one: it operates only when one of the participants is a location noun, which leaves the common case of two ordinary-noun third-person arguments to plausibility and discourse context .
Its full treatment is in and .
A referent that is being introduced as the topic of a sustained passage, or that re-enters discourse salience after an interval, is often fronted and marked by the adverbial particle anak(ne).

The particle functions comparably to Japanese は in establishing a topic for the clauses that follow, but it is used more sparingly — it carries the weight of "as for (X), specifically" rather than neutral givenness marking, and it is not re-applied clause by clause to a topic already active in the discourse ; .

Community practice corroborates this: an established topic does not need to be re-marked; omitting anakne when the referent is clear from context is normal (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-09, asserted; ) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The attested corpus contains topicalized possessed-subject NPs of precisely this type.

In an uwepeker narrated by Kawakami Matsuko, the sentence a=kor seta anakne i=oyakke oma ka somo ki p ne kusu i=sam ta ukasuy ipe=an — 'my dog, as for it, never left my side, so it ate (together) with me' — introduces the dog as topic with anakne and then tracks it by zero anaphora and person indices through the remainder of the episode (Kawakami Matsuko, AA研アイヌ語資料, Saru [aa-irc/009#393]).
forms: a=kor seta anakne i=oyakke oma ka somo ki p ne kusu i=sam ta ukasuy ipe=an

text: The full syntax of anak(ne), including its scope, its interaction with focus particles, and its distributional limits, is treated in and .

Participant continuity within a narrative episode is sustained by clause-chaining with wa and hine: where person indices remain constant across chained clauses, a single participant is tracked through a sustained sequence.

The statistical tendency of wa toward same-subject reference — approximately 90% of wa-chained clauses in Refsing's Shizunai data share their subject — reflects a discourse-structural preference rather than a grammatical constraint; different-subject sequences with wa are attested ‹corpus-suggested›.
See .
Episode and actor changes are marked by the construction a p / a korka, comprising the perfective auxiliary a followed by the nominalizer p or the adversative particle korka.
Bugaeva describes this construction as marking "the point at which the scene, topic, or actor in the story changes," typically followed by the orienting adverb tane 'now' .
The mechanism operates at the narrative-structural level, above the clause-linkage system, and is developed in .
Ainu has no morphological switch-reference system ; .
In switch-reference languages, a clause-linking morpheme encodes whether the subject of the dependent clause is the same as or different from the subject of an adjacent clause.
No such morpheme exists in Ainu.

The clause-linking particles wa, hine, kor, and kane are linkers between finite clauses, not non-finite subordinators with an obligatory co-reference specification; and the language has no converbs — non-finite verbal forms that typically carry switch-reference morphology — in the relevant typological sense ; .

The functions that switch-reference systems serve elsewhere are distributed across the cluster of mechanisms described in this chapter: the obligatory person indices identify participants at each verb; zero anaphora propagates known referents; the fourth-person form signals the story-internal perspective and the logophoric reported-speaker; the location noun class resolves two zero-marked third-person roles; topic-fronting with anak(ne) re-establishes prominence; and the a p construction flags episode boundaries.
None of these constitutes switch-reference in the typological sense, and the differences matter for comparing Ainu with its geographically adjacent languages ‹consensus›.

Ijäs correctly describes Ainu reference tracking as a discourse-pragmatic matter without positing a switch-reference system, noting the topic particle and the person-form contrast without conflating them with morphological switch-reference .
The formal typological comparison is available in .

Hokkaido Ainu encodes information structure — topic, focus, and contrast — through a class of delimiting particles (副助詞) that adjoin to a noun phrase, postpositional phrase, or verb phrase and add meaning without changing the host's grammatical category ; ; .

The language carries no morphological case on core arguments and no topic or focus inflection on the verb; the agreement a verb shows with its arguments is governed by valency, not by whether one of those arguments has been focus- or topic-marked .

The word-order consequences of topic marking — the strong tendency for a topicalized phrase to occur clause-initially, and the patterns of left- and right-dislocation — are treated in ; the present chapter is restricted to the particles themselves and their semantic scope.
One structural property shared by all delimiting particles is that they cannot host a clause-linking suffix directly when they follow a verb phrase.
The verb phrase must first be re-verbalised by the dummy light transitive before the connective attaches (ki-support).
Fukuda's foundational treatment of the Saru particle system already identifies this as the single clearest diagnostic of the 副助詞 class ; .

The kakari-musubi emphatic concord particles (ta, tasi, tap) and the focus-concord sentence-final particles that pair with them are treated in ; the nominalization-based focus construction (…p ne, …hi ne) is in .
and mark the 提題 ('topic-raising') function: a phrase is singled out as the current topic of talk and implicitly set in contrast to other possible topics .
Nakagawa and Satō agree that the two forms carry no difference in meaning: "whether anak and anakne differ at all is an open question" ; .
The particle follows its host immediately.
Three attachment sites are documented: after a bare noun phrase, after a postpositional phrase (noun + relational noun), and after a verb phrase that functions as the topic of the sentence .
Ijäs's online pedagogical grammar gives a learner-oriented account of the same functions .
The particle does not mark the grammatical role of its host.
A topicalized phrase may be the agent, the patient, or an oblique of the comment predicate, and the verb's person agreement is determined entirely by its valency, not by topic status.

This is consistent with the absence of morphological case on core arguments and with the head-marking profile of the language described in : it is the verb that tracks participants through its prefixal paradigm, and a separate topic particle does not alter that tracking.
Satō distinguishes two uses of a single form: plain topic (主題) and contrastive topic (対照) .
In contrastive use, two phrases each receive or and the comment clauses are set in explicit opposition, typically with :
A contrastive pair does not require both members to be overtly topic-marked.

requires a referent that the hearer can already be assumed to know .

Satō illustrates with a pointing context: a demonstrative like toan pe 'that thing' is situationally identifiable but is being raised as a topic for the first time, so is blocked even though the referent is visible.
The constraint is sharper than Japanese 「は」, which permits 'あれは何だ?' in the same situation; Ainu does not allow the equivalent construction ; .

A participant already mentioned or recoverable from context can freely be topic-marked; given that Hokkaido Ainu regularly omits core arguments when they are contextually recoverable (see ), signals that the referent is being made the active topic in contrast to something else, not merely that it is recoverable.
Nakagawa notes that is used considerably less than Japanese 「は」: a word-for-word substitution of 「は」 with produces unnatural Ainu sentences .
The particle carries something of the weight of '〜というものに関しては' ('as for the thing that is X'), marking a topic that is actively contrasted with alternatives.
Once a topic has been established in discourse, it need not be re-marked on subsequent clauses within the same topic chain.

This assessment is corroborated by community linguistic discussion: the particle is reserved for contexts where singling-out or contrast is genuinely intended, and omitting it when topic continuity is clear from context is the natural choice (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-11-09; ) ‹corpus-suggested›.
A delimiting particle cannot attach to a person-agreement prefix.
Those prefixes are bound indexes that form a morphological unit with the stem; they are not free words and cannot host a postposition or particle.
Topicalizing a first- or second-person participant therefore requires the free independent pronoun (, , etc.) as the syntactic host .
The construct *ku= anakne or *en= anakne, where the particle would attach to a bare prefix, is ungrammatical :
The same constraint applies to all persons.

Etymologically, derives from an-yak — the existential verb an plus the conditional/contrastive particle — as recorded in the Saru dictionary (corroborated by nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2023-12-08; ) ‹speculative›.

The corresponding Sakhalin forms have been proposed as neyke or neanpe (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-12-27; ) ‹speculative›; the correspondence remains to be established through systematic comparative work.
marks the exclusion of all alternatives: the domain of the focus contains one item and nothing else ; ; .

The particle has a high degree of autonomy: it may attach to a noun phrase, an adverb phrase, or a verb phrase (with ki-support before any following connective), and it can carry its own accent and appear without a following clause.
Tamura (via ) places at the boundary between adverb and delimiting particle for this reason.
Two near-synonyms with different morphosyntactic behaviour are documented for parts of Hokkaido.

(possessed form ), restricted to western Hokkaido (Horobetsu, Saru, Chitose), is more noun-like than : after a verb phrase it requires ne-support (the copula, not ki), it has a possessed-form variant, and it cannot follow an adverb phrase — properties that place it between noun, 名助詞, and 副助詞 ; .
(eastern variant ) denotes the minimal threshold: 'at least, even just this much'.
Its use is restricted to contexts where the speaker demands realisation of a minimum requirement or embeds it in a negation; it does not appear with already-accomplished events ; .
poka is the western form; pokay is found at Samani, Tokachi, Shiranuka, and Asahikawa .
A community observation notes that traditional Hokkaido Ainu texts favour ani patek (instrumental + ) while modern community usage shows increased patek ani.

The order reversal may reflect the influence of Japanese 「だけ」, which derives from a grammaticalized noun and can appear as a free NP before に; cannot function as a noun headword, so the rising frequency of patek ani is interpreted as contact-induced reanalysis (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-12-16; ) ‹contested›.
The core point — that does not nominalize — is consistent with Nakagawa's and Fukuda's analyses ; .
(southeastern Hokkaido variant ) adds the host to a contextually established set and carries a scalar or contrary-to-expectation force: 'also, even, and — perhaps surprisingly' ; ; .

Fukuda formulates its Saru semantics as 'beyond or contrary to expectation' , and Satō illustrates with examples carrying emotional weight: 'even a dog won't eat it'; 'even two or three young men came' .
This distinguishes from the plain additive (§ below).
In negative clauses, reinforces the negation with a scalar 'not even' reading.

The combination of an indefinite pro-form with produces an indefinite or negative-polarity series: nep ka 'something / anything', nen ka 'someone / anyone', ney ta ka 'somewhere / anywhere'; under negation these shift to 'nothing / no-one / nowhere' ; .

In a paired construction X hem Y hem 'both X and Y', each member carries and the reading is symmetrical addition ; .
The particle is attested only in Saru and Chitose; elsewhere plain juxtaposition or, in Tokachi and Kushiro, the coordinator serves the same function.

A repeated hene … hene presents two or more members as mutually interchangeable options, as in nisatta hene oyasim hene 'tomorrow or the day after' ; ; .
Hokkaido Ainu has no morphological focus affix and no dedicated cleft particle.
The work of marking focus, asserting propositions, and identifying referents falls to the same nominalization-plus-copula architecture that underlies the evidential system.
A finite clause is nominalized by a light formal noun — p/pe, hi, or one of the four evidential heads ruwe, hawe, siri, humi — and the result is predicated with the copula ne ; .

The copula predicates the nominalized proposition as an asserted or identified fact, and the choice of formal noun and of the post-nominal predicate (ne, an, or bare) encodes illocutionary force — declarative, content question, or polar question (§5 below).

This chapter treats the information-structural function of three overlapping constructions: (a) the p/pe and hi nominalization cleft, which throws assertive or identificational focus onto a participant or proposition; (b) the naming cleft sekor a=ye p/hawe/katu ne, which identifies or labels a referent; and (c) the evidential frame as an assertion-focus device, with cross-references to the evidential chapters.
Focus particles (, ) and the kakari-musubi emphatic concord are surveyed in §7 with a pointer to , where their full treatment appears.
The structural mechanics of p/hi as nominalizers are in and ; the copula is treated in .
The minimal frame is a person-marked VP followed by the nominalizer (after a vowel) or (after a consonant), and then the copula .

The nominalizer has the arity of a formal noun (−1 on Nakagawa's arity scale), so it saturates a gap left by one participant in the embedded clause — producing a relative-clause reading ('the one who …', 'the thing that …') — or nominalizes a whole saturated clause — producing a complement reading ('the fact that …') ; .
When the result is predicated with ne, the copular sentence frames the nominalized content as an assertable fact and throws focus onto either the predicate nominal or the proposition as a whole .
Ijäs's lesson on adnominal clauses presents the same pre-head gap strategy without treating the copular focus function explicitly .
The arity principle that distinguishes relative-clause from complement uses is stated precisely only in and , and is the lens through which the focus function is understood here.
Two focus readings arise depending on whether a participant gap remains in the embedded VP.

In the argument-focus reading the nominalizer heads a relative clause: the embedded VP lacks one of its required participants, and the focused element — supplied as the predicate nominal of the copula — identifies that participant.
A minimal constructed illustration:

In the predicate-focus reading the embedded VP is fully saturated — the fourth person a= indexes the generic agent — and the nominalizer nominalizes the whole proposition; the predicate nominal then supplies a property or category asserted of the nominalized event:
The abstract nominalizer works in the same slot but is more abstract: Satō glosses it as 'こと / の / 時' and notes that it "has almost no concrete meaning and nominalizes the whole clause" .
The distinction between p/pe and hi is one of concreteness: p/pe identifies a person, thing, or event; hi identifies a fact, time, or circumstance.
Both combine with ne for declarative force and with an for content-question force (§5).
When the topical item is itself a nominalized clause, the topic particle can mark it, producing a construction that combines topic and focus in a single sentence.
Satō's example of contrastive anak illustrates this interaction:
The naming cleft identifies a referent by the name or label applied to it.
Its standard formula is [label] sekor a=ye [formal-noun] ne, 'the [word/fact] of calling [something] [label] is'.

The quotative complementizer introduces the quoted name (see ), and a formal noun — most commonly p/pe, or the voice-noun hawe 'word of', or the manner-noun katu 'way of calling' — nominalizes the whole sekor a=ye clause.
The copula ne then predicates it:

The variant with p produces the most common naming formula — [name] sekor a=ye p ne — which the community has discussed for its valency structure: the nominalizer p here is analysed as zero-valent (not filling an object slot in a=ye), because the transitive verb ye (+2) is already saturated by the fourth-person agent a= (−1) and the implicit zero third-person object (−1), leaving p to nominalize the whole proposition rather than fill a participant gap (nukopoli, 2024-11-09) ‹contested›.
This analysis aligns with Nakagawa's arity account: the embedded clause is saturated (arity 0), so p functions as a complement nominalizer rather than a relative-clause head .
The logophoric narration that pervades yukar oral literature produces naming-cleft structures in contexts where the fourth-person a= references the narrator voicing a protagonist (see and ).
In such passages sekor a=ye p ne and its variant with hawe are a stock device for supplying proper names and category labels within the narrative .

Whether [VP] p/hi ne should be called a cleft, a pseudocleft, or a nominal predication depends on two analytical choices that remain unresolved in the literature: the structural status of the copula ne, and the source-language content of "cleft" as a cross-linguistic category.
The nominal-predication position, implicit in Nakagawa's arity account, treats [VP] p ne as a copular sentence with the nominalized NP [VP] p as one argument and the predicate nominal as the other.
Nothing biclausal is required; the embedded VP is a finite clause that happens to be nominalized, and ne is the ordinary copula .

On this reading the construction is formally parallel to any other copular sentence — 'the thing one eats is fish' is no different in type from 'this thing is a fish' — and calling it a cleft imports a typological category from languages with a structurally distinct cleft construction.

The biclausal cleft position holds that the embedded clause bears the full person and TAM marking of a main clause, and the copula is a full predicate verb; the resulting structure is therefore biclausal — a main copular clause whose subject is a nominalized subordinate clause.
This is the reading Shibatani adopts when he calls -p(e) and -i "nominationalizers" and treats the construction as "appositive nominalization" .

The embedded clause retains full finiteness (person marking, number-sensitive verb choice, aspect, negation), which Bugaeva treats as the defining typological feature of Ainu nominalization: because there is no finite/non-finite morphological contrast, every embedded VP looks like a main clause, and nominalization is always formally overt, never zero .
Neither analysis settles whether these are "true" clefts in the narrow sense of a bi-clausal structure with an empty-headed relative clause as one component.

In many typological frameworks a cleft requires a relativized pivot; in [VP] p ne the nominalizer p may head a relative clause (when the embedded VP is unsaturated) or a complement clause (when it is saturated).
On Nakagawa's arity principle, the choice is grammatically determined case by case, so some tokens of the surface pattern are structurally clefts and others are nominal predications ‹contested›.
Satō's diagnostic — a nominalizer nominalizes a complete clause; a formal noun heads a relative clause with a recoverable antecedent — attempts to sort the cases but concedes the boundary is blurry .

Whether or not the label "cleft" applies, the IS function is consistent: the copular frame [nominalized-clause] ne focuses the predicate nominal and foregrounds the nominalized content as a recoverable, asserted fact ‹consensus›.
The debate over the structural label does not affect the description of that function.
The copula ne and the question of its verbal status are treated in ; the analysis of the embedded clause's finiteness and constituency bears on the unresolved questions there.
The tightest structural fact about the formal-noun system is that the copula slot following the formal noun determines the illocutionary type of the whole clause.
Satō and Nakagawa document a four-way paradigm shared by all formal nouns ; :

Satō's motivation for the three-way split is precise: the declarative ne predicates the subject's nature or identity; the content-question an asserts that the described entity exists while its nature is the open question; and when even existence is at issue, the copula drops entirely for the polar question .
The content-question frame obligatorily uses the existential an: the frame *ruwe ne with a wh-word in the same clause is ill-formed; the wh-word forces the switch to an.
This is a rare case in Ainu where the choice of formal-noun copula is not freely pragmatic but grammatically determined by the presence of an interrogative pro-form (see ).

The same paradigm extends to p/pe: a content question uses p an (with a wh-word) and the polar question uses bare p or pe, while pe ne ya? with the question final particle ya is also attested for content questions .
The full range of interrogative strategies, including the polar-question particle and its interaction with the bare formal-noun frame, is in .

The four evidential formal nouns ruwe, hawe, siri, and humi build exactly the same nominalization-plus-copula frame, and they carry a corresponding IS contribution: they frame the embedded proposition as established, speaker-endorsed fact.
Nakagawa explicitly treats these formal nouns as complementizers of the same type as p/hi .
The IS function of each evidential frame differs by the nature of the speaker's epistemic access.

ruwe ne, the most common and most grammaticalized of the four (comprising roughly 86% of evidential tokens in the Hokkaido corpus; ), presents the content as a known or inferred fact — 'it is the trace/fact that …' — and serves as the workhorse of narrative assertion and scene-boundary marking.

Community discussion confirms that ruwe ne does scene-shift and summary (総括) work, is particularly frequent in folktales and legends, and is used notably more by male speakers in oral literature than by female (nukopoli, 2024-11-09) ‹corpus-suggested›.
Hirosawa connects this to its information-structural role as a marker of discourse-new content within the speaker's territory of information .

The full semantics, the male-register skew (a register fact of the evidential system, distinct from the gendered sentence-final particles treated in ; compare ), and the interaction with mirativity are described in the evidential chapters: , , , , .

One cross-cutting point that bears on this chapter: the ordering constraint that places the evidential frame below connectives and final particles (kusu ne ruwe ne ✓, *ruwe ne kusu ne ✗) is a syntactic reflex of the same nominalization architecture — the evidential NP is itself an argument position in the clause-linkage hierarchy, not a free adjunct.
Community discussion confirms this ordering (nukopoli, 2024-11-09) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

Hokkaido Ainu marks delimiting and scalar focus with a class of adverbial particles (副助詞) that add interpretive nuance to a following verb phrase, noun, or adverb without changing its grammatical category ; ; .
The core focus particles — , , — are described with their full distributional and discourse properties in .
The present section notes only the points where they interact with the nominalization-based focus system.
patek 'only/nothing but' marks exhaustive focus.
It attaches after a VP with the support of dummy ki 'do' to re-verbalize the construction for downstream connectives ; .

The community notes that patek is an adverb and cannot itself be nominalized as 'the only one of —' (unlike Japanese だけ, which derives from a noun); the rising modern pattern patek ani instead of traditional ani patek is attributed to Japanese-contact influence (nukopoli, 2024-12-16) ‹contested›.

Closer to a grammaticalized focus-concord is the kakari-musubi (係り結び) system first identified by Chiri and described for Saru by Fukuda : a small set of emphatic particles concords with a specific sentence-final particle at the clause end.
Nakagawa and Satō document the two productive Saru pairings ; :
The closing particle is optional in Saru — "not necessarily present" — which complicates calling this a true productive focus-concord on the model of Japanese kakari-musubi.
Whether the HA system constitutes a grammaticalized construction or a set of frozen collocations is open ; ‹contested›.

Satō also documents a more specialized kakari-musubi-like construction in which the concept-form nouns ru 'trace', hum 'sound', sir 'appearance', or haw 'voice' precede the emphatic particle konna/kan, and the clause ends with a verb in the suffix -natara, -atki, or -rototke .

This construction is restricted to oral literature and its grammatical status is unclear; the nouns before konna appear in their concept form (ru, not ruwe), unlike their use as evidential formal nouns, a distribution that Satō flags as unexplained ‹contested›.
Hokkaido Ainu has one rigid clause-level constraint: the verb phrase — together with any evidential — comes last, and all other elements precede it .
Within the preverbal domain, however, the relative sequence of nominal and adverbial phrases is not grammatically fixed.

Because grammatical roles are indexed on the verb by obligatory person affixes (see ), and overt NPs stand in an appositional relation to those affixes rather than filling assigned slots (see ), the preverbal domain is available for information structure to impose its own ordering — independently of the S/A/O distinctions encoded morphologically.
Several distinct operations occupy this space.
Topical elements tend to appear at the left edge of the preverbal sequence, most visibly when marked by the topic particle .
A contrastively stressed indirect object may be fronted and receive an allative postposition it would otherwise lack.
An adverbial complex can appear in any order relative to the NPs around it.

And a third-person NP can be placed after the verb and re-predicated by the light verb — a right-dislocation strategy that Bugaeva connects to processing and to the disambiguating function that verb-initial order performs in other head-marking languages .
This chapter describes those positional operations and the discourse conditions that license each.
The topic-particle system — anak(ne), the additive-focus particle , and the exclusive-focus adverb — is treated in full in ; cleft and nominalization-based focus constructions belong to .

Argument ellipsis proper — the conditions under which a recoverable NP is simply omitted — is covered in and ; what this chapter addresses is how ellipsis conditions the use (and non-use) of fronting and dislocation.
The most consistently stated pragmatic generalization in the literature on Ainu word order is that topical NPs tend to come first .

Nakagawa frames the same observation structurally: rather than a subject-before-object preference, the preverbal sequence is organized by information status, so that the element made topic by anak(ne) or ka tends to occupy the initial position .

His Chitose paradigm — the same ditransitive event narrated with the three arguments of in three different orders — makes the point directly: the order shifts with the topic-marking, and order alone cannot determine which argument is agent or recipient (Nakagawa 2024: 363, exx.700–702; see ).
Three corpus examples from different narrators and registers show the range of what can be fronted:
All three share the positional structure — topic + anak(ne) at the left edge — but the fronted constituent varies: a possessed noun phrase, a relative-clause head, and a bare lexical noun.
The register likewise varies: oral narrative, a modern written newsletter, and a generic statement in the same newsletter.

The anak(ne) particle itself appears in different clause types and carries a pragmatic weight closer to Japanese '～に関しては (as for, regarding —)' than to the bare thematic は; once a topic is established in discourse, re-marking with anak on a continuing topic is unnecessary (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-11-09; asserted; consistent with ).
The full distributional and functional account of anak(ne) is in .

The anak form is etymologically transparent: Tamura's Saru dictionary derives it from an-yak 'if it is so / as for it being' (reported in , nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2023-12-08, asserted; after ).
This diachronic source is consistent with the particle's evidential weight and its less-grammaticalized status relative to Japanese は ‹speculative›.
Topic-initial order occurs without the overt particle when context already establishes the topic.

The particle-free pattern is indistinguishable in position from neutral order or from unmarked focus preposing, and in practice it is the particle that signals topicalization as distinct from simple preverbal adjacency to the verb.
Left-fronting is available to focused constituents as well as to topics.

Refsing observes that an indirect object, normally embedded among the preverbal NPs without any postpositional marking, "may, when stressed, be moved to the beginning of the sentence and marked with an allative case postposition" (§13.4.3, Shizunai data).

The allative marking is the diagnostic: core arguments are never flagged by a case postposition in neutral order, so when one appears on a fronted IO it signals a positional operation driven by focus or contrast, not by grammatical role ‹contested›.
This pattern is phonologically and semantically driven — it signals narrow focus on the indirect-object referent.
Content-question words, by contrast, remain in situ: they occupy the same preverbal position as the corresponding non-question constituent, and "questions do not involve any distinctive word order" .
No wh-movement applies.
The interrogative system — including the question particles ya and ya an and the content-question pro-forms (hunna 'who', hemanta 'what', hunak 'where') — is treated in .
In the majority of cases, focus is conveyed in situ through the focus particle ka 'also/even/indeed' or the exclusive adverb patek 'only', rather than by a positional operation.
When a cleft or pseudocleft construction is used to identify a focus referent, the nominalization-based apparatus described in is employed; this chapter does not treat those constructions.

The mirror image of topic-initial order is a pattern documented by Bugaeva in which the predicate comes first and the disambiguating subject or object NP appears after the verb, re-predicated by the light verb .

Bugaeva analyses this as right-dislocation: a discourse or processing device that "mimics the verb-initial strategy of establishing relations at the outset" even in a verb-final language, allowing the hearer to know the event-type before the participant-identities are supplied.

The following passage from a Chitose narrative has the predicate phrase he=tuk-pa pa 'they all grew (plural, perfective)' before the two subject NPs, which are then introduced as afterthoughts via the ki construction:

Bugaeva connects this pattern typologically to Nichols's observation that head-marking languages, in which relations are established on the verb rather than on NPs, have the greatest freedom to put the verb first — "establishing relations at the outset" — and that this is the functional pay-off of verb-initial order in many head-marking families .

Verb-final Ainu achieves a structurally parallel effect through right-dislocation: the event is predicated and the argument-tracking indices are on the verb; the NP appears afterward as a lexical specification that allows the hearer to recover participant identity .

The pattern is attested but not quantified: only two examples are documented in the sources consulted (Bugaeva 2022 ch.1, exx.18–19), both from Chitose narrative texts, so its frequency and range are open ‹corpus-suggested›.

No right-dislocation marker has grammaticalized; the ki that closes the afterthought is the ordinary light verb 'do', and the construction has no dedicated morphological signature distinct from any other ki-predicated clause.
Its identification as right-dislocation rests on the discourse position of the NP relative to the preceding predicate.
The fourth-person affixes are central to what makes right-dislocation functional in Ainu narration.

Third-person arguments carry a zero index — no morphological trace of their identity — and it is precisely this zero-marking that motivates the afterthought: the hearer cannot identify the participant from the affix and so the lexical NP is supplied after the fact.
See for the agent-defocusing and narrator-tracking functions of the fourth person, and for the broader discourse role of the a=/=an forms in oral narrative.
Time adverbs, manner adverbs, and postpositional adjunct phrases are all preverbal in Hokkaido Ainu, but their order within the preverbal domain is unconstrained.

Nakagawa's sentence template allows zero to any number of adverbials (副詞句 0…x) in any order relative to one another and relative to the argument NPs (名詞句 0…n), with the only requirement being that all precede the verb phrase .
Refsing states the same freedom empirically: her grammar does not account for adjunct order because she found it "very free" (§2.4).
Negators and likewise precede the verb as adverbs; they occupy no fixed structural slot beyond the general Adv–V requirement .
One specific pair of adverbial forms illustrates how adjunct order can be sensitive to contact-induced change.
In traditional Ainu texts the complex ani patek '(INS) only' — the instrumental postposition ani following its nominal complement and followed by the exclusive adverb patek — is the normal sequence.
Modern speakers show roughly equal frequency of the reverse order patek ani.

The reversal is attributed to Japanese influence: patek is an adverb and cannot be nominalised as Japanese 丈/だけ can, so the Japanese-modelled patek ani sequence imports a word-order pattern that is category-inappropriate for the Ainu form (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-12-16; proposed) ‹contested›.
The positional operations described above are not alternatives to one another but alternatives to argument ellipsis.

An argument NP that is fully recoverable from context — whether from a shared index on the verb, from the established discourse referent, or from plausibility — is simply absent: "it is not necessary in Ainu for a noun phrase that is clear from the context to appear in a sentence, and such a noun phrase is not even represented by a pronoun" .
Fronting or topic-marking therefore signals something beyond what the obligatory person indices already convey.

Typically it marks re-establishment of a topic after a scene-switch or topic-lapse, the introduction of a new referent that the hearer cannot retrieve from the index alone, or contrastive focus on a participant against an alternative set.
See for the full system of how participant continuity is maintained across clauses.
The discourse function of each operation is approximate rather than categorical:

Topic-initial with anak(ne) — marks a discourse-topic at the start of a new unit, after a gap, or when shifting from a previous topic; the particle has the weight of 'as for (X)' and is not re-applied on every subsequent mention of the same topic.

In-situ order — the default when participants are known and the predicate is the communicative center; any preverbal arrangement is grammatical as long as roles are recoverable from the indices and context.
Focus preposing with allative — reserved for the indirect object under narrow contrastive focus; the allative postposition is the marker that distinguishes this from ordinary topic-initial position.

Right-dislocation with ki — supplies a participant lexically after the predicate has committed to an event-type; attested in narrative contexts where the third-person zero index is insufficient for disambiguation.
The interaction between information structure and the nonconfigurationality question is addressed in .

The head-marking analysis of Ainu (see ; ) predicts precisely the observed pattern: because roles are encoded on the predicate, overt NPs are free to appear, be omitted, or be placed wherever information structure directs them.
The clause-chaining apparatus — wa, hine, kor — maintains participant continuity across linked clauses and thereby reduces the need for topic re-introduction within a chain (see ).
Fronting and dislocation are most active at chain boundaries and at discourse transitions, not inside the chain itself.
Hokkaido Ainu has a closed class of sentence-final particles (終助詞, hereafter SFPs) that occupy the outermost position in the finite clause.
The distributional test for the class, first systematised by , is that an SFP follows a predicate and closes the utterance: nothing may follow within the same clause ; .

This positional exclusivity distinguishes SFPs from the adverbial particles (副助詞) treated in and , which are category-preserving and do not close a clause; a 副助詞 attached to a verb phrase must be re-verbalised by the light verb ki before a clause-linker may attach, while a SFP makes that attachment impossible altogether ; .
Two frequency generalizations apply across the class.
SFPs are less frequent in Hokkaido Ainu than in Japanese: a bare finite predicate routinely ends a sentence, and SFP absence signals nothing marked ; ; .
Stacking is also restricted: only freely follows another SFP (na hani, yan hani); no other combination is freely productive ; ; .

The class encodes the speaker's illocutionary intent — command, invitation, question, assertion, admonition — and a stratum of discourse tuning that softens, reinforces, or appeals for a response from the addressee ; .
The Saru–Chitose baseline inventory is given below; dialect variants are noted where documented ; ; .
The polite imperative requires the plural verb stem even when the addressee is one person: arki yan 'please come' uses the suppletive plural stem arki, not singular ek ; .
Imperative predicates take no subject person-index; *a=arki yan is ungrammatical — the full morphological constraint is set out in .
When the stem ends in a consonant, yan reduces to an.
Ijäs's pedagogical grammar title a-eyaypakasnu ro 'let us learn [it]' illustrates the hortative in natural use (see below).
Ishikari has a distinct singular-addressee command ya — formally identical to the Q-particle but functionally opposed to it ; .
The two yas are disambiguated by the predicate type that precedes them (imperative vs. declarative) and by dialect; the Q-particle treatment is in the section on boundary cases below.
The hortative (‹TOK›
Shiranuka rok; Urakawa/Samani no) seeks the addressee's assent for a proposed joint action ; ; .
An earlier analysis held that ro is a "first-plural-inclusive command particle", a claim advanced in and repeated in .

rejects this: the particle is attested after first-singular, second-person, and third-person predicates, not only after the fourth-person (inclusive) plural; the frequent co-occurrence with the fourth person reflects the hortative meaning 'let us …', not a morphosyntactic person restriction ; ‹contested›.
Further discussion is in .
The deliberative converts a predicate into a self-addressed musing — consideration of an action for one's own benefit, not aimed at an interlocutor ; ; .
The assertive-appeal particle rouses the hearer's attention and implies a response — verbal or behavioural — is expected ; ; .
It attaches to declarative and command predicates alike and is among the most frequent SFPs in the Saru and Chitose corpus.
The softening particle adds a mild conversational tone to a declarative, serving the function Nakagawa calls 談話調整 (discourse tuning) ; ; .
It is restricted to declarative predicates: neither questions nor imperatives take it.
In answers and in-dialogue assertions, wa is particularly frequent, pulling blunt propositions toward a gentler register:
The soft-address particle conveys gentle appeal or mild affirmation and is unusual in the inventory for attaching to nouns and adverbs as well as to VPs ; ; .
The sequence an un (existential + un) serves as a polite dubitative.
In the affirmative-answer frame of the evidential tail (§evidential-frame below), un follows the formal noun directly: ku=nu ruwe un 'yes, I heard it' .
The admonitive adds gentle urging to commands and admonitions — a 'won't you; I hope you will' coloring ; ; .
Its structural property is free stacking after na or yan, yielding bipartite clusters na hani and yan hani; the latter contracts to yanani in Chitose.
hani is not restricted to imperatives, as the following shows:

Members of the Discord-based aynu-corpora community have proposed that hani derives from the motion verb hanke 'approach, come near' by grammaticalization into a command particle, parallel to the proposed path of yan from a lexical verb meaning 'come up from the water' (antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-11-18; ) ‹speculative›.

Both etymologies are plausible given the cross-linguistically common motion-verb-to-imperative cline, but neither has been established in the primary literature; the proposals are leads for diachronic work.

Three pairs in the Ainu particle inventory exhibit a concord relationship structurally parallel to Japanese 係り結び: an emphatic adverbial particle (副助詞) inside the clause licenses or requires a specific SFP at sentence end.
The 係助詞 label for the emphatic members of these pairs was introduced by (via ) and is endorsed by ; .

In Saru the concordant SFP is optional — the closing particle "is not necessarily present" — which raises the question of whether the concord is a productive grammatical constraint or a set of conventionalized collocations.
The sources consulted do not settle this ‹contested›.

identifies a structurally more opaque intensification construction in oral-literary register: a bare concept-form noun (hum 'sound', ru 'trace') followed by the particle konna/kan and a verb ending in the concord suffix -natara, -atki, or -rototke:
The formal noun / possessed-form puzzle that the konna construction poses is discussed in ; the construction is also adjacent to the kakari-musubi debate in ‹contested›.
Whether any of these three concord pairs constitute a productive focus-concord (like Japanese 係り結び) or merely a set of frozen collocations remains an open descriptive question ; ‹contested›.
The emotive particle attaches after a clausal nominalizer (p/pe or hi) and signals strong affective involvement — reminiscence, wonder, or pathos .
Its position after the nominalizer, rather than directly after the verb, makes it one of the few SFPs whose attachment site is lexically conditioned.
See for the nominalizer inventory.
The formal-register marker tapan replaces ne, an, or un after the evidential formal nouns ruwe, hawe, and siri, yielding the ございます-register frame ruwe tapan .
It is the one SFP that enters the evidential tail proper (the predicator slot of the formal noun) rather than stacking outside it.
The general clause-final ordering runs: verb stem → TAM auxiliaries → evidential tail (ruwe/hawe/siri/humi + ne/an) → SFP.
The ordering is confirmed by the grammaticality of … ruwe ne na and the ungrammaticality of *… na ruwe ne ; .
The two exceptions within this slot are un and tapan, which intrude into the evidential predicator position itself (ruwe un, ruwe tapan) rather than stacking outside it — see and .
Within the outer SFP slot, only hani freely follows another SFP .
No other combination of two SFPs is freely attested in the sources consulted; longer stacks have not been systematically studied in the Hokkaido corpus ‹corpus-suggested›.
tapan does not add to the outer SFP slot: it occupies the predicator position of the formal noun and is not a stacking particle in the same sense.

When na immediately precedes a command clause, it functions as a clause-boundary signal rather than a sentence-closing SFP: … na [command] reads 'since … / because … [do X]', where na provides the motivating ground for the instruction ; .
The following corpus instance shows na closing a declarative clause inside a direct quote, where the SFP value is foregrounded by the sekor hawean framing:
The ambiguity between the SFP and connective readings is resolved by whether a further clause follows: sentence-final na ends the utterance, while the connective na always precedes something else.
The connective function is treated fully in and .
The Q-particle / closes a polar question as a SFP ; .
The same ya (but not a) also nominalizes a clause as an embedded polar question ('whether …'), functioning as a complementizer; in that use it is not a SFP because the clause it heads is embedded ; .
The category of ya/a is therefore function-dependent: SFP in main clauses, COMP in embedded indirect questions ‹contested›
The Q-副助詞 and the Q-SFPs ya/a occupy distinct positions: he attaches to the constituent in doubt and can appear mid-clause, while ya/a are clause-final ; .
The full interrogative strategy — the polar vs. content split, wh-in-situ, and the ne/an/∅ alternation on the evidential tail — is in .
The SFP wa (soft assertive, §assertive-softening) is formally identical to the sequential clause-linker wa (CONJ 'and then, having done X') treated in .
They are distinguished by position: the linker always precedes another predicate, the SFP ends the utterance.
In many Hokkaido dialects the wa morpheme surfaces phonologically as ma (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-07-09, asserted; ).

Whether this phonological shift applies equally to both the connective and the SFP, or whether only one of the two undergoes it in a given dialect, is not documented in the sources consulted ‹speculative›.

The community discussion has also proposed a morphological analysis of newa 'and' as ne + wa (copula + sequential linker) and neya 'or' as ne + ya (copula + Q-SFP) (aomidori_cs_ and nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2023-12-12; ) ‹contested›.

If correct, the SFP ya would participate directly in the formation of a common NP-coordinator — but the analysis remains community-proposed and the morphological reanalysis of these particles has not been verified in the primary literature.

The evidential formal nouns (ruwe, hawe, siri, humi) that anchor the nominalization-plus-copula evidential construction (see and ) also host a sentence-type switch: the predicator following the formal noun — copula ne, existential an, or zero — signals declarative, content-question, or polar-question force respectively ; .

proposes that in a declarative the copula predicates the subject's nature; in a content question the existential asserts that the subject exists while its nature is questioned; in a polar question even existence is at issue, so the verb is omitted.
The un and tapan entries in the table are the two SFPs that enter this predicator slot.
The outer SFPs (na, wa, hani, …) stack outside the evidential frame: ruwe ne na is grammatical; *na ruwe ne is not .
The quotative is sometimes encountered in clause-final position of a quoted clause, preceding a speech verb (sekor hawean 'said, …').
It is not a SFP: it functions as a quotative adverb/particle (QUOT) that heads the quoted clause as an adverbial, not as a particle that closes a main clause ; .

The etymological analysis sekor < se 'make a sound' + kor 'while' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-11-09; , asserted, corroborated by Nakagawa 2024: 470) confirms its adverbial origin: it is 'saying while', not a clause-closing illocutionary marker.
The full syntactic and typological treatment of sekor is in and .
SFPs in Hokkaido Ainu are not conditioned by the speaker's biological sex.

states this explicitly: "Ainu final particles are in principle used by both sexes; there is no particle specific to men or women" — a direct contrast with Japanese, where particles are gender-indexed.
noted that the SFP wa carries a feel similar to the Tokyo-female / Hokkaido-unisex Japanese「わ」, but did not claim the Ainu particle is female-restricted.
The two descriptions converge: HA SFPs are gender-neutral ‹consensus›.
A register observation does correlate with speaker sex, but at the level of the evidential tail, not the SFP class.

Community discussion in the aynu-corpora Discord identifies ruwe ne as "used for objective fact, frequent in folktales/legends, favoured by men, like のだ, and doing scene-shift and summary work" (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-11-09; ) ‹corpus-suggested›.
This skew belongs to the evidential-nominal layer, not to the SFP layer; it does not contradict Satō's gender-neutrality claim for SFPs, which operates at a different level of the clause.
The sociolinguistic conditions behind the ruwe ne frequency pattern, and register differences in evidential and particle use across genres, are treated in and .
Mirative meaning in Hokkaido Ainu is carried by the perfective auxiliary aan/anan, not by a dedicated SFP ; .
When ruwe ne appears in surprising contexts the surprise comes from the discourse frame, not from the formal noun itself.
The mirativity–evidentiality interface is in .

The Shizunai dialect materials in contain an SFP inventory that likely includes forms not in the Saru–Chitose baseline described above; the Refsing treatment (pp.253, 265–267) was not re-read for this chapter and the Shizunai inventory has not been compiled at Fukuda's level of rigour.

Whether a form glossable as awa belongs to the Shizunai SFP inventory is one unsettled gap; the present description is limited to the Saru–Chitose core supplemented by documented dialect variants ‹speculative›.

Hokkaido Ainu marks clause-level interrogation through four intersecting mechanisms: rising intonation alone, sentence-final particles, a constituent-scoping focus-question particle, and the sentence-type alternation on the formal-noun evidential tail.
Wh-pro-forms remain in their canonical argument or adjunct position throughout — there is no wh-movement and no obligatory cleft for question formation ; .

The wh-pro-form inventory — , , , , and their dialectal alternants — is documented in ; this chapter describes the clause-level framing strategies, the interrogative particles, and the conventions for answering questions.
Two particles carry most of the segmental interrogative work.

(post-consonant allomorph ) is a true sentence-final particle that also nominalizes a clause as 'whether …' in embedded questions .

The deepest structural mechanism, however, is the alternation among the copula , the existential , and the ∅-tail on the formal nouns , , , and : the same nominal that closes a declarative as ruwe ne becomes a polar question as bare ruwe and a content question as ruwe an.
The inferential evidential and its frame alternations are treated fully in ; the full sentence-final particle inventory is in .
A pedagogical overview of question formation is in .

Strategy (a) — rising intonation without any segmental reflex — is the unmarked polar-question device ; .
It leaves no trace that would survive in written documentation; Fukuda's treatment of sentence melody carefully separates prosodic questioning from the particle system .

When a clause is nominalized by one of the four formal nouns, the predicate following the nominal determines sentence type.
Satō documents the three-way pattern for all four formal nouns , confirmed in detail by Nakagawa :

Satō proposes a structural motivation: the copula predicates the nature of the subject, so the declarative asserts what something is; the existential asserts that a situation exists while its nature remains open to the wh-word in a content question; and the bare formal noun without either predicate treats even the existence of the described state as the open question — the polar reading ‹speculative›.
The account is Satō's own working hypothesis, not a derivation shared across the sources consulted.
Nakagawa gives the content question an additional expansion: NMLZ an hi an — existential, then the formal noun , then existential again — emphasizes the facthood of the unknown element .

The alternation also disambiguates near-identical wh-clauses: hemanta an? = 'what (is there)?' versus hemanta ne? = 'what is it?' / 'why?' — the choice of vs after a wh-word marks open-existence question vs identification .
The evidential-tail system and the semantics of vs are set out in the frames section and in .

Fukuda classifies as a 副助詞 on distributional grounds: it attaches after any constituent — noun, postpositional phrase, verb, adjective, or conditional clause — and marks that constituent as the locus of uncertainty, so it may stand inside the clause rather than at the sentence boundary ; .

When it happens to fall at the clause end Fukuda notes a category straddle toward the sentence-final class ‹contested›; Nakagawa and Satō describe it functionally rather than categorially, emphasizing its constituent-scoping behaviour ; .

This etymology is consistent with the pattern but is not independently documented in the sources consulted.
Content questions retain the wh-pro-form in its canonical argument or adjunct position.
Nothing moves.
When a formal-noun tail is present, the copula is replaced by the existential , producing ruwe an / hawe an etc., or the expanded NMLZ an hi an frame ; .
Without a formal-noun tail, any of the polar-question devices — rising intonation, , or on the focal wh-element — also marks a content question.

The indefinite shapes combine with the additive particle to produce 'someone/something/somewhere' in positive contexts and 'no one/nothing/nowhere' under negation ; .

The declarative hemanta ne? = 'what is it?' / 'why?' The complementizers , , and introduce indirect-speech and indirect-question complements under transitive reporting verbs such as or ; .

These contrast with the quotative particle , which introduces direct and semi-direct speech under intransitive verbs; the transitivity split ( ⇒ intransitive reporter, ⇒ transitive reporter) is confirmed by community observation (nukopoli, 2024-11-09) ‹speculative›.
The direct/semi-direct/indirect speech continuum, person-switching in logophoric speech, and the / contrast are treated in .
Hokkaido Ainu has no grammaticalized 'yes' and 'no' particles used crosslinguistically to confirm or deny a proposition directly.
The standard response to a polar or content question repeats the relevant verb — in its positive form to confirm, or with negation to deny — and may add a reason clause .

Community documentation from across several dialects corroborates this: in most dialects outside Saru, bare affirmative or negative interjections are not used to answer a question, and the verb-repetition strategy is employed exclusively.
Saru aligns more closely with Japanese-style polarity responses.
Forms such as e, ho, and m are responses to being addressed or called, not affirmation/denial particles (nukopoli, 2024-12-04) ‹speculative›.
One attested affirmative-response frame retains the formal noun and adds the sentence-final particle :
The particle (soft assertive) also frequently closes replies, softening the declarative force of a repeated or corrective statement ; .
Neither the Q-particles nor the response particles are gender-restricted: HA has no sentence-final particle specific to men or women .

The male-register skew noted for ruwe ne in oral narrative is a property of the evidential class, not of the SFP class, and the two systems should not be conflated ‹corpus-suggested›; see for oral-register distinctions and the semantics of ruwe ne for the gendered-register side of the evidential.
The most thoroughly documented gender dimension of Hokkaido Ainu is the performance norm that distributes oral-literary genres by the sex of the traditional narrator.

Satō's table for Chitose specifies narrator sex as a genre-diagnostic parameter alongside melody, , and rhythm-tapping ; Endō's synthesis confirms the same allocation across the Hidaka–Iburi region and notes that the norm applies to both the content and the formal-poetic apparatus of each genre .
(After and .) The allocation is not symmetrically two-way.
Several genres are open to performers of either sex; the two genres allocated exclusively to men are heroic verse (yukar) and prayer (kamuy nomi).
Prayer is improvised with a personal melody and structurally distinct from the fixed, shared incantation, which any speaker may perform .

Genre norms operated as conventions, and their social character is clear from modern practice: Endō notes that modern revitalization recordings document women reciting verse yukar; the performers themselves recognized this as a departure from tradition .
The grammar and genre taxonomy of each form, including the narrator-person conventions and the sakehe refrain, are treated in , , and .
The retains the verse architecture of the standard yukar — notably the — while replacing the battle theme with marriage.
Its female protagonist holds the same superhuman capacities as the male hero of the standard epic, including , but the narrative turns on a marriage outcome .
The genre is documented for mid-Saru (沙流中流); its presence in other Hokkaido regions is not established from the sources read for this chapter ‹speculative›.

A Saru speaker's metalinguistic testimony illustrates the sakehe distinction. 川上まつ子 described the menoko yukar as a genre one properly performs with the sakehe, and noted that she was narrating one without it — treating it as an uwepeker — and that with the sakehe the performance would be long, whereas without it, short (AA研アイヌ語資料 「menokoyukar 神謡6（節なし）」, 沙流, aa-irc/019, ll. 0, 66).
This metalinguistic testimony aligns with Satō's genre-feature table : the sakehe defines the genre boundary, not the thematic content.
A speaker switching off the refrain performs the same story in a different register.
Grammatically, the menoko yukar is not differentiated from the male-narrator yukar by any morphological marker of the narrator's sex.
Both use the fourth-person narrator voice (a=/=an) and the elevated register () in the same way ; .
The narrator fourth person and its logophoric function in oral epic are described in ; the elevated register and its grammatical hallmarks in .
Two sets of thanks-expressions and accompanying gestures are sex-differentiated in traditional practice.
When receiving food or a gift, women say (lower-Saru hunna) while performing , stroking below the nose with the index finger; men perform without this interjection.
A lesser degree of gratitude uses hioy'oy; a stronger reduplicated form hinna hinna marks stronger feeling (scale: hioy'oy < hinna hinna).

Formal thanks in ceremonial contexts uses , applicable by either sex (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-26; asserted; consistent with Endō's account of gendered oral-literature performance ) ‹corpus-suggested›.

A revitalization-era speaker attests the full gesture-and-word complex in use: the palm-up hand motion accompanies the interjection, and the speaker describes it as a candidate for animated depiction:

The women's formal greeting gesture is likewise attested in the oral-literary register, where a female narrator describes performing raymik as part of the conventionalised greeting routine of oral narrative:
The greeting was traditionally a man's formula, delivered with onkami.
In the revitalization period it has come into gender-neutral use, recognized by speakers as a shift from traditional practice .
These gendered formulae belong to the broader system of deferential address that includes the honorific fourth-person forms and prayer-specific epithets for the deities, treated in and .

Whether specific sentence-final particles carry a sex-of-speaker feature in Hokkaido Ainu — a structural parallel to the Japanese feminine わ versus masculine ぞ/ぜ — cannot be answered from the sources read for this chapter.

Satō , Endō , and Nakagawa supply no systematic gender-indexed inventory of sentence-final particles for Hokkaido Ainu, and a search of the grammar literature yielded no attested sex-conditioned particle pair ‹speculative›.
For the pedagogical grammar, Ijäs likewise addresses Hokkaido speech norms without specifying gendered SFP contrasts .

Three primary sources that might bear on this question were not read for this chapter: Fukuda's (Tamura's) 1961 description of the Saru SFP system , Kindaichi's writings on elegant-language and genre-specific grammar , and Hattori's 1957 monograph on the 'special language of the older generations' (nenchōshasō tokushugo), the primary source on age- and register-conditioned lexical repertoires.
These constitute the main empirical gap.
Any future study would need to work from conversational recordings, which are sparse in the available Hokkaido documentation relative to the predominantly oral-literary aligned corpus.
The SFP inventory — , , , , and their illocutionary values — is treated without sex-of-speaker stratification in .
The evidential formal nouns that grammaticalize into sentence-final positions (ruwe, hawe) are covered in .
Age- and status-conditioned register is distinct from sex-of-speaker conditioning and is better documented.
The fourth-person affix set (a=/=an) functions as a second-person honorific in respectful address, drawing on the same forms that serve as the narrator's voice in oral epic .
Satō lists the elegant-language pronoun set — asinuma, aoka(y), eani, ecioka(y) — as drawn from the fourth-person paradigm and used in contexts of respectful address without sex-specificity .
The full treatment of these honorific-fourth-person forms is in ; their intersection with kinship-term morphology in .

Kindaichi's genre-density ranking — the density of elegant-language features increases from greetings through prayer and incantation to negotiation () and peaks in heroic verse (via ) — overlaps with the narrator-sex allocation above: prayer and heroic verse, the male-allocated genres, occupy the high-density end of the scale.

The elegant register (atomte itak) and its grammatical hallmarks — applicative case-marking by prefix rather than particle, number-agreement override, and the distinct poetic lexicon — are described in .
The register is not itself sex-indexed: a narrator of either sex performing a genre that uses atomte itak uses the same elevated morphology ‹consensus›.
The gendered-register evidence for Hokkaido Ainu stratifies by quality.

Genre allocation by narrator sex rests on genre tables, fieldwork descriptions, and native metalinguistic statements extending from early twentieth-century documentation through Satō's Chitose-based grammar and Endō's Handbook synthesis ; it is the most robustly documented layer.
The ritual speech-act differentiation (hinna/onkami) is attested in community discussion consistent with the ethnographic picture but would benefit from independent primary documentation.
Sentence-final particle gender-indexing remains open and unconfirmed ‹speculative›.
Two further documentary gaps limit what can be said.

First, Hattori 1957 on the elders' special register — the key inventory of age- and sex-conditioned non-everyday vocabulary — is not held in the project repository and was not read; Fukuda/Tamura 1961 on Saru SFPs and Kindaichi on elegant language are held but were not read for this chapter.
Second, the aligned Hokkaido corpus is overwhelmingly oral-literary and genre-coded, so conversational distribution of any potential gendered particle cannot be quantified from it directly.
Together these gaps mean that a strong claim about sex-indexed particles or a full inventory of gendered register features in Hokkaido Ainu remains beyond what the present evidence supports.
Revitalization-era usage may be leveling some traditional allocations.
The irankarapte greeting is the clearest documented case; it is possible but undocumented that other sex-specific formulae are similarly shifting ‹speculative›.
The sociolinguistic context of the revitalization is treated in the opening chapter of the grammar.
Hokkaido Ainu adverbs modify verb phrases, carry arity zero — they neither serve as predicate heads nor fill argument slots — and take no nominative person prefix ; .
The class boundary with prenominals (連体詞) turns on target: adverbs attach to the VP, prenominals to the NP, and prenominals additionally bear no person prefix of any kind .

Postpositional adverbs form a subclass that co-indexes a nominal antecedent; when that antecedent is pronominal the postpositional adverb receives an objective person prefix — a morphological signature shared with locative nouns and distinct from verbal person inflection .

Because this grammar assigns no adjective class to property-concept words — treating them as stative intransitive verbs (see ) — the adverb–verb boundary matters directly for the description of manner and degree.
A property verb such as predicates with full person marking; the deadverbal form pirka-no 'well, nicely' derived from it carries arity zero and no person affix.
Kindaichi, who did posit an adjective class, treated these same forms as adjective-derived adverbials ; in the modern analysis the derivation is uniform verb → adverb .
Nakagawa identifies five formation routes for adverbs proper, plus a distinct postpositional subclass treated below .

The five are: (i) basic/lexical adverbs (本来型); (ii) intransitive verb + the suffix ; (iii) bare intransitive conversion; (iv) transitive verb conversion; and (v) directional formations built on locative roots with pronominal prefixes and directional suffixes.
The full account of the suffix belongs to ; the present chapter surveys its output alongside the other types, then the degree and comparison systems.

Satō additionally distinguishes a demonstrative adverb subtype (指示副詞) and an interrogative subtype (疑問副詞) alongside the basic and postpositional divisions ; Nakagawa subsumes both into the basic and prenominal classes respectively .
Refsing, working on Shizunai, groups adverbs with conjunctions and interjections in a single particle category ‹contested›.
Nakagawa and Satō instead distribute conjunctive-meaning items between conjunctive particles (接続助詞) and adverbs, leaving no independent conjunction class ; .
Basic lexical adverbs form a closed set spanning temporal, degree, and modal functions.

The degree adverbs and are cross-class items: both also function as general prenominals meaning 'real, true' when preceding a noun phrase (sonno menoko 'a real woman') .

The adverb provides an instructive contrast with Japanese だけ: patterns as a pure adverb and cannot head a nominal phrase, whereas Japanese だけ is a grammaticalized noun.

Community corpus analysis records the traditional order ani patek 'with only this' in classical texts (one token against zero of the reversed patek ani), with near-equal counts of both orders in modern learner material; the reversal is attributed to nominal influence from Japanese (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024; ) ‹corpus-suggested›.
The suffix attaches to intransitive verbs — most productively to property verbs — to derive manner and degree adverbs: → pirka-no 'well, nicely'; → moyre-no 'gently, slowly'; → tunas-no 'quickly'.
The resulting forms are adverbs with arity zero and no person affix.
