The most frequently attested members of this bare-conversion pattern are , , , and .
Bare and -no forms often co-occur in the same dialect without semantic contrast; the choice may reflect prosodic context or register ‹corpus-suggested›.
Transitive verb conversion produces a third group, whose members surface mainly as postpositional adverbs (e.g., , ) and are documented in the following section .
Directional adverbs derived from locative roots are treated immediately below.

A productive series of directional adverbs is built by prefixing e- (allative) or o- (ablative) to a Type-2 locative noun root and adding the directional suffix -ne or -un; a second pattern uses he- / ho- before the root plus -asi .
In Ishikari, Tokachi, and eastern Hokkaido dialects the initial h- drops, so herepasi 'seaward' appears as erepasi .

Postpositional adverbs (後置副詞) take a nominal antecedent — typically the immediately preceding NP — and carry the objective person prefix when the antecedent is pronominal .

Two diagnostics distinguish them from case postpositions: they can stand independently at the head of a clause, and they do not require a 〈place〉-marked antecedent, unlike the locative case particles , , and .

Compare: ruyka kari 'across the bridge' (postpositional adverb with a bare noun antecedent; no 〈place〉 required) vs riyopa or peka (the perlative case particle requires the 〈place〉-marked locative noun ) .
Nakagawa divides postpositional adverbs into two formation types: a basic (本来型, 表70) and a transitive-verb-conversion type (他動詞転換型, 表71) .
The member of the basic type builds the degree clauses treated in ; of the conversion type serves as the standard-of-comparison marker (see comparison section below):
With a pronominal antecedent, the objective prefix attaches to the postpositional adverb: en=akkari 'more than me', en=sam 'beside me', un=koraci 'like us'.
The same en= / un= series that marks objects of transitive verbs appears here, confirming the objective rather than nominative slot .
With a noun antecedent the noun simply precedes without marking: seta koraci 'like a dog'.
Degree in Hokkaido Ainu is expressed through lexical degree adverbs, through property verbs themselves (which predicate directly as intransitives), and in some contexts through reduplication.
The lexical degree adverbs and precede the modified predicate exactly as manner adverbs do: sonno poro 'truly big / really large', earkinne pirka 'very beautiful' .

At the lower end of degree, — a stative property verb meaning 'be small' — is used prenominally (pon hekaci 'small child', ) and, in its adverbial bare-conversion use, as a diminutive degree modifier meaning 'a little, slightly' ‹corpus-suggested›.
Its logical counterpart in the degree domain is , which in composition and derivation conveys augmentative force; neither is a bound degree morpheme.
Reduplication of property verbs and ideophonic forms yields intensified or expressive degree readings — the patterns are analysed together with the broader reduplication system in .
The superlative degree adverb immediately precedes the modified property predicate: iyotta tanne 'the longest', iyotta pirka 'the most beautiful' .
No comparative morpheme competes for this slot, so bears the superlative function without formal ambiguity with a comparative form.
The superlative construction is amply attested in the oral corpus.

Hokkaido Ainu has no dedicated comparative morpheme — no suffix or particle whose sole function is to inflect a property predicate for comparison.

The analysis follows directly from the no-adjective-class thesis: because property-concept words are intransitive verbs, they carry no adjectival inflection and therefore no comparative inflection ; .

In Stassen's cross-linguistic survey of comparison strategies , this places Ainu in the large type that expresses comparison via a separate particle or postpositional element rather than by morphological marking on the predicate.
The primary comparison construction uses the postpositional adverb (表71 above) as the standard-of-comparison marker.
The standard NP immediately precedes ; when the standard is pronominal, the objective prefix attaches to in the usual postpositional pattern:
carries the full comparative meaning; the property verb itself (, , etc.) is unchanged from its predicative form.
Comparison is thus encoded entirely in the postpositional layer rather than in predicate morphology.
For equative comparison ('as … as'), the postpositional adverbs and (basic type, 表70) serve as the standard marker: seta koraci poro 'as big as a dog' .

The overlap between the equative 'as … as' and the manner 'like' reading of is common in languages that use manner adverbs for equative comparison, and has not been distinguished as a formal ambiguity in the sources read for this chapter ‹speculative›.
Degree and extent comparison using — yielding proportional and scalar clauses — is treated in .

Juxtaposition without an explicit standard marker also operates as a comparison strategy in discourse contexts where the contrasted entities have been introduced: two property predicates in adjacent clauses can be read as comparative without any occurrence of ‹corpus-suggested›.
Its pragmatic frequency relative to the construction has not been quantified from the sources read for this chapter.
Hokkaido Ainu has no dedicated word class of conjunctions (接続詞).
Nakagawa folds the clause-initial discourse connectives treated here into the adverb class (副詞) and concludes that no separate conjunction category is warranted .

The structural ground for this classification is the independence of these forms: they need no host predicate, impose no morphological requirement on the following clause, and can occur sentence-initially after a pause or paragraph break.
This distinguishes them from the bound post-predicate 接続助詞 (clause-linking particles) — , , , , and their relatives — which attach directly to a verbal stem and cannot stand alone.
A further diagnostic is stacking: the free connectives can follow a 接続助詞 without any intervening predicate, yielding attested sequences such as … hine, orano … 'and then, after that …' ‹consensus›.
The bound clause-linkers and the switch-reference-like behaviour of versus are treated in and ; the sequential particle as a clause-chaining device in its own right is in .

The present chapter covers only the free, clause-initial layer, grouping its members by discourse function: the sequential– temporal pair and ; the scene-shift adverb ; the anaphoric-resumptive ; the NP coordinators and ; and the demonstrative-adjacent forms and .

Its etymology is transparent: the relational-locative noun combined with the ablative source particle yields orowano 'from that place/point onwards', which has grammaticalized to a purely sequential reading.

The syncopated form orano is the most frequent in the aligned corpus (rank 114; 1,927 tokens across Hokkaido and Sakhalin data); further reductions to ora and oraun are dialectally attested ‹corpus-confirmed›.

The function of such sequences in maintaining episode cohesion is developed further in .

Both derive transparently from the locative noun extended by a locative or temporal suffix, following the same etymological pattern as from .
Their frequency in the aligned corpus is considerably lower than that of , and they appear primarily in narrative prose rather than conversation.
Nakagawa gives no dialect restriction for these forms.
is the general temporal adverb 'now'; its discourse-connective use emerges when it opens a new clause after a completed prior episode.

In this position — particularly after a clause nominalized by or after an episode-closing evidential frame — signals a shift in scene, time reference, or central participant, functioning as a narrative reset .
There is no separate discourse-particle lexeme: it is the ordinary temporal adverb 'now' that acquires connective force from its position and the completion of the preceding unit.
The corpus rank (54; 4,272 tokens) therefore conflates the temporal-adverb and scene-shift uses ‹speculative›; per-function counts would require disambiguation across individual texts.
The interaction of with the aspectual and TAM apparatus of the verb it introduces belongs to ; its role in signalling participant change across episodes is taken up in and .
is the form most distinctively positioned at the clause boundary as a cohesive device, yet it is best analysed as an anaphoric demonstrative NP rather than a pure conjunction.
Its composition is transparent: + + = 'that existing thing/fact'.

The whole form occupies nominal position, refers anaphorically to a proposition or entity just established in the prior clause, and introduces the clause that predicates something of it — yielding a resumptive-cohesive function glossed 'and as for that / and as for that (fact)' .
Its connective feel is structural (clause-boundary position + invariably anaphoric reference) rather than intrinsic to its lexical class.
Corpus rank 1,349 (84 tokens) reflects the more specialized, narrative-internal role of compared with .
The form has low homonymy — unlike or — so the count is a relatively clean estimate of its frequency ‹corpus-confirmed›.

The boundary between 'resumptive demonstrative NP' and 'discourse connective proper' is not drawn in the available sources; the form participates in both the demonstrative system () and in discourse-structural patterns that overlap with topic marking ().

Whether to treat it as a connective or as an instance of an anaphoric topic-NP in clause-initial position is a matter of descriptive standpoint rather than an empirical question the present data resolve ‹speculative›.
Two additional forms operate at the level of nominal coordination rather than at the clause boundary.
'and' joins two NPs into a single conjunctive NP and marks the first member; it does not appear after the last member of the conjunction .
A sharp regional restriction applies: the Saru and Chitose dialects use bare NP juxtaposition for nominal coordination and lack in this function .

Community discussion corroborates the restriction independently — as an explicit 'and'-coordinator is little used in modern Ainu and its distribution is dialectally conditioned (nukopoli, 2023-12-12) ‹corpus-suggested›.
A proposed morphological decomposition ne + wa — with and — has been noted in community discussion as consistent with the connective meaning 'it being so, and …' (aomidori_cs_, 2023-12-12).
This decomposition is an informal proposal unsupported by a published etymological study ‹contested›.
'and, as well as, both … and …' serves as the Tokachi/Kushiro counterpart for listing.

Unlike , which marks only the first member, can appear after each coordinated element, and it extends to verbal predicates as well as nominal ones; in western Hokkaido the same form functions as an adverb rather than a particle .

The anaphoric determiner 'that (aforementioned)' is not a connective in its own right but the demonstrative stem that underlies both (§ above) and topic-resumption constructions where an anaphoric NP headed by opens the next clause.
The demonstrative system and the proximal/distal/anaphoric paradigm are in .

Interjections (間投詞) occupy the most peripheral position in Hokkaido Ainu's part-of-speech system.
The diagnostic is syntactic: an interjection enters no grammatical relation with any other clause element and constitutes a complete utterance by itself ; .
This separates them from adverbs, which share the arity-zero slot but modify a VP, and from particles, which attach to an autonomous element.
The six-class system and its diagnostics are laid out in .
Refsing, working on Shizunai, treated interjections as a member of a single nominal macro-class together with conjunctions and adverbs, rather than as an independent class .
Nakagawa and Satō reject the lumping: adverbs and conjunctions enter syntactic relations; canonical interjections do not .

The categories do, however, grade into each other at the margin — directive words like hetak and hokure can immediately precede an imperative verb, functioning as manner adverbs, while retaining their classification as interjections in Nakagawa's analysis ‹contested›

The class is large and heavily dialect-specific: the same expressive domain may be covered by phonologically unrelated forms in different Hokkaido varieties, and many items have no straightforward equivalents across dialects .
Nakagawa organises the inventory under three functional types: response words, calls, and emotion expressions .

The following table synthesizes the forms attested in the best-documented Hokkaido varieties, drawing on Nakagawa and Tamura for Saru ; , and the pedagogical grammar of Ijäs for the broader revitalization inventory .
The two response words e and ho are distinguished by their discourse trigger: e responds to a proposition (assent), while ho responds to a direct call or address.
Both are monomorphemic and stand alone as complete utterances.
is the pan-Hokkaido greeting formula in the modern documentary record and is the form standard in revitalization pedagogy ; .

The Shizunai variety uses ikatay in the same function; community discussion reports that Asahikawa speakers use a phonologically distinct greeting not shared by southern varieties (palestine_2026, aynu-corpora Discord, 2025-09-22, asserted; ).
This strong dialect-specificity in the expressive vocabulary extends to the whole interjection class .
The morphological structure of irankarapte is not decomposed in the descriptive grammars consulted, which treat it as a frozen formula.

A community analysis proposes i=rankarap-te, applying an i=…-te causative construction to the verb rankarap 'approach, greet formally', yielding something like 'let me greet you / the act of greeting' (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-25; ) ‹contested›.
The same analysis is proposed for as i=yairayke-re from , analogous to the pattern 'the thing one ought to be grateful for' — a parallel noted there with English excited / exciting ‹contested›.
Neither proposal has been tested against corpus attestations of the component morphemes, and they are best treated as working hypotheses.
Among the thank-you forms, a pragmatic scale runs from informal to formal.

Community discussion documents the Saru hierarchy as: hioy'oy — a light acknowledgment appropriate for ordinary exchanges — is less formal than hinna (lower-stream Saru hunna), which in turn is reinforced by reduplicated hinna hinna for greater warmth, with iyayiraykere as the most formal register expression (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-26, asserted; ) ‹corpus-suggested›.

The form hinna is specifically associated with women's speech and accompanies the gesture raymik (touching the index finger beneath the nose) when receiving gifts or food; the corresponding male gesture is onkami (both hands).
The gender-register conditioning of these forms is treated in .

The affirmative response word in dialogue is typically the bare assent particle e, but the reduced formal-noun form ruwe appears in some spoken contexts as a compact affirmative response — a final-particle use of the same element that heads the inferential evidential construction.
Its relation to the full evidential predicate is treated in .
and are directive interjections urging speed or movement .
Both appear most commonly as standalone utterances, but hetak can also precede an imperative verb, where it functions as a manner adverb rather than as a pure interjection.

Old documentary sources include sequences interpretable as hetak ek 'come quickly' and hetak hosipi 'go home quickly', where hetak modifies the following imperative (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-24, proposed; ) ‹contested›.
The animal call coco — used to summon a dog — is phonologically stable across the documented Hokkaido varieties .
Its CVCV shape is shared with the reduplicative mimetics discussed in the following section, though no etymological connection is documented ‹speculative›.
A small set of nouns encodes inherent plurality or collective multiplicity through reduplication — what Kindaichi and Chiri's grammar calls 疊語法 (reduplicative word formation).
The following inventory is drawn from their survey of Hokkaido forms .
These are nouns, not adverbs or particles; they occur as arguments of the verb rather than as depictive adjuncts.

Their shared morphological character — a CVC(V) base doubled to form a disyllabic or tetrasyllabic whole — encodes the dispersed or multiple nature of the referent: twigs as opposed to a single branch, hailstones as a mass, intestines as a coiled plurality.

Kindaichi and Chiri note that some inherently-plural nouns of this kind trigger a plural verb form in the governing predicate, though the reduplicative noun itself carries no obligatory agreement marking .
The cross-chapter treatment of reduplication phonology — including the templates, base-copy processes, and their interaction with morphophonological sandhi — is in .

These lexically closed reduplicative nouns are distinct from two other reduplication phenomena in the language: verbal reduplication, which encodes iterativity or distributive plurality (see ), and pragmatic intensification by repetition of an interjection or adverb (as in hinna hinna above).
The reduplicative nouns do not extend to new bases by productive rule; they are individually listed in dictionaries rather than derived by a synchronic morphological operation ; .

Whether Hokkaido Ainu has a productive phonesthemic system — systematic associations between phonological shape and semantic value, of the kind extensively described for Japanese and Korean — cannot be established from the descriptive literature accessible for this grammar.

The reduplicative nouns show that the language uses phonological form to encode distributed plurality and collectivity, but whether the individual consonant or vowel choices within those forms carry meaning independently of the reduplication is not demonstrated by any primary source consulted ‹speculative›.

The closest approximation to size or intensity gradation in the available data is pragmatic intensification through repetition: the scale hioy'oy < hinna < hinna hinna represents gradient expressiveness through reduplication of the base form rather than through vowel or consonant substitution ‹corpus-suggested›.
The adverb inventory includes words with degree-sensitive semantics (), but no primary source analyses these as phonesthemic.

Ideophones and formulaic refrain syllables in oral poetry — the ritual repetition units of kamuy yukar and the formulaic diction of uwepeker — constitute a distinct expressive register that intersects with this chapter's topic.
Their analysis as a poetic and ritual phenomenon belongs to .
Canonical interjections integrate into discourse by standing outside clause structure entirely; they do not head a predicate, fill an argument position, or modify a noun or VP.
Mimetic words, when used depictively, can integrate at three positions.
The most common integration is the adverbial slot (arity zero): a mimetic word appears immediately before the verb it qualifies, in the same position as a common adverb.
The adverb class and its arity-zero definition are set out in .
Manner adverbs like , , and show that the preverbal modifier slot is productive for motion- and manner-qualifying expressions .
A second strategy uses the quotative postposition followed by a light verb, typically .
The construction [depictive] sekor ki predicts a depicted action or produced sound as something 'thus performed': the depictive content is quoted under sekor and then asserted through the light verb.
This is the Ainu quotative frame analysed in ; its applicability to sound-depicting content specifically rests on limited corpus evidence ‹corpus-suggested›.
The third strategy embeds an ideophonic content in the standard nominalization apparatus — under a formal noun like or — and then uses the nominalized clause as a clause argument.
This integration route is not specific to ideophones and does not mark depictive status specially; it is shared with all clause types.
The formal-noun complement system is described in .
No single Ainu term covers oral-literary activity as a whole; the domain is delimited descriptively.

The most widely adopted modern taxonomy, developed by Nakagawa and followed by , organizes oral activity into four macro-categories by communicative purpose: songs (seated upopo, dance songs rimse / horippa, lyric yaysama, lullabies), word play (kikinasi bird-cry mimicry, tongue-twisters, riddles), chants directed to gods or humans (prayer kamuy nomi itak / inonno itak, incantation, dispute-speech caranke, funeral words, greeting words), and narrative (prose tales, divine epics, heroic epics, legend).

Within the narrative category the formal parameters that differentiate genres are: presence or absence of melody; presence or absence of a refrain; rhythmic tapping () with a stick (); typical length; and narrator gender ; .

The table below gives the Chitose-based three-way split of the narrative genres and its primary formal diagnostics, which constitute the empirical baseline from which dialect variants and contested cases depart .
The table identifies the sakehe as the primary formal divide between yukar and kamuy yukar: both are sung genres with melody, but yukar carries no sakehe while kamuy yukar does.
A fourth narrative form, irupaye, presents yukar content in a prose frame with no melody or refrain; it was available to women narrators for whom verse yukar was conventionally restricted .

Two further genres stand outside the main three: upaskuma / ucaskuma (oral tradition, legend, historical lore), which makes no fixed verse or performance demands, and the coastal-Hidaka/Iburi oyna (culture-hero epic with a distinct protagonist class), treated separately below.
The grammatical consequences of the sung/prose distinction — person-marking conventions, evidential defaults, and metrical packaging — are surveyed in .
The Ainu genre vocabulary is not uniform across Hokkaido.
Terms shift across dialect areas in ways that reflect both sound change and the independent naming of genre categories by distinct communities.
The principal dialect correspondences, as documented by and , are:
Two naming collisions make this geography analytically difficult ‹contested›.

First, the term oyna covers different genres in different areas: in Tokachi and Sakhalin it functions as a synonym of kamuy yukar (a divine epic with sakehe), while in coastal Hidaka and Iburi it designates a distinct genre whose protagonist is a culture-hero (Aynurakkur / Okikurmi / Oynakamuy) and which uses no sakehe ; .
Second, the term tuytak means 'prose tale' across most of eastern Hokkaido but 'divine epic' in Samani — the same form names metrically and functionally opposite genres depending on locality .

These are not irregular synonymies; they reflect genre systems that were named independently in different dialect communities, a distribution that Nakagawa treated as a problem in dialect linguistic geography .
The classification also shifts within a single dialect tradition.

In Tamura's Saru materials, informant 平賀サダモ (Sadamo) does not use oyna as a genre label at all: the divine and culture-hero epics that Kindaichi and Kubodera classed as oyna are subsumed under yúkar in her usage ; .
This shows that even the yukar/kamuy-yukar boundary, presented as basic in the Chitose table above, is not imposed uniformly on all bearers of the Saru tradition.

provides a metalinguistic definition of yukar as a practice of imitation and transmission: "誰かが聞かせてくれた長い長い物語，それを真似て次に誰か に聞かせる，それをユカㇻと言う" ('the long story that someone told you, which you imitate and tell the next person — that is called yukar').
The same entry records the dream-transmission convention: a yukar heard in a dream (wentarap or ta a=nu yukar) must be retold at once or it is lost.

The yukar is the longest and formally most demanding of the sung genres: an epic sung to a melody that is specific to the narrator (not fixed to the story and subject to change mid-performance), stretching from a single evening to several nights .
Its defining formal features in the Saru/Chitose baseline are the absence of a sakehe refrain and the presence of rhythmic tapping with a on the hearth-rim throughout the performance .
Listeners may add a chorus call ().

The narrator is traditionally a man; women conventionally told the prose form irupaye when they wished to narrate yukar content , though modern documentation records women reciting verse yukar knowingly against that convention .

The protagonist is a parentless superhuman youth — in Saru texts canonically Poy-ya-un-pe or Pon Sinutapka-un-kur, in eastern Hokkaido Pon Otasam-un-kur — who flies, dives, travels underground, and battles without moral framing (heroes may annihilate whole villages; the worldview is entertainment, not instruction) .
The sub-genre menoko yukar ('women's heroic epic') keeps the format but replaces battle with marriage as its thematic core; female heroes wield shamanistic power (tusu) and foresight .

A speaker of the Saru dialect, 川上まつ子, recorded an explicit account of the menoko yukar genre: the genre is told with a sakehe refrain (sakekoye), but the narrator herself preferred to deliver it without the sakehe, as an uwepeker .
In eastern and central Hokkaido — Tokachi and adjacent areas — the heroic epic is named sakorpe (the eastern term for this genre; its internal morphology is debated) .

For the lexical domain of 'hero', the noun can stand alone as 'brave person / hero' in epic contexts, attested with modifiers such as kamuy rametok and sonno rametok; a further term cipapa appears in but is absent from other dictionaries and texts (gengojiro, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-02-13; ) ‹speculative›.

The Abuta dialect (Iburi, 虻田) yukar narrated by 遠島タンケ attests the same aspectual and comparative apparatus as Saru/Chitose verse narrative, including durative kor okay, resultative wa okay / wa an, and the comparative particle .
The prospective is also documented.
A striking lexical item in this text is the genre-specific verb sakehawki 'to sing / recite a yukar' — a denominal verb built on the eastern heroic-epic root .
A residual opening formula, the eyororpe, may repeat at the start of a yukar performance.

The kamuy yukar is shorter than the yukar (from a few minutes to around an hour), told mainly by women, and sung to a melody fixed per story — in contrast to the narrator-specific melody of the heroic epic .
Its protagonist is a (animal, plant, fire, water, weather, household object) narrating its own experiences in the first person.
The genre's primary formal diagnostic is the sakehe (折り返し, burden, refrain): a fixed string, typically inserted after every line or every few lines, fixed per story ; .
is the possessed form of sake; marks the refrain sense with a distinct pitch accent (sákehe) to distinguish it from the homophonous 'for the sake of —'.

Sakehe range from transparent onomatopoeia (the cuckoo-god's sakehe han kakkok kakkok imitates the bird's cry; the thunder-god's hum pakpak is the sound of rain or thunder, glossed by its narrator as humihiruy 'it's a loud sound' ) to completely opaque compounds such as the long sakehe recorded by : tunoyake renoyake kutunke kamuyke kamuy cikappo hum hum hum.

The function of the sakehe is disputed ‹contested›.
proposed that sakehe originally served as an index of the protagonist.

Against this, the marlin-tuna data above show that the same story-type can carry different sakehe in different performance areas, and that the protagonist may shift between variants (Chitose changes the fish species and replaces the sakehe).
The correspondence between story-type and sakehe is therefore not fixed, and many sakehe cannot be related to the protagonist through any recoverable semantic link .

The Ainu Shin'yōshū () — Iburi (Horobetsu) kamuy yukar compiled and translated into Japanese by 知里幸惠 (Chiri Yukie, 1903–1922) — is the canonical first published Ainu-language oral-literature collection and remains a primary grammatical resource for Iburi kamuy yukar.
Its narrator consistently uses the exclusive first-person plural prefix ci= / suffix =as as a singular hero-narrator marker, throughout every text ; .

Table-of-contents titles in the collection such as AEKIRUSHI have been morphologically reanalysed as a=e-kir-usi 'the place one has memory of' (0penke, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-03-19, after 片山龍峯 2003; ; ‹contested›) rather than the earlier parsing from ekiru 'turn back'.
The coastal-Hidaka/Iburi oyna is a distinct genre with a culture-hero protagonist (Aynurakkur, Okikurmi, Oynakamuy) and no sakehe, making it formally closer to the yukar than to the kamuy yukar ; .
It should not be conflated with the eastern use of oyna as a synonym of kamuy yukar.

The grammatical analysis of the logophoric narrator's voice (the protagonist's first-person perspective) and the evidence for classifying the narrator function as logophoric rather than indirect is in .
The prose tale — in Saru/Chitose, in most of eastern Hokkaido — uses no verse, no melody, and no sakehe.
Length is intermediate.

The narrative range runs from near-conversational to lightly elevated prose; corpus token counts give uwepeker 104 tokens and tuytak 24 tokens in the aligned Hokkaido corpus (the counts conflate metalinguistic and performance contexts).
identifies four sub-genres within the prose tradition:
Human prose tales (the default): an unnamed human protagonist narrates in the first person within a 'real event' frame, typically with a reward-virtue / punish-vice arc.
Kamuy prose tales (kamuy uwepeker): a deity narrates; the register leans toward elegant language (atomte itak), paralleling kamuy yukar in prose form.
Japanese-borrowed prose tales: Ainu-ized versions of Japanese story types, told in the third person.

Pananpe–Penanpe tales: the dyadic pair 'downstream-dweller' / 'upstream-dweller', opening with the formula pananpe an penanpe an hine … 'there were Panampe and Penampe, and …', told in the third person and recognized as a children's genre.

The standard human prose tale is bracketed by formulaic structure: an opening that establishes the protagonist's family and lifestyle ("I had father, mother, elder brother; father hunted bear and deer; we lacked nothing…") and a closing identification formula in which the first-person narrator discloses its own identity via the reportative quotative frame sekor … isoytak / ye ('so X said / told'), revealing retrospectively who the "I" was throughout .
This closure connects to the broader system of narrative reference tracking treated in .
The opening move of a Saru uwepeker shows the narrator naming the genre in the first person before the tale proper begins — the performative self-announcement that frames the prose narration:

Ucaskuma / upaskuma designates a looser genre of oral tradition, legend, and historical account; it imposes no fixed verse or performance constraints and covers knowledge about places, events, and customs passed down across generations .
The intonational profile of prose narration differs observably from conversation.

reports that uwepeker narration uses a one-directional, low-variation melodic line, contrasting with the rising contour of conversation that seeks a response; within the Saru basin, upper-Saru (mid-river) narration tends toward near-monotone, while lower-Saru shows more pitch undulation (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-11-16; ) ‹corpus-suggested›.
The full TAM and evidential patterning by genre is in .
All three principal narrative genres are told in the first person from the protagonist's viewpoint, but the person prefix used for that first person is not the everyday ku=.

In Saru and Chitose both verse and prose narrative, the protagonist is indexed by the fourth-person prefix/suffix a= / =an — the form that in conversational Ainu marks an indefinite or inclusive-plural subject or, with a second-person referent, a deferential addressee ; ; .
The full paradigm and typological analysis of this device are in , , and ; the present section notes only the genre-conditioned contrasts.

names the use of non-everyday person marking in oral literature the "indirection principle" (間接性の原理): on his hypothesis, the narrative was originally framed as a god or spirit speaking to a human inside a dream, and the non-everyday first-person signals the taboo-laden indirectness of that divine address.
The competing "shamaness-oracle-origin" account holds that the form arose from a ritual medium's stance ‹contested›.

The relationship between this narrator-perspective device and typological logophoricity is analysed by , who argue that logophoric speech constructions in Ainu are direct — not indirect — reported speech; the consequences for the genre-narration system are pursued in .
Region and genre interact on the person marking.
In Iburi (Horobetsu) kamuy yukar — the tradition documented in — the hero-narrator consistently uses the exclusive first-person plural forms ci= / =as as a singular narrator throughout each text .
In Chitose, ci= / =as may appear only at the narrative opening, with the body of the text reverting to a= / =an .
The hero-person choice is thus both genre-conditioned (verse vs prose may condition the choice in Chitose) and region-conditioned (Iburi vs Saru/Chitose use different forms throughout).
A second genre-conditioned morphological feature is the number-agreement override.
In everyday Saru/Chitose, the suffix =an never co-occurs with a singular verb root: one says k=ek 'I come.SG' in conversation, and =an appears only with the suppletive plural (arki=an 'we come.PL').

The broader elegant-register morphology (applicative case-marking by prefixes e- / o- / ko- rather than particles, more polysynthetic words, genre-specific lexicon) is covered in .
Verse in Hokkaido Ainu is not organized by rhyme.

noted the absence of systematic rhyme; , following Philippi (1979), confirms that repetition in Ainu poetry largely reflects the small vowel inventory and widespread reduplication rather than a prosodic constraint ‹contested›.

Against this consensus, Tangiku (2020) argues that an 18th-century yukar text (ルウェサニウンクㇽ) uses deliberate head-rhyme, end-rhyme, and imperfect rhyme — a finding that, if sustained, would require revising the standard account (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2023-12-13; ) ‹contested›.
argues that Hokkaido Ainu verse deploys two metrically distinct systems, genre-differentiated.
The first, syllable-count orientation, targets five syllables per line as basic (four-to-seven is the attested range), as described by and ; it is characteristic of lyric songs (yaysama).

The second, accent orientation, places the first pitch accent in a fixed rhythmic slot (the first disyllabic foot) and admits four-syllable lines when the accent is line-initial; it characterizes divine epics (kamuy yukar).
Heroic epics (yukar) use both systems depending on the musical rhythm of the performance ‹contested›.

Okuda reports no other language in which one reciter alternates between two distinct metrical systems — a typological claim that rests on an argument from the present state of the literature rather than exhaustive survey ‹speculative›.

Techniques for achieving the five-syllable target in syllable-count verse include: the insertion of the light verb between a verb and a following element, uncontracted person prefixes, a prefixed initial u-, and retention of vowels that elide in conversational speech ; .
These techniques are also poetic-register diagnostics; they are analysed as part of the couplet and formulaic system in .
Each major scholar of Ainu oral literature has organized the genre system around different primary criteria.
and Kubodera classified the corpus primarily by protagonist type (human vs divine vs culture-hero).
Chiri Mashiho () supplied the dialect-distribution data that revealed the naming mismatches across regions.
showed that the Saru category of oyna is absent from at least one primary narrator's repertoire.
established the four-function classification adopted by and followed here.
These schemes are not mutually falsifying — they weight different parameters — but they produce different genre maps and different descriptions of what counts as a variant of what.
At the level of individual texts, genre boundaries can be indeterminate.

A kamuy yukar from the Shizunai collection narrated by 織田ステノ, titled "怠け者の子供" ('The lazy child'), carries a long sakehe (manayta sanke tar panke tar kocupu) but is shorter than typical kamuy yukar and concludes as a yayeisoytak (first-person self-narration) by a single human boy rather than a divine protagonist.
forms: manayta sanke tar panke tar kocupu

text: Having melody rules out classification as prose, yet the text fits neither standard kamuy yukar (wrong protagonist type) nor yukar (carries a sakehe) (gengojiro, aynu-corpora Discord 2025-12-12; ) ‹contested›.
Such cases show that the sakehe-vs-no-sakehe and divine-vs-human-protagonist parameters do not always co-vary as the taxonomy predicts.
The elegant-vs-everyday register distinction (see ) raises a related question.
ranked the density of elegant-language features across genres from least to most: greeting < prayer < incantation < caranke < yukar, treating the gradation as qualitative differences.

Nakagawa (2001a[1987]: 222, cited via ) argues instead that elegant and everyday language are points on a continuum keyed to verse/prose and fixedness/improvisation, and proposes further that a genre-phrase classification (yukar-phrase vs prayer-phrase) may be more analytically effective than the elegant/everyday binary ‹contested›.

That proposal predicts that the register differences between yukar and prayer, though real, are not of the same kind as the difference between elegant and everyday language generally; the evidential and TAM consequences of this distinction are tracked in .
The Ijäs pedagogical grammar () does not present a systematic genre taxonomy and is focused on spoken, conversational Ainu rather than the verse tradition.
Where vocabulary or constructions associated with the oral-literature register appear in that work, the present chapter routes the reader to the philological and descriptive literature treated here.
Hokkaido Ainu marks reported discourse with a quotative index (QI): a quotative marker that follows the quoted string and is in turn followed by a speech or cognition verb.
The central marker is sekor, an adverbial conjunction that is obligatory in direct and semi-direct constructions.
A structurally separate class of constructions uses bound complementizers (kunak, yak, kuni) with transitive reporting verbs and is treated as a complementation device in and .

This chapter covers the sekor-mediated system: the transitivity split among reporting verbs, the direct/semi-direct/indirect distinction, the 1st-to-4th-person shift inside quotes, the logophoricity debate, the first-person narration convention of yukar and uwepeker, and the hawe family of forms that bridges the quotative and evidential systems.
The evidential architecture within which hawe ne and hawe as sit is described in and .

The quotative and evidential systems intersect at the noun : the intransitive report verb hawean ('a voice exists' → 'say'), the reportative evidential hawe ne ('it is a voice/report that'), and the hearsay form hawe as ('a voice arises') all derive from the possessed form haw-e 'the voice of —' .
Reference-tracking across narrative spans, which the quotative machinery helps manage, is described in .
The etymology of sekor is transparent: it derives from se 'make a sound / say' + kor 'while / while holding', yielding roughly 'while saying' (nukopoli, , 2024) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
In the southern Hokkaido dialects it is fully grammaticalized as the quotative particle and no longer carries its compositional meaning.
The form following sekor is the reporting verb, and its transitivity determines the construction type.
The constraint was first stated by and systematized by : sekor co-occurs with intransitive reporting verbs because the quoted string is adverbial — it is not the object of the reporting verb.
The complementizer constructions (kunak/yak/kuni) take transitive verbs (ye 'say', ramu 'think') because the complement clause is the object.

The community discussion confirms this: *sekor a=ramu is ungrammatical — ramu requires a nominal object; the correct form is kuni a=ramu or, with the intransitive cognate, sekor yaynu=an (nukopoli, , 2024) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

The apparent exception is sekor a=ye: the transitive verb ye occurs after sekor in a lexicalized frame that is more frequent in the corpus than the intransitive alternative sekor itak=an (nukopoli, , 2024; thegodofneet, , 2025) ‹corpus-confirmed›.
acknowledges sekor a=ye as a lexicalized exception to the transitivity constraint.
presents both sekor hawean and sekor a=ye as the two standard quotative frames in her pedagogical grammar.
identifies three construction types for Hokkaido Ainu, distinguished by the treatment of person inside the quote and by the syntactic integration of the complement.

The DRD/SDRD distinction rests on person: when the current narrator quotes herself, 1st-person forms inside the quote are retained, and the construction is direct.

When she quotes a different speaker, the original 1st-person of the quoted speaker is replaced by the 4th/indefinite person — the pronoun asinuma for the singular logophoric-like reference, the prefix a= on transitive stems, and the suffix =an on intransitive stems — and the result is semi-direct ; .
The free pronoun asinuma and the 4th-person affix paradigm are described in and .
is explicit that the 4th-person-in-quote is not indirect narration.
formalizes a semi-direct category: the syntax of the quote is direct, but the person form signals that the source of the quoted content is a participant other than the current narrator.

sharpen the analysis: across languages, logophoric speech shares its syntax with direct speech and none with indirect; the Ainu semi-direct construction is syntactically direct-like and its person shift is a logophoric device, not a symptom of syntactic subordination ‹contested›.
The clause-integration mechanics of the three types are treated in .
Two analyses of the 4th-person-in-quote compete.
calls it the 'quotative first person' (引用の1人称), treating it as a sub-use of the 4th person alongside the inclusive, impersonal, and honorific uses.
lists the quotative use as use ⑤ of the 4th person without positing a dedicated logophoric category.
argues for a genuinely logophoric analysis: the pronoun asinuma (literally a=sinuma 'the self of one') is the singular logophoric form, invariably glossed by the speaker Mrs.
Ito Oda as じぶん 'self' rather than わたし 'I'; it tracks the original speaker of the quoted discourse, not the current narrator ‹contested›.
and treat the same forms as polysemous, deriving the narrative-first-person use from a first-person-plural (inclusive) strategy in which the 4th-person affixes index both protagonist and audience.
The whole-range of the 4th person and the competing analyses of its referential extent are laid out in .
The available evidence leaves several points unsettled.
The logophoric analysis is based on Saru–Chitose data (Mrs.
Ito Oda, Biratori); whether asinuma carries the same dedicated 'original speaker' meaning in other Hokkaido dialects is unverified ‹speculative›.
notes the same dialect gap.

The best-supported claim is: in southern Hokkaido, when a narrator quotes a speaker other than herself, the quoted speaker's 1st-person morphology is systematically replaced by the 4th-person set, and this replacement is not optional ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Whether the replacing forms constitute a grammaticalized logophoric subsystem or are a deployment of the general 4th person is the contested analytical choice.

The narrative first-person convention of yukar (heroic and divine epic) and uwepeker (prose tale) consists in the reciter voicing the protagonist through the 4th/indefinite person forms (a=, =an, i=) rather than the narrator's own 1st-person forms ; .

The mechanism is structurally parallel to the semi-direct shift in §3: the protagonist's perspective is indexed by the 4th-person set throughout the tale, while any stepping-out narrator commentary, where it appears, uses the 1st person.
The oral-literature genres and their registers are described in , and the TAM and evidential patterns by genre in .
The analytical question is whether the convention is a genre-bound pragmatic device or a grammaticalized logophoric system.

Several observations favour a convention-first reading: (a) the 4th-person forms are identical to those marking indefinite agents in everyday speech; (b) the distribution skews heavily by genre — the pattern is densest in yukar, lighter in uwepeker, lighter still in everyday quoted speech ‹corpus-suggested›; (c) derives the narrative use from the inclusive reading, on which the protagonist is voiced as 'we' (protagonist and audience together).
Against this, notes occurrences of asinuma as the logophoric form outside oral literature, which would push toward a grammatical analysis that is not genre-defined ‹contested›.

The chapter's conclusion is that a genre-convention analysis accounts for the distribution but does not preclude a logophoric analysis of the form: the two claims are compatible if the logophoric device originated in the narrative genre and extended into everyday quotation ‹speculative›.
All three members of the family derive from the possessed form haw-e 'the voice of —'.
They differ in the predicate that follows the possessed noun and, correspondingly, in what they assert about the source of information:

The reportative evidential hawe ne differs from the quotative frame in scope: sekor … hawean presents a specific attributed speech event, while hawe ne predicates the whole proposition as something the speaker knows through words, without identifying a specific utterer .
The hearsay form hawe as extends further: it reports ambient or indirectly received information, the 'sound' of something being said rather than a specific attributed utterance:
The naming cleft X sekor a=ye hawe ne 'it is what is called X — so it is said' layers both systems.
The inner sekor a=ye lexicalized frame embeds the name; the outer hawe ne frames the whole as a conventionally reported fact:
A related but structurally distinct naming frame is X sekor a=ye p ne 'it is the thing that is called X'.
Here p is the nominalizer 'thing / the one', and ne is the copula (see ).
The community discussion raises a valency point: in this frame the nominalizer p is zero-valent — it is not the object of ye.

The transitive verb ye (+2) has its two valency slots filled by the agent a= (−1) and the implicit 3rd-person zero-object (−1), and p then nominalizes the whole clause from outside (nukopoli, , 2024) ‹contested›.
If correct, the frame has the same underlying structure as the general predicate-nominalization cleft described in , with sekor embedded inside.
Sekor is the quotative marker of the southern Hokkaido dialects.
Other Hokkaido varieties use ari or ani in the same quotative slot.
notes the dialect distribution.

The community discussion proposes that ari/ani is the older pan-Ainu quotative and that sekor is a Saru-region innovation: an analytical form built from se + kor that replaced ari/ani as the Saru dialect grew as the cultural centre (nukopoli, , 2024) ‹contested›.

The directionality of change is not independently datable from the available sources, and the claim rests on internal evidence (the composition of sekor) and the dialect distribution, not comparative-historical reconstruction.
The equivalent in Sakhalin varieties (nah), occupying the same functional slot, is cited for typological contrast only; its morphology and distribution belong to the Sakhalin contrast chapter.
Three significant uncertainties bear on the analysis of this chapter.
First, the logophoric vs. 4th-person debate (§4) remains open: the key evidence for a dedicated logophoric pronoun asinuma comes from Saru–Chitose (Mrs.
Ito Oda), and no study has verified that the same 'self / original speaker' reading is obligatory in other dialects .

Second, the distributional boundary between the genre-bound narration convention (§5) and a grammaticalized logophoric device is not resolved: quantified evidence of asinuma in everyday versus oral-literary speech is not available in the sources consulted ‹speculative›.

Third, the non-Saru dialect behaviour of the quotative system — what role ari/ani plays in the DRD/SDRD/IRD split, and whether the same transitivity constraint holds — has not been described at the same level of detail as the Saru–Chitose baseline in and .
Melody presence is the most grammar-relevant parameter dividing Hokkaido Ainu oral genres.
Three verse-and-narrative traditions each carry a distinct constellation of features — melody, the refrain, and rhythm-tapping — that co-condition the grammar of the text ; .
(After , table of Chitose oral-literature genres and features.
Genre taxonomy, regional dialect-term variation, and the oyna nomenclature debate are covered in .)
The sung/prose split is not merely a performance fact.

Sung verse genres deploy the poetic register (atomte itak, 'ornamented language') with its distinct morphological and lexical features, while prose (yayan itak, 'ordinary language') does not — even when the prose narrator's voice rises and falls with a narrative lilt ; .
The elevated register is described in ; its TAM and evidential patterning by genre in .

Folktale intonation — one-directional, low-variation melody, with upper-Saru narration more monotone than lower-Saru — sits apart from the strict melodic structure of sung verse (, nukopoli 2024, asserted, after ).

The verb (E-Iburi) captures the sung dimension lexically; it appears in a Abuta yukar passage meaning 'about to sing a yukar' (sakehawki anki), confirming that for at least the eastern Iburi dialects, sung performance was lexically distinguished from prose narration .
The term is morphologically the possessed form of sa (Japanese Wiktionary: "sa の所属形").

Tamura's Saru dictionary records a prosodic distinction: the genre-refrain sense carries initial accent (sákehe) while the common-noun sense 'sake (the beverage)' is unaccented, creating near-homophones that occasionally coincide within a single verse line (see the hancikiki example below) .

The corpus registers fifteen tokens of the form (rank 4,602 among 45,225 distinct tokens), spanning both senses; the refrain sense is attested in narrator metalinguistic commentary (see example below) ‹corpus-suggested›.

In kamuy yukar, the sakehe is a fixed refrain per story, inserted into the narration — every line or every few lines depending on the text — and held constant throughout one performance of that story ; .
The melody to which the text is sung is equally fixed per story (contrast yukar, where each narrator deploys a personal tune that may change mid-performance; see the melody section below).
Together, the fixed melody and the fixed sakehe define the formal identity of a kamuy yukar text: a reciter who knows a story knows both its sakehe and its melody as an inseparable package .
A canonical instance of sakehe-every-line placement comes from a marlin-tuna kamuy yukar narrated by Nabezawa Nepuki (鍋沢ネブキ) of Biratori.

The sakehe tusunapanu precedes every narrative word-group, producing a strict alternation of refrain and narrative that generates the rhythmic frame of the performance (, reporting ; narrator 鍋沢ネブキ, Biratori):
('Okikurmi and Samayunkur went offshore to fish, so… before that… ahead of [them]…'; the sakehe in capitals precedes every narrative phrase.)
Attested sakehe from the aligned Hokkaido corpus and oral-literature archives show the range from onomatopoeic to opaque.

The story-type and sakehe are demonstrably not in fixed correspondence: the same narrative situation (marlin-tuna confrontation) carries sakehe tusunapanu in Saru (Biratori), tussay turi tussay matu in Horobetsu, and nissō in Chitose (where the protagonist is swapped for the fish okina) .

Kayano's Saru dictionary preserves a long multi-word sakehe (tunoyake renoyake kutunke kamuyke kamuy cikappo hum hum hum) as one illustration of the form's capacity for extended, rhythmically organized strings .

text: The melodic contrast between kamuy yukar and yukar is the clearest formal divide in the genre system.
A kamuy yukar text comes with a melody that is bound to that story and is transmitted alongside the words and the sakehe; a performer who learns the story learns all three as an integrated unit .

Prayer (kamuy nomi) also has a melodic delivery, but its melody is improvised and personal — different each time and not transmitted with the words — a property Nakagawa (via ) uses to distinguish prayer from the fixed-word, fixed-melody incantation.
Yukar stands apart: each narrator constructs or inherits his own tune for a borrowed story, and the melody is liable to change mid-performance .

The absence of a sakehe in yukar corresponds to this melodic instability: where the kamuy yukar uses the repeating sakehe to bind melody, narrative line, and rhythmic unit together, the yukar uses rhythm-tapping ( / — 'the act of keeping time', confirmed in the Mukawa-dialect dictionary as 拍子棒 ) to provide rhythmic scaffolding without a textual refrain.
Listeners add a sung chorus (; corpus count 13) during yukar performance, a further rhythmic layer absent from kamuy yukar .
Satō notes that an opening formula — the — may recur at the start of a yukar and could represent a vestige of a refrain that yukar once possessed ‹speculative›.
The inference is Satō's own and rests on structural analogy with kamuy yukar rather than on textual attestation.
The functional motivation of the sakehe has generated competing accounts.

Nakagawa proposes that it originally indicated the protagonist: the refrain was an identifying tag that signalled whose voice or experience was being narrated , reporting Nakagawa 2001b: 7 ‹contested›.

The counter-evidence is substantial: the same story-type does not consistently carry the same sakehe across dialects (the marlin-tuna case above), and many sakehe have no recoverable semantic or deictic link to their protagonist.

The thunder-god's hum pakpak can be read as onomatopoeia of thunder's sound (the narrator's own gloss supports this), but that is iconic, not indexical, and it is not generalizable to the full sakehe inventory .

A performer's own metalinguistic statement, recorded in the AA研 archive, puts the sakehe at the centre of the sung/prose boundary: the narrator Kawakami Matsuko explains that a menoko yukar is performed sakekoye ('told with the refrain'), and that when the refrain is omitted the same material is told as uwepeker:
The community discussion archives one live genre-boundary case that bears on the sakehe's defining role.

A kamuy yukar narrated by Oda Suteno (織田ステノ, 'Lazybones Child') carries a long sakehe (manayta sanke tar panke tar kocupu) but an unusually short narrative body, and its closing move — the protagonist self-identifying as a human boy (sine wen toranne hekaci, 'a single weak miserable child') — formally resembles a yayeisoytak (self-narration) rather than a divine-epic conclusion (, gengojiro 2025-12-12, proposed).
forms: manayta sanke tar panke tar kocupu

text: This text, with melody and a long sakehe but a human-protagonist resolution, resists placement in either kamuy yukar or yukar, illustrating that the sakehe alone does not uniquely define genre membership ‹contested›.

One additional philological datum: the title-line AEKIRUSHI in Chiri Yukie's has been proposed to parse as a=e-kir-usi 'the place one has memory of' (, 0penke 2024-03-19, proposed, after 片山龍峯 2003) rather than deriving from ekiru 'turn back'.
If correct, the title-line encodes the hero's logophoric self-location, consistent with the divine-epic pattern of first-person self-presentation ‹contested›.
The metrical organization of HA verse has been described under two competing frameworks.
The long-standing analysis treats verse as syllable-count oriented, with five syllables per line as the basic unit.
Okuda's more recent work identifies a second system, accent oriented, in which the first pitch-accent falls in a fixed rhythmic position regardless of line length.
The two frameworks are not simply rival accounts of the same data: Okuda argues they are genre-differentiated and co-active within a single performer's repertoire ‹contested›
The syllable-count description goes back to Kindaichi (1931: 165, via ) and was adopted by Tamura (1973: 56, via ): the basic line unit is five syllables, with four to seven as the attested range.
The five-syllable target is met through a set of compositional techniques catalogued by Tamura and Satō ; :
use of formulaic verse phrases already calibrated to syllable count;
choice between synonyms for their syllable count;
insertion or omission of final particles;
insertion of the dummy verb between a verb and its following element;
use of the uncontracted ku- person prefix rather than its reduced form;
prefixing an initial u to a line when reciting;
splitting a long phrase across two five-syllable lines;
not eliding vowels that would contract in everyday speech;
not pronouncing the line-final syllable (a performance strategy, not a morphological rule).
These techniques confirm that the syllable target is a compositional constraint on the verse line rather than a property of the grammar at large.
They are the mechanisms through which the sung verse actively shapes morphosyntax: word choice, prefix realization, and particle use are all subordinated to the five-syllable frame.
This is the most direct route by which genre conditions grammatical form in Hokkaido Ainu.

Okuda's comparative analysis of divine epics and lyric songs identifies a second system that he terms accent-orientation (アクセント指向): the first pitch-accent of the line falls in the first disyllabic foot, regardless of how many syllables the line contains .
Under this system, a four-syllable line is metrically well-formed as long as the accent is initial; the syllable-count system, by contrast, disfavours four-syllable lines.
The scansion evidence comes from divine epics recorded by narrators in Monbetsu and Chitose.

In the divine epic Amamecikappo narrated by Hatozawa Wateke (幌別/Monbetsu; text in Tamura 2001, via ), of 90 non-refrain lines, 14 are four-syllable lines; of these 14, twelve carry initial accent on the first syllable, matching the accent-orientation prediction.
