In Chitose divine epics, the pattern holds with similar consistency.
The text Wawo kamuy (Shirasawa Nabe; 226 lines) has 62 four-syllable lines, of which 56 carry initial accent; Apehuci kamuy (same narrator; 220 lines) has 79 four-syllable lines, of which 71 do .

The same reciters' lyric songs (yaysama) are overwhelmingly five-syllable (e.g., 33 of 34 lines in Hatozawa Wateke's lyric sample), confirming that the same performer switches between systems by genre .
Okuda maps the two systems onto genres and musical rhythms :
Okuda's claim that a single performance tradition deploys two such metrically distinct systems is, on his own account, without parallel in the reported typological literature ‹contested›.

The traditional syllable-count description (Kindaichi, Tamura) remains well evidenced for lyric and prayer; the accent-orientation analysis adds explanatory coverage for the divine and heroic epics, where four-syllable lines with initial accent resist treatment under a pure syllable-count rule.
The two analyses are therefore complementary across genres rather than mutually exclusive ‹contested›.

A further hypothesis, explicit in Okuda and flagged as conjectural, relates the syllable-count system to Japanese 7-5 mora metre: the contact with Japanese literary tradition could have reinforced or introduced the strict syllable target ‹speculative›.
No positive evidence is offered and the hypothesis rests on structural analogy alone.
Philippi's influential judgment (1979, via ) was that rhyme in Ainu poetry is 'quite accidental' and alliteration 'sporadic' — not prosodically functional as in Mongolic or Tungusic traditions.

Okuda formalizes the reasoning: given five vowels and roughly twelve onset consonants, chance repetition in a corpus of five-syllable lines is high, and a sequence counts as technique only when it demonstrably exceeds chance and is not forced by morphological reduplication, which is pervasive in Ainu .
A counter-position has been raised in the community literature.

Tangiku (2020, 北大言語 アーカイヴ報告書) argues that an 18th-century Ainu yukar — ルウェサニウンクㇽ — uses deliberate head-rhyme, end-rhyme, and imperfect rhyme as compositional devices (, nukopoli 2023-12-13, asserted, after Tangiku 2020).

If the Tangiku analysis survives scrutiny, it would demonstrate at least one historical period or textual tradition in which rhyme was a conscious structural choice rather than an artefact of phonological probability ‹contested›.
The Tangiku source has not been consulted directly for this grammar; the claim is flagged as needing verification against the primary text.
Both yukar and kamuy yukar are narrated in the first person from the protagonist's viewpoint.
The grammatical marker of this 'first person' is, in Saru and Chitose, the fourth-person prefix a= and suffix =an, not the everyday first person ku= ; .

The choice of the fourth-person forms is grammatically productive: in elegant language, =an combines with singular verbs (e.g., ek-an 'I come.SG'), a combination that everyday Saru disallows (*ek-an is ill-formed there but arki-an 'we come.PL' is fine) .
This number-agreement override is a diagnostic of the elegant register in sung verse — see .

The Iburi dialect tradition, canonically represented by Chiri Yukie's , uses instead the exclusive first-person plural ci= / =as as a singular hero-narrator marker, consistently throughout the collection ; .

The regional split is systematic: a= / =an in Saru and Chitose; ci= / =as in Iburi (Horobetsu and related traditions) — with Chitose showing an intermediate pattern where ci= / =as may appear in the opening lines before reverting to a= / =an .

The motivation for the non-everyday person-marking in oral narrative is discussed under two competing accounts: the shamaness-oracle origin theory (standard), in which the verse is framed as spirit-speech, and Satō's 'indirection principle' (間接性の原理), in which the god's first-person speech inside a dream required indirectness to soften the taboo on direct divine address ‹contested›.
The logophoric and direct-speech dimensions of the fourth person as used in narration are treated in and ; reference tracking across verse episodes in ; the full paradigm in .
One grammatically significant consequence of sung-verse performance is quotative density.

Because narration is cast as direct speech and closes with a self-identification formula (…sekor … isoytak 'so X told the story'), the quotative particle with speech verbs (, , ) clusters heavily in verse text-closings.
The evidential tail hawe ne / hawe as (< + possessed form) carries much of the reportative marking in these contexts ; the broader evidential system is treated in and .

Hokkaido Ainu verse genres — the heroic epic (yukar / sakorpe), the divine epic (kamuy yukar / oyna), and ritual speech (prayer, caranke) — are performed in an elevated register, atomte itak 'decorated language', distinct from everyday prose speech (yayan itak) ; .

The primary rhetorical device of this register is parallelism: two or more consecutive verse lines share the same syntactic frame while one or more lexical positions are filled by semantically related but distinct words ; ; .
Phonological matching plays no constitutive role: "for lines to match or rhyme is not required" .
The device is syntactic and lexical, not phonological.
Parallelism in Ainu verse is described in the Japanese scholarship as 対句 (taigu) and treated alongside formulaic phrasing and periphrasis as the core of the poetic apparatus ; .
A minimal pair of parallel lines — a couplet — is the basic unit.
The device is "pervasive in divine and heroic epics" and extends into prayer and incantation; it is absent from everyday prose (uwepeker folktale, conversation).

For the verse genres and their grammatical signatures, see ; for verse metre, the sakehe refrain, and sung-verse structure, see ; for the full elevated-register morphological and lexical cluster, see .

The canonical couplet pairs two lines that are syntactically identical or near-identical, with one lexical position — typically a modifier or head noun — replaced by a semantically contrasted or associated word.
The simplest attested type fills the modifier slot with a spatial antonym pair:
The same antonymic pair extends to a larger syntactic frame with incorporated nouns and causative morphology.
Endō 2022: ch.10 §4, ex.19 gives: hanke kotan sonko-kama-re / tuyma kotan e-sonko-ciw-re — glossable as 'send word to the near village / drive word into the far village'.
forms: hanke kotan sonko-kama-re / tuyma kotan e-sonko-ciw-re

text: Here both the spatial modifier (hanke vs tuyma) and the verb differ, while the nominal skeleton (___ kotan '___ village') and the incorporated noun are constant .
A couplet may extend to a three-line set (tricola) in which the first two parallel lines lead into a shared predicate.
A Chitose text gives:
A carving couplet attested in Endō 2022: ch.10 §4, ex.17 shows synonymic elaboration rather than antonymy: tomika nuye / ikorka nuye 'carve the sword-sheath / carve the treasure-sword-sheath'.
The verb is constant; and name the same type of decorated sheath at a plain and an elaborated grade .
The sources and document the following structural types, which may co-occur within a single couplet:
Antonymic parallelism pairs words that occupy opposite poles of a semantic domain — spatial ( // ), quantitative, or social.
The two lines collectively cover the full extent of the relevant domain.
Synonymic / elaborating parallelism pairs a plain term with a more specific or more elevated one referring to the same referent (tomika // ikorka).
The second member typically adds a qualifier marking prestige or preciousness — a common escalation pattern in heroic and divine verse.
Numeral parallelism deploys the // pair as an intensifying doublet meaning 'many' rather than encoding an exact count (see §below).
This is the most formulaic type and the most pervasive in the corpus.
Endō 2022 does not sort these into discrete sub-types, treating all three under the single label 対句.
The distinction between antonymic and synonymic types is analytical, not a native speaker's metalinguistic category ‹contested›.
The numeral doublet tu // re ('two' // 'three') is a stock parallel pair that functions as a hyperbolic expression of multiplicity rather than a precise count.

Used across a couplet — as in Satō 2008: 264: otu maw-kur-puni kane / ore maw-kur-puni kane 'raising two winds / raising three winds' — the pair means 'many winds', the adjacent small numerals intensifying the predicate by iteration ; .
forms: otu maw-kur-puni kane / ore maw-kur-puni kane

text: In that same example, Satō 2008 notes the archaic counting forms otu and ore rather than the everyday tu and re; the archaic variants are themselves markers of the elevated register .

The Chitose tricola above (tu imeru kur / re imeru kur) uses the everyday numeral forms, showing that the intensifying function of the doublet does not depend on the archaic variants — it resides in the adjacent-numeral pattern itself.
forms: tu imeru kur / re imeru kur

text: The tu // re device belongs to the broader strategy of hyperbole and escalation that Satō 2008: 264 identifies alongside periphrasis and metaphor as the defining rhetorical inventory of atomte itak.

Both the individual lexical pairs and the templates in which they appear show varying degrees of fixedness: some pairs are fully conventional and recur across reciters and texts; others are the productive application of the parallelism template to any semantically contrasted pair of words.
The table below collects the pairs directly attested in the primary sources read for this chapter ; ; ; .

The elegant-register kin terms // — contrasting with the colloquial / — constitute a lexical register pair rather than a verse-line couplet proper, but they belong to the same broader phenomenon of paired synonymic substitution by which atomte itak systematically replaces everyday vocabulary with a distinct poetic word-stock ; (nukopoli, 2026, asserted; corroborates Endō 2022: §3, characteristic 4).
The morphosyntax of kin terms in honorific contexts is treated in .
Couplets in Ainu verse are typically also formulae: fixed word sequences learned as units and redeployed across performances and across reciters, matching the available metrical slot .

The Hokkaido Ainu Center 2000 documentation (via Endō 2022: §4) describes these phrases as "learned in bulk" — a reciter acquires a stock of ready-made pairs and deploys whichever fits the narrative moment.

An illustrative stock phrase is tuk-no pinni si-kopa-yar / aynu pito 'a fine person like a grown Manchurian-ash tree' (featuring the poetic similative si-kopa-yar, absent from everyday speech), which serves as a portable hero-praise formula .
The formulaic character of couplets serves at least three functions in performance.

First, mnemonic: in yukar performances lasting several hours or multiple nights (see ), prefabricated phrase-pairs reduce the cognitive load of real-time composition, allowing the reciter to reproduce long texts with exactitude.

Second, intensifying: repetition of a semantic content across two adjacent syntactic slots (with controlled lexical variation) constitutes verse-internal emphasis; the tu // re doublet works by doubling the iteration rather than by selecting a single emphatic word.
Third, cohesive: paired lines frame episodes and signal transitions within the narrative, binding adjacent performance segments through structural symmetry ; .
Nakagawa (via ) identifies couplets as one of the sub-devices enabling "one phrase → multi-phrase expansion": a single semantic content is projected across two lines, satisfying the metre.

The syllable-count and accent-orientation metrical constraints described in motivate this expansion directly — the choice between the tu and re variants, or between a short and an elaborated form, can resolve a metrical insufficiency ‹corpus-suggested›.
Parallelism and couplets are confined to atomte itak and are absent from prose folktale (uwepeker) and everyday conversation.

The register is not, however, a discrete switch: Nakagawa 2001a[1987]: 222 (via ) treats elegant and everyday language as points on a continuum defined by the degree of verse vs prose and of fixed vs improvised delivery; couplet density tracks this continuum, reaching its maximum in heroic epic ‹contested›.

Kindaichi's hierarchy — greeting < prayer < incantation < caranke < yukar, each richer in elegant language than the last (, via ) — implies a comparable gradient of couplet density, but this has not been quantified on a genre-tagged corpus ‹speculative›.

Parallelism co-occurs with the other grammatical hallmarks of atomte itak: applicative case-marking by prefixes e-/o-/ko- in place of case particles, longer polysynthetic words, number-agreement override (the singular verb with -an for the 1SG hero-narrator), and a distinct elevated lexicon ; .
The couplet is thus one component of a co-occurring cluster, not an isolated device.
The full cluster is treated in ; the number-agreement override belongs to .
Within verse narration, couplets typically accompany the fourth-person (a=/-an) hero-narrator marking that indexes the logophoric first person.
The interaction of this narrative convention with reported-speech structure is described in and .

The evidential frame ruwe ne, which predicates narrative events as established facts (see and ), is the unmarked clause-final frame in verse narration and thus the primary syntactic environment in which couplets appear; the sentence-final particle inventory of verse is treated in .

Paired-line organization of the type found in Ainu verse — a fixed syntactic frame with one or more varying lexical slots, without phonological matching as a constitutive requirement — is documented in many oral-poetic traditions worldwide.

Whether the Hokkaido Ainu pattern shares an origin with neighboring North Pacific verse traditions or developed independently is an open question: no source read for this grammar addresses the diachrony or areality of the couplet device directly, and the primary comparative literature on verse parallelism lies outside the sources available here ‹speculative›.

The absence of a phonological requirement, confirmed for Hokkaido Ainu by and consistent with the contested evidence on rhyme and alliteration reviewed in , is in itself typologically diagnostic and merits future systematic comparison.

Hokkaido Ainu distinguishes two named registers: atomte-itak (アトゥㇺテイタㇰ, lit. 'decorated/ornamented speech'; Japanese 雅語, the elegant or poetic register) and yayan-itak (ヤヤニタㇰ, lit. 'ordinary speech'; 口語/日常語, the everyday register) ; .

The term atomte-itak is attested in metalinguistic use by native speakers and in modern community discussion, where it is explicitly applied to the speech of verse and prayer genres (成田英敏 / asirso, 2024).

The distinction is grammar-diagnostic across four dimensions: (1) applicative prefixes replace postpositional case particles; (2) the fourth-person suffix =an co-occurs with singular verb stems that exclude it in conversation; (3) words are longer and more morphologically elaborated; (4) a verse-specific vocabulary replaces everyday lexemes ; .
The boundary between the two registers is not categorical.
Nakagawa argues that elegant and everyday Ainu are stages on a continuum keyed to two axes — verse vs prose, and fixed vs improvised — rather than two discrete levels ‹contested›
He further proposes that a classification by genre (yukar-vocabulary vs prayer-vocabulary) may prove more analytically useful than the single-level atomte-itak label .
Genre taxonomy and the performance context of each verse genre are described in ; the metrical and refrain structure of verse in ; the parallel and formulaic rhetoric of verse in .

Kindaichi established that elegant-language density varies across chant and verse genres in a consistent gradient, rising from greeting speech through prayer (kamuy nomi itak) and incantation to dispute negotiation (caranke), with the heroic epic (yukar) carrying the highest concentration of atomte-itak features ; .
Prose folktale (uwepeker) falls largely in the everyday register; the sub-genre of divine-protagonist prose tales (kamuy uwepeker) is an exception, narrated in elegant language throughout .
Two parameters drive the gradient.

The first is fixity: incantations are word-for-word memorised and deploy dense elegant morphology; prayers are improvised — "not memorised like scripture; spun out by improvisation, different each time", in Nakagawa's characterisation — yet draw on the same feature inventory with more personal melody.
The second is the verse/prose divide: all melodic, sung genres (yukar, kamuy yukar, prayer) signal their generic status partly through grammar, not only through melody and metre .
The heroic and divine epics are described in .

The formal/ceremonial evidential frame ruwe tapan, which Tamura's dictionary registers as register-marked, is one illustration of how elegance inflects evidential choice across genres; it is analysed in and situated among genre-conditioned TAM choices in .

Satō lists four grammatical hallmarks of the poetic register , which align with Nakagawa's four defining traits of atomte-itak as reported in Endō : (1) applicative case-marking in place of particles; (2) number-agreement override; (3) greater polysynthetic complexity and periphrasis; (4) a distinct verse/prayer lexicon.
Features (1) and (2) are directly grammar-diagnostic.
In everyday speech, oblique relations — location, direction, goal — are expressed by postpositional particles: ta (locative), un (allative), and others.
In atomte-itak, the same relations are instead encoded by applicative prefixes on the verb: , , .

The register diagnostic is the substitution of prefix for particle, which simultaneously increases syllabic weight — a functional fit with both the metrical preference for longer units and the 5-syllable line ; .
Prayer text is particularly applicative-dense.
Endō's example from a Monbetsu prayer (鍋澤モトゾウ / Motoanrek) shows stacked applicative layers within a single verb: ku=e-ko-pase- and k=e-ko-onkami '(I) reverently worship' .
The applicative morphemes and their stacking interactions are described in , , and .

In Saru and Chitose everyday speech, the fourth-person intransitive suffix =an attaches only to plural verb stems: suppletive plural arki 'come.PL' gives arki=an 'we/they come', while singular ek 'come.SG' does not combine with =an in conversation .

In the poetic register this restriction is suspended: the hero-narrator uses the singular stem together with =an, yielding ek=an 'I came', a formulaic feature of first-person verse narration throughout Saru and Chitose ‹consensus›.
The override is confined to varieties that use a=/=an for the hero-narrator (Saru, Chitose).
Outside those varieties, =an attaches only to plural stems without exception, so this pattern is simultaneously a register and a dialect marker .
Suppletive plural verb pairs are described in ; the fourth-person paradigm in .

The third hallmark is the formation of morphologically heavier words than everyday speech permits, achieved partly through periphrasis — spreading an everyday lexeme across a complex verbal construction.
Two attested examples from Satō illustrate the device :

The periphrasis kamuy ne manu p (lit. 'what is said to be a god') inserts an evidential distancing element (manu 'it is said/alleged') between predicate and nominalized head, simultaneously filling the 5-syllable metrical target and conferring a deferential, distanced quality on divine reference.

Satō also documents the poetic use of kane 'as if, to the extent that' as a simile device in the Abuta (虻田/Iburi) yukar of narrator 遠島タンケ — urar ruyka a=turi kane 'stretching the mist as if it were a bridge' (l. 136) — where kane shades from its circumstantial into a comparative-poetic value .
The interaction of periphrasis with couplet structure is treated in .
The person set used for the narrative hero is the most salient grammatical marker of verse register.
All three primary narrative genres are performed from the protagonist's viewpoint in the first person, but the affix set used for the hero differs from everyday ku=/=en.
The full paradigm and its logophoric analysis are treated in and ; what concerns this chapter is the register conditionality of the choice.
In Saru and Chitose, the hero-narrator uses the fourth-person prefix a= and suffix =an rather than the everyday first person ; .
A framing utterance outside the narration uses ordinary ku=:

Satō explains the hero's non-everyday person marking through what he terms the "indirection principle" (間接性の原理): oral literature was framed — in his hypothesis — as a god's telling inside a dream, and the avoidance of ordinary first-person marking increases indirectness, softening the taboo of a divine being addressing a living human directly ‹speculative›
The competing "shamaness-oracle origin" account (巫女の託宣), which Satō dissents from, locates the origin in shamanic ritual; neither is established ‹contested›

The Iburi kamuy yukar collected by Chiri Yukie — , the first published Ainu-language oral-literature collection — uses a distinct convention: the hero-narrator employs the exclusive first-person plural ci=/=as consistently as a singular, throughout each text ; .
In Chitose, ci= may appear at the opening and then give way to a=/=an .

The hero-person marker is therefore simultaneously genre-conditioned (narrative verse, not prayer or conversation), dialect-conditioned (Saru/Chitose vs Iburi), and register-conditioned (verse or verse-grade prose, not everyday speech) ‹consensus›.

The pronoun set of elegant language likewise draws on the fourth-person and honorific domain: Satō lists asinuma, aoka(y), eani, and ecioka(y) as the elegant-register free-pronoun set, the same forms that function as second-person honorifics in conversation .
The convergence of elevated and honorific function in the fourth-person paradigm is described in .
The distinctive verse and prayer vocabulary is documented across the sources consulted in scattered but consistent testimony.
The table below collects attested everyday–elegant word pairs with genre specification and source attribution.

The elegant parental terms ona 'father' and unu 'mother' are confirmed as literary register forms by community discussion: nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-06-15) asserts that both are 文語的雅語 contrasting with colloquial haca/hapo, and that the plural forms onautari/unuutari can extend to mean 'parents together' .
The observation aligns with Endō's characterisation of a distinct verse lexicon (§3 characteristic 4) without being independently stated there ‹corpus-suggested›.
The possessed-form morphology of forms like i-resu huci ('the-one-who-raised-me grandmother') is described in .
The fire-deity substitutions reveal a genre division within atomte-itak itself.

The everyday address ape huci is the default in heroic and divine epic; prayer substitutes i-resu huci, foregrounding the personal bond between worshipper and deity, and adds the prayer-exclusive epithet mosir kor huci 'grandmother who holds the land', documented for the Monbetsu (Biratori) prayer tradition and described as absent from every other genre .
Conversely, the adnominal kamuy = 'splendid' appears in heroic epic but is absent from prayer, where a deferential petitionary address would not employ such a modifier .
The taboo and honorific extensions of the prayer address system are treated in .
Within the verse lexicon, hero-praise formulae are also genre-specific.

The formula tuk-no pinni si-kopa-yar aynu pito 'a fine person like a grown Manchurian-ash tree' — containing si-kopa-yar 'like', a form not attested in everyday speech — is used for hero description in heroic and divine epics and is not productive outside that genre .
Prayer (kamuy nomi itak, inonno itak) is improvised rather than memorised, which distinguishes it formally from incantation (fixed word-for-word) and from the more formulaic yukar.
Despite this improvisation, prayer deploys atomte-itak features throughout: heavy applicative-prefix stacking in place of postpositions, the elegant vocabulary set, and verse-grade prosody ; .

The address structure of prayer is genre-governed and register-distinctive in its own right: the fire deity (ape huci / i-resu huci) is addressed first in every prayer, acting as intermediary to the other gods .

Genre-conditioned connective inventory is an additional sub-register signal: Endō notes that conjunctive-phrase distributions differ across heroic epic, kamuy yukar, and prayer in ways that go beyond vocabulary differences (Endō 2015, as cited in ).
Prayer is the domain in which the restriction of kamuy as 'splendid' is blocked (§ register lexicon above), and in which the applicative stacking is densest.
The sentence-final particles associated with formal and ceremonial illocution in prayer are treated in .
Register as dichotomy or continuum. Kindaichi's framing treats elegant and everyday as two discrete levels ; .

Nakagawa dissents: the gradient runs continuously through multiple genres, and a yukar-vocabulary/prayer-vocabulary classification may be more tractable than the single atomte-itak rubric ‹contested›.
The practical implication is that claims about "elegant language" should specify which genre is the source.

Origin of non-everyday person marking in verse. Two accounts compete for the historical motivation behind the hero's use of fourth-person affixes: the "shamaness-oracle origin" theory (the consensus framing) and Satō's "indirection/dream-framing" hypothesis.
Both treat the fourth-person marking as motivated by an avoidance principle, but their reference to different social institutions makes them empirically distinct ; ‹contested›.
The honorific dimension of the fourth-person paradigm that underlies both accounts is described in .

Residual refrain in yukar. The opening formula eyororpe in yukar is read by Satō as a vestige of a former refrain, suggesting that heroic and divine epics diverged from a common refrain-bearing ancestor ‹speculative›.
The claim is an inference, not independently supported by text-comparative evidence.
The sakehe system is described in .
Hokkaido Ainu speech is sociolinguistically stratified along three partially independent axes.

The poetic/everyday axis — the contrast between (雅語, poetic–elegant register) and (日常語/口語) — is the broadest division, shared across verse and prayer genres; its archaic morphology and formulaic vocabulary are treated in , and the genre system that controls which register is appropriate is described in .
The honorific/deferential axis, realized through the fourth-person address forms and the associated pronoun set, is analysed formally in and .

The ritual-substitution and taboo axis, in which specific vocabulary items are replaced or avoided in ceremonial, deity-address, or kinship contexts, is the focus of the present chapter, set against the sociolinguistic conditioning shared by all three axes.
The three axes do not constitute a clean binary of "high" versus "low" language.

(via ) argues that elegant and everyday Ainu occupy positions on a continuum keyed to verse-vs-prose and fixedness-vs-improvisation, and proposes that a classification by genre-type — yukar-specific phrases versus prayer-specific phrases — may be more analytically effective than the elegant/everyday dichotomy alone ‹contested›.

The substitution phenomena treated here are social rather than metrical: the determining factor is the relationship between speaker and addressee — between worshipper and deity, between kin-avoidance pairs, between the hunter and the spirit of the quarry.

The deferential or honorific address register routes second-person reference through the fourth-person prefix a= and suffix =an rather than the everyday second-person affixes, producing a construction where 'you did X' or 'you are Y' is morphologically encoded as if the agent were fourth-person ; .

The same prefix-set indexes the indefinite agent-defocusing function in everyday speech and the first-person hero-narrator in oral literature; its deferential reading arises specifically in contexts where the referent is identifiable and the social relationship calls for deference — address to an elder, to a chief (nispa), or to a deity (see and ).
A dedicated honorific pronoun set co-occurs with these verbal affixes.

The everyday second-person pronouns eani and ecioka(y) share morphological origin with the second-person verbal affixes.

The honorific alternatives asinuma and aoka(y) are drawn from the fourth-person paradigm and function as free pronouns in deferential speech — between a junior and a senior speaker, or between a human worshipper and a divine interlocutor .

The structural convergence of the honorific second-person, the indefinite agent-defocusing, and the oral-literary hero-narrator on a single morphological paradigm is the subject of ; for the distribution by genre see .

The permissive–sociative causative -yar functions additionally as a register device in formal speech: the causee, when it is the deferential addressee, may be left implicit rather than named directly, heightening the indirection appropriate to the social relationship .
This strategy is treated in .
A small set of kinship terms participates in the everyday/elegant distinction as straightforward register alternants.

The terms and are the literary or elegant (文語的雅語) kin terms for 'father' and 'mother', attested in verse and formal contexts; the everyday equivalents and vary more strongly by dialect and belong primarily to everyday speech ; (nukopoli, 2026-06-15, asserted).

The possessed forms and are the grammatically standard affiliative kin-noun forms; the collective compounds and each carry the extended meaning 'parents (both)' alongside the primary 'fathers' and 'mothers' readings (nukopoli, 2026-06-15, asserted) ‹corpus-suggested›.
In the oral-literary register these forms surface with the fourth-person possessive prefix a= in a dignified self-reference, as when a narrator names her parents as deities:

The colloquial term shows conspicuous dialect variation: it means 'mother' in most Hokkaido varieties but 'father' in Chitose and Horobetsu, while in the Kuril varieties it denotes 'elder sibling' (thegodofneet, 2026-06-08, asserted, citing Chiri Mashiho's comparative data).

This lexical instability of the colloquial terms against the relative stability of the elegant pair ona/unu across verse traditions provides a further diagnostic value for the register distinction: the literary terms are fixed precisely where the colloquial terms shift.
The possessive morphology and the full kinship-possession system are treated in .

The most extensively documented register-substitution phenomenon in Hokkaido Ainu is the genre-conditioned alternation of fire-deity epithets across the performance contexts of divine epic and prayer.
In kamuy yukar (divine epic), the fire deity is addressed as , the kin-term-based epithet shared with everyday speech.

In formal prayer (kamuy nomi / inonno itak), the same deity is addressed by the relational epithet or , and the prayer text of 鍋沢モトゾウ (Motoanrek, Monbetsu) preserves an additional prayer-only form, , described in as "not found in any other genre".
Conversely, the modifier functioning as an intensifier glossed 'splendid' occurs in the heroic epic but is absent from prayer .
The full inventory of substitution pairs for this deity is:

The relational epithet i-resu huci encodes the deity-to-worshipper bond explicitly: the prefix i- (antipassive / indefinite-object marker) indexes 'me' as the implicit object, so the form is lexically 'the grandmother who raised [me]', positioning the prayer as a speech-act by a person acknowledging filial dependence on the deity.
Using the everyday ape huci in formal prayer would constitute a register mismatch; the substitution is not stylistic variation but a categorical genre requirement .

A self-composed prayer by a Saru–Chitose speaker attests the relational epithet in active ritual use, addressing the fire deity first as the 'raising-deity' and then by the weighty honorific epithet, before the first-person worship verb:
Prayer language is morphologically marked beyond the lexical substitutions.

The inonno itak register is applicative-heavy, encoding the case frame of the verb by applicative prefixes (e-, o-, ko-) rather than by case particles — a hallmark of atomte-itak generally, but especially concentrated in prayer .
The prayer text cited in (§2.3) preserves doubled applicative prefixes on a single verb:

The formal sentence-final frame marks utterances as ceremonial assertions in ritual speech contexts, carrying the assertive-present reading appropriate to public declaration rather than the ordinary inferential use of ruwe ne .
The evidential system underpinning this frame is described in and ; a fully glossed prayer text is given in .

proposes that the non-everyday person marking in Ainu oral literature — the use of fourth-person a=/=an where everyday first-person would use ku= — is rooted in a cultural taboo: a deity or spirit (kamuy) addressing a living human directly transgresses a boundary, and the non-everyday person marking softens that transgression by increasing indirectness.

Satō labels this the indirection principle (間接性の原理), contrasting it with the standard "shamaness-oracle origin" (巫女の託宣起源) theory and presenting it explicitly as a hypothesis rather than an established result ‹speculative›.
For the heroic and divine epic genres that most visibly deploy this device, see .

Whether or not Satō's diachronic hypothesis is accepted, the synchronic functional overlap between the fourth person's honorific use (deferential address to human superiors) and its oral-literary use (narration by divine or supernatural heroes) is structurally coherent: both exploit the same fourth-person paradigm to mediate the speech-act through a form not claimed by the ordinary grammatical first person of the interaction.

The prayer epithet alternation described above operates on the same logic at the lexical level: the worshipper who addresses the fire deity as i-resu huci rather than ape huci likewise routes the address through a relational frame encoding the deity's prior act toward the worshipper, rather than naming the deity in a neutral noun .
Ritual speech-acts are differentiated by the performer's sex in ways that partly overlap with, and partly extend beyond, the narrator-gender allocation for oral-literary genres (treated in ).

Two complementary deferential-acknowledgment acts are documented for the Saru basin: women utter (lower-Saru variant: hunna; degree form < hinna hinna) while performing , a gesture of acceptance offered when receiving food or a gift; men instead perform .
The formal general thanks-form is unmarked for gender (nukopoli, 2024-12-26, asserted).

The polite greeting was traditionally a male greeting accompanied by onkami; its current use across genders in contemporary Ainu speech is described as a "transformed usage" in the context of revitalization .
Prayer (kamuy nomi) is performed exclusively by adult men; seated songs (upopo) are primarily women's performative domain .
The sentence-final particles associated with each genre and gender are treated in .
The existence of a special taboo vocabulary in Hokkaido Ainu — restricted word-forms for hunting, bear-ceremony, and kinship-avoidance contexts — is attested independently in several sources.
catalogues "special terminology including taboo and prayer words" as a vocabulary class of the language.
The 1795 Edo-period record Ezoki is reported in as describing "a kind of secret language" observed among Ainu speakers — an early external testimony to a restricted speech variety.

The primary monographic treatment of this vocabulary is Hattori (1957), "Special language of the older generations among the Ainu" (nenchōshasō tokushugo, 年長者層特殊語), which was not held or consulted in the preparation of this grammar.
No systematic hunting-substitute or in-law name-avoidance word list was recoverable from the read grammars or the aligned corpus ‹speculative›.

What the sources consulted make available is the mechanism — lexical substitution by a genre- or context-conditioned alternate form — and several attested examples from the prayer and epic registers, as described above.
The hunting and bear-ceremony vocabulary, and the kinship-avoidance pairs, remain a gap pending access to Hattori (1957) and to the taboo-marked entries in .

Structurally, the attested substitution cases share a common property: the replacement is a different lexeme or an elaborated periphrastic construction, not a phonological modification of the everyday form.

This is illustrated by the elegant-register periphrases documented in : everyday is replaced in the elegant register by an elaborate circumlocution; everyday is replaced by kamuy ne manu p 'what is said to be a god'.

In each case the substitute form encodes a relational or evaluative frame around the concept rather than naming it directly — a structural parallel to the fire-deity epithet alternation and, plausibly, to the bear-ceremony and hunting-taboo substitutions whose inventory remains undocumented in the consulted sources.
For the broader system of elegant periphrasis and archaic morphology, see ; for the genre contexts in which these registers are activated, see .
The Hokkaido Ainu evidential system — four formal nouns (ruwe, hawe, siri, humi) closing nominalized clauses with the copula or an existential — does not distribute evenly across connected discourse.

Prose folktale (uwepeker), divine epic (kamuy yukar), heroic epic (yukar/ sakorpe), and ritual prayer each impose a characteristic profile on the clause-final slot: which evidential nominal dominates the main-clause boundary, how dense quotative embedding is, and which register-specific frames appear or are blocked.
The constructions themselves are treated in the evidential chapters: the semantics and morphosyntax of ruwe ne in , the reportative frame hawe ne/hawe as in , and the full four-term paradigm in .
Fourth-person narrator marking and its logophoric analysis are treated in and .
The genre taxonomy and verse structure are in , , and .
The present chapter maps those systems onto genre-by-genre distribution.
Across all three narrative genres — uwepeker, kamuy yukar, and yukar — ruwe ne is the unmarked main-clause clause-final.

Dal Corso's Hokkaido reference texts yield 1,508 tokens of ruwe ne out of 2,232 evidential tokens (roughly two-thirds), with the form dominating wherever the narrator presents story-world events as established fact .
In the present Hokkaido corpus the skew is steeper still: 16,350 tokens of ruwe ne beside 796 hawe ne, 607 siri ne, and 200 humi ne ‹corpus-confirmed›.

Community discussion corroborates the distributional pattern: ruwe ne is especially frequent in folktale and legend narration and collocates with the narrative connective akusu 'thereupon' to move the storyline forward (nukopoli, , 2024-11-09, asserted).
Two accounts of this dominance are available and they partially conflict.

Hirosawa argues that ruwe ne marks discourse-new content that the speaker claims as personal knowledge — the form presents a proposition as belonging to the speaker's information territory, which is exactly what a narrator does when introducing each new story-world event .

Dal Corso, treating the same form as a direct evidential of reasoning and knowledge, notes separately that it serves as "the default predicate of the narrative frame-text" because the narrator presents traditional narrative content as shared, knowable fact rather than as ongoing perception or hearsay .
Yoshikawa analyses ruwe ne as the semantically unmarked member of the evidential series, functioning like Japanese のだ/んです to mark episode boundaries and scene transitions ‹contested›.
The three accounts share the structural observation — ruwe ne is the default at main-clause boundaries in narrative — while differing on its semantic driver; the debate is treated in .
The opening frame of prose tales characteristically sets the scene with ruwe ne, sometimes followed by hike 'although; and yet' to signal the adversative turn that opens the main narrative sequence .
Within the episode, ruwe ne marks the close of each foregrounded event unit; the narrative proceeds by chaining these clause-final assertions with akusu or hine into a sequenced storyline.
The perfective a may follow ruwe ne in the post-evidential slot to flag a temporally anterior proposition before the next episode opens, as in … ruwe ne a p 'and (having done) that …' .
Hokkaido Ainu has no tense morphology.
Temporal sequencing in narrative rests instead on the conjunction-aspect apparatus treated in and .
In practice, the distinction between storyline (foreground) and setting (background) falls out from the aspect constructions selected and the connective that links clauses.

Foreground events — the sequential actions that advance the plot — are typically expressed with a bare, uninflected verb form closing the clause, chained into sequences by hine, wa, or akusu, and closed at episode boundaries with ruwe ne ; .

Background material — ongoing states, framing circumstances, simultaneous action — is expressed with durative or resultative aspect constructions: kor okay (have + exist.PL, durative), wa okay or wa an (resultative continuative), and kor an (possessive existential, stative frame).

Satō's analysis of the Abuta/Iburi heroic epic text (narrator 遠島タンケ) shows the same aspect inventory in verse as in prose, confirming that the foreground/background distinction is not genre-specific grammar but the same aspectual system deployed under metrical constraints .
The durative kor okay frames backgrounded action:
The resultative wa okay similarly backgrounds a settled outcome: rok wa okay 'is sitting (has sat down)' (l. 192), yaykoan wa an 'living alone (has settled alone)' (l. 481) .

The pattern is: background clauses use existential-aspect constructions and are embedded under the ongoing narrative frame; storyline clauses use bare verbs (or the prospective anki 'about to') closing with ruwe ne when they constitute an asserted episode-boundary fact.

The prospective auxiliary anki also appears in the Abuta yukar to mark an imminent action — paye-an anki 'I am about to go' (l. 113) — representing the hero's stated intention within direct speech, which is the immediate context for all narrative action in these verse genres .
All three major narrative genres share a defining grammatical feature: the protagonist is indexed not by the everyday first person ku=/=an but by the fourth person a=/=an (Saru and Chitose) ; .

The form is the same prefix set that encodes indefinite reference, second-person honorific address, and inclusive first plural in other contexts; in narrative it indexes the protagonist as logophoric — cast as the direct speech of the hero-narrator — rather than as the actual speaker ; .
See and for the paradigm and its syntactic analysis.

Satō connects the non-everyday person marking to what he calls the indirection principle: the genre convention that the narrative voice is not the actual reciter's but a god's or spirit's (possibly transmitted in a dream), and the non-everyday marker increases the indirectness of that address and softens the implied taboo on a deity speaking directly to a living human ; .
This remains Satō's own hypothesis and stands as an alternative to the older "shamaness-oracle origin" account ‹contested›.
The choice of marker shows a regional split without altering the narrative function.
Saru/Chitose prose tales and heroic epics use a=/=an.

Iburi kamuy yukar — canonically the collection compiled by Chiri Yukie (Ainu Shin'yōshū, 1923, Horobetsu) — uses the exclusive first plural ci=/=as as the singular hero-narrator marker consistently throughout ; .
In Chitose ci=/=as may appear only at the opening before reverting to a=/=an .
A second genre-diagnostic agreement property follows from the use of a=/=an.
In everyday Saru/Chitose =an never combines with a singular verb: the singular form ek 'come' takes ku=/=en (1SG), while arki=an 'we come' (plural + fourth) is well-formed.
In the atomte-itak (elegant) register of verse, ek-an 'I come.SG' is grammatical and serves as the hero's first person, overriding the number-agreement constraint .
This number-agreement override is a diagnostic of verse language and does not appear in prose .
See for the paradigm.
The narrative closes with a retrospective identification formula.

The fourth-person "I" who has narrated throughout is revealed at the end: the narrator supplies the protagonist's name or nature with sekor followed by a speech verb (isoytak 'narrate', ye 'say', hawki 'recite/utter').
At that moment the narration shifts from fourth-person to everyday first person as the reciter resumes her or his own voice ; .

Because narrative runs in direct speech of the protagonist throughout, the quotative is dense at clause boundaries: every speech act, thought, or action declared by the hero-narrator is formally attributed to that voice by sekor + a speech or cognitive verb .
The closing identification formula (sekor isoytak 'so X narrated'; sekor ye 'so X said') terminates the logophoric frame.

isoytak and ye carry different semantics: isoytak means specifically 'narrate/tell a story', while ye is the general speech verb; both are attested at the close of uwepeker (nukopoli and thegodofneet, , 2025-06-03, asserted).

Within the narrator's frame, characters' utterances and attributed knowledge are marked by the reportative evidential hawe ne (direct reportative, voice-POSS + copula) or hawe as (indirect reportative, voice-POSS + existential).
hawe as typically frames a character's state as known by hearsay or mediated inference rather than direct witness ; .
The full morphological analysis is in .

Double evidentiality is a distinctive feature of narrative: a character's hearsay frame hawe as is embedded inside the narrator's assertive ruwe ne, yielding sequences of the type … hawe as ruwe ne 'it is established fact that (it was said that …)'.

Dal Corso identifies this as the pattern in which the narrator ratifies a character's indirect source as shared narrative knowledge — the operator ruwe ne scoping over the already-evidentially-marked inner proposition ‹corpus-confirmed›.

In contrast, the low-reliability indirect frame hawe ne nankor ruwe ne ('it is fact that (it seems to be said that …)') reinforces an uncertain report by wrapping it in the direct evidential, marking that the narrator vouches for the report even if its original source is uncertain .
The four major performative genres differ structurally in metre, refrain ( sakehe), narrator gender, and the clause-final evidential profile.
The following table summarises the genre-conditioned grammatical features documented for Saru/Chitose; regional variants (Iburi ci=/=as, E-Hokkaido sakorpe) are noted in §4 above ; .
Several patterns stand out.

First, ruwe ne is the main-clause evidential across all three narrative genres (uwepeker, kamuy yukar, yukar), confirming that genre does not differentiate the basic narrative evidential but does condition every other structural parameter in the table.

Second, the sakehe refrain inserts between predicate lines in kamuy yukar without interacting morphosyntactically with the evidential construction: the refrain occupies a line-level slot, the evidential closes the predicate, and neither constrains the other .

Third, prayer diverges sharply: the narrator is the human speaker (everyday first person ku=) rather than a logophoric protagonist, and the preferred ceremonial tail is ruwe tapan — a register-marked frame consisting of the trace formal noun plus the demonstrative tapan 'this' (ru-we tapan = 'such is the trace/fact') — rather than plain ruwe ne ; .

Verse genres (kamuy yukar, yukar, prayer) require the atomte-itak (elegant/poetic register), which is distinguished from everyday yayan-itak by four properties: development in 5-syllable verse units, dense use of formulaic phrases to meet syllable count, longer polysynthetic word-forms than colloquial usage, and a distinct poetic lexicon ; .

Register is a continuum keyed to verse-vs-prose and improvisation-vs-fixedness, not a binary: Nakagawa argues that elegant and everyday mark stages on this cline, with prayer phrases and yukar phrases constituting sub-variants of the elegant pole rather than a unified "poetic register" distinct from prayer ‹contested›.
See .

Grammatically, the most diagnostic elegant-register feature is the applicative case-marking system: locative, directional, and other oblique relations that prose encodes with postpositional particles are encoded in verse by the prefixes e-, o-, and ko- applied to the verb .
The choice between prefix and particle is therefore a genre diagnostic — prefix = verse; particle = prose — and applies equally across kamuy yukar, yukar, and prayer.

Prayer is additionally characterised by e-ko- stacks: the Monbetsu prayer text cited by Endō shows ku-e-ko-pase- and k-e-ko-onkami '(I) respectfully worship', layering applicative prefixes in a way unattested in conversational register .
The applicative system is treated in the valency chapters; its genre-distribution is noted here as a cross-cutting marker of elegant language.
The comparative / likening particle kane takes a poetic value in verse that extends beyond its everyday circumstantial use.

In the Abuta yukar, kane introduces similes of the type urar ruyka a-turi kane 'stretching the mist as if a bridge' (l. 136) and kamuy takaramono esik kane 'as if filled with divine treasure' (l. 182) — a comparative use that Satō treats as a yukar-specific extension of the circumstantial particle ‹corpus-suggested›.
A phonetic correlate of genre is the sentence intonation contour.
In conversational register, utterances addressed to an interlocutor tend toward rising intonation, marking expectation of a response.
Folktale narration (uwepeker) is one-directional and shows a flat, low-variation melodic line — a register correlate of the absent interlocutor and the unidirectional narrative address.

Within the Saru basin itself there is geographic variation: upper-Saru (middle-river) narrators are more monotone, lower-Saru narrators more melodically undulating (nukopoli, , 2024-11-16, asserted, citing ).
The verse genres, sung to fixed or narrator-specific melodies, impose melody over phonetic intonation; prose prayer is improvised with a personal melody but is not strictly syllable-metered .
Three issues remain contested or under-documented.

First, the semantic status of ruwe ne in narrative — whether it is an evidential that happens to dominate narrative or a discourse-boundary marker that has been reanalysed from evidential source — is unresolved in the literature: Dal Corso's source-reliability account and Hirosawa's territory-of-information account both handle the distribution but make different predictions at the discourse level ; ‹contested›.
This question cannot be settled here; it is flagged in .
Second, per-genre corpus frequencies of the evidential and TAM constructions are not directly queryable from the available corpus, which is not genre-tagged as a facet.

The whole-corpus token counts reported above (ruwe ne 16,350; hawe ne 796, etc.) include both narrative and non-narrative contexts, and the 86% share of ruwe ne among evidential forms is an upper bound that folds in homophonous lexical uses of the noun ruwe.
Genre-internal counts — confirming, for example, that prayer shows lower ruwe ne density than uwepeker — remain to be computed on a genre-tagged subcorpus ‹speculative›.
Third, the grammar of eastern Hokkaido verse (sakorpe, Tokachi and Kushiro) is documented from few texts.

The Sakaguchi 2018 Tokachi sakorpe (narrator 山本多助) and the Nakagawa white-heron text series (2000–2025) contain the relevant material but have not been fully analysed for evidential and TAM distribution ; .
Whether the Tokachi bare-concept-form preference (ru/sir/haw rather than possessed ruwe/siri/hawe) found in Takahashi's elicited data also holds in sakorpe verse is unknown ‹speculative›.
Ainu is a language isolate: all attempts to establish a genetic relationship with any other language or family have failed .
For an isolate, the comparative method — which enables deep-time reconstruction by aligning cognate sets across related branches — cannot apply when only a single lineage survives.

Three instruments remain available : internal reconstruction, which Alonso de la Fuente calls "by far the most powerful" tool; contact-induced-change analysis, chiefly against Japanese and, on Sakhalin, against Nivkh; and typological reasoning, which carries no independent probatory weight and must be handled with caution.

The reconstruction surveyed here is accordingly shallow in time depth: internal evidence licenses proposals reaching roughly a thousand years into the past, and the one firm external anchor is the thirteenth-century Great Migration that separated the Hokkaido, Sakhalin, and Kuril varieties .
Deeper pre-history — the Pre-Proto-Ainu stage — is reachable only "ad nauseam by internal reconstruction" and cannot be independently validated .
The two primary sources for this chapter are — the monograph-length reconstruction of Proto-Ainu, abbreviated RPA — and the critical revision by (abbreviated "New").

The RPA monograph is not held in the project repository; all RPA reconstructions and associated table references are taken from Alonso de la Fuente's reproductions, and citations of Vovin 1993 therefore carry the reported-evidence status already assigned to that entry.

The genetic-isolate question and the failed macro-comparisons are treated in ; grammaticalization pathways for individual morphemes (the affiliative, the applicatives, the evidential nominals) are in .

Alonso de la Fuente distinguishes three stages , drawing an analogy with the Slavic case (Pre-PA ≈ PIE, PA ≈ Proto-Slavic, Common Ainu ≈ Common Slavic), while noting that only Common Ainu and later can claim anything resembling a running comparative method:

The CA innovations listed by Alonso de la Fuente (Table 19) are: merger of *l and *ɾ to *ɾ; merger of palatalized and plain sibilants (*sʸ, *s > *s); shift of the sibilant before *i; aspiration of *h; and the collapse of *tʸ, *pʸ to *c.
These CA-level changes account for the shared features of all attested Hokkaido lects relative to the older reconstructed stage.
The Hokkaido-internal dialect archaeology built on this foundation is treated in .
Every documented Ainu lect — Hokkaido, Sakhalin, Kuril — has exactly five vowel qualities, a e i o u.

Vovin posited a seventeen-vowel PA system (twelve short plus five long: i ü e ö E a ï ë A O o u plus long counterparts) to regularize what he called the "chaotic" distribution of the affiliative suffix -V: in Vovin's account, the suffix vowel is selected by the last vowel of the base according to a vowel-harmony-like table (RPA; reproduced in Alonso 2022, Table 2).

text: Alonso rejects the seventeen-vowel system on phonetic and historical grounds: the proposed extra vowel qualities leave no trace in the oldest Nara-period loanword layer, and the distributional alternations attributed to them are reassignable to the five basic vowels without residue ‹contested›.

An alternative account of the affiliative -(V)hV shape comes from Janhunen's vowel-dropping hypothesis (Janhunen 2020, reported via Alonso 2022 §2.1): the marker was originally an undefined final consonant *-x; the synchronic shape reflects the lost second vowel of a once-disyllabic base — *CVC.Vx > CVC, but *CVC.Vx > CVC-Vx when the marker follows — and the sequence later fused with the noun hi 'time, place, thing' to yield the current possessive shape.
Alonso calls this "a triumph of internal reconstruction" .

Community discussion on the aynu-corpora Discord has independently noted this as the more parsimonious account, opposing the introduction of a phonemically unmotivated *H (antitwilight, 2024-12-23 ‹contested›).
The morphophonology of the affiliative suffix — its echo vowels, allomorphic conditioning, and distributional constraints — is treated in .
The reconstructed PA vowel system is the same five-quality inventory that all modern lects share ‹consensus›.
Whether PA also had distinctive vowel length is the central suprasegmental dispute, addressed in §6 below.

Contemporary reviews of RPA raised two structural objections: the absence of *w, a phoneme present in every attested Ainu lect (Sidwell 1996, via Alonso 2022 §2.2.3); and the background assumption of an Austroasiatic affiliation that distorted the consonant correspondences (Sidwell 1996, Abondolo 1997, Witczak 1999; all via ).
Alonso de la Fuente's revision addresses eleven correspondence classes .

The most consequential revisions are summarised in the subsections below.
Vovin's word-initial *d- is reinterpreted as a lateral *l- .
Ainu synchronically lacks /l/ — a typological rarity shared in the immediate region only with Japanese.
The key evidence is the Nairo subdialect of ‹SA›, where this class surfaces as t- where all other lects have r-: ‹SA›
Nairo taarak 'smooth' : raarak elsewhere; teera 'wind' : rera.
A lateral that becomes a tap [ɾ] in most environments but a dental stop word-initially in Nairo parallels the Korean lateral distribution.
Early Ainu-to-Ghilyak loans showing Proto-Ghilyak *l- corresponding to RPA *d- provide an independent, contact-based check (RPA 160, via ; for the Nivkh contact background, see ).

Community observation on the aynu-corpora Discord that retar ~ tretar ~ tetar 'white' shows the same initial-consonant split — reconstructing the initial as PA *l (Alonso "New") — is consistent with this analysis (antitwilight, 2024-11-24 ‹contested›).
Vovin's cluster notation *tr- is reanalysed as a single retroflex stop *ʈ- (or retroflex flap ~*ʈɽ) .
The cluster form never appears in ‹SA› sources, where Dobrotvorskij and Piłsudski recorded [tr]~[r].

Decisive phonetic attestation comes from the Bihoro-dialect idiolect of Ginosuke Kikuchi, where the voiced retroflex [ɖ] was still audible when Hattori's team collected data (Hattori 1964: 34, cited via ).
Cognate sets include PA *ʈam.u 'soul', *ʈek.e 'drumstick', *ʈus 'skin' .

Three RPA classes — *g, *hd, and one reflex of *s — converge on h- and s- before i in the attested lects, reflecting the change *w > *h before front vowels (parallel to Greek spiritus asper or Slavic prothetic *h-).
Rather than adjudicating between the two economical analyses, Alonso presents them side by side ‹contested›:
Scenario 1: *hd → *kʷ; *g → *w; one *s class.
Scenario 2: *hd → *w; *g → *s; a palatalized sibilant *sʸ alongside *s.
Both scenarios restore a *w absent from Vovin's inventory — a phoneme present in every attested Ainu lect — which is the principal structural advance over RPA.
Vovin treated word-initial *h- and medial *-ʔ- as separate phonemes.

Following Shiraishi (1999, via Alonso 2022 §2.2.4), Alonso argues they are in complementary distribution: the glottal stop has no lexical function, plays no role in morphonology, and is epenthetic in modern Hokkaido Ainu .
In most HA dialects the initial *h- and *ʔ- merged as laryngeal h-, while medial *ʔ was lost or preserved as an epenthetic glottal.
The phonemic status of the glottal stop in the modern Hokkaido system is discussed in .
Vovin posited a PA consonant *H to account for Bihoro prothetic h- before original vowel-initial stems: Bihoro haspa 'deaf' : aspa, ham 'nail' : am.

Alonso rejects this: prothetic h- in Bihoro is an independent innovation triggered by initial-syllable stress (the typologically common #V → hV tendency, citing Blevins 2008 via Alonso 2022 §2.2.5), and it functions to disambiguate homophones (Bihoro ham 'claw' vs am 'nail', Alonso 2022 Table 8) .
Kuril lects show the converse pattern independently — prothetic h- alongside loss of original h- (Alonso 2022 Table 9) — which further undermines the *H analysis.
Hokkaido microvariation in word-initial h-, including h-elision in eastern standard-accent dialects, is treated in .
Alonso proposes a full Pre-PA palatalized consonant set — *pʸ *tʸ *kʸ *hʸ *sʸ (and possibly *mʸ *nʸ) — which collapsed into modern /c/ etc., analogously to the Latin palatal series in Spanish .
The evidence for *pʸ comes from correspondence class #6 in the table above: southwestern Hokkaido par 'mouth' : northeastern and Kuril car, with Nayoro and Asahikawa having both forms.

This distribution, called the pa-:ca- "pseudo-correspondence" in the dialectological literature because it does not extend to words with other vowels, has at least four competing analyses : Kindaichi and Chiri's diachronic change (*pa → ca); Kirikae's (1994) two-morpheme-ab-initio account; Nakagawa's (1996) priority for ca-; and Fukazawa's (2014/2017) separate-morpheme analysis.
Alonso reconstructs *pʸaɾ as a fifth account, attributing the southwest/northeast split to the collapse of the palatalized labial .
The palatalized-series hypothesis is explicitly typology-driven — posited because the *s/sʸ and *t/tʸ doublets make it typologically expected, not because reflex distributions force it ‹speculative›.
Shiratori's (2026) proposal of PA *ia as a new diagnostic for the palatalized series adds independent support for at least *pʸ and *tʸ ‹speculative›.

Hokkaido Ainu h is an onset segment.
It occurs word-initially — hapo 'mother', huci 'grandmother' — and as the opening consonant of the affiliative suffix -hi/-he/-hu/-ha.
It does not occur as a syllable coda .

The descriptive gap between the two scripts — Hokkaido retaining original coda consonants, Sakhalin replacing them with h — makes the phoneme appear to play an outsized role in cross-dialect description, yet for Hokkaido the question is straightforward: the h visible inside forms such as tek-ehe 'hand (of someone)' or sik-ihi 'eye (of someone)' is suffix-initial, not base-final.
The base consonants — k in tek, k in sik — surface unchanged across all Hokkaido morphological environments ‹consensus›.
The analysis that makes this transparent is Janhunen's (2020, via ) account of the affiliative -VhV.
The proto-Ainu noun base was disyllabic — *tek.e 'hand', *sik.i 'eye' — with a final vowel subsequently lost in the citation form.
When the noun hi 'thing, place, time' fused with the base, the lost base-vowel was restored before the suffix-initial h: *tek.e → tek-ehe, *sik.i → sik-ihi.
The h in the affiliative is therefore the onset of hi, and the suffix vowel harmonises with the base's final vowel: -ehe (base e), -ihi (base i), -uhu (base u), -aha (base a).
The full morphology belongs in and ; the point here is that HA morphology provides no surface evidence for an underlying word-final /h/ on noun stems ‹consensus›.

A separate h-related phenomenon in Hokkaido — the prothetic h- of the Bihoro dialect (haspa 'deaf' : aspa; ham 'nail' : am) — has been analysed as an independent Bihoro innovation driven by disambiguation of initial-stressed forms, not as an archaism or an echo of any coda laryngeal .
It is discussed in the broader consonant inventory in .

In Sakhalin Ainu a systematic coda-weakening rule applies: stop and fricative codas debuccalize to h (p, t, k → h), nasal m merges with n, and coda r is followed by a vowel that opens the syllable ; .
A secondary rule then shifts the resulting coda h to s after a front vowel: HA sik → *sih → sis (‹SA›RA).

Community members nukopoli and aldehyde8908 independently documented these alternations in the aynu-corpora Discord — kor → koh (nukopoli, 2024) and the sik / sis split (aldehyde8908, 2025) — both fully corroborated by ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The mat / mah / mac-ihi triplet is the strongest case for internal reconstruction via the affiliative.
The ‹SA›RA surface form mah would predict an affiliative *mah-ihi, but the attested form is mac-ihi, with an affricate c absent from the citation form of both dialects ; .

The affricate arises from the regular t → c alternation before front i that applies at the morpheme boundary when the ‹SA› uniform affiliative suffix -ihi is appended: the underlying *t surfaces as c before the connecting -i-.
The affiliative therefore functions as a transparent window onto the base consonant that debuccalization hides on the citation form.
In HA, where the affiliative connecting vowel matches the base's own final vowel (a for mat), the same alternation does not arise: HA mat-aha keeps t.

The practical consequence — noted by community member nukopoli (2023, ) ‹corpus-confirmed› — is that ‹SA› concept-form etymology is often unrecoverable from the citation form alone: a surface -h coda could descend from any of p, t, k, or (via the secondary rule) any front-vowel-final stem whose coda lenited to h then shifted to s.
The HA cognate or the ‹SA› affiliative — often both — supply the disambiguation.
The phonemic status of ‹SA› coda h is itself debated.
Alonso de la Fuente transcribes it as a velar fricative /x/, reflecting its realization as [ax], [iɕ], [uf] conditioned by the preceding vowel.

Tangiku and community member thegodofneet (2025, ) treat it as a glottal or pharyngeal breath [h], citing the dialect dictionary's description that only breath, not modal voicing, exits, and raising the further question of whether the coda segment and the word-initial onset h are the same phoneme ‹contested›.

The two transcriptions have no consequence for the diachronic correspondences laid out here, since both agree on the underlying source consonants; but they diverge in the phonological analysis of contemporary ‹SA›
Ainu and its segmental inventory.
The broader consonant inventory discussion is in .
‹SA›-internal variation further limits how far back the debuccalization can be projected.
The Taraika (east coast) and Tarantomari dialects preserve p / t / k in coda position where the main ‹SA› dialects have h, and Esutoru distinguishes -is from -ih .
Debuccalization thus developed within the Sakhalin branch rather than in the common ancestor, and the HA forms represent the conservative retention of whatever coda consonants Proto-Ainu had.
Alongside the consonant correspondences, Hokkaido and Sakhalin diverge in their prosodic systems.
Sakhalin Ainu carries phonemic vowel length in open stem syllables (a aa e ee i ii o oo u uu); Hokkaido Ainu has a pitch accent and no contrastive length ; .

text: Hattori (1967, via ; ) first stated the systematic correspondence: a ‹SA› long vowel in an open stem syllable aligns with a HA high-pitch syllable in the same position.

A closed-syllable constraint qualifies the generalization: where the stem syllable carries a coda consonant (retained in HA, debuccalized to h in ‹SA›), the ‹SA› vowel is short while HA retains the high pitch on that syllable .
The súpki / suhki pair illustrates the closed-syllable constraint directly.

The compound *sup+ki 'reed' keeps a closed first syllable regardless of dialect: in HA, p closes the syllable and the pitch falls on súp-; in ‹SA›, p → h closes the syllable differently but the syllable remains closed, so the vowel is short.
The resulting ‹SA› form suhki shows a short vowel in the first syllable and a coda h, while HA súpki shows high pitch and the original coda p.
The diachronic interpretation of the length–pitch correspondence is the most contested point in proto-Ainu suprasegmental reconstruction.
Three positions are current in the literature, surveyed comprehensively in and addressed in detail in :

(a) Length-first (Hattori 1967; De Boer 2010, both via ): Proto-Ainu had contrastive vowel length and no pitch accent; Hokkaido acquired its pitch system through prolonged contact with Japanese, while Sakhalin preserved the older length contrast.

(b) Both length and pitch (Vovin 1993, via ; ): Proto-Ainu carried both phonemic length and pitch simultaneously; the Sakhalin branch lost pitch under Amur–Sakhalin contact pressure, retaining length; Hokkaido retained pitch and neutralised length.

(c) Pitch-first (Satō 2015–2016, via ): Proto-Ainu had pitch accent only; ‹SA› length is a phonetically conditioned phenomenon restricted to open syllables and represents a Sakhalin-internal development — possibly compensatory lengthening following coda weakening — rather than an inherited contrast.

Alonso de la Fuente's own treatment is internally divided: §2.3 endorses view (c) as "most economical", while §2.4 states that "Hattori was right when he suggested Proto-Ainu had only vowel length, and no pitch accent; pitch accent may be the result of language contact after Japanese influence" — a restatement of view (a) ‹contested›.
The two sections advocate opposite positions without reconciliation; neither can be taken as Alonso's settled conclusion.

Itabashi provides the dedicated historical treatment of the SA-length ↔ HA-pitch diachronic relation; its arguments should be weighed before any definitive account of PA prosody is committed to, and the fuller treatment belongs in .

A trochaic-to-iambic shift hypothesis (Satō 2015–2016; Shiraishi 2017, both via ) adds a further layer: if Proto-Ainu or Common Ainu was trochaic and the pitch accent spread rightward, the resulting iambic system would leave certain archaisms — ‹SA›
noociw : HA nocíw, ‹SA›
niisew : HA niséw (length ↔ low pitch in HA) — as the recoverable fingerprints of the older system.
Community member nukopoli (2023, ) noted the Hattori/Satō dispute directly, identifying the competing claims from within the community's reading of the literature ‹contested›.

Antitwilight (2024, ) takes a position against Satō's posited `*H` segment and prefers Janhunen's vowel-dropping account (see also §1 on the affiliative), arguing that introducing an unattested consonant for the purpose of accounting for exceptional accent is less economical than assuming base-vowel loss ‹contested›.
The pitch-accent system of Hokkaido, including the placement rules and the dialect-internal variation among standard-accent, irregular, and unaccented dialects, is treated in full in and .
The proto-Ainu segmental reconstruction on which the coda correspondences above rest is in , and the broader Hokkaido–Sakhalin dialect picture in and .

For Hokkaido, the orthographic consequences of the debuccalization asymmetry are minimal: HA retains original coda consonants on the surface, and the citation forms write exactly what is heard — tek, sik, cup, mat.
The apparent h that appears medially in affiliative forms is always the onset of the suffix -hi and is morphologically transparent.
For Sakhalin orthography the picture is more consequential.
Writing the citation form as mah, cuh, teh follows the phonetic surface but conceals the base consonant that the affiliative restores and the Hokkaido cognate corroborates.

Thegodofneet (2025, ) proposed writing the underlying p/t/k values directly and reading them as h by convention — a strategy with analogues in French and Korean orthographic traditions, which preserve historically silent consonants as relics of earlier forms.

Aldehyde8908 (2025, ) countered that some ‹SA› subdialects genuinely surface with p/t/k (Taraika, Tarantomari), so writing the surface form is the accurate representation of those dialects, while the uniform h convention would misrepresent them ‹contested›.
The dispute reflects the genuine ‹SA›-internal variation noted above and has no consensus resolution in the sources consulted.
Ijäs addresses the SA–HA affiliative alternation in pedagogical terms, making the base-consonant restoration accessible to learners encountering ‹SA› citation forms for the first time.
Typologically, the ‹SA› debuccalization belongs to a widespread class of coda-weakening processes in which place distinctions are neutralised toward a laryngeal default.

The resulting system — a single coda h for historically distinct p, t, k — would be irrecoverable from ‹SA› alone; the Hokkaido cognates and the ‹SA› affiliative together supply the two independent verification routes that Alonso de la Fuente calls an illustration of internal reconstruction for an isolate.

The genetic position of Ainu — an isolate for which no comparative method in the strict sense applies — makes this type of internal, morphologically mediated evidence especially load-bearing; for the macro-comparative context see .
Ainu is a language isolate (): the comparative method, which requires a set of related languages with regular correspondences, is unavailable.

Three tools remain for recovering Ainu prehistory: internal reconstruction, which exploits alternations, paradigm irregularities, and dialect differences within Ainu itself; contact-induced-change analysis, drawing on the documented Japanese, Nivkh, and Tungusic contact layers; and typological inference, useful as a heuristic but carrying no independent probatory value .
Internal reconstruction is by far the most powerful of the three, accounting for essentially all dialectal differences that can be connected to recoverable earlier forms.
The time depth it can reach is shallow — roughly 1,000 years — bounded by the 13th-century Great Migration that separated Common Ainu into its Hokkaido and Sakhalin branches .

The reconstructible ancestor of the modern Hokkaido varieties is termed Proto-Ainu (PA); the immediate pre-Migration common ancestor is Common Ainu (CA); what internal reconstruction reaches beyond PA through recursive application is termed Pre-Proto-Ainu (Pre-PA).
The segmental inventory and the contested suprasegmental reconstruction (length versus pitch) are treated in ; the SA/KU contrast arising from the 13th-century split is treated in .

This chapter focuses on grammatical morphology: what the alternation patterns within Hokkaido Ainu, together with the SA contrast, allow us to infer about the diachronic sources of bound morphemes and the grammaticalization clines that produced them.
The etymology of Hokkaido Ainu functional morphology is, by comparative standards, unusually transparent.
As Alonso observes, "when it comes to functional words and TAM formatives, the etymology is still transparent" .
The major pathways fall into four structural types.
The theoretical framework for grammaticalization clines, layering, and renewal drawn on here is .
The affiliative (possessed) suffix surfaces in modern Hokkaido dialects as -(V)hV, where both vowels vary with the base in complex ways.
Two analyses of this distribution have been proposed, and the choice between them has direct consequences for the PA vowel inventory.
Vovin (1993, via ) attributed the distributional complexity to a 17-vowel PA system: the suffix vowel was selected through vowel harmony with the final vowel of the base.

The machinery was extensive — twelve short and six long vowels — but all three major reviewers of the 1993 monograph found it unmotivated by the available evidence (Sidwell 1996; Abondolo 1997; Witczak 1999, all via ).
Janhunen (2020, via ) offers a more economical account via internal reconstruction.
Pre-PA nouns were disyllabic: stem *CVC.V#.
When the second syllable reduced and was eventually lost, the lost vowel was reanalysed as an incipient affiliative marker.
Subsequently, the common noun fused with this stranded vowel: base vowel + hi → -(V)hV.
The word illustrates the pathway: PA *tek.e (disyllabic) → tek with loss of second syllable; lost e + hi → affiliative -ehe.
Alonso calls this "a triumph of internal reconstruction" and adopts it as the preferred account, concluding that the PA vowel system contained only the modern five vowels .

Convergent evidence from the ‹SA› varieties supports the underlying hi analysis: in ‹SA›, the base consonant resurfaces in the affiliative form even when it is otherwise debuccalized — sik-ihi 'eye-POSS' rather than the expected *sis-ihi, which would follow from ‹SA›'s regular k → s/_i rule (see ).
The affiliative suffix must therefore preserve access to the underlying base consonant that is otherwise hidden by final debuccalization .
Community discussion records the same pattern: ‹SA›
san + hi = sanihi, makan + hi = makanihi (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-16) , consistent with the hi-fusion account ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The morphophonological details of the modern affiliative paradigm are treated in .

The debate between the two accounts is ultimately ‹contested› rather than resolved: the five-vowel reconstruction has the stronger case given the reviewers' response to Vovin's system, but the internal reconstruction of a lost disyllabic base rests on inferences that cannot be confirmed without a comparative method.

The four formal nouns that build the Hokkaido evidential system — ruwe, hawe, siri, humi — are the possessed forms of four sensory nouns, each of which has grammaticalized into a clause-final evidential predication marker.
The grammaticalization path in each case runs: sensory noun → possessed formal noun → clause-final evidential marker ; ; .

The grammaticalization is not complete: the lexical source meaning remains recoverable, and the formal nouns retain nominal properties (they take the full affiliative suffix: ruwehe, humihi) while losing others (they do not accept demonstrative or attributive modification in their evidential function) .

This partial grammaticalization is reflected in synchronic dialect layering: Tokachi and Ishikari use the bare concept forms ru / sir / haw / hum where Saru and Chitose use the possessed forms, and Horobetsu has extended the possessed forms into conjunctive and adverbial-clause roles ; .
Chiri (1936, via ) already noted the cline from 'there is a trace of X' to 'there is a fact of X' for ruwe.

The dialect distribution encodes the grammaticalization timeline as a spatial stratigraphy: bare concept forms (Tokachi) represent the least grammaticalized stage; possessed forms (Saru) the next; conjunction/adverbial function (Horobetsu) the most advanced.
All three stages coexist synchronically across the Hokkaido dialect space — a textbook case of layering ‹corpus-confirmed›
