The copula that closes the evidential predication also has a grammaticalization history: Alonso identifies it as an anaphoric pronoun that developed a copular function .
This shift is treated in ‹speculative›.
The most transparent set of grammaticalization events in Ainu involves free verbs reanalysed as derivational suffixes on nouns and verbs.
Alonso documents six such suffixes with unambiguous lexical sources (Alonso 2022 §3.1, Table 16; drawing on Dettmer 1989):
The same free verbs continue in full predication and in compound verb constructions, maintaining a synchronic continuum between free and bound use rather than a categorical split.
The morpheme database (mdb.aynu.org) corroborates the overlap: honkor = hon 'stomach' + kor 'have' (conf. 0.85), and the compound verb kor an (progressive) shows the same root in its free form .

Community discussion adds evidence for ongoing productivity of the -kar suffix in action-verbalizer derivations (nimawekar, osorokar, sikayekar, yaykara; nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-12) ‹corpus-confirmed›.

Related pathways in the functional vocabulary follow the same template: > instrumental/comitative particle 'with, by'; > causal conjunction 'because'; hon + tom 'belly + middle' > locative 'in the middle of' .
These are treated in the postposition and clause-linkage chapters; they confirm that the free-to-bound pathway is an ongoing mechanism, not a closed Pre-PA residue.
The existential verb derives from a posture verb meaning 'sit down (SG)'; the suppletive plural corroborates the source, since the SG/PL suppletion retains the posture semantics .
From existential predication, an extends to durative and progressive aspect in the constructions kor an and wa an (see ).
A contested question is whether the personal suffix =an (4th-person intransitive subject; also the inchoative -an in the table above) derives from the same a=~an root.
Nakagawa and Itabashi treat an= as the historically older form from which the reduced a= prefix descends ; .

This derivation is disputed: nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-04-29) notes that the high productivity of a= as an independent prefix weighs against deriving it from the longer an= form, and proposes an independent origin from the existential/aspectual root ‹contested›.
The synchronic person paradigm, where the question bears on its distribution, is treated in .
The nominalizer suffix -p/-pe derives participant nouns and thing-nouns from predicates.
Its lexical source is the free noun , which shifted from independent nominal to clause-final derivational suffix by the same pathway as the evidential formal nouns above .
The synchronic distribution of -p/-pe and the co-occurring event/place nominalizer -i/-hi (< hi 'thing, place') is treated in .

Its morphological analysis is:
The three-way comparison — Saru cep, Horobetsu ciʔep, SA ceh — is Alonso's flagship illustration of the CA→dialect split .
Horobetsu retains the glottal stop *ʔ from CA */ciʔep/, Saru has lost it, and the SA debuccalization (final p > h) is the regular ‹SA› reflex.
That three independent phonological processes left distinct residues corroborates the reconstruction in a way that a single-dialect analysis could not.

A community refinement (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-21) proposes that the ci= prefix in this reconstruction reflects a middle/anticausative rather than resultative function — the same ci= that produces intransitive/middle stems in modern Ainu (see ) — with the semantic reading 'the thing that gets-eaten (by itself)' rather than 'the thing that all eat' ‹speculative›.

Both readings yield 'fish'; the middle-voice alternative is of interest because ci= as a middle prefix is otherwise well-attested in the modern grammar, whereas the resultative/inclusive reading presupposes a PA function of ci= that is less clearly distinct in the modern system.
The applicative prefixes e-, o-, and ko- introduce oblique arguments as core verbal arguments.
They are treated functionally in and individually in , , ; and remain the primary analytical references.
Their diachronic origin Alonso assigns to the grammaticalization of locative/relational nouns into verb prefixes, a widespread pathway typologically ; .

The correspondence is transparent in type — relational nouns shifting into applicative prefixes — but the specific source nouns for e- and o- have not been individually identified with confidence, making the claim ‹speculative› for those two prefixes.
A more structurally ambitious proposal appears in the community discussion.

Antitwilight (aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-06-04) argues that the applicative prefixes were originally pre-nominal, not pre-verbal: certain compound nouns and fixed adverbs of the form *e-ka-nok, *ka-o-suy would then be nominal collocations later reanalysed as verb-prefix constructions when the prefix migrated leftward to the verbal host ‹speculative›.

The hypothesis draws on the well-attested presence of applicative-prefix forms inside nominal compounds in the modern language (see ) but has no direct support in the Handbook sources read for this chapter.
It is noted here as a community-generated lead that warrants investigation of the old compound-noun record before further evaluation.

Internal reconstruction in Ainu proceeds primarily through the synchronic dialect record, where different dialects have advanced different distances along the same grammaticalization clines, leaving stages of a single pathway distributed across the Hokkaido dialect space.
Two contrasting patterns emerge: layering (coexistence of older and newer forms with overlapping function) and renewal (the newer form replaces, rather than supplements, the older).
The evidential nominals are the clearest layering case.

The Tokachi bare concept forms ru / sir / haw / hum, the Saru possessed forms ruwe / siri / hawe / humi, and the Horobetsu conjunctive extensions of the same possessed forms coexist synchronically as three stages of one cline.

The forms at each stage are not synonymous across all contexts, and the distributional differences between stages reveal the grammaticalization constraints: the possessed form (ruwe) has wider contextual distribution than the bare concept form (ru), and the bare form retains combinatorial restrictions that the possessed form has shed ; .
The plural marker in the Saru/Ishikari region illustrates renewal rather than layering.

The older plural form ci (surviving in Horobetsu, Shizunai, Shiranuka) was replaced in the Saru/Ishikari core by an innovated pa, which spread and displaced the older form in those dialects rather than accumulating beside it .
The corresponding ‹SA› form (a)hci is likely the archaic stage, placing ci as intermediate .

The free-verb-to-bound-suffix pathways (§ above) offer the purest layering: the root functions simultaneously as a free transitive verb, as a compound element in the progressive kor an, and as the bound possessive-verbalizer suffix -kor.
No Hokkaido dialect has lost any of these uses; the layers accumulated without replacement.

Reconstruction of a relative chronology for these layers — which function is oldest, and when the bound use separated from the free — remains out of reach given the approximately 1,000-year horizon of reliable internal reconstruction and the absence of any direct chronological evidence internal to Hokkaido Ainu .

Alonso (2022 §3.2), following Austerlitz, Kindaichi, and Chiri (1936), considers whether certain final consonants of body-part and nature nouns are relics of an earlier classifier or noun-class system in Pre-PA.

The proposed class markers include: *k (body/round: tek 'hand', sik 'eye', nok 'egg'); *t (long/rolling: pet 'river', not 'chin', at 'cord'); *m (long/small: kem 'needle', yam 'chestnut'); and *r (elongated: ker 'footwear', sir 'rock') .

Alonso himself rejects the hypothesis on diagnostic grounds: classifier systems typically require that the class marker occur independently as a free morpheme or in some derivational use beyond noun-final position.
Ainu's proposed class-final consonants fail this test — they are invariably noun-final and never function as independent words or derivational triggers.
He concludes that the pattern "illustrates the dangers of wishing to see too much in the data" (Alonso 2022 §3.2).
The word-final consonant inventory of Hokkaido Ainu is phonologically constrained (see and ) but does not cross-classify nouns in any grammatically active synchronic sense.

The productive numeral classifiers of modern Hokkaido Ainu — -p~-pe (things) and -n~-iw (people, from ) — derive from the common nouns pe and aynu through the noun-to-nominalizer pathway already attested in the -p/-pe nominalizer above; they are treated in ‹speculative›.

The Ainu communities documented across Hokkaido in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries show both continuous gradient variation and a set of discrete isoglosses whose distributions do not coincide.

Three research traditions have engaged this situation on different terms: pre-war geography-based groupings; post-war quantitative lexicostatistics producing numerical similarity matrices and dendrograms; and more recent statistical reanalyses of those same matrices with spectral clustering and correspondence analysis, which contest the canonical groupings at several points.
This chapter traces the classification debate and the phonological and morphological isoglosses that underlie it.

The proportional weighting of each variety in the aligned corpus used throughout this grammar is specified in .

applied a 200-item Swadesh-based word list to nineteen localities: thirteen Hokkaido sites — Yakumo, Oshamambe, Horobetsu, Biratori, Nukibetsu, Niikappu, Samani, Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro, Asahikawa, Nayoro, and Sōya — together with six Sakhalin sites and Torii's 1903 Kuril materials.
Cognacy was scored ternarily: matched, unmatched, or uncertain (uncertain = 0.5), and lexical similarity was then the percentage of shared items.
A practical constraint limits the analysis: only 91 of the 200 items actually entered the count, since the remainder showed no cross-dialect stem difference and were uninformative for comparison .
Four conclusions emerged from the Hattori–Chiri matrix .
The gap between Hokkaido and Sakhalin varieties constituted the sharpest division in the data.
Within Hokkaido, Sōya was the variety closest to Sakhalin.
Internal Hokkaido varieties clustered into groupings: {Yakumo, Oshamambe}; {Nukibetsu, Biratori, Niikappu}; and {Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro}.

An east–west gap opened at the Shizunai–Niikappu line — the same boundary that had demarcated the eastern Menas un kur 'people of the east' from the western Sum un kur 'people of the west' during Shakushain's War in 1669 .
recalculated the Hattori–Chiri data by cluster analysis, adding Chitose, and proposed the grouping known as the Major Division.

The first split placed {Hokkaido + North Kuril} against {Sakhalin}; Hokkaido itself divided into four zones: North (Sōya), East (Obihiro / Kushiro / Bihoro / Asahikawa / Nayoro), Central-South (Yakumo / Oshamambe / Horobetsu / Biratori / Nukibetsu / Niikappu), and a marginal position for Samani .
The North Kuril group appeared closer to the NE-Hokkaido cluster than to the Central-South cluster.
Several features of the dataset limit what the cluster analysis can show .
The Sea-of-Japan and Sea-of-Okhotsk coasts have almost no post-Meiji speech records, and several "dialect" rows represent a single consultant's idiolect rather than a community variety.
The site matrix is therefore geographically skewed and thin at the margins ‹contested›.
The most widely cited informal classification, , moves beyond lexicostatistics to incorporate morphological and particle-level indicators.
Tamura divides Hokkaido into two broad zones, with Shizunai on the boundary line:
Northeast: North (Sōya), Central (Teshio, Ishikari), East (Tokachi, Kitami, Kushiro, Eastern Hidaka);
Southwest: South (Western Hidaka, Eastern Iburi), West (Shiribeshi).

The NE/SW axis also tracks the distribution of culture-hero names in oral literature — Okikurmi in the southwest, Samayekur in the northeast — and, more broadly, the genre designations that differ between the two halves .
Whether the literary distribution reflects linguistic divergence, independent areal diffusion, or some combination is not settled by the available sources ‹speculative›.
reanalyses Asai's cognacy matrix (110 items over 21 lects) with Spectral Clustering (MinmaxCut / Mcut algorithm).

The methodological argument is that Asai's matrix is a commutative monoid: only addition and comparison of cognacy percentages are linguistically meaningful; converting them to "dissimilarity" by subtraction destroys information.

Ono further shows that both of Asai's clustering methods (large-linkage, small-linkage) lack identifiability — they produce identical dendrograms for very different matrices because they ignore mid-range values.
Spectral Clustering does not share this limitation.
The result is two groups, not three: Hokkaido (including North Kuril) versus Sakhalin.
The three-way Major Division is not statistically supported ‹contested›.
Within the Hokkaido cluster, North Kuril patterns most strongly with the northeast Hokkaido group — Samani, Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro, Sōya — while southwest Hokkaido forms a second tier.

Ono notes this converges with earlier work placing North Kuril close to northeast Hokkaido, while a separate observation by Satō and Bugaeva (via ) clusters 19th-century Kuril items with the Saru/Chitose zone — a tension the 2020 study does not resolve ‹contested›.
Ono also cautions that Asai's cluster analysis may never have been intended to establish a canonical classification; its standard status in subsequent literature may exceed its original scope.

takes a further methodological step: rather than assigning dialects to groups — which forces a decision about where "boundary dialects" belong — the framework selects a reference dialect, computes similarity from all other lects to that centre, and visualises each variety's "central-dialect-likeness" via correspondence analysis (対応分析) and projection pursuit (射影追跡法).

Applied to Ainu with Sōya (the Sakhalin-facing margin) and Asahikawa (the NE–SW junction) as reference centres, the approach reframes these "boundary dialects" as analytically primary objects rather than residue from a grouping procedure.

The published abstract reports that the isogloss topology around Sōya and Asahikawa is more complex than any single bipartition captures; the full empirical dataset has not been assessed here ‹speculative›.
extends the quantitative tradition to 75 localities, substantially broadening the geographic coverage of the Hattori–Chiri / Asai matrix.
The study — published in Japanese — has not been assessed in full for this chapter; its specific sub-groupings and methodological choices remain to be synthesised ‹speculative›.
