The pitch-accent placement rules are developed in .
Three accent types are attested across Hokkaido :
Standard (Saru, Chitose, Horobetsu, Asahikawa, Nayoro, Obihiro, Sōya): two placement rules — a closed first syllable takes high pitch on σ1; an open first syllable takes high pitch on σ2.
Irregular (Yakumo, Oshamambe): when both σ1 and σ2 are open, high pitch falls on σ3.
Saru ipérekut corresponds to Yakumo iperékut; Saru hopúni to Yakumo hopuní.
Unaccented (Shizunai, Urakawa, Samani, Bihoro, Kushiro, Shiranuka): pitch is non-distinctive.
Samani tends toward final-syllable high; Shizunai shows no syllable-position relation to pitch at all.
The origin of the unaccented type in Hokkaido differs from the Sakhalin unaccented system, where the driver is loss of vowel length rather than loss of pitch (see ).

In the eastern standard-accent dialects, initial h is elided when the pitch accent falls on the second syllable : Saru/Horobetsu huráye 'wash' → uráye in Asahikawa/Nayoro; Saru hokú 'husband' → okú; hekáci 'child' → ekáci.
The conditioning is accentual and areal: Horobetsu, Biratori, Nukibetsu, Niikappu, Samani, and Sōya retain initial h, while Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro, Asahikawa, and Nayoro do not.

The eastern dialects, most extensively Bihoro, show regressive consonant assimilation at morpheme and compound boundaries : hotke 'lie' → hokke (Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro); sirsesek 'hot' → sissesek (Bihoro, Asahikawa, Nayoro); tupte → tutte (Bihoro); upsor → ussor 'bosom'.
The active patterns include tk → kk, pt → tt, rs → ss, ps → ss, kp → pp, and kt → tt.
treats these as historical word-form changes rather than productive synchronic sandhi rules.

A community reading, noting that Bihoro's patterns are non-conditional and lexeme-specific, proposes them as evidence for a distinct underlying Proto-Ainu consonant series (antitwilight, November 2024); the proposal goes beyond the sources consulted and awaits verification ‹speculative›.
A small set of words in the mouth-region semantic field shows a geographic alternation: par (southwest) : car (northeast and Kuril) for 'mouth'; papus / patoy : capus / catoy for 'lip'.
Nayoro and Asahikawa attest both forms.

The alternation affects the labial–alveolar onset position within this semantic field only; there is no comparable p-/c- alternation for e-, i-, o-, u-initial words, which is why call it a pseudo-correspondence rather than a sound correspondence in the comparative linguistic sense.

Place-name evidence from supplies a geographic profile: in the Ishikari watershed, par-type toponyms predominate (11 : 0 against car-type), while Nemuro–Kushiro coast place names are exclusively car-type (13 occurrences).
Community observation independently noted that place names favour car broadly across the northeast and the Kuril data (nishiyasu, May 2026), consistent with ‹corpus-suggested›.
Four analyses of the alternation appear in the literature, and they are genuinely incompatible ‹contested›:
Diachronic merger (Kindaichi, Chiri, Naert 1958, via ): either pa- > ca- historically, or both trace to a single proto-form *Xa-.
Two lexical items from the start (Kirikae 1994, via ): Proto-Ainu already had distinct p- and c- 'mouth' words, later sorted geographically.
ca- as older (Nakagawa 1996, via ): ca- is attested inside par-region place names (e.g.
sanca or ta), suggesting it was the earlier form in that area too.

Separate morphemes ab initio (Fukazawa 2014/2017, via ): ca- and pa- are independent morphemes throughout their full distribution — pa- also means 'head'; irreducible lexical pairs exist (can : pan 'thin', cas : pas 'run').
adds a reconstruction perspective: the split reflects a palatalized series in Proto-Ainu, with *pʸaɾ as the reconstructed form and *pʸ > ca- in one regional stream, *p > pa- in another.

This account integrates the two-morpheme view with the palatalized-series hypothesis (see ), but Alonso himself flags the full palatalized series as typologically motivated rather than philologically forced ‹speculative›.
Additional phonological isoglosses documented by include:
-iw : -uy metathesis — Bihoro and Kushiro: siwnin → suynin 'green'; ciw → cuy 'stab'; nociw → nocuy 'star' (Kushiro); riwka → ruyka 'bridge'.
Vowel alternations — u:o (Sōya opas : standard upas 'snow'); o:e (Yakumo etop : otop 'hair'); V(e,u):i (Samani / eastern sitá : setá 'dog').
Consonant alternations — y:w (Yakumo puwar, nuwe vs standard puyar, nuye); n:m (nimak : mimak 'tooth' — Yakumo, Nukibetsu, and Niikappu use mimak; Sōya ónke : ómke 'cough').
-y elision and extension — Saru/Chitose: plural existential okay → oka, extended to the pronoun ciokay → coka.
Eastern dialects (Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro) show the inverse: particles ka and korka acquire -kay extensions .
Community observation confirms ka → kay as a Kushiro-diagnostic marker (thegodofneet, February 2026) ‹corpus-suggested›.

No phonological isogloss replicates the NE/SW bipartition exactly; each cuts the map at a slightly different line, which is the fundamental reason that "bundle of isoglosses" descriptions are more accurate than a single dividing line.
The sharpest morphological isogloss separates Saru and Chitose from every other Hokkaido variety.
In Saru and Chitose, transitive-verb person marking is carried entirely by prefixes; all other Hokkaido dialects use circumfixes — an object prefix before the stem and a subject suffix after it .
The 'I give to you' cell illustrates the contrast: Saru/Chitose eci=kore (prefix only) versus Horobetsu e=kore=as and Ishikari e=kore=an (circumfix in both).
The implication is that Horobetsu patterns morphologically with the geographically distant Ishikari and Tokachi varieties, not with the adjacent Saru region ‹contested›.

The basic-vocabulary lexicostatistic matrix does not capture this: Hattori–Chiri's 200-item list excluded grammatical words and inflectional paradigms, so the morphological and lexical isogloss pictures diverge at this point.
Horobetsu is lexically Central-South but morphologically northeast.
The full person-marking paradigm and the architectural implications are treated in .
The verbal plural morpheme shows a three-way geographic split :
Sakhalin: (a)hci / hcin (the ‹SA› form; see );
Shizunai, Horobetsu, Shiranuka: ci;
Saru, Chitose, Ishikari: pa.
The historical direction is recoverable: ci is the older Hokkaido form, cognate with Sakhalin (a)hci, and pa is an innovation that spread within the Saru–Ishikari corridor, displacing ci there .
The verbal number system that houses these morphemes and their interaction with the possessed form paradigm are treated in .

Several grammatical morphemes distribute along isoglosses that match neither the NE/SW bipartition nor the lexicostatistic clusters, illustrating how the different layers of dialectal organisation fail to converge .
The allative particle ('toward') takes four attested forms:
un — Yakumo, Horobetsu, Chitose, Biratori, Shizunai;
en — Urakawa, Tokachi, Eastern Hidaka;
(e)ne — Shiranuka, Kushiro, Nemuro, Bihoro, Asahikawa, Sōya, and also Sakhalin and Kuril;
ekota — an Asahikawa alternative form.
The examples below illustrate two of the attested allative forms in running discourse:
The juxtapositional particle newa (and/with) is absent in Saru and Chitose, where bare juxtaposition does the same work.

The successive particle tek functions as a conjunction ('and then') in Shizunai, Samani, Tokachi, Kushiro, Shiranuka, and Ishikari, but as an auxiliary meaning 'do briefly' in Saru, Chitose, and Horobetsu; the Sakhalin cognate teh is the older form (see ).

The conditional particle shows a three-way split: ko (Abuta, Horobetsu, Samani, Kushiro, Shiranuka) vs kor (Tokachi, Ishikari, Saru, Chitose) vs Shizunai konno (< kor-no); ko is reconstructed as the older form .
The cohortative particle is ro in Saru, Chitose, Horobetsu, Yakumo, Asahikawa, Nayoro, and Sōya; rok in Asahikawa, Nayoro, and Obihiro; and no in Urakawa and Samani.
The imperative particle ya (singular) is specific to Ishikari — another morphological feature that cross-cuts the lexical clusters .
, drawing on Nakagawa 1996, classifies the geographic distribution patterns of Hokkaido isoglosses into six types:
Eastern–Western (approximating the NE/SW bipartition): par / car 'mouth'; hempak / nempak 'how many'; hempara / nempara 'when'.
The western form nempara itself derives by analogy with the ne- indefinite root (h- → n-) and is therefore a secondary innovation even within the western zone.
ABA (peripheral conservatism, central innovation): aw (peripheral) vs parunpe (central) 'tongue'.
The compound parunpe (lit. 'mouth-inside-thing') spread from the par-region and displaced aw in the centre while the older form survived at the edges.
Saru–Chitose island: interrogatives hemanta 'what', hunna 'who'; plural existential oka; indefinites nep / nen; prefix-only person marking.
These features cluster in Saru–Chitose but are absent or replaced in surrounding varieties.

Saru–Chitose + Sakhalin: the interrogative hemata 'what' and the prefix eci- '1→2' appear in Saru–Chitose and distant Sakhalin but not in the geographically intervening Hokkaido varieties — a bridge distribution that describe as "hard to believe independent", though the historical mechanism is unresolved ‹speculative›.
Pacific Coast: mici 'father' in a strip running from the Kuriles through Horobetsu, crossing the east–west divide; the place-name cluster koyka / koypok (Yamada 1982) follows a similar path.
Ishikari Watershed: isolated innovations within an inland corridor, e.g.
iyapo 'father' at the Saru river mouth.

The interrogative morphology receives special attention in : most Hokkaido interrogatives are historically indefinite pronouns repurposed via focus particles, while Saru and Chitose retain a two-stem system with a distinct interrogative root hVm / hVn and an indefinite root ne-.
Community discussion independently segmented hunna as hun + na, hunak as hun + yak, and hempak as hem + pak (nukopoli, December 2023), corroborated by the sources.

A community-proposed case for a 'bone' ABA distribution is worth noting: pone in Hokkaido versus poni in Sakhalin and Kuril, with La Pérouse 1787 Pauni as a candidate early Sakhalin attestation (antitwilight, June 2026 ‹speculative›).
The ABA reasoning is methodologically sound, but the forms and site attestations require independent verification before the proposal can be taken further.

Saru and Chitose emerge from all classification approaches as a coherent subgroup, though the extent to which this distinguishes them from all other Hokkaido varieties or only from their immediate neighbours remains contested.
The lexicostatistic matrix places Saru and Chitose together with Biratori, Nukibetsu, and Niikappu in the Central-South cluster.

Morphological features — prefix-only transitive marking, plural pa, the contracted pronouns kani (< kuani) and coka (< ciokay), distinct interrogative stems, and the 4th-person singular pronoun asinuma — constitute a cluster that maps poorly onto the lexical groupings ‹contested›.
The Saru–Chitose + Sakhalin bridge (shared hemata, eci-) is the outstanding puzzle in the classification.
Parallel independent retention of an archaic form, coastal-route areal contact, or early divergence before the northeast varieties had innovated are all consistent with the distribution.
The genetic relationship between Hokkaido and Sakhalin and the historical branching order are discussed in and .
Sakhalin and Kuril data appear in the classification literature as calibration points for Hokkaido-internal distances.
The one result robust across all methods is that the Hokkaido cluster is more internally cohesive than its gap from Sakhalin ; .

places Sakhalin's divergence from Common Ainu at roughly 800 years and Kuril's at under 600, consistent with the Satsumon-culture migration chronology — Kuril is historically as well as structurally closer to Hokkaido.
The Sakhalin-specific features that calibrate the gap — final-consonant debuccalization (sik 'eye' → ‹SA›
sis; cup 'sun/moon' → ‹SA›
cuh), the vowel-length to pitch-accent correspondence, and the Nairo r- → t- archaism — are documented in full in and .
The reconstruction of the stage from which Hokkaido, Sakhalin, and Kuril all diverged is the subject of .
Northern contact (Nivkh, Tungusic, Manchu) is primarily a Sakhalin phenomenon and is treated in .
All quantitative classifications rest on the matrix of , collected at thirteen Hokkaido sites.
The matrix has documented limitations .
The Sea-of-Japan and Sea-of-Okhotsk coasts lack post-Meiji speech records; only one northern site, Sōya, is included, and it was documented from a single consultant.
Several "dialect" rows represent a single speaker's idiolect rather than a community variety.
Place-name evidence from supplements documentary records for areas without spoken materials, but place-name attestations and 20th-century speech data are chronologically incommensurable.
The corpus used throughout this grammar (209,878 sentences) is weighted heavily toward Saru (77,964 sentences) and Shizunai (43,346), with all other varieties together making up the remainder.
Eastern and northern forms — Tokachi allative en, the Kushiro particle extension kay — appear too infrequently for distributional analysis.
The corpus weighting and its implications for frequency counts are specified in .

The philological programme initiated by and the Chiri-family manuscript archive offer one corrective: historical documents (Kaga-ke, Matsuura, Mamiya) and the Hattori 1964 comparative dialect dictionary preserve regional forms not captured in post-WWII speech data.
Lexical dialectology drawing on these sources is treated in .

The thirteen Hokkaido Ainu localities surveyed by show fine-grained phonological differences that cross-cut — and in some cases run orthogonal to — the northeast/southwest bipartition established by .
§3 catalogues these systematically in a set of isogloss tables whose data derive ultimately from and .

Four domains carry the phonological distinctiveness: suprasegmental type (pitch-accent vs unaccented), word-initial consonant elision, consonant-cluster assimilation, and a pair of well-known segmental alternations (pa- ~ ca- and -iw ~ -uy).
Vowel quality and the distribution of a few morphophonological alternations add further dimensions.
None of the isoglosses coincides precisely with the others, which is why prefer a framework of gradient boundary dialects over a partition into discrete named groups.

The consonant inventory common to all Hokkaido dialects is set out in ; the vowel system in ; pitch-accent placement rules of the dominant standard type in ; and the overarching dialectometric classification in .
Proto-Ainu reconstructions invoked here are from .

The most fundamental suprasegmental split within Hokkaido divides the field into three accent types: a standard type shared by the majority of documented localities, an irregular type in the far southwest, and a set of unaccented varieties on the east coast and in part of the west .
In the standard type, a closed first syllable draws the high pitch to σ1; an open first syllable places it on σ2.
The rules operate on the bare lexical stem; cliticized person prefixes shift the accent domain (see ).
The Saru–Chitose instantiation of this type is the baseline described by and the system treated in .
The geographic spread of the standard type is non-contiguous.

The Saru–Chitose group in south-central Hokkaido, Horobetsu on the west coast, the inland Asahikawa–Nayoro corridor, and the eastern Obihiro dialect share identical accent rules despite the intervening unaccented belt.

Sōya, at the northern tip of Hokkaido, also belongs here — a significant fact given that Sōya is the Hokkaido locality most closely cognate to Sakhalin in the lexicostatistic matrices of and the dialectometric reanalysis of .
When both the first and second syllables of a word are open, Yakumo and Oshamambe place the high pitch on the third syllable rather than the second.
The contrast with the standard type is audible on identical lexical stems :
The contrast recurs in verbs: Saru hopúni 'fly' vs Yakumo hopuní.

Whether the irregular pattern is a phonological innovation at Yakumo/Oshamambe or an archaic retention from a stage before the standard rule spread has not been settled; neither has any synchronic account of what structural property of consecutive open syllables triggers the shift ‹contested›
Six localities — Shizunai, Urakawa, Samani, Bihoro, Kushiro, and Shiranuka — have been described as lacking phonologically contrastive pitch at the lexical level.
The description requires qualification: Samani tends toward a final-high pattern in practice; Shizunai shows no stable positional pattern across the lexicon .

These varieties did not lose their accent through the same mechanism as Sakhalin Ainu, where the absence of pitch correlates with the retention of vowel length (and a long-vowel/high-pitch correspondence with the standard Hokkaido type; see ).

In Hokkaido, the unaccented dialects appear to represent a secondary pitch-neutralization within a variety that had already developed the pitch-accent system — the opposite direction from Sakhalin's retention of length as the suprasegmental distinction ‹contested›
The broader prosodic comparison with Sakhalin is taken up in .
In eastern standard-accent dialects — Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro, Asahikawa, and Nayoro — a word-initial h is absent when the accent falls on σ2, that is, when σ1 is open.

The elision environment is exactly the standard-type accent context where the initial consonant carries no pitch-peak information; western and southern dialects (Horobetsu, Biratori, Nukibetsu, Niikappu, Samani, Sōya) retain h throughout :

The synchronic status of the glottal onset that phonetically precedes the initial vowel in some realizations of the eastern forms varies by dialect and speaker and connects to the analysis of ; the relevant point here is that h is absent as a segment, not merely reduced ‹corpus-suggested›

The most geographically concentrated consonant alternation in the Hokkaido field is a set of regressive assimilation processes converting heterorganic clusters at morpheme junctions into geminates or homorganic sequences.
The alternations are confined to the northeast and are most extensive in Bihoro :

treats these as historically altered word-forms specific to those localities — lexical entries in the Bihoro dialect — rather than as the output of a productive synchronic sandhi rule applying across the board.

A community discussant takes a different interpretive direction, suggesting that the geographic concentration of the pattern in Bihoro points to an underlying "proto-phoneme" (an ancestor consonant distinct from both of the modern alternants) whose collapse produced the heterorganic clusters later simplified by assimilation ‹speculative›
(antitwilight, 2024-11-17).
The relationship of the assimilated forms to the broader coda-sandhi phenomena described in has not been worked out.

One of the most discussed phonological isoglosses in the Hokkaido field is the distribution of pa- and ca- in a small set of words related to 'mouth': par (southwest) and car (northeast) 'mouth', papus ~ capus ~ patoy ~ catoy 'lip'.
Nayoro and Asahikawa attest both forms, marking the interior transition zone .

The phenomenon is formally restricted: there is no comparable pe-/ce-, pi-/ci-, or po-/co- correspondence in the lexicon, which is why call it a "pseudo-correspondence" rather than a sound correspondence in the strict sense.
Place-name evidence corroborates the geographic split: records eleven par-type place names against zero car-type in Ishikari; in Nemuro and Kushiro the ratio reverses (thirteen car-type).
The Kuril attestations — Krasheninnikov 1738 and Golovnin 1811 — record car for 'mouth', consistent with the northeastern and eastern distribution.
gives par as the Saru concept-form, with the possessed form paro-ho.
Four analyses of the alternation have been proposed ‹contested›:
Kindaichi, Chiri, and Naert 1958 (via ): a diachronic change pa → ca, or the reconstruction of a single Proto-Ainu syllable *Xa (with an indeterminate initial consonant).
: Proto-Ainu already had two distinct 'mouth' lexemes; the par and car forms are not cognates but separate vocabulary items with overlapping reference.

Nakagawa 1996 (via ): the ca- form is the older one, evidenced by its appearance in place-names and formulaic expressions (sanca or ta) inside otherwise par-using regions — an ABA distribution where a central innovation displaced the peripheral retention.
: ca- and pa- were always distinct morphemes, with irreducible minimal pairs can:pan 'thin' and cas:pas 'run' coexisting in the same dialects with distinct phonological histories.

§2.2.6 reconstructs PA *pʸaɾ for 'mouth', treating the p/c split as a relic of a Proto-Ainu palatalized consonant series in which *pʸ shifted toward c in the northeast; this reconstruction is typologically motivated rather than philologically forced ‹speculative›.

A community discussant proposes a related but distinct mechanism: that the alternation reflects a Proto-Ainu syllable *ti, whose labialized variant underwent palatalization via an intermediate glide (*pj → *tj → c), overlapping with Alonso's palatalized-series account but positing a glide intermediate ‹speculative›
None of the four analyses has achieved consensus.
Bihoro and Kushiro show a systematic alternation in which the sequences -iw and -uy are transposed relative to the forms recorded elsewhere :
The base form has a glide following the vowel (iw); the Bihoro/Kushiro form has the vowel following the glide (uy = u + y).
The alternation is limited to these two unaccented eastern dialects; standard-accent dialects do not participate.

Additional, lexically specific metatheses occur in other dialects without forming a regular alternation: piyar / puyar / puray 'window' (three variants across the field), nipek / nupek / nikep 'light', and askepet / aspeket 'finger' (Horobetsu) .
Their relationship to the -iw/-uy set is unclear.
Two further consonant alternations are documented across the dialect field.
First, y and w alternate in a small set of lexical items in the Yakumo area: puyar and nuye where most dialects have puwar and nuwe .
This remains lexically specific.
Second, n and m vary in particular words and localities: nimak ~ mimak 'tooth' (Yakumo, Nukibetsu, and Niikappu favour mimak); and ómke ~ ónke 'cough' at Sōya versus other dialects .

A community discussant observes that the change mi → ni (or its inverse) appears broadly in Hokkaido and suggests the epicentre may lie in the Horobetsu area, where long-distance assimilation could be the operative mechanism ‹corpus-suggested›
That hypothesis is consistent with the nimak/mimak distribution but requires systematic corpus verification before it can be stated as established.

An isolated consonant-copying phenomenon produces Sōya purár against the more widespread puwar 'fog/mist'; and the alternation hútne ~ Bihoro húpne 'narrow' represents a C:p correspondence that remains lexically isolated .

Simeon's fieldwork of June–July 1967 on Hiratori, Horobetsu, and Higashi-Shizunai — the informants were Kayano Shigeru, Itaku Haru, and Sasaki Taro — records a set of sub-phonemic differences among three southern dialects that later descriptions rarely separate .

Intervocalic voicing of the obstruents runs along a gradient: Higashi-Shizunai shows [b d g dʑ] most freely (hapo [habo] 'mother', ante [ande] 'put down', yakun [jagun] 'if', eci [edʑi] 'you (pl.)'), Horobetsu less often, and Hiratori hardly at all.

The [ɸ] realization of /h/ before /u/ is constant in Horobetsu and Higashi-Shizunai and optional in Hiratori (hure [ɸure] 'red'); final /n/ surfaces as [ŋ] in Horobetsu and Higashi-Shizunai (kotan [kotaŋ]); and in Horobetsu the contrast of /h/ and /s/ is neutralized before /i/, giving free variation of the type unihi ~ unisi '(my) home' — the same sibilant–laryngeal instability treated in .
These observations carry a caveat.

Except for Kayano, Simeon's informants had seldom spoken Ainu for decades, all were bilingual, and no acoustic verification was made; a gradient of intervocalic voicing in particular could reflect Japanese interference or moribund-speaker variability as easily as an old isogloss.
The record is best read as a dated snapshot of individual speakers, valuable precisely because each is localized and named ‹speculative›.
Vowel quality shows inter-dialectal variation without organizing into simple geographic zones.
§3.5 (Tables 9–11) documents three vowel-pair alternations:
These vowel variations do not produce a coherent geographic split comparable to the accent types or the h-elision isogloss.

Sōya (northwest) and Yakumo (southwest) both show o/e alternations but in different lexical items and different directions; Bihoro (northeast unaccented) and Samani (east unaccented) share i-raising in different words.

The irregularity is consistent with the lexicostatistic picture: only 91 of the 200 Swadesh-list items used by showed any cross-dialect stem differentiation, meaning that the majority of the basic vocabulary is shared across all localities without alternation .

One fine-phonetic observation, currently unsystematically documented, concerns the Mukawa recordings, where i is realized as [e] and e as [ɛ] throughout — a general-lowering pattern not reported from other localities and suggesting a dialect-level phonetic shift beyond the sporadic lexical alternations above ‹corpus-suggested›
In Saru and Chitose, the plural existential okay reduces to oka by elision of the final -y; the same elision extends to the pronoun ciokay → coka .
This is not a general rule affecting all -ay-final sequences; it is confined to this functional item and its derivatives.
In the eastern dialects (Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro), the pattern runs in the opposite direction.
Particles that appear as ka, yakka, and korka in standard dialects acquire a final -y: kay, yakkay, korkay .

The geographic separation of the two changes — southwest elision, east extension — argues against treating them as a single diachronic development; they are most plausibly independent innovations at opposite ends of the dialect field.
The isoglosses surveyed above do not partition Hokkaido into a clean binary or ternary arrangement.
Each phenomenon has its own geographic distribution, and the bundles of overlapping isoglosses reproduce only approximately the northeast/southwest bipartition of .
A summary of the main isoglosses and their geographic alignment:
Bihoro occupies a distinctive structural position.
It is unaccented, shows the -iw/-uy metathesis, and carries the most extensive cluster assimilation — yet also shares the car-type 'mouth' with the northeast and the eastern particle extension.

The independent prothetic h that Bihoro developed on certain vowel-initial forms (Bihoro haspa 'deaf', ham 'nail' vs general aspa, am) is a separate localized innovation analysed by §2.2.5 as a prothetic strategy to disambiguate homophones — distinct from the original h elided in the surrounding eastern dialects.
Two "boundary dialect" positions merit specific mention.

Sōya (the ‹SA›–HA border) combines standard-type accent and h-retention with some northeastern vowel forms (opas for 'snow') and one cluster-assimilation form (sirpokke), placing it between northeast and northwest on multiple phonological parameters simultaneously.
Asahikawa (the NE/SW interior border) has standard accent, eastern h-elision, both par and car, and the rs→ss assimilation — again a profile that spans the main isogloss bundles.
argue that such localities are better treated as reference points for measuring gradient similarity than as dialect members to be assigned to one group.
The car-type's correlation with Kuril forms — Krasheninnikov (1738) and Golovnin (1811) ‹KU› both record car — and the Sōya–Sakhalin closeness in the lexicostatistic matrices are taken up in .
The morphological isoglosses that partially parallel the phonological division — in particular the Saru/Chitose prefix-only person marking — are described in .
The overall picture is one of overlapping, non-coextensive isoglosses producing a dialect continuum rather than discretely bounded varieties.

This is consistent with 's finding that the three-way "Major Division" (Hokkaido/Sakhalin/Kuril) does not survive statistical testing and that even within Hokkaido the internal structure is gradient — a conclusion that the multi-parameter isogloss geography here supports at the segmental and prosodic levels ; .
The systematic comparison of lexical variation across Hokkaido Ainu rests on a survey carried out by Hattori Shirō and Chiri Mashiho in 1960.

Working from a 200-item basic-vocabulary list elicited at 19 localities — 13 across Hokkaido and 6 in Sakhalin ‹SA› — together with Torii's 1903 Kuril ‹KU› materials, they scored each item for cross-dialectal cognacy as positive, negative, or partial ().
The 13 Hokkaido localities were Yakumo, Oshamambe, Horobetsu, Biratori, Nukibetsu, Niikappu, Samani, Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro, Asahikawa, Nayoro, and Sōya.

The resulting cognacy percentages supplied the first quantified measure of lexical distance between Hokkaido varieties and remain the empirical layer beneath every subsequent dialectometric classification.
The survey's reach is narrower than the item count suggests.
Of the 200 elicited items, only 91 actually contributed to the cognacy matrix — the remaining 109 showed no cross-dialectal stem difference and therefore carried no discriminating information ().

Those 91 variable items are the effective data for Hokkaido lexical dialectology: a diagnostically rich but typologically restricted window, concentrated on body parts, basic environmental vocabulary, and core verbal concepts.
Two further resources expand and document the survey results.
Hattori's 1964 dialect dictionary () organized the comparative material across the 19 localities into a single reference work, giving paradigmatic forms and attestations for each item.

Fukazawa (2025) has since brought to light a previously unpublished document: Chiri Mashiho's own handwritten and annotated copy of the basic-vocabulary survey tables, preserved at the National Ainu Museum ().

These tables, covering at minimum the Yakumo, Oshamambe, and Horobetsu localities, carry Chiri's marginal variant readings and hesitation marks, providing a check on the published cognacy scores and revealing forms that may have been suppressed in the final scoring.
The geographic distribution of the 13 Hokkaido localities is uneven.
The Pacific coast and the Ishikari–Hidaka corridor are represented by multiple sites; the Sea-of-Japan coast contributes only Yakumo, and the Sea-of-Okhotsk coast only Bihoro.
The northernmost point, Sōya, was effectively a single speaker — Ben Kashiwagi — so its data reflect an idiolect rather than a community sample ().
Many areas that certainly held Ainu-speaking populations into the nineteenth century, particularly along the Sea-of-Japan coast, left no post-Meiji lexical record at all ‹corpus-suggested›.

Kasuga's 2026 expansion to 75 localities, incorporating place-name evidence and historical documents, begins to fill some of these gaps (), but systematic multi-speaker lexical data from the poorly attested regions remain largely absent.

The place-name record is geographically broader than the spoken-language survey, though it introduces its own complications: toponyms reflect an earlier language state, their orthographic conventions vary across sources, and phonological changes may have operated differently on frozen names than on the living lexicon ‹speculative›.
Mapping the 91 variable items across the 13 survey localities produces several recurrent distribution patterns.
Nakagawa and Fukazawa, building on Nakagawa's earlier geographic analysis, distinguish five types ():
These five types do not bundle neatly into coinciding isoglosses.
Each lexical item can produce a different boundary, with particular localities appearing in opposite groups depending on which item is considered.
This non-congruence is consistent with a dialect continuum undergoing diffusion from multiple centers rather than a single ancestral branching event (; ) ‹contested›.
The most robust lexical signal dividing northeastern from southwestern Hokkaido is a set of interrogative and temporal stems.
The southwestern dialects (including Saru, Chitose, Horobetsu, and Yakumo) use interrogative stems beginning in hem- / hen-: 'when' is hempara and 'how many' is hempak.
The northeastern dialects (Asahikawa, Nayoro, Sōya, Obihiro, Kushiro, and Bihoro) use ne--initial forms: nempara and nempak ().
The Saru–Chitose group adds its own specific interrogatives: hemanta 'what', hunna 'who'.
Nakagawa and Fukazawa read the interrogative distribution as a diachronic contrast.

The Saru–Chitose group preserves two etymologically distinct stems — an interrogative hVm- / hVn- base and a separate indefinite ne- base — while most northeastern dialects generalized the indefinite stem to interrogative function, yielding ne-mpara by analogy with other ne- indefinites ().
On that analysis the southwestern and Saru–Chitose patterns are retentions and the northeastern forms are innovations ‹contested›.

Community discussion at the aynu-corpora Discord independently arrived at the same two-stem analysis — interrogative hem / hun versus indefinite ne — and further segmented hunna as hun + na and hempak as hem + pak (, nukopoli 2023-12-08, proposed).
The segmentation is corroborated by the comparative data in Nakagawa and Fukazawa's analysis ‹corpus-confirmed›.
A morphological item that closely parallels the lexical NE/SW divide is the allative postposition.

Southwestern dialects use un; eastern Hidaka and Tokachi use en; and the northern and far-eastern dialects (Sōya, Asahikawa, Bihoro, Kushiro, Nemuro) use ne or its extended form, with Asahikawa additionally using ekota ().

Because this particle distribution matches no other lexical or morphological isogloss exactly, it functions as one of the single clearest indicators for locating an undescribed text within the Hokkaido dialect area.
The allative alternation is treated as a morphological isogloss here rather than a purely lexical one because the variation involves bound grammatical morphemes, not independent lexical stems.

Its geographic distribution nevertheless contributes to the same east–west picture that the basic-vocabulary survey drew, and the two types of variation align without being identical — a further demonstration that no single isogloss bundle defines the Hokkaido dialect area as a whole.
Among the lexical differences documented by the survey, the word for 'mouth' has attracted the most analytical attention.
Southwestern Hokkaido dialects use and its affiliative form paro; northeastern dialects, Sakhalin ‹SA›, and Kuril ‹KU› varieties use and caro.
The related body-part terms follow the same division: 'lip' is papus / capus or patoy / catoy depending on region ().
The contrast superficially resembles a regular sound correspondence between a southwestern /p/-initial and a northeastern /c/-initial dialect group, but it does not behave like one.

No other set of unrelated Hokkaido words shows the same /p/ ∼ /c/ alternation in any systematic pattern; the variation is restricted to the 'mouth' semantic cluster and a small number of body-part and motion terms (can / pan 'thin'; cas / pas 'run').
Nakagawa and Fukazawa therefore call it a "pseudo-correspondence": it is geographically distributed like a sound change but is not phonologically general ().
Four analytical positions have been advanced for the origin of the split, all reported here via Nakagawa and Fukazawa ():
Single-change account (Kindaichi, Chiri, Naert 1958): a historical change *pa > ca propagated through the northeastern region, or both derive from a single ancestral form *Xa.
Two-'mouth'-words account (Kirikae 1994): Proto-Ainu already had two distinct words for 'mouth'; their regional distribution is a fossilized retention of this original synonymy.
Age-area / ABA account (Nakagawa 1996): car is the older form, preserved at the northeastern periphery and in ‹SA›/‹KU›, and retained in Saru-region place names (e.g.
sancaorta); par is a Saru-Hidaka innovation that spread through the southwest, eventually producing the compound par-unpe 'tongue' (lit. 'that-which-lies-in-the-par-region').

Two-morpheme account (Fukazawa 2014/2017): ca- and pa- were separate morphemes from the outset, each appearing across a range of body-part and spatial vocabulary (pa- also meaning 'head'), so the alternation reflects a productive morphemic distinction rather than a lexical split or sound change.
All four accounts rest on the same survey dataset and on place-name evidence with its own chronological uncertainties; none can be ruled out on the available materials ‹contested›.

Place-name counts — 11:0 in favor of par- in the Ishikari basin, 13 instances of car- in Nemuro and Kushiro combined (Kirikae 1994, reported via ) — are consistent with a sharp geographic boundary but do not settle the mechanism.

A community discussion at the aynu-corpora Discord (nishiyasu 2026-05-07, proposed) independently observed that place-name distributions favor car in the northeast and east, strengthening the place-name evidence without resolving the analytical question () ‹corpus-suggested›.

A further phonological account, not among the four original proposals, reconstructs a Proto-Ainu palatalized initial *pʸaɾ, whose northeastern reflex yielded /c/ while the southwestern region generalized plain /p/ (reported via ) ‹speculative›.

A community member (nukopoli 2023-12-08) independently proposed a related palatalization pathway via a reconstructed intermediate *ti (, proposed) ‹speculative›; the two mechanisms converge in positing a palatal intermediate but differ in the structural details.
Several variable items show an ABA distribution: the same form occurs at the geographic margins of Hokkaido — both east and west — while a different form occupies the center.

Under the wave-model reading standard in Japanese dialectology and adopted here by Nakagawa (reported via ), the peripheral form (A) is typically the older retention and the central form (B) is an innovation that has not yet completed its spread to the edges.
The word for 'tongue' is the primary example.
The peripheral dialects — Yakumo in the southwest, Kushiro and Bihoro in the east — retain .
The central dialects, including Saru, Chitose, Horobetsu, and Asahikawa, use parunpe, a transparent compound: literally 'that which lies inside the par region / the mouth-interior'.

The ABA reading takes aw as the form reconstructable for pre-innovation Hokkaido and parunpe as an innovation coined in the par-using southwestern area and spreading outward without displacing aw at the farthest edges () ‹speculative›.

That interpretation is also consistent with the Nakagawa 1996 age-area account of the par / car alternation: if par 'mouth' is itself an innovation displacing car, then parunpe 'tongue' (par + locative/relational element) is a secondary compound built on that innovation and will share the same geographic profile — which is exactly what the survey data show ‹speculative›.
The 'father' terms offer a second, less clear-cut case.
The form mici appears along the Pacific Coast arc from the Kuril Islands through the eastern coast to Horobetsu, a distribution that cuts across the NE/SW divide.
The form iyapo is recorded at an isolated inland point near the Saru river mouth.

Yamada's proposed "Pacific Tribe" — a hypothetical coastal population whose lexical traces are visible in forms like mici and in place-name elements (koyka / koypok) — is a speculative interpretation of this coastal continuity (reported via ) ‹speculative›.
The 91-item variation set is limited to high-frequency basic vocabulary.

Systematic cross-dialectal comparison in other semantic fields — animal and plant names, technological vocabulary, ceremony-related terms — is absent from the survey, and the dialect dictionary () covers the same 19 localities but does not extend systematically beyond the survey items.

The domain of place names has been used as a partial supplement: because toponyms encode older vocabulary and are geographically pinnable, they allow isoglosses to be reconstructed for areas with no living-speaker data.
Fukazawa's 2025 edition of Chiri Mashiho's annotated survey tables () adds a qualitative dimension to the Yakumo, Oshamambe, and Horobetsu data.

Chiri's marginal notes reveal the range of variant forms that a skilled lexicographer heard during elicitation but collapsed in the final binary cognacy score — information that the published 1960 dataset conceals.

This document is a significant resource for reassessing the resolution of the survey data, though it covers only three southwestern localities and cannot compensate for the absent data from underattested regions.

One kinship term deserves note as a clear inter-dialectal lexical isogloss outside the basic-vocabulary list: the terms for 'father' (see above, §aba-patterns) and the broader kinship vocabulary in general have not been systematically mapped across the survey localities.
Regional variation in kinship terminology is attested in scattered sources but lacks a comprehensive comparative treatment comparable to the basic-vocabulary survey ‹corpus-suggested›.

Within the southwestern zone, the Saru–Chitose group shows a cluster of lexical and morphosyntactic innovations that set it apart from neighboring Horobetsu and Biratori, even though basic-vocabulary cognacy alone would place Saru, Chitose, and Horobetsu in a common southwestern group.

The distinctively Saru–Chitose items include the interrogative forms hemanta 'what' and hunna 'who', the existential plural oka, the indefinites nep 'something' and nen 'someone', and the prefix eci- 'I to you (pl)' ().
Several of these Saru–Chitose forms recur in ‹SA›
Sakhalin: the form hemata (the Sakhalin cognate of hemanta) 'what' and the prefix eci- appear in both Saru–Chitose and ‹SA›, yet are absent from much of northeast Hokkaido.
Nakagawa and Fukazawa find this distribution "hard to believe [is] independent" and leave it as an unresolved puzzle about the internal phylogeny of Ainu () ‹contested›.

One reading is that these forms are innovations shared by an ancestral coastal or southern group before the Sakhalin branch diverged; another is that they are archaisms preserved separately in Saru–Chitose and ‹SA› while the northeast innovated.
Neither account has been demonstrated from the available data.
The cognacy matrix computed from the 91 variable items has been the primary input for the main proposals about how Hokkaido dialects group.

Asai's 1974 cluster analysis of this matrix proposed a partition into northern (Sōya), eastern (Obihiro / Kushiro / Bihoro / Asahikawa / Nayoro), central-southern (Yakumo / Oshamambe / Horobetsu / Biratori / Nukibetsu / Niikappu), and eastern-Hidaka (Samani) zones for Hokkaido, together with a major split between the Hokkaido+Kuril group and Sakhalin (reported via ; ).

Ono's 2020 statistical reanalysis demonstrates that the claimed three-way "Major Division" of Hokkaido / North Kuril / Sakhalin is not supported when methodologically appropriate algorithms are applied to Asai's original data.

Asai's linkage methods (single-linkage and complete-linkage agglomerative clustering) ignore mid-range cognacy values that are precisely where the evidence for sub-groupings lies; spectral clustering over the same matrix yields two groups — Hokkaido plus North Kuril vs Sakhalin — without any robust internal three-way split () ‹contested›.

Within the Hokkaido+Kuril group, North Kuril clusters with the northeastern Hokkaido localities (Samani, Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro, Sōya) rather than with the southwestern group, while the southwestern and Saru–Chitose varieties form the second sub-cluster.
Ono also notes that Asai (1974) may never have intended to canonize a tripartite dialect classification, yet his result became the standard reference beyond its original purpose.
Fukazawa and Ono's 2024 paper takes a complementary methodological direction ().

Rather than assigning each locality to a group, it maps the similarity of every Hokkaido point to two "boundary" reference dialects — Sōya (the Hokkaido/Sakhalin boundary variety) and Asahikawa (the NE/SW boundary variety) — through correspondence analysis combined with projection pursuit.
This dissolves the unresolvable question of which group a boundary dialect belongs to and instead treats geographic gradience as the object of description.
The resulting picture is one of overlapping similarity fields converging on the boundary localities rather than a set of discrete blocs.
A persistent tension runs through the classification literature: lexical and morphosyntactic isoglosses do not always converge on the same groupings.
The clearest case is Horobetsu.

Basic-vocabulary cognacy places Saru, Chitose, and Horobetsu together in a southwestern cluster; person-marking morphology (Horobetsu uses prefix–suffix circumfixes while Saru–Chitose use prefix-only marking) places Horobetsu with the geographically distant Ishikari and Tokachi varieties () ‹contested›.
Lexical distance is the broadest signal; finer grammatical features track different, partly independent histories.
The morphosyntactic dimension is developed in , and the full statistical classification debate in .
The 1960 survey included six Sakhalin localities and the Torii 1903 Kuril materials alongside the 13 Hokkaido points, giving the lexical comparisons a triangulable external dimension.
For the present chapter, two findings are directly relevant.

First, the form — northeastern in Hokkaido — is the standard word for 'mouth' in ‹KU› and ‹SA›, attested in early Kuril sources including Krasheninnikov (1738) and Golovnin (1811) and throughout the Sakhalin records (reported via ).

If the age-area account of the par / car split is correct (§mouth-isogloss), the agreement between northeastern Hokkaido, ‹SA›, and ‹KU› in using car supports reading that form as older, and par as an innovation limited to southwestern Hokkaido ‹speculative›.

Second, Ono's reanalysis of the full dataset, including the Sakhalin and Kuril points, places North Kuril lexically closer to northeastern Hokkaido than to southwestern Hokkaido, with Sakhalin forming a clearly separated external group ().

This topological finding — NE Hokkaido+Kuril as one cluster, SW Hokkaido as a second, Sakhalin as the external comparator — is the most statistically defensible summary of the lexical evidence as the dataset currently stands ‹contested›.
The Sakhalin and Kuril varieties in their full phonological and morphosyntactic dimensions are treated in .
Ainu has no demonstrated genetic relatives and is treated as a language isolate ; the failed macro-comparisons are surveyed in .
Internally the language forms a small family — sometimes labelled Ainuic — of three entities: Hokkaido (HA), Sakhalin, and the Northern Kuril varieties .
The tripartition was formalised on geographic grounds in the early twentieth century and appeared to receive objective support from the lexicostatistic studies of and .

demonstrates with spectral-clustering methods, however, that the three-way "Major Division" carries no statistically robust support: the cleaner two-way structure is Hokkaido (including the Kuril varieties) versus Sakhalin.
The internal Hokkaido classification and the dialectometry underlying that finding are treated in ; the boundary-dialect methodology is refined further by .

The branching order follows the archaeological record of the Satsumon culture's northward expansion from Honshu: the language reached Hokkaido from around the seventh century CE, southern Sakhalin around the thirteenth century, and the Northern Kuriles around the fifteenth to sixteenth century .
The Sakhalin branch diverged from Common Ainu approximately 800 years ago; the Kuril varieties diverged later and cluster more closely with northeast Hokkaido in the lexicostatistic data ; .
Both the Sakhalin and Kuril varieties ceased to be community languages during the twentieth century.

The primary Sakhalin documentation consists of the grammar and texts of and the folkloric corpus of ; the Kuril varieties are known only from questionnaire records assembled by eighteenth- and nineteenth-century travellers.
Within Hokkaido, the dialect geographically and lexically closest to Sakhalin is Sōya, at the northern tip of the island .

The Sakhalin varieties have a vowel-length contrast on the five vowels a e i o u, with long vowels occurring only in open stem syllables; Hokkaido has a pitch-accent system and no distinctive vowel length.

Hattori (1967) first established the correspondence: a Sakhalin long vowel corresponds to a Hokkaido high pitch, and a Sakhalin short vowel in a closed-syllable stem likewise corresponds to Hokkaido high pitch in the same environments ; .
The pitch-accent rules are described in ; the diachronic account of the length–pitch relationship is the subject of .
Three competing reconstructions of Proto-Ainu prosody account for this correspondence.
(a) Hattori (1967) and De Boer (2010) held that Proto-Ainu had vowel length alone and Hokkaido developed pitch accent through contact with Japanese.
(b) and argued that Proto-Ainu had both length and pitch, with the Sakhalin branch losing accent under Amur-Sakhalin contact.
(c) Satō (2015, 2016) proposed Proto-Ainu had pitch and no length, the Sakhalin vowel length being a phonetically conditioned open-syllable phenomenon.
Alonso de la Fuente endorses view (c) in the body of his chapter but (a) in the conclusion, leaving the question unresolved ‹contested›.
Community discussion (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2023; ) arrives at the same impasse, recognising both the Hattori and the Satō positions as defensible.
The phonological signature of the Sakhalin varieties relative to Hokkaido is systematic debuccalization of coda obstruents.
Where Hokkaido has a word-final or syllable-final p, t, or k, the core Sakhalin varieties produce h; final m becomes n; and final r receives a following vowel, keeping the syllable open ; .
A secondary rule applies within Sakhalin: the h produced by debuccalization becomes s following i (h > s / i__), yielding alternants such as sis for HA sik 'eye'.
Alonso de la Fuente uses this set of alternations as his illustration of what internal reconstruction can accomplish for a language isolate without recourse to the comparative method .
The correspondences are set out in Table 2; the coda consonants of the Hokkaido system are described in .
The Hokkaido forms in the first column are corpus-attested throughout; the constructed example below places cep in a transitive clause to show the coda -p in context.
The corresponding Sakhalin Raiciska form ceh is the regular debuccalization reflex .

Community corroboration: the kor > koh change and the general pattern of coda-consonant debuccalization in Sakhalin are noted, with examples, in aynu-corpora Discord discussion (nukopoli 2024-12-19, aldehyde8908 2025-04-22; ), consistent with .
The debuccalization applies across the Sakhalin varieties with notable subdialect variation.
The eastern coast varieties Taraika and Tarantomari preserve the coda stops p/t/k like Hokkaido; the Esutoru subdialect distinguishes -is from -ih .

The phonological status of SA coda h itself is disputed: Alonso de la Fuente treats it as a velar fricative /x/ (with realisations [ax], [iɕ], [uf]), while Tangiku and community members analyse it as a laryngeal breath h ; ‹contested›.
The possessed (affiliative) form of Sakhalin nouns reveals the base consonant that debuccalization masks in the independent form.

The affiliative suffix -ihi / -ehe attaches directly to the underlying stem: the noun whose independent form is sis 'eye' (< *sih, with h > s before i) surfaces in the possessed form as sik-ihi — the base /k/ restored — not as the unattested *sis-ihi.
The underlying consonant is thus directly recoverable from morphological alternation even where phonology has eliminated it from the independent form ; .
The Hokkaido Saru counterpart is identical: sik-ihi.
Sakhalin uses only the long affiliative form — there is no short/long alternation of the kind found in Hokkaido .

The affiliative insert is transparently the suffix -hi 'thing, trace' attached to the base: san+hi = sanihi, makan+hi = makanihi — a pathway corroborated in community analysis (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-12-16; ), and consistent with the general account of the affiliative's origin from the noun hi 'thing, trace' argued by Janhunen (2020) via .

Within Sakhalin, the Nairo subdialect (eastern Sakhalin) shows word-initial t- where Hokkaido and the remaining Sakhalin varieties have r-: Nairo teera 'wind' corresponds to HA rera and non-Nairo SA reera; Nairo taarak 'smooth' corresponds to HA raarak .

Alonso de la Fuente interprets this as retention of a Proto-Ainu lateral *l that merged with r in most dialects but with t in Nairo — on this account Nairo preserves the most archaic reflex for the relevant set ‹contested›.
The PA consonant reconstruction, including the evidence from Ainu→Ghilyak loans showing Proto-Ghilyak *l- opposite these forms, is treated in .
Hokkaido Ainu counts in a vigesimal (base-20) system; Sakhalin diverges above ten.
The Sakhalin varieties use a decimal structure for eleven and above, with kunkutu '10' and tanku '100' as the key items .

The word tanku '100' is a Tungusic borrowing; kunkutu '10' may derive from Itelmen (the language of the Kamchatka Peninsula), on the basis of a resemblance to forms recorded by Krasheninnikov in 1755 — this is a comparison, not a demonstrated etymology ‹speculative›.
Community discussion (antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord 2024-11-22; ) also notes the Itelmen resemblance for kunkutu, attributing the decimal restructuring to Sakhalin trade contact ‹speculative›.
The Hokkaido vigesimal system is described in .
The Sakhalin varieties lack the first-person-plural-exclusive forms that Hokkaido marks with ci= / =as .
In an "elders' style" of Sakhalin speech, the fourth-person forms an= / =an cover first-singular reference alongside the dedicated ku= .
The Hokkaido first-person plural and the exclusive/inclusive distinction are described in .
Plural marking across the three Ainuic entities shows a layered historical picture.
Sakhalin uses the suffix -hci / -hcin; most Hokkaido dialects outside Saru–Chitose use ci; Saru, Chitose, and Ishikari use pa ; .
Nakagawa establishes that Hokkaido ci is the older Hokkaido form, and pa is an innovation that spread through the Saru and Ishikari regions .

Sakhalin uses the allative particle (e)ne, which coincides with the form found in northern and eastern Hokkaido (Sōya, Asahikawa, Bihoro, Kushiro, Shiranuka) rather than the southwestern HA forms un (Horobetsu, Chitose, Yakumo) or en (Tokachi) .

Other shared features between Sakhalin and the geographically distant southern Hokkaido dialects (Saru–Chitose) are harder to explain: the interrogative form hemata 'what' and the second-person-plural object prefix eci= occur in both Saru–Chitose and Sakhalin, a distribution that Nakagawa and Fukazawa describe as "hard to believe independent" ‹contested›.
Whether these features reflect retention in peripheral varieties, a contact relic, or convergence is treated in .

The Northern Kuril varieties are known only from questionnaire records compiled by eighteenth- and nineteenth-century travellers — abbreviated in Alonso de la Fuente's discussion as KD (Dybowski), KK (Krašeninnikov), KL (Klaproth), KT (Torii), and KV (Voznesenskij) .

The lexicostatistic reanalysis of finds the Kuril varieties clustering with the northeast Hokkaido group — Samani, Obihiro, Kushiro, Bihoro, Sōya — rather than with Sakhalin, supporting a two-way Hokkaido-plus-Kuril versus Sakhalin division over the classic three-way one.

A separate analysis using nineteenth-century Kuril material by Satō and Bugaeva (2019) places the Kuril items closer to southern Hokkaido (Saru/Chitose); the two results rest on different data sets and are not directly comparable ‹contested›.

Phonologically the Kuril varieties largely preserve the coda stops p/t/k that Sakhalin debuccalises, but they also show prothetic h- in some forms alongside loss of original h- in others — an independent innovation parallel to the prothetic h- found in the Bihoro dialect of Hokkaido .

The word for 'mouth' appears as car in Kuril records (aligning with northeastern HA and Sakhalin against the southwestern HA form par), an isogloss documented in place-name data by (via ) and diachronically accounted for as a palatalized-series relic *pʸaɾ by .
The diachrony of that split is treated in .
Hokkaido phonological microvariation, including the Bihoro and northeastern features that align partially with Kuril, is described in .
A Kuril contrast text appears in .
Sakhalin was the primary zone of Ainu contact with Nivkh (Ghilyak), Uilta (Tungusic), and Manchu-mediated trade vocabulary from Qing China.
The multilingualism was "extremely limited and localised", concentrated among individual interpreters rather than being community-wide .
Most of the resulting loanword layer remained specific to the Sakhalin varieties; the full contact account belongs in .
The items with a direct reflex in Hokkaido are:
— borrowed on Sakhalin from Nivkh, reaching Hokkaido with the specialised sense 'sail' only ;
— morphologically unanalysable in Ainu, possibly connected to the Eurasian sanduk Wanderwort, also appearing as Nivkh sinduχ ;
— Nivkh cʰaŋ, Uilta saan ;
— from Pre-Proto-Ghilyak *tola-ŋa.y, also the source of Japanese トナカイ .

In the reverse direction, several Ainu lexical items passed into Nivkh and Uilta on Sakhalin ; the directionality in each case is argued from morphological analysability, plausible sound correspondences, and the dialect distribution of the forms across Sakhalin versus the continent.
Vovin characterizes the lexical impact of Japanese on Hokkaido Ainu as making modern Ainu "inundated by loanwords from Japanese" .

The flow has been almost entirely one-directional for the modern period: domestic animals, trade goods, administrative vocabulary, and — from the Meiji era onward — the full terminology of modern institutions all entered Ainu from Japanese.

The reverse direction, Ainu elements entering Japanese through place names and regional vocabulary, is treated in ; contact with Nivkh and Uilta, which shaped the Sakhalin lexicon but has no Hokkaido counterpart, is discussed in .
Vovin himself acknowledges that "there is no comprehensive study" of Japanese loanwords in Ainu .
The account below draws on the etymology tags in Chiri's classified dictionary , the word-formation remarks in Nakagawa , and attested corpus examples.

Ainu is a language isolate with no genetic relationship to Japanese (see ), so the loans are a contact phenomenon and bring Japanese phonological structures that require systematic restructuring to fit the Ainu syllable canon.
Nakagawa states the diagnostic plainly: free lexical words of three or more syllables are often loanwords (3音節以上の自立語は外来語であることが多い), citing as a typical case .
The underlying phonological mismatch is clear: Japanese contrasts voiced and voiceless obstruents; Ainu has no phonemic voicing (see ).
Japanese also permits nasal-mora and long-vowel mora types that fall outside the Ainu (C)V(C) canon.
Every borrowed form is therefore reshaped by one or more of the following repair operations, documented in Chiri's etymology tags and in Nakagawa .
The obstruent repairs reflect Ainu's lack of phonemic voicing: Japanese voiced stops surface voiceless or prenasalized (b → p / mp, d → t / nt, g → k).
Prenasalization is the preferred repair for medial voiced stops in a nasal-compatible environment, as both and confirm ‹corpus-confirmed›.

Consonant clusters outside the (C)V(C) template are broken by epenthesis; the default epenthetic vowel is o or a copy vowel — a pattern attested in community comparisons of loanword shapes from multiple source languages ‹contested›
(nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-11 [227]).
A further substitution affects the Japanese rhotic: Japanese /r/ has an [l]-allophone that maps to Ainu n rather than to Ainu r (a flap with no lateral allophone) ‹contested›
(antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, 2025-01-02 [400]).
The nasal spelling of prenasalized loans is an active orthographic debate.
Nakagawa's convention writes the etymological labial nasal (hence tampaku, kampi, umma), because /n/ and /m/ neutralize to [m] before /p/ and /m/.
Kana orthography uses ン throughout since kana encodes a single nasal mora.
The choice between kampi and kanpi reflects an etymological or neutralization-based orthographic stance, not a phonological difference ‹contested›
(nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-16 [216, 217]).

One community-proposed case suggests that voicing may occasionally survive in a borrowed form: the garment term cinciri has been proposed as a loan of Japanese 綴れ (tsuzure) with the voiced affricate retained ‹speculative›
(scheuewsuiski, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-05 [215]).
The etymology is unverified against a primary dictionary source.
The earliest stratum consists of culture-contact vocabulary that is fully integrated into Ainu phonology and morphology.
These forms appear in the nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century texts collected by Chiri and Batchelor and are attested across multiple dialects.
The core items are animals not native to pre-contact Hokkaido, material-culture goods brought by trade, and administrative terminology tied to the Wajin presence.
The animal loans — , , — fill gaps in the Ainu fauna lexicon for mainland domestic species absent from Hokkaido before sustained contact.
The corpus shows with 146 tokens (rank 882 in the full vocabulary), making it the most frequent Japanese animal loan by a large margin.

The administrative items reflect the institutional structure of Wajin–Ainu trade: titles the Japanese trade-post supervisor, and names the bilingual go-between required in formal dealings — plausibly < archaic Japanese 通事/通詞 tsūji ‹speculative›
(thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-06-14).
Early loans also appear as components in native compound and incorporation structures.
The corpus records both tampaku-op 'tobacco pouch' and toy-ta-tampaku 'home-grown tobacco' .
The following example shows two animal loans and an administrative loan co-occurring in a single clause:
The noun is attested in the older sense of 'written order, official document' in oral-literature contexts, where the Wajin administrative apparatus is a recurring plot element:
Meiji-era colonization and the assimilation policy that followed (documented in ) ended the productive nativization of new Japanese vocabulary.

Concepts introduced during the decades when Ainu was no longer used in daily life simply appear as untranslated Japanese forms: terebi 'television', sinbun 'newspaper', zeikin 'tax', ginkō 'bank', denwa 'telephone'. Ōno's formulation is precise: "no Ainu vocabulary has been found to refer to televisions or computers … during the period when these things became widespread, the Ainu language was rarely used in Ainu daily lives" .

The untranslated character of modern loans distinguishes them from the early stratum: early loans received full phonological repair; modern loans often retain Japanese syllable structure intact ‹corpus-confirmed›.
The contrast is visible when modern and early loans appear in the same sentence.
An Ainu Times text places the fully nativized early loan alongside three unrepaired modern loans:

Contrast the handful of native-era coinages for Meiji-period technology, which show that Ainu was still spoken when those concepts spread: tunas-kampi 'telegram' (literally 'fast paper/letter', Asahikawa) and a-e-y-nu-p 'telephone' (literally 'the thing with which we hear one another') are built from native and nativized material rather than borrowed from Japanese .
Their existence marks the relative chronology of language shift across technology domains.

Loans cluster in the semantic fields where post-contact material and administrative culture arrived: domestic animals, trade goods, clothing, tools, money and administration, and in the modern stratum technology and institutions .
Core vocabulary — body parts, kinship terms, the natural-world lexicon, basic verbs, the native numerals one through ten, and pronouns — is native.
The vigesimal numeral system treated in is entirely native in its derivational base; classifiers and ordinals in likewise draw on native morphology.
Property-concept predicates in are native verbal predicates.
The pattern is the classic "borrow the culture, keep the core" profile of contact lexicon.
The noun illustrates how a fully nativized loan can become a productive morphological base.

Borrowed early as 'paper' (< kami 紙), it has generated a set of neologisms for educational and museum contexts in the revitalization period: kampi-nukat-cise 'school' (paper–look-at–house), kanpi pu 'library' (paper–storehouse), imeru-kampi 'email' (lightning–paper) .
A loanword functioning as a stem in noun incorporation and in productive compounding is indistinguishable in its morphological behavior from a native root.
Early loans are fully integrated.

They bear Ainu accentuation according to the prosodic rules described in : the geminate in creates a heavy first syllable that receives the accent nucleus by the default rule for CVC.CV words, so the form sounds native, not Japanese.
Early loans also participate freely in compounding and incorporation (see examples in §3.1 above).

Native obligatorily-possessed nouns carry affiliative suffixes in possessed contexts; borrowed nouns such as and are not obligatorily possessed and do not display this morphology — a diagnostic that separates many loans from native inalienable nouns.
Modern loans are less integrated.

They frequently retain Japanese syllable structure, and in the new-speaker texts produced in language-revitalization contexts, the boundary between a nativized loanword and a code-switch from Japanese is structurally difficult to establish ‹speculative›.

The compound umma menoko illustrates how native and loan morphology interact productively: the bare juxtaposition is ambiguous between 'horse and girl' (appositive) and 'horse-girl' (compound); inserting the copula explicitly as umma-ne-menoko removes the ambiguity ‹speculative›
(nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-12 [356]).
Four properties together identify a form as a Japanese loan in Hokkaido Ainu:
Syllable count. A free lexical root of three or more syllables is a strong prior for borrowing .
Native Ainu roots are predominantly mono- or disyllabic; polysyllabic roots arise through borrowing or through productive — and morphologically transparent — affixal derivation.

Recognizable phonological repair. Prenasalization of a medial voiced stop (-mp-, -nt-), gemination of a stem-initial nasal consonant, or an unexpected initial m- where a Japanese source has n- all point to a Japanese etymon.
Absence of affiliative morphology. Obligatorily-possessed native nouns display a concept/affiliative alternation (所属形; see ).
Most Japanese loans are not obligatorily possessed and lack this alternation.
Chiri dictionary etymology tags. The tags [<日本語…] and [<Jap.…] in mark the identified Japanese-loan inventory and remain the most systematic primary record.
Vovin notes the lack of a comprehensive successor survey .
The name for the source language itself illustrates one of the finer integration distinctions.

The two-word phrase sisam itak 'the speech of the Wajin' (a descriptive NP) and the single compound sisamitak 'Japanese [language]' (a language name) are argued to differ semantically and phonologically: the former has two independent accentual words, while the latter functions as a single compound with one accent domain.
Writing them together obscures the accentuation and conflates the two meanings ‹speculative›
(nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-05 [299]; 2024-12-20 [549]).

Ochiai's study of demonstrates a methodological corollary from the reverse direction: a Japanese dialect tree-name preserving a reconstructible intermediate Ainu form — *si kor pe before the change to sikerpe — can be used both to date the borrowing and to anchor the proto-Ainu reconstruction .
The evidence for Ainu loans in Old Japanese, including Vovin's Man'yōshū material, is taken up in and .
Ainu's classification as a language isolate, surveyed in , means that no genetic relationship accounts for resemblances between Ainu and Japanese vocabulary.
Demonstrable shared items are contact loans, and the directionality of that contact is asymmetric by period and domain.

The companion chapter documents the large stratum of Japanese vocabulary that entered Ainu after sustained post-medieval contact with the Wajin: domesticated animals, material culture, administrative titles, and, from the Meiji era onward, unmarked quotations of modern Japanese terms.
The reverse current — Ainu material entering Japanese — is narrower in scope and less systematically studied.
Its primary evidence is toponymic, and lexical loans proper are few.

Vovin observes that "it is silently assumed that there are no Ainu loanwords in Japanese" and acknowledges the absence of any comprehensive study; the same observation is echoed in Ijäs's typological overview of the language .
The geographical distribution of Ainu-origin place names testifies to a former Ainu presence across a wider area than the historically documented homeland.

records that the toponymic distribution across Hokkaidō is extensive and that "many place names in the northern part of Honshū indicate that they might have once lived in that region as well"; Ainu place names also occur in southern Kamchatka.
Chiri Mashiho devoted major scholarly effort to this toponymic substrate , and that dictionary remains the standard reference for individual etymologies.

Individual toponyms cited in this chapter as examples have been verified only at the level of their Ainu component elements through the Tamura and Nakagawa dictionaries, not against the primary place-name sources.
A small set of Ainu geographic roots recur as diagnostic final elements in Japanese place names, constituting the backbone of the toponymic substrate.

Because these elements are independently attested in the Ainu lexicon with stable meanings ; , the toponymic analysis rests on solid morphological footing at the elemental level even where the etymology of a specific place name requires verification against .
