text: Japanese reflexes typically show rendaku (sequential voicing: pet → -betsu), phonological reduction, or orthographic regularization through kanji choice — adaptations governed by Japanese phonotactics, not by Ainu phonology .
All etymologies in the table are illustrative; individual place names require verification against and related primary sources.
A specific Japanese name may involve phonological reduction, analogical replacement, or overlay by later Japanese morphology that obscures the Ainu source compound.
The component Ainu forms are well attested in the living lexicon; it is the mapping from a given Japanese string to those components that calls for caution.
The contrast between and reflects a live semantic distinction in the Ainu lexicon, not merely the presence of two suffix shapes.
Tamura (1996, s.v.

pet) characterizes it from the Saru area: pet designates the representative waterway of a locality — the Saru, Mukawa, and Monbetsu rivers all carry this label — while a branch stream or tributary is nay.
The criterion is typicality, not size: even a small stream that defines its valley is pet, while a large tributary of a major river remains nay.
Corpus frequencies reflect this asymmetry: pet occurs 1,344 times (rank 140) against nay's 559 (rank 312) in the Hokkaido text corpus, consistent with the broader referential range of the former.
The semantic distinction matters for toponymic analysis: a -nai place name designates a tributary or smaller mountain stream, while a -betsu name marks the primary waterway of its valley.

A common folk-etymological error equates nay with 'pond'; nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-11, corroborating Tamura 1996) registers this as a mistaken conflation: 'pond' or 'lake' is , a semantically distinct root with its own toponymic reflex ‹corpus-confirmed›.
Two further formatives encode habitual or permanent location and are productive in place-name formation.
The verbal element (Tamura 1996, s.v.
us) means 'be habitually attached to, grow at'; the suffix -us(i) nominalizes this to 'place where X habitually grows or is found'.
The compound ni-kap-us-i — ni 'tree' + kap 'bark' + -us-i 'habitually-at' — yields 'place where bark trees stand', commonly cited as the source of Niikappu 新冠 (illustrative only; ).
The suffix also surfaces in Usu 有珠 and several other Hokkaido names.
The element 'be located in, be contained in' (Tamura 1996, s.v.
oma; Nakagawa 1995, s.v.
oma) forms the nominalized oma-i 'place where X is located', the source of the Japanese -omai / -oma endings.
In Ainu syntax, oma also appears in postpositional constructions expressing containment; this overlap between its lexical geographic use and its grammatical locative function is discussed in .
A further geographic compound illustrates the compounding pattern that underlies Hokkaido toponymy:

This compounding pattern — a landscape attribute or associated entity plus a geographic generic (nay, pet, to, etc.) — is the typical structure of an Ainu place name; the phonological adaptation that Japanese applies when borrowing such compounds is treated in .
The toponymic data extend beyond Hokkaidō into northern Honshū.
observes that many place names in northern Honshū suggest historical Ainu presence there as well.

Vovin extends the argument into the philological record: he proposes that a number of items in Eastern Old Japanese — texts preserved in Man'yōshū books 14 and 20, compiled in the 8th century — are Ainu loans, reflecting a prehistoric Ainu substrate in the Kantō and Tōhoku regions ‹contested›.
Vovin also argues that modern Japanese iruka 'dolphin' is an Ainu loan, "isolated in Japonic; cf.
Saru rika / Kuril rika 'whale meat'" ‹contested›.
This programme forms a minority and contested position.

Vovin (2022 Ch.6 §1) himself acknowledges the prevailing working assumption against Ainu loans in Japanese, and individual etymologies in the table are disputable on grounds of sound correspondence and comparative methodology; the full debate on Ainu's historical position and the validity of deep-contact proposals belongs to ‹contested›.

At the community level, nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-01-22) proposes that the Iwate place name Otomonai (乙茂内) — both a surname and a stream name in an area dense with -nai endings — derives from Ainu o-tum-nay 'head-middle-stream'.
The analysis is morphologically plausible within Ainu and consistent with the Tōhoku -nai substrate, but has not been verified against or published place-name catalogues ‹speculative›.
Ochiai (2026) provides a model of rigorous Ainu → Japanese lexical identification.

The Ainu form — fruit of the Amur cork tree (キハダ Phellodendron amurense) — is analysed as a reflex of Proto-Ainu *siw kor pe 'thing that holds bitterness': siw 'bitter' + kor 'hold, have' + pe 'thing'.
The proto-form shifted to sikerpe through w-deletion and regressive vowel assimilation (o → e) .

A cluster of Japanese dialectal names for the same tree — most conservatively sikorope in Akita, with reduced forms sikoro, sikonohe, siko no ki elsewhere — are loans from Ainu *si kor pe, borrowed before the Ainu vowel change to *si ker pe had completed .
Two complementary arguments support the claim.

First, the Japanese siko- type is morphologically opaque in Japanese and has no Japanese-internal etymology, while the Ainu compound is transparent — the asymmetry that is diagnostic of borrowing direction.

Second, the Japanese form preserves the earlier vowel /o/ in the second syllable, showing that the borrowing antedates the Ainu sound change; this gives a terminus ante quem for the Ainu historical phonology, linking contact evidence to reconstruction .
The reconstruction side of this analysis connects to .
Northern Honshū hunter vocabulary (matagi speech) furnishes candidates for Ainu lexical retention in an area where the toponymic substrate already indicates historical Ainu presence.

Two items are community-proposed: antitwilight (aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-06-09) proposes matagi ɸina 'elder brother (matagi usage)' as a reflex of Ainu , and matagi hatagi/hattagi 'locust' as a reflex of Ainu .

Both proposals are phonologically plausible — the initial p- → ɸ- change and the h- variant reflect regular Japanese alternations — and they are consistent with Vovin's OJ substrate thesis, but neither has been verified against published philological sources for the matagi lexicon ‹speculative›.
Several items in standard Japanese are widely attributed to Ainu origin in the popular literature and encyclopaedic reference works.
None could be verified in the sources consulted for this chapter; they are listed with that status recorded.
Asserting these as Ainu loans without a primary source risks repeating popular etymology.
Vovin's argument that iruka 'dolphin' is an Ainu loan — "isolated in Japonic; cf.
Saru rika / Kuril rika 'whale meat'" () — belongs to his OJ substrate programme and carries the same contested status ‹contested›.
On Sakhalin, the contact partners were Nivkh and Uilta rather than Japanese, and the Ainu loans that did cross language boundaries there went into those languages, not into Japanese, as surveyed in .
The Hokkaidō → Japanese transfer treated in this chapter is therefore a southern phenomenon without a direct Sakhalin parallel.
Place-name etymology faces several systematic pitfalls that bear on the analysis above.
Japanese phonological adaptation erases information present in the Ainu source.
Coda consonants, the voiced/voiceless distinction absent from Ainu, and syllable-weight differences are all reorganized by Japanese phonotactics, as described in .
Rendaku produces pet → -betsu; recovering the Ainu source requires knowledge of both the Ainu phonological inventory and the Japanese adaptation rules.
Reading Ainu-derived place names through kanji orthography produces folk etymologies — 稚内 as 'young interior'? — that are wholly Japanese in structure and irrelevant to the Ainu source.
A second difficulty is the limited documentation of Ainu as spoken across many areas.

As discussed in , recording of Ainu varieties was geographically uneven, and for areas with no documented variety — Hakodate, Erimo, Rumoi, Otaru — place-name reconstruction by extrapolation from better-recorded dialects is at best speculative.

The constraint that a proposed source compound must be morphologically analysable within Ainu and that phonological correspondences must be regular remains the methodological floor for any specific toponym claim.
A third caution is convergence.
Phonologically similar strings may arise from unrelated sources, and it is possible that some Ainu geographic terms entered Ainu at an earlier period from a continental substrate.
Antitwilight (aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-15) has proposed Korean-origin candidates for several Ainu roots, including nay, casi, and others .
This is unverified and has not been tested against the comparative literature; it is noted here as an acknowledged edge case, not a claim ‹speculative›.
Three genealogically unrelated languages occupied Sakhalin simultaneously and traded across it: Ainu (an isolate), Nivkh/Ghilyak (an isolate), and Uilta/Orok, a Southern Tungusic language.

Manchu-origin goods and vocabulary reached the island via the Santan trade network from the Qing frontier; Chinese commodities followed the same route without producing direct Ainu–Chinese bilingualism.
Whether this configuration constitutes a linguistic area in the strict sense — a Sprachbund defined by structural convergence — Shiraishi and Tangiku explicitly leave for future research .
What is documented is directional lexical borrowing; the structural case for areal convergence remains under-evidenced.
The contact layer as it reaches Hokkaido is thin.
Most Nivkh, Tungusic, and Manchu vocabulary stayed on Sakhalin, and loanwords travelling in the Ainu-to-continent direction barely reached the mainland .
A small residue — , , , — passed from the Sakhalin contact zone into Hokkaido Ainu, together with the Eurasian Wanderwort and the proposed Tungusic borrowing .

Contact borrowing is distinct from genetic relatedness: all proposals linking Ainu genetically to Nivkh or any other northern family have failed, and the Ainu–Nivkh relationship is one of early lexical interaction between two isolates ‹consensus›.
The genetic question is addressed in .
Borrowing between Ainu and Nivkh ran in both directions on Sakhalin.
Standard directionality diagnostics — geographic spread within each family, morphological analysability, sound-change plausibility, and dialect correspondences — must be applied case by case .

Multilingualism on the island was not a general social condition: before the late nineteenth century it was "extremely limited and localized", mediated by individual interpreters and trading contacts rather than widespread bilingualism .
The west-coast Sakhalin group called Sirunkur, described as "originally Ainu but Nivkh-ized", documents a sociolinguistic boundary zone rather than a stable bilingual population .
Items that passed from Nivkh into Ainu on Sakhalin include nuso/nuhsu 'dog sled' (‹SA›; < Nivkh nuci), hankata 'birch-bark plate' (< Nivkh haŋr̥), and ka 'sable trap' (< Nivkh ha).
In the reverse direction, Sakhalin Ainu tonto, sinduχ, upun 'winter storehouse', nikar 'ladder', and muks 'swaddling cloth' appear in Nivkh .

Of the Nivkh-into-Ainu items, is the one with a clear Hokkaido reflex: Batchelor's dictionary documents kaya in Sakhalin with the meaning 'fish-skin garment', and Hokkaido retained the word with the narrower meaning 'sail' ; .
The early Ainu–Ghilyak contact layer reaches deeper than the Sakhalin trade period.

Alonso de la Fuente, revising Vovin's Proto-Ainu reconstruction, argues that Ainu-into-Ghilyak loans preserve the proto-lateral PA *l- before its merger with *r in all Hokkaido reflexes: the Proto-Ghilyak reflex *l- corresponding to Vovin's PA *d- makes sense if Ainu lent these words to Ghilyak before the lateral–flap merger had run its course .
This is a secondary use of contact evidence to triangulate segmental reconstruction; the reconstruction itself is treated in .
Among the deeper shared items, tunakay 'reindeer' — source of Japanese トナカイ tonakai (treated in ) — is linked by Janhunen, following Austerlitz (1976), to Pre-Proto-Ghilyak *tola-ŋa.y ‹contested›
The Sakhalin-only parallel kaco 'shaman's drum', shared with ‹SA›
Ghilyak *kaco, points to a similar early contact stratum .
The reindeer was not native to Hokkaido proper; tunakay passed through the Sakhalin trade route into Ainu cultural vocabulary and then into Japanese.

The community note that Sakhalin Ainu nikubun 'a Nivkh person' derives from the Sakhalin Nivkh form ɲiɣvŋ — distinct from the Amur-dialect form ɲivx — is consistent with the Sakhalin contact setting and is corroborated by Shiraishi and Tangiku's discussion of Ainu ethnonyms ‹contested›
(nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-11); .
The Santan trade (山丹交易) was the channel through which Qing-dynasty Manchu goods reached Sakhalin and, through Sakhalin, the northern coast of Hokkaido.
Uilta (Orok), a Southern Tungusic language closely related to Evenki, occupied the east and central coast of Sakhalin alongside Ainu communities.

Direct Ainu–Uilta exchange, Manchu-mediated trade contact, and the downstream movement of Chinese goods via the Santan network are distinguishable layers even though the documentary record conflates them.
The offering shelf has cognates in both Nivkh (cʰaŋ) and Uilta (saan), making the direction of borrowing difficult to establish without further philological evidence ‹contested›.
The comparison of person and number marking across Uilta, Sakhalin Ainu, and Nivkh has been carried out systematically and is addressed in .
Manchu proper was reached through trade rather than direct contact.

The Manchu word hasaha 'scissors' entered Nivkh as haza; the Hokkaido Ainu word for the same object, hasami, is a Japanese borrowing from the same Manchu ultimate source — showing that the same trade good reached Ainu and Nivkh through different intermediaries .
The ritual vocabulary item has been proposed as a Tungusic borrowing by Ikegami (1980), cited by Janhunen ‹speculative›

If correct, ināw/inaw — central to Ainu ceremonial life and frequent throughout the corpus — is among the oldest identifiable northern borrowings in the Hokkaido lexicon, pre-dating the Sakhalin trading system.
The Sakhalin Ainu numeral system carries the clearest structural trace of northern contact.

Hokkaido Ainu counts vigesimally; Sakhalin uses a decimal system above ten, with the word for 'hundred', tanku, established as a Tungusic borrowing, and the word for 'ten', kunkutu, proposed on the basis of early records as a loan from Itelmen/Kamchadal ‹contested›.
The community analysis of kunkutu as an Itelmen item independently converges with Tangiku's hedged position (antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-22).
The Sakhalin Ainu vocabulary of neighbouring peoples is richer than its Hokkaido counterpart, reflecting the island's position in the Qing-era trade network.
Attested ‹SA› forms include manciw 'Manchu', canta 'Santan person', kakan 'Khan', and nuca 'Russian'; the word kawren 'Korean' has been speculatively connected to 高麗 Kōrai ‹speculative›
(thegodofneet, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-10); .
Hokkaido Ainu has no equivalent vocabulary at this density: Japanese-mediated contact, treated in , was the channel through which the wider world reached HA.
The following table summarises the northern loanwords with clear or well-argued Hokkaido reflexes together with the principal ‹SA› items.
Sakhalin-only forms are marked ‹SA›; confidence grades follow the evidence-grade conventions of this grammar.
The Wanderwort is the northern-contact item most deeply embedded in the Hokkaido lexicon.

It ranks 56th by corpus frequency (4,210 tokens), is pervasive in oral literature as a geographic and social term, and its opaque internal structure in Ainu points to external origin — though the ultimate source cannot be identified ‹speculative›.
The community observation that kotan is a continental loan is corroborated by Janhunen's Eurasian Wanderwort characterization (antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-15).
The word is fully integrated morphologically, taking possessive prefixes and entering compounds freely; the compound illustrates this integration:

Whether Sakhalin constituted a Sprachbund has two separable sub-questions: whether Sakhalin Ainu shows contact-induced structural changes attributable to Nivkh or Tungusic, and whether the three languages converged as an areal unit.
Shiraishi and Tangiku leave the Sprachbund label for future research ; on current evidence, lexical exchange is real and directional, while the structural case is thin.
Person and number marking across Uilta, Sakhalin Ainu, and Nivkh has been compared directly .
All three languages mark third person with zero or near-zero morphology, and all three attach plural affixes at the outer edge of the person-marked verbal complex.
Whether these parallel patterns reflect contact, shared typological pressures on head-marking systems, or independent development cannot be resolved from the existing data ‹speculative›.

The phonological innovations distinguishing Sakhalin from Hokkaido Ainu — final-consonant debuccalization, the vowel-length system — are internal to Ainuic and independent of northern contact; their diachrony is treated in .
The claim in one view of the prosodic debate that Hokkaido pitch accent arose through contact with Japanese concerns the HA end, not Sakhalin ‹contested›; that debate is reviewed there and in .

The primary source for northern-contact data is Shiraishi and Tangiku's survey , which draws on Piłsudski's early-twentieth-century Sakhalin corpus , post-war word-list records, and secondary comparative Nivkh and Tungusic material.
Three limits bound what can be established.
First, the documentation of Sakhalin contact vocabulary is uneven across the island's dialects and social groups.
Second, directionality of individual loans is difficult to verify without comprehensive comparative Nivkh fieldwork, some of which remains unpublished.
Third, individual interpreters working between Ainu, Nivkh, and Uilta could have introduced phonologically irregular intermediary forms that complicate the etymological record .
For Hokkaido, the corpus gives little direct traction on the northern loanword layer.
Items such as kaya, sintoko, and san are cultural vocabulary with low narrative frequency; only is a corpus staple.
Dictionary evidence — and — together with the secondary literature remain the principal witnesses for most items.
Japanese-mediated contact, which produced a larger and better-attested Hokkaido loanword layer, is treated in .
The Ainu contribution to Japanese in the reverse direction, including tonto → Japanese todo 'sea lion' and tunakay → tonakai 'reindeer', is treated in .
Macro-comparison proposals that would extend the lexical Ainu–Nivkh relationship into a genetic one are catalogued and critiqued in .
Ainu has no confirmed genetic relative.

Every proposal to link it to another language family has been examined and set aside; Janhunen's verdict — that Ainu "does not show unambiguous indications of being associated with any other language family" — expresses the current consensus ‹consensus›
Within its own lineage Ainu constitutes a small family — sometimes called Ainuic or Kurilic — of three closely related varieties: Hokkaido, Sakhalin, and the Northern Kuriles ().

The question addressed here is not the isolate status itself, which is settled, but two connected and genuinely open questions: the nature and direction of contact between Ainu and neighbouring languages, especially Japonic; and whether any proposed deep-time comparison or areal alignment survives methodological scrutiny.
The isolate status and its evidential basis are set out in ; the ethnolinguistic context in .
For an isolate the comparative method is unavailable: there is no sister language against which to project correspondences back into a proto-system.

Three analytic tools remain — internal reconstruction, contact-induced-change analysis, and typology — with the important qualification that typological reasoning carries no probatory weight for genetic questions and must be used "with utmost caution" .

The methodologically recoverable depth is also shallow: internal reconstruction reaches approximately 1,000 years without unsupported extrapolation, terminating at a Common Ainu stage no earlier than the thirteenth-century CE branching that separated the Sakhalin varieties from Hokkaido .
The reconstruction of Proto-Ainu and Common Ainu is treated in and .
The table below surveys the external comparisons that have been proposed for Ainu and records their current status.
Judgements follow Janhunen , Alonso de la Fuente , and the three published reviews of Vovin (1993): Sidwell (1996), Abondolo (1997), and Witczak (1999), all cited second-hand via Alonso .
A structural point underlies the table.

Proposing a genetic relationship for an isolate places the entire burden of proof on the proposer, because the null hypothesis — independent origin — accounts for all of the data without additional apparatus.

Lexical resemblances between any two languages occur by chance at a predictable rate; only systematic sound-to-sound correspondences across a significant portion of core vocabulary, independent of areal diffusion, constitutes evidence for common descent .
No proposal for Ainu has satisfied this standard.
Contact between Ainu and Japonic is the best-documented diachronic layer in Ainu's external history, and the directionality is not in dispute for the early stratum.

A set of Ainu items preserve phonological features of Old Japanese or Pre-Old-Japanese that had disappeared from Japanese before the Nara period, placing the borrowing events "around the middle of the first millennium CE" .
The diagnostics are the retention of a labial stop where later Japanese shows a fricative (Pre-OJ *p- → later Japanese /h-/), and the preservation of sequences that subsequently monophthongized.
The regularly cited items are:
— preserves Pre-OJ *siopo before the labial lenition that yields Modern Japanese 塩 shio .
— compared with OJ hashi 'chopstick'; Ainu retains the original stop p- lost in Japanese .
— an early cultural borrowing whose deep distribution across all Ainu lects confirms a pre-branching age .
These items are morphologically opaque in Ainu — no segment maps onto a recoverable Ainu morpheme — whereas inherited vocabulary often remains internally analyzable.

Compare , reconstructed as Pre-PA *ti=(ʔ)e pe 'the thing eaten by everyone' (< fourth-person prefix ci= + + nominalizer -p), whose internal structure remains transparent after a millennium of phonological change .
(.) Opacity versus transparency of this kind is a standard heuristic for separating loans from inherited vocabulary.

Later loanwords from Japanese, received after the post-Nara sound changes, carry the expected modern phonological shapes: cikenki (Saru; < Standard Japanese 付け木 tsukegi 'matches'), antuki (Saru; < 小豆 azuki 'azuki bean', with prenasalization from Tōhoku Japanese) .
The two strata — pre-Nara and post-Nara — are therefore separable through phonological shape alone.
The Eurasian Wanderwort — attested throughout Hokkaido and appearing at 4,210 corpus tokens — sits outside this Japanese-specific stratum.
Janhunen (2022 §5) classifies it as a continental Wanderwort; whether it entered Ainu via Japanese, via Tungusic, or through an older continental network is unresolved ‹speculative›
; the community has raised the same question without resolving it (antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-15, speculative).
The word is, by contrast, an Ainu coinage: reconstructible as Pre-PA *sii+sam/o with native Ainu morphology, surviving in the Yakumo dialect as samó .

The claim that Ainu was once spoken more broadly across the Japanese archipelago and left loanwords in Old Japanese is the most contested diachronic proposal currently appearing in peer-reviewed Ainu scholarship.

Vovin (2022) argues that Ainu extended through Kantō and Tōhoku before the Yayoi expansion, and that the Man'yōshū — particularly East Old Japanese (EOJ) in books 14 and 20 and West Old Japanese (WOJ) in books 17 and 19 — contains loans from this substrate ‹contested›
Among the specific etymologies Vovin proposes:
EOJ kuta 'house' ← Ainu (village→house shift parallel to Latin vicus/villa) .
WOJ porö 'big' ← Ainu .
OJ iruka 'dolphin' ← Ainu rika 'whale-fat' .
OJ kanimba 'cherry' ← Ainu karinpa 'cherry' .
Place names in Man'yōshū: Kanipa ← Ainu ka-ne-pa 'upper bank'; Ikuri ← Ainu ikure .

The loan-phonology proposed is systematic: Ainu geminate clusters simplify across the borrowing boundary (Ainu -kk- → OJ -k-); Ainu word-final consonants are lost in EOJ surface forms; and the Proto-Japonic vowel shifts *o > u and *e > i in EOJ environments are said to reflect the Ainu source shapes .
The argument has not been independently corroborated in either Old Japanese philology or Ainu linguistics.

The structural problem is that short monosyllabic resemblances — like WOJ porö ~ Ainu — fall within the range expected by chance between unrelated languages, and the required semantic shifts must be stipulated rather than derived from cross-linguistically attested patterns.

Janhunen (2022) characterises the shared features under the more general rubric of "Jōmonization of Japanese" — Ainu-type languages influencing Japonic typologically — without endorsing individual lexical etymologies of this kind .

The substrate hypothesis and the lexical-etymology program address different phenomena and should be kept analytically separate: the former has structural support; the latter remains unconfirmed ‹contested›.
Independent of the lexical-etymology debate, Janhunen (2022) develops a substrate account of Japonic that is better evidenced and more broadly accepted.

The Japonic family arrived on the archipelago with the Yayoi agricultural expansion from the Korean Peninsula, roughly between 900 BCE and 500 CE, and displaced the earlier "Jōmonic" linguistic communities whose long prior presence shaped Japonic phonology, morphology, and vocabulary in ways that remain incompletely disentangled ‹contested›
On this account, Ainu is the sole surviving Jōmon language — its survival "an accident" in the northeast while the Japonic expansion replaced the other Jōmon languages of the archipelago .
The ethnolinguistic implication is that the Ainu homeland was not Hokkaido but Honshu.

The present Hokkaido distribution results from northward movement: the Satsumon culture (c. 700–1200 CE) carried the Ainu linguistic ancestors northward, reaching northern Hokkaido around 1000 CE, southern Sakhalin around 1300 CE, and the Kuriles around 1500–1600 CE .
The Emishi (蝦夷) of northern Honshu are most plausibly treated as a proto-historical complex partly ancestral to the Ainu .

The Okhotsk culture (c. 600–1600 CE), whose language Janhunen associates with early Ghilyak/Amuric, was absorbed by the Satsumon population in northern Hokkaido and Sakhalin, contributing a borrowing residue treated in .
Community discussion connects the OJ ethnonym emi₁si with the Sakhalin Ainu ethnonym enciw.

Antitwilight (aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-23) proposes that OJ emi₁si borrows from a pre-Proto-Ainu form *æmi-ti, with the segmentation *ti = first-person plural, regularly giving > enciw ‹speculative›.

This partially converges with Janhunen's (2022 §4) note that enciw ~ Emishi/Ebisu/Ezo *emisV~*emiciV (citing Kindaichi 1960), though the specific morpheme segmentation proposed by the community goes beyond the published source and cannot be verified against it.
The word — which entered Japanese as tonakai — is a probable loan from a pre-Proto-Ghilyak source into Ainu, illustrating contact at the Okhotsk cultural interface ‹contested›
A Honshu Ainu homeland should have left a toponymic residue; place-name substrates are well attested where a speech community has been displaced but not entirely erased.

Two bodies of candidate evidence circulate in the literature: analysis of Tōhoku place names with elements cognate with productive Ainu geographical vocabulary, and Vovin's (2022 §3) identifications of Ainu-origin proper names in the Man'yōshū (§4 above).
Ainu geographical vocabulary is morphologically productive and well-documented in Hokkaido: , , , , and appear in hundreds of Hokkaido place names.

The community has noted specific Tōhoku cases: nukopoli (aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-01-22, proposed) analyses the Iwate surname and toponym 乙茂内 (Otomonai) as Ainu o-tum-nay 'head-middle-stream', citing the concentration of 内 (-nai) toponyms in the surrounding area as convergent evidence ‹speculative›.
The morphological segmentation is plausible against known Ainu geographical morphology, but confirmation requires independent phonological correspondence evidence that is not yet available.
A systematic survey of Tōhoku toponymy against the Ainu geographical lexicon remains a research gap.

The existing evidence — from the matagi hunter-gatherer vocabulary of Tōhoku, from the Emishi cultural zone extending considerably south of modern Hokkaido, and from the individual proposals above — is suggestive but not yet probative ‹speculative›.

The central methodological problem for all the proposals above is the triage between three origins for any given resemblance: inheritance from a common ancestor; borrowing through contact; and chance.
For an isolate, the inheritance route is ruled out by definition for resemblances with established families.
The issue is therefore always whether a similarity is contact-induced or accidental.
The standard diagnostics applied in the Ainu contact literature are:
Direction of spread: does the item appear only in lects geographically adjacent to the supposed source, or is it pan-Ainu?
A pan-Ainu distribution implies a pre-branching (Common Ainu or Proto-Ainu) age, excluding recent contact.
Morphological analyzability: inherited vocabulary tends to be internally structured; loans tend to be opaque.
carries no recoverable Ainu morpheme; (< ci=e-p) is fully transparent — see .
Loan phonology: for a directed borrowing, the donor-language form and the recipient-language form must be connected by phonologically plausible, preferably recurrent, processes.
Ad hoc adjustments stipulated for a single item weaken the case considerably.
Systematic correspondence: a genetic or deep-contact relationship requires recurrent sound-to-sound correspondences across a significant portion of core vocabulary, not sporadic resemblances.
By these criteria the early Japanese→Ainu stratum (§3) meets most diagnostics and is well established ‹consensus›.
Vovin's reverse-direction program (§4) proposes systematic loan-phonology but produces thin correspondence sets and semantically variable links, and has not been replicated ‹contested›.

The Jōmon-substrate thesis (§5) operates at a depth that forecloses direct lexical testing; it is evaluated primarily through population history and typological alignment and is best treated as a working hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result ‹contested›.
Two community discussions illustrate the methodological divide.

The proposal that Ainu si= (reflexive prefix, treated in ) is cognate with Korean and Old Japanese reflexive pronouns — aomidori_cs_, aynu-corpora Discord, 2023-12-08 — invokes forms short enough to match by chance and a semantic field (self-reference) common enough to arise independently; without a systematic correspondence framework the proposal cannot advance beyond conjecture ‹speculative›.

The set of proposed Korean-origin vocabulary items (casi, notak, mose, nay, toy — antitwilight, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-15, proposed ) faces the same difficulty: casi 'fortification' in particular has a plausible Ainu-internal structure and is not compelled to be a contact loan ‹contested›.
Both sets are the kind of etymologies that Alonso (2022 §1) and Janhunen (2022 §2) explicitly bracket as undemonstrable under the current methodological standard for Ainu.

At the typological level Ainu shares features with North Pacific Rim languages — polysynthetic morphology, head-marking, verb-final word order, extensive nominalization-based clause linkage — that place it loosely within a broad Northeast Asian typological zone, though Janhunen (2022 §3c) notes that Ainu "stands apart" even within that grouping.
The typological characterisation is descriptive, not a genetic or even a firm areal claim.
The contact-driven Amur areal layer has a real lexical residue, but its Hokkaido signature is thin.
The primary northern-contact zone was Sakhalin, where Ainu, Nivkh, Uilta, and Manchu (via the Santan trade) met; the lexical traffic is documented in .

The items that reached Hokkaido Ainu directly — (< Nivkh, with the 'fish-skin garment' sense retained in Sakhalin but reduced to 'sail' in Hokkaido), (morphologically opaque; possible ultimate Eurasian Wanderwort), (< Nivkh cʰaŋ, Uilta saan) — are documented borrowings, not indicators of genetic relationship .
Whether the Sakhalin contact situation constituted a true Sprachbund is left open by the most recent survey .

Alonso de la Fuente (2022 §2.4) observes that the reconstructed Proto-Ainu consonant inventory looks typologically like a mixed Southwest/Northeast Eurasian language that may have acquired some Southeast Asian-type features through contact: the merger of *l and *ɾ, the single fricative /s/, and the bare stop series /p t k/ are consistent with this areal profile.
The observation is typological inference, not a contact-language argument, and it post-dates the genetic-affiliation question addressed in this chapter.

The native core of the Hokkaido Ainu lexicon is organized around a small number of semantic fields whose internal structure feeds directly into the grammar.
Kinship terms and body-part nouns constitute the obligatorily-possessed (bound) noun class.
Motion verbs supply the primary paradigm of singular/plural stem suppletion.
Colour terms and property-denoting natural-world vocabulary are encoded as stative verbs, with no separate adjectival category.
Demonstratives, locative nouns, and postpositions combine into a layered spatial-deictic system anchored to river orientation.

The spatial deictic system has three interacting layers: a demonstrative series, a set of obligatorily-possessed locative nouns, and a small set of postpositions.

Within the proximal slot, the longer form taan has been proposed to carry greater information content or emphasis relative to tan, and a sound-symbolic account has been proposed in which narrow front vowels index proximity and broader back vowels index distance (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord 2025-12-27, proposed; ) ‹contested›.

Hokkaido Ainu oral narrative divides into three major genres: the heroic epic, the divine epic, and the prose folktale.

The prose folktale is designated in the Saru and Chitose dialects of southwestern Hokkaido and across much of southern Hidaka; the eastern dialects — Ishikari, Teshio, Kitami, Kushiro, Tokachi, and eastern Hidaka east of Shizunai — use tuytak for the same genre.
The two terms are geographically distributed, not functionally distinct ‹consensus›
(Confusingly, tuytak designates the divine epic in Samani; the term's referent is therefore dialect-specific — see .)

What distinguishes the prose tale from the two sung genres is the complete absence of three formal features: a fixed melody, a cyclically recurring refrain (), and the rhythm-stick () that performers and listeners use to keep time during heroic-epic recitation.
The narrator speaks in an ordinary, near-conversational voice.

The sakehe refrain and metre of the sung genres are treated in .
An additional prose sub-form, , carries heroic-epic content in prose delivery, enabling women narrators to perform yukar material without contravening the convention that verse yukar belongs to men .
The gendered allocation of genres is discussed in .
Speakers themselves characterise the prose tale as serious, factual narration rather than fiction.
Osuka Rieko of Shiraoi insists on the genre's truth-status, contrasting it with fabricated talk:
Endō identifies four sub-categories within the uwepeker heading :
Human prose tales (the default type).
The protagonist is an unnamed human — "the chief of ___", "a poor young man" — and the narration is in the first person with a retrospective identification at the close.

The most pervasive narrative shape is the impoverished-hero tale: a young man in reduced circumstances acquires power or a spouse through courage, divine favour, or correct conduct; the arc broadly rewards good behaviour and punishes bad.
Kamuy prose tales (kamuy uwepeker).
A deity narrates in the first person, aligning these tales with the world of divine epics despite their prose format; the language may reach into the elevated register .
Japanese-borrowed tales.
Adapted Japanese narratives told in the third person — "In a certain place there lived a young lord…" — with an Ainu-inflected worldview.
Pananpe–Penanpe tales.
A dyadic genre built around the archetypal pair ('downstream-dweller', pana-n-pe) and ('upstream-dweller', pena-n-pe).
Variant forms panakuru / penakuru, with kur 'person' rather than pe 'thing, person', also occur.
These tales are narrated in the third person, open with a formulaic pair-announcement, and are regarded as a children's genre .
The Pananpe–Penanpe opening is among the most stable formulae in the repertoire.
Both characters are introduced with the existential verb in succession, joined by a conjunctive clause.
The inferential evidential ruwe ne predicated over the whole opening grounds the state of affairs as established narrative fact (on this function see ):

Human prose tales open with a scene-setting passage establishing the protagonist's household and livelihood: an enumeration of family members, the father's hunting activities, the household's prosperity or poverty.
This is a learned formula, not an improvised description, and it recurs across narrators and dialect areas in broadly stable shape .
The closing formula works in the opposite direction.
The narrator, who has spoken throughout as the protagonist "I", reveals the protagonist's identity at the tale's end through a retrospective disclosure.
The pattern takes the shape of a quotative wrap: the protagonist's name or description appears inside a frame, which is closed by a verb of telling — typically — with explicit person marking.
The formula … sekor … isoytak ('…so [so-and-so] told the story') simultaneously attributes the performance to its narrator and discloses the fourth-person protagonist's identity .
The grammar of sekor and the interaction of the closing frame with the logophoric fourth person are treated in and .

The default prose tale is narrated in the first person from the protagonist's viewpoint, but the person marking on verbs is the fourth person — a= (transitive subject and possessor) and =an (intransitive subject) — not the everyday first-person singular ku=.
This fourth-person-as-narrative-'I' convention holds across all three major Saru/Chitose narrative genres and is the defining feature of Ainu oral narrative person-marking ‹consensus›

Within the prose tale, the same fourth-person forms also serve as a deferential honorific when the narrator-protagonist refers to a revered figure — an elder chief, a deity encountered in the story world, or a powerful adversary.
Here a= encodes not narrative self-reference but respectful distance ; .
Both functions, the logophoric and the honorific, are realised by the same set of forms and are distinguished by context.
The full paradigm and its referential range are set out in and ; the narrator-as-protagonist analysis and its relation to logophoricity are treated in .
Why a= rather than ku=?
Two competing accounts circulate in the literature ‹contested›.

The standard explanation traces the convention to a "shamaness-oracle" origin: the narrative voice is a possessing spirit speaking through the teller, making everyday first-person marking inappropriate.

Satō argues instead for an indirection principle (間接性の原理): the genre originated as a god's telling inside a dream addressed to a living human, and since direct god-to-human address is taboo, the non-everyday person marking adds the necessary indirectness .

Bugaeva and Nikitina reanalyse the narrator-protagonist using the framework of logophoricity: the "I" of the tale is a logophoric controller, the narration is direct-style throughout, and the fourth person is the Ainu mechanism for maintaining logophoric reference across the embedded narrative ; .
Whether Ainu oral narrative therefore qualifies as genuine "first-person literature" (一人称体) in the typological sense remains an open question ; ‹contested›.
The person-marking architecture that makes all these functions possible is surveyed in .
One feature distinguishes prose-tale person-marking from that of the sung genres: the number-agreement profile.

In the elevated register of heroic and divine epics, =an appears freely with a syntactically singular verb (ek-an 'I come', singular verb stem), overriding the everyday restriction that bars =an from singular stems in Saru/Chitose.
Prose uwepeker does not generally exploit this override; its number agreement follows the everyday pattern ‹corpus-suggested›
Because the prose tale maintains direct-voice narration throughout, and because embedded dialogue is a constant feature of the genre, the quotative complementizer sekor is dense.
Speech and thought reports are framed with sekor followed by one of a small set of reporting verbs: ye 'say', hawki 'recite/say', or isoytak 'narrate'.
The same frame reappears at the close of the whole performance in the retrospective identification formula discussed above .
The construction grammar of sekor, its position with respect to tense and aspect, and the distinction between direct and indirect-style reporting in prose narrative are treated in .

Participant tracking across extended prose narration — keeping the listener oriented among multiple characters when several embedded speakers each use "I" — relies on the fourth-person / first-person contrast in conjunction with the quotative frame.
The narrator-protagonist's embedded direct speech remains under the logophoric fourth person; secondary characters may receive everyday person marking.
The reference-tracking apparatus is treated in .

The TAM and evidential profile of prose tales — the predominance of ruwe ne as narrative-frame predicate, the aspectual distribution, and the sequencing role of conjunctive hine and akusu — is the topic of .
Human prose tales operate in (口語・日常語), the ordinary register, in contrast to the elevated poetic language (, 雅語) of heroic and divine epics ; .

Prose narration therefore avoids the hallmarks of the elevated register: the applicative case-marking prefixes (e-, o-, ko-) in place of spatial particles, the polysynthetic formulaic periphrases, and the elegant kin-term vocabulary (ona 'father', unu 'mother' as literary-register forms, against colloquial dialect variants) (nukopoli, 2024-06-15).
The elevated register and its structural diagnostics are surveyed in .
The boundary is not absolute.
Kamuy prose tales (kamuy uwepeker), in which a deity narrates, may draw on the elevated register, aligning their language with that of divine epics despite their prose format .

Narrators with a broad stylistic range may also import elevated vocabulary or formulae into human prose tales, and the register of any given performance reflects the individual narrator's competence and choices.
The elegant/everyday register boundary is a continuum keyed to verse-vs-prose and improvisation-vs-fixedness rather than a clean binary ‹contested›
The prosodic correlate of the everyday register is a characteristic intonation pattern.

Tamura notes that uwepeker narration is unidirectional — the teller speaks to an audience rather than seeking a response — and the voice falls to a flat, low-variation melodic contour across sentences, in contrast to the rising contour of conversational speech where the speaker solicits a reaction ; the community discussion in the aynu-corpora Discord (nukopoli, 2024-11-16) confirms this datum from Tamura's account .

Within the Saru basin, upper-Saru (mid-river) narrators tend toward a monotone delivery while lower-Saru (downriver) narrators show more melodic undulation; this microvariation does not affect the structural grammar of the genre.
Among Hokkaido Ainu narrative genres, two are sung verse: the heroic epic (yukar / sakorpe) and the divine epic (kamuy yukar / oyna).

Both are performed in the elevated register (atomte-itak), both narrate their story in the first person from the protagonist's viewpoint, and both draw on a dense stock of formulaic couplets and parallelism.
They diverge in several formal parameters that are diagnostically useful ; :
Both genres are narrated in the first person using the fourth-person (indefinite) prefixes a= / =an (see the section on the fourth-person narrator, below) rather than the everyday first-person ku=.
The register, verse form, and grammatical hallmarks they share are treated jointly here; the full genre taxonomy — including prose tales, prayer, and song — is set out in .
The yukar is the longest and most prestigious genre in Hokkaido Ainu oral literature.
The name itself encodes performance: Kayano glosses it as 'to imitate / mimic' — the narrator heard the story (perhaps in a dream) and now re-tells it .
In south-west Hokkaido the Saru and Chitose term yukar is standard; eastern varieties use sakorpe (lit. 'the thing with sakor') in Tokachi .
The Samani term yayerap and the prose-content alternative irupaye (yukar material recited without melody) mark additional regional and performative variation.
A yukar performance is sung to a melody that belongs to the narrator rather than to the story: each performer re-melodizes a borrowed narrative, and the tune may shift mid-performance .
The narrator and listeners keep time by beating the hearth-rim with a stick, repni ('rhythm-stick'), the act called .
Listeners may add a chorus (hetce).
There is no fixed sakehe refrain, which is the single clearest formal contrast with the divine epic.

Satō notes an opening formula eyororpe that may repeat at the very start of a performance and reads it as a possible vestige of a refrain that the heroic epic once shared with the divine epic ‹speculative›
The protagonist is a parentless superhuman youth — in Saru texts typically Poy-ya-un-pe or Pon Sinutapka-un-kur; in eastern Hokkaido Pon Otasam/Otasut-un-kur.
The hero flies, dives, and travels underground; battles are not governed by a good-vs-evil worldview but by heroic competition .
Female protagonists appear in the menoko yukar subgenre, which keeps the heroic format but centres on marriage rather than battle.

The term (ram-etok 'spirit-tip') stands alone for the hero-concept; a second term cipapa appears in Chiri Mashiho's Shinyōshū annotations but is not documented in other dictionaries (gengojiro, 2024-02-13, asserted) ‹speculative›.
The yukar is traditionally narrated by men; women tell the prose equivalent irupaye instead .
Modern revitalization practices have women reciting verse yukar, knowingly departing from the traditional allocation .
The gendered narrator convention connects to the broader pattern of genre allocation by sex treated in .
In the divine epic the narrator speaks in the voice of a deity — a kamuy: an animal, plant, fire, water, weather phenomenon, or object — telling its own story.
The Saru/Chitose term is kamuy yukar; Tokachi uses oyna for the same genre .

The term oyna is, however, ambiguous across the dialect area: in coastal Hidaka and Iburi it labels a distinct genre whose protagonist is the culture-hero Oynakamuy (Aynurakkur / Okikurmi) and which uses no sakehe, while in Tokachi and Sakhalin it covers the divine epic proper ; .

At Saru, the term is absent from Hiraga Sadamo's (平賀サダモ) usage — she subsumed what Kindaichi and Kubodera classified as sacred biographies under her yukar label, a dialectally conditioned genre-boundary that resists a single universal taxonomy ‹contested›.
In contrast to the heroic epic, each kamuy yukar is sung to a fixed melody that belongs to the story itself, not to the narrator .
Performances are shorter (minutes to roughly an hour) and are associated traditionally with women narrators, though men may also perform them .
The canonical published collection is Chiri Yukie's アイヌ神謡集 (Ainu Shin'yōshū, 1923) , thirteen Horobetsu/Iburi kamuy yukar with parallel Japanese translation.

Compiled by Yukie Chiri (知里幸恵, 1903–1922), it remains the most widely read primary text of Ainu oral literature and provides the main evidence for the Iburi convention of using the exclusive first-plural ci= / =as as a singular deity-narrator marker (see the section on fourth-person narration, below).

The chapter title formulae in this collection — for example AEKIRUSHI — have been analysed as a=e-kir-usi 'the place one has memory of' (after 片山龍峯 2003) rather than as a reflex of ekiru 'turn back' (0penke, 2024-03-19, proposed) ‹contested›.
The sakehe (variant saha, Chiri 1955) is the defining feature of the kamuy yukar: a fixed, often semantically opaque refrain inserted into the narration.
It is fixed per story — the same kamuy yukar story-type may carry a different sakehe in different localities .
See for verse-structural detail; the present section concerns the grammatical and philological facts.
The word sakehe is the possessed form of : sake-he, 'the sake of (something)'.
Tamura's Saru dictionary distinguishes this accented form (sákehe 'melody; refrain') from the unaccented noun for 'sake-rice-wine' (also sake) .
The formal identity of the two is reflected in line-internal puns where both readings are live simultaneously.
The sakehe is inserted every line or every few lines, depending on the story; the insertion pattern is fixed for a given text but not uniform across the genre .
The content ranges from the transparently onomatopoeic — the cuckoo-deity's sakehe han kakkok kakkok imitates its own call — to the semantically opaque.

The function of the sakehe is debated: Nakagawa (2001b, via ) holds that it originally indexed the protagonist, but many sakehe have no recoverable referential link; and the same story-type does not carry the same sakehe across localities ‹contested›.

The Biratori corpus preserves the narrator 貝澤とぅるしの (Kaizawa Turushino) explicitly labelling the phenomenon: after reciting the thunder-deity's refrain hum pakpak, she glosses it humihiruy だわ。sakehe. 'it's a loud sound — [that's] the sakehe' .
This is one of the clearest native metalinguistic testimonies on the genre term itself.

Similarly, the mid-Saru narrator 川上まつ子 (Kawakami Matsuko, ILCAA corpus) describes how the menoko yukar ('female heroic epic') differs from the prose alternative she uses: one is told with the sakehe (sakekoye), the other as an uwepeker (prose tale), and the version with sakehe runs long while the prose version is short .
Okuda's analysis of Hokkaido Ainu verse identifies two distinct metrical systems, deployed by genre and musical rhythm :
The syllable-count metre — with its 5-syllable basic line — was the established description from Kindaichi (1931) and Tamura (1973) onward .
Okuda's addition is the accent-orientation metre identified in divine-epic texts.

In his scansion of Amamecikappo narrated by Hatozawa Wateke (Monbetsu; Tamura 2001), 14 of 90 non-refrain lines are 4 syllables, and 12 of those 14 carry their first accent on syllable 1 — consistent with accent-orientation rather than syllable-count .
The scansion pattern is illustrated below (● = first accented syllable):
Okuda further reports that the same reciters' lyric poems are overwhelmingly 5-syllable, confirming that the two systems are not speaker-dependent but genre- and rhythm-dependent .
He claims no other language is documented to use two such metre types by one reciter .

A further hypothesis holds that the syllable-count system entered Ainu via contact with the Japanese 7-5 mora metre, with accent-orientation as the native baseline — but Okuda notes there is no direct evidence for this at present ‹speculative›.
On the question of rhyme and alliteration: Philippi (1979, via ) held that rhyme in Ainu verse is 'quite accidental' and alliteration 'sporadic'.

Tangiku (2020), as reported from community discussion, argues that an 18th-century yukar text (ルウェサニウンクㇾ) shows deliberate head-rhyme, end-rhyme, and imperfect rhyme (nukopoli, 2023-12-13, asserted, citing Tangiku 2020) ‹contested›.
The question of whether Ainu verse rhyme is a real compositional device or an artefact of a small phoneme inventory remains open.

To hit the target syllable count, poets employ a recognized set of techniques: formulaic verse phrases, syllable-appropriate word choice, presence/absence of final particles, insertion of the dummy verb between verb and following element, uncontracted ku- person marker, a line-initial prefixed u, and the suppression of vowel elision that occurs freely in prose speech ; .
All sung verse genres, and prose narrative as well, are told in the first person from the protagonist's point of view throughout, with a closing identification formula revealing who 'I' was ; .
The 'first person' is, however, expressed not by everyday ku= (1SG) but by the fourth-person set: transitive-subject a=, intransitive-subject =an, object i= (Saru / Chitose baseline) ; .

The typological status of this convention — whether it represents genuine first-person narration throughout or a logophoric construction framing the whole text as a reported speech act — is unsettled ; ‹contested›.
The logophoric analysis is developed in .

Satō (2008: 259–261) offers a pragmatic motivation he calls the indirection principle (間接性の原理): oral literature originated as a deity's narration inside a dream, and the taboo on a deity addressing a living human directly motivates a non-everyday first-person marker that increases indirectness .
He presents this explicitly as a hypothesis of his own, dissenting from the standard 'shamaness-oracle origin' theory (巫女の託宣起源説) ‹contested›.
The discourse–narration connection is taken up in .

In Saru and Chitose yukar and kamuy yukar the hero or deity is indexed throughout by the fourth-person prefixes a= (transitive subject) and =an (intransitive subject), identical in form to the everyday indefinite and inclusive uses of the fourth person .
Corpus attestation of the narrative a= comes predominantly from prose tale (uwepeker) texts , where the same convention applies.
The Abuta (虻田, Iburi) yukar narrated by Tōshima Tanke shows the same set: rek kor okay 'is crying' (durative; l.46), paye=an anki 'I am about to go' (prospective; l.113) .
The verb sakehawki 'to sing/recite (a yukar)' appears in the same text, an Iburi-specific term .
In Iburi kamuy yukar — above all in Chiri Yukie's アイヌ神謡集 (Horobetsu, 1923) — the deity-narrator uses the exclusive first-plural ci= / =as consistently as a singular first person ; .
In Chitose, ci= / =as may appear at the opening and then revert to a= / =an .
The hero-person marker is thus both genre-conditioned and regionally conditioned, forming a two-way system across Hokkaido:
The architecture of these person cells is developed in ; the honorific and logophoric readings of the fourth-person set in .
Everyday Saru/Chitose allows the intransitive suffix =an only with plural verb stems: arki=an 'we come (PL)', never *ek=an (the singular stem ek 'come.SG' does not take =an in prose).
In the elevated verse register, =an does combine with singular stems to mark the hero-narrator as fourth person :
This override extends to non-Saru/Chitose dialects which in prose also attach =an only to plurals; the singular-stem combination is a verse-register diagnostic across southern Hokkaido .
Both genres use the elevated register (atomte-itak, lit. 'decorated language'), which differs from everyday speech (yayan-itak) along four grammatical parameters identified by Satō :
Everyday Ainu marks locatives and goals by free particles (ta for locative, un for goal, etc.).
The verse register replaces these with applicative verbal prefixes (e-, o-, ko-), producing longer, morphologically heavier verb forms .
The contrast is attested in the Chitose data Satō provides:
The applicative system itself is described in , and its interaction with the verse register in .
Verse register words are structurally heavier than their everyday counterparts through elaborated prefixation and the use of periphrastic expressions where prose would use a single stem.
Satō's examples include soyna-sanma o-si-ray-e (lit. 'let oneself be pushed out') for everyday soyne 'go out', and kamuy ne manu p (lit. 'what is said to be a god') for kamuy 'god/deity' .
The periphrastic tendency also serves the syllable-count metre (§ above).
The verse register maintains a vocabulary stratum not used in everyday speech.

Genre-specific terms include the elegant kin terms and , contrasting with the colloquial and regionally variable haca/hapo (nukopoli, 2026-06-15, asserted; consistent with the distinct elegant lexicon described in ).

The modifier kamuy meaning 'splendid' (as opposed to its deity meaning) is attested in heroic epic but not in prayer — an instance of genre-internal lexical differentiation within the elevated register itself .
This register lexicon is catalogued in .
Couplets and parallel lines are the backbone rhetorical device of both sung genres ; .
Lines do not need to rhyme or metrically match to count as a couplet — the requirement is semantic or structural correspondence only.

The most productive template is tu … / re … 'two … / three …', which does not mean an exact count but a rhetorical plural ('many'): otu maw-kur-puni kane / ore maw-kur-puni kane 'raising two winds / raising three winds' (= many winds) .
forms: otu maw-kur-puni kane / ore maw-kur-puni kane

text: Formulaic descriptive phrases are memorized in bulk and redeployed across texts, serving syllable-count requirements while conveying conventional praise or scene-setting; for example, tuk-no pinni si-kopa-yar / aynu pito 'a fine person like a grown Manchurian-ash tree' (containing si-kopa-yar 'like', not used in everyday speech) .
The full couplet and word-pair inventory is treated in .

Reference-tracking across the long stretches of yukar narration relies on the same fourth-person set throughout, with quotative sekor + speech verb (ye, hawki, isoytak) closing and re-opening direct-speech frames.
The density of sekor in verse is addressed under and ; the reportative tail hawe ne / hawe as as a narration-closure device is treated in .
Several questions about the verse genres remain open in the literature:
Is Ainu oral literature genuine first-person literature? The uniform use of the fourth-person set throughout all three narrative genres is typologically unusual.
Whether it constitutes true first-person (direct-style) narration or a logophoric construction that frames the entire text as reported speech is unsettled ; ‹contested›.

Genre-boundary cases. The aynu-corpora community has identified 織田ステノ's kamuy yukar '怠け者の子供' as resistant to genre classification: it has a long sakehe (*manayta sanke tar panke tar kocupu*) but a short body and ends as a yayeisoytak (self-narration) by a human boy — 'neither kamuy yukar nor yukar, and (having a melody) not prose' (gengojiro, 2025-12-12, proposed) ‹contested›.
This is consistent with Endō's own caveat that regional genre inventories do not map cleanly onto any single scheme .
The residual refrain. Satō's reading of the opening eyororpe as a vestige of a lost yukar refrain is an inference without independent textual support ‹speculative›.

Two metres or one? The long-standing syllable-count description (Kindaichi 1931; Tamura 1973, via ) and Okuda's accent-orientation metre are treated as genre- and rhythm-differentiated by Okuda himself, but the relationship between them — whether one is derivative of the other or they are independent — is not settled ‹contested›

Prayer speech — or — belongs to the chant (唱え言) macro-category of Ainu oral performance, whose distinguishing feature is that the speaker's will is directed toward a non-present audience: deities, spirits, the dead, or distant humans .
The chant category is set out alongside the narrative and song categories in ; the present chapter treats the grammatical and register properties of prayer speech specifically.

Within the chant sub-system, prayer () is distinguished from incantation by improvisation: a prayer is composed fresh each time, to the worshipper's own melody, whereas an incantation is memorised word-for-word and shared with a fixed community tune .
Prayer is further distinguished from the speech-act of public negotiation () by its divine addressee.
The genre boundaries are set out in the table below.
(After .) Both and name the prayer register, the former foregrounding the act of worship and the latter the word-substance of the address.

The corpus of 209,878 sentences returns 405 times (rank 405) and 203 times (rank 675), though these counts fold together metalinguistic mentions in narrative texts with tokens in actual prayer performance ‹corpus-suggested›.
A is an address to the divine world conducted at the altar () or the hearth.
The fire deity () is invoked first in every prayer, as the goddess who relays human words to the gods; all subsequent divine recipients are addressed through her .
Prayer is structurally a two-stage act of communication: worshipper → fire deity → target deity.

The right to lead prayer is restricted to adult men ‹consensus›; women's formal expression of gratitude takes the verbal gesture of accompanied by , while men perform (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-12-26, asserted; ).
The material offerings that accompany prayer — , fermented millet wine (), and dumplings () — are enumerated in narrative prose when speakers describe the ceremony from outside it.

In one Saru uwepeker, the narrator 川上まつ子 lists the offerings: kamuynomi atpa ne, a=nomi wa inaw ne ciki sake ne ciki sito ne ciki pirka uske 'at the start of the kamuy-nomi, [we] worship and (offer) fine things — inaw, sake, dumplings…' (川上まつ子, AA研 uwepeker 12, Saru).

text: The disjunctive X ne ciki 'whether it be X' is an enumerating formula in elevated narrative, not specific to prayer speech itself — see the genre taxonomy chapter.
The ceremonies associated with prayer speech include the seasonal worship calendars (, , ; nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-03-18, asserted; ) and the bear-sending ceremony.
The verb forms for the sending ceremonies are semantically distinct: / / (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2024-11-17, asserted, citing 欠ヶ端和也 2016; ).
The prayer speech that accompanies these ceremonies follows the same grammatical register as all kamuy-nomi, regardless of the ceremony type.
Prayer speech belongs to the elevated register (雅語), which is distinguished from everyday speech () by a set of grammatical and lexical properties described in .
Kindaichi's ranking of genres by elegant-language density — greeting < prayer < incantation < < — places prayer above everyday greeting speech but below the heaviest verse genres .

In Nakagawa's reformulation, elegant and everyday language are not a binary but stages on a verse/improvisation continuum, and the prayer sub-register is sufficiently distinct from the yukar sub-register that Nakagawa proposes a prayer-word vs. yukar-word classification as more analytically useful than the simple elegant/everyday dichotomy ‹contested›.

Four defining properties of (as formulated in Nakagawa 2001a[1987], via ) apply to prayer speech: (1) verse structure built on five- or four-syllable line units; (2) formulaic phrases deployed to meet the syllable count; (3) morphologically more complex and polysynthetic forms than their everyday equivalents; and (4) a distinct, genre-conditioned vocabulary.
Properties (3) and (4) are examined in §§ applicative morphology and prayer vocabulary below; property (2) in .

The most striking person-marking contrast between prayer speech and narrative oral literature is that prayer uses the first-person singular prefix (and suffix in singular intransitives) where verse narrative uses the fourth person .

In narrative genres — heroic epic, divine epic, and prose tale — the protagonist narrates in a non-everyday first person realized by the fourth-person affixes / , which indexes the narrative voice with a degree of indirection compatible with the "dream-origin" hypothesis for oral literature ; the full account of this fourth-person narrative function is given in and .
Prayer speech addresses the deities directly in the worshipper's own voice, and uses accordingly.

An attested prayer text from the Monbetsu region (鍋澤モトゾウ /Motoanrek, narrator; cited via ) shows the forms ku-e-ko-pase-… and k=e-ko-onkami 'I reverently worship [you]' — both built on the first-person singular prefix / (reduced allomorph before a vowel-initial stem), not the fourth person.
The contrast with narrative is thus: fourth person in narrative oral literature, first singular in prayer ‹corpus-suggested›.
See and for the person paradigm.
Attested narrative prose confirms the iterative worship pattern with the fourth-person index.

Prayer belongs to the elevated register's most characteristic morphological pattern: locative and goal relations are expressed by applicative prefixes (, , ) rather than by postpositional case particles ; .

The applicative system is described in ; what is distinctive in prayer is the density of stacked applicatives — two or more prefixes on the same verb, encoding simultaneously the goal deity and the manner of approach.
The Monbetsu prayer text cited above shows k=e-ko-onkami: the goal applicative marks the deity as the target of worship, and the additional encodes the dimension of address .

The contrast between everyday and elevated locative marking is illustrated in : the everyday form uses the particle — tanto Ukurmem ta ku-sirepa 'I arrived at Ukurmem today' — whereas the elevated form marks the same relation with the goal applicative :
The same goal-applicative pattern recurs in narrative prose.
A Saru uwepeker records the iterative worship frame with the applicative prefix on the verb and the fourth-person narrative index:
In prayer speech the same applicative morphology applies, but with the first-singular prefix.
The pattern k=e-ko- combines two applicative prefixes: for the divine recipient and for the domain of address.
Multiple applicative stacking is an established property of the elevated register and is treated typologically in .

The lexical register of prayer is genre-conditioned in a stronger sense than the elevated/everyday dichotomy alone would predict: certain epithets and noun phrases occur only in prayer and are not found in everyday speech or in other verse genres.
Endō identifies this as a property that motivates treating prayer vocabulary as a distinct sub-class of the elevated register rather than simply a variety of the yukar lexicon .
The fire deity provides the clearest documented case.
In everyday speech and in the divine epic (), the fire deity is called .
In prayer, two distinct epithets replace this:
The epithet 'grandmother who rules the land' was documented in the prayer text of 鍋澤モトゾウ (Motoanrek, Monbetsu; cited via ) and is described by Endō as "not found in any other genre".

The epithet (where = 1.O-raise = 'the one who raised me') or its kamuy-variant references the fire deity's role as the deity who reared and protects the community, a relationship that everyday does not encode .

Endō (2009, cited via ) further notes that the modifier with the meaning 'splendid' or honorific intensifier occurs in heroic epics but not in prayer, a further sub-register distinction within elevated speech ‹corpus-suggested›.

The elegant kin terms documented in the lexicon also belong to this prayer-adjacent register: and are the elevated equivalents of the colloquial / (nukopoli, aynu-corpora Discord, 2026-06-15, asserted; ).

Their attestation in prayer contexts has not been independently verified from prayer texts, but the community observation is consistent with the elegant-register lexical substitution described in ‹corpus-suggested›.
Prayer utterances, and formal speech-acts that invoke prayer register, frequently close with the frame ruwe tapan na, a ceremonial assertion tail.

In the frame is marked as a register-specific feature of formal/ ceremonial speech; it appears in prayer contexts and is also documented in other elevated speech (the greeting and negotiation genres).
The frame combines the evidential formal noun — the same element treated as an inferential evidential in — with the proximate demonstrative in place of the copula .
The effect is to assert the clause content as an already-established fact that the addressee can witness directly; in prayer speech, the deity is the witness ; .
The full evidential system built on formal nouns is set out in .
What the prayer use adds is that ruwe tapan (versus the more common ruwe ne) is register-marked: it is a ceremonial variant found in formal genres and not in everyday assertion.

Whether the selection of 'this' over (copula) encodes a special speech-act value — presenting the prayer content as observable to the divine audience — or whether it is simply a lexically frozen formulaic closure is not settled by the available sources ‹speculative›.

A diagnostic of elevated speech reported for both Saru and Chitose is the number-agreement override: in everyday speech, the suffix combines only with a plural verb form (e.g., 'we come'), never with a singular stem (*ek=an would be ungrammatical in conversation).
In the elevated register, may appear on a singular verb form — ek=an 'I come (sg.)' — to index the first-person narrative voice of the verse persona ; .

As prayer speech uses the first-singular rather than the fourth-person , the number-agreement override in its narrative form does not apply within prayer itself; but the wider pattern of agreement relaxation is part of the atomte-itak grammar that prayer shares with yukar and kamuy yukar.

The prayer/incantation contrast rests on a single axis: prayer is improvised ("not memorised like scripture; spun out by improvisation, different each time", Nakagawa 2016: 16, cited via ), while incantation is word-for-word fixed and communally shared.
Both use melody; both address deities; both belong to the chant category.
Grammatically, the shared elevated-register morphology (applicatives, archaic vocabulary, number override) applies to both, since both are composed in .

The improvised character of prayer means that no canonical prayer text has the status of a fixed literary work in the way that a kamuy yukar or yukar text does: prayers are attested only as specimens preserved in recordings or transcriptions, not as memorized texts reproduced with authority by named successors .
At the same time, prayer is heavily formulaic at the level of the phrase and the opening sequence (address to the fire deity; enumeration of offerings), even though the full utterance is improvised.
This is the pattern Nakagawa identifies for the elevated register generally: formulae — fixed verse phrases that are learned and re-deployed — are the unit of memorisation, not the text .

The formulaic patterns in prayer overlap with those in yukar and kamuy yukar (couplet structures, tu ~ / re ~ 'two ~ / three ~' intensification doublets, applicative periphrases) and are described in .

Actual prayer texts preserved in audio or transcription are sparser in the accessible Hokkaido corpus than narrative texts, for reasons Endō notes: prayer is a performative act tied to ceremony, not a memorised genre reproduced for entertainment or transmission .
The Hokkaido corpus (209,878 sentences) contains metalinguistic mentions of prayer words embedded in narrative (uwepeker, kamuy yukar) rather than extended stretches of prayer speech itself.

The primary documented prayer text accessible for grammatical analysis is the Monbetsu (Biratori) example attributed to 鍋澤モトゾウ (Motoanrek), cited and analysed by ; further attested prayer language appears in the Biratori oral-literature archives and in the ILCAA Ainu language materials through prosodic and formulaic phrases embedded in narrators' own metalinguistic commentary.

The renewal of prayer speech in the revitalisation era has produced written specimens — the periodical includes self-composed prayer formulas by speakers including 大野徹人 (Samani) — but these are modern compositions; they attest living competence in the prayer register rather than traditional continuous transmission.
The evidential tail ruwe tapan na glossed above (§ruwe tapan) comes from such a modern specimen.

The distinction between documented traditional prayer texts and revitalisation-era compositions is maintained throughout; the register properties described in this chapter are drawn from traditional materials unless stated otherwise.
