The passage glossed in this chapter is drawn from the Asahikawa section of , a conversational textbook produced by the Hokkaidō Utari Kyōkai to accompany a set of VHS recordings.
Two speakers are documented: Sugimura Fusa (杉村フサ) and Kawamura Tome (川村トメ), both of Asahikawa (旭川市).

The exchange depicts a neighbour's visit — calling at the door, being invited in, exchanging a well-being greeting, and closing with a weather remark — and brings into a single connected stretch several constructions that are analysed in separate chapters of this grammar: the polar-question frame of the evidential, the 1SG and 2SG person prefixes, the causal connective kusu, and the inferential auxiliary nankor.
The dialect is Asahikawa (), a northern Hokkaido variety; the transcription uses the romanization conventions of the original publication, with small-kana codas rendered as their consonant values.
The register is everyday colloquial speech, sharply distinct from the elevated vocabulary of oral-literature genres (; ) and from the gendered-register differences documented in .
The published source is ; Asahikawa section, speakers Sugimura Fusa and Kawamura Tome.
Sugimura calls through the closed door, addressing her friend as sapo (older sister, a close-kin address term).

The existential verb appears without a person prefix: in Hokkaido Ainu, the 3rd person is zero-marked (), and the intended referent — the woman inside — is a 3rd-person entity from the caller's perspective.
The formal noun in its bare clause-final position, without the following copula ne, builds the polar-question frame rather than the declarative evidential (the polar-question frame).
Kawamura responds and invites her visitor in.

The directive particle in Asahikawa corresponds to in Saru and most other varieties (a difference noted in a footnote of the original publication ); it functions as a polite imperative softener, not as the default bare imperative ().
The motion verb is the singular form; its suppletive plural is .
A single visitor is addressed, hence the singular ().
Later in the visit Sugimura enquires after Kawamura's well-being, now with an explicit 2nd-person prefix on the same existential verb .

The contrast between the zero-marked opening question (an ruwe?, §2) and the prefix-marked well-being question shows the full range of the person system operating on a single verb stem: 3rd-person referents are zero-marked, while 1SG and 2SG carry distinct prefixes throughout Hokkaido ().

Person marking in the Ainu verb is obligatory in careful speech; its omission in the opening formula above reflects conversational reduction where the referent is fully recoverable from the situation (; ).
The conjunctive particle connecting or closing clauses is treated in .
The visit closes with a brief weather exchange.
Kawamura's remark is a biclausal construction: a causal adverbial clause in followed by a main-clause assertion.
The causal connective belongs to the pattern treated in .
The property verb is an intransitive predicate whose subject — the weather — is zero-marked at 3rd person.
Sugimura's agreeing response uses the same property verb with the 4th-person intransitive suffix .
The 4th / indefinite person, whose S-role index is =an, shifts the perspective from a specific 3rd-person subject to a general experiencer ().
The existential-type aspect form V=an is the same suffix in its aspectual function, discussed in .
Kawamura rounds off the exchange with a prediction, using the inferential auxiliary .

Unlike ruwe ne, which presents content as already-established knowledge (), nankor encodes a tentative, inference-based assertion: the speaker reasons from current conditions rather than perceiving or reporting the future event directly.
The auxiliary is discussed as part of the epistemic-modal paradigm in and at the evidential-mirative interface in .
The Asahikawa form undergoes sandhi: nankor followed by the final particle na surfaces as nankornā, rendered in the source's Katakana as ナンコンナー.
The seven utterances above cover a cluster of constructions whose full analyses belong to separate chapters.
The table maps each to its primary grammatical feature.

The passage also illustrates a characteristic feature of Ainu conversational structure: each turn-final predicate controls the evidential or modal framing for the whole turn — ruwe in the questions, wa in the open-chain response, bare na in the assertions, and nankor na in the inference.
The parallel between this conversational pattern and the evidential-turn structure of oral-literature frame-text is noted in ; the contrast with oral-literature patterning is illustrated in .
The sentences glossed in this chapter come from , Murasaki Kyōko's revised introductory textbook of West-Sakhalin (Enciw) Ainu.

The primary data were elicited at Tokoro on the Sea of Okhotsk coast, chiefly from Fujiyama Haru (c. 1895–1974) and Asai Take (c. 1916–1994), the two principal consultants in Murasaki's fieldwork programme spanning 1960–1994.
A small number of illustrations also draw on Nagara Iso (Shiretoko/Chirijiri).

The dialect represented is the western coastal (Raichiishka/Laichiśka) variety; minor contrasts with the slightly more southerly Maoka variety and the northeastern Taraika variety are noted where they bear on the comparisons below .
The orthography follows Hattori's phonemic transcription , as adopted by Murasaki.
Long vowels are written double (aa ee oo etc.); every vowel-initial syllable carries the glottal onset written ʼ; the six permissible coda consonants are -h -m -n -s -w -y.
A person prefix is separated from its verb stem by =.

Piłsudski's 1912 Sakhalin corpus , the earliest substantial Enciw text collection, uses a different Romanization; forms cited from that source elsewhere in this grammar have been converted to the Hattori convention following .
No Cyrillic script is reproduced.
The broader typological and diachronic profile of Sakhalin Ainu relative to Hokkaido is developed in .
Five sentences drawn from Murasaki's lesson dialogues are glossed below.
Together they sample existential predication, attributive and locative structure, equational copula, analytic negation, suppletive verbal number, and the first-person object prefix.
Each sentence was produced by Fujiyama Haru or Asai Take in elicitation sessions conducted by Murasaki .
The most immediately audible distinction between SA and Hokkaido (HK) Ainu is prosodic.

Where Saru and other HK varieties carry a lexically contrastive pitch accent on stems, West-Sakhalin has phonemic vowel quantity — long vowels (written double) versus short vowels — with no accentual contrast.
The two systems correspond diachronically: what HK encodes as a high pitch on a short vowel, SA encodes as length on that vowel ; .
A selection of cognate pairs from Murasaki's textbook illustrates the pattern :
A second phonological divergence involves the coda consonants.
HK retains the Proto-Ainu coda obstruents /-p -t -k -r/ directly in the citation form of nouns and verb stems.
SA replaces all four with a single surface segment /-h/, which is the reflex of the historical closure when no vowel follows; the original coda emerges when a vowel-initial suffix is added ; .
The affiliative (possessed) suffix therefore restores the underlying consonant, as the table of nominal pairs shows:
The SA citation forms ceh teh sih kah all surface with /-h/; the historical /-p -k -k -p/ re-emerge in the affiliative.
HK retains the coda obstruents in the citation form itself.

The HK affiliative suffix morphophonology is described in ; the diachronic correspondence between the SA surface /-h/ and the HK retained obstruents, with its implications for the internal reconstruction of Proto-Ainu codas, is the subject of ‹consensus›.
Example (3) illustrates the SA negative copula construction.

The sequence ka hannehka (nee) negates an equational proposition: ka is the focus particle, and hannehka is the negative predicate, historically the copula root with the negative prefix han- prefixed .
The same prefix attaches directly to verb stems for verbal negation: hannehka ku='oman 'I did not go'.
The copula nee following the negative is frequently omitted in conversational speech.
HK Saru negates an equational predicate with the independent negative particle somo before the copula, yielding somo ne (NEG COP).
The HK somo particle and its distribution across existential, copular, and verbal contexts are described in .
Dal Corso's study of SA negation treats the structural history of the SA han- series and its divergence from the Hokkaido system in detail ‹contested›.

The SA person-prefix inventory parallels HK in its core forms — first-person singular ku= (A/S), first-person singular object 'en= — but diverges in what it assigns to the paradigm cell that HK labels 'fourth person' or 'indefinite'.
In SA the morpheme 'an-/='an functions as first-person plural in the speech of younger speakers, and as first-person singular in the elderly register, the inverse of its value in HK ; .
SA accordingly has no productive indefinite/fourth-person paradigm of the HK type; the HK system is described in and .
Example (4) shows the SA third-person plural subject suffix =hci cliticizing to the verb: 'ariki=hci 'they came'.

HK grammars report no cognate suffix in this structural position; Dal Corso's alignment study traces the SA morpheme to a grammaticalized pronoun and argues that the SA system encodes a richer nominal-tracking morphology than any Hokkaido variety.
Sakaguchi provides the most detailed morphological analysis of the SA person–number paradigm to date ‹speculative›.
SA and HK share suppletive verbal number — distinct verb stems indexed to the number of the core argument — but enforce it differently.
In SA, grammatical number agreement is strict: a plural subject requires the plural verb form, with no tolerance for the singular at low counts that is documented in Hokkaido .
The existential opposition in examples (1) and (2) — singular 'an versus plural 'okay — is cognate with HK an versus oka=an .
Similarly, 'eh (singular 'come') and 'ariki (plural 'come') in example (4) are cognate with HK ek / arki.
The final long vowel in SA 'ariki versus the short vowel in HK arki is consistent with the length-accent correspondence noted in the preceding section.
The HK suppletive verbal number system is described in ‹consensus›.
This glossary defines the grammatical and linguistic terms used throughout the grammar.
Entries are alphabetized by the English head-term.

Each entry gives a concise definition oriented to Hokkaido Ainu, notes where the analysis is unsettled ‹contested›, and cross-references the chapter or chapters where the term is most fully analyzed and exemplified.
Ainu forms follow the Latin transcription adopted in ; grammatical abbreviations used here follow the inventory in .
The grammar's interlinear examples follow the Leipzig Glossing Rules , adapted for the morphological structure of Ainu.
A minimal example has three aligned lines: a morphemic segmentation line (m), a gloss line (g), and a free translation (tr).

An optional surface-form line (ain) appears where the orthographic surface differs from the segmentation; an original-script line (orig) preserves katakana source text where the segmentation is editorial.
The methodology governing source attribution, example selection, and the layout of example headers is set out in .
Three symbols mark morpheme structure within a word:
The personal indexes (ku=, e=, eci=, a=, =an, =as, and the object prefixes) are uniformly marked with = throughout the grammar.

This follows the orthographic convention begun by Nakagawa (from his 1980s data-management practice, promulgated in the 1986 語りの中の生活誌 and now dominant in Hokkaidō teaching and descriptive materials): the = keeps inflectional person marking visually distinct from derivation and makes the dictionary headword recoverable.
It is expressly not the Leipzig-glossing clitic boundary — Nakagawa himself notes his usage is unrelated to that convention .
Other sources notate the same elements differently: Satō and Ijäs write them with hyphens, Hattori and Tamura solid, Kirikae with a space; examples quoted from those sources are renotated to = here.
The markers' actual morphological status — clitic-like for =an, affix-like for the prefixal set — is mixed and contested, and is treated in and .
Derivational material — applicative prefixes, the causative suffix -ke, the reflexive and reciprocal prefixes, and the plural stem suffix -pa — is separated with -.
The portmanteau dot . joins fused atoms within a single gloss position without inserting a morpheme boundary on the morphemic line.

Two uses arise: (1) person-and-role portmanteaux (1sg.a for a single morpheme encoding both first-person singular and agent), and (2) a lexical-root gloss combined with a grammatical atom (track.poss for ru-we 'the trace of —').
Every atom in a dot-joined sequence must exist in the inventory below.
All grammatical-category labels in gloss lines are drawn from the table below.
The grammar's <Ex> component validates every uppercase token at build time and throws if an atom is absent.
Lexical glosses — the ordinary English words that translate roots and stems — are lowercase and do not require registration.
The inventory follows the Leipzig Glossing Rules base set extended with categories specific to the description of Hokkaido Ainu.

A, S, and O are the core argument-role labels of the S/A/O framework used throughout the grammar: A for the transitive subject (agent), S for the sole argument of an intransitive verb, and O for the transitive object (patient).

The choice of these labels over erg and abs reflects the mixed alignment of the Hokkaido paradigm — where 1SG is nominative–accusative (S=A≠O), the second and third persons are neutral (S=A=O), and the first-person plural exclusive and the fourth person are tripartite (S≠A≠O) — so neither an ergative nor a nominative characterization covers the whole system.
The paradigm and the alignment question are set out in .
4 labels the formal fourth person by form class, following Nakagawa's framework of four numbered persons .
INDEF is used when the gloss targets the referential value — indefinite or impersonal — rather than the form class.
The two atoms may appear in portmanteau sequences: 4.A, 4.S, and 4.O index the three role slots of the fourth-person form set.
The full referential range of the fourth person — inclusive 'we', impersonal agent-defocusing, honorific second person, narrative first person, and logophoric reference — is treated in .

POSS glosses two distinct but related phenomena: the person-possessive prefix slot (ku=cise, 1sg.poss=house 'my house'), and the affiliative/possessed suffix that marks the "belonging form" of a noun or that nominalizes a clause-internal constituent (ru-we, track-poss, 'the trace of —').

The concept form versus the affiliative (possessed) form is defined in ; the English label POSS here corresponds to what the Japanese tradition calls 所属形 shozokuei, sometimes rendered AFF (affiliative) in English-medium work .
ANTIP glosses the detransitivizing prefix i- throughout the grammar, following Bugaeva's explicit antipassive analysis .
Its analysis and its boundary with the homophonous fourth-person object prefix i= are treated in .
REFL, AUTOC, ANTIC, REFL.POSS, and MID are separated by construction rather than by surface form.
Verbal yay- is glossed REFL, following Bugaeva's contrast between reflexive proper and the si- line.

Verbal si- is normally AUTOC (autocausative, self-induced motion or change) in Bugaeva's 2025 analysis, with an emerging or lexicalized ANTIC use; it keeps the gloss REFL where it fills a genuinely self-coreferent object slot, as in the 'pretend to' construction with causative -re/-ka.
Nominal si- and yay- are glossed REFL.POSS when they mark a subject-coreferent possessor.
The suffix -ke is the primary ANTIC/INTR.SG marker in Bugaeva's anticausative paper, while the homophonous lexical-transitive -ke is glossed TR or CAUS.LEX.
The prefix ci- is kept separate as MID/RES, because it suppresses the agent/resultatively profiles the affected participant rather than marking self-causation ; .

Four labels cover the Hokkaido Ainu evidential system: INFR (inferential), REP (reportative), PERS (personal — evidential of direct personal knowledge), and EVID (generic evidential, used where the specific type is not at issue or is analytically undifferentiated in the source).
These map onto the nominalization-plus-copula evidential construction described in .
The relationship to the more fine-grained labeling of Dal Corso (2018) is set out in the concordance section below.
Every interlinear example carries a dialect tag indicating which variety of Ainu it represents.
The closed set of recognized tags is listed below; the tag appears in the example header as the dial attribute.
Finer locality — the specific community, speaker, or recording site — is recorded in the place field rather than as a new dialect tag.
The dialect survey and the principles governing example selection are set out in .
The tag HK is used where a source covers more than one Hokkaido locality or where the specific site cannot be determined.
Sakhalin (SA) and Kuril (KU) examples appear only to illuminate contrasts with the Hokkaido system and are always tagged as such.
No ad-hoc locality tags are introduced; the place field carries any further detail.

The Latin-script phonemic transcription — the grammar's primary writing system for Ainu forms — is described in .
Orthographic variation, word-division conventions, and the relationship between different romanization standards in the literature are covered in .
Technical grammatical terms used throughout the grammar are defined in .
The descriptive literature on Hokkaido Ainu uses divergent glossing conventions.

English-medium typological treatments and Japanese-medium reference grammars do not share a unified standard, and examples drawn from these sources and re-glossed here may carry different labels than the originals.
The table below maps the most consequential divergences.
The evidential labels warrant the most attention for readers moving between this grammar and Dal Corso (2018).

Dal Corso employs a fine-grained eight-term system organized by two parameters — source reliability and event accessibility — yielding dir.rsn (direct/reasoning), dir.knw (direct/knowledge), ind.vis (indirect/visual), ind.rep (indirect/reportative), ind.sens (indirect/sensory), and their extensions .

This grammar uses four simplified labels (INFR, REP, PERS, EVID) that correspond to the grammatical construction rather than to Dal Corso's semantic parameters; the mapping is discussed alongside the construction in .

Refsing (1986) predates the Leipzig Glossing Rules and uses a non-standardized labeling system with lowercase labels; readers consulting her Shizunai paradigm tables should use this grammar's abbreviation inventory as the mapping reference.

The Japanese-medium grammars of Satō (2008) and Nakagawa (2024) work predominantly with Japanese metalanguage rather than Latin-script gloss abbreviations ; ; where they do supply English-style labels in comparative sections, these are generally compatible with the inventory here.
The AFF (affiliative) versus POSS (possessive) difference reflects a genuine terminological divergence between traditions.

Bugaeva aligns with the Japanese 所属形 (shozokuei) label — translating it as "affiliative" — while this grammar uses POSS to emphasize the morphological category (the "belonging form" that the noun takes when possessed or when it heads a nominalized constituent).
The concept form versus affiliative-form opposition, and the morphological evidence bearing on the choice, are defined in .
